title: 42  Lecture 20.1: Cramer’s LDP-Part I
text:
42.1 Introduction: Rare Events and SLLN
Let \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 1}\) be an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sequence of random variables in \(L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\), and define the partial sums: \[S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n X_k\]
By the Strong Law of Large Numbers (SLLN), the sample average converges almost surely to the expected value: \[\frac{S_n}{n} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} \mathbb{E}[X_1] \quad \text{as } n \to \infty\]
If we further assume \(X_1 \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) with \(\operatorname{Var}(X_1) = \sigma^2 < \infty\), then, because the \(X_k\) are independent and identically distributed, variances add: \[\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{S_n}{n}\right) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{k=1}^n \operatorname{Var}(X_k) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.\] Since \(\mathbb{E}[S_n/n] = \mathbb{E}[X_1]\), Chebyshev’s inequality gives, for every fixed \(\epsilon > 0\), \[\mathbb{P}\left(\left| \frac{S_n}{n} - \mathbb{E}[X_1] \right| > \epsilon \right) \le \frac{\operatorname{Var}(S_n/n)}{\epsilon^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n \epsilon^2} = O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\]
Thus, the event \(\left\{ \left| \frac{S_n}{n} - \mathbb{E}[X_1] \right| > \epsilon \right\}\) is a rare event as \(n \to \infty\).
To understand the exact decay rate of such rare events without pathological behavior, we impose a stronger regularity condition on \(X_n\).

title: 42  Lecture 20.1: Cramer’s LDP-Part I
text:
Definition 42.1 (Exponential Integrability) A random variable \(X\) is called exponentially integrable if \[
\mathbb{E}\left[e^{t|X|}\right]<\infty
\quad\text{for every }t>0.
\]


Remark 42.1. Exponential integrability implies the existence of moments of all orders. Indeed, fix an integer \(p \ge 1\) and any \(t > 0\). Since every term of the series \(e^{s} = \sum_{j \ge 0} s^j/j!\) is nonnegative for \(s = t|X| \ge 0\), retaining only the \(j = p\) term gives the pointwise bound \[
e^{t|X|} \geq \frac{(t|X|)^p}{p!}.
\] Both sides are nonnegative, so monotonicity of the expectation applies and yields \[
\mathbb{E}[|X|^p] \leq \frac{p!}{t^p}\mathbb{E}\left[e^{t|X|}\right] <\infty.
\] Therefore \(X \in L^p(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) for every integer \(p \ge 1\), and hence for every real \(p \ge 1\) by \(|X|^p \le 1 + |X|^{\lceil p \rceil}\).

title: 42  Lecture 20.1: Cramer’s LDP-Part I
text:
42.2 Moments and Cumulant Generating Functions
When \(X\) is exponentially integrable, its moment-generating properties are exceptionally well-behaved.

Definition 42.2 (MGF and CGF) Let \(X\) be an exponentially integrable random variable.

The Moment Generating Function (MGF) of \(X\) is defined as: \[M_X(t) := \mathbb{E}\left[e^{tX}\right], \quad t \in \mathbb{R}\]
The Cumulant Generating Function (CGF) of \(X\) is defined as: \[\Psi_X(t) := \log M_X(t) = \log \mathbb{E}\left[e^{tX}\right], \quad t \in \mathbb{R}\] The number \(C_k(X) := \Psi_X^{(k)}(0)\) is called the \(k\)-th cumulant of \(X\).



Proposition 42.1 (Regularity of the MGF and CGF) Let \(X\) be exponentially integrable. Then:

\(M_X(t) \in (0, \infty)\) for every \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), and \(M_X\) is entire (real-analytic on all of \(\mathbb{R}\)) with the globally convergent power series \[M_X(t) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{E}[X^k] \frac{t^k}{k!} = 1 + \mathbb{E}[X]t + \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[X^2]t^2 + \dots\]
\(\Psi_X = \log M_X\) is real-analytic on all of \(\mathbb{R}\), and it admits a Taylor expansion \[\Psi_X(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} C_k(X) \frac{t^k}{k!}\] valid on some interval \((-r, r)\) with \(r > 0\). (The radius \(r\) need not be infinite: the Taylor series of \(\log M_X\) at \(0\) is limited by the complex zeros of \(M_X\), even though \(\Psi_X\) itself is analytic on all of \(\mathbb{R}\).)



Proof. (1) Positivity is clear since \(e^{tX} > 0\) pointwise. Finiteness: \(0 < e^{tX} \le e^{|t||X|}\) pointwise, so \(M_X(t) \le \mathbb{E}[e^{|t||X|}] < \infty\) for \(t \ne 0\) by Definition 42.1, and \(M_X(0) = 1\). For the series, apply Tonelli’s theorem to the nonnegative terms \(|X|^k|t|^k/k!\): \[\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{|t|^k}{k!}\mathbb{E}[|X|^k] = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(|t||X|)^k}{k!}\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[e^{|t||X|}\right] < \infty .\] This absolute convergence licenses Fubini’s theorem for the interchange of \(\mathbb{E}\) and \(\sum\) applied to \(e^{tX} = \sum_k (tX)^k/k!\), giving the stated series for every \(t \in \mathbb{R}\). A power series convergent on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) defines a real-analytic function there.
(2) \(\log\) is analytic on \((0,\infty)\) and \(M_X > 0\) by part (1), so the composition \(\Psi_X = \log \circ M_X\) is real-analytic on \(\mathbb{R}\); in particular it is \(C^\infty\), so all cumulants \(C_k(X) = \Psi_X^{(k)}(0)\) exist, and analyticity at \(0\) gives convergence of the Taylor series on some interval \((-r,r)\), \(r > 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: 42  Lecture 20.1: Cramer’s LDP-Part I
text:
42.4 Chernoff’s Bound for Upper Deviations
Throughout this section, \(\{X_n\}_{n\ge1}\) is i.i.d. and \(X_1\) is exponentially integrable, and \(\epsilon > 0\) is fixed. How rare is it for \(\frac{S_n}{n} - \mathbb{E}[X_1] > \epsilon\)?
Define the centered random variables: \[\dot{X}_k := X_k - \mathbb{E}[X_1], \quad \text{so that } \mathbb{E}[\dot{X}_k] = 0\] \[\dot{S}_n := \sum_{k=1}^n \dot{X}_k = S_n - n\mathbb{E}[X_1]\]
Two facts we will use repeatedly, both immediate but worth stating:

The \(\dot X_k\) are i.i.d. Each \(\dot X_k = f(X_k)\) for the same Borel function \(f(x) = x - \mathbb{E}[X_1]\), and measurable functions of independent random variables are independent; identical distribution is preserved likewise.
\(\dot X_1\) is exponentially integrable. Writing \(m := \mathbb{E}[X_1]\), the triangle inequality gives \(|\dot X_1| \le |X_1| + |m|\), hence for every \(t > 0\) \[\mathbb{E}\left[e^{t|\dot X_1|}\right] \le e^{t|m|}\,\mathbb{E}\left[e^{t|X_1|}\right] < \infty .\] So Proposition 42.1 applies to \(\dot X_1\), and \(M_{\dot X_1}, \Psi_{\dot X_1}\) are finite on all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

The event of interest becomes: \[\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{S_n}{n} - \mathbb{E}[X_1] > \epsilon\right) = \mathbb{P}(\dot{S}_n > n\epsilon)\]
Fix \(t > 0\). Since \(s \mapsto e^{ts}\) is strictly increasing for \(t > 0\), the events \(\{\dot S_n > n\epsilon\}\) and \(\{e^{t\dot S_n} > e^{tn\epsilon}\}\) coincide. Applying Markov’s inequality to the nonnegative random variable \(e^{t\dot S_n}\) (which is integrable by exponential integrability of \(\dot X_1\)):
\[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\dot{S}_n > n\epsilon) &= \mathbb{P}\left(e^{t\dot{S}_n} > e^{tn\epsilon}\right) \quad \text{(valid because } t > 0) \\
&\le e^{-tn\epsilon} \, \mathbb{E}\left[e^{t\dot{S}_n}\right] \quad \text{(by Markov's inequality)}
\end{aligned}\]
By independence of \(\dot{X}_1, \dots, \dot{X}_n\) (the factors \(e^{t\dot X_k}\) are independent, nonnegative and integrable, so the expectation of the product is the product of the expectations), and by their identical distribution: \[\mathbb{E}\left[e^{t\dot{S}_n}\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{k=1}^n e^{t\dot{X}_k}\right] = \prod_{k=1}^n \mathbb{E}\left[e^{t\dot{X}_k}\right] = \left(M_{\dot{X}_1}(t)\right)^n\]
Substituting \(M_{\dot{X}_1}(t) = e^{\Psi_{\dot{X}_1}(t)}\): \[\mathbb{P}(\dot{S}_n > n\epsilon) \le e^{-tn\epsilon} \left(e^{\Psi_{\dot{X}_1}(t)}\right)^n = \exp\left(-n \left( t\epsilon - \Psi_{\dot{X}_1}(t) \right)\right)\]
Since this inequality holds for every \(t > 0\), we may take the infimum of the right-hand side over \(t > 0\): \[\mathbb{P}(\dot{S}_n > n\epsilon) \le \inf_{t>0} \exp\left(-n(t\epsilon - \Psi_{\dot X_1}(t))\right) = \exp\left(-n \sup_{t > 0} \{ t\epsilon - \Psi_{\dot{X}_1}(t) \} \right)\] where the last equality uses that \(u \mapsto e^{-nu}\) is decreasing.

title: 42  Lecture 20.1: Cramer’s LDP-Part I
section: 42.5 The Legendre Transform and Properties of \(\Psi_{\dot{X}}\)
text:
42.5 The Legendre Transform and Properties of \(\Psi_{\dot{X}}\)

Definition 42.3 (Legendre Transform (Convex Conjugate)) Let \(\psi: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a convex function. Its Legendre transform (convex conjugate) is the function \(\psi^*: \mathbb{R} \to (-\infty, +\infty]\) defined by \[\psi^*(\eta) := \sup_{t \in \mathbb{R}} \{ \eta t - \psi(t) \}\] The value \(+\infty\) is genuinely allowed (take \(\psi \equiv 0\)), so the codomain must be the extended half-line. The value \(-\infty\) never occurs, since \(\psi^*(\eta) \ge \eta\cdot 0 - \psi(0) = -\psi(0) > -\infty\). As a pointwise supremum of the affine functions \(\eta \mapsto \eta t - \psi(t)\), \(\psi^*\) is automatically convex and lower semicontinuous.


Example 42.1 (Example: Gaussian Distribution) Let \(\sigma^2 > 0\) and \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\). Then \(Z\) is exponentially integrable and \(\Psi_Z(t) = \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 t^2\). Fix \(\eta \in \mathbb{R}\) and set \[h(t) := \eta t - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 t^2 .\] Since \(h''(t) = -\sigma^2 < 0\), \(h\) is strictly concave, and \(h(t) \to -\infty\) as \(|t| \to \infty\); hence the supremum is attained at the unique stationary point. Solving \(h'(t) = \eta - \sigma^2 t = 0\) gives \(t^* = \eta/\sigma^2\), and substituting back: \[\Psi_Z^*(\eta) = h(t^*) = \eta\left(\frac{\eta}{\sigma^2}\right) - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\left(\frac{\eta}{\sigma^2}\right)^2 = \frac{\eta^2}{2\sigma^2}\] In particular the supremum in Definition 42.3 is a maximum here, and it is finite for every \(\eta\).


Theorem 42.1 (Convexity of the Cumulant Generating Function) For any exponentially integrable random variable \(X\), its CGF \(\Psi_X(t)\) is convex on \(\mathbb{R}\). If additionally \(\operatorname{Var}(X) > 0\) (i.e., \(X\) is non-degenerate), then \(\Psi_X(t)\) is strictly convex.


Proof. Step 1 (differentiation under the expectation). Fix \(t_0 \in \mathbb{R}\) and let \(\delta := 1\). For \(|t - t_0| \le \delta\) we have the domination \[\left|\frac{\partial}{\partial t} e^{tX}\right| = |X| e^{tX} \le |X| e^{(|t_0|+1)|X|} \le e^{(|t_0|+2)|X|},\] using \(|x| \le e^{|x|}\), and the right-hand side is integrable by Definition 42.1. The same bound with \(X^2\) in place of \(|X|\) (and \(|t_0|+3\) in the exponent) handles the second derivative. Hence \(M_X\) is twice differentiable with \[M_X'(t) = \mathbb{E}\left[X e^{tX}\right], \qquad M_X''(t) = \mathbb{E}\left[X^2 e^{tX}\right],\] both finite for every \(t \in \mathbb{R}\). (This also follows from Proposition 42.1.)
Step 2 (the second derivative of the CGF). Since \(M_X(t) > 0\), the quotient rule applied to \(\Psi_X'(t) = M_X'(t)/M_X(t)\) gives, for an arbitrary \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), \[\Psi_X''(t) = \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X^2 e^{tX}\right]\mathbb{E}\left[e^{tX}\right] - \left(\mathbb{E}\left[X e^{tX}\right]\right)^2}{\left(\mathbb{E}\left[e^{tX}\right]\right)^2} = \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X^2 e^{tX}\right]}{M_X(t)} - \left( \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X e^{tX}\right]}{M_X(t)} \right)^2\]
Step 3 (the tilted measure). Introduce the exponentially tilted probability measure \(\mathbb{P}_t\) via the Radon-Nikodym derivative: \[\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_t := \frac{e^{tX}}{M_X(t)} \, \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}\]
The density is nonnegative and \(\mathbb{P}\)-integrable, and \(\mathbb{P}_t(\Omega) = \int d\mathbb{P}_t = M_X(t)/M_X(t) = 1\), so \(\mathbb{P}_t\) is indeed a probability measure on \((\Omega,\mathcal{F})\). By the change-of-measure formula, and since \(X, X^2\) are \(\mathbb{P}_t\)-integrable by Step 1, \[\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_t}[X] = \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X e^{tX}\right]}{M_X(t)}, \qquad \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_t}[X^2] = \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X^2 e^{tX}\right]}{M_X(t)}\]
Hence \(\Psi_X''(t) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_t}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_t}[X])^2 = \operatorname{Var}_{\mathbb{P}_t}(X) \ge 0\) for every \(t \in \mathbb{R}\). A twice-differentiable function with nonnegative second derivative on \(\mathbb{R}\) is convex, establishing convexity.
Step 4 (strict convexity). Since \(d\mathbb{P}_t/d\mathbb{P} = e^{tX}/M_X(t) > 0\) everywhere, \(\mathbb{P}_t\) and \(\mathbb{P}\) are mutually absolutely continuous (\(\mathbb{P}_t \sim \mathbb{P}\)). They therefore share the same null sets, so \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mathbb{P}_t}(X) = 0 \iff X\) is \(\mathbb{P}_t\)-a.s. constant \(\iff X\) is \(\mathbb{P}\)-a.s. constant \(\iff \operatorname{Var}(X) = 0\). When \(\operatorname{Var}(X) > 0\), we conclude \(\Psi_X''(t) = \operatorname{Var}_{\mathbb{P}_t}(X) > 0\) for every \(t \in \mathbb{R}\); a positive second derivative on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) gives strict convexity. \(\blacksquare\)

title: 42  Lecture 20.1: Cramer’s LDP-Part I
section: 42.7 Main Result: Cramér’s Large Deviation Theorem
text:
42.7 Main Result: Cramér’s Large Deviation Theorem

Theorem 42.2 (Cramér’s Large Deviation Theorem (Upper Bound & Exact Rate)) Let \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 1}\) be an i.i.d. sequence of exponentially integrable random variables which are non-degenerate, i.e. \(\operatorname{Var}(X_1) > 0\). Let \(\dot{X}_n := X_n - \mathbb{E}[X_1]\), \(\dot{S}_n := \sum_{k=1}^n \dot{X}_k\), and set \[b := \operatorname*{ess\,sup} \dot X_1 \in (0, +\infty] .\] (Non-degeneracy together with \(\mathbb{E}[\dot X_1] = 0\) forces \(b > 0\).) Then for every \(\epsilon\) with \(0 < \epsilon < b\): \[\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mathbb{P}\left( \frac{\dot{S}_n}{n} > \epsilon \right) = -\Psi_{\dot{X}_1}^*(\epsilon)\] with the conventions \(\log 0 := -\infty\) and \(-(+\infty) := -\infty\).


Remark 42.2. The restriction \(\epsilon < b\) is needed for the strict inequality \(\dot S_n/n > \epsilon\) used here. If \(b < \infty\) and \(\mathbb{P}(\dot X_1 = b) > 0\), then at \(\epsilon = b\) the left-hand side equals \(-\infty\) (the event is empty), whereas \(\Psi_{\dot X_1}^*(b) = -\log \mathbb{P}(\dot X_1 = b)\) is finite, so the identity fails at that single point. For \(\epsilon > b\) both sides equal \(-\infty\), so the statement remains true there. Only the upper bound \[\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log\mathbb{P}(\dot S_n > n\epsilon) \le -\Psi^*_{\dot X_1}(\epsilon)\] is proved above; it requires no assumption beyond exponential integrability and holds for every \(\epsilon > 0\). The matching lower bound is proved in Part 2.

title: 43  Lecture 20.2: Cramer’s LDP-Part II
text:
43.1 Theorem Statement & Context
Let \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be a sequence of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), exponentially integrable random variables defined on a probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\). We assume throughout that \(X_1\) is non-degenerate, i.e. \(\operatorname{Var}(X_1) > 0\).
Define the centered random variables and their sample sum: \[
\dot{X}_n := X_n - \mathbb{E}[X_1], \quad \text{and} \quad \dot{S}_n := \sum_{i=1}^n \dot{X}_i .
\] As shown in Part I, each \(\dot X_n\) is again exponentially integrable, the \(\dot X_n\) are i.i.d., and \(\mathbb{E}[\dot X_1] = 0\).
Also recall that the moment generating function (MGF) and cumulant generating function (CGF) of \(\dot{X}_1\) are defined as: \[
M_{\dot{X}_1}(t) := \mathbb{E}\left[e^{t\dot{X}_1}\right], \quad \text{and} \quad \Psi_{\dot{X}_1}(t) := \log M_{\dot{X}_1}(t),
\] both finite for every \(t \in \mathbb{R}\).
The Legendre-Fenchel transform of the CGF is given by: \[
\Psi_{\dot{X}_1}^*(\epsilon) := \sup_{t \in \mathbb{R}} \left\{\epsilon t - \Psi_{\dot{X}_1}(t)\right\} = \sup_{t \ge 0} \left\{\epsilon t - \Psi_{\dot{X}_1}(t)\right\},
\] where the second equality holds for every \(\epsilon > 0\) and was proved in Part I (the concave function \(t \mapsto \epsilon t - \Psi_{\dot X_1}(t)\) vanishes at \(t=0\), has positive derivative there, and lies below the line \(t \mapsto \epsilon t\), so nothing is lost by restricting to \(t \ge 0\)).
Finally, set \[
b := \operatorname*{ess\,sup} \dot X_1 \in (0, +\infty] ,
\] which is strictly positive because \(\mathbb{E}[\dot X_1] = 0\) and \(\dot X_1\) is not a.s. constant, so \(\mathbb{P}(\dot X_1 > 0) > 0\).
Then, Cramér’s Large Deviation Principle (LDP) states that the tail probability of the sample sum \(\dot{S}_n\) decays exponentially with rate \(\Psi_{\dot{X}_1}^*(\epsilon)\):
From Part I, we have already established the upper bound: \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mathbb{P}\left(\dot{S}_n > n\epsilon\right) \le -\Psi_{\dot{X}_1}^*(\epsilon).
\]
Thus, to complete the proof of Cramér’s Theorem, it suffices to prove the matching lower bound: \[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mathbb{P}\left(\dot{S}_n > n\epsilon\right) \ge -\Psi_{\dot{X}_1}^*(\epsilon).
\]

title: 43  Lecture 20.2: Cramer’s LDP-Part II
section: 43.3 Key Observations about the Rate Function \(\Psi^*(\epsilon)\)
text:
43.3 Key Observations about the Rate Function \(\Psi^*(\epsilon)\)
Since \(\Psi(t) = \log M(t)\) is smooth and strictly convex for non-degenerate distributions:

The supremum defining the Legendre transform is attained at a unique maximizer \(t_\epsilon > 0\): \[
\Psi^*(\epsilon) = \sup_{t \ge 0} \left\{\epsilon t - \Psi(t)\right\} = \epsilon t_\epsilon - \Psi(t_\epsilon).
\]
The First-Order Condition (FOC) with respect to \(t\) yields: \[
0 = \left. \frac{d}{dt} \left(\epsilon t - \Psi(t)\right) \right|_{t = t_\epsilon} = \epsilon - \Psi'(t_\epsilon) \implies \Psi'(t_\epsilon) = \epsilon.
\]

title: 43  Lecture 20.2: Cramer’s LDP-Part II
text:
43.4 Essential Construct: Exponential Tilting (Esscher Transform)
Given an exponentially integrable random variable \(Y\) on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\), we construct a family of exponentially tilted probability measures \(\mathbb{P}_t\) on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) parameterized by \(t \in \mathbb{R}\):
\[
d\mathbb{P}_t := \frac{e^{tY}}{M_Y(t)} \, d\mathbb{P}.
\]






NoteVerification of Probability Measure



The density \(e^{tY}/M_Y(t)\) is nonnegative, \(\mathbb{P}\)-integrable, and in fact strictly positive everywhere. Integrating over the entire sample space \(\Omega\): \[
\int_{\Omega} d\mathbb{P}_t = \int_{\Omega} \frac{e^{tY}}{M_Y(t)} \, d\mathbb{P} = \frac{1}{M_Y(t)} \int_{\Omega} e^{tY} \, d\mathbb{P} = \frac{M_Y(t)}{M_Y(t)} = 1.
\] This confirms that \(\mathbb{P}_t\) is a valid probability measure for any \(t\) with \(M_Y(t) < \infty\), which by exponential integrability means every \(t \in \mathbb{R}\). Strict positivity of the density further gives \(\mathbb{P}_t \sim \mathbb{P}\) (mutual absolute continuity), so \(\mathbb{P}\)-a.s. statements and \(\mathbb{P}_t\)-a.s. statements are interchangeable.

title: 43  Lecture 20.2: Cramer’s LDP-Part II
text:
43.6 Detailed Proof
Throughout the proof \(\epsilon \in (0,b)\) is fixed, and we freeze the tilting parameter at the maximizer \(t_\epsilon\) once and for all. This matters: the auxiliary variables constructed below depend on \(t_\epsilon\), so the parameter cannot be left free and optimized afterwards.

43.6.1 Step 1: Characterization of the Tilted Measure
By Lemma 43.1 the maximizer \(t_\epsilon > 0\) satisfies the first-order condition \(\Psi'(t_\epsilon) = \epsilon\). Unpacking the derivative of the CGF (differentiation under the expectation being justified in Part I by exponential integrability): \[
\begin{align*}
\Psi'(t) &= \frac{d}{dt} \log M(t) = \frac{M'(t)}{M(t)} = \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\dot{X}_1 e^{t\dot{X}_1}\right]}{M(t)} \\
&= \int_{\Omega} \dot{X}_1 \frac{e^{t\dot{X}_1}}{M(t)} \, d\mathbb{P} = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_t}[\dot{X}_1].
\end{align*}
\]
Therefore, setting \(t = t_\epsilon\) explicitly forces the expectation under the tilted measure to equal \(\epsilon\): \[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{t_\epsilon}}[\dot{X}_1] = \epsilon.
\]
Denote by \(\mu := \mu_{\dot X_1}\) the law of \(\dot X_1\) under \(\mathbb{P}\) and define the tilted law on \((\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\): \[
\nu(dx) := \frac{e^{t_\epsilon x}}{M(t_\epsilon)}\, \mu(dx) .
\] This is the law of \(\dot X_1\) under \(\mathbb{P}_{t_\epsilon}\), and it is a probability measure by the callout above. Since its density is strictly positive, the relation inverts: \[
\mu(dx) = M(t_\epsilon)\, e^{-t_\epsilon x}\, \nu(dx) .
\]
Let \(\{W_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be an i.i.d. sequence with common law \(\nu\), realised on an auxiliary probability space \((\tilde\Omega, \tilde{\mathcal{F}}, \tilde{\mathbb{P}})\) (take the product space \((\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})^{\otimes\mathbb{N}}, \nu^{\otimes\mathbb{N}})\) with the coordinate maps); expectations on this space are written \(\tilde{\mathbb{E}}\). Keeping the two spaces distinct is what makes the change-of-measure identity of Step 2 an honest statement rather than a notational coincidence.
The \(W_n\) inherit the following three properties, all of which are used later:

Mean. \(\tilde{\mathbb{E}}[W_n] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{t_\epsilon}}[\dot X_1] = \Psi'(t_\epsilon) = \epsilon\). This is the point of tilting: the rare event \(\{\dot S_n > n\epsilon\}\) becomes the typical event \(\{T_n > n\epsilon\}\).
Finite variance. \(\tilde{\mathbb{E}}[W_1^2] = \mathbb{E}[\dot X_1^2 e^{t_\epsilon \dot X_1}]/M(t_\epsilon) < \infty\), since \(\dot X_1^2 e^{t_\epsilon\dot X_1} \le e^{(2 + t_\epsilon)|\dot X_1|}\) is integrable by exponential integrability.
Non-degeneracy. \(\sigma_W^2 := \operatorname{Var}_{\tilde{\mathbb{P}}}(W_1) = \operatorname{Var}_{\mathbb{P}_{t_\epsilon}}(\dot X_1) = \Psi''(t_\epsilon) > 0\), by the strict convexity of \(\Psi\) established in Part I. Hence \(\sigma_W^2 \in (0,\infty)\) and the CLT of Step 5 applies.




43.6.2 Step 2: Change of Measure for \(n\)-dimensional Product Space
Let \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to [0, \infty]\) be Borel measurable and non-negative (so that every integral below is defined in \([0,\infty]\) and Tonelli’s theorem licenses the factorisation). Because \(\dot X_1,\dots,\dot X_n\) are i.i.d. with law \(\mu\), their joint law is the product measure \(\mu^{\otimes n}\); likewise \(W_1,\dots,W_n\) are i.i.d. with joint law \(\nu^{\otimes n}\). Substituting \(\mu(dx) = M(t_\epsilon)e^{-t_\epsilon x}\nu(dx)\) coordinatewise:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\left[f(\dot{X}_1, \dots, \dot{X}_n)\right] &= \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x_1, \dots, x_n) \, \mu(dx_1) \cdots \mu(dx_n) \\
&= \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x_1, \dots, x_n) \prod_{i=1}^n \left( M(t_\epsilon) e^{-t_\epsilon x_i} \nu(dx_i) \right) \\
&= M(t_\epsilon)^n \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x_1, \dots, x_n) e^{-t_\epsilon \sum_{i=1}^n x_i} \, \nu(dx_1) \cdots \nu(dx_n) \\
&= M(t_\epsilon)^n \, \tilde{\mathbb{E}}\left[f(W_1, \dots, W_n) e^{-t_\epsilon T_n}\right],
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(T_n := \sum_{i=1}^n W_i\). Note that the identity relates an expectation on \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb{P})\) to one on the auxiliary space \((\tilde\Omega,\tilde{\mathcal F},\tilde{\mathbb{P}})\).



43.6.3 Step 3: Bounding the Indicator Function
Apply the identity to the (non-negative, Borel) indicator \(f(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \mathbb{I}_{\{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i > n\epsilon\}}\):
\[
\mathbb{P}\left(\dot{S}_n > n\epsilon\right) = M(t_\epsilon)^n \, \tilde{\mathbb{E}}\left[ e^{-t_\epsilon T_n} \mathbb{I}_{\{T_n > n\epsilon\}} \right].
\]
Now fix \(\delta > 0\) and shrink the domain of integration to the slice \(\{n\epsilon < T_n \le n(\epsilon+\delta)\}\). The strict lower endpoint is essential: this slice is a subset of \(\{T_n > n\epsilon\}\), whereas the closed slice \(\{n\epsilon \le T_n \le \cdots\}\) need not be, since the law of \(T_n\) may carry an atom at \(n\epsilon\). On the slice \(e^{-t_\epsilon T_n} \ge e^{-t_\epsilon n(\epsilon+\delta)}\), because \(t_\epsilon > 0\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}\left(\dot{S}_n > n\epsilon\right) &\ge M(t_\epsilon)^n \, \tilde{\mathbb{E}}\left[ e^{-t_\epsilon T_n} \mathbb{I}_{\{n\epsilon < T_n \le n(\epsilon + \delta)\}} \right] \\
&\ge M(t_\epsilon)^n e^{-t_\epsilon n(\epsilon + \delta)} \, \tilde{\mathbb{P}}\left(n\epsilon < T_n \le n(\epsilon + \delta)\right) \\
&= e^{n(\Psi(t_\epsilon) - t_\epsilon\epsilon)} e^{-n t_\epsilon \delta} \, \tilde{\mathbb{P}}\left(n\epsilon < T_n \le n(\epsilon + \delta)\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
using \(M(t_\epsilon)^n = e^{n\Psi(t_\epsilon)}\) in the last line. Since \(\Psi(t_\epsilon) - t_\epsilon \epsilon = -\Psi^*(\epsilon)\) by Lemma 43.1,
\[
\mathbb{P}\left(\dot{S}_n > n\epsilon\right) \ge e^{-n \Psi^*(\epsilon)} e^{-n t_\epsilon \delta} \, \tilde{\mathbb{P}}\left(n\epsilon < T_n \le n(\epsilon + \delta)\right).
\]



43.6.4 Step 4: Taking the Logarithmic Limit
Step 5 shows the last factor is eventually positive, so the right-hand side is eventually strictly positive and we may apply the increasing map \(\frac{1}{n}\log(\cdot)\) to both sides. This turns the product into a sum, and taking \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}\) (using superadditivity of \(\liminf\)) gives:
\[
\begin{align*}
\liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mathbb{P}\left(\dot{S}_n > n\epsilon\right) &\ge -\Psi^*(\epsilon) - t_\epsilon \delta \\
&+ \liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \tilde{\mathbb{P}}\left(n\epsilon < T_n \le n(\epsilon + \delta)\right) \quad (\star)
\end{align*}
\]



43.6.5 Step 5: Asymptotic Analysis of the Probability Term via CLT
To complete the proof, we show that the last probability term in \((\star)\) vanishes on the log scale as \(n \to \infty\); equivalently, that it stays bounded away from \(0\).
By Step 1, \(\tilde{\mathbb{E}}[T_n] = \sum_{i=1}^n \tilde{\mathbb{E}}[W_i] = n\epsilon\) and \(\sigma_W^2 = \operatorname{Var}(W_1) \in (0,\infty)\). Write the normalised sum \[
Z_n := \frac{T_n - n\epsilon}{\sigma_W\sqrt{n}} ,
\] so that, splitting the slice into two half-lines, \[
\tilde{\mathbb{P}}\left(n\epsilon < T_n \le n(\epsilon + \delta)\right)
= \tilde{\mathbb{P}}\!\left(Z_n \le \frac{\delta\sqrt{n}}{\sigma_W}\right) - \tilde{\mathbb{P}}\left(Z_n \le 0\right).
\]
The two terms are handled by different theorems.

Second term (CLT). The \(W_i\) are i.i.d. with finite, non-zero variance, so the Lindeberg-Lévy CLT gives \(Z_n \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,1)\). The limit distribution function \(\Phi\) is continuous, so \(0\) is a continuity point and \[
\tilde{\mathbb{P}}(Z_n \le 0) \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} \Phi(0) = \frac{1}{2}.
\]
First term (WLLN). Here the threshold \(\delta\sqrt{n}/\sigma_W \to \infty\), so the CLT cannot be invoked at a fixed point; use instead the weak law of large numbers, \(T_n/n \to \epsilon\) in \(\tilde{\mathbb{P}}\)-probability: \[
\tilde{\mathbb{P}}\!\left(Z_n > \frac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma_W}\right) = \tilde{\mathbb{P}}\!\left(\frac{T_n}{n} - \epsilon > \delta\right) \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} 0,
\] so the first term tends to \(1\).

Combining, \[
\lim_{n \to \infty}\tilde{\mathbb{P}}\left(n\epsilon < T_n \le n(\epsilon + \delta)\right) = 1 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2} > 0 ,
\] which is the rigorous form of the heuristic \(\int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2 / 2} \, dx = \frac{1}{2}\). In particular the probability exceeds \(\tfrac14\) for all large \(n\), so the sandwich
\[
0 \ge \frac{1}{n} \log \tilde{\mathbb{P}}\left(n\epsilon < T_n \le n(\epsilon + \delta)\right) \ge \frac{\log(1/4)}{n} \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} 0
\]
gives \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \tilde{\mathbb{P}}\left(n\epsilon < T_n \le n(\epsilon + \delta)\right) = 0 .
\]
Substituting back into \((\star)\):
\[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mathbb{P}\left(\dot{S}_n > n\epsilon\right) \ge -\Psi^*(\epsilon) - t_\epsilon \delta
\]
The left-hand side does not depend on \(\delta\), and \(t_\epsilon\) is a fixed finite number, so letting \(\delta \downarrow 0\) yields the desired lower bound:
\[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mathbb{P}\left(\dot{S}_n > n\epsilon\right) \ge -\Psi^*(\epsilon) \quad \blacksquare
\]
Together with the upper bound from Part I, this proves Theorem 43.1 for every \(\epsilon \in (0,b)\).

44.1 Convergence Revisited
In earlier sections, we considered several modes of convergence for random variables \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) to \(X\) defined on a common probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\):

title: 44  Lecture 21.1: Total Variation
text:
44.3 Scheffé’s Lemma
The following lemma, known as Scheffé’s Lemma, provides an important characterization of the total variation distance in terms of densities with respect to a dominating measure.

Lemma 44.1 (Scheffé’s Lemma) Let \(\mu, \nu \in \text{Prob}(S, \mathcal{B})\) and let \(\alpha\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite measure on \((S, \mathcal{B})\) such that \(\mu \ll \alpha\) and \(\nu \ll \alpha\). By the Radon-Nikodym theorem there exist non-negative densities \(u, v \in L^1(\alpha)\) with \(d\mu = u \, d\alpha\), \(d\nu = v \, d\alpha\) and \(\int_S u \, d\alpha = \int_S v \, d\alpha = 1\). Then: \[
d_{\text{TV}}(\mu, \nu) = \frac{1}{2} \|u - v\|_{L^1(\alpha)} = \frac{1}{2} \int_S |u - v| \, d\alpha.
\]


Proof (Proof of Scheffé’s Lemma). For any event \(B \in \mathcal{B}\): \[
|\mu(B) - \nu(B)| = \left| \int_B u \, d\alpha - \int_B v \, d\alpha \right| \le \int_B |u - v| \, d\alpha
\tag{44.1}\]
Similarly, applying (1) to the complement \(B^c \in \mathcal{B}\) and using \(\mu(B^c) = 1 - \mu(B)\), \(\nu(B^c) = 1 - \nu(B)\) (here we use that \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are probability measures): \[
\begin{aligned}
|\mu(B) - \nu(B)| &= |(1 - \mu(B)) - (1 - \nu(B))| \\
&= |\mu(B^c) - \nu(B^c)| \le \int_{B^c} |u - v| \, d\alpha
\end{aligned}
\tag{44.2}\]
Adding inequalities Equation 44.1 and Equation 44.2: \[
\begin{aligned}
2 |\mu(B) - \nu(B)| &\le \int_B |u - v| \, d\alpha + \int_{B^c} |u - v| \, d\alpha\\
& = \int_S |u - v| \, d\alpha = \|u - v\|_{L^1(\alpha)}
\end{aligned}
\] Taking the supremum over all \(B \in \mathcal{B}\) yields: \[
d_{\text{TV}}(\mu, \nu) \le \frac{1}{2} \|u - v\|_{L^1(\alpha)}
\]
To achieve equality, define \(A := \{x \in S : u(x) > v(x)\}\). Since \(\int_S u \, d\alpha = \int_S v \, d\alpha = 1\), we have \(\int_S (u - v) \, d\alpha = 0\). Thus: \[
\int_A (u - v) \, d\alpha + \int_{A^c} (u - v) \, d\alpha = 0 \implies \int_A |u - v| \, d\alpha = \int_{A^c} |u - v| \, d\alpha
\] Evaluating \(|\mu(A) - \nu(A)|\): \[
\begin{aligned}
|\mu(A) - \nu(A)| &= \int_A (u - v) \, d\alpha \\
&= \frac{1}{2} \left( \int_A |u - v| \, d\alpha + \int_{A^c} |u - v| \, d\alpha \right)\\
&= \frac{1}{2} \int_S |u - v| \, d\alpha
\end{aligned}
\] Since \(A \in \mathcal{B}\), the upper bound is attained, establishing \(d_{\text{TV}}(\mu, \nu) = \frac{1}{2} \|u - v\|_{L^1(\alpha)}\). \(\blacksquare\)







NoteConstruction of a Dominating Measure \(\alpha\)



A common dominating measure always exists for a countable family. For any sequence \(\{\mu_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset \text{Prob}(S, \mathcal{B})\), set: \[
\alpha = \sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n} \mu_n .
\] This is a well-defined measure with \(\alpha(S) = \sum_{n \ge 1} 2^{-n} = 1\), so \(\alpha\) is finite (indeed a probability measure). If \(\alpha(B) = 0\) then \(2^{-k}\mu_k(B) \le \alpha(B) = 0\), hence \(\mu_k \ll \alpha\) for every \(k\), and by the Radon-Nikodym theorem \(d\mu_k = u_k \, d\alpha\) with \(u_k \ge 0\) and \(\int_S u_k \, d\alpha = \mu_k(S) = 1\).
(For a sequence of general finite measures one normalizes first, e.g. \(\alpha = \sum_{n \ge 1} 2^{-n} \mu_n / (1 + \mu_n(S))\).)

title: 44  Lecture 21.1: Total Variation
44  Lecture 21.1: Total Variation
text:
44.7 Example 1: Bernoulli Distributions
Let \(\mu_p \triangleq \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) and \(\mu_q \triangleq \text{Bernoulli}(q)\) for \(p, q \in [0, 1]\). Using Lemma 44.2 on \(S = \{0, 1\}\): \[
\begin{align*}
d_{\text{TV}}(\mu_p, \mu_q) &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{x=0}^1 |\mu_p(\{x\}) - \mu_q(\{x\})|\\
&= \frac{1}{2} \left( |(1 - p) - (1 - q)| + |p - q| \right) = |p - q|
\end{align*}
\]

text:

u_\lambda 	riangleq 	ext{Poisson}(\lambda)\) where \(

The last two bounds are justified as follows. Assume without loss of generality that \(\lambda \le \eta\) and let \(X \sim 	ext{Poisson}(\lambda)\) and \(Z \sim 	ext{Poisson}(\eta - \lambda)\) be independent, so that \(Y := X + Z \sim 	ext{Poisson}(\eta)\) by the convolution property of Poisson laws. title: 44  Lecture 21.1: Total Variation
text:
44.9 Example 3: Bernoulli vs. Poisson Comparison
Fix \(p \in [0, 1]\) and regard both laws as elements of \(\text{Prob}(\mathbb{N}_0, 2^{\mathbb{N}_0})\). Consider \(d_{\text{TV}}(\mu_p, \nu_p)\) where \(\mu_p = \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) and \(\nu_p = \text{Poisson}(p)\). Since \(\mu_p(\{k\}) = 0\) for all \(k \ge 2\), Lemma 44.2 gives:
\[
\begin{align*}
d_{\text{TV}}(\mu_p, \nu_p) &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{x=0}^\infty |\mu_p(\{x\}) - \nu_p(\{x\})| \\
&= \frac{1}{2} |\mu_p(\{0\}) - \nu_p(\{0\})| \\
&\quad + \frac{1}{2} |\mu_p(\{1\}) - \nu_p(\{1\})| + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k \ge 2} \nu_p(\{k\}).
\end{align*}
\]
Evaluating individual terms:

\(\mu_p(\{0\}) - \nu_p(\{0\}) = 1 - p - e^{-p}\)
\(\mu_p(\{1\}) - \nu_p(\{1\}) = p - p e^{-p} = p(1 - e^{-p}) \ge 0\)
\(\sum_{k \ge 2} \nu_p(\{k\}) = 1 - \nu_p(\{0\}) - \nu_p(\{1\}) = 1 - e^{-p} - p e^{-p} \ge 0\)

Using the standard inequality \(1 - p \le e^{-p}\), we have \(1 - p - e^{-p} \le 0\), so \(|1 - p - e^{-p}| = e^{-p} + p - 1\).
Combining all components: \[
\begin{aligned}
d_{\text{TV}}(\mu_p, \nu_p) &= \frac{1}{2} (e^{-p} + p - 1) + \frac{1}{2} p(1 - e^{-p}) + \frac{1}{2} (1 - e^{-p} - p e^{-p}) \\
&= \frac{1}{2} e^{-p} + \frac{1}{2} p - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} p - \frac{1}{2} p e^{-p} + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} e^{-p} - \frac{1}{2} p e^{-p} \\
&= p (1 - e^{-p}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, the exact total variation distance is: \[
d_{\text{TV}}(\text{Bernoulli}(p), \text{Poisson}(p)) = p (1 - e^{-p}).
\]

title: 74  Lecture 34.1: Probability Kernels-Part II
text:
74.1 Probability Kernels and Bounded Measurable Functions
Let \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) and \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) be measurable spaces, and let \(Q: S_1 \times \mathcal{B}_2 \to [0, 1]\) be a probability kernel. Recall that
Given any bounded, \(\mathcal{B}_2\)-measurable function \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\), we can integrate \(f\) against \(Q(x, \cdot)\) for each fixed \(x \in S_1\): \[
(L_Q f)(x) := \int_{S_2} f(y) \, Q(x, dy) \quad \forall x \in S_1.
\] The resulting function \(L_Q f: S_1 \to \mathbb{R}\) is a new \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable function of \(x \in S_1\). Furthermore, this operation preserves boundedness: \[
\begin{align*}
|(L_Q f)(x)| &= \left| \int_{S_2} f(y) \, Q(x, dy) \right| \\
&\le \int_{S_2} |f(y)| \, Q(x, dy) \\
&\le \sup_{y \in S_2} |f(y)| \\
&= \|f\|_\infty \quad \forall x \in S_1.
\end{align*}
\]

title: 74  Lecture 34.1: Probability Kernels-Part II
text:
For each fixed \(x \in S_1\), \(Q(x, \cdot)\) is a probability measure on \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\).
For each fixed \(B \in \mathcal{B}_2\), \(Q(\cdot, B)\) is a \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable function on \(S_1\).
We can integrate bounded measurable functions against probability kernels: \[
\int f(y) \, Q(x, dy),
\] where \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) is a bounded \(\mathcal{B}_2\)-measurable function. This integral is well-defined for each fixed \(x \in S_1\) because \(Q(x, \cdot)\) is a probability measure. The resulting function of \(x \in S_1\) is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable and \[
\left|\int f(y) \, Q(x, dy)\right|\le \int |f(y)| \, Q(x, dy) \le \sup_{y \in S_2} |f(y)| = \|f\|_\infty.
\]



Definition 74.1 (Markov Operator) Equip the space of bounded measurable functions \(\mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) with the supremum norm: \[
\|f\|_\infty := \sup_{x \in S} |f(x)|.
\] For a probability kernel \(Q\) from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\), the linear mapping \[
L_Q: \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1), \quad f \mapsto L_Q f
\] defined by \((L_Q f)(x) = \int_{S_2} f(y) \, Q(x, dy)\) is called the Markov operator (or transition operator) associated with \(Q\). It satisfies \(\|L_Q f\|_\infty \le \|f\|_\infty\).


Example 74.1 Let \(S_1=S_2=\mathbb R\) and define the probability kernel \[
Q(x,dy)=\phi(y-x)\,dy,
\] where \(\phi\) is the standard normal density. Thus, \(Q(x,\cdot)=N(x,1)\). In probabilistic language, \(Y\mid X=x\sim N(x,1)\). The associated Markov operator is \[
(L_Qf)(x) = \int_{\mathbb R}f(y)\phi(y-x)\,dy.
\] So the Markov operator takes a function \(f\) and returns its conditional expectation under the transition distribution \(Q(x,\cdot)\).
Now take \(f(y)=y^2\). Since \(Y\mid X=x\sim N(x,1)\), \[
\begin{aligned}
(L_Qf)(x) &=\int_{\mathbb R}y^2\phi(y-x)\,dy\\
&=\mathbb E[Y^2\mid X=x]\\ &=x^2+1.
\end{aligned}
\] Thus, \(L_Q(y^2)(x)=x^2+1\). This is a nice illustration of why \(L_Q\) is closely connected to conditional expectation.
As another example, consider an indicator function: \(f(y)=\mathbf 1_{\{y\leq a\}}\). Then \[
\begin{aligned}
(L_Qf)(x) &= \int_{\mathbb R} \mathbf 1_{\{y\leq a\}} \phi(y-x)\,dy\\
&= \int_{-\infty}^a\phi(y-x)\,dy\\ &= \Phi(a-x).
\end{aligned}
\] Hence \(L_Q\mathbf 1_{(-\infty,a]}(x)=\Phi(a-x)\). But this has an immediate probabilistic interpretation: \(L_Q\mathbf 1_{\{y\leq a\}}(x) = P(Y\leq a\mid X=x)\). So the Markov operator turns an event indicator into its conditional probability.

title: 34  Lecture 34.1: Probability Kernels-Part II
text:
34.2 Axiomatic Properties of Markov Generators
In the following proposition, we summarize the structural properties of the Markov generator \(L_Q\) associated with a probability kernel \(Q\).

Proposition 34.1 (Properties of the Associated Markov Generator) Let \(Q\) be a probability kernel from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\). The associated Markov generator operator \(L_Q: \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) satisfies the following structural properties:

Linearity: \(L_Q(\alpha f + \beta g) = \alpha L_Q(f) + \beta L_Q(g)\) for all \(\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(f, g \in \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\).
Preservation of Constants (Normalization): \(L_Q(\mathbb{I}_{S_2}) = \mathbb{I}_{S_1}\).
Positivity (Monotonicity): If \(f \ge 0\), then \(L_Q(f) \ge 0\). Consequently, if \(f \le g\), then \(L_Q(f) \le L_Q(g)\).
Boundedly Monotone / Pointwise Continuity: If \(f_n \to f\) boundedly (i.e., \(f_n(y) \to f(y)\) pointwise and \(\sup_n \|f_n\|_\infty < \infty\)), then \(L_Q f_n \to L_Q f\) boundedly on \(S_1\).



Proof. 

Linearity: Follows directly from the linearity of integration with respect to the integrand: \[
(L_Q(\alpha f + \beta g))(x) = \int_{S_2} (\alpha f(y) + \beta g(y)) \, Q(x, dy) = \alpha (L_Q f)(x) + \beta (L_Q g)(x).
\]
Normalization: Since \(Q(x, \cdot)\) is a probability measure for each \(x \in S_1\): \[
(L_Q \mathbb{I}_{S_2})(x) = \int_{S_2} 1 \, Q(x, dy) = Q(x, S_2) = 1 = \mathbb{I}_{S_1}(x) \quad \forall x \in S_1.
\]
Positivity: If \(f(y) \ge 0\) for all \(y \in S_2\), integrating a non-negative function against a non-negative probability measure yields \((L_Q f)(x) = \int_{S_2} f(y) \, Q(x, dy) \ge 0\).
Boundedly Monotone Continuity: Suppose \(f_n \to f\) pointwise with \(\|f_n\|_\infty \le M < \infty\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). For each \(x \in S_1\), applying the classical Dominated Convergence Theorem (DCT) to the probability measure \(Q(x, \cdot)\) yields: \[
(L_Q f_n)(x) = \int_{S_2} f_n(y) \, Q(x, dy) \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} \int_{S_2} f(y) \, Q(x, dy) = (L_Q f)(x),
\] pointwise on \(S_1\) by the Dominated Convergence Theorem. Furthermore, \(\|L_Q f_n\|_\infty \le \|f_n\|_\infty \le M\), so the convergence \(L_Q f_n \to L_Q f\) is bounded.



Remark 34.1 (Implication of Positivity). If a linear operator \(L: \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) satisfies positivity (\(f \ge 0 \implies L f \ge 0\)) and normalization (\(L \mathbb{I} = \mathbb{I}\)), then for any \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\): \[
-|f| \le f \le |f| \implies -L(|f|) \le L f \le L(|f|) \implies |L f| \le L(|f|).
\] Because \(|f| \le \|f\|_\infty \mathbb{I}_{S_2}\), monotonicity implies: \[
|L f| \le L(|f|) \le L(\|f\|_\infty \mathbb{I}_{S_2}) = \|f\|_\infty L(\mathbb{I}_{S_2}) = \|f\|_\infty \mathbb{I}_{S_1}.
\] Hence \(\|L f\|_\infty \le \|f\|_\infty\), demonstrating that every positive normalized linear operator is automatically a contraction with \(\|L\| = 1\).

title: 34  Lecture 34.1: Probability Kernels-Part II
section: 34.3 Duality: Bijection Between Probability Kernels and Markov Generators
text:
34.3 Duality: Bijection Between Probability Kernels and Markov Generators
In the next proposition, we show that the mapping \(Q \mapsto L_Q\) is a bijection between probability kernels and Markov generators. This is a duality result: every probability kernel defines a Markov generator, and conversely, every Markov generator arises from a unique probability kernel.

Proposition 34.2 (Representation Theorem for Markov Generators) Let \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be a measurable space. Let \(L: \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) be an operator satisfying:

\(L\) is linear.
\(L(\mathbb{I}_S) = \mathbb{I}_S\).
\(L f \ge 0\) whenever \(f \ge 0\).
If \(f_n \to f\) boundedly in \(\mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\), then \(L f_n \to L f\) boundedly in \(\mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\).

Then there exists a unique probability kernel \(Q\) over \((S, \mathcal{B})\) such that \(L = L_Q\). Explicitly, \(Q\) is given by: \[
Q(x, B) := (L \mathbb{I}_B)(x) \quad \forall x \in S, \; B \in \mathcal{B}.
\]


Proof. We construct \(Q(x, B) := (L \mathbb{I}_B)(x)\) and check the defining properties of a probability kernel:

Measurability: For every fixed \(B \in \mathcal{B}\), \(\mathbb{I}_B \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\). By definition of the domain/codomain of \(L\), \(Q(\cdot, B) = L(\mathbb{I}_B)(\cdot) \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\), so \(x \mapsto Q(x, B)\) is \(\mathcal{B}\)-measurable.
Probability Measure Properties for \(Q(x, \cdot)\):

Normalization: \(Q(x, S) = (L \mathbb{I}_S)(x) = 1\) by Property 1.
Non-negativity: For any \(B \in \mathcal{B}\), \(\mathbb{I}_B \ge 0 \implies Q(x, B) = (L \mathbb{I}_B)(x) \ge 0\) by Property 2.
Countable Additivity: Let \((B_k)_{k=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{B}\) be pairwise disjoint sets, and let \(B = \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty B_k\). Define \(f_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb{I}_{B_k} = \mathbb{I}_{\bigcup_{k=1}^n B_k}\). Then \(f_n \uparrow \mathbb{I}_B\) boundedly as \(n \to \infty\). By Property 3 (boundedly monotone continuity) and linearity of \(L\): \[
\begin{align*}
Q(x, B) &= (L \mathbb{I}_B)(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} (L f_n)(x)\\
& = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k=1}^n (L \mathbb{I}_{B_k})(x) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty Q(x, B_k) \quad \forall x \in S.
\end{align*}
\] Thus \(Q(x, \cdot)\) is a probability measure on \((S, \mathcal{B})\) for every fixed \(x \in S\).

Verification of \(L = L_Q\): We need to show \(L f = L_Q f = \int_S f(y) \, Q(\cdot, dy)\) for all \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\).

For indicator functions \(f = \mathbb{I}_B\): \(\int_S \mathbb{I}_B(y) \, Q(x, dy) = Q(x, B) = (L \mathbb{I}_B)(x)\).
By linearity, \(L f = L_Q f\) for all simple functions \(f = \sum_{i=1}^m c_i \mathbb{I}_{B_i}\).
For an arbitrary bounded measurable \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\), there exists a sequence of simple functions \(f_n\) such that \(f_n \to f\) boundedly. Applying Property 3 to both \(L\) and \(L_Q\) yields \(L f = \lim_{n \to \infty} L f_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} L_Q f_n = L_Q f\).



Thus, the mapping \(Q \mapsto L_Q\) defines a bijection between probability kernels and Markov generators: \[
\begin{align*}
&Q \mapsto L(f) = \int_S f(y) \, Q(\cdot, dy).\\
& L \mapsto Q(\cdot, B) = (L \mathbb{I}_B)(\cdot).
\end{align*}
\]

title: 74  Lecture 34.1: Probability Kernels-Part II
text:
74.4 Composition of Probability Kernels
The algebraic correspondence between probability kernels and linear operators allows us to define the product or composition of probability kernels via operator composition.

Corollary 74.1 (Kernel Composition via Operator Composition) Let \(Q_1\) be a probability kernel from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\), and let \(Q_2\) be a probability kernel from \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) to \((S_3, \mathcal{B}_3)\). Then there exists a unique probability kernel \(Q\) from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_3, \mathcal{B}_3)\) such that its associated Markov operator equals the composition of the individual operators: \[
L_Q = L_{Q_1} \circ L_{Q_2}.
\] We write \(Q = Q_1 Q_2\) or \(Q = Q_1 \cdot Q_2\). In the special case \(S_1=S_2=S_3=S\), this is the composition of kernels on the same space.


Proof (Proof of Corollary 74.1). Consider the operator \(L := L_{Q_1} \circ L_{Q_2}: \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\). We verify that \(L\) satisfies properties 0–3 of Proposition 74.2:

Linearity: Composition of linear operators is linear.
Normalization: \((L \mathbb{I}_S) = L_{Q_1}(L_{Q_2} \mathbb{I}_S) = L_{Q_1}(\mathbb{I}_S) = \mathbb{I}_S\).
Positivity: If \(f \ge 0\), then \(g := L_{Q_2}(f) \ge 0\) by positivity of \(L_{Q_2}\). Then \(L f = L_{Q_1}(g) \ge 0\) by positivity of \(L_{Q_1}\).
Boundedly Monotone Continuity: If \(f_n \to f\) boundedly, then \(g_n := L_{Q_2}(f_n) \to g := L_{Q_2}(f)\) boundedly by property 3 of \(L_{Q_2}\). Subsequently, \(L_{Q_1}(g_n) \to L_{Q_1}(g)\) boundedly by property 3 of \(L_{Q_1}\).

By Proposition 74.2, there exists a unique probability kernel \(Q\) such that \(L_Q = L_{Q_1} \circ L_{Q_2}\).


Remark 74.2 (Explicit Integral Formula for Kernel Composition). The kernel corresponding to the composed Markov operator \[
L_{Q_1Q_2}=L_{Q_1}\circ L_{Q_2}
\] can be obtained by evaluating the operator at the indicator function \(\mathbb{I}_B\). For \(B\in\mathcal{B}_3\), \[
\begin{aligned}
(Q_1Q_2)(x,B)
&= (L_{Q_1Q_2}\mathbb{I}_B)(x)\\
&= (L_{Q_1}(L_{Q_2}\mathbb{I}_B))(x)\\
&= \int_{S_2} Q_2(y,B)\,Q_1(x,dy).
\end{aligned}
\] Thus, the composition of two kernels is given explicitly by \[
(Q_1Q_2)(x,B) =\int_{S_2} Q_2(y,B)\,Q_1(x,dy).
\] More generally, for any \(f\in\mathcal{B}_b(S_3,\mathcal{B}_3)\), \[
\begin{aligned}
(L_{Q_1Q_2}f)(x)
&= (L_{Q_1}(L_{Q_2}f))(x)\\
&= \int_{S_2}
\left(
\int_{S_3} f(z)\,Q_2(y,dz)
\right)
Q_1(x,dy).
\end{aligned}
\] Equivalently, this can be written as the iterated integral \[
(L_{Q_1Q_2}f)(x)
=
\int_{S_2\times S_3}
f(z)\,Q_1(x,dy)\,Q_2(y,dz).
\] Thus, kernel composition corresponds to two successive transitions: \[
x \xrightarrow{Q_1} y \xrightarrow{Q_2} z.
\]


Example 74.2 (Matrix Multiplication Analogy for Discrete Spaces) When \(S\) is countable and \(\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{P}(S)\), a probability kernel is fully specified by a stochastic matrix \((Q(x, y))_{x, y \in S}\) where \(Q(x, y) = Q(x, \{y\})\).
Evaluating the kernel composition formula (from Remark 74.2) at \(B = \{z\}\) gives the \((x,z)\) entry of the composed kernel: \[
Q(x, z) := Q(x, \{z\}) = \int_S Q_2(y, \{z\}) \, Q_1(x, dy) = \sum_{y \in S} Q_1(x, y) \, Q_2(y, z).
\] This is precisely the \((x, z)\) entry of the matrix product \(Q_1 Q_2\), confirming that kernel composition is matrix multiplication. The associated generator then acts on \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) by: \[
(L_Q f)(x) = \sum_{z \in S} f(z) \, Q(x, z) = \sum_{z \in S} f(z) \sum_{y \in S} Q_1(x, y) \, Q_2(y, z).
\]


Example 74.3 (Composition of Two Discrete Kernels) Let \(S=\{1,2,3\}\) and consider two probability kernels \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) on \(S\), represented by the stochastic matrices \[
Q_1=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.5 & 0.3 & 0.2\\
0.1 & 0.6 & 0.3\\
0.2 & 0.2 & 0.6
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Q_2=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.7 & 0.2 & 0.1\\
0.3 & 0.4 & 0.3\\
0.1 & 0.2 & 0.7
\end{pmatrix}.
\] Suppose the process starts at state \(x=1\). The first kernel \(Q_1\) determines the distribution of the intermediate state \(Y\): \(Q_1(1,\cdot)=(0.5,0.3,0.2)\). The second kernel \(Q_2\) then determines the distribution of the final state \(Z\), conditional on \(Y\). For example, the probability of ending at state \(z=3\) is \[
\begin{aligned}
(Q_1Q_2)(1,3)
&=
\sum_{y\in S}Q_1(1,y)Q_2(y,3)\\
&=
Q_1(1,1)Q_2(1,3)
+Q_1(1,2)Q_2(2,3)
+Q_1(1,3)Q_2(3,3)\\
&=
(0.5)(0.1)+(0.3)(0.3)+(0.2)(0.7)\\
&=0.28.
\end{aligned}
\] Thus, \(P(Z=3\mid X=1)=0.28\). The three terms correspond to the three possible intermediate states: \[
\begin{aligned}
P(X=1\to Y=1\to Z=3)&=(0.5)(0.1)=0.05,\\
P(X=1\to Y=2\to Z=3)&=(0.3)(0.3)=0.09,\\
P(X=1\to Y=3\to Z=3)&=(0.2)(0.7)=0.14.
\end{aligned}
\] Adding these mutually exclusive paths gives \[
0.05+0.09+0.14=0.28.
\] More generally, the composition kernel is \[
(Q_1Q_2)(x,z)
=
\sum_{y\in S}Q_1(x,y)Q_2(y,z).
\] Hence, in this example, \[
Q_1Q_2=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.40 & 0.26 & 0.34\\
0.22 & 0.32 & 0.46\\
0.26 & 0.28 & 0.46
\end{pmatrix}.
\] For instance, the first row gives the distribution of \(Z\) after two transitions when \(X=1\): \[
(Q_1Q_2)(1,\cdot)=(0.40,0.26,0.34).
\] Thus, kernel composition combines all possible intermediate states, weighting each two-step path by the probability of reaching that intermediate state under \(Q_1\).

title: 74  Lecture 34.1: Probability Kernels-Part II
section: 74.5 Construction of Finite-Dimensional Distributions on Path Spaces
text:
74.5 Construction of Finite-Dimensional Distributions on Path Spaces
Probability kernels provide the building block for constructing finite-dimensional joint distributions of Markov processes.

Proposition 74.3 (Finite-Dimensional Path Distribution) Let \((S_0, \mathcal{B}_0), (S_1, \mathcal{B}_1), \dots, (S_n, \mathcal{B}_n)\) be measurable spaces. Let \(\nu \in \mathcal{P}(S_0, \mathcal{B}_0)\) be an initial probability measure, and let \(Q_k\) be a probability kernel from \((S_{k-1}, \mathcal{B}_{k-1})\) to \((S_k, \mathcal{B}_k)\) for \(k = 1, \dots, n\).
Then there exists a unique joint probability measure \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}(S_0 \times S_1 \times \dots \times S_n, \mathcal{B}_0 \otimes \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \mathcal{B}_n)\) such that for all bounded measurable functions \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S_0 \times \dots \times S_n)\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\int f \, d\mu &= \int_{S_0} \int_{S_1} \dots \int_{S_n} f(x_0, x_1,\dots, x_n) \, Q_n(x_{n-1}, dx_n)\\
& \dots Q_1(x_0, dx_1) \, \nu(dx_0).
\end{aligned}
\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 74.3). We construct \(\mu\) iteratively using kernels lifted to product spaces. For \(k \ge 2\), define the lifted kernel \[
\widetilde Q_k\big((x_0,\dots,x_{k-1}), A\big) := Q_k(x_{k-1}, A), \qquad A \in \mathcal{B}_k.
\] This is a probability kernel from \((S_0\times\cdots\times S_{k-1}, \mathcal{B}_0\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathcal{B}_{k-1})\) to \((S_k,\mathcal{B}_k)\).
Then the construction proceeds as follows:

Define \(\mu_1 = \nu \otimes Q_1 \in \mathcal{P}(S_0 \times S_1, \mathcal{B}_0 \otimes \mathcal{B}_1)\).
Define \(\mu_2 = \mu_1 \otimes \widetilde Q_2 \in \mathcal{P}(S_0 \times S_1 \times S_2, \mathcal{B}_0 \otimes \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\).
Continuing inductively, set \[
\mu_k = \mu_{k-1} \otimes \widetilde Q_k \in \mathcal{P}(S_0 \times \cdots \times S_k), \qquad k=1,\dots,n.
\] The resulting measure \(\mu := \mu_n\) is the desired finite-dimensional distribution.

To verify the integral identity, start with product functions \[
f(x_0,\dots,x_n) = f_0(x_0) f_1(x_1) \cdots f_n(x_n),
\] where each \(f_i\) is bounded and measurable. Applying Fubini/Tonelli successively gives \[
\begin{aligned}
\int f \, d\mu &= \int_{S_0} f_0(x_0) \left( \int_{S_1} f_1(x_1) \dots \left( \int_{S_n} f_n(x_n) \, Q_n(x_{n-1}, dx_n) \right) \dots Q_1(x_0, dx_1) \right) \nu(dx_0) \\
&= \int_{S_0} f_0(x_0) \Big( L_{Q_1} \big( f_1 \cdot L_{Q_2}( \dots (f_{n-1} \cdot L_{Q_n} f_n)\dots ) \big) \Big) (x_0) \, \nu(dx_0).
\end{aligned}
\] This is the claimed iterated-integral representation on tensor-product functions.
To extend from product functions to arbitrary bounded measurable \(f\), define \[
\mathcal{C} := \left\{E \in \mathcal{B}_0\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathcal{B}_n : \int \mathbf{1}_E \, d\mu = \int \mathbf{1}_E \, d\mu' \right\},
\] where \(\mu'\) is the measure defined by the right-hand side of the formula. One checks that \(\mathcal{C}\) is a \(\lambda\)-system, and it contains the class of finite rectangles (equivalently, cylinder sets) because the identity has already been verified on tensor-product functions. Since the rectangles form a \(\pi\)-system generating the product \(\sigma\)-algebra, Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem yields \(\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{B}_0\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathcal{B}_n\). Thus the two finite measures agree on all measurable sets, and therefore on all bounded measurable functions by standard measure-theoretic extension.

title: 49  Lecture 23.2: Prokhorov’s Compactness Theorem
text:
49.1 Motivation & Counterexample
Some sequences of probability measures have no weakly convergent subsequences.

title: 49  Lecture 23.2: Prokhorov’s Compactness Theorem
section: 49.4 Step 1: Cantor’s Diagonal Method on Rational Numbers
text:
49.4 Step 1: Cantor’s Diagonal Method on Rational Numbers
Enumerate the countable set of rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\): \[
\mathbb{Q} = \{q_1, q_2, q_3, \dots, q_j, \dots\}
\]

For \(q_1\): The numerical sequence \(\{F_n(q_1)\}_{n=1}^\infty\) is bounded in \([0, 1]\). By the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, there exists a convergent subsequence: \[
\{F_{m_1(k)}(q_1)\}_{k=1}^\infty
\]
For \(q_2\): Extract a sub-subsequence \(\{m_2(k)\}_{k=1}^\infty \subset \{m_1(k)\}_{k=1}^\infty\) such that \(\{F_{m_2(k)}(q_2)\}_{k=1}^\infty\) converges.
Inductively: For each \(j \ge 1\), \(\{m_j(k)\}_{k=1}^\infty\) is a subsequence of \(\{m_{j-1}(k)\}_{k=1}^\infty\) such that \(F_{m_j(k)}(q_i)\) converges as \(k \to \infty\) for all \(1 \le i \le j\).

Define the diagonal sequence \(n_k := m_k(k)\). By construction, \(\{n_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\) is eventually a subsequence of \(\{m_j(k)\}_{k=1}^\infty\) for any fixed \(j\). Therefore, the pointwise limit exists on all of \(\mathbb{Q}\): \[
F_{n_k}(q) \xrightarrow{k\to\infty} G(q) \in [0, 1], \quad \forall q \in \mathbb{Q}
\] Since each \(F_{n_k}\) is non-decreasing on \(\mathbb{R}\), the pointwise limit \(G\) is non-decreasing on \(\mathbb{Q}\).

title: 49  Lecture 23.2: Prokhorov’s Compactness Theorem
text:
49.5 Step 2: Extension from \(\mathbb{Q}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\)
We wish for the limiting object to define a valid CDF on \(\mathbb{R}\). To ensure it is right-continuous, define the function \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) by: \[
F(x) := \inf \{G(q) : q \in \mathbb{Q}, q > x\}
\]

title: 49  Lecture 23.2: Prokhorov’s Compactness Theorem
section: 49.7 Step 3: Convergence at Continuity Points of \(F\)
text:
49.7 Step 3: Convergence at Continuity Points of \(F\)
To complete the proof of vague/weak convergence (Theorem 48.3 and Theorem 51.1), it suffices to show that: \[
F_{n_k}(b) - F_{n_k}(a) \longrightarrow F(b) - F(a), \quad \forall a, b \in \text{Cont}(F)
\] In fact, we prove the stronger claim that: \[
F_{n_k}(x) \longrightarrow F(x), \quad \forall x \in \text{Cont}(F)
\] Fix \(x \in \text{Cont}(F)\). Choose rational sequences \(q_j, r_j \in \mathbb{Q}\) such that: \[
q_j \uparrow x \quad \text{and} \quad r_j \downarrow x \quad \implies \quad q_j < x < r_j
\] Since each \(F_{n_k}\) is non-decreasing: \[
F_{n_k}(q_j) \le F_{n_k}(x) \le F_{n_k}(r_j)
\] Taking the limit superior and limit inferior as \(k \to \infty\): \[
G(q_j) = \lim_{k \to \infty} F_{n_k}(q_j) \le \liminf_{k \to \infty} F_{n_k}(x) \le \limsup_{k \to \infty} F_{n_k}(x) \le \lim_{k \to \infty} F_{n_k}(r_j) = G(r_j)
\]
Since this holds for all \(j\):

Upper bound — \(G(r_j) \to F(x)\): Each \(G(r_j) \ge F(x)\) because \(r_j > x\), so \(G(r_j)\) belongs to the infimum set defining \(F(x)\). For any rational \(r^{*} > x\), since \(r_j \downarrow x < r^{*}\), eventually \(r_j < r^{*}\); non-decreasingness of \(G\) on \(\mathbb{Q}\) then gives \(G(r_j) \le G(r^{*})\). Hence \(\limsup_j G(r_j) \le G(r^{*})\) for every rational \(r^{*} > x\), so \(\limsup_j G(r_j) \le \inf_{r^{*} > x} G(r^{*}) = F(x)\). Combined with \(G(r_j) \ge F(x)\): \(G(r_j) \downarrow F(x)\).
Lower bound — \(G(q_j) \to F(x)\): Since \(G\) is non-decreasing on \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(q_j\) is increasing, \(G(q_j)\) is non-decreasing and bounded, so \(L := \lim_j G(q_j)\) exists.

\(L \le F(x)\): For any rational \(r > x\), we have \(r > q_j\) for all \(j\), so \(G(r) \ge G(q_j)\) for all \(j\), hence \(G(r) \ge L\). Taking the infimum over all rational \(r > x\) gives \(F(x) \ge L\).
\(L \ge F(x)\): For any \(z < x\), choose a rational \(r \in (z, x)\). Eventually \(q_j > r\), so \(G(q_j) \ge G(r)\); and since \(r > z\), non-decreasingness places \(G(r)\) in the infimum set for \(F(z)\), giving \(G(r) \ge F(z)\). Thus \(L \ge F(z)\) for every \(z < x\). Taking \(z \uparrow x\) and using continuity of \(F\) at \(x\) (i.e.~\(F(x^-) = F(x)\)): \(L \ge F(x)\).
Hence \(G(q_j) \uparrow F(x)\).


Hence, taking \(j \to \infty\): \[
F(x) \le \liminf_{k \to \infty} F_{n_k}(x) \le \limsup_{k \to \infty} F_{n_k}(x) \le F(x).
\] By squeeze theorem: \[
\lim_{k \to \infty} F_{n_k}(x) = F(x), \quad \forall x \in \text{Cont}(F).
\]

Example 49.1 (A tight sequence with an oscillating mean) Let \[
\mu_n =
\begin{cases} N(0,1), & n \text{ even},\\
N(1,1), & n \text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\] Equivalently, if \(X_n\sim\mu_n\), \[
X_n\sim
\begin{cases}
N(0,1), & n \text{ even},\\
N(1,1), & n \text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\] The full sequence does not converge weakly, because the even and odd subsequences have different limits: \(\mu_{2k}=N(0,1)\) and \(\mu_{2k+1}=N(1,1)\).
But the sequence is tight. Indeed, given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(M\) sufficiently large. Then \(\sup_n \mu_n([-M,M]^c) \leq P(|Z|>M-1)\), where \(Z\sim N(0,1)\). Note that the right-hand side tends to zero as \(M\to\infty\). Hence \(\{\mu_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) is tight.
Therefore, by Corollary 49.1, there must be a weakly convergent subsequence. And we can see exactly what the subsequences are: \(\mu_{2k}\xrightarrow{w}N(0,1)\) and \(\mu_{2k+1}\xrightarrow{w}N(1,1)\). Both limits are proper probability measures.
This example demonstrates an important distinction: tightness does not imply convergence of the entire sequence. Rather, tightness guarantees the existence of a weakly convergent subsequence. The sequence can oscillate between different probability distributions, but because its mass cannot escape to infinity, some subsequence must settle down to a genuine probability distribution.
For contrast, consider \(\mu_n=\delta_n\). Here the mass moves farther and farther to the right: \(\delta_1,\delta_2,\delta_3,\ldots\) and the sequence is not tight. It has no weakly convergent subsequence in \(\operatorname{Prob}(\mathbb R)\). Its vague limit is instead \(\delta_n\xrightarrow{v}0\), where \(0\) is the zero measure, not a probability measure.

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
50.1 Introduction & Motivation
For random variables defined on a common probability space, almost sure convergence and \(L^p\) convergence (for \(1 \le p < \infty\), assuming the relevant moments are finite) each imply convergence in probability, which in turn implies weak convergence (\(\mu_n \Rightarrow \mu\), or \(X_n \xrightarrow{d} X\)). None of the converse implications holds in general, so weak convergence is the weakest of these modes. Note also that, unlike the other three, weak convergence depends only on the laws of the random variables and does not require them to be defined on a common space.
However, there is a fundamental connection back to almost sure convergence that serves as a powerful analytical tool in many stochastic contexts.

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
50.3 Technical Properties of \(F^\leftarrow\) and \(F^\rightarrow\)

Ordering: \[
F^\leftarrow(u) \le F^\rightarrow(u), \quad \forall u \in (0, 1).
\]
Equivalence & Flat Spots: Say that \(u\) is the height of a flat spot of \(F\) if \(F \equiv u\) on some nonempty open interval. Then \(F^\leftarrow(u) < F^\rightarrow(u)\Longleftrightarrow  u\) is the height of a flat spot of \(F\). Consequently, define \[
E := \{u\in(0,1):F^\leftarrow(u)<F^\rightarrow(u)\}.
\] For each \(u\in E\), the interval \(\bigl(F^\leftarrow(u),F^\rightarrow(u)\bigr)\) is a nonempty open interval on which \(F\) is constant and equal to \(u\). These intervals are pairwise disjoint. Hence, since every nonempty open interval in \(\mathbb R\) contains a rational number, \(E\) is at most countable. Therefore, \(\lambda(E)=0\).
Key Inequality: For all \(u \in (0, 1)\), \[
\lim_{y \uparrow F^\leftarrow(u)} F(y) \le u \le F\left(F^\leftarrow(u)\right)
\] together with the two implications

If \(y > F^\leftarrow(u)\), then \(F(y) \ge u\);
If \(y < F^\leftarrow(u)\), then \(F(y) < u\).

The two implications and the left-hand inequality use only the definition of the supremum and the monotonicity of \(F\). Right-continuity of \(F\) is needed only for the right-hand inequality \(u \le F\left(F^\leftarrow(u)\right)\).







Figure 50.1: Generalized CDF Inverses




Proof (Proof of Technical Properties of \(F^\leftarrow\) and \(F^\rightarrow\)). Proof of 1: Fix \(u\in(0,1)\) and define \(A_u:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:F(x)<u\}\) and \(B_u:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:F(x)>u\}\). Take any \(a\in A_u\) and \(b\in B_u\). Then \(F(a)<u<F(b)\). Since \(F\) is nondecreasing, we must have \(a<b\). Otherwise, if \(b\leq a\), then \(F(b)\leq F(a)\), which contradicts \(F(a)<u<F(b)\). Thus every element of \(A_u\) is less than every element of \(B_u\). Therefore, \(\sup A_u\leq\inf B_u\). By the definitions of the lower and upper quantile functions, \[
F^\leftarrow(u)=\sup A_u\leq\inf B_u=F^\rightarrow(u).
\] Hence \(F^\leftarrow(u)\leq F^\rightarrow(u)\).
Proof of 2: Fix \(u\in(0,1)\) and write \(a:=F^\leftarrow(u)\) and \(b:=F^\rightarrow(u)\). Suppose first that \(a<b\). Take any \(x\in(a,b)\). Since \(x>a\) and \(a=\sup\{y:F(y)<u\}\), we cannot have \(F(x)<u\). Otherwise, \(x\) itself would belong to \(\{y:F(y)<u\}\), implying \(x\leq a\), which contradicts \(x>a\). Similarly, since \(x<b\) and \(b=\inf\{y:F(y)>u\}\), we cannot have \(F(x)>u\). Otherwise, \(x\) would belong to \(\{y:F(y)>u\}\), implying \(b\leq x\), which contradicts \(x<b\). Therefore, \(F(x)=u\) for \(x\in(a,b)\). Thus \(F\) is constant and equal to \(u\) on the nonempty open interval \((a,b)\); that is, \(u\) is the height of a flat spot of \(F\).
Conversely, suppose that \(F\) has a flat spot at height \(u\). That is, there exist \(a<b\) such that \(F(x)=u\) for \(x\in(a,b)\). We claim that \(\{y:F(y)<u\}\subseteq(-\infty,a]\). Indeed, no \(x\in(a,b)\) belongs to this set, since \(F(x)=u\); and if \(z\geq b\), then monotonicity gives \(F(z)\geq F(x)=u\) for any \(x\in(a,b)\), so \(z\) does not belong to it either. Taking suprema yields \(F^\leftarrow(u)\leq a\). Symmetrically, \(\{y:F(y)>u\}\subseteq[b,\infty)\), so \(F^\rightarrow(u)\geq b\). Hence \[
F^\leftarrow(u)\leq a<b\leq F^\rightarrow(u).
\] Therefore, \(F^\leftarrow(u)<F^\rightarrow(u)\). This proves \(F^\leftarrow(u)<F^\rightarrow(u)\Longleftrightarrow u\) is the height of a flat spot of F.
Now consider \[
E=\{u\in(0,1):F^\leftarrow(u)<F^\rightarrow(u)\}.
\] For each \(u\in E\), define \[
I_u:=\bigl(F^\leftarrow(u),F^\rightarrow(u)\bigr).
\]
Each \(I_u\) is a nonempty open interval on which \(F(x)=u\). Moreover, these intervals are pairwise disjoint. Indeed, suppose that \(u,v\in E\) with \(u<v\). If \(I_u\) and \(I_v\) had a common point \(x\), then the flat-spot property would give \(F(x)=u\) and \(F(x)=v\), which is impossible because \(u\neq v\). Thus \(\{I_u:u\in E\}\) is a collection of pairwise disjoint nonempty open intervals in \(\mathbb R\).
Every nonempty open interval in \(\mathbb R\) contains a rational number. Since the intervals are pairwise disjoint, we can associate a distinct rational number with each \(u\in E\). Because \(\mathbb Q\) is countable, \(E\) must be at most countable. Consequently, \(\lambda(E)=0\).
Proof of 3: Fix \(u\in(0,1)\), set \(A_u:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}:F(y)<u\}\), and let \(q:=F^\leftarrow(u)=\sup A_u\), which is finite by the finiteness remark following Definition 50.1.
Second implication. Let \(y<q\). By definition of the supremum there exists \(z\in A_u\) with \(y<z\leq q\). Monotonicity of \(F\) then gives \[
F(y)\leq F(z)<u.
\] Hence \(F(y)<u\) whenever \(y<q\). Letting \(y\uparrow q\) in this inequality gives \[
\lim_{y\uparrow q}F(y)\leq u,
\] which is the left-hand inequality of the display. (The limit exists because \(F\) is nondecreasing and bounded.) Note that only monotonicity and the definition of the supremum were used.
First implication. Let \(y>q\). Since every element of \(A_u\) is at most \(q\), we have \(y\notin A_u\), which by the definition of \(A_u\) means exactly \(F(y)\geq u\).
Right-hand inequality. Apply the first implication along any sequence \(y_k\downarrow q\) with \(y_k>q\), obtaining \(F(y_k)\geq u\) for every \(k\). Since \(F\) is right-continuous, \[
F(q)=\lim_{k\to\infty}F(y_k)\geq u.
\] Combining the two inequalities gives \[
\lim_{y\uparrow F^\leftarrow(u)}F(y)\leq u\leq F\left(F^\leftarrow(u)\right),
\] as claimed. \(\blacksquare\)

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
50.5 Proof of Lemma 50.1
For any \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), we claim the fundamental equivalence: \[
\{ x \in (0, 1) : Y(x) \le t \} = (0, 1) \cap (0, F(t)].
\]

\((\subseteq)\): If \(Y(x) \le t\), then by right-continuity and monotonicity of \(F\), \(x \le F(F^\leftarrow(x)) \le F(t)\), so \(x \in (0, F(t)]\).
\((\supseteq)\): If \(x \le F(t)\), then every \(y\) with \(F(y) < x\) satisfies \(y \le t\): if \(y > t\), then non-decreasingness of \(F\) gives \(F(y) \ge F(t) \ge x\), contradicting \(F(y) < x\). Thus \(t\) is an upper bound for \(\{y : F(y) < x\}\), so \(Y(x) = \sup\{y : F(y) < x\} \le t\).

Taking the Lebesgue measure of this set gives: \[
\lambda(\{ x \in (0, 1) : Y(x) \le t \}) = \lambda((0, F(t)]) = F(t) = F_\mu(t).
\] Thus, \(\mu_Y = \mu\).

Corollary 50.1 (Inverse Transform Sampling) If \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})\) has CDF \(F\), and \(U \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1)\), then \(F^\leftarrow(U) \sim \mu\).

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
50.7 Step 1: Lower Bound (\(\liminf_{n\to\infty} Y_n(x) \ge Y(x)\))
Fix \(x \notin E\). Choose \(y \in \text{Cont}(F)\) such that \(y < Y(x) = F^\leftarrow(x)\). By Property 3 of \(F^\leftarrow\), since \(y < F^\leftarrow(x)\), we have \(F(y) < x\).
Since \(y\) is a continuity point of \(F\) and \(\mu_n \Rightarrow \mu\), we have \(F_n(y) \to F(y)\). Because \(F(y) < x\), for all sufficiently large \(n\), we have \(F_n(y) < x\). Therefore, by definition of \(Y_n(x) = F_n^\leftarrow(x)\): \[
Y_n(x) = \sup \{ y' : F_n(y') < x \} \ge y.
\] Taking the limit inferior as \(n \to \infty\) gives: \[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} Y_n(x) \ge y.
\] Since this holds for all \(y \in \text{Cont}(F)\) with \(y < Y(x)\), and continuity points of \(F\) are dense in \(\mathbb{R}\), taking \(y \uparrow Y(x)\) yields: \[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} Y_n(x) \ge Y(x).
\]

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
50.8 Step 2: Upper Bound (\(\limsup_{n\to\infty} Y_n(x) \le Y(x)\))
Now choose \(y \in \text{Cont}(F)\) such that \(y > Y(x)\). Since \(x \notin E\), we have \(Y(x) = F^\leftarrow(x) = F^\rightarrow(x) = \inf \{ y' : F(y') > x \}\). Thus \(y > F^\rightarrow(x)\). Since the set \(\{y': F(y') > x\}\) is closed upward (non-decreasingness of \(F\): if \(F(z)>x\) and \(z'\ge z\) then \(F(z')\ge F(z)>x\)) and \(F^\rightarrow(x)\) is its infimum, any \(y > F^\rightarrow(x)\) belongs to the set, i.e.~\(F(y) > x\).
Since \(y \in \text{Cont}(F)\), \(F_n(y) \to F(y) > x\), so for all sufficiently large \(n\), \(F_n(y) > x\). Because \(F_n\) is non-decreasing, \(F_n(y) > x\) makes \(y\) an upper bound for \(\{z : F_n(z) < x\}\) (any \(z > y\) satisfies \(F_n(z) \ge F_n(y) > x\)), so \(Y_n(x) = \sup\{z : F_n(z) < x\} \le y\). Taking the limit superior as \(n \to \infty\) gives: \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} Y_n(x) \le y
\] Taking \(y \downarrow Y(x)\) over continuity points \(y \in \text{Cont}(F)\) yields: \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} Y_n(x) \le Y(x)
\]
Combining both steps: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} Y_n(x) = Y(x), \quad \forall x \in (0, 1) \setminus E
\] Since \(\lambda(E) = 0\), \(Y_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} Y\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: 13  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
13.10 Proof of Corollary 13.2

13.10.1 Step 0: Skorohod Coupling
Since \(X_n \xrightarrow{d} X\), Skorohod’s Representation Theorem provides a common probability space \(((0, 1), \mathcal{B}(0,1), \lambda)\) and random variables \((Y_n, Y)\) satisfying: \[Y_n \overset{d}{=} X_n \quad \forall n, \qquad Y \overset{d}{=} X, \qquad \text{and} \qquad Y_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} Y.\] That is, there exists a set \(\Omega_1 \subset (0,1)\) with \(\lambda(\Omega_1) = 1\) such that \(Y_n(\omega) \to Y(\omega)\) for all \(\omega \in \Omega_1\).



13.10.2 Step 1: The Composition \(g \circ f\) is Continuous \(\lambda\)-a.s. at \(Y\)
Let \(g \in C_b(\mathbb{R})\) be any bounded continuous test function. Since \(g\) is everywhere continuous, any point of continuity of \(f\) is also a point of continuity of \(g \circ f\): \[x \in \text{Cont}(f) \implies g \circ f \text{ is continuous at } x \implies x \notin \text{Disc}(g \circ f).\] Taking complements: \(\text{Disc}(g \circ f) \subseteq \text{Disc}(f)\). Therefore: \[\lambda(Y \in \text{Disc}(g \circ f)) = \mu_X(\text{Disc}(g \circ f)) \le \mu_X(\text{Disc}(f)) = P(X \in \text{Disc}(f)) = 0.\] So there exists \(\Omega_2 \subset (0,1)\) with \(\lambda(\Omega_2) = 1\) and \(Y(\omega) \notin \text{Disc}(g \circ f)\) for all \(\omega \in \Omega_2\).



13.10.3 Step 2: Pointwise A.S. Convergence of \(g \circ f\)
The set \(\Omega^* := \Omega_1 \cap \Omega_2\) satisfies \(\lambda(\Omega^*) = 1\). Fix any \(\omega \in \Omega^*\):

\(Y_n(\omega) \to Y(\omega)\) (since \(\omega \in \Omega_1\)).
\(g \circ f\) is continuous at \(Y(\omega)\) (since \(\omega \in \Omega_2\)).

By the definition of continuity, \(y_n \to y\) and \(h\) continuous at \(y\) implies \(h(y_n) \to h(y)\). Applying this with \(y_n = Y_n(\omega)\), \(y = Y(\omega)\), \(h = g \circ f\): \[(g \circ f)(Y_n(\omega)) \longrightarrow (g \circ f)(Y(\omega)).\] Since this holds for all \(\omega \in \Omega^*\): \[(g \circ f)(Y_n) \xrightarrow{a.s.} (g \circ f)(Y).\]



13.10.4 Step 3: Dominated Convergence
Since \(g \in C_b(\mathbb{R})\), there exists \(M < \infty\) with \(|g(y)| \le M\) for all \(y\). Thus: \[|(g \circ f)(Y_n(\omega))| \le M \quad \text{for all } n \text{ and all } \omega \in (0,1).\] The constant function \(M\) is integrable on \(((0,1), \lambda)\). By the Dominated Convergence Theorem: \[\mathbb{E}_\lambda[(g \circ f)(Y_n)] \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}_\lambda[(g \circ f)(Y)].\]



13.10.5 Step 4: Transfer Back to \((X_n, X)\)
Since \(Y_n \overset{d}{=} X_n\), for any Borel-measurable bounded function \(h\): \[\mathbb{E}[h(Y_n)] = \int h \, d\mu_{Y_n} = \int h \, d\mu_{X_n} = \mathbb{E}[h(X_n)],\] and similarly \(\mathbb{E}[h(Y)] = \mathbb{E}[h(X)]\). Applying this with \(h = g \circ f\): \[\mathbb{E}[g(f(X_n))] = \mathbb{E}[(g \circ f)(Y_n)] \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}[(g \circ f)(Y)] = \mathbb{E}[g(f(X))].\]



13.10.6 Step 5: Conclusion of Part 1
Since \(g \in C_b(\mathbb{R})\) was arbitrary and \(\mathbb{E}[g(f(X_n))] \to \mathbb{E}[g(f(X))]\) for every such \(g\), the definition of weak convergence gives \(f(X_n) \xrightarrow{d} f(X)\).



13.10.7 Step 6: Part 2 — Bounded \(f\) Implies \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_n)] \to \mathbb{E}[f(X)]\)
Suppose \(|f| \le M\) for some \(M < \infty\). From Step 2 (with \(g = \text{id}\) applied informally, or directly): for all \(\omega \in \Omega^*\), \(Y_n(\omega) \to Y(\omega)\) and \(f\) is continuous at \(Y(\omega)\), so \(f(Y_n(\omega)) \to f(Y(\omega))\). Hence: \[f(Y_n) \xrightarrow{a.s.} f(Y).\] The uniform bound \(|f(Y_n)| \le M\) provides a dominating function, so by DCT: \[\mathbb{E}[f(Y_n)] \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}[f(Y)].\] Transferring back via Step 4 (with \(h = f\), which is bounded Borel): \[\mathbb{E}[f(X_n)] = \mathbb{E}[f(Y_n)] \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}[f(Y)] = \mathbb{E}[f(X)]. \quad \blacksquare\]

title: 51  Lecture 24.1: Complex Integration and Dynkin’s Theorem
text:
52 Integration of Complex-Valued Functions
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space. Consider a complex-valued function \(f: \Omega \to \mathbb{C}\) that is \(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{C})\)-measurable, where \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{C}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^2)\) under the usual identification \(\mathbb{C} \cong \mathbb{R}^2\). Throughout, “measurable” for a \(\mathbb{C}\)-valued function means \(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{C})\)-measurable.
We can write \(f\) in terms of its real and imaginary components: \[
f(\omega) = u(\omega) + i v(\omega), \qquad u := \operatorname{Re} f, \quad v := \operatorname{Im} f,
\] where \(u, v: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\). Since \(\mathbb{C}\) is a separable metric space, \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{C}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) \otimes \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\); consequently \(f\) is measurable if and only if \(u\) and \(v\) are \(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\)-measurable.
crumbs: 51  Lecture 24.1: Complex Integration and Dynkin's Theorem

title: 51  Lecture 24.1: Complex Integration and Dynkin’s Theorem
text:
52.1 Norm Equivalence & Triangle Inequality
Let \(f = u + iv : \Omega \to \mathbb{C}\) be measurable, so that \(|f| = \sqrt{u^2 + v^2}\) is measurable as a continuous function of \(f\). Using the bounds relating the components to the magnitude: \[\max\{|u|, |v|\} \le \sqrt{u^2 + v^2} \le \sqrt{2} \max\{|u|, |v|\}\]
it follows that a measurable \(f\) satisfies \(f \in L_{\mathbb{C}}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) if and only if \(|f| \in L_{\mathbb{R}}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), i.e.,: \[\|f\|_{L_{\mathbb{C}}^1} := \int_{\Omega} |f| \, d\mu < \infty\]
The measurability hypothesis cannot be omitted: on a probability space one may have \(|f| \equiv 1\) integrable while \(u\) is non-measurable. As in the real case, \(\|\cdot\|_{L_{\mathbb{C}}^1}\) is only a seminorm on functions; it is a norm on \(L_{\mathbb{C}}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) once functions agreeing \(\mu\)-a.e. are identified, and we adopt this identification throughout.
It is routine to verify that \(\int_{\Omega} \cdot \, d\mu\) is \(\mathbb{C}\)-linear on \(L_{\mathbb{C}}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\). Standard integration theorems transfer to complex-valued functions by applying them separately to real and imaginary parts. For instance, in the Dominated Convergence Theorem, if \(f_n \to f\) pointwise with \(|f_n| \le g\) for some \(g \in L_{\mathbb{R}}^1\), then \(|\operatorname{Re} f_n| \le g\) and \(|\operatorname{Im} f_n| \le g\), so the real theorem applies componentwise and yields \(\int_{\Omega} f_n \, d\mu \to \int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu\).

Theorem 52.1 (Triangle Inequality for Complex Integrals) If \(f \in L_{\mathbb{C}}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), then: \[\left| \int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu \right| \le \int_{\Omega} |f| \, d\mu\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 52.1). If \(\int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu = 0\), the inequality holds trivially.
Suppose \(\int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu \ne 0\). Express the complex number \(\int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu\) in polar form: \[\int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu = r e^{i\theta}, \quad \text{where } r = \left| \int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu \right| > 0 \text{ and } \theta \in [0, 2\pi)\]
Multiplying by \(e^{-i\theta}\), we obtain a real non-negative quantity: \[r = e^{-i\theta} \int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu = \int_{\Omega} e^{-i\theta} f \, d\mu\]
Since \(r \in \mathbb{R}\), taking the real part of both sides yields: \[r = \operatorname{Re}\left( \int_{\Omega} e^{-i\theta} f \, d\mu \right) = \int_{\Omega} \operatorname{Re}\left( e^{-i\theta} f \right) d\mu\]
Using the pointwise real part bound \(\operatorname{Re}(z) \le |z|\) for any \(z \in \mathbb{C}\): \[\operatorname{Re}\left( e^{-i\theta} f(\omega) \right) \le \left| e^{-i\theta} f(\omega) \right| = |e^{-i\theta}| \cdot |f(\omega)| = |f(\omega)|\]
Both \(\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta} f)\) and \(|f|\) lie in \(L_{\mathbb{R}}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), so integrating the pointwise bound and using monotonicity of the real integral gives: \[
\left| \int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu \right| = r = \int_{\Omega} \operatorname{Re}\left( e^{-i\theta} f \right) d\mu \le \int_{\Omega} |f| \, d\mu.
\]
