title: 65  Lecture 30.1: Conditional Probability
text:
65.1 Foundations of Conditional Probability
Given a underlying probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) and an event \(B \in \mathcal{F}\) with non-zero probability (\(\mathbb{P}(B) > 0\)), we can define a updated probability measure \(\mathbb{P}_B: \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]\).

title: 65  Lecture 30.1: Conditional Probability
text:
65.3 Applied Example: Unfair Coin Collection
Suppose you find a coin on the street selected from a mixed population:

Fair Coins (\(B_1\)): \(90\%\) of coins (\(\mathbb{P}(B_1) = 0.90\)), with \(\mathbb{P}(\text{Heads} \mid B_1) = 0.50\).
Biased Coins Type 1 (\(B_2\)): \(9\%\) of coins (\(\mathbb{P}(B_2) = 0.09\)), with \(\mathbb{P}(\text{Heads} \mid B_2) = 0.60\).
Biased Coins Type 2 (\(B_3\)): \(1\%\) of coins (\(\mathbb{P}(B_3) = 0.01\)), with \(\mathbb{P}(\text{Heads} \mid B_3) = 0.80\).

What is the overall probability \(P(H)\) that a randomly selected coin turns up heads?
Applying the Law of Total Probability:
\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(H) &= \mathbb{P}(B_1)\mathbb{P}(H \mid B_1) + \mathbb{P}(B_2)\mathbb{P}(H \mid B_2) + \mathbb{P}(B_3)\mathbb{P}(H \mid B_3) \\ &= (0.90)(0.50) + (0.09)(0.60) + (0.01)(0.80) \\ &= 0.450 + 0.054 + 0.008 = 0.512 \quad (51.2\%). \end{aligned}\]

title: 65  Lecture 30.1: Conditional Probability
text:
65.4 Example 1: Updating the Coin Beliefs
Given that the picked coin comes up heads on a single toss, what is the probability that it is the heavily biased coin (\(B_3\))?
\[\mathbb{P}(B_3 \mid H) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(H \mid B_3) \, \mathbb{P}(B_3)}{\mathbb{P}(H)} = \frac{(0.80)(0.01)}{0.512} = \frac{0.008}{0.512} \approx 0.0156 \quad (1.56\%).\]
Notice that even though \(\mathbb{P}(H \mid B_3) = 80\%\), \(\mathbb{P}(B_3 \mid H) \neq 80\%\) due to the low prior probability of picking \(B_3\).

title: 65  Lecture 30.1: Conditional Probability
text:
65.5 Example 2: Demographic Inversion (Billionaires)
According to Forbes data (April 2019), there are \(2,208\) billionaires globally, of whom \(1,964\) are men.

Let \(B\) be the event of being a billionaire, and \(M\) be the event of being male.
\(\mathbb{P}(M \mid B) = \frac{1964}{2208} \approx 88.95\%\).
Crucially, \(\mathbb{P}(M \mid B) \neq \mathbb{P}(B \mid M)\), as \(\mathbb{P}(B \mid M)\) represents the probability that a randomly chosen male is a billionaire (which is near zero).

title: 65  Lecture 30.1: Conditional Probability
text:
65.6 Epidemiological Fallacy (Base Rate Neglect)
Consider a medical diagnostic test for HIV with the following specifications:

Accuracy: \(99\%\) sensitivity (\(\mathbb{P}(T \mid H) = 0.99\)) and \(99\%\) specificity (\(\mathbb{P}(T^c \mid H^c) = 0.99\), implying a false-positive rate \(\mathbb{P}(T \mid H^c) = 0.01\)).
Prevalence (Base Rate): \(0.33\%\) of the population has HIV (\(\mathbb{P}(H) = 0.0033\)).

If an individual tests positive (\(T\)), what is the probability that they actually have HIV (\(\mathbb{P}(H \mid T)\))?
\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(H \mid T) &= \frac{\mathbb{P}(T \mid H) \mathbb{P}(H)}{\mathbb{P}(T \mid H)\mathbb{P}(H) + \mathbb{P}(T \mid H^c)\mathbb{P}(H^c)} \\ &= \frac{(0.99)(0.0033)}{(0.99)(0.0033) + (0.01)(1 - 0.0033)} \\ &= \frac{0.003267}{0.003267 + 0.009967} = \frac{0.003267}{0.013234} \approx 24.69\%. \end{aligned}\]

65.6.1 Structural Insight
Even though the false-positive rate is only \(1\%\), the healthy population \(H^c\) is so much larger than \(H\) (\(99.67\%\) vs. \(0.33\%\)) that false positives outnumber true positives nearly \(3\) to \(1\). This demonstrates the high sensitivity of posterior probabilities to low prior base rates.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

labels = ['True Positives P(H ∩ T)', 'False Positives P(H^c ∩ T)']
sizes = [0.003267, 0.009967]
colors = ['#2ca02c', '#d62728']

plt.figure(figsize=(5, 5))
plt.pie(sizes, labels=labels, colors=colors, autopct='%1.1f%%', startangle=140)
plt.title('Composition of Positive Test Results (P(H|T) = 24.7%)')
plt.show()







Figure 65.1: Visual Breakdown of Positive HIV Test Results

title: 65  Lecture 30.1: Conditional Probability
text:
70.1 Game Setup and Event Definitions

Player Choice: Without loss of generality, assume you originally choose Door #1.
Host Action: Monty, who knows what is behind all doors, must open one of the two unchosen doors (#2 or #3) to reveal a goat.
Observed Event: Let \(A = \{\text{Monty opens Door \#2}\}\).
Decision: Should you stick with Door #1 or switch to Door #3?

We evaluate the posterior probability \(\mathbb{P}(B_3 \mid A)\) that the car is behind Door #3 given that Monty opened Door #2.

title: 65  Lecture 30.1: Conditional Probability
text:
70.2 Host Behavior Conditional Probabilities
To apply Bayes’ Rule, we determine \(\mathbb{P}(A \mid B_i)\) for each hypothesis \(B_i\):

Case 1 (\(B_1\) is true): If the car is behind Door #1, both Door #2 and Door #3 hide goats. Monty chooses randomly between them with equal probability: \[\mathbb{P}(A \mid B_1) = \frac{1}{2}\]
Case 2 (\(B_2\) is true): If the car is behind Door #2, Monty cannot open Door #2 because he must reveal a goat: \[\mathbb{P}(A \mid B_2) = 0\]
Case 3 (\(B_3\) is true): If the car is behind Door #3, Monty cannot open Door #1 (your choice) or Door #3 (car location). He is forced to open Door #2: \[\mathbb{P}(A \mid B_3) = 1\]

title: 65  Lecture 30.1: Conditional Probability
text:
70.3 Posterior Calculation via Bayes’ Rule
Applying Bayes’ Theorem to compute \(\mathbb{P}(B_3 \mid A)\):
\[
\mathbb{P}(B_3 \mid A) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(B_3 \cap A)}{\mathbb{P}(A)} = \frac{\mathbb{P}(B_3) \mathbb{P}(A \mid B_3)}{\mathbb{P}(B_1)\mathbb{P}(A \mid B_1) + \mathbb{P}(B_2)\mathbb{P}(A \mid B_2) + \mathbb{P}(B_3)\mathbb{P}(A \mid B_3)}
\]
Substituting the known probabilities into the formula:
\[
\mathbb{P}(B_3 \mid A) = \frac{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \cdot 1}{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)(0) + \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)(1)} = \frac{\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{1}{6} + 0 + \frac{1}{3}} = \frac{\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{2}{3}
\]
Similarly, for staying with your original choice:
\[
\mathbb{P}(B_1 \mid A) = \frac{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{\frac{1}{6}}{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{3}
\]

title: 65  Lecture 30.1: Conditional Probability
text:
70.4 Conclusion
Since \(\mathbb{P}(B_3 \mid A) = \frac{2}{3}\) and \(\mathbb{P}(B_1 \mid A) = \frac{1}{3}\), you should switch doors. Switching doubles your chance of winning the car.

title: 66  Lecture 30.2: Conditional Expectation-Part I
text:
66.1 Conditioning on a Single Event
Given a probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) and an event \(A \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(\mathbb{P}(A) > 0\), recall the conditional probability measure on \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\): \[
\mathbb{P}_A(B) = \mathbb{P}[B \mid A] = \frac{\mathbb{P}(A \cap B)}{\mathbb{P}(A)},
\qquad B\in\mathcal F.
\]
We can evaluate the expected value of an integrable random variable \(X \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}_A)\) under this updated measure:
\[
\mathbb{E}_A[X] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid A] := \int_\Omega X \, d\mathbb{P}_A.
\]

title: 66  Lecture 30.2: Conditional Expectation-Part I
text:
66.3 \(\sigma\)-Algebras Generated by Partitions
Instead of indexing by the explicit set sequence \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\), it is more natural to label the operator using the sub-\(\sigma\)-algebra generated by the partition:
\[
\mathcal{G} = \sigma(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty).
\]
We write the preceding random variable as \[
\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]:=\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]
:=\mathbb{E}_{\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty}[X].
\] Using the fact that \(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\) is constant on each \(A_n\), it can be shown that \(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\) is integrable because the triangle inequality and the single-event formula give \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\left[\left|\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\right|\right]
&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left|\mathbb E_{A_n}[X]\right|\mathbb P(A_n) \\
&\le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb E_{A_n}[|X|]\mathbb P(A_n)\\
&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\mathbb E[|X|\mathbb I_{A_n}]}{\mathbb P(A_n)}\mathbb P(A_n)\\
&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb E[|X|\mathbb I_{A_n}]\\
&=\mathbb E[|X|].
\end{aligned}
\]

Exercise 66.1 (Structure of Partition \(\sigma\)-Algebras) If \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) forms a partition of \(\Omega\) into nonempty sets, then:
\[
\sigma(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty) = \left\{ \bigcup_{n \in \Lambda} A_n : \Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{N} \right\}.
\]
Thus, each \(A_n\) is an atom of \(\mathcal G\), and every element of \(\mathcal G\) is a union of these atoms.


Corollary 66.1 (Measurability of Conditional Expectation) If \(\mathcal{G} = \sigma(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty)\), then \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable and, for every \(B\in\mathcal G\), \[
\mathbb E\left[\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]\mathbb I_B\right]
=\mathbb E[X\mathbb I_B].
\]


Proof (Proof of Corollary 66.1). For \(m\ge1\), the partial sum \[
S_m=\sum_{n=1}^m \mathbb{E}_{A_n}[X]\mathbb I_{A_n}
\] is \(\mathcal G\)-measurable. Since every \(\omega\in\Omega\) belongs to exactly one \(A_n\), \(S_m(\omega)\) converges pointwise to \(\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X](\omega)\). Therefore, \(\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]\) is \(\mathcal G\)-measurable.
For \(B\in\mathcal G\), the partition description above gives \(B=\bigcup_{n\in\Lambda}A_n\) for some \(\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N\). The series below are absolutely convergent because \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty\left|\mathbb E[X\mathbb I_{A_n}]\right|
\le\sum_{n=1}^\infty\mathbb E[|X|\mathbb I_{A_n}]
=\mathbb E[|X|]<\infty.
\] Thus, \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\left[\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]\mathbb I_B\right]
&=\sum_{n\in\Lambda}\mathbb E_{A_n}[X]\mathbb P(A_n) \\
&=\sum_{n\in\Lambda}\mathbb E[X\mathbb I_{A_n}] \\
&=\mathbb E\left[X\mathbb I_{\bigcup_{n\in\Lambda}A_n}\right]\\
&=\mathbb E[X\mathbb I_B].
\end{aligned}
\] Together with the preceding integrability estimate, this verifies that the displayed random variable is a version of \(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\).

title: 67  Lecture 31.1: Orthogonal Projection
text:
67.1 Introduction: From Finite Dimensions to Hilbert Spaces
In a finite-dimensional inner product space \(H\), any linear subspace \(K \subseteq H\) admits an orthogonal projection operator \(P_K: H \to K\).
We extend this geometric concept to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, specifically the space of square-integrable random variables \(H = L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\).

title: 68  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation-Part II
text:
68.1 Background: Hilbert Space Projections
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) be a probability space. The space \(H = L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) equipped with the inner product \[\langle X, Y \rangle = \mathbb{E}[XY]\] and induced norm \(\|X\|_{L^2} = \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X^2]}\) is a Hilbert space.
For any closed subspace \(K \subseteq H\), the Orthogonal Projection Theorem guarantees the existence of a unique linear operator \(P_K: H \to K\) such that for every \(X \in H\):

title: 68  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation-Part II
text:
68.4 Geometric Intuition

\(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) is the \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable random variable closest to \(X\) in \(L^2\): \[
\|X - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\|_{L^2} = \min_{Y \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)} \|X - Y\|_{L^2}.
\] In information-theoretic terms, \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) is the “best guess” or best mean-squared estimation of \(X\) given only the information in \(\mathcal{G}\).
By the orthogonal projection property, the error \(X - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]=X - P_{L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)}(X)\) is orthogonal to all \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable random variables: \[
\begin{aligned}
&\langle X - P_{L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)}(X), Y \rangle = 0 \\
&\iff \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]) Y] = 0 \\
&\iff \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] Y] = \mathbb{E}[XY] ,
\end{aligned}
\] for all \(Y \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\).

title: 68  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation-Part II
text:
68.5 Concrete Example: Partition Sub-\(\sigma\)-field
Let \(\Omega = \{1, 2, 3\}\), \(\mathcal{F} = 2^{\Omega}\), and \(P\) be the uniform distribution \(P(\{i\}) = \frac{1}{3}\) for \(i \in \{1, 2, 3\}\).
Consider the sub-\(\sigma\)-field generated by the partition \(A_1 = \{1, 2\}\) and \(A_2 = \{3\}\): \[
\mathcal{G} = \sigma(\{1, 2\}, \{3\}) = \{ \emptyset, \{1, 2\}, \{3\}, \Omega \}.
\]
Any \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable function \(X\) must be constant on the atoms of \(\mathcal{G}\), meaning \(X(1) = X(2)\). Thus, \[
L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P) \cong \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} x \\ x \\ y \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid x, y \in \mathbb{R} \right\}.
\]
An orthogonal basis for this subspace under the standard inner product \(\mathbb{E}[XY] = \frac{1}{3}\sum_{i=1}^3 X(i)Y(i)\) is given by the indicator functions: \[
u_1 = \mathbb{1}_{\{1, 2\}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad u_2 = \mathbb{1}_{\{3\}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
For any random variable \(X = \begin{bmatrix} X(1) \\ X(2) \\ X(3) \end{bmatrix} \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), the projection onto \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\) is: \[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] = \frac{\mathbb{E}[X u_1]}{\|u_1\|_{L^2}^2} u_1 + \frac{\mathbb{E}[X u_2]}{\|u_2\|_{L^2}^2} u_2 = \frac{\mathbb{E}[X \mathbb{1}_{\{1, 2\}}]}{P(\{1, 2\})} \mathbb{1}_{\{1, 2\}} + \frac{\mathbb{E}[X \mathbb{1}_{\{3\}}]}{P(\{3\})} \mathbb{1}_{\{3\}}.
\]
Evaluating the components explicitly: \[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X](1) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X](2) = \frac{X(1) + X(2)}{2}, \quad \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X](3) = X(3).
\]

title: 28  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation - II
text:
36.1 Proof of (1) Monotonicity:
Let \(Z = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[Y - X] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[Y] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\), where the equality holds by linearity of \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}\). We wish to show \(Z \ge 0\) a.s.
Define the “negative part” event \(B = \{Z < 0\}\). Since \(Z\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, \(B \in \mathcal{G}\), so \(\mathbb{1}_B \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\).
Step 1 (averaging forces non-negativity). Apply the averaging property of \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[Y-X]\) with test function \(\mathbb{1}_B\): \[
\mathbb{E}[Z \mathbb{1}_B] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[Y - X] \cdot \mathbb{1}_B] = \mathbb{E}[(Y - X) \cdot \mathbb{1}_B] \ge 0,
\] where the final inequality uses \(Y - X \ge 0\) a.s.
Step 2 (definition of \(B\) forces non-positivity). On \(B = \{Z < 0\}\) we have \(Z < 0\), and off \(B\) the factor \(\mathbb{1}_B = 0\). Hence \(Z \mathbb{1}_B \le 0\) everywhere, so: \[\mathbb{E}[Z \mathbb{1}_B] \le 0.\]
Step 3 (conclude \(P(B) = 0\)). Steps 1 and 2 together give \(\mathbb{E}[Z \mathbb{1}_B] = 0\). Since \(-Z \mathbb{1}_B \ge 0\) pointwise and has expectation zero, a non-negative random variable with zero expectation must vanish a.s.: \[-Z \mathbb{1}_B = 0 \quad \text{a.s.}\] But on \(B\), \(-Z \mathbb{1}_B = -Z > 0\). Therefore \(P(B) = P(Z < 0) = 0\), so \(Z \ge 0\) a.s., i.e. \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[Y] \ge \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) a.s. \(\blacksquare\)

title: 28  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation - II
text:
36.2 Proof of (2) Triangle Inequality:
Note that \(X \le |X|\) and \(-X \le |X|\) a.s.
By Monotonicity (1): \[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \le \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[|X|] \quad \text{and} \quad -\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[-X] \le \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[|X|]\] Combining both yields \(|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]| \le \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[|X|]\) a.s.
If \(|X| \le M\) a.s., then \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[|X|] \le \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[M] = M\) a.s. \(\blacksquare\)

title: 28  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation - II
28  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation - II
text:
36.4 Proof of (5) Tower Property:
Let \(\mathcal{H} \subseteq \mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\).
For any \(Z \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{H})\), since \(\mathcal{H} \subseteq \mathcal{G}\), we also have \(Z \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\).
Using the averaging property at level \(\mathcal{H}\), then level \(\mathcal{G}\): \[\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]] Z\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] Z\right] = \mathbb{E}[X Z] = \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X] Z\right]\] By uniqueness of the conditional expectation onto \(\mathcal{H}\), we conclude: \[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X] \quad \text{a.s.}\] For the second equality, note that \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X]\) is \(\mathcal{H}\)-measurable, hence \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable (since \(\mathcal{H} \subseteq \mathcal{G}\)). More generally, any \(W \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[W] = W\) a.s.: indeed, \(W\) itself satisfies the averaging characterization trivially, since \(\mathbb{E}[W \cdot Z] = \mathbb{E}[W \cdot Z]\) for all \(Z \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\), so uniqueness (Theorem 34.1) forces \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[W] = W\). Applying this with \(W = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X]\) gives \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X]] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X]\) a.s. \(\blacksquare\)

title: 72  Lecture 33.1: Probability Kernels-Part 1
text:
72.1 Introduction to Probability Kernels
In this lecture, we study probability kernels, which are a generalization of conditional distributions. We will define probability kernels, discuss their measurability and integration properties, and construct the semi-direct product measure \(\mu \otimes Q\) associated with a probability kernel \(Q\) and a probability measure \(\mu\). We will also establish a generalized Fubini’s theorem for integration with respect to \(\mu \otimes Q\).
Recall that if a random vector \((X, Y)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^k\) possesses a joint probability density \(f_{X,Y}(x, y)\), then for any \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^k)\), where \(\mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^k)\) is the space of bounded, Borel-measurable functions on \(\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^k\), we have \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X = x] = \int_{\mathbb{R}^k} f(x, y) f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) \, dy,
\] where the conditional density is given by \(f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x, y)}{f_X(x)}\) whenever \(f_X(x) > 0\).
That is, for each fixed \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\), we can define a probability measure \(Q_x\) on \((\mathbb{R}^k, \mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}^k})\) via \[
Q_x(B) = \int_B f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) \, dy.
\] Then \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X = x] = \int_{\mathbb{R}^k} f(x, y) \, Q_x(dy).
\] The family \(\{Q_x\}_{x \in \mathbb{R}^d}\) provides a concrete instance of a conditional probability distribution or probability kernel.

title: 69  Lecture 32.1: Conditioning as Partial Integration
text:
69.1 The Averaging Property as the Primary Workhorse
In this lecture, we explore the concept of conditional expectation as a form of partial integration in the context of product probability spaces. We will see how conditioning on a sub-\(\sigma\)-field can be interpreted as integrating out certain variables while retaining measurability with respect to others.
In measure-theoretic probability, the Averaging Property serves as the central operational characterization of conditional expectation.
crumbs: 69  Lecture 32.1: Conditioning as Partial Integration

title: 69  Lecture 32.1: Conditioning as Partial Integration
text:
69.2 Example 1.0 (Averaging Property in Action)
Let \(X \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\). Consider \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[X]\). By definition, \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[X]\) is the unique \(\mathcal{F}\)-measurable random variable satisfying: \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[X] Y] = \mathbb{E}[XY] \quad \forall Y \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{F}).
\] Since \(\mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) contains all bounded \(\mathcal{F}\)-measurable random variables, we can take \(Y = \mathbb{1}_A\) for any \(A \in \mathcal{F}\), yielding: \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[X] \mathbb{1}_A] = \mathbb{E}[X \mathbb{1}_A] \quad \forall A \in \mathcal{F}.
\] This is precisely the defining property of \(X\) itself, so we conclude: \[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[X] = X \quad \text{a.s.}
\]
For uniqueness, if \(Z \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) also satisfies the averaging property, then \(\mathbb{E}[(Z - X) Y] = 0\) , where \(Y\in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{F})\). Taking \(Y = \text{sign}(Z - X) \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\{|Z - X| \leq n\}}\) gives \[
0=\mathbb{E}[(Z - X) Y] = \mathbb{E}[|Z - X| \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\{|Z - X| \leq n\}}] \to \mathbb{E}[|Z - X|],
\] by the Dominated Convergence Theorem (DCT). Thus, \(Z = X\) a.s., proving uniqueness.
crumbs: 69  Lecture 32.1: Conditioning as Partial Integration

title: 69  Lecture 32.1: Conditioning as Partial Integration
text:
69.3 Example 1.1 (Trivial/Constant Case)
If \(X\) is already \(\mathcal{F}\)-measurable and we condition on the trivial \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{G} = \{\emptyset, \Omega\}\), then any \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable function must be constant almost surely: \[
L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P) = \{ c \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\Omega} \mid c \in \mathbb{R} \}.
\] Thus any \(\mathcal G\)-measurable random variable must be constant almost surely. Then, for some constant \(c\in\mathbb R\), \(\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]=c\) \(a.s.\) Now take \(Y=1_{\Omega}\). The averaging property gives \[
\mathbb E[\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]] = \mathbb E[X].
\] Since \(\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]=c\) a.s., we have \(\mathbb E[\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]] = \mathbb E[c] = c\). Therefore, \(c=\mathbb E[X]\), and hence \[
\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]=\mathbb E[X] \qquad\text{a.s.}
\]
So the intuition is:

conditioning on \(\mathcal F\): you retain all information, so \(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]=X\);
conditioning on the trivial \(\sigma\)-field: you retain no information, so the conditional expectation must be a constant, and that constant is chosen to preserve the unconditional mean: \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid\{\emptyset,\Omega\}]=\mathbb{E}[X]\).
crumbs: 69  Lecture 32.1: Conditioning as Partial Integration

title: 69  Lecture 32.1: Conditioning as Partial Integration
text:
69.4 Example 1.2 (Total Expectation Law)
Setting \(Y = \mathbb{1}_{\Omega} \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\) in the averaging property for any arbitrary sub-\(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{G}\) recovers the Law of Total Expectation: \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]] = \mathbb{E}[X].
\] This reflects the inner product identity \(\langle P_K(X), \mathbb{1} \rangle = \langle X, \mathbb{1} \rangle\) when \(\mathbb{1} \in K\) by self-adjointness of the orthogonal projection \(P_K\).
crumbs: 69  Lecture 32.1: Conditioning as Partial Integration

title: 69  Lecture 32.1: Conditioning as Partial Integration
text:
69.7 Product Space Setup
Let \((\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1, P_1)\) and \((\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2, P_2)\) be two probability spaces.
Define the product probability space: \[
\Omega = \Omega_1 \times \Omega_2, \quad \mathcal{F} = \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2, \quad P = P_1 \otimes P_2.
\] Consider the sub-\(\sigma\)-field generated by events in the first coordinate: \[
\mathcal{G} = \{ A_1 \times \Omega_2 \mid A_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1 \}.
\] Notice that \(\mathcal{G}\) contains information only about \(\omega_1 \in \Omega_1\), leaving \(\omega_2 \in \Omega_2\) unobserved.
crumbs: 69  Lecture 32.1: Conditioning as Partial Integration

title: 69  Lecture 32.1: Conditioning as Partial Integration
text:
69.8 Derivation of \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) as Partial Integration
Let \(X \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), where \(X = X(\omega_1, \omega_2)\). We seek a \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable random variable \(Z(\omega_1, \omega_2) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X](\omega_1, \omega_2)\).
Since \(Z\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, \(Z\) must depend only on the first component \(\omega_1\); that is, \(Z(\omega_1, \omega_2) = Z(\omega_1)\).
Using Lemma 69.1, \(Z(\omega_1)\) is uniquely determined by testing against set indicators \(B = A_1 \times \Omega_2 \in \mathcal{G}\) for arbitrary \(A_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1\): \[
\mathbb{E}[Z \mathbb{1}_{A_1 \times \Omega_2}] = \mathbb{E}[X \mathbb{1}_{A_1 \times \Omega_2}].
\]
Evaluating the left-hand side using Fubini’s Theorem: \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[Z \mathbb{1}_{A_1 \times \Omega_2}] &= \int_{\Omega_1} \int_{\Omega_2} Z(\omega_1) \mathbb{1}_{A_1}(\omega_1) \, dP_2(\omega_2) dP_1(\omega_1) \\
&= \int_{A_1} Z(\omega_1) \, dP_1(\omega_1).
\end{align*}
\]
Evaluating the right-hand side using Fubini’s Theorem: \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[X \mathbb{1}_{A_1 \times \Omega_2}] &= \int_{\Omega_1} \int_{\Omega_2} X(\omega_1, \omega_2) \mathbb{1}_{A_1}(\omega_1) \, dP_2(\omega_2) dP_1(\omega_1) \\
&= \int_{A_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} X(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, dP_2(\omega_2) \right) dP_1(\omega_1)
\end{align*}
\]
Equating the two integral representations for all \(A_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1\): \[
\int_{A_1} Z(\omega_1) \, dP_1(\omega_1) = \int_{A_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} X(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, dP_2(\omega_2) \right) dP_1(\omega_1) \quad \forall A_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1.
\]
Since this equality holds for all \(A_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1\), the integrands must agree \(P_1\)-almost surely: \[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X](\omega_1, \omega_2) = Z(\omega_1) = \int_{\Omega_2} X(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, dP_2(\omega_2) \quad \text{a.s.}\]

Key takeaway: \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) integrates out the unobserved degrees of freedom (\(\omega_2\)) while holding the observed structure (\(\omega_1\)) fixed.

71.1 Conditional Expectation and Independence
The conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\) represents the “best guess” or optimal \(L^2\) projection of \(X\) given the information contained in the sub-\(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{G}\). A natural question arises: What if \(\mathcal{G}\) contains no information about \(X\)?

title: 73  Lecture 33.2: Regular Conditional Distributions
text:
73.1 Probability Kernels and Conditional Expectation
In this lecture, we define regular conditional distributions (RCDs), which provide a rigorous framework for conditioning on random variables. We explore the relationship between RCDs and probability kernels, and we discuss the existence and uniqueness of RCDs in various settings.
Probability kernels provide a powerful general framework for evaluating conditional expectations of joint functions \(\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X]\). The following theorem shows that if the joint distribution of \((X,Y)\) can be disintegrated into a product measure \(\mu_X \otimes Q\), then the conditional expectation can be computed using the kernel \(Q\).

title: 73  Lecture 33.2: Regular Conditional Distributions
text:
73.4 Case 1: Absolutely Continuous Distributions (Radon-Nikodym Construction)

Example 73.2 (RCD for Absolutely Continuous Measures) Let \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1, \nu_1)\) and \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2, \nu_2)\) be \(\sigma\)-finite measure spaces. Let \((X, Y)\) have joint distribution \(\mu_{(X,Y)} \ll \nu_1 \otimes \nu_2\) with joint density \(f_{X,Y} = \frac{d\mu_{(X,Y)}}{d(\nu_1 \otimes \nu_2)}\).
Define the marginal density \(f_X(x) = \int_{S_2} f_{X,Y}(x, y) \, \nu_2(dy)\) so that \(d\mu_X = f_X \, d\nu_1\). Define the conditional density: \[
f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) := \begin{cases}
\dfrac{f_{X,Y}(x, y)}{f_X(x)} & \text{if } f_X(x) > 0, \\[8pt]
f_0(y) & \text{if } f_X(x) = 0,
\end{cases}
\] where \(f_0(y)\) is any arbitrary probability density on \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2, \nu_2)\).
Then the mapping \[
Q(x, B) := \int_B f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) \, \nu_2(dy)
\tag{73.5}\] is a Regular Conditional Distribution of \(Y\) given \(X\).


Proof. We verify \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes Q\) by checking on measurable rectangles \(A \times B \in \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\) (which generate \(\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\), so equality on rectangles implies equality on the whole product \(\sigma\)-algebra by Dynkin’s theorem): \[
\begin{aligned}
(\mu_X \otimes Q)(A \times B)
&= \int_A Q(x, B) \, \mu_X(dx) \\
&= \int_A Q(x, B) \, f_X(x) \, \nu_1(dx) \\
&= \int_A \left( \int_B f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) \, \nu_2(dy) \right) f_X(x) \, \nu_1(dx).
\end{aligned}
\] On the set \(\{x : f_X(x) > 0\}\), substituting \(f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}\) gives \(f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) \cdot f_X(x) = f_{X,Y}(x,y)\). On the set \(\{x : f_X(x) = 0\}\), \(f_X(x) = \int_{S_2} f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, \nu_2(dy) = 0\) implies \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 0\) for \(\nu_2\)-a.e. \(y\), so both sides contribute zero. Hence: \[
(\mu_X \otimes Q)(A \times B) = \int_A \int_B f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, \nu_2(dy) \, \nu_1(dx) = \mu_{(X,Y)}(A \times B),
\] where the last equality uses the Fubini–Tonelli theorem (since \(f_{X,Y} \ge 0\)) and the fact that \(f_{X,Y}\) is the joint density of \((X,Y)\). Thus \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes Q\), and by Proposition 73.1, \(Q\) is an RCD of \(Y\) given \(X\).

title: 73  Lecture 33.2: Regular Conditional Distributions
text:
73.5 Case 2: Discrete Distributions

Example 73.3 (RCD for Discrete Random Variables) Let \(Y\) be a discrete random variable taking values in a countable set \(S_2 = \{y_1, y_2, \dots\} \subset \mathbb{R}\). For \(x \in S_1\) where \(\mathbb{P}(X = x) > 0\), define the point probabilities: \[
Q(x, \{y\}) = \mathbb{P}(Y = y \mid X = x) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(X = x, Y = y)}{\mathbb{P}(X = x)}.
\] Then for any \(B \in \mathcal{B}_2\): \[
Q(x, B) = \sum_{y \in B \cap S_2} \mathbb{P}(Y = y \mid X = x).
\] For \(x\) where \(\mathbb{P}(X = x) = 0\), set \(Q(x, \cdot)\) to be any fixed probability measure on \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\). Evaluating this kernel at \(X\) yields: \[
\mathbb{P}(Y \in B \mid X) = Q(X, B) = \sum_{y \in B \cap S_2} Q(X, \{y\}) \quad \text{a.s.}
\]


Proof. We verify \(Q\) is an RCD by checking \(\mathbb{P}(Y \in B \mid X) = Q(X, B)\) a.s. for each \(B \in \mathcal{B}_2\). Since \(Y\) takes values in the countable set \(S_2\), we have \(\mathbb{P}(X = x) > 0\) for at most countably many \(x\). For any such \(x\): \[
\begin{align*}
Q(x, B)
&= \sum_{y \in B \cap S_2} Q(x, \{y\})\\
&= \sum_{y \in B \cap S_2} \frac{\mathbb{P}(X = x,\, Y = y)}{\mathbb{P}(X = x)}\\
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}(X = x,\, Y \in B)}{\mathbb{P}(X = x)}\\
&= \mathbb{P}(Y \in B \mid X = x),
\end{align*}
\] where the third equality uses countable additivity (the events \(\{Y = y\}\) for \(y \in B \cap S_2\) are pairwise disjoint). For \(x\) with \(\mathbb{P}(X = x) = 0\), the value of \(Q(x, \cdot)\) does not affect any a.s. statement since \(\mathbb{P}(X = x) = 0\). Hence \(Q(X, B) = \mathbb{P}(Y \in B \mid X)\) a.s., so \(Q\) is an RCD of \(Y\) given \(X\).







NoteProcedural Order in Discrete Conditioning



When evaluating discrete RCD expressions in practice:

First compute the two-variable deterministic function \(Q(x, \{y\}) = \mathbb{P}(Y = y \mid X = x)\) on \(\{x: \mathbb{P}(X=x) > 0\}\).
Then evaluate \(Q(X, \{y\})\) at the random variable \(X\).
Sum over \(y \in B \cap S_2\) to obtain \(\mathbb{P}(Y \in B \mid X) = \sum_{y \in B \cap S_2} Q(X, \{y\})\) a.s.

title: 74  Lecture 34.1: Probability Kernels-Part II
text:
74.6 Takeaways

Markov generators encode kernels. Every probability kernel \(Q\) from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) induces a bounded linear operator \(L_Q: \mathcal{B}_b(S_2) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S_1)\), \((L_Q f)(x) = \int f \, dQ(x, \cdot)\), satisfying four structural properties: linearity, normalization (\(L_Q \mathbb{I} = \mathbb{I}\)), positivity (\(f \ge 0 \Rightarrow L_Q f \ge 0\)), and continuity under bounded pointwise convergence (via DCT). These properties imply the contraction bound \(\|L_Q\|_\infty \le 1\).
Representation theorem (duality). The four properties characterize Markov generators completely. Every operator \(L: \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) satisfying them arises from a unique probability kernel, recovered by the formula \(Q(x, B) = (L \mathbb{I}_B)(x)\). The countable additivity of \(Q(x, \cdot)\) follows from the bounded-convergence property of \(L\) applied to the partial sums \(\sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb{I}_{B_k} \uparrow \mathbb{I}_B\).
Composition of kernels. The product \(Q = Q_1 Q_2\) is the unique kernel whose generator is \(L_Q = L_{Q_1} \circ L_{Q_2}\). Explicitly, \((Q_1 Q_2)(x, B) = \int_S Q_2(y, B) \, Q_1(x, dy)\). For countable \(S\) this reduces to matrix multiplication: \((Q_1 Q_2)(x, z) = \sum_{y \in S} Q_1(x, y) \, Q_2(y, z)\).
Path-space distributions. Given an initial distribution \(\nu \in \mathcal{P}(S_0)\) and transition kernels \(Q_k\) from \(S_{k-1}\) to \(S_k\) (\(k = 1, \dots, n\)), there exists a unique probability measure \(\mu\) on the product space \(S_0 \times \cdots \times S_n\) satisfying the iterated-integral formula \(\int f \, d\mu = \int_{S_0} \cdots \int_{S_n} f(x_0, \dots, x_n) \, Q_n(x_{n-1}, dx_n) \cdots Q_1(x_0, dx_1) \, \nu(dx_0)\). This provides the foundation for constructing finite-dimensional distributions of Markov processes.

title: 74  Lecture 34.1: Probability Kernels-Part II
text:
74.2 Axiomatic Properties of Markov Operators
In the following proposition, we summarize the structural properties of the Markov operator \(L_Q\) associated with a probability kernel \(Q\).

Proposition 74.1 (Properties of the Associated Markov Operator) Let \(Q\) be a probability kernel from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\). The associated Markov operator \(L_Q: \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) satisfies the following structural properties:

Linearity: \(L_Q(\alpha f + \beta g) = \alpha L_Q(f) + \beta L_Q(g)\) for all \(\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(f, g \in \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\).
Preservation of Constants (Normalization): \(L_Q(\mathbb{I}_{S_2}) = \mathbb{I}_{S_1}\).
Positivity (Monotonicity): If \(f \ge 0\), then \(L_Q(f) \ge 0\). Consequently, if \(f \le g\), then \(L_Q(f) \le L_Q(g)\).
Boundedly Monotone / Pointwise Continuity: If \(f_n \to f\) boundedly (i.e., \(f_n(y) \to f(y)\) pointwise and \(\sup_n \|f_n\|_\infty < \infty\)), then \(L_Q f_n \to L_Q f\) boundedly on \(S_1\).



Proof (Proof of Proposition 74.1). 

Linearity: Follows directly from the linearity of integration with respect to the integrand: \[
\begin{aligned}
(L_Q(\alpha f + \beta g))(x) &= \int_{S_2} (\alpha f(y) + \beta g(y)) \, Q(x, dy) \\
&= \alpha (L_Q f)(x) + \beta (L_Q g)(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Normalization: Since \(Q(x, \cdot)\) is a probability measure for each \(x \in S_1\): \[
(L_Q \mathbb{I}_{S_2})(x) = \int_{S_2} 1 \, Q(x, dy) = Q(x, S_2) = 1 = \mathbb{I}_{S_1}(x) \quad \forall x \in S_1.
\]
Positivity: If \(f(y) \ge 0\) for all \(y \in S_2\), integrating a non-negative function against a non-negative probability measure yields \((L_Q f)(x) = \int_{S_2} f(y) \, Q(x, dy) \ge 0\).
Boundedly Monotone Continuity: Suppose \(f_n \to f\) pointwise with \(\|f_n\|_\infty \le M < \infty\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). For each fixed \(x \in S_1\), we have \(|f_n(y)| \le M\) for all \(y \in S_2\), and therefore \[
\int_{S_2} M \, Q(x, dy) = M \, Q(x, S_2) = M < \infty.
\] Hence the constant function \(M\) is integrable with respect to the probability measure \(Q(x,\cdot)\), so the Dominated Convergence Theorem applies and yields \[
(L_Q f_n)(x) = \int_{S_2} f_n(y) \, Q(x, dy) \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} \int_{S_2} f(y) \, Q(x, dy) = (L_Q f)(x).
\] Since this holds for every \(x \in S_1\), the convergence is pointwise on \(S_1\). Moreover, \[
\|L_Q f_n\|_\infty \le \|f_n\|_\infty \le M,
\] so the convergence \(L_Q f_n \to L_Q f\) is bounded.



Remark 74.1 (Implication of Positivity). If a linear operator \(L: \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) satisfies positivity (\(f \ge 0 \implies L f \ge 0\)) and normalization (\(L \mathbb{I} = \mathbb{I}\)), then for any \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\): \[
-|f| \le f \le |f| \implies -L(|f|) \le L f \le L(|f|) \implies |L f| \le L(|f|).
\] Because \(|f| \le \|f\|_\infty \mathbb{I}_{S_2}\), monotonicity implies: \[
|L f| \le L(|f|) \le L(\|f\|_\infty \mathbb{I}_{S_2}) = \|f\|_\infty L(\mathbb{I}_{S_2}) = \|f\|_\infty \mathbb{I}_{S_1}.
\] Hence \(\|L f\|_\infty \le \|f\|_\infty\) for every \(f\), so \(\|L\|_\infty \le 1\). Since \(L\mathbb{I}_{S_2} = \mathbb{I}_{S_1}\), we also have \(\|L\|_\infty = 1\). Thus every positive normalized linear operator is automatically a contraction.

title: 74  Lecture 34.1: Probability Kernels-Part II
section: 74.3 Duality: Bijection Between Probability Kernels and Markov Operators
text:
74.3 Duality: Bijection Between Probability Kernels and Markov Operators
In the next proposition, we show that the mapping \(Q \mapsto L_Q\) is a bijection between probability kernels and Markov operators. This is a duality result: every probability kernel defines a Markov operator, and conversely, every Markov operator arises from a unique probability kernel.

Proposition 74.2 (Representation Theorem for Markov Operators) Let \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be a measurable space. Let \(L: \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) be an operator satisfying:

\(L\) is linear.
\(L(\mathbb{I}_S) = \mathbb{I}_S\).
\(L f \ge 0\) whenever \(f \ge 0\).
If \(f_n \to f\) boundedly in \(\mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\), then \(L f_n \to L f\) boundedly in \(\mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\).

Then there exists a unique probability kernel \(Q\) over \((S, \mathcal{B})\) such that \(L = L_Q\). Explicitly, \(Q\) is given by: \[
Q(x, B) := (L \mathbb{I}_B)(x) \quad \forall x \in S, \; B \in \mathcal{B}.
\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 74.2). We construct \(Q(x, B) := (L \mathbb{I}_B)(x)\) and check the defining properties of a probability kernel:

Measurability: For every fixed \(B \in \mathcal{B}\), \(\mathbb{I}_B \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\). By definition of the domain/codomain of \(L\), \(Q(\cdot, B) = L(\mathbb{I}_B)(\cdot) \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\), so \(x \mapsto Q(x, B)\) is \(\mathcal{B}\)-measurable.
Probability Measure Properties for \(Q(x, \cdot)\):

Normalization: \(Q(x, S) = (L \mathbb{I}_S)(x) = 1\) by Property 1.
Non-negativity: For any \(B \in \mathcal{B}\), \(\mathbb{I}_B \ge 0 \implies Q(x, B) = (L \mathbb{I}_B)(x) \ge 0\) by Property 2.
Countable Additivity: Let \((B_k)_{k=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{B}\) be pairwise disjoint sets, and let \(B = \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty B_k\). Define \(f_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb{I}_{B_k} = \mathbb{I}_{\bigcup_{k=1}^n B_k}\). Then \(f_n \uparrow \mathbb{I}_B\) boundedly as \(n \to \infty\). By Property 3 (boundedly monotone continuity) and linearity of \(L\): \[
\begin{align*}
Q(x, B) &= (L \mathbb{I}_B)(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} (L f_n)(x)\\
& = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k=1}^n (L \mathbb{I}_{B_k})(x) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty Q(x, B_k) \quad \forall x \in S.
\end{align*}
\] Thus \(Q(x, \cdot)\) is a probability measure on \((S, \mathcal{B})\) for every fixed \(x \in S\).

Verification of \(L = L_Q\): We need to show \(L f = L_Q f = \int_S f(y) \, Q(\cdot, dy)\) for all \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\).

For indicator functions \(f = \mathbb{I}_B\): \(\int_S \mathbb{I}_B(y) \, Q(x, dy) = Q(x, B) = (L \mathbb{I}_B)(x)\).
By linearity, \(L f = L_Q f\) for all simple functions \(f = \sum_{i=1}^m c_i \mathbb{I}_{B_i}\).
For an arbitrary bounded measurable \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\), there exists a sequence of simple functions \(f_n\) such that \(f_n \to f\) boundedly. Applying Property 3 to both \(L\) and \(L_Q\) yields \(L f = \lim_{n \to \infty} L f_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} L_Q f_n = L_Q f\).



Thus, the mapping \(Q \mapsto L_Q\) defines a bijection between probability kernels and Markov operators: \[
\begin{align*}
&Q \mapsto L(f) = \int_S f(y) \, Q(\cdot, dy).\\
& L \mapsto Q(\cdot, B) = (L \mathbb{I}_B)(\cdot).
\end{align*}
\]

title: 75  Lecture 34.2: Random Dynamics
text:
75.1 Motivation: Dynamical Systems
Dynamical systems can generally be classified into two broad (and often interwoven) categories: discrete-time and continuous-time systems.

title: 75  Lecture 34.2: Random Dynamics
text:
75.2 Discrete Dynamics
Let \(S\) be a state space and let \(x_0 \in S\) be an initial state. Consider a function \(f: S \to S\). We study the asymptotic and qualitative behavior of the deterministic sequence \(\{x_n\}_{n \ge 0}\) defined recursively by: \[
x_{n+1} = f(x_n), \quad n \ge 0.
\tag{75.1}\]

title: 75  Lecture 34.2: Random Dynamics
text:
75.3 Continuous Dynamics
Let \(S\) be a state space (typically \(S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) or a smooth manifold \(M\)) and let \(x_0 \in S\). Let \(f: S \to T S\) be a vector field on \(S\). We study the behavior of the continuous trajectory \(x(t)\) governed by the differential equation: \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}x(t)}{\mathrm{d}t} = f(x(t)), \quad t \ge 0, \quad x(0) = x_0.
\tag{75.2}\]
In both deterministic settings, if the initial state \(x_0\) and the evolution function \(f\) are known with perfect precision, the full trajectory of the system is uniquely determined for all time.
However, in realistic physical, economic, or biological modeling, systems are subject to ambient noise, random environmental fluctuations, or measurement errors. To incorporate these effects, we consider dynamical systems driven by stochastic perturbations.

title: 75  Lecture 34.2: Random Dynamics
section: 75.4 A Rigorous Model for Noisy (Discrete) Dynamics
text:
75.4 A Rigorous Model for Noisy (Discrete) Dynamics
To model noisy discrete dynamics, we wish to iterate state transitions of the form \(x_{n+1} = f_n(x_n)\), where each \(f_n: S \to S\) is a random function. To make this mathematically precise and analytically tractable, we formulate the system within a measure-theoretic framework.

Definition 75.1 (Random Dynamical System / Iterated Function System) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space. Consider:

A state space \((S, \mathcal{B}_S)\), where \(S\) is a measurable space equipped with its \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}_S\) (typically a Polish space endowed with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra).
A noise state space \((R, \mathcal{G})\), equipped with its \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{G}\).
An independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sequence of random elements \(\{\xi_n\}_{n \ge 0}\) defined on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) taking values in \((R, \mathcal{G})\), so that \(\xi_n: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (R, \mathcal{G})\) for all \(n \ge 0\).
A jointly measurable transition map \(f: S \times R \to S\).

Given an initial random variable \(X_0: \Omega \to S\) (measurable with respect to \(\mathcal{B}_S\)) independent of the sequence \(\{\xi_n\}_{n \ge 0}\), the random dynamical system \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 0}\) is defined recursively by: \[
X_{n+1} = f(X_n, \xi_n), \quad n \ge 0.
\tag{75.3}\]

title: 75  Lecture 34.2: Random Dynamics
text:
75.5 Unfolding and Measurability Properties
By induction, the random state \(X_n\) at step \(n \ge 1\) can be expressed directly in terms of the initial state \(X_0\) and the sequence of noise variables \(\xi_0, \xi_1, \dots, \xi_{n-1}\).
Let \(F_n: S \times R^n \to S\) be the \(n\)-fold iterated composition maps defined recursively as follows:

\(F_1(x, y_0) := f(x, y_0)\),
\(F_2(x, y_0, y_1) := f(f(x, y_0), y_1)\),
\(F_n(x, y_0, \dots, y_{n-1}) := f(F_{n-1}(x, y_0, \dots, y_{n-2}), y_{n-1})\) for \(n \ge 2\).

By standard measure theory, since \(f\) is jointly measurable, each \(F_n: (S \times R^n, \mathcal{B}_S \otimes \mathcal{G}^{\otimes n}) \to (S, \mathcal{B}_S)\) is a measurable function.
Consequently, for every \(n \ge 1\), we can write: \[
X_n = F_n(X_0, \xi_0, \xi_1, \dots, \xi_{n-1}).
\tag{75.4}\]

title: 75  Lecture 34.2: Random Dynamics
text:
75.6 Filtration and Markov Property
Let \(\mathcal{F}_n\) denote the natural filtration generated by the state history up to time \(n \ge 0\): \[
\mathcal{F}_n := \sigma(X_0, X_1, \dots, X_n).
\tag{75.5}\]
Because each \(X_j = F_j(X_0, \xi_0, \dots, \xi_{j-1})\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_0, \xi_0, \dots, \xi_{j-1})\) by Equation 75.4, we have \[
\sigma(X_j) \subseteq \sigma(X_0, \xi_0, \dots, \xi_{j-1}) \subseteq \sigma(X_0, \xi_0, \dots, \xi_{n-1})
\] for all \(0 \le j \le n\), and hence \[
\mathcal{F}_n = \sigma(X_0, X_1, \dots, X_n) \subseteq \sigma(X_0, \xi_0, \dots, \xi_{n-1}).
\]

Lemma 75.1 (Independence of Future Noise) For every \(n \ge 0\), the random driver \(\xi_n\) is independent of the \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F}_n\).


Proof. By construction, \(\{\xi_k\}_{k \ge 0}\) is an i.i.d. sequence, and \(X_0\) is independent of \(\{\xi_k\}_{k \ge 0}\). Thus, the collection \((X_0, \xi_0, \dots, \xi_{n-1})\) is independent of \(\xi_n\). Since \(\mathcal{F}_n \subseteq \sigma(X_0, \xi_0, \dots, \xi_{n-1})\), it follows directly that \(\xi_n\) is independent of \(\mathcal{F}_n\).

Define \[
\mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}_S) := \{g:S \to \mathbb{R} : g \text{ is bounded and } \mathcal{B}_S\text{-measurable}\}.
\] When the underlying \(\sigma\)-algebra is clear, we write simply \(\mathcal{B}_b(S)\).

Definition 75.2 (Markov Transition Operator) For any \(x \in S\) and any measurable set \(A \in \mathcal{B}_S\), define \[
Q(x, A) := \mathbb{P}(f(x, \xi_0) \in A).
\tag{75.6}\] Because \(f\) is jointly measurable and \(\xi_0\) is a random element, for each fixed \(A \in \mathcal{B}_S\) the map \(x \mapsto Q(x,A)\) is \(\mathcal{B}_S\)-measurable, while for each fixed \(x \in S\), the set function \(A \mapsto Q(x,A)\) is a probability measure on \((S, \mathcal{B}_S)\). Thus \(Q\) is a probability kernel from \((S,\mathcal{B}_S)\) to itself.
For any \(g \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}_S)\), define the associated Markov operator \(L: \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}_S) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}_S)\) by: \[
(L g)(x) := \mathbb{E}[g(f(x, \xi_0))] = \int_S g(y) Q(x, \mathrm{d}y).
\tag{75.7}\]


Theorem 75.1 (Markov Property) Let \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 0}\) be the random dynamical system defined by Equation 75.3. Then \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 0}\) is a time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel \(Q(x, \cdot)\) and Markov operator \(L\).
Specifically, for any \(g \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}_S)\) and \(n \ge 0\): \[
\mathbb{E}[g(X_{n+1}) \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = \mathbb{E}[g(X_{n+1}) \mid X_n] = (L g)(X_n) \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{75.8}\]


Proof. Let \(g \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}_S)\). By definition of the process: \[
g(X_{n+1}) = g(f(X_n, \xi_n)) = (g \circ f)(X_n, \xi_n).
\] Since \(X_n\) is \(\mathcal{F}_n\)-measurable and \(\xi_n\) is independent of \(\mathcal{F}_n\) (by Lemma 75.1), we apply the standard freezing lemma for conditional expectations: if \(Z\) is \(\mathcal{F}\)-measurable and \(Y\) is independent of \(\mathcal{F}\), then for bounded measurable \(\phi\), \[
\mathbb{E}[\phi(Z,Y) \mid \mathcal{F}] = \psi(Z) \quad \text{a.s.},
\qquad \psi(z):=\mathbb{E}[\phi(z,Y)].
\] Here \(Z=X_n\), \(Y=\xi_n\), and \(\phi(z,y) = g(f(z,y))\). Therefore, \[
\mathbb{E}[g(X_{n+1}) \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = h(X_n) \quad \text{a.s.},
\] where \[
h(x) := \mathbb{E}[g(f(x,\xi_n))] = \mathbb{E}[g(f(x,\xi_0))] = (L g)(x),
\] using that \(\xi_n \stackrel{d}{=} \xi_0\) because \(\{\xi_k\}\) is i.i.d.
Because \((L g)(X_n)\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_n) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_n\), taking the conditional expectation with respect to \(\sigma(X_n)\) yields: \[
\mathbb{E}[g(X_{n+1}) \mid X_n] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[g(X_{n+1}) \mid \mathcal{F}_n] \mid X_n] = \mathbb{E}[(L g)(X_n) \mid X_n] = (L g)(X_n) \quad \text{a.s.}
\] This establishes Equation 75.8.

Taking the expectation on both sides of Equation 75.8, using the law of total expectation, yields: \[
\mathbb{E}[g(X_{n+1})] = \mathbb{E}[(L g)(X_n)].
\tag{75.9}\]
