text:
36.8 Summary of Transcriptions & Reconstructions

Explicit Rigor Added:

Stated precise measure spaces \(((S, \mathcal{B}_S)\) and \((R, \mathcal{G}))\) and measurability conditions for \(f\), \(X_0\), and \(\xi_n\).
Explicitly invoked the Freezing/Independence Lemma for conditional expectation when establishing \(\mathbb{E}[g(X_{n+1}) \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = (L g)(X_n)\).
Formally proved the iterated identity \(\mathbb{E}[g(X_n) \mid \mathcal{F}_k] = (L^{n-k} g)(X_k)\) using the tower property of conditional expectation.

Handwriting / Typo Corrections:

In the original handwritten notes, \(Q_{n+1}(x, \mathrm{d}y)\) and \(L_{n+1}\) were initially written with subscript \(n+1\); since \(\xi_n\) are i.i.d., the kernel \(Q(x, \cdot)\) and generator \(L\) are time-homogeneous. The notation was unified to \(Q\) and \(L\).
Corrected notation for the natural filtration \(\mathcal{F}_n = \sigma(X_0, \dots, X_n)\) and restored mathematical notation throughout.

title: 36  Lecture 34.2: Random Dynamics
text:
36.9 Items Requiring Verification

State Space Topology: The notes specify general measurable spaces \((S, \mathcal{B}_S)\) and \((R, \mathcal{G})\). If continuous state space dynamics (e.g., Feller properties or invariant measures) are considered in subsequent sections, assuming \(S\) is a Polish space with Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(S)\) would be recommended.

title: 76  Lecture 35.1: Stochastic Processes
text: 76.1 Mathematical Foundations of Stochastic Processes

title: 76  Lecture 35.1: Stochastic Processes
text:
Definition 76.1 (Stochastic Process) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space, and let \((S, \mathcal{B}_S)\) be a measurable space (referred to as the state space). Let \(T\) be an index set. When the process is time-indexed, \(T\) is typically equipped with an order \(\le\). Examples include:

\(\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\) or \(\mathbb{Z}_+\) (discrete time),
\([0, b]\) or \([0, \infty)\) (continuous time).

A stochastic process is a collection of random variables indexed by \(T\), denoted by: \[
\{X_t\}_{t \in T},
\] where for each \(t \in T\), \(X_t: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (S, \mathcal{B}_S)\) is a measurable mapping.

title: 76  Lecture 35.1: Stochastic Processes
text:
76.2 Finite-Dimensional Distributions
The fundamental finite-dimensional statistical behavior of a stochastic process is captured by its finite-dimensional distributions (f.d.d.s).

Definition 76.2 (Finite-Dimensional Distributions) For any nonempty finite subset \(A \subseteq T\), choose an enumeration \(A=\{t_1, t_2, \dots, t_n\}\). The finite-dimensional distribution associated with this ordered list is the joint probability measure \(\mu_A\) on \((S^n, \mathcal{B}_S^{\otimes n})\) defined by the law of \((X_{t_1},\dots,X_{t_n})\). If \(T\) is ordered, we use the increasing order on \(A\) by convention: \[
\begin{align*}
\mu_A &:= \mathrm{Law}(X_{t_1}, X_{t_2}, \dots, X_{t_n})\\
& = \mathbb{P} \circ (X_{t_1}, X_{t_2}, \dots, X_{t_n})^{-1}.
\end{align*}
\tag{76.1}\] Explicitly, for any measurable set \(B \in \mathcal{B}_S^{\otimes n}\): \[
\mu_A(B) = \mathbb{P}\left( (X_{t_1}, X_{t_2}, \dots, X_{t_n}) \in B \right).
\]


Remark 76.1 (Limitations of Finite-Dimensional Distributions). The finite-dimensional distributions of an existing process are consistent and uniquely determine its law on \((S^T, \bigotimes_{t\in T}\mathcal{B}_S)\), the product sigma-algebra generated by finite-coordinate cylinders. Conversely, an abstract consistent family of finite-dimensional distributions admits an extension under the hypotheses of the Kolmogorov Extension Theorem; for example, a standard Borel state space is a common sufficient setting. These distributions alone generally do not settle pathwise regularity, such as continuity or boundedness, when \(T\) is uncountable. Sample-path measurability also requires specified measurable or topological structures on the index and state spaces. Appropriate regularity assumptions, such as a càdlàg version in a suitable state space, can provide additional pathwise control.

title: 76  Lecture 35.1: Stochastic Processes
section: 76.3 Example: Sums of Independent Random Variables
text:
76.3 Example: Sums of Independent Random Variables
Consider \(T = \mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\). Let \(\{\xi_k\}_{k=1}^{\infty}\) be an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sequence of random vectors taking values in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), with common distribution \(\mu = \mathrm{Law}(\xi_1)\).
Define the process \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 0}\) by setting \(X_0 = 0\) and: \[
X_n := \sum_{k=1}^n \xi_k, \quad n \ge 1.
\tag{76.2}\]
For any finite sequence of time indices \(0 < n_1 < n_2 < \dots < n_m\), the joint law \(\mathrm{Law}(X_{n_1}, X_{n_2}, \dots, X_{n_m})\) can be explicitly derived via the joint distribution of independent increments: \[
(X_{n_1}, X_{n_2} - X_{n_1}, \dots, X_{n_m} - X_{n_{m-1}}).
\] For instance, the joint distribution of \((X_1, X_2, X_3)\) is completely determined by the independent components: \[
(X_1, X_2, X_3) = \left(\xi_1, \, \xi_1 + \xi_2, \, \xi_1 + \xi_2 + \xi_3 \right).
\] For any bounded measurable function \(g: (\mathbb{R}^d)^3 \to \mathbb{R}\): \[
\mathbb{E}[g(X_1, X_2, X_3)] = \int_{(\mathbb{R}^d)^3} g(y_1, y_1 + y_2, y_1 + y_2 + y_3) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y_1) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y_2) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(y_3).
\]
As seen in previous discussions on random dynamics, studying the joint asymptotic behavior of \((X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)\) as \(n \to \infty\) requires systematic conditional structure, leading directly to the concept of filtrations.

title: 76  Lecture 35.1: Stochastic Processes
text:
76.4 Filtrations and Adapted Processes

Definition 76.3 (Filtration and Filtered Probability Space) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space and \(T\) an ordered index set.

A filtration is an increasing family of \(\sigma\)-subalgebras of \(\mathcal{F}\), denoted by \(\mathbb{F} = \{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \in T}\), such that: \[
\mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t \subseteq \mathcal{F} \quad \text{for all } s, t \in T \text{ with } s \le t.
\tag{76.3}\]
A tuple \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \in T}, \mathbb{P})\) equipped with a filtration is called a filtered probability space.



Definition 76.4 (Adapted Process) A stochastic process \(\{X_t\}_{t \in T}\) taking values in \((S, \mathcal{B}_S)\) defined on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \in T}, \mathbb{P})\) is said to be adapted to the filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \in T}\) if, for every \(t \in T\), the random variable \(X_t\) is \(\mathcal{F}_t/\mathcal{B}_S\)-measurable: \[
\sigma(X_t) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t \quad \text{for all } t \in T.
\]


Example 76.1 (Natural Filtration) For any stochastic process \(\{X_t\}_{t \in T}\), its natural filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_t^X\}_{t \in T}\) is defined by: \[
\mathcal{F}_t^X := \sigma(X_s : s \le t, s \in T).
\tag{76.4}\]

By construction, \(\{X_t\}_{t \in T}\) is always trivially adapted to its natural filtration \(\mathcal{F}_t^X\).
Note that taking \(\mathcal{F}_t = \sigma(X_t)\) does not generally form a filtration because \(\sigma(X_s) \subseteq \sigma(X_t)\) does not necessarily hold for \(s \le t\).
When multiple processes are studied simultaneously, a larger, common background filtration \(\mathcal{F}_t\) containing information from all processes is used.

title: 76  Lecture 35.1: Stochastic Processes
section: 76.5 Markov Property for Sums of Independent Variables
text:
76.5 Markov Property for Sums of Independent Variables
Let \(\{\xi_k\}_{k=1}^{\infty}\) be i.i.d. \(\mathbb{R}^d\)-valued random vectors on a common probability space, and let \(X_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \xi_k\) with \(X_0 = 0\). Set \(\mathcal{F}_0 = \{\varnothing,\Omega\}\) and, for \(n\ge 1\), let \(\mathcal{F}_n = \sigma(\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n) = \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_n)\).
For any \(n \ge k \ge 0\) and any bounded Borel measurable function \(g: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\): \[
X_n = X_k + \sum_{j=k+1}^n \xi_j.
\]
Since \(X_k\) is \(\mathcal{F}_k\)-measurable and the sum \(\sum_{j=k+1}^n \xi_j\) is independent of \(\mathcal{F}_k\), the standard conditional-expectation identity for a measurable function of an \(\mathcal{F}_k\)-measurable variable and an independent random vector gives: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[g(X_n) \mid \mathcal{F}_k] &= \mathbb{E}\left[g\left(X_k + \sum_{j=k+1}^n \xi_j\right) \,\middle|\, \mathcal{F}_k\right] \\
&= h(X_k) \quad \text{a.s.},
\end{aligned}
\] where \(h(a) := \mathbb{E}\left[g\left(a + \sum_{j=k+1}^n \xi_j\right)\right]\).
Furthermore, since \(h(X_k)\) is \(\sigma(X_k)\)-measurable, the tower property (using \(\sigma(X_k) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_k\)) gives: \[
\mathbb{E}[g(X_n) \mid X_k] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[g(X_n) \mid \mathcal{F}_k] \mid X_k] = \mathbb{E}[h(X_k) \mid X_k] = h(X_k) \quad \text{a.s.}
\] Thus, we obtain the Markov property: \[
\mathbb{E}[g(X_n) \mid \mathcal{F}_k] = \mathbb{E}[g(X_n) \mid X_k] \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{76.5}\]

This process fits precisely into the random dynamics framework \(X_{n+1} = f(X_n, \xi_{n+1})\) where \(f(x, y) = x + y\) and \(X_0 = 0\).

title: 76  Lecture 35.1: Stochastic Processes
text:
76.6 Special Case: Simple Random Walk

Definition 76.5 (Simple Random Walk) For an integer \(d\geq1\), let \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) denote the standard coordinate basis vectors of \(\mathbb R^d\). Suppose that \(\{\xi_k\}_{k\geq1}\) are i.i.d. random vectors taking values in \(\{\pm e_1,\ldots,\pm e_d\}\), with \[
\mathbb P(\xi_k=e_j) = \mathbb P(\xi_k=-e_j) = \frac{1}{2d}, \qquad j=1,\ldots,d.
\] Starting from \(X_0=0\), define \(X_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\xi_k\) for \(n\geq1\). The process \(\{X_n\}_{n\geq0}\) is called the simple random walk on \(\mathbb Z^d\).

title: 76  Lecture 35.1: Stochastic Processes
text:
76.7 Arrival, Counting, and Renewal Processes

Definition 76.6 (Arrival Process) On a common probability space, let \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 0}\) be nonnegative real-valued random variables satisfying \(X_0=0\) and, almost surely, \(X_n\le X_{n+1}\) for every \(n\ge 0\): \[
0 = X_0 \le X_1 \le X_2 \le \dots \le X_n \le \dots \quad \text{a.s.}
\] The sequence \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 0}\) is called an arrival process, where \(X_n\) represents the arrival time of the \(n\)-th event.


Definition 76.7 (Counting Process) Given an arrival process \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 0}\), suppose additionally that \(X_1>0\) a.s. and \(X_n\to\infty\) a.s. The associated finite-valued counting process \(\{N_t\}_{t \ge 0}\) is defined by: \[
N_t := \sup \{ n \ge 0 : X_n \le t \}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{I}_{\{X_n\leq t\}}, \quad t \ge 0.
\tag{76.6}\] \(N_t\) counts the total number of arrivals that have occurred up to and including time \(t\), and \(N_0=0\) a.s. Without the condition \(X_n\to\infty\) a.s., the same formula defines an extended-valued count that may be infinite. For every integer \(n\ge 1\), the duality relation is: \[
\{ N_t \ge n \} = \{ X_n \le t \}.
\tag{76.7}\]


For an integer \(n\ge 1\), the statement \(N_t\geq n\) means that at least \(n\) arrivals have occurred by time \(t\). Since \(X_n\) is the time of the \(n\)-th arrival, having at least \(n\) arrivals by time \(t\) means precisely that the \(n\)-th arrival has occurred by time \(t\). Therefore \[
N_t\geq n \iff X_n\leq t.
\]


Definition 76.8 (Inter-arrival Times and Renewal Process) For an arrival process \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 0}\), define the inter-arrival times \(\{\xi_n\}_{n \ge 1}\) by: \[
\xi_n := X_n - X_{n-1}, \quad n \ge 1.
\tag{76.8}\] Consequently, \(X_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \xi_k\).

If the inter-arrival times \(\{\xi_n\}_{n \ge 1}\) are i.i.d. finite, strictly positive random variables, then \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 0}\) is called a renewal process. In this case, \(X_n\to\infty\) a.s.: for some \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\mathbb{P}(\xi_1\ge\varepsilon)>0\), so independence and the second Borel–Cantelli lemma imply that infinitely many inter-arrival times are at least \(\varepsilon\).
The counting process \(\{N_t\}_{t \ge 0}\) associated with a renewal process is called a renewal counting process.
The homogeneous Poisson process of rate \(\lambda>0\) is the renewal counting process whose inter-arrival times are i.i.d. exponential random variables with rate \(\lambda\).

title: 37  Lecture 35.1: Stochastic Processes
text:
37.8 Summary of Transcriptions & Reconstructions

Explicit Rigor Added:

Rigorously formulated the definition of stochastic processes, probability spaces \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\), state spaces \((S, \mathcal{B}_S)\), and finite-dimensional distributions.
Formalized filtrations, adapted processes, and natural filtrations using standard measure-theoretic probability notation.
Proved the Markov property for sums of independent random variables using the Freezing/Independence Lemma for conditional expectations.
Rigorously stated the duality relation \(\{N_t \ge n\} = \{X_n \le t\}\) between arrival processes and counting processes.

Handwriting & Notation Clean-up:

Resolved notation for sequences \((\xi_k)_{k \ge 1}\) and partial sums \(X_n\).
Expanded initial abbreviations (e.g., “f.d. distributions”, “rv’s”, “iid”, “p.m.”) into complete, clear terminology.

title: 37  Lecture 35.1: Stochastic Processes
text:
37.9 Items Requiring Verification
Continuity of Paths for Continuous-Time Processes: When moving to continuous-time processes like the Poisson process \(\{N_t\}_{t \ge 0}\), paths are typically assumed to be right-continuous with left limits (cadlag). This path property will be formally introduced in subsequent lectures.

title: 77  Lecture 35.2: Poisson Process
text:
77.1 Review of the Exponential Distribution
The exponential distribution serves as the foundational building block for renewal and Poisson processes.
The exponential distribution frequently models waiting times because it is the unique continuous distribution possessing the memoryless property. Specifically, for any \(t, s \ge 0\): \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(\xi > t + s \mid \xi > s) &= \frac{\mathbb{P}(\xi > t + s)}{\mathbb{P}(\xi > s)}\\
&= \frac{e^{-\lambda(t+s)}}{e^{-\lambda s}} \\
&= e^{-\lambda t} \\
&= \mathbb{P}(\xi > t).
\end{align*}
\tag{77.2}\]
Rearranging Equation 77.2 yields the functional equation: \[
\mathbb{P}(\xi > t + s) = \mathbb{P}(\xi > t) \mathbb{P}(\xi > s).
\tag{77.3}\]

title: 77  Lecture 35.2: Poisson Process
text:
Definition 77.1 (Exponential Distribution) A random variable \(\xi\) is said to follow an exponential distribution with rate parameter \(\lambda > 0\), denoted \(\xi \sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\), if its tail probability is given by: \[
\mathbb{P}(\xi > t) = e^{-\lambda t}, \quad t \ge 0.
\tag{77.1}\]

title: 77  Lecture 35.2: Poisson Process
text:
77.2 Characterization via Differential Equations
Let \(f(t) := \mathbb{P}(\xi > t)\) for a continuous cumulative distribution function with \(f: [0, \infty) \to [0, 1]\). Assuming \(f\) is differentiable almost everywhere, we differentiate Equation 77.3 with respect to \(s\) at \(s = 0\): \[
\begin{align*}
&f(t + h) - f(t) = f(t)(f(h) - 1) \\
&\implies \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{f(t+h) - f(t)}{h} \\
&= f(t) \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{f(h) - 1}{h}.
\end{align*}
\tag{77.4}\]
This leads directly to the ordinary differential equation: \[
f'(t) = -\lambda f(t),
\tag{77.5}\] where \(\lambda = -\lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{f(h)-1}{h} > 0\). Solving Equation 77.5 with initial condition \(f(0) = 1\) uniquely determines \(f(t) = e^{-\lambda t}\).

title: 77  Lecture 35.2: Poisson Process
section: 77.3 Construction of the Standard Poisson Process
text:
77.3 Construction of the Standard Poisson Process
Let \(\{\xi_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) random variables representing inter-arrival times.
Define the arrival times \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 0}\) by \(X_0 = 0\) and: \[
X_n := \sum_{k=1}^n \xi_k, \quad n \ge 1.
\tag{77.6}\]
The associated renewal counting process \(\{N_t\}_{t \ge 0}\) is defined by: \[
N_t := \sup \{ n \ge 0 : X_n \le t \} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathbb{I}_{\{X_n \le t\}}, \quad t \ge 0.
\tag{77.7}\]
The event that \(N_t = n\) corresponds precisely to the interval of arrival times: \[
\{ N_t = n \} = \{ X_n \le t < X_{n+1} \}.
\tag{77.8}\]

Definition 77.2 (Standard Poisson Process) This renewal counting process \(\{N_t\}_{t \ge 0}\) is called the standard Poisson process of rate \(\lambda\).

title: 77  Lecture 35.2: Poisson Process
section: 77.4 Finite-Dimensional Distributions of the Poisson Process
text:
77.4 Finite-Dimensional Distributions of the Poisson Process
To understand the finite-dimensional distributions of \(\{N_t\}_{t \ge 0}\), it is first useful to compute the joint distributions of the arrival times \(\{X_n\}_{n \ge 1}\).
Notice that the arrival times satisfy \(X_n > X_{n-1} > \dots > X_1 > 0\) almost surely. Consequently, the state space of \((X_1, \dots, X_n)\) is restricted to a simplex rather than the full Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

Definition 77.3 (Arrival Simplex Domains) For \(t > 0\), define the ordered simplex domains:

\(D_n(t) := \{ (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n : 0 < x_1 < x_2 < \dots < x_n \le t \}\).
\(\widetilde{D}_n :=\cup_{t>0}D_n(t) = \{ (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n : 0 < x_1 < x_2 < \dots < x_n \}\).



Lemma 77.1 (Lebesgue Measure of the Simplex) The Lebesgue measure of \(D_n(t)\) is given by: \[
\operatorname{Leb}(D_n(t)) = \frac{t^n}{n!}.
\tag{77.9}\]


Proof (Proof of Lemma 77.1). Write the measure as the iterated integral over the nested inequalities \(0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n \le t\): \[
\operatorname{Leb}(D_n(t))
= \int_0^t \int_0^{x_n} \cdots \int_0^{x_2} 1 \, \mathrm{d}x_1 \, \mathrm{d}x_2 \cdots \mathrm{d}x_{n-1} \, \mathrm{d}x_n.
\] Define \(I_k(s) := \operatorname{Leb}(D_k(s))\) for \(k \ge 1\) and \(s \ge 0\). We prove \(I_k(s) = s^k / k!\) by induction on \(k\).
Base case (\(k = 1\)): \[
I_1(s) = \int_0^s \mathrm{d}x_1 = s = \frac{s^1}{1!}.
\]
Inductive step: Suppose \(I_{k-1}(x) = x^{k-1}/(k-1)!\) for all \(x \ge 0\). The outermost integral peels off the \(x_k\)-integration, with the inner \((k-1)\) integrals giving \(I_{k-1}(x_k)\): \[
I_k(s)
= \int_0^s I_{k-1}(x_k) \, \mathrm{d}x_k
= \int_0^s \frac{x_k^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \, \mathrm{d}x_k
= \frac{1}{(k-1)!} \cdot \frac{s^k}{k}
= \frac{s^k}{k!}.
\]
Applying the result at \(k = n\) and \(s = t\) gives \(\operatorname{Leb}(D_n(t)) = I_n(t) = t^n / n!\).


Proof (Alternative proof of Lemma 77.1). The cube \((0,t)^n\) can be partitioned, up to a Lebesgue-null set, into the \(n!\) regions corresponding to the possible strict orderings of \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). By symmetry of Lebesgue measure each region has the same measure, so \[
\operatorname{Leb}(D_n(t)) =\frac{\operatorname{Leb}((0,t)^n)}{n!}= \frac{t^n}{n!}.
\]


Lemma 77.2 (Joint Density of Arrival Times) If \(g\in\mathcal{B}_b\left(\widetilde{D}_n,\mathcal{B}(\widetilde{D}_n)\right)\) is a bounded measurable function, then: \[
\mathbb{E}\left[g(X_1, \dots, X_n)\right] = \int_{\widetilde{D}_n} g(x_1, \dots, x_n) \lambda^n e^{-\lambda x_n} \, \mathrm{d}x_1 \dots \mathrm{d}x_n.
\tag{77.10}\]


Proof (Proof of Lemma 77.2). The inter-arrival times \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n\) are i.i.d. exponential random variables with parameter \(\lambda\), so their joint density on \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is \[
\begin{align*}
f_{\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n}(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)&= \prod_{k=1}^n \lambda e^{-\lambda \xi_k}=\lambda^n e^{-\lambda(\xi_1+\cdots+\xi_n)}.
\end{align*}
\] The arrival times are related to the inter-arrival times by \[
X_k=\sum_{j=1}^k \xi_j,
\qquad k=1,\ldots,n.
\] Equivalently, the inverse transformation is \[
\xi_1=x_1,\qquad
\xi_2=x_2-x_1,\qquad
\ldots,\qquad
\xi_n=x_n-x_{n-1}.
\] Since \(\xi_k>0\) for every \(k\), the corresponding \((x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) satisfy \[
0<x_1<x_2<\cdots<x_n,
\] so the transformation maps \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\) onto \(\widetilde{D}_n\). The Jacobian matrix of the inverse transformation is \[
\frac{\partial(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)}
{\partial(x_1,\ldots,x_n)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0\\
-1 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0\\
0 & -1 & 1 & \cdots & 0\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots\\
0 & 0 & \cdots & -1 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\] This matrix is lower triangular with diagonal entries equal to \(1\), and hence \[
\left|\text{det}
\frac{\partial(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)}
{\partial(x_1,\ldots,x_n)}\right|=1.
\] Moreover, \[
\xi_1+\cdots+\xi_n=x_n.
\] Therefore, by the change-of-variables formula, \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\left[g(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\right]
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}_+^n}
g(\xi_1,\xi_1+\xi_2,\ldots,\xi_1+\cdots+\xi_n)
\lambda^n e^{-\lambda(\xi_1+\cdots+\xi_n)}
d\xi_1\cdots d\xi_n\\
&=
\int_{\widetilde{D}_n}
g(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
\lambda^n e^{-\lambda x_n}
dx_1\cdots dx_n.
\end{aligned}
\] This proves the result.


Corollary 77.1 (Poisson Marginal Distribution) For each \(t > 0\) and \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), the counting process variable \(N_t\) follows a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda t\), i.e., \(N_t \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda t)\).


Proof. We compute the probability \(\mathbb{P}(N_t = n)\) using the indicator of the event \(\{X_n \le t < X_{n+1}\}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(N_t = n) &= \mathbb{P}(X_n \le t < X_{n+1})=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{I}_{\{X_n \le t < X_{n+1}\}}\right] \\
&= \int_{\widetilde{D}_{n+1}} \mathbb{I}_{\{x_n\le t\}}\mathbb{I}_{\{x_{n+1} > t\}} \lambda^{n+1} e^{-\lambda x_{n+1}}\mathrm{d}x_1 \dots \mathrm{d}x_{n+1} \\
&= \int_{D_n(t)} \mathrm{d}x_1 \dots \mathrm{d}x_n\int_t^\infty \lambda^{n+1} e^{-\lambda x_{n+1}} \, \mathrm{d}x_{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\] The first integral is the volume of the simplex \(D_n(t)\), which is \(\frac{t^n}{n!}\). The last integral evaluates to \(e^{-\lambda t}\lambda^n\). Multiplying these two factors gives the final result: \[
\mathbb{P}(N_t = n) = e^{-\lambda t} \frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!}.
\] This confirms that \(N_t \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda t)\).

title: 77  Lecture 35.2: Poisson Process
section: 77.5 Order Statistics Property of Arrival Times
text:
77.5 Order Statistics Property of Arrival Times

Proposition 77.1 (Uniform Order Statistics Property) Let \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) and \(t > 0\). Let \(U_1, \dots, U_n\) be independent and identically distributed \(\operatorname{Unif}(0, t)\) random variables. Then, conditioned on the event \(\{N_t = n\}\), the joint distribution of \((X_1, \dots, X_n)\) is identical to the joint distribution of the order statistics of \((U_1, \dots, U_n)\) (i.e., the values sorted in non-decreasing order).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 77.1). First note that if \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\sim\text{Unif}(0, t)\), then their joint density is \[
f_{U_1,\ldots,U_n}(u_1,\ldots,u_n)=\frac{1}{t^n}\mathbb{I}_{(0,t)^n}(u_1,\ldots,u_n).
\] Thus the vector \((U_1,\ldots,U_n)\) is uniformly distributed on the cube \((0,t)^n\). The order statistics \((U_{(1)},\ldots,U_{(n)})\) are obtained by sorting the \(U_i\)’s in non-decreasing order. The joint density of the order statistics is given by \[
f_{U_{(1)},\ldots,U_{(n)}}(u_1,\ldots,u_n)=\frac{n!}{t^n}\mathbb{I}_{D_n(t)}(u_1,\ldots,u_n),
\] where the factor of \(n!\) accounts for the \(n!\) possible permutations of the \(U_i\)’s that yield the same order statistics.
For any bounded measurable function \(f: D_n(t) \to \mathbb{R}\): \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_1, \dots, X_n) \mid N_t = n] = \frac{\mathbb{E}[f(X_1, \dots, X_n)\,\mathbb{I}(X_n \le t < X_{n+1})]}{\mathbb{P}(N_t = n)}.
\] For the numerator, apply Lemma 77.2 to \((X_1,\dots,X_{n+1})\) and separate the \(x_{n+1}\)-integration over \((t,\infty)\) (exactly as in the proof of Corollary 77.1): \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_1,\dots,X_n)\,\mathbb{I}(X_n\le t<X_{n+1})]
= \lambda^n e^{-\lambda t}\int_{D_n(t)} f(x_1, \dots, x_n) \, \mathrm{d}x_1 \cdots \mathrm{d}x_n.
\] Dividing by \(\mathbb{P}(N_t = n) = e^{-\lambda t} \frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!}\) gives: \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_1, \dots, X_n) \mid N_t = n]
= \frac{n!}{t^n} \int_{D_n(t)} f(x_1, \dots, x_n) \, \mathrm{d}x_1 \cdots \mathrm{d}x_n.
\] The right-hand side is exactly \(\mathbb{E}[f(U_{(1)}, \dots, U_{(n)})]\), where \(U_{(1)} \le \dots \le U_{(n)}\) are the order statistics of \(n\) independent \(\operatorname{Unif}(0, t)\) variables. Indeed, \((U_{(1)},\dots,U_{(n)})\) has joint density \(\frac{n!}{t^n}\) on \(D_n(t)\) (the \(n!\) comes from symmetry: the \(n!\) possible orderings of \((U_1,\dots,U_n)\) each occupy the same Lebesgue measure \(t^n/n!\) within \((0,t)^n\)). Since the identity holds for every bounded measurable \(f\), the conditional distribution of \((X_1,\dots,X_n)\) given \(N_t=n\) equals the distribution of the order statistics \((U_{(1)},\dots,U_{(n)})\).

title: 39  Lecture 35.2: Poisson Process
text:
39.6 Uniform Order Statistics Property
Let \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) and \(t > 0\). Let \(U_1, \dots, U_n\) be independent and identically distributed \(\operatorname{Unif}(0, t)\) random variables. Then, conditioned on the event \(\{N_t = n\}\), the joint distribution of \((X_1, \dots, X_n)\) is identical to the joint distribution of the order statistics of \((U_1, \dots, U_n)\) (i.e., the values sorted in non-decreasing order).

title: 77  Lecture 35.2: Poisson Process
section: 77.6 Stochastic Counting Measure and Independent Increments
text:
77.6 Stochastic Counting Measure and Independent Increments
To study spatial or temporal distributions more generally, we generalize the counting process to a stochastic counting measure.
For any Borel set \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}_+)\), define \(N(B)\) as the number of arrival points \(X_n\) falling within \(B\): \[
N(B) := \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb{I}_B(X_n) = N\left(B \cap [0, t]\right) \quad \text{(for bounded sets $B \subset [0, t]$)}.
\]

Theorem 77.1 (Independence and Poisson Increments Theorem)  

If \(B_1, \dots, B_k\) form a disjoint partition of an interval \([0, t]\), then the random variables \(N(B_1), \dots, N(B_k)\) are mutually independent.
If \(\operatorname{Leb}(B) < \infty\), then \(N(B) \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda \operatorname{Leb}(B))\).
In particular, for any \(0 \le s < t\), the increment \(N((s, t]) = N_t - N_s\) is independent of \(\mathcal{F}_s\) and follows \(\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda(t - s))\).



Proof (Proof of Theorem 77.1). Parts 1 and 2.
Write \(\ell_j := \operatorname{Leb}(B_j)\) and note \(\sum_{j=1}^k \ell_j = t\). For \(u_1, \dots, u_k \in \mathbb{R}\), define \[
\tilde{u}(x) := \sum_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j}\,\mathbb{I}_{B_j}(x), \quad x \in [0, t].
\] Since the \(B_j\) partition \([0, t]\), exactly one indicator is non-zero for each \(x\), so \(\tilde{u}\) is well-defined. We compute the joint characteristic function \[
\phi(\mathbf{u}) := \mathbb{E}\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j N(B_j)}\right].
\]
Step 1: Conditional expectation on \(\{N_t = n\}\).
On the event \(\{N_t = n\} = \{X_n \le t < X_{n+1}\}\), the arrivals that fall in \([0,t]\) are exactly \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) (since \(X_{n+1} > t\)). Because \(B_1, \dots, B_k\) partition \([0,t]\) and every \(X_m \in [0,t]\), the count of arrivals in \(B_j\) is: \[
N(B_j) = \sum_{m=1}^n \mathbb{I}_{B_j}(X_m), \quad j = 1, \dots, k.
\] Substituting and rearranging the product: \[
\prod_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j N(B_j)}
= \prod_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j \sum_{m=1}^n \mathbb{I}_{B_j}(X_m)}
= \prod_{j=1}^k \prod_{m=1}^n e^{i u_j \mathbb{I}_{B_j}(X_m)}
= \prod_{m=1}^n \prod_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j \mathbb{I}_{B_j}(X_m)}.
\] For each fixed \(m\), the sets \(B_j\) partition \([0,t]\), so \(X_m\) belongs to exactly one set, say \(X_m \in B_{j_0}\). Then \(\mathbb{I}_{B_j}(X_m) = \mathbf{1}_{j=j_0}\), and: \[
\prod_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j \mathbb{I}_{B_j}(X_m)}
= e^{i u_{j_0} \cdot 1} \prod_{j \ne j_0} e^{i u_j \cdot 0}
= e^{i u_{j_0}}.
\] On the other hand, the definition of \(\tilde{u}\) gives: \[
\tilde{u}(X_m) = \sum_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j} \mathbb{I}_{B_j}(X_m) = e^{i u_{j_0}}.
\] Therefore \(\prod_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j \mathbb{I}_{B_j}(X_m)} = \tilde{u}(X_m)\) for every \(m\), and: \[
\prod_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j N(B_j)} = \prod_{m=1}^n \tilde{u}(X_m) \quad \text{on } \{N_t = n\}.
\] Applying Lemma 77.2 to \((X_1, \dots, X_{n+1})\): \[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j N(B_j)}\,\mathbb{I}(N_t = n)\right]
= \int_{\widetilde{D}_{n+1}} \prod_{m=1}^n \tilde{u}(x_m)\cdot\mathbb{I}(x_n \le t < x_{n+1})
  \cdot\lambda^{n+1} e^{-\lambda x_{n+1}}\,dx_1\cdots dx_{n+1}.
\] The constraint \(x_{n+1} > t\) decouples the \(x_{n+1}\)-integration from the rest: \[
= \lambda^{n+1}\int_{D_n(t)}\prod_{m=1}^n \tilde{u}(x_m)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n
  \cdot\int_t^\infty e^{-\lambda x_{n+1}}\,dx_{n+1}.
\] Since \(\displaystyle\int_t^\infty e^{-\lambda x}\,dx = \frac{e^{-\lambda t}}{\lambda}\), the \(\lambda^{n+1}\) and \(1/\lambda\) cancel to give: \[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j N(B_j)}\,\mathbb{I}(N_t = n)\right]
= \lambda^n e^{-\lambda t}\int_{D_n(t)}\prod_{m=1}^n \tilde{u}(x_m)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n.
\tag{77.11}\]
Step 2: Evaluating the simplex integral.
The integrand \(\prod_{m=1}^n \tilde{u}(x_m)\) is symmetric in \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\) (each factor depends on a single variable and is unaffected by permuting the others). The simplex \(D_n(t) = \{0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n \le t\}\) is exactly one of the \(n!\) equal-measure regions obtained by partitioning \((0,t)^n\) according to the ordering of the coordinates. By symmetry, the integral over each such region is the same, so \[
\int_{D_n(t)}\prod_{m=1}^n \tilde{u}(x_m)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n
= \frac{1}{n!}\int_{(0,t)^n}\prod_{m=1}^n \tilde{u}(x_m)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n.
\] The integrand factors over coordinates, so Fubini gives \[
\int_{(0,t)^n}\prod_{m=1}^n \tilde{u}(x_m)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n
= \prod_{m=1}^n\int_0^t \tilde{u}(x)\,dx
= \left(\int_0^t \tilde{u}(x)\,dx\right)^n.
\] Since the \(B_j\) are disjoint, \[
\int_0^t \tilde{u}(x)\,dx = \sum_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j}\int_{B_j}dx = \sum_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j}\ell_j.
\] Substituting back into Equation 77.11: \[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j N(B_j)}\,\mathbb{I}(N_t = n)\right]
= \frac{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda t}}{n!}\left(\sum_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j}\ell_j\right)^n.
\]
Step 3: Summing over \(n \ge 0\).
Since \(\{N_t = n\}_{n \ge 0}\) are disjoint events whose union is the whole sample space, the total expectation decomposes as: \[
\phi(\mathbf{u})
= \mathbb{E}\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j N(B_j)}\right]
= \sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb{E}\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j N(B_j)}\,\mathbb{I}(N_t = n)\right].
\] Substituting the result of Steps 1 and 2: \[
= \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda t}}{n!}\left(\sum_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j}\ell_j\right)^n.
\] Set \(c := \lambda\sum_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j}\ell_j\). Since \(|c| \le \lambda\sum_j \ell_j = \lambda t < \infty\), the series converges absolutely and equals \(e^c\) by the Taylor expansion of the exponential: \[
\phi(\mathbf{u})
= e^{-\lambda t}\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{c^n}{n!}
= e^{-\lambda t} e^{c}
= e^{-\lambda t}\exp\!\left(\lambda\sum_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j}\ell_j\right).
\] Since the \(B_j\) partition \([0,t]\), we have \(\sum_{j=1}^k \ell_j = t\), so \(-\lambda t = -\lambda\sum_{j=1}^k \ell_j\). Combining the exponents: \[
\phi(\mathbf{u})
= \exp\!\left(-\lambda\sum_{j=1}^k \ell_j + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^k e^{i u_j}\ell_j\right)
= \exp\!\left(\lambda\sum_{j=1}^k \ell_j(e^{i u_j}-1)\right).
\] The exponent is a sum of \(k\) independent terms, so the exponential factors into a product: \[
\phi(\mathbf{u})
= \prod_{j=1}^k \exp\!\left(\lambda\ell_j(e^{i u_j}-1)\right).
\tag{77.12}\]
Conclusion for Parts 1 and 2. The joint characteristic function \(\phi(\mathbf{u})\) is the product over \(j\) of \(\exp(\lambda\ell_j(e^{iu_j}-1))\), which is exactly the characteristic function of a \(\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda\ell_j)\) random variable. By uniqueness of characteristic functions:

(Part 1) \(N(B_1), \dots, N(B_k)\) are mutually independent.
(Part 2) Each marginal satisfies \(N(B_j) \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda\ell_j) = \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda\operatorname{Leb}(B_j))\).

Part 3.
Fix \(0 \le s < t\). For any finite partition \(0 < r_1 < \cdots < r_{m-1} < s\) of \([0,s]\), apply Part 1 to the partition \[
\bigl\{[0, r_1],\,(r_1, r_2],\,\dots,\,(r_{m-1}, s],\,(s, t]\bigr\}
\] of \([0, t]\). This gives mutual independence of all the increment counts, and in particular shows that \(N((s,t])\) is independent of the finite family \[
\bigl\{N([0,r_1]),\,N((r_1,r_2]),\,\dots,\,N((r_{m-1},s])\bigr\}.
\] The \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F}_s = \sigma(N_r : r \le s)\) is generated by all such families (as the partition of \([0,s]\) is refined). By the \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem, \(N((s,t])\) is independent of the entire \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F}_s\). Part 2 applied to \(B = (s,t]\) with \(\operatorname{Leb}((s,t]) = t-s\) gives \(N((s,t]) = N_t - N_s \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s))\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: 71  Lecture 32.3: Conditioning on Random Variables
text:
Proposition 71.1 (Independence Characterization via Conditional Expectation) Let \(X: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}) \to (S, \mathcal{B}_S)\) be a random variable (or measurable map), and let \(\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a sub-\(\sigma\)-field.

If \(\sigma(X)\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) are independent, then for any bounded measurable function \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}_S)\) (or \(f \ge 0\)), \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X) \mid \mathcal{G}] = \mathbb{E}[f(X)] \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{71.1}\]
Conversely, if Equation 71.1 holds for all \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}_S)\), then \(\sigma(X)\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) are independent.



Proof. \((\Longrightarrow)\) Forward Direction: Assume \(\sigma(X)\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) are independent. Let \(Y\) be any bounded, \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable random variable (or set \(Y = \mathbb{I}_B\) for \(B \in \mathcal{G}\)). Since \(f(X)\) is \(\sigma(X)\)-measurable and \(Y\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, independence implies: \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X) Y] = \mathbb{E}[f(X)] \mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}\big[ \mathbb{E}[f(X)] Y \big].
\] Because \(\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\) is a constant (hence trivially \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable) and satisfies the defining integration property for all bounded \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable \(Y\), uniqueness of conditional expectation implies: \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X) \mid \mathcal{G}] = \mathbb{E}[f(X)] \quad \text{a.s.}
\]
\((\Longleftarrow)\) Reverse Direction: Assume \(\mathbb{E}[f(X) \mid \mathcal{G}] = \mathbb{E}[f(X)]\) a.s. for all \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}_S)\). Fix \(A \in \mathcal{B}_S\) and \(B \in \mathcal{G}\). Setting \(f = \mathbb{I}_A\) and \(Y = \mathbb{I}_B\): \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(X \in A, B) &= \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_A(X) \mathbb{I}_B] \\
&= \mathbb{E}\big[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_A(X) \mid \mathcal{G}] \mathbb{I}_B \big] \\
&= \mathbb{E}\big[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_A(X)] \mathbb{I}_B \big] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_A(X)] \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_B] \\
&= \mathbb{P}(X \in A) \mathbb{P}(B).
\end{align*}
\] Since this holds for all \(A \in \mathcal{B}_S\) and \(B \in \mathcal{G}\), the \(\sigma\)-fields \(\sigma(X)\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) are independent.

text:
71.2 Conditioning on a Random Variable / Vector

Definition 71.1 (Conditioning on a Random Vector) Let \(X: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}) \to (S, \mathcal{B}_S)\) (where typically \(S = \mathbb{R}^d\)) and let \(Y \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\). We denote the conditional expectation of \(Y\) given \(X\) as: \[
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] := \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \sigma(X)].
\] By definition, \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] \in L^1(\Omega, \sigma(X), \mathbb{P})\) and is \(\sigma(X)\)-measurable.
By the Doob-Dynkin Lemma, there exists a measurable function \(g: S \to \mathbb{R}\) (where \(g \in \mathcal{B}(S, \mathcal{B}_S)\)) such that: \[
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] = g(X) \quad \text{a.s.}
\] We denote \(g(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]\).


Remark 71.1 (Equivalence of Conditional Expectations). The three expressions represent the same random variable (up to a.s. equality): \[
\mathbb E[Y\mid X] = \mathbb E[Y\mid\sigma(X)] = g(X).
\]

The first expression emphasizes the information being conditioned on;
the second emphasizes that the information is generated by \(X\); and
the third emphasizes that the resulting random variable must be a measurable function of \(X\).
Then \(g(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]\) is the function-level representation of that conditional expectation.



Remark 71.2 (Characterization of \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]\)). Equivalently, the factor function \(g = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = \cdot]: S \to \mathbb{R}\) is characterized up to \(\mu_X\)-null sets (where \(\mu_X = \mathbb{P} \circ X^{-1}\)) by the integration identity: \[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{E}[Yh(X)]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]h(X)]=\mathbb{E}[g(X)h(X)]\\
&=\int_S g(x) h(x) \, \mu_X(dx), \quad \forall h \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}_S).
\end{aligned}
\] In particular, for indicator functions \(h = \mathbb{I}_A\) with \(A \in \mathcal{B}_S\): \[
\mathbb{E}[Y \mathbb{I}_{\{X \in A\}}] = \int_A g(x) \, \mu_X(dx).
\] This says that \(g(x)\) is the function that reproduces the conditional averages of \(Y\) over every event determined by \(X\).

text:
71.3 Product Spaces, Independence, and Substitution Rules
When \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, “\(Y\) is constant with respect to \(X\)” in a probabilistic sense. We make this precise using product measures and Fubini’s Theorem.

Proposition 71.2 (Disintegration / Substitution under Independence) Let \(X: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (S, \mathcal{B}_S)\) and \(Y: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (T, \mathcal{B}_T)\) be independent random variables defined on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\). Let \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S \times T, \mathcal{B}_S \otimes \mathcal{B}_T)\) (or \(f \ge 0\)).
Then: \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X = x] = \mathbb{E}[f(x, Y)] = \int_T f(x, y) \, \mu_Y(dy),
\tag{71.2}\] and consequently, \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X] = g(X) \quad \text{a.s., where } g(x) = \mathbb{E}[f(x, Y)].
\]


Proof. Since \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, their joint pushforward distribution factors into a product measure: \[
\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes \mu_Y.
\] To verify that \(g(x) = \int_T f(x, y) \, \mu_Y(dy)\) gives the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X]\), take an arbitrary test function \(h \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}_S)\). Applying Fubini-Tonelli Theorem on the product measure \(\mu_X \otimes \mu_Y\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y) h(X)] &= \int_{S \times T} f(x, y) h(x) \, \mu_{(X,Y)}(dx \, dy) \\
&= \int_S \left( \int_T f(x, y) \, \mu_Y(dy) \right) h(x) \, \mu_X(dx) \\
&= \int_S g(x) h(x) \, \mu_X(dx) \\
&= \mathbb{E}[g(X) h(X)].
\end{aligned}
\] Since \(g(X)\) is \(\sigma(X)\)-measurable and satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y) h(X)] = \mathbb{E}[g(X) h(X)]\) for all \(h \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\), by uniqueness of conditional expectation we conclude \(\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X] = g(X)\) a.s.

title: 71  Lecture 32.3: Conditioning on Random Variables
text:
71.4 Explicit Computation via Joint Densities

Proposition 71.3 (Conditional Expectation with Respect to Absolutely Continuous Distributions) Let \((X, Y)\) be a random vector in \(\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^k\) with joint probability density function \(f_{X,Y}(x, y)\) relative to Lebesgue measure.
Let \(f_X(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^k} f_{X,Y}(x, y) \, dy\) denote the marginal density of \(X\). Define the conditional density \(f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x)\) by: \[
f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) := \begin{cases}
\dfrac{f_{X,Y}(x, y)}{f_X(x)} & \text{if } f_X(x) > 0, \\[8pt]
0 & \text{if } f_X(x) = 0.
\end{cases}
\tag{71.3}\]
For any \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{R}^{d+k})\), \(\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X] = g(X)\) a.s., where: \[
g(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^k} f(x, y) f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) \, dy.
\tag{71.4}\]


Proof. We must show that for every bounded measurable function \(h \in \mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{R}^d)\): \[
\mathbb{E}\big[ g(X) h(X) \big] = \mathbb{E}\big[ f(X, Y) h(X) \big].
\] Using the joint density \(f_{X,Y}(x, y)\), the right-hand side is: \[
\mathbb{E}\big[ f(X,Y) h(X) \big] = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \int_{\mathbb{R}^k} f(x, y) h(x) f_{X,Y}(x, y) \, dy \, dx.
\] Now compute the left-hand side using the definition of \(g(x)\) in Equation 71.4 and the marginal density \(f_X(x)\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\big[ g(X) h(X) \big] &= \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} g(x) h(x) f_X(x) \, dx \\
&= \int_{\{x: f_X(x) > 0\}} \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}^k} f(x, y) \frac{f_{X,Y}(x, y)}{f_X(x)} \, dy \right) h(x) f_X(x) \, dx \\
&= \int_{\{x: f_X(x) > 0\}} \int_{\mathbb{R}^k} f(x, y) h(x) f_{X,Y}(x, y) \, dy \, dx.
\end{aligned}
\]






NoteClaim on Null Sets



Claim: On the set \(N = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d : f_X(x) = 0\}\), the integral vanishes: \[
\int_N \int_{\mathbb{R}^k} f(x, y) f_{X,Y}(x, y) \, dy \, dx = 0.
\] Proof of Claim: Since \(f_{X,Y}(x, y) \ge 0\), Fubini’s theorem gives: \[
\int_N f_X(x) \, dx = \int_N \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}^k} f_{X,Y}(x, y) \, dy \right) dx = 0.
\] Since \(f_{X,Y}(x, y) = 0\) for Lebesgue-almost-every \((x, y) \in N \times \mathbb{R}^k\), any integral of \(f(x, y) h(x) f_{X,Y}(x, y)\) over \(N \times \mathbb{R}^k\) is identically 0.


Hence, integrating over \(\{x: f_X(x) > 0\}\) is equal to integrating over all of \(\mathbb{R}^d\): \[
\mathbb{E}\big[ g(X) h(X) \big] = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \int_{\mathbb{R}^k} f(x, y) h(x) f_{X,Y}(x, y) \, dy \, dx = \mathbb{E}\big[ f(X, Y) h(X) \big].
\] By the uniqueness of conditional expectation, \(g(X) = \mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X]\) a.s.

title: 71  Lecture 32.3: Conditioning on Random Variables
text:
71.5 Takeaways

Conditioning on a random variable reduces to conditioning on a \(\sigma\)-field. \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] := \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \sigma(X)]\). By the Doob-Dynkin lemma, every \(\sigma(X)\)-measurable function has the form \(g \circ X\), so there exists a measurable \(g: S \to \mathbb{R}\), unique up to \(\mu_X\)-null sets, such that \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] = g(X)\) a.s. The function \(g\) is characterized by \(\mathbb{E}[Y h(X)] = \int_S g(x) h(x) \, \mu_X(dx)\) for all \(h \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\).
Independence is equivalent to conditional expectation collapsing to the unconditional mean. \(\sigma(X)\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) are independent if and only if \(\mathbb{E}[f(X) \mid \mathcal{G}] = \mathbb{E}[f(X)]\) a.s. for every \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\). The forward direction follows because independence gives \(\mathbb{E}[f(X) Y] = \mathbb{E}[f(X)] \mathbb{E}[Y]\) for all bounded \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable \(Y\), and the constant \(\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\) satisfies the defining integration identity. The reverse direction is verified by testing \(f = \mathbb{I}_A\) and applying the tower property to recover \(\mathbb{P}(X \in A, B) = \mathbb{P}(X \in A)\mathbb{P}(B)\).
Substitution rule under independence. If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then \(\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X] = g(X)\) where \(g(x) = \mathbb{E}[f(x, Y)] = \int_T f(x, y) \, \mu_Y(dy)\). The proof factors the joint law \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes \mu_Y\) and applies the Fubini-Tonelli theorem to match the integration identity \(\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y) h(X)] = \mathbb{E}[g(X) h(X)]\) for all \(h \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\).
Computation via conditional densities. When \((X, Y)\) has joint density \(f_{X,Y}\) relative to Lebesgue measure, the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y) \mid X] = g(X)\) a.s., where \(g(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^k} f(x, y) f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) \, dy\) and \(f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) = f_{X,Y}(x,y)/f_X(x)\) on \(\{f_X > 0\}\). The set \(N = \{f_X = 0\}\) is a \(\mu_X\)-null set: since \(f_{X,Y} \ge 0\) and \(\int_N \int f_{X,Y} \, dy\, dx = \int_N f_X(x)\, dx = 0\), we have \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 0\) for a.e. \((x,y) \in N \times \mathbb{R}^k\), so the definition of \(g\) on \(N\) is irrelevant.

title: 70  Lecture 32.2: Conditional MCT, Fatou, DCT, Jensen
text:
Definition 70.1 (Conditional Expectation for Non-Negative Random Variables) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space, and let \(\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a sub-\(\sigma\)-field. If \(X \ge 0\) almost surely (not necessarily in \(L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\)), there exists a unique (up to \(\mathbb{P}\)-almost sure equivalence) \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable random variable, denoted \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\), such that for every non-negative \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable random variable \(Y\) (or equivalently, every \(B \in \mathcal{G}\)), \[
\mathbb{E}[X \mathbb{I}_B] = \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \mathbb{I}_B\big].
\tag{70.1}\] If \(X \in L^1\), \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\) coincides with the standard \(L^1\) conditional expectation.


Proposition 70.1 (Well-Definedness of Conditional Expectation for \(X \ge 0\)) If \(X \ge 0\) almost surely, and \(\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) is a sub-\(\sigma\)-field, then there exists a unique (up to \(\mathbb{P}\)-null sets) \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable random variable \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\) satisfying: \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \mathbb{I}_B] = \mathbb{E}[X \mathbb{I}_B], \quad \forall B \in \mathcal{G}.
\]


Proof. Existence:
To define \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\), consider the truncated sequence \(X_n = X \wedge n\) for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). Since \(0 \le X_n \le n\), we have \(X_n \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\), so the standard conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X_n \mid \mathcal{G}]\) exists for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).
By the monotonicity of conditional expectation on \(L^1\), the sequence \((\mathbb{E}[X_n \mid \mathcal{G}])_{n=1}^\infty\) is non-decreasing almost surely. Therefore, we may define: \[
\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] := \lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[X_n \mid \mathcal{G}] \quad \text{a.s.}
\]
Now, fix \(B \in \mathcal{G}\). Applying the classical Monotone Convergence Theorem (MCT) twice—first for the integrated sequence of non-negative \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable functions, and second for \(X_n \mathbb{I}_B\): \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \mathbb{I}_B\big] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[X_n \mid \mathcal{G}] \mathbb{I}_B\right]\\
& \stackrel{\text{MCT}}{=} \lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[X_n \mid \mathcal{G}] \mathbb{I}_B\big] \\
&= \lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[X_n \mathbb{I}_B]\\
& \stackrel{\text{MCT}}{=} \mathbb{E}[X \mathbb{I}_B].
\end{align*}
\] This establishes the defining property.
Uniqueness:
Let \(W=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\). Suppose \(Z\ge0\) is \(\mathcal G\)-measurable and satisfies \(\mathbb E[Z1_B]=\mathbb E[X1_B]\) for all \(B\in\mathcal G\). We want to show \(Z=W\) a.s.
For the finite-valued part, define \(B_m=\{Z>W\}\cap\{Z\le m\}\). On \(B_m\), we have \[
0\le W<Z\le m,
\] so both \(Z1_{B_m}\) and \(W1_{B_m}\) are integrable. Therefore \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Z-W)1_{B_m}] &=\mathbb E[Z1_{B_m}]-\mathbb E[W1_{B_m}]\\
&=\mathbb E[X1_{B_m}]-\mathbb E[X1_{B_m}]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\] Since \((Z-W)1_{B_m}\ge0\), it follows that \((Z-W)1_{B_m}=0\) a.s. But \(Z>W\) on \(B_m\), so \(P(B_m)=0\). Hence \(P(Z>W,\;Z<\infty)=0\).
We still need to deal with \(Z=\infty\). Define \(C_m=\{Z=\infty,\;W\le m\}\). If \(P(C_m)>0\), then \(\mathbb E[Z1_{C_m}]=\infty\), whereas \(\mathbb E[W1_{C_m}]\le mP(C_m)<\infty\). But both quantities must equal \(\mathbb E[X1_{C_m}]\), a contradiction. Hence \(P(C_m)=0\) for all \(m\). Since \(\{Z=\infty,\;W<\infty\} = \bigcup_{m=1}^\infty C_m\), we obtain \(P(Z=\infty,\;W<\infty)=0\). The same argument with \(Z\) and \(W\) interchanged gives \(P(W>Z)=0\). Thus \(Z=W \quad\text{a.s.}\)


Remark 70.1 (Monotonicity of Extended Conditional Expectation). The extended conditional expectation is monotone: if \(0 \le X \le Y\) a.s., then \[
\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] = \lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[X \wedge n \mid \mathcal{G}] \le \lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[Y \wedge n \mid \mathcal{G}] = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{G}] \quad \text{a.s.}
\]

text:
70.3 Conditional Jensen’s Inequality and \(L^p\) Contractions

Theorem 70.2 (Conditional Jensen’s Inequality) Let \(X \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) and let \(\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a sub-\(\sigma\)-field. If \(\varphi: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is convex and \(\varphi(X) \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\), then \[
\varphi(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]) \le \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X) \mid \mathcal{G}] \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{70.2}\] In particular, \(\mathbb{E}[\varphi(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}])] \le \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X)]\).


Proof. To illustrate the underlying mechanism, we first consider the smooth case where \(\varphi \in C^2(\mathbb{R})\) with \(\varphi'' > 0\). By Taylor’s theorem, for any \(x, y \in \mathbb{R}\): \[
\varphi(y) = \varphi(x) + \varphi'(x)(y - x) + \int_x^y (y - t) \varphi''(t) \, dt \ge \varphi(x) + \varphi'(x)(y - x).
\] Substituting \(y = X\) and \(x = \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\) (which is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable): \[
\varphi(X) \ge \varphi(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]) + \varphi'(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]) (X - \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]) \quad \text{a.s.}
\] Taking conditional expectations with respect to \(\mathcal{G}\) on both sides, and noting that \(\varphi(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}])\) and \(\varphi'(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}])\) are \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X) \mid \mathcal{G}] &\ge \mathbb{E}\left[ \varphi(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]) + \varphi'(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]) (X - \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]) \;\middle|\; \mathcal{G} \right] \\
&= \varphi(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]) + \varphi'(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]) \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[X - \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \mid \mathcal{G}]}_{= 0} \\
&= \varphi(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]) \quad \text{a.s.}
\end{aligned}
\]
For a general convex function \(\varphi\), recall that \(\varphi\) is the supremum of a countable collection of affine lines: \(\varphi(t) = \sup_{k \in \mathbb{N}} (a_k t + b_k)\). For each \(k \in \mathbb{N}\): \[
\varphi(X) \ge a_k X + b_k \implies \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X) \mid \mathcal{G}] \ge \mathbb{E}[a_k X + b_k \mid \mathcal{G}] = a_k \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] + b_k \quad \text{a.s.}
\] Taking the supremum over \(k \in \mathbb{N}\) yields: \[
\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X) \mid \mathcal{G}] \ge \sup_{k \in \mathbb{N}} \left( a_k \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] + b_k \right) = \varphi(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]) \quad \text{a.s.}
\] Taking total expectations on both sides yields \(\mathbb{E}[\varphi(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}])] \le \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X)]\).


Corollary 70.1 (\(L^p\) Contraction Property) For \(1 \le p < \infty\), the conditional expectation operator \(\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot \mid \mathcal{G}]: L^p(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}) \to L^p(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, \mathbb{P})\) is a non-expansive contraction; that is, for all \(X \in L^p\): \[
\|\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\|_p \le \|X\|_p.
\tag{70.3}\]


Proof. Consider the function \(\varphi(x) = |x|^p\). Since \(p \ge 1\), \(\varphi\) is convex on \(\mathbb{R}\). If \(X \in L^p\), then \(\varphi(X) = |X|^p \in L^1\).
Applying Conditional Jensen’s Inequality (Equation 70.2): \[
\left| \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \right|^p \le \mathbb{E}\left[ |X|^p \;\middle|\; \mathcal{G} \right] \quad \text{a.s.}
\] Taking total expectations on both sides: \[
\mathbb{E}\left[ \left| \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \right|^p \right] \le \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}\left[ |X|^p \;\middle|\; \mathcal{G} \right] \right] = \mathbb{E}\left[ |X|^p \right].
\] Taking the \(p\)-th root gives \(\|\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\|_p \le \|X\|_p\).

70.4 Takeaways

Extension to \(X \ge 0\). Conditional expectation extends beyond \(L^1\) by setting \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] := \lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[X \wedge n \mid \mathcal{G}]\) a.s. The limit is non-decreasing; MCT applied twice (once to \(\mathbb{E}[X_n \mid \mathcal{G}]\mathbb{I}_B\) and once to \(X_n \mathbb{I}_B\)) verifies the defining identity, and uniqueness follows by truncating to bounded sets in \(\mathcal{G}\).
Conditional MCT and Fatou. If \(0 \le X_n \uparrow X\) a.s., then \(\mathbb{E}[X_n \mid \mathcal{G}] \uparrow \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\) a.s. (Conditional MCT), proved by fixing \(B \in \mathcal{G}\) and applying ordinary MCT to pass the limit through the integral on both sides. Conditional Fatou follows by setting \(Y_k = \inf_{n \ge k} X_n \uparrow \liminf_n X_n\): monotonicity gives \(\mathbb{E}[Y_k \mid \mathcal{G}] \le \inf_{n \ge k} \mathbb{E}[X_n \mid \mathcal{G}]\) a.s. (by a countable intersection of null sets), and Conditional MCT takes the limit on the left.
Conditional DCT. If \(X_n \to X\) a.s. and \(|X_n| \le Y \in L^1\), then \(\mathbb{E}[X_n \mid \mathcal{G}] \to \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\) in \(L^1\) and a.s. The \(L^1\) part uses \(|\mathbb{E}[Z \mid \mathcal{G}]| \le \mathbb{E}[|Z| \mid \mathcal{G}]\) a.s. (from monotonicity applied to \(\pm Z \le |Z|\)), giving \(\|\mathbb{E}[Z \mid \mathcal{G}]\|_1 \le \|Z\|_1\). The a.s. part applies Conditional Fatou to the non-negative sequences \(Y \pm X_n\): the two inequalities \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \le \liminf_n \mathbb{E}[X_n \mid \mathcal{G}]\) and \(\limsup_n \mathbb{E}[X_n \mid \mathcal{G}] \le \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\) are obtained by subtracting \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{G}] < \infty\) a.s. (since \(Y \in L^1\)).
Conditional Jensen and \(L^p\) contraction. For convex \(\varphi\) with \(\varphi(X) \in L^1\): \(\varphi(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]) \le \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X) \mid \mathcal{G}]\) a.s. The proof represents \(\varphi = \sup_k (a_k t + b_k)\) as a countable supremum of affine functions; linearity of conditional expectation gives the inequality for each affine minorant, and taking the supremum recovers \(\varphi(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}])\). As a special case with \(\varphi(t) = |t|^p\) (\(p \ge 1\)): \(\|\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\|_p \le \|X\|_p\).
