title: 68  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation-Part II
text:
68.2 \(L^2\) Subspaces Defined by Sub-\(\sigma\)-Fields
Let \(\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a sub-\(\sigma\)-field of \(\mathcal{F}\). We define the subset of \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable \(L^2\)-random variables: \[L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P) \coloneqq \{ X \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P) \mid X \text{ is } \mathcal{G}\text{-measurable} \}\]

Theorem 68.1 (Closure of Sub-\(\sigma\)-Field \(L^2\) Spaces) The subset \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\) is a closed linear subspace of \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 68.1). 

Subspace Property:
If \(X, Y \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\) and \(\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}\), then \(\alpha X + \beta Y\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable. Moreover, by Minkowski’s inequality: \[\|\alpha X + \beta Y\|_{L^2} \le |\alpha| \|X\|_{L^2} + |\beta| \|Y\|_{L^2} < \infty\] Thus, \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\) is a vector subspace of \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\).
Closedness Property:
Let \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty} \subset L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\) be a sequence such that \(X_n \to X\) in \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\). Convergence in \(L^2\) implies convergence in probability, which guarantees the existence of a subsequence \(\{X_{n_k}\}\) converging almost surely to \(X\): \[X_{n_k} \xrightarrow{a.s.} X \quad \text{as } k \to \infty\] Since each \(X_{n_k}\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, the almost sure limit \(X\) is also \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable (modulo null sets under completion). Hence, \(X \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\), showing that \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\) is closed.

title: 68  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation-Part II
text:
68.3 Definition of Conditional Expectation in \(L^2\)

Definition 68.1 (Conditional Expectation in \(L^2\)) For any \(X \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) and sub-\(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\), the conditional expectation of \(X\) given \(\mathcal{G}\), denoted \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) or \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\), is defined as the orthogonal projection of \(X\) onto \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\): \[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \coloneqq P_{L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)}(X).
\]
By Theorem 67.1 and Theorem 67.2, \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) is the unique \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable random variable satisfying the orthogonality condition: \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] Y] = \mathbb{E}[XY] \quad \forall Y \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P).
\]

title: 68  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation-Part II
text:
68.6 Extension of Conditional Expectation to \(L^1\)
To extend the definition from \(L^2\) to \(L^1\), we first establish a contractivity lemma in \(L^1\).

Lemma 68.1 (\(L^1\)-Contraction Lemma) For any \(X \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), \[
\mathbb{E}\left[|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]|\right] \le \mathbb{E}[|X|].
\] That is, \(\|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\|_{L^1} \le \|X\|_{L^1}\).


Note that the \(L^1\) norms are

\(\|X\|_{L^1} = \mathbb{E}[|X|]=\int_\Omega |X| dP\), and
\(\|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\|_{L^1} = \mathbb{E}[|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]|] = \int_\Omega |\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]| dP\) is the \(L^1\) norm of the conditional expectation.

The lemma states that the conditional expectation operator is a contraction in \(L^1\).


Proof (Proof of Lemma 68.1). Set \(Y = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\). Consider the sign function \(Z = \operatorname{sgn}(Y)\), defined as: \[
\begin{align*}
Z(\omega) &= \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } Y(\omega) > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } Y(\omega) = 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } Y(\omega) < 0 \end{cases}\\
&=\mathbb{I}_{\{Y\ne0\}} \frac{Y}{|Y|}.
\end{align*}
\] Since \(Y\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, \(Z\) is also \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable. Furthermore, \(|Z(\omega)| \le 1\), so \(Z \in L^\infty(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P) \subset L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\).
Using \(Z\) as a test function in the orthogonality characterization of \(L^2\) conditional expectation: \[
\mathbb{E}[|Y|] = \mathbb{E}[Y \cdot \operatorname{sgn}(Y)] = \mathbb{E}[Y Z] = \mathbb{E}[X Z].
\] Since \(|Z(\omega)| \le 1\), we have \[
\mathbb{E}[|Y|] = \mathbb{E}[X Z] \le \mathbb{E}[|X Z|] \le \mathbb{E}[|X| \cdot 1] = \mathbb{E}[|X|].
\] Hence, \(\|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\|_{L^1} \le \|X\|_{L^1}\).

title: 68  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation-Part II
text:
68.7 Extension Procedure via Density
Note that \(L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\subset L^1(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\). Indeed, by Cauchy–Schwarz, \[
\mathbb E[|X|] = \mathbb E[|X|\cdot 1] \leq \sqrt{\mathbb E[X^2]}\sqrt{\mathbb E[1]} = \sqrt{\mathbb E[X^2]}.
\] So \(X\in L^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad X\in L^1\). But the converse is not true. For example, a random variable can have a finite first moment but an infinite second moment. So the hierarchy is: \(L^2 \subsetneq L^1\). This distinction is important: \(L^1\) is the natural space for defining conditional expectation in general, whereas \(L^2\) is the natural space when we want the geometric interpretation as an orthogonal projection.
In this section, we will discuss how to extend the definition of conditional expectation from \(L^2\) to \(L^1\) using the density of \(L^2\) in \(L^1\).

Density of \(L^2\) in \(L^1\): For any \(X \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), define \(X_n = X \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\{|X| \le n\}}\). Each \(X_n\) is bounded, hence \(X_n \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\). By the Dominated Convergence Theorem (DCT): \[
\|X - X_n\|_{L^1} = \mathbb{E}[|X| \mathbb{1}_{\{|X| > n\}}] \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0.
\] Therefore, \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) is dense in \(L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\). That is, for any \(X \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), there exists a sequence \(\{X_n\} \subset L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) such that \[
\|X - X_n\|_{L^1} \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0.
\]
Definition in \(L^1\): Given \(X \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), select any sequence \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) converging to \(X\) in \(L^1\). By Lemma 68.1: \[
\|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X_n] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X_m]\|_{L^1} = \|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X_n - X_m]\|_{L^1} \le \|X_n - X_m\|_{L^1}.
\] Thus, \(\{\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X_n]\}_{n=1}^\infty\) is a Cauchy sequence in the complete space \(L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\). We define: \[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \coloneqq L^1\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X_n]= L^1\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} P_{L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)}(X_n).
\] That is, we have \[
\|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X_n]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\|_{L^1} = \mathbb{E}\left[\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X_n]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\right|\right] \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0.
\]
Well-Definedness: If \(\{Y_n\}\) is another sequence in \(L^2\) converging to \(X\) in \(L^1\), then: \[
\|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X_n] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[Y_n]\|_{L^1} \le \|X_n - Y_n\|_{L^1} \to 0.
\] The limit is unique and independent of the choice of approximating sequence.
Conclusion: This gives the standard \(L^1\)-conditional expectation as an extension of the \(L^2\) orthogonal-projection operator. That is, conceptually,

\(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] = P_{L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)}(X) \quad \text{for } X \in L^2\), and
\(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] = L^1\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} P_{L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)}(X_n) \quad \text{for } X \in L^1\), where \(X_n \in L^2\) and \(X_n \to X\) in \(L^1\).


So structurally, we have the following hierarchy and extension process: \[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c} X\in L^2 \\[2mm] \downarrow \\ \mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G] =P_{L^2(\Omega,\mathcal{G},P)}(X) \\[2mm] \downarrow\quad\text{\(L^1\)-contraction} \\ \text{continuous extension} \\[2mm] \downarrow \\ X\in L^1 \\[2mm] \mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G] = L^1\!-\!\lim_n\mathbb E[X_n\mid\mathcal G]= L^1\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} P_{L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)}(X_n).
\end{array}
}
\] That gives a very clean geometric-to-measure-theoretic construction of conditional expectation.

title: 68  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation-Part II
text:
68.8 Averaging Property / Characterization
By Definition 68.1, the orthogonality condition gives the following averaging property for conditional expectation: \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] Y] = \mathbb{E}[XY] \quad \forall Y \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P).
\] In the case of \(L^1\), the averaging characterization uses \(Y\in\mathcal B_b(\Omega,\mathcal G)\). This change is important. For \(X\in L^1\), the product \(XY\) is guaranteed to be integrable when \(Y\) is bounded: \[
|XY|\leq \|Y\|_\infty |X|\in L^1.
\] So bounded \(\mathcal G\)-measurable functions are exactly the natural test functions for the \(L^1\) definition.

Theorem 68.2 (Averaging Property) For \(X \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) and sub-\(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\), the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) is the unique \(L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\) random variable satisfying: \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] Y] = \mathbb{E}[XY] \quad \forall Y \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G}),
\] where \(\mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\) denotes the space of bounded, \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable random variables.


Proof (Proof of Theorem 68.2). 

Existence:
For \(X \in L^2\), this holds directly by Definition 68.1. For general \(X \in L^1\), let \(X_n \in L^2 \to X\) in \(L^1\). For each \(n\), since \(X_n \in L^2\), the \(L^2\) definition gives: \[\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X_n] Y] = \mathbb{E}[X_n Y].\] We pass to the limit \(n \to \infty\) on both sides. Fix any \(Y \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\) with \(|Y| \le M\). On the left side: \[|\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X_n] Y] - \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] Y]| \le M \|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X_n] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\|_{L^1} \to 0.\] On the right side: \[|\mathbb{E}[X_n Y] - \mathbb{E}[XY]| \le M \|X_n - X\|_{L^1} \to 0.\] Since both sides converge to the same quantity in the limit, we conclude \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] Y] = \mathbb{E}[XY]\).
Uniqueness:
Suppose \(Z_1, Z_2 \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\) both satisfy the property. Then \(\mathbb{E}[(Z_1 - Z_2) Y] = 0\) for all \(Y \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\).
Choose \(Y_n = \operatorname{sgn}(Z_1 - Z_2) \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\{|Z_1 - Z_2| \le n\}} \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\). Then: \[0 = \mathbb{E}[(Z_1 - Z_2) Y_n] = \mathbb{E}[|Z_1 - Z_2| \mathbb{1}_{\{|Z_1 - Z_2| \le n\}}]\] By Monotone Convergence Theorem (MCT) as \(n \to \infty\), \(\mathbb{E}[|Z_1 - Z_2|] = 0\), implying \(Z_1 = Z_2\) almost surely.



Remark 68.1 (Remark on Averaging Property with Indicator Functions). The averaging property can be particularly useful when \(Y\) is taken as an indicator function of a \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable set \(A \in \mathcal{G}\): \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \mathbb{1}_A] = \mathbb{E}[X \mathbb{1}_A].
\] This shows that the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) correctly averages \(X\) over the sets in \(\mathcal{G}\).
In terms of integral notation, the averaging property with indicator functions can be written as: \[
\int_A \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \, dP = \int_A X \, dP.
\] Thus, the conditional expectation preserves the integral of \(X\) over every event whose occurrence can be determined from \(\mathcal G\). That is why it is called the averaging property.
Finally, note that the indicator function characterization is equivalent to the averaging property for all bounded \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable functions, since any such function can be approximated by linear combinations of indicator functions.

title: 68  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation-Part II
text:
68.9 Fundamental Properties of Conditional Expectation

Theorem 68.3 Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) be a probability space, \(\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) a sub-\(\sigma\)-field, and \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}: L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P) \to L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\) the linear operator.

Monotonicity:
If \(X \le Y\) a.s., then \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \le \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[Y]\) a.s.
Triangle Inequality:
\(|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]| \le \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[|X|]\) a.s. If \(|X| \le M\) a.s., then \(|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]| \le M\) a.s.
Averaging Property:
\(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] Y] = \mathbb{E}[XY]\) for all \(Y \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\).
Product Rule (Taking out what is known):
If \(Y \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\), then \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[XY] = Y \cdot \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) a.s.
Tower Property (Iterated Expectations):
If \(\mathcal{H} \subseteq \mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) are sub-\(\sigma\)-fields, then: \[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X]] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X] \quad \text{a.s.}\]

title: 68  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation-Part II
text:
68.10 Detailed Proofs of Fundamental Properties
Property (3) is exactly the averaging characterization established in Theorem 68.2, so the only remaining properties to verify here are (1), (2), (4), and (5).

68.10.1 Proof of (1) Monotonicity:
First, we establish the positivity of conditional expectation. Suppose \(Z\ge0\) a.s. Define \(A=\{\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal G]<0\}\). Since \(\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal G]\) is \(\mathcal G\)-measurable, \(A\in\mathcal G\). By the averaging property, \[
\mathbb E\left[\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal G]1_A\right] = \mathbb E[Z1_A].
\] The right-hand side is nonnegative because \(Z\ge0\) a.s. However, on \(A\), \(\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal G]1_A<0\). Therefore, if \(P(A)>0\), \[
\mathbb E\left[\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal G]1_A\right]<0,
\] which contradicts \(\mathbb E[Z1_A]\ge0\). Hence \(P(A)=0\), so \[
Z\ge0\quad\text{a.s.} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal G]\ge0\quad\text{a.s.}
\] Now, since \(X\le Y\) a.s., we have \(Y-X\ge0\quad\text{a.s.}\). By positivity, \(\mathbb E[Y-X\mid\mathcal G]\ge0\quad\text{a.s.}\). Using linearity, \[
\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G]-\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\ge0 \quad\text{a.s.}
\] Therefore, \(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\le \mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.}\). So the essential argument is positivity first, then apply it to \(Y-X\). \(\blacksquare\)


68.10.2 Proof of (2) Triangle Inequality:
Note that \(X \le |X|\) and \(-X \le |X|\) a.s.
By Monotonicity (1): \[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \le \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[|X|] \quad \text{and} \quad -\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[-X] \le \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[|X|]\] Combining both yields \(|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]| \le \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[|X|]\) a.s.
If \(|X| \le M\) a.s., then \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[|X|] \le \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[M] = M\) a.s. \(\blacksquare\)


68.10.3 Proof of (4) Product Rule:
Let \(Y \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\) with \(|Y| \le M\). Since \(X \in L^1\) and \(Y\) is bounded, \(XY \in L^1\), so \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[XY]\) is well-defined. We prove the claim by verifying that \(Y \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) satisfies the two conditions that uniquely characterize \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[XY]\) via Theorem 68.2.
\(\mathcal{G}\)-measurability: Both \(Y\) and \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) are \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, so their product \(Y \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable. Moreover, \(\|Y \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\|_{L^1} \le M \|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\|_{L^1} \le M \|X\|_{L^1} < \infty\), so \(Y \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\).
Averaging property: For any test function \(Z \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\), the product \(YZ\) is also bounded and \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, i.e. \(YZ \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\). Since \(|XYZ| \le M\|Z\|_\infty |X|\), all expectations below are finite. Therefore: \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\left[(Y \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]) \cdot Z\right] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \cdot (YZ)\right] && \text{(rearranging)} \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[X \cdot (YZ)\right] && \text{(averaging property)} \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[(XY) \cdot Z\right]. && \text{(rearranging)}
\end{align*}
\] Since \(Y \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable and satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \cdot Z] = \mathbb{E}[XY \cdot Z]\) for all \(Z \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\), uniqueness in Theorem 68.2 gives \(Y \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[XY]\) a.s. \(\blacksquare\)


68.10.4 Proof of (5) Tower Property:
Let \(\mathcal{H} \subseteq \mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\).
Since \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P) \subseteq L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) and \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X] \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{H}, P)\), both iterated conditional expectations are well-defined. For any \(Z \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{H})\), since \(\mathcal{H} \subseteq \mathcal{G}\), we also have \(Z \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\).
Using the averaging property at level \(\mathcal{H}\), then level \(\mathcal{G}\): \[\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]] Z\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] Z\right] = \mathbb{E}[X Z] = \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X] Z\right]\] By uniqueness of the conditional expectation onto \(\mathcal{H}\), we conclude: \[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X] \quad \text{a.s.}\] For the second equality, note that \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X]\) is \(\mathcal{H}\)-measurable, hence also \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable because \(\mathcal{H} \subseteq \mathcal{G}\). More generally, if \(W \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\), then \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[W] = W\) a.s.: \(W\) is already \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable and, for every \(Z \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\), it satisfies the averaging identity \[
\mathbb{E}[WZ] = \mathbb{E}[WZ].
\] Therefore, by uniqueness in Theorem 68.2, \(W\) must equal its own conditional expectation given \(\mathcal{G}\). Applying this fixed-point property with \(W = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X]\) yields \[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X]] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X] \quad \text{a.s.}
\] Combining the two identities proves \[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X]] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}}[X] \quad \text{a.s.}
\] The first equality is the substantive tower property; the second follows from the fact that conditioning does nothing to a random variable that is already measurable with respect to the conditioning \(\sigma\)-field. \(\blacksquare\)

title: 68  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation-Part II
text:
68.11 Takeaways
1. Conditional expectation as orthogonal projection in \(L^2\).
For \(X \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[X]\) is defined as the orthogonal projection onto the closed subspace \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\). The closedness of this subspace — proved by extracting an a.s.-convergent subsequence from any \(L^2\)-Cauchy sequence of \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable functions — is precisely what makes the Hilbert-space projection theorem applicable.
2. The averaging property is the universal characterization.
\(\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[X]\) is the unique \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable \(L^1\) random variable satisfying \[\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[X] \cdot Y] = \mathbb{E}[XY] \quad \forall Y \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{G}).\] This is orthogonality rewritten in \(L^1\) language. Uniqueness uses the sign-function test: setting \(Y_n = \operatorname{sgn}(Z_1 - Z_2)\mathbb{1}_{\{|Z_1-Z_2| \le n\}}\) and applying MCT forces \(\mathbb{E}[|Z_1 - Z_2|] = 0\), hence \(Z_1 = Z_2\) a.s.
3. Extension from \(L^2\) to \(L^1\) rests on three steps.

\(L^1\)-contraction: \(\|\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[X]\|_{L^1} \le \|X\|_{L^1}\) for \(X \in L^2\), proved by using \(\operatorname{sgn}(\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[X])\) as a bounded \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable test function and applying Hölder.

Density: the truncations \(X_n = X \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\{|X| \le n\}}\) show \(L^2\) is dense in \(L^1\) via DCT.

Cauchy completion: the contraction makes \(\{\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[X_n]\}\) Cauchy in the complete space \(L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, P)\); well-definedness follows because any two approximating sequences yield the same \(L^1\) limit.

4. Monotonicity is proved by a zero-integral sandwich argument.
To show \(X \le Y\) a.s. implies \(\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[X] \le \mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[Y]\) a.s., let \(B = \{\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[Y-X] < 0\}\). Using \(\mathbb{1}_B\) as a test function gives \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[Y-X]\mathbb{1}_B] = \mathbb{E}[(Y-X)\mathbb{1}_B] \ge 0\), while the definition of \(B\) forces the same quantity to be \(\le 0\). Hence \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[Y-X]\mathbb{1}_B] = 0\), so \(P(B) = 0\).
5. The product rule and tower property both reduce to the uniqueness of conditional expectation.

Product rule: verify that \(Y\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[X]\) satisfies the averaging characterization of \(\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[XY]\) by testing against \(Z \in \mathcal{B}_b(\mathcal{G})\): the product \(YZ\) is bounded \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, so the averaging property applies to shift \(Y\) inside.

Tower property (\(\mathcal{H} \subseteq \mathcal{G}\)): \(\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{H}[\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[X]] = \mathbb{E}_\mathcal{H}[X]\) because both satisfy the same \(\mathcal{H}\)-averaging property (since every \(Z \in \mathcal{B}_b(\mathcal{H}) \subseteq \mathcal{B}_b(\mathcal{G})\) can be used to apply \(\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}\) and then \(\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{H}\) in sequence). The reverse identity \(\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{H}[X]] = \mathbb{E}_\mathcal{H}[X]\) follows from idempotency: any \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable \(W \in L^1\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{G}[W] = W\) by uniqueness, since \(W\) trivially satisfies its own averaging characterization.

title: 1  Lecture 0: Banach Tarski
text:
1.1 Introduction to Measurement
To motivate the mathematical necessity of measure theory, consider the fundamental problem of measuring the length (or proportion) of subsets of the unit circle in the complex plane \(\mathbb{C}\): \[
S^1 := \{ z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| = 1 \}.
\tag{1.1}\]
For any given subset \(E \subseteq S^1\), we would like to assign a real number \(\mu(E) \ge 0\) representing the “proportion of the circle” covered by \(E\) (so that \(0 \le \mu(E) \le 1\)).

title: 1  Lecture 0: Banach Tarski
section: 1.2 Axiomatic Properties of a Measurement Function
text:
1.2 Axiomatic Properties of a Measurement Function
An ideal measurement function \(\mu: 2^{S^1} \to [0, 1]\) on the power set of \(S^1\) should satisfy the following natural axioms:

Definition 1.1 (Properties of Measurements) Let \(S^1\) be the unit circle. A set function \(\mu: 2^{S^1} \to [0, 1]\) is a valid measurement if:

Normalization: \[
\mu(S^1) = 1.
\tag{1.2}\]
Finite Additivity (\(2'\)): If \(E_1, E_2 \subseteq S^1\) are disjoint (\(E_1 \cap E_2 = \emptyset\)), then: \[
\mu(E_1 \cup E_2) = \mu(E_1) + \mu(E_2).
\tag{1.3}\]
Countable Additivity (\(2\)): If \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty\) is a countable sequence of pairwise disjoint subsets of \(S^1\) (\(E_i \cap E_j = \emptyset\) for all \(i \neq j\)), then: \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu(E_j).
\tag{1.4}\]
Rotational Invariance (\(3\)): If two subsets \(E_1, E_2 \subseteq S^1\) are congruent (i.e., \(E_2\) is obtained from \(E_1\) by a rigid rotation \(u \in S^1\)), then: \[
\mu(E_1) = \mu(E_2).
\tag{1.5}\] Explicitly, for any \(u \in S^1\) and \(E \subseteq S^1\), defining \(u E := \{ u z : z \in E \}\), rotational invariance requires \(\mu(u E) = \mu(E)\).

title: 1  Lecture 0: Banach Tarski
text:
1.3 Non-Existence Theorem (Vitali-Type Construction)

Theorem 1.1 (Non-Existence of a Universally Defined Measure) There is no set function \(\mu: 2^{S^1} \to [0, 1]\) that simultaneously satisfies Normalization (Equation 1.2), Countable Additivity (Equation 4.1), and Rotational Invariance (Equation 1.5).


Proof. Consider the countable dense subgroup of rotations \(T \subset S^1\) corresponding to rational angles in \([0, 2\pi)\): \[
T := \{ e^{2\pi i t} : t \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0, 1) \}.
\tag{1.6}\] Notice that \(T\) is a countable subgroup of \(S^1\) under complex multiplication.
Define an equivalence relation \(\sim\) on \(S^1\) by setting: \[
z \sim w \iff z = u w \text{ for some } u \in T.
\tag{1.7}\]
By the Axiom of Choice, select exactly one representative element \(q\) from each equivalence class in \(S^1 / \sim\), and collect these representatives into a set \(E_0 \subset S^1\): \[
E_0 = \{ q \in S^1 : q \text{ is the chosen representative of its class} \}.
\tag{1.8}\]
We establish two claims regarding \(E_0\):

Disjointness: If \(u_1, u_2 \in T\) with \(u_1 \neq u_2\), then \((u_1 E_0) \cap (u_2 E_0) = \emptyset\).

Proof: If \(z \in (u_1 E_0) \cap (u_2 E_0)\), then \(z = u_1 q_1 = u_2 q_2\) for some \(q_1, q_2 \in E_0\). This implies \(q_1 = (u_1^{-1} u_2) q_2\), so \(q_1 \sim q_2\). By construction of \(E_0\), \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) must be the same representative element, so \(q_1 = q_2\). Thus \(u_1 = u_2\), establishing disjointness.

Partitioning \(S^1\): The rotated copies of \(E_0\) cover the entire circle: \[
S^1 = \bigcup_{u \in T} u E_0.
\tag{1.9}\]

Proof: For any \(z \in S^1\), \(z\) belongs to some equivalence class with representative \(q \in E_0\). Thus \(z \sim q\), which means \(z = u q \in u E_0\) for some \(u \in T\).


Now, apply the measurement function \(\mu\) to Equation 1.9. By normalization (Equation 1.2) and countable additivity (Equation 4.1): \[
1 = \mu(S^1) = \mu\left( \bigcup_{u \in T} u E_0 \right) = \sum_{u \in T} \mu(u E_0).
\tag{1.10}\]
By rotational invariance (Equation 1.5), \(\mu(u E_0) = \mu(E_0)\) for all \(u \in T\). Substituting this into Equation 1.10 yields: \[
1 = \sum_{u \in T} \mu(E_0).
\tag{1.11}\]
Since \(T\) is countably infinite, the constant sum \(\sum_{u \in T} \mu(E_0)\) presents a contradiction:

If \(\mu(E_0) = 0\), then \(\sum_{u \in T} 0 = 0 \neq 1\).
If \(\mu(E_0) > 0\), then \(\sum_{u \in T} \mu(E_0) = \infty \neq 1\).

Thus, no such measurement function \(\mu\) can exist on all subsets of \(S^1\).

title: 1  Lecture 0: Banach Tarski
text:
1.4 Resolution: \(\sigma\)-Algebras and Non-Measurable Sets
The measurement function \(\mu(E) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_E \mathrm{d}\theta\) is used daily in ordinary calculus. How can it fail to exist?
The answer lies in an important subtlety: the definition of the Riemann integral only works over “nice” sets. The Vitali-type set \(E_0\) is logically well-defined — its construction requires only the Axiom of Choice — but it is measure-theoretically pathological: it is non-measurable and cannot be assigned a consistent length.
Much of measure theory is spent extending the Riemann integral to the Lebesgue integral over a restricted, rich family of sets called a \(\sigma\)-algebra (\(\mathcal{F}\)). BUT there is a fundamental limit: there’s only so far it can be extended.

title: 1  Lecture 0: Banach Tarski
section: 1.5 The Moral of the Story and Kolmogorov’s Probability Theory
text:
1.5 The Moral of the Story and Kolmogorov’s Probability Theory
This non-existence result might seem like a bad sign… but it is actually a foundational truth for Kolmogorov’s modern probability theory.

Key Takeaway: In probability theory, we do not always have complete information about the world, which means there may be some events (subsets of \(\Omega\)) to which we simply cannot assign probabilities. Consequently, probability measures \(\mathbb{P}\) must be defined on a designated \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F} \subset 2^\Omega\) of measurable events, rather than the full power set \(2^\Omega\).

title: 1  Lecture 0: Banach Tarski
text:
1.6 The Banach–Tarski Paradox
The existence of non-measurable sets leads to paradoxical decompositions in higher dimensions.

Theorem 1.2 (Banach–Tarski Paradox (Banach & Tarski, 1924)) Given any two bounded subsets \(E, F \subset \mathbb{R}^d\) (\(d \ge 3\)) with non-empty interior, there exist finite partitions: \[
E = \bigcup_{j=1}^n E_j \quad \text{and} \quad F = \bigcup_{j=1}^n F_j
\tag{1.12}\] with \(E_i \cap E_j = \emptyset\) and \(F_i \cap F_j = \emptyset\) for \(i \neq j\), such that \(E_j\) is congruent to \(F_j\) via rigid rotations and translations for each \(1 \le j \le n\).


Remark (Robinson’s Refinement, 1947): If \(E\) is a solid ball in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) and \(F\) consists of two disjoint solid balls of the same radius, the Banach–Tarski theorem holds explicitly with as few as \(n = 5\) non-measurable pieces!

title: 1  Lecture 0: Banach Tarski Banach Tarski
text:
1.7 Summary of Transcriptions & Reconstructions

Explicit Rigor Added:

Rigorously formulated the non-existence proof (Vitali set construction on \(S^1\)) using the rational rotations subgroup \(T\)[cite: 4].
Added step-by-step verification showing that \(E_0\) forms a partition of \(S^1\) via disjoint rotated translates \(u E_0\)[cite: 4].
Contextualized the breakdown of universal measures as the foundational motivation for \(\sigma\)-algebras in Kolmogorov’s probability theory[cite: 4].
Formalized the Banach–Tarski Paradox and Robinson’s 5-piece sphere duplication theorem[cite: 4].

Handwriting & Notation Clean-up:

Fixed notation for unit circle elements \(z \in S^1\), rotation subgroups \(T \subset S^1\), and equivalence classes \(S^1 / \sim\)[cite: 4].
Corrected historical citation dates (Banach–Tarski Paradox published in 1924; Raphael M. Robinson’s 5-piece proof in 1947)[cite: 4].

title: 1  Lecture 0: Banach Tarski
text:
1.7 Takeaways

No universal measure exists on \(S^1\). No set function \(\mu: 2^{S^1} \to [0,1]\) can simultaneously satisfy normalization, countable additivity, and rotational invariance. The proof constructs a Vitali set \(E_0\) using the Axiom of Choice by selecting one representative from each orbit of \(T = \{e^{2\pi i t} : t \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1)\}\). The rotated copies \(\{uE_0 : u \in T\}\) are disjoint (since \(q_1 \sim q_2\) and both in \(E_0\) forces \(q_1 = q_2\)) and cover \(S^1\), so countable additivity and rotational invariance force \(1 = \sum_{u \in T} \mu(E_0)\), which is impossible for any constant \(\mu(E_0) \ge 0\).
Resolution via \(\sigma\)-algebras. The Lebesgue measure \(\mu(E) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_E d\theta\) is well-defined on the \(\sigma\)-algebra of Lebesgue-measurable sets, which excludes non-measurable sets like \(E_0\). Measure theory resolves the paradox by restricting \(\mu\) to a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F} \subsetneq 2^{S^1}\) rather than attempting to measure every subset.
Banach–Tarski paradox. In \(\mathbb{R}^d\) for \(d \ge 3\), any two bounded sets with non-empty interior are equidecomposable into finitely many pieces related by rigid motions. In particular, a solid ball can be reassembled into two balls of the same size. This is not physically realizable because the pieces are non-measurable — the usual principle that rigid motions preserve volume does not apply to them.
Kolmogorov’s framework. The non-existence result is a foundational feature of modern probability: not all subsets of the sample space \(\Omega\) can be assigned probabilities. The probability triple \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) restricts \(\mathbb{P}\) to a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F} \subset 2^\Omega\) of measurable events. This is not a limitation but a necessity imposed by the structure of the real line.

title: 2  Lecture 1.1: Probability Motivation
text:
2.1 Experiments, Sample Spaces, and Events
Probability theory provides a mathematically rigorous language for modeling non-deterministic phenomena or “experiments”.

title: 2  Lecture 1.1: Probability Motivation
text:
Definition 2.1 (Outcome, Sample Space, and Event)  

An outcome \(\omega\) is a single possible result of a random experiment.
The sample space \(\Omega\) (or \(\mathcal{S}\)) is the set of all possible outcomes of the experiment.
An event \(E\) is a measurable subset of the sample space, i.e., \(E \subseteq \Omega\) (\(E \in \mathcal{F}\) for a given \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F}\) on \(\Omega\)).

title: 2  Lecture 1.1: Probability Motivation
text:
2.2 Motivating Examples

2.2.1 Example 1: Discrete Finite Sample Space (Coin Tossing)
Consider tossing a fair coin \(N = 4\) times. The sample space \(\Omega = \{H, T\}^4\) contains \(2^4 = 16\) equally likely outcomes.
Consider the event \(E \subset \Omega\): “Obtaining exactly 3 heads and 1 tail.” \[
E = \{ HHHT, \, HHTH, \, HTHH, \, THHH \}.
\tag{2.1}\]
Since all \(16\) elementary outcomes are equiprobable, the probability of the event \(E\) is: \[
\mathbb{P}(E) = \frac{\vert{}E\vert{}}{\vert{}\Omega\vert{}} = \frac{4}{16} = \frac{1}{4}.
\]



2.2.2 Example 2: Continuous Sample Space (Geometric Probability)
Throw a dart at a circular target of radius \(R > 0\). Modeling the point of impact as a uniform continuous random variable over the target, the sample space is: \[\Omega = \{ (x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : x^2 + y^2 \le R^2 \}.\] {#eq-dart-space}
For any measurable region \(E \subseteq \Omega\), the probability of the dart landing in \(E\) is given by the ratio of two-dimensional Lebesgue measures (areas): \[
\mathbb{P}(E) = \frac{\operatorname{Leb}(E)}{\operatorname{Leb}(\Omega)} = \frac{\operatorname{Area}(E)}{\pi R^2}.
\tag{2.2}\]

title: 2  Lecture 1.1: Probability Motivation
section: 2.3 Finite vs. Countably Infinite Sample Spaces
text:
2.3 Finite vs. Countably Infinite Sample Spaces
Consider an experiment that continues indefinitely until a specific condition is met.

Example 2.1 (Coin Tossing Until First Tail) Suppose a fair coin is tossed repeatedly until Tails (\(T\)) appears for the first time.
What is the probability that the total number of tosses required is odd?

2.3.1 Formalization
Let \(\Omega\) be the space of infinite binary sequences \(\omega = (\omega_1, \omega_2, \dots) \in \{H, T\}^{\mathbb{N}}\). The countable subset of sequences where \(T\) eventually appears can be indexed by \(n \ge 1\), where \(n\) represents the stopping time: \[
E_j := \{ \omega \in \Omega : \omega_1 = H, \dots, \omega_{2j} = H, \omega_{2j+1} = T \}, \quad j \ge 0.
\tag{2.3}\] \(E_j\) represents the outcome where the first Tail occurs on precisely the \((2j+1)\)-th toss (an odd index).
Since the coin is fair and tosses are independent, the probability of \(E_j\) is: \[\mathbb{P}(E_j) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2j+1} = \frac{1}{2^{2j+1}}, \quad j \ge 0. \tag{2.4}\]
The event \(E\) that the total number of tosses is odd is the countable disjoint union: \[
E = \bigcup_{j=0}^\infty E_j.
\tag{2.5}\]


2.3.2 Calculation via Countable Additivity
Applying countable additivity and summing the resulting geometric series: \[
\begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(E) &= \sum_{j=0}^\infty \mathbb{P}(E_j) = \sum_{j=0}^\infty \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2j+1} \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j=0}^\infty \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^j \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - 1/4} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{4}{3} = \frac{2}{3}. \end{aligned}
\tag{2.6}\] Thus, the probability that the total number of tosses is odd is \(\frac{2}{3}\).

title: 2  Lecture 1.1: Probability Motivation
section: 2.4 Formal Definition of a Probability Measure
text:
2.4 Formal Definition of a Probability Measure

Definition 2.2 (Probability Measure (Kolmogorov Axioms)) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and \(\mathcal{F}\) be a \(\sigma\)-algebra of subsets of \(\Omega\). A set function \(\mathbb{P}: \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]\) is called a probability measure if it satisfies:

Normalization: \[
\mathbb{P}(\Omega) = 1.
\tag{2.7}\]
Countable Additivity (\(\sigma\)-Additivity): For any countable sequence of pairwise disjoint events \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subset \mathcal{F}\) (where \(E_i \cap E_j = \emptyset\) for all \(i \neq j\)): \[
\mathbb{P}\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mathbb{P}(E_j). \tag{2.8}\]

title: 2  Lecture 1.1: Probability Motivation
text:
2.5 Elementary Consequences of the Axioms
From the core axioms (Equation 2.7 and Equation 2.8), fundamental rules of probability immediately follow:

Proposition 2.1 (Basic Rules of Probability) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space.

Finite Additivity: If \(E_1, E_2 \in \mathcal{F}\) are disjoint (\(E_1 \cap E_2 = \emptyset\)), then: \[
\mathbb{P}(E_1 \cup E_2) = \mathbb{P}(E_1) + \mathbb{P}(E_2).
\tag{2.9}\]
Complement Rule: For any event \(E \in \mathcal{F}\), let \(E^c = \Omega \setminus E\) denote its complement. Then: \[
\mathbb{P}(E^c) = 1 - \mathbb{P}(E).
\tag{2.10}\]
Empty Set Probability: The probability of the empty set \(\emptyset\) is zero: \[
\mathbb{P}(\emptyset) = 0.
\tag{2.11}\]



Proof. 

Set \(E_3 = E_4 = \dots = \emptyset\) in Equation 2.8. Countable additivity reduces directly to finite additivity.
For any \(E \in \mathcal{F}\), \(E\) and \(E^c\) are disjoint, and \(E \cup E^c = \Omega\). By finite additivity and normalization: \[
\mathbb{P}(E) + \mathbb{P}(E^c) = \mathbb{P}(E \cup E^c) = \mathbb{P}(\Omega) = 1 \implies \mathbb{P}(E^c) = 1 - \mathbb{P}(E).
\]
Taking \(E = \Omega\) in the complement rule gives \(\mathbb{P}(\emptyset) = \mathbb{P}(\Omega^c) = 1 - \mathbb{P}(\Omega) = 1 - 1 = 0\).

title: 2  Lecture 1.1: Probability Motivation
text:
2.6 Basic Rules of Probability
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space.

Finite Additivity: If \(E_1, E_2 \in \mathcal{F}\) are disjoint (\(E_1 \cap E_2 = \emptyset\)), then: \[
\mathbb{P}(E_1 \cup E_2) = \mathbb{P}(E_1) + \mathbb{P}(E_2).
\tag{2.9}\]
Complement Rule: For any event \(E \in \mathcal{F}\), let \(E^c = \Omega \setminus E\) denote its complement. Then: \[
\mathbb{P}(E^c) = 1 - \mathbb{P}(E).
\tag{2.10}\]
Empty Set Probability: The probability of the empty set \(\emptyset\) is zero: \[
\mathbb{P}(\emptyset) = 0.
\tag{2.11}\]

title: 3  Lecture 1.2: Sigma Algebra
text:
3.1 Fields and \(\sigma\)-Fields (\(\sigma\)-Algebras)
Let \(\Omega\) be a non-empty sample space (any set). We aim to define structured collections of subsets of \(\Omega\) that behave predictably under standard set-theoretic operations.

title: 3  Lecture 1.2: Sigma Algebra
text:
Definition 3.1 (Field (Algebra of Sets)) A collection \(\mathcal{F} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) of subsets of \(\Omega\) is called a field (or an algebra) over \(\Omega\) if it satisfies the following three conditions:

Entire Space Inclusion: \[
\Omega \in \mathcal{F}.
\tag{3.1}\]
Closure under Complement: \[
\text{If } E \in \mathcal{F}, \quad \text{then } E^c \in \mathcal{F},
\tag{3.2}\] where \(E^c := \Omega \setminus E\).
Closure under Finite Unions: \[
\text{If } E_1, E_2, \dots, E_n \in \mathcal{F}, \quad \text{then } \bigcup_{j=1}^n E_j \in \mathcal{F}.
\tag{3.3}\]



Definition 3.2 (\(\sigma\)-Field (\(\sigma\)-Algebra)) If, instead of condition (3) in Definition 3.1, \(\mathcal{F}\) satisfies the stronger property of closure under countable unions, then \(\mathcal{F}\) is called a \(\sigma\)-field (or a \(\sigma\)-algebra) over \(\Omega\):

Closure under Countable Unions: \[
\text{If } \{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}, \quad \text{then } \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \in \mathcal{F}.
\tag{3.4}\]



De Morgan’s Laws: By De Morgan’s laws, closure under complements and unions implies closure under intersections for both fields and \(\sigma\)-fields: \[
\left( \bigcup_{j} E_j \right)^c = \bigcap_{j} E_j^c.
\tag{3.5}\]

title: 3  Lecture 1.2: Sigma Algebra
text:
3.2 Canonical Examples of \(\sigma\)-Fields

Power Set \(\sigma\)-Field: For any sample space \(\Omega\), the full power set \(2^\Omega\) is the largest possible \(\sigma\)-field over \(\Omega\).
Trivial \(\sigma\)-Field: The collection \(\mathcal{F} = \{\emptyset, \Omega\}\) is the smallest possible \(\sigma\)-field over \(\Omega\).
Finite Discrete Example: Let \(\Omega = \{1, 2, 3\}\). Then \(\mathcal{F} = \{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2, 3\}, \Omega\}\) is a valid \(\sigma\)-field over \(\Omega\).
Cofinite / Countable-Cocountable \(\sigma\)-Field: Let \(\Omega\) be an uncountable set. Define: \[
\mathcal{F} = \{ B \subseteq \Omega : B \text{ is countable or } B^c \text{ is countable} \}.
\tag{3.6}\] Then \(\mathcal{F}\) is a valid \(\sigma\)-field over \(\Omega\).


Proof (Proof of Countable-Cocountable \(\sigma\)-Field). We verify the three conditions of Definition 3.2.
1. \(\Omega \in \mathcal{F}\): \(\Omega^c = \emptyset\) is finite, hence countable. Therefore \(\Omega \in \mathcal{F}\).
2. Closure under complements: Let \(B \in \mathcal{F}\). By definition, either \(B\) is countable or \(B^c\) is countable.

If \(B\) is countable: then \((B^c)^c = B\) is countable, so \(B^c \in \mathcal{F}\).
If \(B^c\) is countable: then \(B^c\) is directly countable, so \(B^c \in \mathcal{F}\).

In both cases \(B^c \in \mathcal{F}\).
3. Closure under countable unions: Let \(\{B_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) and set \(B := \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty B_j\). There are two exhaustive cases.

Case 1 — all \(B_j\) are countable. A countable union of countable sets is countable, so \(B\) is countable, hence \(B \in \mathcal{F}\).
Case 2 — some \(B_{j_0}\) has \(B_{j_0}^c\) countable. By De Morgan’s law: \[
B^c = \left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty B_j\right)^{\!c} = \bigcap_{j=1}^\infty B_j^c \;\subseteq\; B_{j_0}^c.
\] Since \(B_{j_0}^c\) is countable and \(B^c \subseteq B_{j_0}^c\), the set \(B^c\) is countable, so \(B \in \mathcal{F}\).

Since every sequence in \(\mathcal{F}\) falls into Case 1 or Case 2 (or both), the union \(B \in \mathcal{F}\) in all cases. \(\square\)

title: 3  Lecture 1.2: Sigma Algebra
text:
3.3 Properties and Generation of \(\sigma\)-Fields

Lemma 3.1 (Arbitrary Intersection of \(\sigma\)-Fields) Let \(I\) be an arbitrary (possibly uncountable) index set, and let \(\{\mathcal{F}_i\}_{i \in I}\) be a collection of \(\sigma\)-fields over \(\Omega\). Then their intersection: \[
\mathcal{F} := \bigcap_{i \in I} \mathcal{F}_i
\tag{3.7}\] is also a \(\sigma\)-field over \(\Omega\).


Proof. We verify the three conditions of Definition 3.2:

Since \(\mathcal{F}_i\) is a \(\sigma\)-field for every \(i \in I\), \(\Omega \in \mathcal{F}_i\) for all \(i \in I\). Thus, \(\Omega \in \bigcap_{i \in I} \mathcal{F}_i = \mathcal{F}\).
Let \(E \in \mathcal{F}\). Then \(E \in \mathcal{F}_i\) for every \(i \in I\). Since each \(\mathcal{F}_i\) is closed under complements, \(E^c \in \mathcal{F}_i\) for all \(i \in I\). Therefore, \(E^c \in \bigcap_{i \in I} \mathcal{F}_i = \mathcal{F}\).
Let \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\). Then for each fixed \(i \in I\), \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}_i\). Since \(\mathcal{F}_i\) is closed under countable unions, \(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \in \mathcal{F}_i\) for all \(i \in I\). Hence, \(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \in \bigcap_{i \in I} \mathcal{F}_i = \mathcal{F}\).

title: 3  Lecture 1.2: Sigma Algebra
text:
3.4 The \(\sigma\)-Field Generated by a Collection

Proposition 3.1 (Generated \(\sigma\)-Field) Let \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) be any collection of subsets of \(\Omega\). There exists a unique, smallest \(\sigma\)-field containing \(\mathcal{E}\), denoted by \(\sigma(\mathcal{E})\). It is called the \(\sigma\)-field generated by \(\mathcal{E}\).


Proof. Define \(\sigma(\mathcal{E})\) as the intersection of all \(\sigma\)-fields over \(\Omega\) that contain \(\mathcal{E}\): \[
\sigma(\mathcal{E}) := \bigcap \left\{ \mathcal{F} \subseteq 2^\Omega : \mathcal{F} \text{ is a } \sigma\text{-field over } \Omega \text{ and } \mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{F} \right\}.
\tag{3.8}\]

Non-emptiness of Index Set: The family of \(\sigma\)-fields containing \(\mathcal{E}\) is non-empty because \(2^\Omega\) is a valid \(\sigma\)-field containing \(\mathcal{E}\).
Validity: By Lemma 3.1, \(\sigma(\mathcal{E})\) is a valid \(\sigma\)-field.
Minimal Property: By construction, any \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{G}\) containing \(\mathcal{E}\) is part of the intersection, so \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}) \subseteq \mathcal{G}\).



3.4.1 Concrete Example
Let \(\Omega = \{1, 2, 3\}\) and let \(\mathcal{E} = \{\{1\}\}\). The generated \(\sigma\)-field is: \[
\sigma(\mathcal{E}) = \{\emptyset, \, \{1\}, \, \{2, 3\}, \, \{1, 2, 3\}\}.
\tag{3.9}\]


Exercise 3.1 (Exercise: Equivalence of Generated \(\sigma\)-Fields) Let \(\mathcal{E}_1, \mathcal{E}_2 \subseteq 2^\Omega\) be two collections of subsets. Prove that \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}_1) = \sigma(\mathcal{E}_2)\) if and only if \(\mathcal{E}_1 \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E}_2)\) and \(\mathcal{E}_2 \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E}_1)\).


Proof. 

(\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}_1) = \sigma(\mathcal{E}_2)\), then since \(\mathcal{E}_1 \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E}_1)\), we have \(\mathcal{E}_1 \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E}_2)\). Similarly, \(\mathcal{E}_2 \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E}_1)\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) If \(\mathcal{E}_1 \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E}_2)\), then since \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}_2)\) is a valid \(\sigma\)-field containing \(\mathcal{E}_1\), by minimality of \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}_1)\), we must have \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}_1) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E}_2)\). Reversing the roles for \(\mathcal{E}_2 \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E}_1)\) gives \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}_2) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E}_1)\). Combining both inclusions yields \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}_1) = \sigma(\mathcal{E}_2)\).

title: 3  Lecture 1.2: Sigma Algebra
text:
3.5 Generated \(\sigma\)-Field
Let \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) be any collection of subsets of \(\Omega\). There exists a unique, smallest \(\sigma\)-field containing \(\mathcal{E}\), denoted by \(\sigma(\mathcal{E})\). It is called the \(\sigma\)-field generated by \(\mathcal{E}\).

title: 3  Lecture 1.2: Sigma Algebra
text:
3.5 Topological Spaces and the Borel \(\sigma\)-Field

Definition 3.3 (Borel \(\sigma\)-Field) Let \(X\) be a topological space (e.g., Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^d\) equipped with the standard metric topology). The Borel \(\sigma\)-field on \(X\), denoted by \(\mathcal{B}(X)\), is the \(\sigma\)-field generated by all open subsets of \(X\): \[
\mathcal{B}(X) := \sigma(\{ U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } X \}).
\tag{3.10}\] Elements of \(\mathcal{B}(X)\) are called Borel sets.


Proposition 3.2 (Countable Generators of \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\)) In Euclidean space \(X = \mathbb{R}^d\), every open set \(U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) can be expressed as a countable union of open balls with rational centers and rational radii: \[
U = \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty B(x_i, r_i), \quad x_i \in \mathbb{Q}^d, \, r_i \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}.
\tag{3.11}\]
Consequently, \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\) is generated by the countable collection of open balls: \[
\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \sigma\left( \{ B(x, r) : x \in \mathbb{Q}^d, r \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0} \} \right).
\tag{3.12}\]
For the real line \(d = 1\), the Borel \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) can be equivalently generated by open intervals, half-open intervals, or rays: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) &= \sigma(\{ (a, b) : a < b \}) \\
&= \sigma(\{ (a, b] : a < b \}) \\
&= \sigma(\{ (-\infty, a] : a \in \mathbb{R} \}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.13}\]

title: 3  Lecture 1.2: Sigma Algebra
text:
3.7 Countable Generators of \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\)
In Euclidean space \(X = \mathbb{R}^d\), every open set \(U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) can be expressed as a countable union of open balls with rational centers and rational radii: \[
U = \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty B(x_i, r_i), \quad x_i \in \mathbb{Q}^d, \, r_i \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}.
\tag{3.11}\]
Consequently, \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\) is generated by the countable collection of open balls: \[
\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \sigma\left( \{ B(x, r) : x \in \mathbb{Q}^d, r \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0} \} \right).
\tag{3.12}\]
For the real line \(d = 1\), the Borel \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) can be equivalently generated by open intervals, half-open intervals, or rays: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) &= \sigma(\{ (a, b) : a < b \}) \\
&= \sigma(\{ (a, b] : a < b \}) \\
&= \sigma(\{ (-\infty, a] : a \in \mathbb{R} \}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.13}\]

title: 4  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
4.1 Definition of Measure and Measure Spaces
Measure theory generalizes the intuitive geometric concepts of length, area, volume, and probability mass to abstract set structures.

title: 4  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
Definition 4.1 (Measure and Measure Space) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and \(\mathcal{F}\) be a \(\sigma\)-field (\(\sigma\)-algebra) over \(\Omega\). The pair \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) is called a measurable space, and elements \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) are called measurable sets (or events).
A set function \(\mu: \mathcal{F} \to [0, \infty]\) is called a measure if it satisfies the following two conditions:

Empty Set: \(\mu(\emptyset) = 0\).
Countable Additivity (\(\sigma\)-additivity): For any countable sequence of pairwise disjoint sets \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (i.e., \(E_i \cap E_j = \emptyset\) for all \(i \neq j\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu(E_j).
\tag{4.1}\]







Note



The condition \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) is independent of countable additivity for general measures: without it, the constant function \(\mu \equiv \infty\) satisfies countable additivity but violates the empty-set condition. For finite measures \(\mu(\Omega)<\infty\), the condition can be derived by applying countable additivity to \(\Omega = \Omega \cup \emptyset \cup \emptyset \cup \cdots\).


The triple \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called a measure space.


Definition 4.2 (Finite and Probability Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

\(\mu\) is a finite measure if \(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\).
\(\mu\) is a probability measure if \(\mu(\Omega) = 1\). In this case, \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called a probability space.

title: 4  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
4.2 Canonical Examples of Measures

4.2.1 Trivial Measure
On any measurable space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), the constant zero function \(\mu(E) \equiv 0\) for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is trivially a valid measure.


4.2.2 Point Mass (Dirac Measure)

Definition 4.3 (Dirac / Point Mass Measure) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space and fix a point \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\). The Dirac measure (or point mass) at \(\omega_0\), denoted by \(\delta_{\omega_0}: \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]\), is defined by: \[
\delta_{\omega_0}(E) := \begin{cases}  1 & \text{if } \omega_0 \in E, \\  0 & \text{if } \omega_0 \notin E.  \end{cases}
\tag{4.2}\]


Proposition 4.1 (Validity of Dirac Measure) For any \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\), \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 4.1). First, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(\Omega) = 1\) since \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\).
Next, let \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a countable sequence of pairwise disjoint measurable sets. Since the sets are disjoint, the point \(\omega_0\) can belong to at most one set \(E_k\):

Case 1: There exists a unique index \(k \ge 1\) such that \(\omega_0 \in E_k\). Then \(\omega_0 \in \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 1\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) = 1\) and \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \neq k\). Thus: \[\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = \delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) + \sum_{j \neq k} 0 = 1 + 0 = 1.\]
Case 2: \(\omega_0 \notin E_j\) for all \(j \ge 1\). Then \(\omega_0 \notin \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 0\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \ge 1\), yielding \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\).

In both cases, \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j)\), proving countable additivity.

title: 4  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
4.3 Validity of Dirac Measure
For any \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\), \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).

title: 4  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
section: 4.3 Constructing New Measures from Existing Measures
text:
4.3 Constructing New Measures from Existing Measures

Theorem 4.1 (Linear Combinations and Sums of Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space.

Scalar Multiplication: If \(\mu\) is a measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(a \in (0, \infty)\), then \(a\mu\) defined by \((a\mu)(E) := a \cdot \mu(E)\) is a valid measure.
Countable Linear Combinations: If \(\{\mu_j\}_{j=1}^\infty\) is a countable collection of measures on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(\{c_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, \infty)\), then the set function: \[
\mu := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j
\tag{4.3}\] defined by \(\mu(E) := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E)\) for \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is a valid measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).



Proof (Proof of Theorem 4.1). Because all terms \(c_j \mu_j(E)\) are non-negative (\(c_j \mu_j(E) \in [0, \infty]\)), all infinite sums consist of non-negative real/extended terms, which guarantees that sums are well-defined and order of summation can be interchanged by Tonelli’s theorem for series.
Let \(\{E_k\}_{k=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be pairwise disjoint events. Using countable additivity of each individual measure \(\mu_j\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \left( \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu_j(E_k) \right) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E_k) \quad \text{(interchanging non-negative double summation)} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu(E_k).
\end{aligned}
\] Hence, \(\mu\) is countably additive and constitutes a valid measure.

title: 4  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
4.4 Discrete Probability Measures

Corollary 4.1 (Discrete Probability Measures) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and let \(\{\omega_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \Omega\) be a countable sequence of points. Let \(\{p_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, 1]\) be weights satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j = 1\).
Then \(\mu := \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j \delta_{\omega_j}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 4.1). By Theorem 4.1, \(\mu\) is a valid measure. Evaluating \(\mu\) on the entire space \(\Omega\) gives: \[
\mu(\Omega) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j \delta_{\omega_j}(\Omega) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j (1) = 1.
\] Thus, \(\mu\) is a normalized probability measure.

title: 4  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
4.5 Basic Properties of Measures
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

Proposition 4.2 (Fundamental Properties of Measures)  

Monotonicity: If \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(A \subseteq B\), then: \[
\mu(A) \le \mu(B).
\tag{4.4}\] If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), then \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion Rule (Addition Rule): For any \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\): \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\tag{4.5}\] When \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), this is written as \(\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\).
Countable Sub-Additivity (Boole’s Inequality): For any countable sequence of measurable sets \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (not necessarily disjoint): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\tag{4.6}\]



Proof (Proof of Proposition 4.2). 

Monotonicity: Decompose \(B\) into the disjoint union \(B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\). By countable additivity (applied to the two-set partition, using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) to pad with empty sets): \[
\mu(B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] Since \(\mu(B \setminus A) \ge 0\), it immediately follows that \(\mu(A) \le \mu(B)\). If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), subtracting \(\mu(A)\) from both sides gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion: Decompose \(A \cup B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint) and \(B = (A \cap B) \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint). By countable additivity applied to each two-set partition: \[
\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A), \quad \text{and} \quad \mu(B) = \mu(A \cap B) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] The second equation gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\) (valid when \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), which is the stated hypothesis). Substituting into the first: \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\]
Countable Sub-additivity: Disjointify the sequence \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) by defining: \[
A_1 := B_1, \quad A_n := B_n \setminus \left( \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1} B_j \right) \quad \text{for } n \ge 2.
\tag{4.7}\] By construction, \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are pairwise disjoint measurable sets, \(A_n \subseteq B_n\) for all \(n\), and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\). Applying countable additivity and monotonicity (\(A_n \subseteq B_n \implies \mu(A_n) \le \mu(B_n)\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\]

text:
4.7 Fundamental Properties of Measures

Monotonicity: If \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(A \subseteq B\), then: \[
\mu(A) \le \mu(B).
\tag{4.4}\] If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), then \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion Rule (Addition Rule): For any \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\): \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\tag{4.5}\] When \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), this is written as \(\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\).
Countable Sub-Additivity (Boole’s Inequality): For any countable sequence of measurable sets \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (not necessarily disjoint): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\tag{4.6}\]
