title: 86  Lecture 40.1: Operator Norm Continuity
text:
86.1 Introduction to Markov Generators and Continuity
Given a family of Markov transition operators \(\{Q_t\}_{t \ge 0}\) on the bounded measurable functions \(\mathcal{B}(S, \mathcal{B})\) over a state space \(S\), the generator \(A\) (should it exist) is defined as the linear operator: \[
A f := \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} Q_t f \right\vert{}_{t=0} = \lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{Q_t f - f}{t}.
\tag{86.1}\]
If \(Q_t\) is differentiable at \(t = 0\), it must also be continuous at \(t = 0\). There are multiple notions of operator continuity available (e.g., pointwise/strong continuity, operator norm continuity). The strongest notion—operator norm continuity—yields the most concrete analytical properties.

title: 86  Lecture 40.1: Operator Norm Continuity
text:
86.2 Operator Norms and Bounded Operators

Definition 86.1 (Bounded Operator and Operator Norm) Let \((B, \Vert{}\cdot\Vert{})\) be a normed space (e.g., \(B = \mathcal{B}(S, \mathcal{B})\) equipped with the supremum norm \(\Vert{}f\Vert{}_\infty := \sup_{x \in S} \vert{}f(x)\vert{}\)). For a linear operator \(A: B \to B\), its operator norm \(\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}\) is defined as: \[
\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} := \sup_{f \neq 0} \frac{\Vert{}A f\Vert{}}{\Vert{}f\Vert{}} = \sup_{\Vert{}f\Vert{} \le 1} \Vert{}A f\Vert{}.
\tag{86.2}\]
\(A\) is called a bounded linear operator if \(\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} < \infty\), which is equivalent to \(A\) being Lipschitz continuous: \[
\Vert{}A f\Vert{} \le \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \Vert{}f\Vert{} \quad \forall f \in B.
\tag{86.3}\]

title: 86  Lecture 40.1: Operator Norm Continuity
text:
86.3 Submultiplicativity of the Operator Norm

Lemma 86.1 (Composition of Bounded Linear Operators) If \(A, T: B \to B\) are bounded linear operators, then their composition \(A T\) is also bounded, and: \[
\Vert{}A T\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \Vert{}T\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}.
\tag{86.4}\]


Proof (Proof of Lemma 86.1). Fix \(f \in B\), \(f \neq 0\). If \(T f = 0\), then \(\Vert{}A T f\Vert{} = \Vert{}A 0\Vert{} = 0 \le \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \Vert{}T\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \Vert{}f\Vert{}\) trivially. If \(T f \neq 0\), then: \[
\frac{\Vert{}A T f\Vert{}}{\Vert{}f\Vert{}} = \frac{\Vert{}A(T f)\Vert{}}{\Vert{}T f\Vert{}} \cdot \frac{\Vert{}T f\Vert{}}{\Vert{}f\Vert{}}.
\] By definition of the operator norm: \[
\frac{\Vert{}A(T f)\Vert{}}{\Vert{}T f\Vert{}} \le \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \quad \implies \quad \frac{\Vert{}A T f\Vert{}}{\Vert{}f\Vert{}} \le \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \cdot \frac{\Vert{}T f\Vert{}}{\Vert{}f\Vert{}} \le \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \Vert{}T\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}.
\] In either case \(\Vert{}A T f\Vert{} \le \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \Vert{}T\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \Vert{}f\Vert{}\). Taking the supremum over all \(f \neq 0\) yields \(\Vert{}A T\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \Vert{}T\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}\).

title: 86  Lecture 40.1: Operator Norm Continuity
text:
86.4 Operator Powers and Matrix Exponentials

Corollary 86.1 (Powers and Exponentials of Operators) If \(A\) is a bounded linear operator, then \(A^n\) is bounded for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), with: \[
\Vert{}A^n\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}^n.
\tag{86.5}\]
Furthermore, on a Banach space \(B\), the operator exponential defined by the power series: \[
e^{t A} := \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^n}{n!} A^n,
\tag{86.6}\] converges in operator norm to a bounded linear operator for all \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), satisfying: \[
\Vert{}e^{t A}\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le e^{\vert{}t\vert{} \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}} < \infty.
\tag{86.7}\]


Proof (Proof of Corollary 86.1). 

By induction on Lemma 86.1 (base case \(n=0\): \(\Vert{}A^0\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} = \Vert{}I\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} = 1 = \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}^0\)), \(\Vert{}A^n\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}^n\).
Since \((\mathcal{B}(S), \Vert{}\cdot\Vert{}_\infty)\) is a complete normed space (Banach space, as uniform limits of bounded functions are bounded and \(\mathbb{R}\) is complete), a standard result in functional analysis guarantees that the operator algebra \((\mathcal{L}(B), \Vert{}\cdot\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}})\) of bounded linear operators on a Banach space is itself a Banach space: if \((A_n)\) is \(\Vert{}\cdot\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}\)-Cauchy, then \((A_n f)\) is Cauchy in \(B\) for each fixed \(f\), hence converges to some \(A f\) by completeness of \(B\); one checks \(A\) is linear, bounded, and \(A_n \to A\) in operator norm.
By completeness of \((\mathcal{L}(B), \Vert{}\cdot\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}})\), it suffices to show the series of norms converges (absolute convergence implies convergence in a Banach space): \[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty \left\Vert{} \frac{t^n}{n!} A^n \right\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\vert{}t\vert{}^n}{n!} \Vert{}A^n\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\vert{}t\vert{}^n \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}^n}{n!} = e^{\vert{}t\vert{} \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}} < \infty.
\] Hence the partial sums of \(e^{t A}\) form a Cauchy sequence in \((\mathcal{L}(B), \Vert{}\cdot\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}})\) and converge to a bounded operator, with \(\Vert{}e^{tA}\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le \sum_{n=0}^\infty \Vert{}t^nA^n/n!\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le e^{\vert{}t\vert{}\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}}\) by the triangle inequality.

title: 86  Lecture 40.1: Operator Norm Continuity
text:
86.5 Discrete Matrix Representations of Operators
When \(S\) is countable, we can represent linear operators on \(\mathcal{B}(S)\) via matrix kernels \(q: S \times S \to \mathbb{R}\): \[
(A f)(i) = \sum_{j \in S} q(i, j) f(j).
\tag{86.8}\]
To ensure that \((A f) \in \mathcal{B}(S)\) and \(A\) is bounded, we define the norm: \[
\Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty := \sup_{i \in S} \sum_{j \in S} \vert{}q(i, j)\vert{}.
\tag{86.9}\]

Proposition 86.1 (Equivalence of Row-Sum Norm and Operator Norm) Let \(S\) be countable and \(q: S \times S \to \mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(\Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty < \infty\). Then \((A f)(i) = \sum_{j \in S} q(i, j) f(j)\) defines a bounded linear operator on \(\mathcal{B}(S)\), and: \[
\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} = \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty = \sup_{i \in S} \sum_{j \in S} \vert{}q(i, j)\vert{}.
\tag{86.10}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 86.1). 

Upper Bound (\(\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty\)): For any \(f \in \mathcal{B}(S)\) and any \(i \in S\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\vert{}(A f)(i)\vert{} &= \left\vert{} \sum_{j \in S} q(i, j) f(j) \right\vert{}\\
& \le \sum_{j \in S} \vert{}q(i, j)\vert{} \vert{}f(j)\vert{} \\
&\le \left( \sum_{j \in S} \vert{}q(i, j)\vert{} \right) \Vert{}f\Vert{}_\infty \\
&\le \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty \Vert{}f\Vert{}_\infty.
\end{aligned}
\] Taking the supremum over \(i \in S\) gives \(\Vert{}A f\Vert{}_\infty \le \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty \Vert{}f\Vert{}_\infty\), so \(\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty\).
Lower Bound (\(\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \ge \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty\)): Fix \(\varepsilon > 0\) and choose \(i \in S\) such that \(\sum_{j \in S} \vert{}q(i, j)\vert{} \ge \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty - \varepsilon\). Define the function \(f_i \in \mathcal{B}(S)\) by setting \(f_i(j) = \operatorname{sgn}(q(i, j))\). Notice \(\Vert{}f_i\Vert{}_\infty \le 1\). Evaluating \((A f_i)(i)\): \[
(A f_i)(i) = \sum_{j \in S} q(i, j) \operatorname{sgn}(q(i, j)) = \sum_{j \in S} \vert{}q(i, j)\vert{} \ge \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty - \varepsilon.
\] Hence \(\Vert{}A f_i\Vert{}_\infty \ge \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty - \varepsilon\). Taking \(\varepsilon \to 0\) yields \(\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \ge \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty\).

Combining both inequalities establishes \(\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} = \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty\).


Caution: Even when \(S\) is countable, not every bounded linear operator on \(\mathcal{B}(S) = \ell^\infty(S)\) can be expressed as such a matrix. This is because the dual space \((\ell^\infty(S))^*\) is strictly larger than \(\ell^1(S)\): it contains singular (finitely additive but not countably additive) functionals, such as Banach limits, that cannot be represented by any row \(q(i, \cdot) \in \ell^1(S)\). Operators built from such functionals (e.g., rank-one operators \(f \mapsto \phi(f) g\) for \(g \in \mathcal{B}(S)\) and \(\phi\) a singular functional) are bounded but admit no matrix representation Equation 86.8.

title: 86  Lecture 40.1: Operator Norm Continuity
section: 86.6 Equivalence of Row-Sum Norm and Operator Norm
text:
86.6 Equivalence of Row-Sum Norm and Operator Norm
Let \(S\) be countable and \(q: S \times S \to \mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(\Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty < \infty\)[cite: 8]. Then \((A f)(i) = \sum_{j \in S} q(i, j) f(j)\) defines a bounded linear operator on \(\mathcal{B}(S)\), and[cite: 8]: \[\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} = \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty = \sup_{i \in S} \sum_{j \in S} \vert{}q(i, j)\vert{}.\] {#eq-norm-equivalence}

title: 86  Lecture 40.1: Operator Norm Continuity
text:
86.6 Uniformly Continuous Markov Semigroups
The following result shows that operator norm continuity at a single point, combined with the semigroup property, forces the entire semigroup to have the simplest possible structure: The entire semigroup collapses to \(Q_t = e^{tA}\) for a single bounded operator \(A\). This means the infinitely many operators \(\{Q_t\}_{t \geq 0}\) are completely encoded in just one object \(A\), and the time evolution is as explicit as it could possibly be.

Theorem 86.1 (Uniformly Continuous Markov Semigroups) Let \(B = \mathcal{B}(S, \mathcal{B})\) and let \(\{Q_t\}_{t \ge 0} \subset \mathcal{L}(B)\) be a semigroup of bounded linear Markov transition operators, i.e. \[
Q_0 = I, \qquad Q_{s+t} = Q_s Q_t \quad \text{for all } s, t \ge 0
\tag{86.11}\] (the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations). Suppose further that \(Q_t\) is operator norm continuous at \(t = 0\): \[
\lim_{t \to 0^+} \Vert{}Q_t - I\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} = 0.
\tag{86.12}\]
Then \(Q_t\) is operator norm continuous for every \(t \ge 0\), and operator norm differentiable on all of \([0, \infty)\) (one-sided at \(t = 0\)). Furthermore, defining the generator \(A := \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} Q_t\right\vert{}_{t=0} = \lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{Q_t - I}{t}\), we have:

\(\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} < \infty\) (the generator is a bounded operator).
\(Q_t = e^{t A} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^n}{n!} A^n\) for all \(t \ge 0\).
\(Q_t\) satisfies the Kolmogorov Forward and Backward Differential Equations: \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} Q_t = Q_t A = A Q_t, \quad \text{with } Q_0 = I.
\tag{86.13}\]



Proof (Proof of Theorem 86.1). Step 1 (A local uniform bound, and continuity on all of \([0,\infty)\)). By Equation 86.12, fix \(\delta > 0\) such that \(\Vert{}Q_s - I\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le 1/2\) for all \(s \in [0, \delta]\); in particular \(M := \sup_{s \in [0,\delta]} \Vert{}Q_s\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le 3/2\). For any \(t \ge 0\), write \(t = n\delta + r\) with \(n \in \mathbb{N}_0\), \(r \in [0, \delta)\); by Equation 87.1 and Lemma 86.1, \(\Vert{}Q_t\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} = \Vert{}Q_\delta^n Q_r\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le M^{n+1} < \infty\). Hence \(\sup_{s \in [0,T]} \Vert{}Q_s\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} < \infty\) for every \(T < \infty\).
For \(t_0 \ge 0\) and \(h \to 0^+\), Equation 87.1 gives \(Q_{t_0+h} - Q_{t_0} = Q_{t_0}(Q_h - I)\), so by Lemma 86.1 and Equation 86.12, \[
\Vert{}Q_{t_0+h} - Q_{t_0}\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le \Vert{}Q_{t_0}\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \Vert{}Q_h - I\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \to 0,
\] which is right continuity at every \(t_0 \ge 0\). For \(0 < h < t_0\), similarly \(Q_{t_0} - Q_{t_0 - h} = Q_{t_0 - h}(Q_h - I)\); since \(\Vert{}Q_{t_0-h}\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}\) stays bounded as \(h \to 0^+\) by the uniform bound on \([0,t_0]\) established above, \(\Vert{}Q_{t_0}-Q_{t_0-h}\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \to 0\) as well: left continuity. Hence \(t \mapsto Q_t\) is operator norm continuous on all of \([0,\infty)\).
Step 2 (Construction of a bounded generator). Since \(s \mapsto Q_s\) is continuous on \([0,\delta]\) (Step 1), the Riemann integral \(S_\delta := \int_0^\delta Q_s \, \mathrm{d}s \in \mathcal{L}(B)\) is well-defined as a limit of Riemann sums in the Banach space \((\mathcal{L}(B), \Vert{}\cdot\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}})\) (cf. Corollary 86.1), and \[
\left\Vert{} \frac{S_\delta}{\delta} - I \right\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} = \left\Vert{} \frac{1}{\delta}\int_0^\delta (Q_s - I) \, \mathrm{d}s \right\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le \frac{1}{\delta}\int_0^\delta \Vert{}Q_s - I\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \, \mathrm{d}s \le \frac{1}{2} < 1.
\] The last inequality uses the uniform bound \(\|Q_s - I\|_\text{op} \leq 1/2\) on \([0, \delta]\) from Step 1. Since we’re in a Banach algebra and \(\|S_\delta/\delta - I\|_\text{op} < 1\), the Neumann series \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty (I - S_\delta/\delta)^n\) converges in operator norm and gives \((S_\delta/\delta)^{-1}\). Hence \(S_\delta\) is invertible with a bounded inverse \(S_\delta^{-1}\). Define the bounded operator \[
A := (Q_\delta - I) S_\delta^{-1}.
\] For \(h > 0\), since the bounded linear operator \(Q_h\) commutes with the Riemann integral and \(Q_h Q_s = Q_{h+s}\), a change of variables \(u = h+s\) gives \[
\frac{Q_h - I}{h} S_\delta = \frac{1}{h}\left( \int_0^\delta Q_{h+s}\,\mathrm{d}s - \int_0^\delta Q_s\,\mathrm{d}s \right) = \frac{1}{h}\left( \int_\delta^{\delta+h} Q_u\,\mathrm{d}u - \int_0^h Q_u\,\mathrm{d}u \right).
\] By continuity of \(u \mapsto Q_u\) at \(u = \delta\) and \(u = 0\) (Step 1), each averaged integral converges in operator norm as \(h \to 0^+\): \(h^{-1}\int_\delta^{\delta+h}Q_u\,\mathrm{d}u \to Q_\delta\) and \(h^{-1}\int_0^h Q_u\,\mathrm{d}u \to Q_0 = I\) (see Remark 86.1). Hence \[
\frac{Q_h-I}{h}S_\delta \to Q_\delta - I \quad \text{in operator norm as } h \to 0^+.
\]

Remark 86.1. Banach-space analogue of the fundamental theorem of calculus: if \(u \mapsto Q_u\) is continuous in operator norm at a point \(u_0\), then \[
\frac{1}{h}\int_{u_0}^{u_0+h} Q_u\, du \xrightarrow{h \to 0^+} Q_{u_0}.
\] Proof of this fact. Write: \[
\begin{aligned}
\left\|\frac{1}{h}\int_{u_0}^{u_0+h} Q_u\, du - Q_{u_0}\right\|_\text{op} &= \left\|\frac{1}{h}\int_{u_0}^{u_0+h}(Q_u - Q_{u_0})\, du\right\|_\text{op} \\
&\leq \frac{1}{h}\int_{u_0}^{u_0+h}\|Q_u - Q_{u_0}\|_\text{op}\, du.
\end{aligned}
\] The first equality uses the fact that \(\frac{1}{h}\int_{u_0}^{u_0+h} Q_{u_0}\, du = Q_{u_0}\) exactly. The inequality is the triangle inequality for Banach-space-valued integrals. Now fix any \(\varepsilon > 0\). Since \(u \mapsto Q_u\) is operator-norm continuous at \(u_0\), there exists \(\eta > 0\) such that \(|u - u_0| < \eta \implies \|Q_u - Q_{u_0}\|_\text{op} < \varepsilon\). For any \(0 < h < \eta\), every \(u \in [u_0, u_0 + h]\) satisfies \(|u - u_0| \leq h < \eta\), so: \[
\frac{1}{h}\int_{u_0}^{u_0+h}\|Q_u - Q_{u_0}\|_\text{op}\, du < \frac{1}{h}\int_{u_0}^{u_0+h} \varepsilon\, du = \varepsilon.
\] Since \(\varepsilon > 0\) was arbitrary, the limit holds.

Right-multiplication by the fixed bounded operator \(S_\delta^{-1}\) is continuous on \(\mathcal{L}(B)\) (Lemma 86.1), so \[
\frac{Q_h-I}{h} = \left[\frac{Q_h-I}{h}S_\delta\right]S_\delta^{-1} \longrightarrow (Q_\delta-I)S_\delta^{-1} = A
\] in operator norm as \(h \to 0^+\). This shows the limit defining \(A\) exists in operator norm, and \(A\) is bounded as a product of bounded operators, proving (1).
Step 3 (Differentiability for all \(t \ge 0\) and the Kolmogorov equations). Fix \(t_0 \ge 0\). For \(h > 0\), Equation 87.1 gives \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{Q_{t_0+h}-Q_{t_0}}{h} = Q_{t_0}\cdot\frac{Q_h-I}{h} \longrightarrow Q_{t_0}A, \\
& \frac{Q_{t_0+h}-Q_{t_0}}{h} = \frac{Q_h-I}{h}\cdot Q_{t_0} \longrightarrow A Q_{t_0}
\end{aligned}
\] as \(h \to 0^+\), using Step 2 and continuity of left- and right-multiplication by the fixed bounded operator \(Q_{t_0}\) (Lemma 86.1). Hence the right-derivative of \(Q_t\) at \(t_0\) equals \(Q_{t_0}A = AQ_{t_0}\). For \(t_0 > 0\) and \(0 < h < t_0\), \[
\frac{Q_{t_0}-Q_{t_0-h}}{h} = Q_{t_0-h}\cdot\frac{Q_h-I}{h}.
\] Since \(Q_{t_0-h}\to Q_{t_0}\) (Step 1) and \((Q_h-I)/h \to A\) (Step 2), and \(\Vert{}Q_{t_0-h}\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}\) is bounded for small \(h\) (Step 1), multiplication in \(\mathcal{L}(B)\) is jointly continuous there (Lemma 86.1), so the left-derivative at \(t_0\) also equals \(Q_{t_0}A\). Thus \(t \mapsto Q_t\) is differentiable in operator norm on \([0,\infty)\) (one-sided at \(t=0\)), with \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}Q_t = Q_t A = A Q_t, \qquad Q_0 = I,
\] proving (3).
Step 4 (\(Q_t = e^{tA}\)). By Corollary 86.1, \(e^{-tA}\) is a well-defined bounded operator for every \(t\), and \(A\) commutes with \(e^{-tA}\) since \(A\) commutes with every power of itself. Define \(F(t) := Q_t e^{-tA} \in \mathcal{L}(B)\). Differentiating the power series for \(e^{-tA}\) term-by-term (justified by the same absolute-convergence argument as in Corollary 86.1) gives \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}e^{-tA} = -Ae^{-tA}\), so by the Leibniz rule for operator-norm-differentiable \(\mathcal{L}(B)\)-valued functions (valid since operator multiplication is bounded bilinear) and Step 3, \[
F'(t) = (Q_tA)e^{-tA} + Q_t(-Ae^{-tA}) = Q_tAe^{-tA} - Q_tAe^{-tA} = 0,
\] for all \(t \ge 0\). Since \(F\) is continuously differentiable with \(F' \equiv 0\) on \([0,\infty)\), the fundamental theorem of calculus for Banach-space-valued functions gives \(F(t) - F(0) = \int_0^t F'(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\), i.e., \(F(t) = F(0) = Q_0 e^0 = I\) for all \(t \ge 0\). Hence \(Q_t = e^{tA}\) for all \(t \ge 0\), proving (2).

title: 86  Lecture 40.1: Operator Norm Continuity
text:
86.7 Remarks

Uniqueness: The argument in Step 4 of the proof above is in fact a general uniqueness argument: for any bounded operator \(A\), the operator-valued ODE \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}X_t = AX_t\), \(X_0 = I\), has \(X_t = e^{tA}\) as its unique solution among operator-norm-differentiable curves \(t \mapsto X_t \in \mathcal{L}(B)\) (apply Step 4’s computation to \(F(t) := X_t e^{-tA}\) to get \(F'\equiv0\), hence \(X_t = X_0 e^{tA} = e^{tA}\)). In particular, \(Q_t = e^{tA}\) is the unique such solution to Equation 87.5.
Unbounded Generators: Without operator norm continuity (e.g., under the weaker notion of strong/pointwise continuity \(\lim_{t \to 0} \Vert{}Q_t f - f\Vert{}_\infty = 0\)), the generator \(A\) may be unbounded and only densely defined on a proper domain \(\mathcal{D}(A) \subset \mathcal{B}(S)\). The key step of the proof above that fails in this setting is Step 2: the Riemann integral \(S_\delta\) is still well-defined (its integrand is only strongly, not uniformly, continuous), but \(S_\delta/\delta\) need not be close to \(I\) in operator norm, so the Neumann-series argument for invertibility of \(S_\delta\) breaks down, and the generator can no longer be extracted as a bounded operator via this construction.

title: 52  Lecture 24.2: Characteristic Function
text:
Definition 52.1 (Fourier Transform of a Measure & Characteristic Function) Let \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\). For \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d\), define the Fourier transform of \(\mu\) as: \[
\hat{\mu}(\xi) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i \xi \cdot x} \, d\mu(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e_\xi \, d\mu.
\]
If \(X: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P) \to (\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) is a random vector, its characteristic function \(\varphi_X: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{C}\) is defined as: \[
\varphi_X(\xi) := \hat{\mu}_X(\xi) = \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{i \xi \cdot X} \right].
\] Here \(\mu_X := P \circ X^{-1}\) is the law of \(X\).


Theorem 52.1 (Injectivity / Uniqueness) The map \(\mu \mapsto \hat{\mu}\) is injective: if \(\hat{\mu}(\xi) = \hat{\nu}(\xi)\) for all \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d\), then \(\mu = \nu\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 52.1). By Corollary 54.1, if \(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i\xi \cdot x} \, d\mu(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i\xi \cdot x} \, d\nu(x)\) for all \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d\), then \(\mu(B) = \nu(B)\) for all \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Thus, \(\mu\) is uniquely determined by \(\hat{\mu}\) (and vice versa).







TipMGF vs. Characteristic Function




Moment Generating Function (MGF): For real \(t\), \(M_X(t) := \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]\) always exists as an extended nonnegative expectation, but it is finite only under the corresponding exponential-integrability condition.
Characteristic Function: \(\varphi_X(\xi) = \mathbb{E}[e^{i\xi X}]\) is always finite since \(|e^{i\xi X}| = 1\). If \(z \mapsto \mathbb{E}[e^{zX}]\) has a well-defined complex extension to the relevant imaginary points, then its value at \(z=i\xi\) equals \(\varphi_X(\xi)\); this does not follow from the real-variable definition of the MGF alone. The characteristic function determines the probability law by Theorem 52.1.

title: 52  Lecture 24.2: Characteristic Function
text:
52.2 Basic Properties of Characteristic Functions

Theorem 52.2 (Basic Properties of Characteristic Functions) Let \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\).

Boundedness: \(\hat{\mu}(0) = 1\), and \(|\hat{\mu}(\xi)| \le 1\) for all \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d\).
Uniform Continuity: \(\hat{\mu} \in C_u(\mathbb{R}^d)\) (uniformly continuous on \(\mathbb{R}^d\)).
Hermitian Symmetry: \(\hat{\mu}(-\xi) = \overline{\hat{\mu}(\xi)}\) for all \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d\). Moreover, \[
\begin{aligned}
&\hat{\mu}(\xi) \in \mathbb{R}\ \text{for every }\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d\\
&\Longleftrightarrow \mu(B)=\mu(-B)\ \text{for every }B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d).
\end{aligned}
\]
Moment Differentiation: Let \(\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)\in\mathbb{N}_0^d\). If \[\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\|x\|^{|\alpha|}\,d\mu(x)<\infty,\] then the mixed derivative \(\partial^\alpha\hat\mu\) exists and \[\partial^\alpha\hat\mu(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}(ix_1)^{\alpha_1}\cdots(ix_d)^{\alpha_d}e^{i\xi\cdot x}\,d\mu(x).\] In particular, if \(\int\|x\|^k\,d\mu(x)<\infty\), then \(\hat\mu\in C^k(\mathbb{R}^d)\) and the preceding formula holds for every multi-index \(\alpha\) with \(|\alpha|\le k\).



Proof (Proof of Theorem 52.2). 

Boundedness: \[\hat{\mu}(0) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i 0 \cdot x} \, d\mu(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} 1 \, d\mu(x) = 1\] \[|\hat{\mu}(\xi)| = \left| \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i \xi \cdot x} \, d\mu(x) \right| \le \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |e^{i \xi \cdot x}| \, d\mu(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} 1 \, d\mu(x) = 1\]
Uniform Continuity: For \(h \in \mathbb{R}^d\), \[
\begin{aligned}
|\hat{\mu}(\xi+h)-\hat{\mu}(\xi)|
&\le \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}|e^{i(\xi+h)\cdot x}-e^{i\xi\cdot x}|\,d\mu(x)\\
&=\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}|e^{ih\cdot x}-1|\,d\mu(x).
\end{aligned}
\] The last expression is independent of \(\xi\), converges pointwise to \(0\) as \(h\to0\), and is dominated by \(2\in L^1(\mu)\). DCT therefore shows that the supremum over \(\xi\) tends to \(0\), proving uniform continuity.
Conjugation & Symmetry: \[\overline{\hat{\mu}(\xi)} = \overline{\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i \xi \cdot x} \, d\mu(x)} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{-i \xi \cdot x} \, d\mu(x) = \hat{\mu}(-\xi)\] Let \(\check\mu(B):=\mu(-B)\) be the reflected measure. If \(\mu\) is symmetric, then \(\check\mu=\mu\), so: \[\hat{\mu}(-\xi) = \int e^{-i\xi\cdot x}\,d\mu(x) = \hat{\mu}(\xi)\] Since \(\hat{\mu}(-\xi) = \overline{\hat{\mu}(\xi)}\), this implies \(\hat{\mu}(\xi) = \overline{\hat{\mu}(\xi)}\), so \(\hat{\mu}(\xi) \in \mathbb{R}\). Conversely, suppose \(\hat\mu(\xi)\in\mathbb{R}\) for every \(\xi\). Then \(\hat\mu(-\xi)=\hat\mu(\xi)\). For the reflected measure \(\check\mu\), \[\hat{\check\mu}(\xi)=\int e^{i\xi\cdot x}\,d\check\mu(x)=\int e^{-i\xi\cdot y}\,d\mu(y)=\hat\mu(-\xi)=\hat\mu(\xi).\] Injectivity gives \(\check\mu=\mu\), which is exactly symmetry.
Differentiation Under the Integral: For a fixed multi-index \(\alpha\), repeated differentiation under the integral sign is justified by the integrable bound \(\|x\|^{|\alpha|}\), which dominates every monomial needed at an intermediate step. This gives \[\partial^\alpha\hat\mu(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}(ix)^\alpha e^{i\xi\cdot x}\,d\mu(x).\] The integrand is continuous in \(\xi\) and dominated by \(|x^\alpha|\), so the derivative is continuous by DCT. If instead \(\int\|x\|^k\,d\mu<\infty\), the same argument applies to every multi-index with \(|\alpha|\le k\), proving the stated \(C^k\) conclusion.

title: 52  Lecture 24.2: Characteristic Function
text:
52.3 Convolutions & Affine Transformations

Theorem 52.3 (Convolutions & Affine Shifts) Let \(\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\). For \(B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\), define their convolution by \[
(\mu*\nu)(B):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\mathbf{1}_B(x+y)\,d\mu(x)\,d\nu(y).
\]

Convolution: The characteristic function of a convolution \(\mu * \nu\) is the product of their characteristic functions: \[\widehat{\mu * \nu}(\xi) = \hat{\mu}(\xi) \cdot \hat{\nu}(\xi)\] Equivalently, if \(X,Y\) are independent \(\mathbb{R}^d\)-valued random vectors with laws \(\mu\) and \(\nu\), then \(\mathcal{L}(X+Y)=\mu*\nu\) and: \[\varphi_{X+Y}(\xi) = \varphi_X(\xi) \cdot \varphi_Y(\xi), \quad \forall \xi \in \mathbb{R}^d\]
Affine Transformation: If \(X\) is an \(\mathbb{R}^d\)-valued random vector, \(a \in \mathbb{R}\), and \(v \in \mathbb{R}^d\), then: \[\varphi_{aX + v}(\xi) = e^{i \xi \cdot v} \, \varphi_X(a\xi)\]



Proof (Proof of Theorem 52.3). 

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then: \[
\begin{align*}
\varphi_{X+Y}(\xi) &= \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{i \xi \cdot (X + Y)} \right] = \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{i \xi \cdot X} e^{i \xi \cdot Y} \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{i \xi \cdot X} \right] \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{i \xi \cdot Y} \right] = \varphi_X(\xi) \varphi_Y(\xi)
\end{align*}
\] Since \(\mathcal{L}(X+Y)=\mu*\nu\) by the definition above, this also proves \(\widehat{\mu*\nu}=\hat\mu\,\hat\nu\).
Direct expectation evaluation: \[
\begin{align*}
\varphi_{aX + v}(\xi) &= \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{i \xi \cdot (aX + v)} \right] = \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{i \xi \cdot v} e^{i (a\xi) \cdot X} \right]\\
& = e^{i \xi \cdot v} \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{i (a\xi) \cdot X} \right] = e^{i \xi \cdot v} \varphi_X(a\xi)
\end{align*}
\]

title: 52  Lecture 24.2: Characteristic Function
section: 52.9 Central Limit Theorem for Rademacher Sums
text:
52.9 Central Limit Theorem for Rademacher Sums
Let \(Y_1, Y_2, \dots\) be i.i.d. Rademacher random variables. Define the scaled sum: \[W_n := \frac{Y_1 + \dots + Y_n}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{S_n}{\sqrt{n}}\]
Using the scaling property of characteristic functions: \[\varphi_{W_n}(\xi) = \varphi_{S_n/\sqrt{n}}(\xi) = \varphi_{S_n}\left( \frac{\xi}{\sqrt{n}} \right) = \left( \cos\left( \frac{\xi}{\sqrt{n}} \right) \right)^n\]
For each fixed \(\xi\), choose \(N(\xi)\) so that \(|\xi|/\sqrt n<\pi/2\) for all \(n\ge N(\xi)\). Then \(\cos(\xi/\sqrt n)>0\), so the following real logarithm is defined for all sufficiently large \(n\); finitely many initial terms do not affect the limit: \[\ln \varphi_{W_n}(\xi) = n \ln \cos\left( \frac{\xi}{\sqrt{n}} \right)\]
Using the Taylor expansion of \(\ln \cos(x)\) near \(x = 0\): \[
\cos(x) = 1 - \frac{x^2}{2} + O(x^4).
\] \[
\ln(1 + u) = u - \frac{u^2}{2} + O(u^3).
\] \[
\begin{aligned}
&\implies \ln \cos(x) = \left(-\frac{x^2}{2} + O(x^4)\right) - \frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{x^2}{2} + O(x^4)\right)^2 + \dots\\
& = -\frac{x^2}{2} + O(x^4).
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting \(x = \frac{\xi}{\sqrt{n}}\): \[
\ln \varphi_{W_n}(\xi) = n \left( -\frac{\xi^2}{2n} + O_\xi\left( \frac{1}{n^2} \right) \right) = -\frac{\xi^2}{2} + O_\xi\left( \frac{1}{n} \right).
\]
Taking the limit as \(n \to \infty\) for fixed \(\xi\): \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \ln \varphi_{W_n}(\xi) = -\frac{\xi^2}{2} \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} \varphi_{W_n}(\xi) = e^{-\frac{\xi^2}{2}}.
\]
Since \(e^{-\xi^2/2}\) is the characteristic function of \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\), by the Continuity Theorem we conclude: \[
\frac{Y_1 + \dots + Y_n}{\sqrt{n}} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, 1).
\]

title: 54  Lecture 25.2: Fourier Inversion
text:
54.2 Lévy’s Fourier Inversion Theorem
A probability distribution can be completely reconstructed from its characteristic function; Lévy’s inversion formula provides an explicit Fourier-integral formula for recovering its interval probabilities.

Theorem 54.1 (Lévy’s Inversion Theorem) Let \(\mu \in \operatorname{Prob}(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) with characteristic function \(\hat{\mu}(\xi)\). For any \(a < b\) in \(\mathbb{R}\):
\[
\lim_{R \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-R}^{R} \frac{e^{-i\xi a} - e^{-i\xi b}}{i\xi} \hat{\mu}(\xi) \, d\xi = \mu((a, b)) + \frac{1}{2}\mu(\{a\}) + \frac{1}{2}\mu(\{b\}),
\] where
\[
\mu(\{c\})=\lim_{R \to \infty} \frac{1}{2R} \int_{-R}^{R} e^{-i\xi c} \hat{\mu}(\xi) \, d\xi, \quad c \in \{a, b\}.
\]
In particular, if \(a\) and \(b\) are continuity points of the cumulative distribution function \(F(x) = \mu((-\infty, x])\), then:
\[
\mu((a, b)) = \lim_{R \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-R}^{R} \frac{e^{-i\xi a} - e^{-i\xi b}}{i\xi} \hat{\mu}(\xi) \, d\xi
\]

Note on Boundedness: The integrand kernel \(\frac{e^{-i\xi a} - e^{-i\xi b}}{i\xi} = \int_a^b e^{-i\xi x} dx\) is bounded by \(|b - a|\) because \[
\left| \frac{e^{-i\xi a} - e^{-i\xi b}}{i\xi} \right| = \left| \int_a^b e^{-i\xi x} dx \right| \le \int_a^b |e^{-i\xi x}| dx = |b - a|.
\] However, it is generally not integrable on \(\mathbb{R}\) with respect to Lebesgue measure (\(\notin L^1(\mathbb{R})\)), which is why we must compute the symmetric limit as \(R \to \infty\).

title: 54  Lecture 25.2: Fourier Inversion
section: 54.3 Key Technical Lemma: The Sine Integral Trick
text:
54.3 Key Technical Lemma: The Sine Integral Trick

Lemma 54.1 (Properties of the Sine Integral Function) For \(r \ge 0\), define the sine integral, interpreting \(\sin(\xi)/\xi\) at \(\xi=0\) by its continuous extension with value \(1\):
\[
S(r) := \int_{-r}^{r} \frac{\sin(\xi)}{\xi} \, d\xi = 2 \int_{0}^{r} \frac{\sin(\xi)}{\xi} \, d\xi
\]
Then \(S(r)\) is continuous on \([0, \infty)\), and \(\lim_{r \to \infty} S(r) = \pi\).


Proof (Proof via the “One Simple Trick”). We express \(\frac{1}{\xi}\) as an exponential integral \(\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-\xi t} \, dt = \frac{1}{\xi}\) (for \(\xi > 0\)), and substitute directly:
\[
\int_{0}^{r} \frac{\sin(\xi)}{\xi} \, d\xi = \int_{0}^{r} \sin(\xi) \left( \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-\xi t} \, dt \right) d\xi
\]
By Fubini’s Theorem (justified since \(\int_0^r\int_0^\infty e^{-\xi t}|\sin\xi|\,dt\,d\xi \le r < \infty\)):
\[
= \int_{0}^{\infty} \left( \int_{0}^{r} e^{-\xi t} \sin(\xi) \, d\xi \right) dt
\]
Evaluating the inner integral via integration by parts:
\[
\int_{0}^{r} e^{-\xi t} \sin(\xi) \, d\xi = \frac{1}{1+t^2} \left[ 1 - e^{-rt}(\cos r + t \sin r) \right]
\]
Substituting back and recalling \(S(r) = 2\int_{0}^{r} \frac{\sin(\xi)}{\xi} \, d\xi\):
\[
S(r) = 2 \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{1+t^2} \left[ 1 - e^{-rt}(\cos r + t \sin r) \right] dt
\]
We now let \(r\to\infty\). For every \(t>0\), \(e^{-rt}(\cos r+t\sin r)\longrightarrow0\). Moreover, for \(r\ge1\), \[
\left| \frac{e^{-rt}(\cos r+t\sin r)} {1+t^2} \right| \le e^{-t}\frac{1+t}{1+t^2}.
\] Note that \(e^{-t}\frac{1+t}{1+t^2} \le 2 e^{-t}\) for \(t \ge 0\). Thus, \[
\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\frac{1+t}{1+t^2}\,dt<\infty.
\] Hence, by the Dominated Convergence Theorem, \[
\int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-rt}(\cos r+t\sin r)}{1+t^2}\,dt \longrightarrow 0.
\] Therefore, \[
\lim_{r \to \infty} S(r) = 2 \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{1+t^2} \, dt = 2 \left[ \arctan(t) \right]_{0}^{\infty} = 2 \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = \pi.
\]

title: 54  Lecture 25.2: Fourier Inversion
section: 54.4 Complete Proof of Lévy’s Inversion Formula
text:
54.4 Complete Proof of Lévy’s Inversion Formula
Let \(I(R)\) be defined as:
\[
I(R) := \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-R}^{R} \frac{e^{-i\xi a} - e^{-i\xi b}}{i\xi} \hat{\mu}(\xi) \, d\xi
\]
The quotient at \(\xi=0\) is understood by continuous extension, with value \(b-a\). We first record the atom identity used in the theorem. For any \(c\in\mathbb R\), Fubini’s theorem gives \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{2R}\int_{-R}^{R}e^{-i\xi c}\hat\mu(\xi)\,d\xi
&=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{2R}\int_{-R}^{R}e^{i\xi(x-c)}\,d\xi\,\mu(dx)\\
&=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\sin(R(x-c))}{R(x-c)}\,\mu(dx),
\end{align*}
\] where the quotient is defined to be \(1\) at \(x=c\). Its absolute value is at most \(1\), and it converges pointwise to \(\mathbf 1_{\{c\}}(x)\). The Dominated Convergence Theorem therefore yields \[
\mu(\{c\})=\lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{1}{2R}\int_{-R}^{R}e^{-i\xi c}\hat\mu(\xi)\,d\xi.
\]
Substitute \(\hat{\mu}(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{i\xi x} \, \mu(dx)\):
\[
I(R) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-R}^{R} \frac{e^{-i\xi a} - e^{-i\xi b}}{i\xi} \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{i\xi x} \, \mu(dx) \right) d\xi
\]
Applying Fubini’s Theorem to swap integration order (justified since \(\left|\frac{e^{i\xi(x-a)}-e^{i\xi(x-b)}}{i\xi}\right| \le |b-a|\), so the double integral over \([-R,R]\times\mathbb{R}\) is absolutely bounded by \(2R|b-a|\mu(\mathbb{R}) < \infty\)):
\[
I(R) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\mathbb{R}} \left( \int_{-R}^{R} \frac{e^{i\xi(x-a)} - e^{i\xi(x-b)}}{i\xi} \, d\xi \right) \mu(dx)
\]

title: 54  Lecture 25.2: Fourier Inversion
text:
54.8 Continuous Densities (\(L^1\) Integrable Characteristic Functions)
If a probability distribution has a sufficiently well-behaved characteristic function—specifically, an integrable characteristic function—then the distribution must have a continuous density, and that density can be recovered explicitly from the characteristic function by Fourier inversion.

Corollary 54.1 (Density Inversion Formula) If \(\mu \in \operatorname{Prob}(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) and its characteristic function satisfies \(\hat{\mu} \in L^1(\mathbb{R})\) (i.e., \(\int_{\mathbb{R}} |\hat{\mu}(\xi)| d\xi < \infty\)), then \(\mu\) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure (\(\mu \ll \lambda\)), and its continuous density function \(g(x) = \frac{d\mu}{dx}\) is given by:
\[
g(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-i\xi x} \hat{\mu}(\xi) \, d\xi
\]

Some Observations:

In other words, the corollary establishes the chain \[
\boxed{ \hat\mu\in L^1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mu\ll\lambda \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mu(dx)=g(x)\,dx }
\] with the density explicitly given by \[
\boxed{ g(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-i\xi x}\hat\mu(\xi)\,d\xi. }
\]
So there are really two messages:

Existence: An integrable characteristic function rules out discrete or singular components; the distribution has a density.
Recovery: The density is not merely known to exist—it can be reconstructed directly from the characteristic function.

The characteristic function contains the entire distribution. When it is integrable, Fourier inversion allows us to recover the distribution’s density directly. This is the key bridge between characteristic functions and densities.


Proof (Proof of Corollary 54.1). Define \(g(x) := \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-i\xi x} \hat{\mu}(\xi) \, d\xi\). Since \(\hat{\mu} \in L^1(\mathbb{R})\), \(g(x)\) is continuous and bounded by the Riemann-Lebesgue Lemma (Theorem 53.1) (\(g \in C_0(\mathbb{R})\)).
For every finite interval \((a,b)\), Fubini’s theorem applies because \[
\int_a^b\int_{\mathbb R}|e^{-i\xi x}\hat\mu(\xi)|\,d\xi\,dx
=(b-a)\|\hat\mu\|_{L^1}<\infty.
\] Therefore,
\[
\begin{align*}
\int_a^b g(x) \, dx &= \int_a^b \left( \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-i\xi x} \hat{\mu}(\xi) \, d\xi \right) dx \\
&= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\mathbb{R}} \left( \int_a^b e^{-i\xi x} dx \right) \hat{\mu}(\xi) \, d\xi \\
&= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\mathbb{R}} \frac{e^{-i\xi a} - e^{-i\xi b}}{i\xi} \hat{\mu}(\xi) \, d\xi\\
& = \lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-R}^{R}\frac{e^{-i\xi a}-e^{-i\xi b}}{i\xi}\hat\mu(\xi)\,d\xi
\end{align*}
\] If \(a\) and \(b\) are continuity points of \(F\), Lévy’s inversion theorem gives \[
\int_a^b g(x)\,dx=\mu((a,b)).
\] The discontinuities of the monotone function \(F\) are countable. Hence, for arbitrary \(a<b\), choose continuity points \(a_n\downarrow a\) and \(b_n\uparrow b\) with \(a_n<b_n\). The intervals \((a_n,b_n)\) increase to \((a,b)\). Continuity from below gives the result for \(\mu\), while the result for the integral of \(g\) follows from the Dominated Convergence Theorem on the bounded interval \((a,b)\), since \(g\) is bounded: \[
\int_a^b g(x)\,dx=\mu((a,b)).
\] In particular, the integral of \(g\) over every bounded interval is real and nonnegative. Since \(g\) is continuous, this implies that \(g\) is real-valued and nonnegative everywhere. Letting the intervals increase to \(\mathbb R\) gives \(\int_{\mathbb R}g\,dx=1\), so \(g\,dx\) is a probability measure. Equality on all bounded intervals then implies \(\mu(dx)=g(x)\,dx\) on \(\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\). Thus, \(g(x)\) is indeed the density of \(\mu\).

55.2 Key Theorems and Technical Lemmas
The characteristic function of one probability measure can be integrated against another probability measure in either order, because the Fourier kernel \(e^{i\xi^\top x}\) is bounded and Fubini’s theorem allows the order of integration to be exchanged.

Lemma 55.1 (Fubini/Fourier Duality Identity) Let \(\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) be probability measures on \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Then: \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \hat{\mu}(\xi) \nu(d\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \hat{\nu}(x) \mu(dx)
\]


Proof (Proof of Lemma 55.1). By definition of the characteristic function \(\hat{\mu}(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i x \cdot \xi} \mu(dx)\), we write: \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \hat{\mu}(\xi) \nu(d\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i x \cdot \xi} \mu(dx) \right) \nu(d\xi)
\] Since \(|e^{i x \cdot \xi}| = 1\), we apply Fubini’s Theorem to interchange the order of integration: \[
= \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \mu(dx) \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i x \cdot \xi} \nu(d\xi) \right) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \hat{\nu}(x) \mu(dx)
\]


Remark 55.1. This identity says that the two measures can be interchanged in the Fourier kernel: \[
\int\!\!\int e^{i\xi^\top x}\,\mu(dx)\nu(d\xi)
\] can be integrated first with respect to either measure. Symbolically, \[
\boxed{ \int \hat\mu\,d\nu = \int \hat\nu\,d\mu. }
\] This is essentially a Fourier duality identity: the characteristic function of \(\mu\), integrated against \(\nu\), equals the characteristic function of \(\nu\), integrated against \(\mu\).

The following corollary shows that the real part of the characteristic function also satisfies a similar duality identity. Using \(\operatorname{Re}\hat\mu(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb R^d}\cos(\xi^\top x)\,\mu(dx)\), we have \[
1 - \operatorname{Re}\hat{\mu}(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \left[ 1 - \cos(\xi^\top x) \right] \mu(dx).
\]

Corollary 55.1 (Real Part Difference Identity) Taking the real part of both sides yields: \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \left[ 1 - \operatorname{Re}\hat{\mu}(\xi) \right] \nu(d\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \left[ 1 - \operatorname{Re}\hat{\nu}(x) \right] \mu(dx)
\]


Proof (Proof of Corollary 55.1). From the previous lemma, \[
\int_{\mathbb R^d}\hat\mu(\xi)\,\nu(d\xi) = \int_{\mathbb R^d}\hat\nu(x)\,\mu(dx).
\] Since both sides are absolutely integrable, we may take real parts: \[
\int_{\mathbb R^d}\operatorname{Re}\hat\mu(\xi)\,\nu(d\xi) = \int_{\mathbb R^d}\operatorname{Re}\hat\nu(x)\,\mu(dx).
\] Now use the fact that both \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are probability measures. Hence \[
\int_{\mathbb R^d}1\,\nu(d\xi)=1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}1\,\mu(dx)=1. \] Subtracting the preceding equality from \(1=1\), we obtain \[ \begin{aligned} \int_{\mathbb R^d} \left[1-\operatorname{Re}\hat\mu(\xi)\right]\nu(d\xi) &= 1-\int_{\mathbb R^d}\operatorname{Re}\hat\mu(\xi)\,\nu(d\xi)\\ &= 1-\int_{\mathbb R^d}\operatorname{Re}\hat\nu(x)\,\mu(dx)\\ &= \int_{\mathbb R^d} \left[1-\operatorname{Re}\hat\nu(x)\right]\mu(dx). \end{aligned} \]

title: 55  Lecture 25.3: The Continuity Theorem
text:
55.5 Main Result: Lévy’s Continuity Theorem
A pointwise limit of characteristic functions is automatically a characteristic function of a probability distribution, provided the limit is continuous at the origin; moreover, the corresponding probability distributions converge weakly.

Theorem 55.2 (Lévy’s Continuity Theorem) Let \(\{\mu_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\). Suppose that \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \hat{\mu}_n(\xi) = \varphi(\xi)\) exists for all \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d\).
If \(\varphi\) is continuous at \(\xi = 0\), then:

\(\varphi\) is the characteristic function of a unique probability measure \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) (i.e., \(\varphi = \hat{\mu}\)).
\(\mu_n \implies \mu\) weakly as \(n \to \infty\).



Proof (Proof Strategy (Subsequence Argument)). 

Tightness: By the Tightness Criterion above, \(\{\mu_n\}\) is tight.
Relative Compactness: By Prokhorov’s Theorem (Theorem 49.1 and Corollary 49.1), tightness implies relative compactness. Thus, every subsequence of \(\{\mu_n\}\) has a further weakly convergent subsequence.
Construction of \(\mu\): By Step 2, pick any subsequence with \(\mu_{n_k} \implies \mu\) for some \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Since \(x \mapsto e^{i\xi\cdot x}\) is bounded and continuous, weak convergence gives \(\hat{\mu}_{n_k}(\xi) \to \hat{\mu}(\xi)\) for every \(\xi\). But by assumption \(\hat{\mu}_{n_k}(\xi) \to \varphi(\xi)\), so \(\hat{\mu} = \varphi\). This establishes Conclusion 1: \(\varphi\) is the characteristic function of \(\mu\), and \(\mu\) is the unique such probability measure (by injectivity of the Fourier transform on \(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)\)).
Uniqueness of Every Subsequential Limit: Suppose for contradiction that \(\mu_n \not\implies \mu\). Then there exist \(f \in C_b(\mathbb{R}^d)\), \(\varepsilon > 0\), and a subsequence \(\{\mu_{n_j}\}\) such that: \[
\left| \int f \, d\mu_{n_j} - \int f \, d\mu \right| \ge \varepsilon \quad \forall j
\] By relative compactness, \(\{\mu_{n_j}\}\) has a further subsequence \(\mu_{n_{j_k}} \implies \nu\) for some \(\nu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)\).
Since \(x \mapsto e^{i\xi\cdot x}\) is bounded and continuous, weak convergence \(\mu_{n_{j_k}} \implies \nu\) gives \(\hat{\mu}_{n_{j_k}}(\xi) \to \hat{\nu}(\xi)\) for all \(\xi\). But \(\hat{\mu}_{n_{j_k}}(\xi) \to \varphi(\xi) = \hat{\mu}(\xi)\) by assumption and Step 3. By uniqueness of limits: \[
\hat{\nu}(\xi) = \varphi(\xi) = \hat{\mu}(\xi)
\] Since characteristic functions uniquely determine probability measures, \(\nu = \mu\).
Conclusion: Since \(\mu_{n_{j_k}} \implies \nu = \mu\) and \(f \in C_b(\mathbb{R}^d)\), we have \(\int f\,d\mu_{n_{j_k}} \to \int f\,d\mu\). This contradicts \(\left|\int f\,d\mu_{n_j} - \int f\,d\mu\right| \ge \varepsilon\) for all \(j\) (in particular for \(j = j_k\) with \(k\) large). Therefore, the entire sequence \(\mu_n \implies \mu\).

title: 56  Lecture 26.1: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
Theorem 56.1 (\(L^2\)-SLLN) Let \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be independent \(L^2\) random variables with common mean \(\mathbb{E}[X_n] = t\). Let \(S_n = X_1 + \dots + X_n\), and let \(\{b_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be a deterministic, nondecreasing sequence such that \(b_n > 0\), \(b_n \to \infty\), and \[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\operatorname{Var}[X_n]}{b_n^2} < \infty \]
Then, defining \(\dot{S}_n = S_n - nt\), we have: \[ \frac{\dot{S}_n}{b_n} = \frac{S_n - nt}{b_n} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s. and } L^2} 0 \]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 56.1). Set \(Y_n = X_n - t\) and \(T_n = \sum_{k=1}^n Y_k\). The variables \(Y_n/b_n\) are independent, centered, and satisfy \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \operatorname{Var}\left[\frac{Y_n}{b_n}\right]
= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\operatorname{Var}[X_n]}{b_n^2}<\infty.
\] Therefore, the hypotheses of Kolmogorov’s Convergence Criterion (Theorem 39.2) are satisfied, and \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty Y_n/b_n\) converges almost surely. Since \(b_n\) is nondecreasing and \(b_n\to\infty\), the hypotheses of Kronecker’s lemma (Lemma 40.1) are also satisfied, so \[
\frac{T_n}{b_n}
= \frac{1}{b_n}\sum_{k=1}^n b_k\frac{Y_k}{b_k}
\longrightarrow 0 \quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
For \(L^2\) convergence, independence and centering give \[
\left\|\frac{T_n}{b_n}\right\|_2^2
= \mathbb{E}\left[\left|\frac{T_n}{b_n}\right|^2\right]
= \frac{1}{b_n^2}\sum_{k=1}^n \operatorname{Var}[X_k],
\] because \(T_n\) is centered. Fix \(K\). For \(n>K\), monotonicity of \(b_n\) yields
\[
\frac{1}{b_n^2}\sum_{k=1}^n \operatorname{Var}[X_k]
\leq \frac{1}{b_n^2}\sum_{k=1}^K \operatorname{Var}[X_k]
+ \sum_{k=K+1}^n \frac{\operatorname{Var}[X_k]}{b_k^2}.
\]
The first term tends to zero as \(n\to\infty\), and the second can be made arbitrarily small by choosing \(K\) large. Hence \(T_n/b_n\to0\) in \(L^2\).

title: 56  Lecture 26.1: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
56.2 Example
For i.i.d. \(L^2\) variables with common variance \(\operatorname{Var}[X_n] = \sigma^2\), the condition \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\operatorname{Var}[X_n]}{b_n^2} < \infty\) reduces to \(\sigma^2 \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{b_n^2} < \infty\).
If \(\alpha > \frac{1}{2}\) and \(b_n = n^\alpha\), then: \[ \sigma^2\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{(n^\alpha)^2} = \sigma^2\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^{2\alpha}} < \infty \] since \(2\alpha > 1\). Thus, by the \(L^2\)-SLLN: \[ \frac{\dot{S}_n}{n^\alpha} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s. and } L^2} 0 \]
However, if \(\sigma^2>0\) and we choose \(b_n = \sqrt{n}\) (i.e., \(\alpha = \frac{1}{2}\)), the condition fails: \[ \sigma^2\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{(\sqrt{n})^2} = \sigma^2\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n} = \infty \] In this critical normalization regime, the \(L^2\)-SLLN above does not apply. The Central Limit Theorem instead gives weak convergence under the nondegeneracy assumption \(\sigma^2>0\).

title: 56  Lecture 26.1: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
56.3 Basic Central Limit Theorem (1D)

Theorem 56.2 (Basic Central Limit Theorem) Let \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be i.i.d. \(L^2\) random variables with common mean \(\mathbb{E}[X_n] = t\) and variance \(\text{Var}[X_n] = \sigma^2>0\). Let \(S_n = X_1 + \dots + X_n\) and \(\dot{S}_n = S_n - nt\). Then: \[ \frac{\dot{S}_n}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} = \frac{S_n - nt}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} \xrightarrow{w} Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) \]



Proof (Proof of Theorem 56.2). Define \(\dot{X}_i = X_i - t\). Then \(\{\dot{X}_i\}\) are i.i.d., centered, and satisfy \(\mathbb{E}[\dot{X}_i^2] = \operatorname{Var}[X_i] = \sigma^2\).
By Lévy’s Continuity Theorem (Theorem 55.2), it suffices to show that the characteristic function of \(\frac{\dot{S}_n}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\) converges pointwise to the characteristic function of \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\): \[
\varphi_{\dot{S}_n / \sigma\sqrt{n}}(\xi) \longrightarrow e^{-\xi^2 / 2}, \quad \forall \xi \in \mathbb{R}.
\]

Factorization via Independence: \[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi_{\dot{S}_n / \sigma\sqrt{n}}(\xi) &= \varphi_{\dot{S}_n}\left( \frac{\xi}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} \right) \\
&= \varphi_{\dot{X}_1 + \dots + \dot{X}_n}\left( \frac{\xi}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} \right) \\
&= \left( \varphi_{\dot{X}_1}\left( \frac{\xi}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} \right) \right)^n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taylor Expansion: Since \(\dot{X}_1 \in L^2\), \(\mathbb{E}[\dot{X}_1^2] = \sigma^2 < \infty\), which implies \(\varphi_{\dot{X}_1} \in C^2(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{C})\) (the derivatives \(\varphi^{(k)}(\xi) = \mathbb{E}[(i\dot{X}_1)^k e^{i\xi\dot{X}_1}]\) exist and are continuous by dominated convergence, since \(|\dot{X}_1|^k e^{i\xi\dot{X}_1}\) is dominated by \(|\dot{X}_1|^k \in L^1\) for \(k\le 2\)). Since \(\varphi_{\dot{X}_1}\) is complex-valued, we apply Taylor’s theorem to its real and imaginary parts separately, yielding the \(o\)-term expansion: \[ \varphi_{\dot{X}_1}(x) = \varphi_{\dot{X}_1}(0) + \varphi_{\dot{X}_1}'(0)\, x + \tfrac{1}{2}\varphi_{\dot{X}_1}''(0)\, x^2 + o(x^2) \quad (x \to 0) \]
Evaluating Derivatives at \(0\):

\(\varphi_{\dot{X}_1}(0) = \mathbb{E}[e^{i \cdot 0 \cdot \dot{X}_1}] = 1\)
\(\varphi_{\dot{X}_1}'(0) = \mathbb{E}[i \dot{X}_1 e^{i \xi \dot{X}_1}]\big|_{\xi=0} = i \mathbb{E}[\dot{X}_1] = 0\)
\(\varphi_{\dot{X}_1}''(0) = \mathbb{E}[(i \dot{X}_1)^2 e^{i \xi \dot{X}_1}]\big|_{\xi=0} = -\mathbb{E}[\dot{X}_1^2] = -\text{Var}[X_1] = -\sigma^2\)

Thus the Taylor expansion simplifies to: \[ \varphi_{\dot{X}_1}(x) = 1 - \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\, x^2 + o(x^2) \quad (x \to 0) \]
Evaluating at \(x = \frac{\xi}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\) and taking \(n \to \infty\): As \(n\to\infty\) the argument \(x = \frac{\xi}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} \to 0\), so the Taylor expansion gives: \[ \varphi_{\dot{X}_1}\!\left(\frac{\xi}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\right) = 1 - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\cdot\frac{\xi^2}{\sigma^2 n} + o\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) = 1 - \frac{\xi^2}{2n} + o\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) \] Define \(a_n := -\frac{\xi^2}{2n} + o\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\), so that \(n\,a_n \to -\frac{\xi^2}{2}\). Since \(a_n\to0\), for all sufficiently large \(n\) the numbers \(1+a_n\) lie in a neighborhood of \(1\) on which a consistent analytic branch of the complex logarithm is defined. Thus the standard complex limit \((1+a_n)^n \to e^L\) whenever \(n\,a_n\to L\) applies, using \(\log(1+a_n)=a_n+O(a_n^2)\): \[ \left( \varphi_{\dot{X}_1}\!\left( \frac{\xi}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} \right) \right)^n = (1 + a_n)^n \longrightarrow e^{-\xi^2/2} \]

By Lévy’s Continuity Theorem (Theorem 55.2), \(\frac{\dot{S}_n}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} \xrightarrow{w} \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\).

title: 56  Lecture 26.1: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
56.4 Multivariate Central Limit Theorem
Before proving the multivariate extension of the CLT, we define the centered multivariate normal distribution and establish the Cramér-Wold device.

Definition 56.1 (Centered Normal Distribution in \(\mathbb{R}^d\)) Let \(Q\) be a positive semi-definite \(d \times d\) matrix, meaning that \(Q\) is symmetric with nonnegative eigenvalues. Equivalently, \(Q = A A^T\) for some \(d \times d\) matrix \(A\). The centered normal distribution of covariance \(Q\) is the unique measure \(\mu \in \text{Prob}(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) whose characteristic function, for \(\xi\in\mathbb{R}^d\), is \[ \hat{\mu}(\xi) = e^{-\frac{1}{2} \xi^T Q\xi} = e^{-\frac{1}{2} |A^T \xi|^2}. \] We denote this as \(\mathcal{N}(0, Q)\).
Existence follows by taking \(AG\), where \(G=(G_1,\dots,G_d)^T\) has independent \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) coordinates, and uniqueness follows from the uniqueness theorem for characteristic functions.

Exercise: If \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q)\), then \(\text{Cov}[X_i, X_j] = Q_{ij}\), \(X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q_{ii})\), and \(Q = \mathbb{E}[X X^T]\).


Lemma 56.1 (Cramér-Wold Device) Let \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) and \(X\) be random vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Then: \[ X_n \xrightarrow{w} X \iff \xi \cdot X_n \xrightarrow{w} \xi \cdot X \quad \forall \xi \in \mathbb{R}^d \]


Proof (Proof of Lemma 56.1). \((\Longrightarrow)\) Fix any \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d\). For any \(g \in C_b(\mathbb{R})\), the composition \(x \mapsto g(\xi \cdot x)\) is bounded and continuous on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (since \(x\mapsto\xi\cdot x\) is a continuous linear map). Therefore, by definition of \(X_n \xrightarrow{w} X\): \[\mathbb{E}[g(\xi \cdot X_n)] \to \mathbb{E}[g(\xi \cdot X)] \quad \forall g \in C_b(\mathbb{R})\] Since this holds for every \(g \in C_b(\mathbb{R})\), we conclude \(\xi \cdot X_n \xrightarrow{w} \xi \cdot X\).
\((\Longleftarrow)\) Conversely, if \(\xi \cdot X_n \xrightarrow{w} \xi \cdot X\) for all \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d\), then for any fixed \(\xi\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(u\in\mathbb{R}\), the hypothesis applied to the vector \(u\xi\) gives, since \(t\mapsto e^{it}\) is bounded and continuous: \[ \varphi_{\xi \cdot X_n}(u) = \mathbb{E}[e^{i (u\xi) \cdot X_n}] \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}[e^{i (u\xi) \cdot X}] = \varphi_{\xi \cdot X}(u) \] Evaluating at \(u=1\) gives \[
\varphi_{X_n}(\xi)=\mathbb{E}[e^{i\xi\cdot X_n}]
\longrightarrow \mathbb{E}[e^{i\xi\cdot X}]=\varphi_X(\xi)
\] for every \(\xi\in\mathbb{R}^d\). By Lévy’s Continuity Theorem (since \(\varphi_X\) is the characteristic function of \(X\), hence continuous at the origin), \(X_n \xrightarrow{w} X\).


Remark 56.1. One conceptual point that is particularly useful: the forward direction is just the continuous mapping theorem (Corollary 50.2), whereas the reverse direction is the substantive content of Cramér–Wold. The characteristic-function argument is what turns convergence of every scalar projection into convergence of the joint distribution.



Theorem 56.3 (Multivariate Central Limit Theorem) If \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are i.i.d. random vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) whose coordinates belong to \(L^2\), with centered mean \(\mathbb{E}[X_n] = 0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and covariance matrix \(Q = \mathbb{E}[X_1 X_1^T]\), then: \[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=1}^n X_j \xrightarrow{w} \mathcal{N}(0, Q) \]



Proof (Proof of Theorem 56.3). Fix \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d\). Define the scalar random variables: \[ X_n^\xi := \xi \cdot X_n \]

Independence and Identical Distribution: Since \(\{X_n\}\) are i.i.d. vectors, \(\{X_n^\xi\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are i.i.d. scalar random variables, with characteristic function: \[ \varphi_{X_n^\xi}(u) = \mathbb{E}[e^{i u \xi \cdot X_n}] = \varphi_{X_n}(u\xi) = \varphi_{X_1}(u\xi) \]
Moments of \(X_n^\xi\):

Mean: \(\mathbb{E}[X_n^\xi] = \mathbb{E}[\xi \cdot X_n] = \xi \cdot \mathbb{E}[X_n] = 0\).
Variance: \[ \text{Var}[X_n^\xi] = \mathbb{E}[(\xi \cdot X_n)^2] - (\xi \cdot \mathbb{E}[X_n])^2 = \mathbb{E}[(\xi \cdot X_n)^2] \] Using the vector identity \((v \cdot w)^2 = v^T (w w^T) v\): \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[(\xi \cdot X_n)^2] &= \mathbb{E}[\xi^T (X_n X_n^T) \xi]\\
& = \xi^T \mathbb{E}[(X_n - \mathbb{E}[X_n])(X_n - \mathbb{E}[X_n])^T] \xi\\
& = \xi^T Q \xi.
\end{align*}
\]

Applying 1D CLT and Cramér-Wold Device: If \(\xi^TQ\xi>0\), the univariate Central Limit Theorem applied to the i.i.d. centered sequence \(\{X_n^\xi\}\) gives \[ \xi \cdot \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=1}^n X_j \right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=1}^n X_j^\xi \xrightarrow{w} \mathcal{N}(0,\, \xi^TQ\xi). \] If \(\xi^TQ\xi=0\), then \(\mathbb{E}[(X_1^\xi)^2]=0\), so \(X_1^\xi=0\) almost surely. Thus every normalized sum of the projections is identically zero, and the same conclusion holds.
For any \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q)\), the projection \(\xi \cdot Z\) has characteristic function \[
\mathbb{E}[e^{iu(\xi\cdot Z)}]
=e^{-\frac{1}{2}u^2\xi^TQ\xi},
\] so \(\xi \cdot Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\xi^TQ\xi)\), including the degenerate case. Therefore, in both cases, \[\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{j=1}^n X_j^\xi \xrightarrow{w} \xi\cdot Z.\]

Since this holds for every fixed \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d\), applying the Cramér-Wold Device yields: \[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=1}^n X_j \xrightarrow{w} \mathcal{N}(0, Q) \] This completes the proof.

title: 57  Lecture 26.2: Infinite Divisibility
text:
Definition 57.1 (Infinitely Divisible Measure) A probability measure \(\mu \in \text{Prob}(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) is infinitely divisible if for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), there exists a probability measure \(\mu_n \in \text{Prob}(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) such that: \[ \mu = \mu_n^{*n} = \underbrace{\mu_n * \mu_n * \dots * \mu_n}_{n \text{ times}} \]
In terms of random variables and characteristic functions, this definition admits two equivalent formulations:

Random Variable Formulation: For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), there exist i.i.d. real-valued random variables \(\{X_{n,k}\}_{k=1}^n\) such that: \[ S_n = X_{n,1} + X_{n,2} + \dots + X_{n,n} \sim \mu \]
Characteristic Function Formulation: \(\mu\) has a characteristic function \(\hat{\mu}(\xi)\) satisfying: \[ \hat{\mu}(\xi) = (\varphi_n(\xi))^n \quad \forall \xi \in \mathbb{R} \] where \(\varphi_n(\xi)\) is the characteristic function of \(\mu_n\).

The equivalence follows from \(\widehat{\mu_n^{*n}}=(\hat\mu_n)^n\) and the uniqueness theorem for characteristic functions.


Remark 57.1. Intuitively, infinite divisibility means that a random quantity can be split into any number of independent, identically distributed pieces without changing its overall distribution. Suppose \(X\sim\mu\). If \(\mu\) is infinitely divisible, then for every \(n=2,3,4,\ldots\), we can find i.i.d. random variables \[ X_{n,1},\ldots,X_{n,n} \] such that \[ X_{n,1}+\cdots+X_{n,n}\overset{d}=X. \]
So you can think of \(X\) as a whole that can be decomposed into \(n\) independent, statistically identical components, for any finite \(n\).
There are really two ideas in the definition:

Divisible: the distribution can be represented as a convolution of smaller distributions.
Infinitely: this can be done for every \(n\), no matter how large.

Graphically, you can think of it as \[ \boxed{\text{whole}} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\text{piece}}+\boxed{\text{piece}}+\cdots+\boxed{\text{piece}} \] with \(n\) identical independent pieces, for any \(n\). The pieces become smaller as \(n\) increases, but their aggregate distribution remains exactly the same.
