title: 45  Lecture 21.2: Law of Rare Events
section: 45.2 Proof of Theorem 45.1 Via Convolution Bound
text:
45.2 Proof of Theorem 45.1 Via Convolution Bound

Lemma 45.1 (Convolution Bound for Total Variation) Let \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n\) and \(\nu_1, \dots, \nu_n\) be probability measures on \((\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\). Then: \[
d_{\text{TV}}(\mu_1 * \mu_2 * \cdots * \mu_n, \, \nu_1 * \nu_2 * \cdots * \nu_n) \le \sum_{j=1}^n d_{\text{TV}}(\mu_j, \nu_j).
\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 45.1). Let \(\{N_j\}_{j=1}^n\) be independent Poisson random variables with \(N_j \sim \text{Poisson}(p_j)\). By the convolution property of Poisson laws, \(\sum_{j=1}^n N_j \sim \text{Poisson}\left(\sum_{j=1}^n p_j\right)\), so \(N \stackrel{d}{=} \sum_{j=1}^n N_j\).
Since the \(X_j\) are independent and the \(N_j\) are independent, the law of each sum is the convolution of the individual laws: \(\mu_{S_n} = \mu_{X_1} * \cdots * \mu_{X_n}\) and \(\mu_{N} = \mu_{N_1} * \cdots * \mu_{N_n}\). Using Lemma 45.1 and the exact Bernoulli–Poisson distance \(d_{\text{TV}}(\text{Bernoulli}(p), \text{Poisson}(p)) = p(1 - e^{-p})\) computed in Lecture 21.1: \[
\begin{aligned}
d_{\text{TV}}(S_n, N) &= d_{\text{TV}}\left(X_1 + \cdots + X_n, \, N_1 + \cdots + N_n\right) \\
&= d_{\text{TV}}(\mu_{X_1} * \cdots * \mu_{X_n}, \, \mu_{N_1} * \cdots * \mu_{N_n}) \\
&\le \sum_{j=1}^n d_{\text{TV}}(\mu_{X_j}, \mu_{N_j}) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^n p_j (1 - e^{-p_j}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(1 - e^{-p_j} = \int_0^{p_j} e^{-x} \, dx \le \int_0^{p_j} 1 \, dx = p_j\), we have \(p_j(1 - e^{-p_j}) \le p_j^2\). Substituting this yields: \[
d_{\text{TV}}(S_n, N) \le \sum_{j=1}^n p_j^2.
\]

title: 45  Lecture 21.2: Law of Rare Events
text:
45.3 Couplings
A coupling puts two random variables with prescribed distributions on the same probability space, so that we can decide how they depend on each other.

Definition 45.1 (Coupling) Given probability measures \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) on \((S, \mathcal{B})\), a coupling of \((\mu, \nu)\) is a pair of random variables \((X, Y)\) defined on a common probability space, taking values in \((S, \mathcal{B})\), such that \(\mu_X = \mu\) and \(\mu_Y = \nu\).


In other words, a coupling is a probability measure on \((S \times S, \mathcal{B} \otimes \mathcal{B})\) whose marginal distributions are \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) respectively. (For instance, the product measure \(\mu \otimes \nu\) is the independent coupling).
For intuition, the coupling determines how \(X\) and \(Y\) are related to each other, while keeping their individual distributions fixed.


Lemma 45.2 (Coupling Inequality) If \((X, Y)\) is any coupling of the probability measures \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) on \((S, \mathcal{B})\), then: \[
d_{\text{TV}}(\mu, \nu) \le \mathbb{P}(X \neq Y)
\] (Here \(\{X \ne Y\}\) is assumed measurable, which holds whenever the diagonal \(\{(x,x) : x \in S\}\) belongs to \(\mathcal{B} \otimes \mathcal{B}\); this is the case, for instance, when \(S\) is a separable metric space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra.)

Taking the infimum over all couplings, the lemma gives \(d_{\text{TV}}(\mu, \nu) \le \inf \{\mathbb{P}(X \ne Y) : (X, Y) \text{ a coupling of } (\mu, \nu)\}\). On a standard Borel space the infimum is in fact attained by the maximal coupling, so equality holds and total variation distance has a probabilistic interpretation:

It is the smallest possible probability that two random variables with distributions \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) must differ, when we are free to choose how they are coupled.


Proof (Proof of Lemma 45.2). Fix any event \(B \in \mathcal{B}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
|\mu(B) - \nu(B)| &= |\mathbb{P}(X \in B) - \mathbb{P}(Y \in B)| \\
&= \left| \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{I}_{\{X \in B\}} - \mathbb{I}_{\{Y \in B\}} \right] \right| \\
&\le \mathbb{E}\left[ \left| \mathbb{I}_{\{X \in B\}} - \mathbb{I}_{\{Y \in B\}} \right| \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{I}_{\{\{X \in B\} \Delta \{Y \in B\}\}} \right] \\
&= \mathbb{P}\left( \{X \in B\} \Delta \{Y \in B\} \right).
\end{aligned}
\] Since \(\{X \in B\} \Delta \{Y \in B\} \subseteq \{X \neq Y\}\), we obtain: \[
|\mu(B) - \nu(B)| \le \mathbb{P}(X \neq Y).
\] Taking the supremum over all \(B \in \mathcal{B}\) completes the proof.

section: 45.4 Proof of Theorem 45.1 Via Explicit Coupling Construction
text:
45.4 Proof of Theorem 45.1 Via Explicit Coupling Construction
We construct a joint probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) carrying i.i.d. Uniform random variables \(U_j \sim \text{Unif}[0, 1]\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n\).

45.4.1 Construction of \(Z_j \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_j)\)
Define \(Z_j := \mathbb{I}_{\{U_j \in (1 - p_j, 1]\}}\). Then: \[
\mathbb{P}(Z_j = 1) = \mathbb{P}(U_j \in (1 - p_j, 1]) = 1 - (1 - p_j) = p_j.
\] So \(Z_j \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_j)\), and since \(Z_j\) is a measurable function of \(U_j\) alone, the \(Z_j\) are independent. Thus \(T := \sum_{j=1}^n Z_j \stackrel{d}{=} S_n\).



45.4.2 Construction of \(M_j \sim \text{Poisson}(p_j)\)
Let \(\alpha_j(k) := \mathbb{P}(\text{Poisson}(p_j) \le k) = \sum_{l=0}^k e^{-p_j} \frac{p_j^l}{l!}\) with \(\alpha_j(-1) := 0\). Define \(M_j := \sum_{k=0}^\infty k \cdot \mathbb{I}_{\{\alpha_j(k-1) < U_j \le \alpha_j(k)\}}\). Since \(\alpha_j\) is strictly increasing with \(\alpha_j(k) \uparrow 1\), the intervals \((\alpha_j(k-1), \alpha_j(k)]\), \(k \ge 0\), partition \((0, 1]\), so exactly one term in the sum is nonzero and: \[
\mathbb{P}(M_j = k) = \mathbb{P}(\alpha_j(k-1) < U_j \le \alpha_j(k)) = \alpha_j(k) - \alpha_j(k-1) = e^{-p_j} \frac{p_j^k}{k!}.
\] So \(M_j \sim \text{Poisson}(p_j)\), and again the \(M_j\) are independent because \(M_j\) depends only on \(U_j\). By the convolution property of Poisson laws, \(M := \sum_{j=1}^n M_j \stackrel{d}{=} N \sim \text{Poisson}\left(\sum_{j=1}^n p_j\right)\).
Note that \(Z_j\) and \(M_j\) are built from the same uniform \(U_j\); this dependence is precisely what makes \((T, M)\) a useful coupling of \((\mu_{S_n}, \mu_N)\).



45.4.3 Visualization of the Joint Coupling \((Z_i, M_i)\)








Figure 45.1: Joint Coupling Construction of Bernoulli (\(Z_i\)) and Poisson (\(M_i\)) random variables.








45.4.4 Evaluating the Difference \(\mathbb{P}(Z_j \neq M_j)\)
Since \(T \stackrel{d}{=} S_n\) and \(M \stackrel{d}{=} N\), the pair \((T, M)\) is a coupling of \((\mu_{S_n}, \mu_N)\), so Lemma 45.2 applies. Moreover \(\{T \ne M\} \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^n \{Z_j \ne M_j\}\), because \(Z_j = M_j\) for every \(j\) forces \(T = M\); the union bound then gives: \[
d_{\text{TV}}(S_n, N) \le \mathbb{P}(T \neq M) \le \sum_{j=1}^n \mathbb{P}(Z_j \neq M_j)
\]
To compute \(\mathbb{P}(Z_j \ne M_j)\), note the elementary inequality \(1 - p_j \le e^{-p_j} = \alpha_j(0) \le \alpha_j(1)\), so the interval \([0,1]\) splits into four consecutive pieces:

Adding the lengths of the two disagreement intervals: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(Z_j \neq M_j) &= [\alpha_j(0) - (1 - p_j)] + [1 - \alpha_j(1)] \\
&= [e^{-p_j} - (1 - p_j)] + [1 - (e^{-p_j} + e^{-p_j} p_j)] \\
&= p_j - p_j e^{-p_j} = p_j (1 - e^{-p_j}) \le p_j^2,
\end{aligned}
\] where the last step again uses \(1 - e^{-p_j} \le p_j\).
Summing over \(j=1, \dots, n\) yields: \[
d_{\text{TV}}(S_n, N) \le \sum_{j=1}^n p_j^2.
\]

title: 45  Lecture 21.2: Law of Rare Events
text:
45.5 Optimal Transport & Wasserstein Distance
Couplings play a foundational role in large deviations, stochastic analysis, and optimal transport.

Definition 45.2 (Wasserstein Distance) For \(p \ge 1\), let \(\text{Prob}_p(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) denote the set of Borel probability measures \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with finite \(p\)-th moment \(\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |x|^p \mu(dx) < \infty\right)\).
The \(p\)-Wasserstein distance between \(\mu, \nu \in \text{Prob}_p(\mathbb{R}^d)\) is: \[
W_p(\mu, \nu) := \left( \inf \left\{ \mathbb{E}\left[|X - Y|^p\right] : (X, Y) \text{ is a coupling of } (\mu, \nu) \right\} \right)^{1/p}.
\]

Unlike \(d_{\text{TV}}\), the metric \(W_p\) incorporates the underlying geometry of \(\mathbb{R}^d\): it measures how far apart \(X\) and \(Y\) are, not merely whether they differ. The two topologies are not comparable on all of \(\text{Prob}_p(\mathbb{R}^d)\):

\(W_p\) convergence does not imply \(d_{\text{TV}}\) convergence: \(W_p(\delta_{1/n}, \delta_0) = 1/n \to 0\), while \(d_{\text{TV}}(\delta_{1/n}, \delta_0) = 1\) for every \(n\).
\(d_{\text{TV}}\) convergence does not imply \(W_p\) convergence: for \(\mu_n := (1 - \tfrac1n)\delta_0 + \tfrac1n \delta_{n^2}\) we have \(d_{\text{TV}}(\mu_n, \delta_0) = \tfrac1n \to 0\), yet \(W_p(\mu_n, \delta_0) = (n^{2p}/n)^{1/p} \to \infty\).

On a set of measures all supported in a fixed bounded set of diameter \(D\), however, the coupling inequality does give \(W_p(\mu, \nu) \le D \cdot d_{\text{TV}}(\mu, \nu)^{1/p}\), so there the \(W_p\)-topology is genuinely weaker than \(d_{\text{TV}}\).

title: 46  Lecture 22.1: Weak Convergence
text:
46.1 Motivation: Limitations of Total Variation Distance
In non-discrete probability settings, Total Variation (TV) convergence is often too strong or restrictive.
If \(\mu(A) = 0\) and \(\nu(A) = 1\) for some set \(A \in \mathcal{B}(S)\), then \(d_{TV}(\mu, \nu) = 1\).

title: 46  Lecture 22.1: Weak Convergence
text:
46.7 Step 1: Proof of \((1 \implies 2)\)
Since every bounded Lipschitz function is bounded and continuous, \(\text{Lip}_b(S) \subseteq C_b(S)\). Thus \((1 \implies 2)\) is immediate.

title: 46  Lecture 22.1: Weak Convergence
text:
46.8 Step 2: Proof of \((2 \implies 3)\)
Goal. Assume \(\int_S f \, d\mu_n \to \int_S f \, d\mu\) for every \(f \in \text{Lip}_b(S)\). Show that \(\limsup_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(F) \le \mu(F)\) for every closed \(F \subseteq S\).
The obstruction. We would like to plug \(f = \mathbf{1}_F\) into hypothesis (2), but \(\mathbf{1}_F\) is not continuous (unless \(F\) is also open). The remedy is to approximate \(\mathbf{1}_F\) from above by a sequence of bounded Lipschitz functions \(f_k \downarrow \mathbf{1}_F\). Each \(f_k\) is a legitimate test function, and the approximation is one-sided, which is exactly why we obtain the one-sided conclusion \(\limsup \mu_n(F) \le \mu(F)\) rather than equality.
If \(F = \emptyset\) both sides equal \(0\), so assume \(F \neq \emptyset\) from now on (this is needed for \(d(x,F)\) to be well defined).


46.8.1 Step 2a: Construction of the test functions
Define the distance to \(F\) by \[d(x, F) := \inf_{y \in F} d(x, y),\] let \(\psi(t) := \max(0, 1 - t)\) for \(t \ge 0\), and set \[f_k(x) := \psi\bigl(k \cdot d(x, F)\bigr), \qquad k \ge 1.\]
Explicitly, \[
f_k(x) =
\begin{cases}
1 - k\,d(x,F), & \text{if } d(x,F) < 1/k,\\[2pt]
0, & \text{if } d(x,F) \ge 1/k.
\end{cases}
\] So \(f_k\) equals \(1\) on \(F\), decays linearly to \(0\) as \(x\) moves away from \(F\), and vanishes entirely outside the open \(\tfrac1k\)-neighborhood \(F^{1/k} := \{x : d(x,F) < 1/k\}\). As \(k\) grows, this collar shrinks down onto \(F\).



46.8.2 Step 2b: Verification that \(f_k \in \text{Lip}_b(S)\)
(i) \(x \mapsto d(x,F)\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz. For any \(z \in F\), the triangle inequality gives \(d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)\), hence \(d(x, F) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)\). Taking the infimum over \(z \in F\) on the right yields \[d(x, F) - d(y, F) \le d(x, y).\] Swapping \(x\) and \(y\) gives the reverse bound, so \(|d(x,F) - d(y,F)| \le d(x,y)\).
(ii) \(\psi\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz. Both \(t \mapsto 0\) and \(t \mapsto 1-t\) are \(1\)-Lipschitz, and the pointwise maximum of two \(1\)-Lipschitz functions is \(1\)-Lipschitz.
(iii) \(f_k\) is \(k\)-Lipschitz. Composing (i) and (ii): \[|f_k(x) - f_k(y)| \le \bigl| k\,d(x, F) - k\,d(y, F) \bigr| = k\,\bigl|d(x,F) - d(y,F)\bigr| \le k\, d(x, y).\]
(iv) \(f_k\) is bounded. Since \(d(x,F) \ge 0\), we have \(\psi(k\,d(x,F)) \in [0,1]\), so \(0 \le f_k \le 1\).
Together, (iii) and (iv) give \(f_k \in \text{Lip}_b(S)\), so hypothesis (2) may be applied to each \(f_k\).



46.8.3 Step 2c: \(f_k\) decreases pointwise to \(\mathbf{1}_F\)
\(f_k \ge \mathbf{1}_F\) everywhere. If \(x \in F\) then \(d(x,F) = 0\), so \(f_k(x) = \psi(0) = 1 = \mathbf{1}_F(x)\). If \(x \notin F\) then \(f_k(x) \ge 0 = \mathbf{1}_F(x)\).
Monotonicity in \(k\). The quantity \(k \, d(x,F)\) is nondecreasing in \(k\) (because \(d(x,F) \ge 0\)), and \(\psi\) is nonincreasing on \([0,\infty)\). Hence \(f_{k+1}(x) \le f_k(x)\) for every \(x\).
Pointwise limit. For \(x \in F\), \(f_k(x) = 1\) for all \(k\). For \(x \notin F\): since \(F\) is closed, its complement is open, so there is \(r > 0\) with \(B(x, r) \subseteq F^c\); every \(y \in F\) therefore satisfies \(d(x,y) \ge r\), giving \(d(x, F) \ge r > 0\). Consequently, as soon as \(k > 1/d(x,F)\) we have \(k\,d(x,F) > 1\) and thus \(f_k(x) = 0\). In particular \(f_k(x) \to 0\).






Note



This is the only place where closedness of \(F\) is used, and it is essential. If \(F\) were not closed, points of \(\bar{F} \setminus F\) would satisfy \(d(x,F) = 0\), forcing \(f_k(x) = 1\) for all \(k\); the limit would then be \(\mathbf{1}_{\bar{F}}\) rather than \(\mathbf{1}_F\).


Combining the three bullets: \[f_k \downarrow \mathbf{1}_F \quad \text{pointwise on } S.\]



46.8.4 Step 2d: Passing to the limit, first in \(n\), then in \(k\)
Fix \(k\). Since \(f_k \ge \mathbf{1}_F\) pointwise and integration is monotone, for every \(n\): \[\mu_n(F) = \int_S \mathbf{1}_F \, d\mu_n \le \int_S f_k \, d\mu_n.\]
Hypothesis (2) applies to \(f_k \in \text{Lip}_b(S)\), so \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_S f_k \, d\mu_n\) exists and equals \(\int_S f_k \, d\mu\). Taking \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}\) of the displayed inequality (the \(\limsup\) of the left side exists in \([0,1]\) even though \(\mu_n(F)\) itself need not converge) gives \[\limsup_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(F) \;\le\; \limsup_{n\to\infty} \int_S f_k \, d\mu_n \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty} \int_S f_k \, d\mu_n \;=\; \int_S f_k \, d\mu.\]
Now let \(k \to \infty\). The left-hand side is a single number \(L := \limsup_{n\to\infty}\mu_n(F)\) that does not depend on \(k\), so the previous display says \[L \le \int_S f_k \, d\mu \qquad \text{for every } k \ge 1.\] By Step 2c, \(f_k \to \mathbf{1}_F\) pointwise with \(0 \le f_k \le 1\); the constant function \(1\) is \(\mu\)-integrable because \(\mu\) is a probability measure. The Dominated Convergence Theorem therefore gives \[\int_S f_k \, d\mu \xrightarrow{k\to\infty} \int_S \mathbf{1}_F \, d\mu = \mu(F).\] (Equivalently, since \(f_k\) is decreasing, the Monotone Convergence Theorem for decreasing sequences applies.)
Taking \(k \to \infty\) in \(L \le \int_S f_k \, d\mu\) yields \(L \le \mu(F)\), that is, \[\limsup_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(F) \le \mu(F) \qquad \text{for every closed } F \subseteq S. \qquad \blacksquare\]







TipWhy only an inequality?



The bound \(\limsup_n \mu_n(F) \le \mu(F)\) cannot be upgraded to equality. Take \(S = \mathbb{R}\), \(\mu_n = \delta_{1/n}\), \(\mu = \delta_0\), and \(F = \{0\}\), which is closed. Then \(\mu_n(F) = 0\) for every \(n\), while \(\mu(F) = 1\), so \[0 = \limsup_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(F) < \mu(F) = 1.\] Mass can “arrive on” a closed set in the limit, but it cannot leak out of one. This is precisely the asymmetry that statement (5) repairs by restricting attention to sets \(A\) with \(\mu(\partial A) = 0\) — and here \(\partial F = \{0\}\) has \(\mu\)-measure \(1\).

title: 46  Lecture 22.1: Weak Convergence
text:
46.9 Step 3: Proof of \((3 \iff 4)\)
Let \(G \subseteq S\) be open, so \(G^c = S \setminus G\) is closed. Using complementation \(\mu_n(G) = 1 - \mu_n(G^c)\): \[\liminf_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(G) = \liminf_{n\to\infty} (1 - \mu_n(G^c)) = 1 - \limsup_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(G^c)\]
Applying (3) to the closed set \(G^c\): \[\limsup_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(G^c) \le \mu(G^c) = 1 - \mu(G)\]
Substituting this back gives: \[\liminf_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(G) \ge 1 - (1 - \mu(G)) = \mu(G)\]
Conversely, if (4) holds and \(F\) is closed, then \(F^c\) is open. Applying (4) to \(F^c\) and taking complements gives \[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\mu_n(F)
=1-\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mu_n(F^c)
\le 1-\mu(F^c)=\mu(F).
\] Thus \((3 \iff 4)\) holds. \(\blacksquare\)

title: 46  Lecture 22.1: Weak Convergence
text:
46.10 Step 4: Proof of \((3 + 4 \implies 5)\)
Let \(A \in \mathcal{B}(S)\) be a \(\mu\)-continuity set, meaning \(\mu(\partial A) = 0\). Recall \(\text{int}(A) \subseteq A \subseteq \bar{A}\), where \(\text{int}(A)\) is open and \(\bar{A}\) is closed.

Using statement (4) on open \(\text{int}(A)\): \[\mu(\text{int}(A)) \le \liminf_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(\text{int}(A)) \le \liminf_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(A)\]
Using statement (3) on closed \(\bar{A}\): \[\limsup_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(A) \le \limsup_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(\bar{A}) \le \mu(\bar{A})\]

Combining the inequalities: \[\mu(\text{int}(A)) \le \liminf_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(A) \le \limsup_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(A) \le \mu(\bar{A})\]
Since \(\mu(\partial A) = 0\), we have \(\mu(\text{int}(A)) = \mu(A) = \mu(\bar{A})\). Therefore, the lower and upper limits collapse to \(\mu(A)\), yielding: \[\lim_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(A) = \mu(A)\] \(\blacksquare\)

title: 46  Lecture 22.1: Weak Convergence
text:
46.11 Step 5: Proof of \((5 \implies 1)\)
Goal. Assume \(\mu_n(A) \to \mu(A)\) for every \(\mu\)-continuity set \(A\). Show that \(\int_S f \, d\mu_n \to \int_S f \, d\mu\) for every \(f \in C_b(S)\).
Strategy. Hypothesis (5) is a statement about sets, while the conclusion is a statement about integrals. The bridge is the layer-cake (horizontal slicing) formula, which rewrites \(\int_S f \, d\mu\) purely in terms of the measures of the superlevel sets \(\{f \ge t\}\). Since \(f\) is continuous, these sets are closed with boundary contained in the level set \(\{f = t\}\), and a counting argument shows \(\{f \ge t\}\) is a \(\mu\)-continuity set for all but countably many \(t\). Hypothesis (5) then applies for Lebesgue-a.e. \(t\), and a convergence theorem in the \(t\) variable finishes the proof.
Fix \(f \in C_b(S)\) and set \(M := \|f\|_\infty = \sup_{x \in S}|f(x)| < \infty\), \(a := -M\), \(b := M\), so that \(a \le f(x) \le b\) for all \(x\). If \(M = 0\) then \(f \equiv 0\) and both sides vanish; assume therefore \(M > 0\), so \(a < b\).


46.11.1 Step 5a: The layer-cake representation
For each fixed \(x \in S\) and \(t \in [a,b]\), the indicator \(\mathbf{1}_{\{f(x) \ge t\}}\) equals \(1\) precisely when \(t \le f(x)\), i.e. for \(t \in [a, f(x)]\), an interval of length \(f(x) - a\). Hence \[f(x) - a = \int_a^b \mathbf{1}_{\{f(x) \ge t\}} \, dt \qquad \text{for every } x \in S.\] This is the “horizontal slicing” identity: instead of adding up the values of \(f\), we add up the heights \(t\) at which \(f\) still exceeds \(t\).



46.11.2 Step 5b: Integrating the identity (Tonelli)
Let \(\nu\) denote either \(\mu_n\) or \(\mu\). The function \[(x,t) \longmapsto \mathbf{1}_{\{f(x) \ge t\}}\] is \(\mathcal{B}(S) \otimes \mathcal{B}([a,b])\)-measurable, since it is the indicator of the set \(\{(x,t) : f(x) - t \ge 0\}\), which is the preimage of \([0,\infty)\) under the jointly measurable map \((x,t) \mapsto f(x) - t\). The integrand is nonnegative, \(\nu\) is a probability measure, and Lebesgue measure on \([a,b]\) is finite, so both measures are \(\sigma\)-finite and Tonelli’s Theorem permits exchanging the order of integration: \[
\int_S \bigl(f(x) - a\bigr) \, \nu(dx)
= \int_S \!\! \int_a^b \mathbf{1}_{\{f(x) \ge t\}} \, dt \, \nu(dx)
= \int_a^b \!\! \int_S \mathbf{1}_{\{f(x) \ge t\}} \, \nu(dx) \, dt
= \int_a^b \nu(\{f \ge t\}) \, dt.
\] Since \(\nu(S) = 1\), this reads \[\int_S f \, d\mu_n = a + \int_a^b \mu_n(\{f \ge t\}) \, dt, \qquad \int_S f \, d\mu = a + \int_a^b \mu(\{f \ge t\}) \, dt.\]
It therefore suffices to prove \[\int_a^b \mu_n(\{f \ge t\}) \, dt \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} \int_a^b \mu(\{f \ge t\}) \, dt.\]



46.11.3 Step 5c: \(\{f \ge t\}\) is a \(\mu\)-continuity set for all but countably many \(t\)
(i) The boundary sits inside the level set. Because \(f\) is continuous, \(\{f \ge t\} = f^{-1}([t,\infty))\) is closed and \(\{f > t\} = f^{-1}((t,\infty))\) is open. An open subset of \(\{f \ge t\}\) is contained in its interior, so \(\{f > t\} \subseteq \text{int}\{f \ge t\}\), and therefore \[\partial \{f \ge t\} = \overline{\{f \ge t\}} \setminus \text{int}\{f \ge t\} = \{f \ge t\} \setminus \text{int}\{f \ge t\} \subseteq \{f \ge t\} \setminus \{f > t\} = \{f = t\}.\]
(ii) Only countably many levels carry mass. Put \[E := \{ t \in [a, b] : \mu(\{f = t\}) > 0 \}, \qquad E_m := \{t \in [a,b] : \mu(\{f = t\}) \ge 1/m\},\] so that \(E = \bigcup_{m \ge 1} E_m\). Each \(E_m\) is finite: if \(t_1, \dots, t_j \in E_m\) are distinct, the level sets \(\{f = t_1\}, \dots, \{f = t_j\}\) are pairwise disjoint, so \[1 = \mu(S) \ \ge \ \sum_{i=1}^j \mu(\{f = t_i\}) \ \ge \ \frac{j}{m},\] forcing \(j \le m\). A countable union of finite sets is countable, so \(E\) is at most countable and in particular has Lebesgue measure zero.
(iii) Conclusion. For every \(t \in [a,b] \setminus E\) — that is, for Lebesgue-a.e. \(t\) — combining (i) and (ii) gives \[\mu\bigl(\partial\{f \ge t\}\bigr) \le \mu(\{f = t\}) = 0,\] so \(\{f \ge t\}\) is a \(\mu\)-continuity set. Hypothesis (5) therefore yields \[\mu_n(\{f \ge t\}) \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} \mu(\{f \ge t\}) \qquad \text{for Lebesgue-a.e. } t \in [a,b].\]






Note



The exceptional set \(E\) cannot be dispensed with. Take \(S = \mathbb{R}\), \(\mu_n = \delta_{1/n}\), \(\mu = \delta_0\) and \(f(x) = e^{-x^2} \in C_b(\mathbb{R})\). At the single level \(t = 1\) we have \(\{f \ge 1\} = \{0\}\), so \(\mu_n(\{f \ge 1\}) = 0\) for all \(n\) while \(\mu(\{f \ge 1\}) = 1\): convergence fails. But \(E = \{1\}\) is a Lebesgue-null subset of \([a,b] = [-1,1]\), so it does not affect the integral over \(t\).





46.11.4 Step 5d: Passing to the limit (Bounded Convergence)
For each \(n\), the map \(t \mapsto \mu_n(\{f \ge t\})\) is nonincreasing (as \(t\) increases the sets \(\{f \ge t\}\) shrink), hence Borel measurable, and it is bounded by \(1\). Lebesgue measure on \([a,b]\) is finite, so the constant \(1\) is an integrable dominating function and the Bounded Convergence Theorem applies to the a.e.-convergence established in Step 5c: \[\int_a^b \mu_n(\{f \ge t\}) \, dt \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} \int_a^b \mu(\{f \ge t\}) \, dt.\]
Adding the constant \(a\) and using the two identities from Step 5b: \[\int_S f \, d\mu_n = a + \int_a^b \mu_n(\{f \ge t\}) \, dt \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} a + \int_a^b \mu(\{f \ge t\}) \, dt = \int_S f \, d\mu.\]
Since \(f \in C_b(S)\) was arbitrary, statement (1) holds. This closes the cycle \((1) \implies (2) \implies (3) \iff (4) \implies (5) \implies (1)\), so all five statements are equivalent. \(\blacksquare\)

title: 46  Lecture 22.1: Weak Convergence
text:
Definition 46.1 (Total Variation Distance) For two probability measures \(\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{P}(S, \mathcal{B}(S))\), the total variation distance is defined as: \[d_{TV}(\mu, \nu) = \sup_{B \in \mathcal{B}(S)} |\mu(B) - \nu(B)|\]




Example 46.1 (Dirac Measures (Point Masses)) Let \(a_n, a \in \mathbb{R}\) with \(a_n \to a\) as \(n \to \infty\), and suppose that \(a_n \neq a\) for infinitely many \(n\). Intuitively, Dirac measures should satisfy \(\delta_{a_n} \to \delta_a\). For every \(n\) such that \(a_n \neq a\), evaluating their total variation distance gives: \[
\begin{align*}
d_{TV}(\delta_{a_n}, \delta_a) &= \sup_{B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})} |\delta_{a_n}(B) - \delta_a(B)| \ge |\delta_{a_n}(\{a\}) - \delta_a(\{a\})|\\
& = |0 - 1| = 1.
\end{align*}
\]
Since \(d_{TV}\) is at most \(1\) for probability measures, \(d_{TV}(\delta_{a_n}, \delta_a)=1\) whenever \(a_n\neq a\). Thus it does not converge to \(0\), even though \(a_n \to a\). (If \(a_n=a\) eventually, then the total variation distance is eventually \(0\).)



Example 46.2 (Discrete Approximation of \(\text{Unif}([0,1])\)) Consider approximating the continuous uniform measure \(\lambda = \text{Unif}([0,1])\) on \([0,1]\) using discrete empirical measures: \[\mu_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \delta_{k/n}\]

Evaluating \(d_{TV}\): Let \(A = \{1/n, 2/n, \dots, n/n\}\). Then \(\mu_n(A) = 1\), but \(\lambda(A) = 0\). \[d_{TV}(\mu_n, \lambda) \ge |\mu_n(A) - \lambda(A)| = 1 - 0 = 1\] Since total variation distance between probability measures is at most \(1\), \(d_{TV}(\mu_n, \lambda) = 1\) for every \(n\).
Evaluating via Integration (Riemann Sums): Recall the integration bound from Lecture 21.1: \[\left| \int_S h \, d\mu - \int_S h \, d\nu \right| \le 2 \, d_{TV}(\mu, \nu) \cdot \sup_{x \in S} |h(x)|\] Since \(d_{TV}(\mu_n, \lambda) = 1\) for every \(n\), this bound degenerates to \(2\sup|h|\) and carries no information. Yet the integrals themselves do converge: since \([0,1]\) is compact, \(C_b([0,1]) = C([0,1])\), and every \(h \in C([0,1])\) is Riemann integrable, so \[\int_{[0,1]} h \, d\mu_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n h\left(\frac{k}{n}\right) \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} \int_0^1 h(x) \, dx = \int_{[0,1]} h \, d\lambda\] because the left-hand side is the right-endpoint Riemann sum of \(h\) over the uniform partition of \([0,1]\) into \(n\) subintervals.
Hence \(\mu_n \implies \lambda\) in the sense of Definition 46.2 below, even though \(d_{TV}(\mu_n, \lambda) = 1\) for all \(n\). Testing against continuous functions captures the limit, whereas \(d_{TV}\) fails due to its extreme sensitivity to singular sets.

title: 46  Lecture 22.1: Weak Convergence
text:
46.2 Weak Convergence of Probability Measures
To bypass the rigidity of \(d_{TV}\), we restrict test functions to bounded continuous functions \(f \in C_b(S)\), which effectively “smear out” point masses.

Definition 46.2 (Weak Convergence (Convergence in Distribution)) Let \((S, d)\) be a metric space, and let \(\mu_n, \mu \in \mathcal{P}(S, \mathcal{B}(S))\). We say \(\mu_n\) converges weakly to \(\mu\), written as \(\mu_n \xrightarrow{w} \mu\) or \(\mu_n \implies \mu\), if: \[\int_S f \, d\mu_n \longrightarrow \int_S f \, d\mu \quad \forall f \in C_b(S)\]


Example 46.3 (Dirac Measures Revisited) If \(a_n \to a\) in \(S\), then for any \(f \in C_b(S)\): \[\int_S f \, d\delta_{a_n} = f(a_n) \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} f(a) = \int_S f \, d\delta_a\] Thus \(\delta_{a_n} \implies \delta_a\) holds under weak convergence.


Theorem 46.1 (TV Convergence Implies Weak Convergence) If \(d_{TV}(\mu_n, \mu) \to 0\), then \(\mu_n \implies \mu\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 46.1). For any \(f \in C_b(S)\), \(\sup |f| < \infty\). By the integration bound: \[\left| \int_S f \, d\mu_n - \int_S f \, d\mu \right| \le 2 \, d_{TV}(\mu_n, \mu) \cdot \sup_{x \in S} |f(x)| \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} 0\] Hence \(\int f \, d\mu_n \to \int f \, d\mu\).

title: 46  Lecture 22.1: Weak Convergence
text:
46.3 Convergence Modes of Random Variables
Let \(X_n, X: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P) \to (S, \mathcal{B}(S))\) be random variables/elements. We write \(X_n \xrightarrow{w} X\) (or \(X_n \xrightarrow{d} X\)) if \(\mu_{X_n} \implies \mu_X\), where \(\mu_{X_n} = P \circ X_n^{-1}\).
Throughout this section \((S,d)\) is assumed separable, so that \(d : S \times S \to \mathbb{R}\) is \(\mathcal{B}(S) \otimes \mathcal{B}(S)\)-measurable and \(d(X_n, X)\) is a genuine random variable. Convergence in probability then means \(P(d(X_n, X) > \epsilon) \to 0\) for every \(\epsilon > 0\).

Lemma 46.1 (Lemma: Preservation of Convergence in Probability) Let \(g : S \to \mathbb{R}\) be continuous. If \(X_n \xrightarrow{P} X\), then \(g(X_n) \xrightarrow{P} g(X)\).


Proof (Proof of Lemma 46.1). To prove convergence in probability, it is enough to show that every subsequence of \((g(X_n))\) has a further subsequence converging almost surely to \(g(X)\). Let \((X_{n_k})\) be any subsequence. Since \(X_n \xrightarrow{P} X\), there exists a further subsequence \((X_{n_{k_j}})\) such that \[X_{n_{k_j}} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}} X.\] On the event of probability one on which this convergence holds, continuity of \(g\) gives \[g(X_{n_{k_j}}) \longrightarrow g(X).\] Thus every subsequence of \((g(X_n))\) has an almost surely convergent further subsequence with limit \(g(X)\), and hence \(g(X_n) \xrightarrow{P} g(X)\).


Proof (Alternative Proof of Lemma 46.1). Fix \(\epsilon>0\). For \(\delta>0\), define \[
B_{\epsilon,\delta}
=\left\{x\in S: \exists\, y\in S \text{ such that } d(x,y)<\delta \text{ and } |g(x)-g(y)|>\epsilon\right\}.
\] The set \(B_{\epsilon,\delta}\) is open: if \(x\in B_{\epsilon,\delta}\) has a witness \(y\), then the same strict inequalities continue to hold for all points sufficiently close to \(x\). In particular, it is Borel measurable. Moreover, as \(m\to\infty\), \[
B_{\epsilon,1/m}\downarrow\emptyset,
\] because continuity of \(g\) at each \(x\) gives a neighborhood on which \(|g(x)-g(y)|\le\epsilon\). Hence, by continuity from above of the probability measure, \[
P(X\in B_{\epsilon,1/m})\longrightarrow0.
\]
For every \(\delta>0\), \[
\{|g(X_n)-g(X)|>\epsilon\}
\subseteq
\{d(X_n,X)\ge\delta\}\cup\{X\in B_{\epsilon,\delta}\}.
\] Indeed, if \(d(X_n,X)<\delta\) and \(X\notin B_{\epsilon,\delta}\), take \(x=X\) and \(y=X_n\) in the definition of \(B_{\epsilon,\delta}\) to obtain \(|g(X_n)-g(X)|\le\epsilon\).
Let \(\eta>0\). First choose \(m\) such that \(P(X\in B_{\epsilon,1/m})<\eta/2\). Since \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}X\), there exists \(N\) such that, for every \(n\ge N\), \[
P\bigl(d(X_n,X)\ge1/m\bigr)<\eta/2.
\] The preceding inclusion then gives \[
P\bigl(|g(X_n)-g(X)|>\epsilon\bigr)<\eta\qquad(n\ge N),
\] which proves \(g(X_n)\xrightarrow{P}g(X)\).


Theorem 46.2 (Convergence in Probability Implies Weak Convergence) If \(X_n \xrightarrow{P} X\), then \(X_n \xrightarrow{w} X\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 46.2). Let \(f \in C_b(S)\).

By Lemma 46.1, \(X_n \xrightarrow{P} X \implies f(X_n) \xrightarrow{P} f(X)\).
If \(M=\|f\|_\infty\), then \(|f(X_n)-f(X)|\le 2M\). Split the expectation on \(\{|f(X_n)-f(X)|>\epsilon\}\) and its complement: for every \(\epsilon>0\), \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\left[|f(X_n)-f(X)|\right]
&=\mathbb{E}\bigl[|f(X_n)-f(X)|
\mathbf{1}_{\{|f(X_n)-f(X)|\le\epsilon\}}\bigr]\\
& +\mathbb{E}\bigl[|f(X_n)-f(X)|
\mathbf{1}_{\{|f(X_n)-f(X)|>\epsilon\}}\bigr]\\
& \le \epsilon+2M\,P\bigl(|f(X_n)-f(X)|>\epsilon\bigr).
\end{align*}
\] The probability on the right tends to \(0\), so \(\limsup_n\mathbb{E}|f(X_n)-f(X)|\le\epsilon\). Letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) shows that \(f(X_n)\to f(X)\) in \(L^1\), and therefore \[\mathbb{E}[f(X_n)] \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}[f(X)].\]
Rewriting in terms of pushforward measures: \[\int_S f \, d\mu_{X_n} = \mathbb{E}[f(X_n)] \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}[f(X)] = \int_S f \, d\mu_X\] Hence \(X_n \xrightarrow{w} X\).



Corollary 46.1 (Almost Sure and \(L^p\) Convergence) If \(X_n \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} X\), then \(X_n \xrightarrow{w} X\). If in addition \(S\) is a normed space (e.g. \(S = \mathbb{R}^d\)) and \(X_n \xrightarrow{L^p} X\) for some \(p \ge 1\), then \(X_n \xrightarrow{w} X\).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 46.1). Almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability: \(\mathbf{1}_{\{d(X_n,X) > \epsilon\}} \to 0\) a.s., so \(P(d(X_n,X)>\epsilon) \to 0\) by dominated convergence. Convergence in \(L^p\) implies convergence in probability by Markov’s inequality, \(P(\|X_n - X\| > \epsilon) \le \epsilon^{-p}\,\mathbb{E}\|X_n - X\|^p \to 0\). In either case Theorem 46.2 applies.

title: 46  Lecture 22.1: Weak Convergence
text:
46.4 Continuity Sets
Total variation distance \(d_{TV}\) fails for sequences of distributions because it evaluates arbitrary sets, including “discontinuity sets”.

Definition 46.3 (Continuity Set) Let \(\mu\) be a Borel probability measure on a metric space \(S\). A set \(A \in \mathcal{B}(S)\) is called a \(\mu\)-continuity set if: \[\mu(\partial A) = 0\] where \(\partial A = \bar{A} \setminus \text{int}(A)\) is the boundary of \(A\). Since \(\text{int}(A) \subseteq A \subseteq \bar{A}\) and \(\bar{A} \setminus \text{int}(A) = \partial A\), this implies \(\mu(A) = \mu(\bar{A}) = \mu(\text{int}(A))\).


Example 46.4 (Examples of Continuity and Non-Continuity Sets)  

Dirac Measure: \((-\infty, a]\) is not a continuity set for \(\delta_a\), since \(\overline{(-\infty,a]} = (-\infty,a]\) and \(\text{int}(-\infty,a] = (-\infty,a)\), so \(\partial(-\infty, a] = \{a\}\) and \(\delta_a(\{a\}) = 1 \neq 0\).
Continuous Distribution on \(\mathbb{R}\): If \(\mu\) has a continuous CDF \(F_\mu\) (equivalently, \(\mu(\{a\}) = 0\) for all \(a \in \mathbb{R}\)), then every interval \(I\) with endpoints \(\alpha \le \beta\) is a \(\mu\)-continuity set, because \(\partial I \subseteq \{\alpha, \beta\}\) and \(\mu(\{\alpha,\beta\}) = 0\).
Rational Numbers: \(A = \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]\) is not a continuity set for any measure \(\mu\) with \(\mu([0,1]) > 0\). Indeed \(\bar{A} = [0,1]\) by density of the rationals and \(\text{int}(A) = \emptyset\) since \(A\) contains no interval, so \(\partial A = [0,1] \setminus \emptyset = [0,1]\) and \(\mu(\partial A) = \mu([0,1]) > 0\).

title: 46  Lecture 22.1: Weak Convergence
text:
46.5 The Portmanteau Theorem
The Portmanteau Theorem provides several equivalent characterizations of weak convergence of probability measures.

Theorem 46.3 (Portmanteau Theorem) Let \((S,d)\) be a metric space and let \(\mu_n, \mu \in \mathcal{P}(S, \mathcal{B}(S))\). The following statements are equivalent:

Definition: \(\int_S f \, d\mu_n \to \int_S f \, d\mu \quad \forall f \in C_b(S)\) (\(\mu_n \xrightarrow{w} \mu\)).
Lipschitz continuous functions: \(\int_S f \, d\mu_n \to \int_S f \, d\mu \quad \forall f \in \text{Lip}_b(S)\) (bounded Lipschitz continuous functions).
Upper bound on closed sets: \(\limsup_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(F) \le \mu(F) \quad \forall \text{ closed } F \subseteq S\).
Lower bound on open sets: \(\liminf_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(G) \ge \mu(G) \quad \forall \text{ open } G \subseteq S\).
Continuity sets: \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(A) = \mu(A) \quad \forall \mu\text{-continuity sets } A \in \mathcal{B}(S)\).

We establish the cycle \((1) \implies (2) \implies (3) \iff (4) \implies (5) \implies (1)\), which yields the equivalence of all five statements.

title: 46  Lecture 22.1: Weak Convergence
text:
46.12 Takeaways

Weak convergence is convergence against every bounded continuous test function. It captures limits such as \(\delta_{a_n}\implies\delta_a\) when \(a_n\to a\), even though total variation convergence can fail completely.
Total variation convergence implies weak convergence, but not conversely: discrete approximations of \(\mathrm{Unif}([0,1])\) converge weakly through Riemann sums while remaining at total variation distance \(1\).
For random elements on a common probability space, convergence in probability, almost sure convergence, and \(L^p\) convergence (\(p\ge1\)) each imply convergence in distribution.
The Portmanteau Theorem gives interchangeable tests for weak convergence: bounded Lipschitz functions, upper bounds on closed sets, lower bounds on open sets, and convergence on every \(\mu\)-continuity set.
Set probabilities should generally be tested only on \(\mu\)-continuity sets. Boundaries with positive limiting mass are precisely where weak convergence need not determine \(\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)\).

title: 77  Lecture 35.2: Poisson Process
text:
77.7 Takeaways

The exponential distribution \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) is the unique continuous distribution satisfying the memoryless property \(\mathbb{P}(\xi>t+s\mid\xi>s)=\mathbb{P}(\xi>t)\). The survival function \(f(t)=e^{-\lambda t}\) is the unique differentiable solution to the functional equation \(f(t+s)=f(t)f(s)\) with \(f(0)=1\).
The Poisson process of rate \(\lambda\) is constructed as the renewal counting process \(N_t=\sup\{n\ge0:X_n\le t\}\) built from i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) inter-arrivals. Arrival times \((X_1,\dots,X_n)\) have joint density \(\lambda^n e^{-\lambda x_n}\) on the ordered simplex \(\widetilde{D}_n\), derived via a change of variables whose Jacobian is \(1\).
The marginal \(N_t\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda t)\) follows by integrating the joint density: the volume of \(D_n(t)\) contributes \(t^n/n!\) and the exponential tail over \((t,\infty)\) contributes \(\lambda^n e^{-\lambda t}\), together yielding \(e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^n/n!\).
Conditioned on \(N_t=n\), the \(n\) arrival times \((X_1,\dots,X_n)\) have joint density \(n!/t^n\) on \(D_n(t)\), which is the density of the order statistics of \(n\) independent \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,t)\) random variables.
For disjoint Borel sets \(B_1,\dots,B_k\) partitioning \([0,t]\), the counts \(N(B_1),\dots,N(B_k)\) are mutually independent with \(N(B_j)\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda\operatorname{Leb}(B_j))\). The proof factorizes the joint characteristic function by symmetrizing the simplex integral and exponentiating the resulting Taylor series.
The increment \(N_t-N_s\) is independent of \(\mathcal{F}_s=\sigma(N_r:r\le s)\) for all \(0\le s<t\), and follows \(\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s))\). This independence follows from applying the disjoint-partition result to any partition that includes \((s,t]\), then extending to all of \(\mathcal{F}_s\) via the \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem.

title: 78  Lecture 36.1: The Markov Property
text:
78.1 The Markov Property
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space equipped with a filtration \((\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \in T}\), where the index set \(T\) is either \(\mathbb{N}\) (discrete time) or \(\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) (continuous time). Let \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be a measurable state space.

title: 78  Lecture 36.1: The Markov Property
text:
Definition 78.1 (Adapted Stochastic Process) A stochastic process \(X = (X_t)_{t \in T}\) taking values in \((S, \mathcal{B})\) is adapted to the filtration \((\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \in T}\) if \(X_t\) is \((\mathcal{F}_t, \mathcal{B})\)-measurable for every \(t \in T\).


Definition 78.2 (The Markov Property) An adapted stochastic process \(X = (X_t)_{t \in T}\) satisfies the Markov property with respect to the filtration \((\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \in T}\) if, for every bounded measurable function \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) and for all \(s, t \in T\) with \(s \le t\), \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{78.1}\]


Remark 78.1. Intuitively, the definition says: Once we know the present state \(X_s\), knowing the entire past up to time \(s\) gives us no additional information about the future state \(X_t\).
Consider the left-hand side: \(\mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid\mathcal F_s]\). \(\mathcal F_s\) represents everything we know from the past and present up to time \(s\). Thus \(\mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid\mathcal F_s]\) is our best prediction of \(f(X_t)\) using the entire history up to time \(s\).
Consider the right-hand side: \(\mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid X_s]\). Here we throw away the entire history and retain only the current state \(X_s\). Thus \(\mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid X_s]\) is our best prediction of \(f(X_t)\) based solely on the current state.
The Markov property says these two predictions are identical.So, schematically, \[
\underbrace{\text{Past history}}_{\mathcal F_s} \longrightarrow \underbrace{X_s}_{\text{present}} \longrightarrow \underbrace{X_t}_{\text{future}}.
\] The past can affect the future only through the information contained in the present state.


Remark 78.2. Why do we use \(f(X_t)\) rather than just \(X_t\)? This is important. Saying \[
\mathbb E[X_t\mid\mathcal F_s] = \mathbb E[X_t\mid X_s]
\] only says that the conditional mean of \(X_t\) depends on the past through \(X_s\). That is not enough to characterize the Markov property. By requiring the equality for every bounded measurable \(f\), \[
\mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid\mathcal F_s] = \mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid X_s],
\] we are effectively saying that the entire conditional distribution of \(X_t\) given the past is determined by \(X_s\). For example, taking \(f(x)=\mathbf 1_A(x)\) gives \[
\mathbb P(X_t\in A\mid\mathcal F_s) = \mathbb P(X_t\in A\mid X_s)
\] for every measurable set \(A\). So an even more intuitive formulation is: Given the present state \(X_s\), the conditional distribution of the future state \(X_t\) does not depend on the history before \(s\).


Proposition 78.1 (Equivalent Characterization via Factorization) An adapted process \((X_t)_{t \in T}\) satisfies Equation 78.1 if and only if for every \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) and all \(s \le t\), there exists a measurable function \(F \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) such that \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = F(X_s) \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{78.2}\]


Proof. \((\Longrightarrow)\) Suppose Equation 78.1 holds. Since \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s]\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_s)\), the Doob–Dynkin Lemma guarantees the existence of a measurable function \(F \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) such that \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] = F(X_s)\) almost surely. Thus, Equation 78.2 holds.
\((\Longleftarrow)\) Conversely, suppose there exists \(F \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) such that \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = F(X_s)\) a.s. By taking conditional expectations with respect to \(\sigma(X_s)\) on both sides and using the tower property (noting that \(\sigma(X_s) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_s\)), we obtain: \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] \mid X_s \right] = \mathbb{E}[F(X_s) \mid X_s] = F(X_s) \quad \text{a.s.}
\] Comparing this with Equation 78.2 yields \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s]\) a.s.


Remark 78.3. Let \(\mathcal{F}_s^X := \sigma(X_r : r \le s)\) denote the natural filtration generated by \(X\). Since \(X\) is adapted, \(\mathcal{F}_s^X \subseteq \mathcal{F}_s\). If the Markov property holds for \((\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \in T}\), then by applying the tower property: \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s^X] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] \mid \mathcal{F}_s^X \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] \mid \mathcal{F}_s^X \right]\\
&= \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] \quad \text{a.s.}
\end{align*}
\] The last step holds because \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s]\) is \(\sigma(X_s)\)-measurable, and \(\sigma(X_s) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_s^X\) (since \(X_s\) is \(\mathcal{F}_s^X\)-measurable), so \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s]\) is already \(\mathcal{F}_s^X\)-measurable and conditioning on \(\mathcal{F}_s^X\) leaves it unchanged. Thus, the Markov property with respect to a general filtration implies the Markov property with respect to the process’s natural filtration.

title: 40  Lecture 36.1: The Markov Property
text:
40.2 Equivalent Characterization via Factorization
An adapted process \((X_t)_{t \in T}\) satisfies Equation 40.1 if and only if for every \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) and all \(s \le t\), there exists a measurable function \(F \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) such that \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = F(X_s) \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{40.2}\]

title: 78  Lecture 36.1: The Markov Property
40  Lecture 36.1: The Markov Property
text:
40.4 One-Step Characterization in Discrete Time
Let \(T = \mathbb{N}\). The process \((X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\) satisfies the Markov property if and only if for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) and every \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\), \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1}) \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = \mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1}) \mid X_n] \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{40.3}\]

title: 78  Lecture 36.1: The Markov Property
text:
78.3 Generalization to Future \(\sigma\)-Fields
The Markov property is often interpreted as stating that “the future depends on the past only through the present.” We now formalize this for arbitrary functions of the future.

Definition 78.3 (Future \(\sigma\)-Field) Given a stochastic process \((X_t)_{t \in T}\) and a fixed time \(s \in T\), the future \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\) (or \(\mathcal{F}_{[s,\infty)}^X\)) is defined by: \[
\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X := \sigma(X_t : t \ge s).
\] (Note: As \(s\) increases, \(s \mapsto \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\) forms a reverse filtration: if \(s_1 \le s_2\), then \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s_2}^X \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{\ge s_1}^X\).)


Theorem 78.1 (Markov Property for General Future Random Variables) Let \((X_t)_{t \in T}\) be an adapted Markov process. Then for any \(s \in T\) and any bounded measurable random variable \(Y \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X)\), \[
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X_s] \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{78.4}\]


Remark 78.4. The original Markov property says: To predict a future state \(X_t\), the entire past can be replaced by the current state \(X_s\). Theorem 78.1 says: To predict anything that depends on the entire future path, the entire past can still be replaced by the current state \(X_s\).

To prove Theorem 78.1, we use a monotone class argument (\(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem / Functional Dynkin System Theorem).

Lemma 78.1 (Multiplicative System Generation) Let \(s \in T\) be fixed. Define the set of finite cylindrical cylinder-type random variables: \[
\mathbb{M} := \left\{ \prod_{i=1}^n g_i(X_{t_i}) : n \in \mathbb{N}, \, s \le t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_n, \, g_i \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}) \right\}.
\] Then \(\mathbb{M}\) is a multiplicative system (i.e., closed under pointwise multiplication) that generates the future \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\).


Proof (Proof of Lemma 78.1). Part 1: \(\mathbb{M}\) is closed under multiplication. Let \(A_1, A_2 \in \mathbb{M}\). Then \(A_1 = \prod_{i=1}^n g_i(X_{t_i})\) and \(A_2 = \prod_{j=1}^m h_j(X_{r_j})\). The product \(A_1 A_2\) is a finite product of bounded measurable evaluations at times in \([s,\infty)\), which can be sorted chronologically. Thus \(A_1 A_2 \in \mathbb{M}\).
Part 2: \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) = \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\).
\((\subseteq)\): Every element of \(\mathbb{M}\) is a finite product \(\prod_{i=1}^n g_i(X_{t_i})\) with each \(t_i \ge s\). Each factor \(g_i(X_{t_i})\) is \(\sigma(X_{t_i})\)-measurable, hence measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_t : t \ge s) = \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\). A finite product of \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\)-measurable functions is \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\)-measurable, so every element of \(\mathbb{M}\) is \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\)-measurable, and therefore \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\).
\((\supseteq)\): It suffices to show that every generator of \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\) lies in \(\sigma(\mathbb{M})\). Fix any \(t \ge s\) and \(B \in \mathcal{B}\). Since \(\mathbf{1}_B \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\), taking \(n = 1\), \(t_1 = t\), \(g_1 = \mathbf{1}_B\) gives: \[
\mathbf{1}_B(X_t) = \mathbf{1}_{\{X_t \in B\}} \in \mathbb{M}.
\] Hence \(\{X_t \in B\} = \{\omega : \mathbf{1}_B(X_t(\omega)) = 1\} \in \sigma(\mathbb{M})\). The collection \(\{\{X_t \in B\} : t \ge s,\, B \in \mathcal{B}\}\) generates \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X = \sigma(X_t : t \ge s)\), so \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X \subseteq \sigma(\mathbb{M})\).


Lemma 78.2 (Monotone Class Setup) Define the functional class \(\mathbb{H}\) as: \[
\mathbb{H} := \left\{ Y \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X) : \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X_s] \text{ a.s.} \right\}.
\] Then \(\mathbb{H}\) is a vector space, contains the constant function \(1\), and is closed under bounded monotone convergence.


Proof (Proof of Lemma 78.2). 

Vector Space: Follows directly from the linearity of conditional expectation.
Contains \(1\): \(\mathbb{E}[1 \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = 1 = \mathbb{E}[1 \mid X_s]\) a.s.
Closed under Bounded Convergence: If \((Y_k)_{k=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{H}\) with \(Y_k \to Y\) pointwise and \(\vert{}Y_k\vert{} \le C < \infty\), then by the Conditional Dominated Convergence Theorem: \[
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \lim_{k\to\infty} \mathbb{E}[Y_k \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \lim_{k\to\infty} \mathbb{E}[Y_k \mid X_s] = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X_s] \quad \text{a.s.}
\]



Proof. Proof of Theorem 78.1. By functional Dynkin system theorem / monotone class theorem, if \(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}\), then \(\mathbb{H}\) contains all bounded \(\sigma(\mathbb{M})\)-measurable functions, so \(\mathbb{H} = \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X)\).
It remains to verify \(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}\). Take \(Y = \prod_{i=1}^n g_i(X_{t_i}) \in \mathbb{M}\) with \(s \le t_1 < \dots < t_n\). Using successive conditioning (tower property): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \left( \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} g_i(X_{t_i}) \right) g_n(X_{t_n}) \;\middle\vert{}\; \mathcal{F}_s \right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}\left[ \left( \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} g_i(X_{t_i}) \right) g_n(X_{t_n}) \;\middle\vert{}\; \mathcal{F}_{t_{n-1}} \right] \;\middle\vert{}\; \mathcal{F}_s \right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \left( \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} g_i(X_{t_i}) \right) \mathbb{E}[g_n(X_{t_n}) \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_{n-1}}] \;\middle\vert{}\; \mathcal{F}_s \right].
\end{aligned}
\] The factoring in the last line is justified because, for each \(i \le n-1\), we have \(t_i \le t_{n-1}\), so \(g_i(X_{t_i})\) is \(\mathcal{F}_{t_i} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t_{n-1}}\)-measurable by adaptedness. Hence the product \(\prod_{i=1}^{n-1} g_i(X_{t_i})\) is \(\mathcal{F}_{t_{n-1}}\)-measurable and bounded, so it can be taken out of \(\mathbb{E}[\cdot \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_{n-1}}]\) by the “taking out what is known” property. By the Markov property at \(t_{n-1}\), \(\mathbb{E}[g_n(X_{t_n}) \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_{n-1}}] = h(X_{t_{n-1}})\) for some \(h \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\). Substituting this reduces the expression to a product of \(n-1\) terms: \[
\mathbb{E}\left[ \left( \prod_{i=1}^{n-2} g_i(X_{t_i}) \right) \cdot \tilde{g}_{n-1}(X_{t_{n-1}}) \;\middle\vert{}\; \mathcal{F}_s \right], \quad \text{where } \tilde{g}_{n-1} = g_{n-1} \cdot h.
\] Repeating this process backward iteratively eliminates terms \(t_{n-1}, \dots, t_1\), ultimately yielding: \[
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = F(X_s) \quad \text{a.s.}
\] for some \(F \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\). Taking conditional expectations with respect to \(X_s\) shows \(F(X_s) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X_s]\) a.s., so \(Y \in \mathbb{H}\).

title: 78  Lecture 36.1: The Markov Property
section: 78.4 Conditional Independence and the Markov Property
text: 78.4 Conditional Independence and the Markov Property

title: 78  Lecture 36.1: The Markov Property
text:
78.5 Conditional Independence

Definition 78.4 (Conditional Independence of \(\sigma\)-Fields) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space and \(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) sub-\(\sigma\)-fields. We say that \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) are conditionally independent given \(\mathcal{G}\) (denoted \(\mathcal{A} \perp\!\!\!\perp \mathcal{B} \mid \mathcal{G}\)) if for all \(A \in \mathcal{A}\) and \(B \in \mathcal{B}\), \[
\mathbb{P}(A \cap B \mid \mathcal{G}) = \mathbb{P}(A \mid \mathcal{G}) \mathbb{P}(B \mid \mathcal{G}) \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{78.5}\]


Proposition 78.3 (Equivalent Characterizations) The following statements are equivalent:

\(\mathcal{A} \perp\!\!\!\perp \mathcal{B} \mid \mathcal{G}\).
For all \(B \in \mathcal{B}\), \(\mathbb{P}(B \mid \mathcal{G} \vee \mathcal{A}) = \mathbb{P}(B \mid \mathcal{G})\) a.s., where \(\mathcal{G} \vee \mathcal{A}\) is the smallest \(\sigma\)-field containing both \(\mathcal{G}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\).
For all bounded \(\mathcal{A}\)-measurable random variables \(Z\) and bounded \(\mathcal{B}\)-measurable random variables \(Y\), \[
\mathbb{E}[Z Y \mid \mathcal{G}] = \mathbb{E}[Z \mid \mathcal{G}] \, \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{G}] \quad \text{a.s.}
\]



Example 78.1 (Counterintuitive Example on Conditional Expectation) Let \(X, Y\) be i.i.d. Rademacher random variables: \(\mathbb{P}(X = 1) = \mathbb{P}(X = -1) = 1/2\). Set \(Z = XY\).
Part 1: \(X\) and \(Y\) are not conditionally independent given \(Z\).
The pair \((X, Y)\) is uniform on \(\{-1,1\}^2\), giving the joint distribution of \((X, Y, Z)\):

Since \(\mathbb{P}(Z = 1 \mid X = 1) = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1) = 1/2 = \mathbb{P}(Z = 1)\), the variable \(Z\) is independent of \(X\) (and similarly of \(Y\)) individually.
However, conditioning on \(Z\) breaks this: given \(Z = 1\), the only possible outcomes are \((X=1,Y=1)\) and \((X=-1,Y=-1)\), each with conditional probability \(1/2\). Therefore: \[
\begin{align*}
&\mathbb{P}(X=1 \mid Z=1) = \tfrac{1}{2},\\
&\mathbb{P}(Y=1 \mid Z=1) = \tfrac{1}{2}, \\
&\mathbb{P}(X=1,\, Y=1 \mid Z=1) = \tfrac{1}{2}.
\end{align*}
\] Since \(\tfrac{1}{2} \neq \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}\), the variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are not conditionally independent given \(Z\). In fact, given \(Z\), the identity \(Y = ZX\) holds deterministically, so \(X\) and \(Y\) are maximally dependent. This shows that marginal independence (\(X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y\)) does not imply conditional independence (\(X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid Z\)).
Part 2: Conditioning on the event \(\{X = Y\}\) vs. a \(\sigma\)-field.
The event \(\{X = Y\} = \{X=1,Y=1\} \cup \{X=-1,Y=-1\}\) has \(\mathbb{P}(X=Y) = 1/2\).
Using the definition of conditional expectation given an event: \[
\mathbb{E}[X \mid X = Y] = \frac{\mathbb{E}[X \,\mathbf{1}_{\{X=Y\}}]}{\mathbb{P}(X=Y)} = \frac{1 \cdot \tfrac{1}{4} + (-1) \cdot \tfrac{1}{4}}{\tfrac{1}{2}} = 0.
\] On the other hand: \[
\mathbb{E}[XY \mid X = Y] = \mathbb{E}[X^2 \mid X = Y] = 1,
\] since \(X^2 = 1\) always. Thus \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid X=Y] \ne \mathbb{E}[XY \mid X=Y]\), even though \(X = Y\) on the conditioning event. This is not a contradiction: the formula \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid X=Y] = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X=Y]\) does hold (both equal \(0\)), but equality of random variables on an event does not transfer inside conditional expectations when the conditioning is on that same event.
This illustrates why in the definition of the Markov property and conditional independence, we always condition on a \(\sigma\)-field (such as \(\sigma(X_s)\)) rather than on a specific event.

41.6 Equivalent Characterizations
The following statements are equivalent:

\(\mathcal{A} \perp\!\!\!\perp \mathcal{B} \mid \mathcal{G}\).
For all \(B \in \mathcal{B}\), \(\mathbb{P}(B \mid \mathcal{G} \vee \mathcal{A}) = \mathbb{P}(B \mid \mathcal{G})\) a.s.
For all bounded \(\mathcal{A}\)-measurable random variables \(Z\) and bounded \(\mathcal{B}\)-measurable random variables \(Y\), \[
\mathbb{E}[Z Y \mid \mathcal{G}] = \mathbb{E}[Z \mid \mathcal{G}] \, \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{G}] \quad \text{a.s.}
\]

title: 78  Lecture 36.1: The Markov Property
section: 78.6 The Poetic Reinterpretation of the Markov Property
text:
78.6 The Poetic Reinterpretation of the Markov Property
The Markov property can be phrased intuitively as: “Given (conditional on) the present, the past and the future are independent.”

Theorem 78.2 (Markov Property as Conditional Independence) Let \((X_t)_{t \in T}\) be an adapted process on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, (\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \in T}, \mathbb{P})\). Then \((X_t)_{t \in T}\) satisfies the Markov property if and only if for each \(s \in T\), the past \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{F}_s\) and the future \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\) are conditionally independent given \(X_s\): \[
\mathcal{F}_s \perp\!\!\!\perp \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X \,\mid \sigma(X_s).
\tag{78.6}\]


Note that \(\sigma(X_t: t \le s )\subseteq\mathcal{F}_s\) and \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X=\sigma(X_t: t \ge s)\). Thus, given \(\sigma(X_s)\), the past and future are independent.


Proof. \((\Longrightarrow)\) Assume the Markov property holds. Let \(Z \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_s)\) and \(Y \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X)\). We evaluate \(\mathbb{E}[Z Y \mid \sigma(X_s)]\): Using the tower property and the fact that \(Z\) is \(\mathcal{F}_s\)-measurable: \[
\mathbb{E}[Z Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = Z \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s].
\] By Theorem 78.1, \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X_s]\) a.s. Substituting this yields: \[
\mathbb{E}[Z Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = Z \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X_s] \quad \text{a.s.}
\] Now take conditional expectations on both sides with respect to \(\sigma(X_s) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_s\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Z Y \mid \sigma(X_s)] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}[Z Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s] \;\middle\vert{}\; \sigma(X_s) \right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}\left[ Z \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X_s] \;\middle\vert{}\; \sigma(X_s) \right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[Z \mid \sigma(X_s)] \, \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \sigma(X_s)] \quad \text{a.s.},
\end{aligned}
\] where \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X_s]\) was pulled out of the conditional expectation since it is \(\sigma(X_s)\)-measurable. This establishes \(\mathcal{F}_s \perp\!\!\!\perp \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X \mid \sigma(X_s)\).
\((\Longleftarrow)\) Conversely, assume \(\mathcal{F}_s \perp\!\!\!\perp \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X \mid \sigma(X_s)\). Let \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) and \(t > s\). Take \(Y = f(X_t) \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X)\). For any \(A \in \mathcal{F}_s\), note that \(\mathbb{I}_A\) is bounded \(\mathcal{F}_s\)-measurable and \(f(X_t)\) is bounded \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\)-measurable. By Proposition 78.3 (condition 3) with \(\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{F}_s\), \(\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\), \(\mathcal{G} = \sigma(X_s)\): \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_A f(X_t) \mid X_s] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_A \mid X_s]\,\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] = \mathbb{P}(A \mid X_s) \, \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s].
\] Taking expectations via the tower property: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_A f(X_t)] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_A f(X_t) \mid X_s] \right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{P}(A \mid X_s) \, \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] \right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_A \mid X_s] \cdot \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] \right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{I}_A \cdot \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] \;\middle\vert{}\; X_s \right] \right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{I}_A \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] \right],
\end{aligned}
\] where the fourth equality uses that \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s]\) is \(\sigma(X_s)\)-measurable, so by the “taking out what is known” property, \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_A \mid X_s] \cdot \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_A \cdot \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] \mid X_s]\). Since this holds for every \(A \in \mathcal{F}_s\), by definition of conditional expectation with respect to \(\mathcal{F}_s\), we conclude: \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] \quad \text{a.s.}
\] This is precisely the Markov property Equation 78.1.

79.1 Introduction and Notation Refinement
In previous discussions, we introduced probability kernels, regular conditional distributions, and their associated integral operators. To prevent confusion in subsequent developments, we establish a standardized notation and terminology convention:

title: 79  Lecture 36.2: Probability Kernels Revisited
text:
Probability Kernel: Denoted by \(q\) (formerly \(Q\)).
Markov (Transition) Operator: Denoted by \(Q\) (formerly \(L\)).

title: 79  Lecture 36.2: Probability Kernels Revisited
text:
79.2 Probability Kernels
Let \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) and \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) be measurable spaces.

Definition 79.1 (Probability Kernel) A function \(q: S_1 \times \mathcal{B}_2 \to [0, 1]\) is a probability kernel (or transition probability kernel) from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) if:

For each fixed \(x \in S_1\), the mapping \(B \mapsto q(x, B)\) is a probability measure on \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\), i.e., \(q(x, \cdot) \in \mathcal{P}(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\).
For each fixed \(B \in \mathcal{B}_2\), the mapping \(x \mapsto q(x, B)\) is \((\mathcal{B}_1, \mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})\)-measurable (automatically bounded, since it takes values in \([0,1]\)).


The following result gives the measurability result for integrating a function against a kernel. The key idea is to regard \(x\longmapsto \int_{S_2}f(y)\,q(x,\mathrm dy)\) as an integration operator indexed by \(x\).

Proposition 79.1 (Integration with Respect to a Kernel) If \(q: S_1 \times \mathcal{B}_2 \to [0, 1]\) is a probability kernel, then for every bounded measurable function \(f: (S_2, \mathcal{B}_2) \to (\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})\), or every non-negative measurable function \(f: (S_2, \mathcal{B}_2) \to ([0,\infty], \mathcal{B}_{[0,\infty]})\), the function defined by \[x \mapsto \int_{S_2} f(y) \, q(x, \mathrm{d}y)\] is \((\mathcal{B}_1, \mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})\)-measurable.


Proof (Proof of Proposition 79.1). See Lemma 72.1.

Some Observations:

For each fixed \(x \in S_1\), \(q(x,\cdot)\) is a probability measure on \((S_2,\mathcal B_2)\). Thus \[
\int_{S_2}f(y)\,q(x,\mathrm dy)
\] is simply the expectation of \(f(Y)\) when \(Y\) has distribution \(q(x,\cdot)\). The nontrivial part of the proposition is that this expectation varies measurably with \(x\).
For example, if \(f=\mathbf 1_B\), then \[
\int_{S_2}\mathbf 1_B(y)\,q(x,\mathrm dy) =q(x,B),
\] which is measurable in \(x\) by the definition of a kernel. The proposition extends this basic property from indicator functions to arbitrary bounded measurable or nonnegative measurable functions, essentially through the usual approximation arguments for measurable functions.
In particular, if \(X\) is an \(S_1\)-valued random variable and \(q(X,\cdot)\) represents the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X\), then \[
x\mapsto \int f(y)\,q(x,\mathrm dy)
\] is the conditional expectation function \(\mathbb{E}[f(Y)\mid X=x]\).

The following result says that a measurable family of probability densities automatically generates a probability kernel.

Example 79.1 (Kernel Defined via Joint/Conditional Density) Let \(\nu_2\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite measure on \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\). If \(q_0: S_1 \times S_2 \to [0,\infty)\) is \((\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\)-measurable and \(\int_{S_2} q_0(x, y) \, \nu_2(\mathrm{d}y) = 1\) for all \(x \in S_1\), then \[q(x, B) = \int_{B} q_0(x, y) \, \nu_2(\mathrm{d}y)\] defines a probability kernel from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\).
There are two properties to verify: (i) \(q(x,\cdot)\) is a probability measure. For fixed \(x\), \(y\mapsto q_0(x,y)\) is measurable, and therefore \[
B\mapsto\int_B q_0(x,y)\,\nu_2(\mathrm dy)
\] is a measure. Moreover, \[
q(x,S_2) = \int_{S_2}q_0(x,y)\,\nu_2(\mathrm dy) =1.
\] Hence \(q(x,\cdot)\) is a probability measure.

\(x\mapsto q(x,B)\) is measurable. For fixed \(B\in\mathcal B_2\), \[
q(x,B) = \int_{S_2}\mathbf 1_B(y)q_0(x,y)\,\nu_2(\mathrm dy).
\] Since \[
(x,y)\mapsto \mathbf 1_B(y)q_0(x,y)
\] is \(\mathcal B_1\otimes\mathcal B_2\)-measurable, the standard measurable-integration theorem implies that \(x\mapsto \int_{S_2}\mathbf 1_B(y)q_0(x,y)\,\nu_2(\mathrm dy)\) is \(\mathcal B_1\)-measurable. Thus \(q\) satisfies both defining properties of a probability kernel.

section: 79.3 Integration with Respect to a Kernel
text:
79.3 Integration with Respect to a Kernel
If \(q: S_1 \times \mathcal{B}_2 \to [0, 1]\) is a probability kernel, then for every bounded measurable function \(f: (S_2, \mathcal{B}_2) \to (\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})\), or every non-negative measurable function \(f: (S_2, \mathcal{B}_2) \to ([0,\infty], \mathcal{B}_{[0,\infty]})\), the function defined by \[x \mapsto \int_{S_2} f(y) \, q(x, \mathrm{d}y)\] is \((\mathcal{B}_1, \mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})\)-measurable.

title: 79  Lecture 36.2: Probability Kernels Revisited
text:
79.3 Regular Conditional Distributions
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space. Let \(X: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) and \(Y: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) be random variables.

Definition 79.2 (Regular Conditional Distribution) A probability kernel \(q_{Y\vert{}X}\) from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) is called a regular conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X\) if for all \(B \in \mathcal{B}_2\), \[
\mathbb{P}(Y \in B \mid X) = q_{Y\vert{}X}(X, B) \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{79.1}\]


Remark 79.1 (Existence of Regular Conditional Distributions). 

One point worth stressing in the surrounding exposition is that \(q_{Y\mid X}(X,B)\) is a random variable, whereas \(q_{Y\mid X}(x,B)\) is a measurable function of the possible value \(x\) of \(X\). Thus the kernel provides a measurable family of conditional distributions: \(x\longmapsto q_{Y\mid X}(x,\cdot)\). For each \(x\), \(q_{Y\mid X}(x,\cdot)\) is a probability measure on \(S_2\), while as \(x\) varies, the probabilities of measurable sets vary measurably. This is precisely why a regular conditional distribution is represented by a kernel, rather than merely by a collection of conditional probabilities.
If \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) is a standard Borel space (e.g., a Polish space equipped with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra), then a regular conditional distribution \(q_{Y\vert{}X}\) of \(Y\) given \(X\) always exists; no topological condition on \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) is required, and the same conclusion holds with \(X\) replaced by an arbitrary sub-\(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{G} \subset \mathcal{F}\).

title: 79  Lecture 36.2: Probability Kernels Revisited
text:
79.4 Disintegration and Expectation
If \(q_{Y\vert{}X}\) is a regular conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X\), then for any \(f \in b(S_1 \times S_2, \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\) (or non-negative measurable \(f\)), \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X] = \int_{S_2} f(X, y) \, q_{Y\vert{}X}(X, \mathrm{d}y) \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{79.2}\] In particular, taking expectations on both sides yields the disintegration formula: \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y)] = \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, q_{Y\vert{}X}(x, \mathrm{d}y) \right) \mathbb{P}_X(\mathrm{d}x).
\tag{79.3}\]

title: 79  Lecture 36.2: Probability Kernels Revisited
text:
79.5 Special Cases

Independent Random Variables: If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent with marginal law \(\mu_Y = \mathbb{P}_Y\), then the constant kernel \(q_{Y\vert{}X}(x,\cdot) := \mu_Y(\cdot)\), independent of \(x\), is a regular conditional distribution: \[q_{Y\vert{}X}(x, B) = \mu_Y(B) = \mathbb{P}(Y \in B) \quad \text{for every } x \in S_1.\]
Absolute Continuity with Respect to Product Measures: Suppose the joint distribution \(\mathbb{P}_{(X,Y)}\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(\nu_1 \otimes \nu_2\) with joint density \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\), and let \(f_X(x) = \int f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, \nu_2(\mathrm{d}y)\) denote the marginal density. For every \(x\) with \(f_X(x) > 0\) (a set of full \(\mathbb{P}_X\)-measure, since \(\mathbb{P}_X(\{f_X=0\})=0\)): \[q_{Y\vert{}X}(x, B) = \int_{B} \frac{f_{X,Y}(x, y)}{f_X(x)} \, \nu_2(\mathrm{d}y);\] on the remaining \(\mathbb{P}_X\)-null set \(\{f_X = 0\}\), set \(q_{Y\vert{}X}(x,\cdot)\) to an arbitrary fixed reference probability measure on \((S_2,\mathcal{B}_2)\), so that \(q_{Y\vert{}X}\) is a genuine probability kernel on all of \(S_1\).
Discrete Spaces: If \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are countable sets with \(\mathcal{B}_1, \mathcal{B}_2\) their power sets, then for any \(x \in S_1\) with \(\mathbb{P}(X = x) > 0\): \[q_{Y\vert{}X}(x, B) = \sum_{y \in B} \mathbb{P}(Y = y \mid X = x);\] on the remaining (necessarily \(\mathbb{P}_X\)-null) set of \(x\) with \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)=0\), set \(q_{Y\vert{}X}(x,\cdot)\) to an arbitrary fixed reference probability measure on \(S_2\).

title: 79  Lecture 36.2: Probability Kernels Revisited
text:
79.6 Markov Transition Operators
Given a probability kernel \(q\) from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\), we associate an operator \(Q\) acting on spaces of bounded measurable functions.

Definition 79.3 (Markov Transition Operator) The Markov transition operator associated with kernel \(q\) is the operator \(Q: \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) defined by \[
(Qf)(x) := \int_{S_2} f(y) \, q(x, \mathrm{d}y), \quad x \in S_1.
\tag{79.4}\] (Note: This operator is contractive on \(\mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\), satisfying \(\Vert{}Qf\Vert{}_\infty \le \Vert{}f\Vert{}_\infty\).)


Theorem 79.1 (Characterization of Transition Operators) Let \(S_1 = S_2 = S\) and \(\mathcal{B}_1 = \mathcal{B}_2 = \mathcal{B}\). An operator \(Q: \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) is a Markov transition operator (i.e., induced by a unique probability kernel \(q\) via \(q(x, B) = (Q\mathbb{I}_B)(x)\)) if and only if it satisfies the following four conditions:

Linearity: \(Q(\alpha f + \beta g) = \alpha Qf + \beta Qg\) for all \(\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(f, g \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\).
Preservation of Constants: \(Q(\mathbb{I}_S) = \mathbb{I}_S\).
Positivity: \(Qf \ge 0\) whenever \(f \ge 0\).
Bounded Pointwise Continuity: If \(f_n \to f\) pointwise with \(\Vert{}f_n\Vert{}_\infty \le C < \infty\) for all \(n\), then \(Qf_n \to Qf\) pointwise. (The bound \(\Vert{}Qf_n\Vert{}_\infty \le C\) is automatic from conditions 0–2 and need not be imposed separately.)



Proof. \((\Longrightarrow)\) If \(Q\) is defined via Equation 79.4, properties (0)–(3) follow directly from the properties of Lebesgue integration with respect to the probability measures \(q(x, \cdot)\).
\((\Longleftarrow)\) Conversely, given such an operator \(Q\), define \(q(x, B) := (Q\mathbb{I}_B)(x)\) for \(x \in S\) and \(B \in \mathcal{B}\). Property (1) implies \(q(x, S) = 1\), property (2) implies \(q(x, B) \ge 0\), and property (3) together with countable additivity of indicator functions ensures that \(B \mapsto q(x, B)\) is a countably additive probability measure. Since \(Q\) maps \(\mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) into \(\mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\), \(x \mapsto q(x, B)\) is \(\mathcal{B}\)-measurable. Linearity extends the identity \((Qf)(x) = \int f(y)\,q(x,\mathrm{d}y)\) from indicators to simple functions, and condition (3) together with dominated convergence for the finite measure \(q(x,\cdot)\) extend it to every \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\).

title: 79  Lecture 36.2: Probability Kernels Revisited
section: 79.7 Composition of Operators and Action on Measures
text:
79.7 Composition of Operators and Action on Measures
A probability kernel \(q: S_1 \times \mathcal{B}_2 \to [0, 1]\) acts on probability measures \(\nu \in \mathcal{P}(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) on the left to produce a probability measure \(\nu q \in \mathcal{P}(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\):
\[
(\nu q)(B) := \int_{S_1} q(x, B) \, \nu(\mathrm{d}x), \quad B \in \mathcal{B}_2.
\tag{79.5}\]

Lemma 79.1 Suppose \(\mathcal{B}_2\) is countably generated, and \(q_1, q_2\) are two probability kernels from \((S_1,\mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2,\mathcal{B}_2)\) such that, for every \(B \in \mathcal{B}_2\), \[q_1(x, B) = q_2(x, B) \quad \text{for } \nu\text{-almost every } x \in S_1\] (the exceptional \(\nu\)-null set may a priori depend on \(B\)). Then there is a single \(\nu\)-null set \(N \subset S_1\) such that \[q_1(x, \cdot) = q_2(x, \cdot) \quad \text{for every } x \notin N.\]

Note: The weaker hypothesis \(\nu q_1 = \nu q_2\), i.e. equality only of the pushed-forward measures \((\nu q_i)(B) := \int_{S_1} q_i(x,B)\,\nu(\mathrm{d}x)\), does not suffice. Example: on \(S_1=S_2=\{1,2\}\) with \(\nu = \tfrac12\delta_1+\tfrac12\delta_2\), the kernels \(q_1(1,\cdot)=\delta_1,\ q_1(2,\cdot)=\delta_2\) and \(q_2(1,\cdot)=\delta_2,\ q_2(2,\cdot)=\delta_1\) satisfy \(\nu q_1 = \nu q_2 = \tfrac12\delta_1+\tfrac12\delta_2\), yet \(q_1(x,\cdot) \ne q_2(x,\cdot)\) for every \(x\).

Definition 79.4 (Composition of Transition Operators) Given two transition operators \(Q_1: \mathcal{B}_b(S_2,\mathcal{B}_2) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S_1,\mathcal{B}_1)\) and \(Q_2: \mathcal{B}_b(S_3,\mathcal{B}_3) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S_2,\mathcal{B}_2)\) induced by kernels \(q_1\) and \(q_2\), their composition \(Q_1 Q_2: \mathcal{B}_b(S_3,\mathcal{B}_3) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S_1,\mathcal{B}_1)\) is defined by: \[
\begin{aligned}
(Q_1 Q_2 f)(x) &= \int_{S_2} q_1(x, \mathrm{d}y) \int_{S_3} f(z) \, q_2(y, \mathrm{d}z)\\
& = \int_{S_3} f(z) \, (q_1 q_2)(x, \mathrm{d}z).
\end{aligned}
\tag{79.6}\]
where \((q_1 q_2)(x, C) := \int_{S_2} q_2(y, C) \, q_1(x, \mathrm{d}y)\) is the Chapman–Kolmogorov composition kernel.


Example 79.2 (A two-step Markov transition) Let \(S_1=S_2=S_3=\{0,1\}\). Suppose the first transition \(q_1\) is given by \[
q_1(0,\{0\})=0.8,\, q_1(0,\{1\})=0.2,\, q_1(1,\{0\})=0.3,\, q_1(1,\{1\})=0.7.
\] Thus its transition matrix is \[
P_1=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.8&0.2\\
0.3&0.7
\end{pmatrix}.
\] Suppose the second transition \(q_2\) is \[
q_2(0,\{0\})=0.6,\, q_2(0,\{1\})=0.4,\, q_2(1,\{0\})=0.1,\, q_2(1,\{1\})=0.9,
\] with transition matrix \[
P_2=
\begin{pmatrix} 0.6&0.4\\
0.1&0.9
\end{pmatrix}.
\] So the system evolves as \(X_1\overset{q_1}{\longrightarrow}X_2 \overset{q_2}{\longrightarrow}X_3\). According to the definition, \[
(q_1q_2)(x,C) = \int_{S_2}q_2(y,C)\,q_1(x,\mathrm dy).
\] Since \(S_2=\{0,1\}\), this is simply \[
(q_1q_2)(x,C) = q_2(0,C)q_1(x,\{0\}) + q_2(1,C)q_1(x,\{1\}).
\] For example, starting from \(x=0\), the probability of ending at \(0\) after two transitions is \[
\begin{aligned}
(q_1q_2)(0,\{0\}) &= q_1(0,\{0\})q_2(0,\{0\}) + q_1(0,\{1\})q_2(1,\{0\})\\
&=(0.8)(0.6)+(0.2)(0.1)\\
&=0.50.
\end{aligned}
\] Similarly, \[
(q_1q_2)(0,\{1\}) =(0.8)(0.4)+(0.2)(0.9) =0.50.
\] For \(x=1\), \[
(q_1q_2)(1,\{0\}) =(0.3)(0.6)+(0.7)(0.1) =0.25,
\] and therefore \((q_1q_2)(1,\{1\})=0.75\). Hence the composition kernel has transition matrix \[
P_1P_2 =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.8&0.2\\
0.3&0.7
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
0.6&0.4\\
0.1&0.9
\end{pmatrix} =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.50&0.50\\
0.25&0.75
\end{pmatrix}.
\] Now look at the transition operators.Take a bounded function \(f:S_3\to\mathbb R\), say \(f(0)=2\) and \(f(1)=5\). The operator \(Q_2\) first transforms \(f\) into a function on \(S_2\): \[
(Q_2f)(y) = \sum_{z\in S_3}f(z)q_2(y,\{z\}).
\] Thus \((Q_2f)(0) =(2)(0.6)+(5)(0.4) =3.2\), while \((Q_2f)(1) =(2)(0.1)+(5)(0.9) =4.7\). Then \(Q_1\) acts on this new function: \[
(Q_1Q_2f)(x) = \sum_{y\in S_2}(Q_2f)(y)q_1(x,\{y\}).
\] For \(x=0\), \[
\begin{aligned}
(Q_1Q_2f)(0) &=(3.2)(0.8)+(4.7)(0.2)\\
&=3.5.
\end{aligned}
\] But using the composition kernel directly, \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{S_3}f(z)(q_1q_2)(0,\mathrm dz) &=(2)(0.50)+(5)(0.50)\\
&=3.5.
\end{aligned}
\] So we have explicitly verified \[
\boxed{ (Q_1Q_2f)(x) = \int_{S_3}f(z)(q_1q_2)(x,\mathrm dz). }
\] This example makes the definition particularly intuitive. If \(X_1=0\), then there are two possible paths to \(X_3\): \(0\longrightarrow0\longrightarrow0\) with probability \((0.8)(0.6)=0.48\), and \(0\longrightarrow1\longrightarrow0\) with probability \((0.2)(0.1)=0.02\). Adding these gives \(P(X_3=0\mid X_1=0)=0.48+0.02=0.50\).
The composition kernel \(q_1q_2\) simply sums over all possible intermediate states. Likewise, the operator composition says that the expected value of \(f(X_3)\), conditional on \(X_1=x\), can be computed in two stages: \[
\boxed{ \mathbb E[f(X_3)\mid X_1=x] = \mathbb E\!\left[ \mathbb E[f(X_3)\mid X_2] \mid X_1=x \right]. }
\] That is the operator version of the Chapman–Kolmogorov idea.

text:
79.10 Action on Measures
A probability kernel \(q: S_1 	imes \mathcal{B}_2 	o [0, 1]\) acts on probability measures \(
u \in \mathcal{P}(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) on the left to produce a probability measure \(
u q \in \mathcal{P}(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\):
\[(
u q)(B) := \int_{S_1} q(x, B) \, 
u(\mathrm{d}x), \quad B \in \mathcal{B}_2.\] {#eq-measure-kernel-action}

Lemma 79.1 If \(\mathcal{B}_1\) and \(\mathcal{B}_2\) are countably generated, and \(q_1, q_2\) are two probability kernels such that \(
u q_1 = 
u q_2\), then: \[q_1(x, \cdot) = q_2(x, \cdot) \quad 	ext{for } 
u	ext{-almost every } x \in S_1.\]

title: 79  Lecture 36.2: Probability Kernels Revisited
text:
79.11 Composition of Operators
Given two transition operators \(Q_1: b\mathcal{B}_2 \to b\mathcal{B}_1\) and \(Q_2: b\mathcal{B}_3 \to b\mathcal{B}_2\) induced by kernels \(q_1\) and \(q_2\), their composition \(Q_1 Q_2: b\mathcal{B}_3 \to b\mathcal{B}_1\) is defined by:
\[(Q_1 Q_2 f)(x) = \int_{S_2} q_1(x, \mathrm{d}y) \int_{S_3} f(z) \, q_2(y, \mathrm{d}z) = \int_{S_3} f(z) \, (q_1 q_2)(x, \mathrm{d}z),\] {#eq-operator-composition}
where \((q_1 q_2)(x, C) := \int_{S_2} q_2(y, C) \, q_1(x, \mathrm{d}y)\) is the Chapman–Kolmogorov composition kernel.

title: 79  Lecture 36.2: Probability Kernels Revisited
text:
79.8 Extension to Finite-Dimensional Product Distributions
Let \(q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n\) be a sequence of probability kernels where, for \(k = 1, \dots, n\), \(q_k: S_k \times \mathcal{B}_{k+1} \to [0, 1]\) is a probability kernel from \((S_k, \mathcal{B}_k)\) to \((S_{k+1}, \mathcal{B}_{k+1})\). Given an initial probability distribution \(\nu \in \mathcal{P}(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\), we define a unique probability measure \(\mu\) on the finite product space \((S_1 \times \dots \times S_{n+1}, \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \mathcal{B}_{n+1})\) via iterated integration:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\int_{S_1 \times \dots \times S_{n+1}} f(x_1, \dots, x_{n+1}) \, \mu(\mathrm{d}x_1, \dots, \mathrm{d}x_{n+1}) := \\
&\int_{S_1} \nu(\mathrm{d}x_1) \int_{S_2} q_1(x_1, \mathrm{d}x_2) \int_{S_3} q_2(x_2, \mathrm{d}x_3) \dots \int_{S_{n+1}} f(x_1, \dots, x_{n+1}) \, q_n(x_n, \mathrm{d}x_{n+1}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{79.7}\]

Proposition 79.2 For product functions \(f(x_1, \dots, x_{n+1}) = f_1(x_1) f_2(x_2) \cdots f_{n+1}(x_{n+1})\) with \(f_k \in \mathcal{B}_b(S_k,\mathcal{B}_k)\), expression Equation 79.7 simplifies in operator notation to: \[
\int f \, \mathrm{d}\mu = \mathbb{E}_\nu \left[ f_1 Q_1 \left( f_2 Q_2 \left( f_3 \dots Q_n(f_{n+1}) \dots \right) \right) \right].
\tag{79.8}\]
