title: 47  Lecture 22.2: Weak Convergence over \(R^d\)
text:
51.1 Takeaways

Smaller test-function classes suffice on \(\mathbb{R}^d\). On \(\mathbb{R}^d\), weak convergence \(\mu_n \implies \mu\) is equivalent to \(\int f \, d\mu_n \to \int f \, d\mu\) for all \(f\) in any of the classes \[C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d) \subsetneq C_c(\mathbb{R}^d) \subsetneq C_b(\mathbb{R}^d), \qquad C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d) \subsetneq \text{Lip}_b(\mathbb{R}^d) \subsetneq C_b(\mathbb{R}^d).\] Note that \(C_c\) and \(\text{Lip}_b\) are not comparable: \(x \mapsto \sqrt{|x|}\) cut off near the origin is in \(C_c(\mathbb{R})\) but is not Lipschitz, while \(x \mapsto \sin x\) is in \(\text{Lip}_b(\mathbb{R})\) but has no compact support. The gain in using \(C_c\) and \(C_c^\infty\) is that their members are compactly supported, hence analytically more tractable.
Tightness underlies the reduction from \(C_b\) to \(C_c\). By Lemma 49.1, weak convergence forces \(\lim_{R\to\infty} \inf_n \mu_n(\bar{B}_R) = 1\): the sequence concentrates uniformly on large balls. This allows tail contributions to be controlled by \(\|f\|_\infty \cdot \sup_n (1 - \mu_n(\bar{B}_{R/2})) \to 0\) as \(R \to \infty\).
Mollification gives the further reduction from \(C_c\) to \(C_c^\infty\). Every \(f \in C_c(\mathbb{R}^d)\) is approximated uniformly by \(f_\epsilon = f * \rho_\epsilon \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)\), with \(\|f - f_\epsilon\|_\infty \to 0\) as \(\epsilon \to 0\) by uniform continuity of \(f\). This reduction is essential for Fourier-analytic methods (e.g., characteristic functions), which test against smooth oscillatory functions.
On \(\mathbb{R}\), weak convergence is equivalent to pointwise CDF convergence at continuity points. By Theorem 51.1, \(\mu_n \implies \mu\) if and only if \(F_n(t) \to F(t)\) for all \(t \in \text{Cont}(F)\). Convergence can fail at discontinuity points of \(F\), as shown in Example 51.1 with \(\delta_{a+1/n} \implies \delta_a\). Since any monotone \(F\) has at most countably many discontinuities, the exceptional set excluded from the convergence requirement is at most countable, and \(\text{Cont}(F)\) is dense in \(\mathbb{R}\).
The full Portmanteau equivalence on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) now has eight conditions. This lecture adds three items to the five Portmanteau conditions from Lecture 22.1: testing against \(C_c(\mathbb{R}^d)\), testing against \(C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)\), and (in dimension \(d = 1\)) CDF convergence at all continuity points of the limit. Each is strictly more convenient to verify than testing all of \(C_b(\mathbb{R}^d)\).

title: 78  Lecture 36.1: The Markov Property
text:
78.7 Takeaways

The Markov property formalises memorylessness.
An adapted process \((X_t)\) is Markov if \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s]\) a.s. for all \(s \le t\) and bounded measurable \(f\). By Proposition 78.1, this is equivalent to the existence of a measurable \(F\) with \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = F(X_s)\) a.s. — the conditional expectation of any future functional depends on the past only through the present state value.
The natural filtration is the smallest that works.
If the Markov property holds for some filtration \((\mathcal{F}_t)\), it automatically holds for the natural filtration \(\mathcal{F}_t^X = \sigma(X_r : r \le t)\). This follows from the tower property and the \(\sigma(X_s)\)-measurability of \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s]\). The Markov property is thus a property of the process itself, not of the choice of filtration.
In discrete time, one-step condition implies the full property.
By Proposition 78.2, checking \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1}) \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = \mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1}) \mid X_n]\) for consecutive times suffices. The extension to all \(s \le t\) is proved by induction: the Doob–Dynkin factorization \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1}) \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = q_{n+1}(X_n)\) enables the tower property to be applied backwards in time.
The Markov property extends to arbitrary future functionals.
By Theorem 78.1, for any bounded \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\)-measurable \(Y\): \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X_s]\) a.s. The proof uses the monotone class theorem (functional Dynkin system): the class \(\mathbb{H}\) of random variables satisfying the identity is a vector space closed under bounded pointwise limits, and the multiplicative system \(\mathbb{M}\) of finite products \(\prod g_i(X_{t_i})\) generates \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\) and is contained in \(\mathbb{H}\) by backward induction via the Markov property.
Conditional independence is the structural characterisation.
By Theorem 78.2, the Markov property is equivalent to \(\mathcal{F}_s \perp\!\!\!\perp \mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X \mid \sigma(X_s)\) for every \(s\): given the present state \(X_s\), the past \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{F}_s\) and the future \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge s}^X\) are conditionally independent. The \((\Longrightarrow)\) direction uses Theorem 78.1 to compute \(\mathbb{E}[ZY \mid \sigma(X_s)] = \mathbb{E}[Z \mid \sigma(X_s)]\,\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \sigma(X_s)]\); the \((\Longleftarrow)\) direction uses Proposition 78.3 (condition 3) and the tower property to recover \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s]\).
Marginal independence does not imply conditional independence.
The Rademacher example shows that \(X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y\) (marginal) does not prevent \(X\) and \(Y\) from being maximally dependent given \(Z = XY\). This illustrates why conditioning on a \(\sigma\)-field (such as \(\sigma(X_s)\)) is structurally distinct from marginal independence, and why the Markov property must be stated in terms of \(\sigma\)-fields rather than events.

title: 48  Lecture 23.1: Vague Convergence
text:
48.1 Motivation: Loss of Mass in the Limit
In previous lectures, we established that on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), weak convergence \(\mu_n \implies \mu\) is equivalent to testing against functions in \(C_c(\mathbb{R}^d)\) provided both \(\mu_n\) and \(\mu\) are probability measures. However, when sequence elements escape to infinity, testing against compactly supported functions \(C_c(\mathbb{R}^d)\) can lead to a limit measure \(\mu\) that fails to preserve total probability mass \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) = 1\).

title: 48  Lecture 23.1: Vague Convergence
text:
Example 48.1 Fix a unit vector \(e_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d\) and let \(\mu_n=\frac{1}{2}\delta_0+\frac{1}{2}\delta_{n e_1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) for \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). Does \(\mu_n\) converge weakly to a probability measure \(\mu\)? For any test function \(f \in C_c(\mathbb{R}^d)\), there exists a radius \(R < \infty\) such that \(\text{supp}(f) \subseteq B_R\). Then for all \(n > R\): \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \, d\mu_n
= \frac{1}{2}f(0) + \frac{1}{2}f(n e_1) = \frac{1}{2}f(0).
\] Thus \(\mu_n \xrightarrow{v} \frac{1}{2}\delta_0\), which is a sub-probability measure with \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) = 1/2 < 1\). Note that \(\mu_n \not\implies \frac{1}{2}\delta_0\), because \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} 1 \, d\mu_n = 1 \nrightarrow \frac{1}{2} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} 1 \, d\mu.
\] In fact, \(\mu_n\) does not possess any weakly convergent subsequence. Indeed, every subsequence is non-tight: for any compact \(K \subset \mathbb{R}^d\), boundedness of \(K\) implies \(n_k e_1 \notin K\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), and hence \(\mu_{n_k}(K) \le 1/2\). Since every weakly convergent sequence of probability measures on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is tight, no subsequence can converge weakly.

title: 48  Lecture 23.1: Vague Convergence
text:
48.2 Vague Convergence
To accommodate limit operations where mass escapes, we introduce the concept of vague convergence for general Radon/Borel measures.

Definition 48.1 (Vague Convergence) Let \(\mu_n, \mu\) be positive Radon measures on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), meaning locally finite regular Borel measures. (In particular, every finite Borel measure on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is Radon.) We say \(\mu_n\) converges vaguely to \(\mu\), denoted \(\mu_n \xrightarrow{v} \mu\), if: \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \, d\mu_n \longrightarrow \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \, d\mu \quad \forall f \in C_c(\mathbb{R}^d)
\]

It is possible to lose mass, but not gain mass under vague convergence. The following proposition formalizes this property.

Theorem 48.1 (One-Sided Conservation of Mass) Let \(\{\mu_n\}\) be a sequence of probability measures on \(\mathbb{R}^d\). If \(\mu_n\xrightarrow{v}\mu\) for some Radon measure \(\mu\), then \[
\mu(\mathbb{R}^d)
\leq
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mu_n(\mathbb{R}^d)
=1.
\] Thus, under vague convergence, total mass can be lost in the limit, but it cannot be gained.


Proof (Proof of Theorem 48.1). Suppose for contradiction that \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) > 1\). Since \(\mu(B_R) \uparrow \mu(\mathbb{R}^d)\) as \(R \to \infty\), there exists some finite radius \(R < \infty\) such that \(\mu(B_R) > 1\). Choose a continuous radial cutoff \(f \in C_c(\mathbb{R}^d)\) that equals \(1\) on \(B_R\), vanishes outside \(B_{R+1}\), and satisfies \(0 \le f \le 1\). Thus \(\mathbf{1}_{B_R} \le f \le 1\). By vague convergence: \[\lim_{n\to\infty} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \, d\mu_n = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \, d\mu \ge \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \mathbf{1}_{B_R} \, d\mu = \mu(B_R) > 1\]
However, for all \(n\): \[\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \, d\mu_n \le \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} 1 \, d\mu_n = \mu_n(\mathbb{R}^d) = 1\] This yields the contradiction \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \int f d\mu_n > 1\), showing \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) \le 1\).

title: 48  Lecture 23.1: Vague Convergence
text:
48.3 Tightness of Probability Measures
To bridge the gap between vague convergence and weak convergence, we need a condition preventing probability mass from fleeing to infinity.

Definition 48.2 (Tightness) A family \(\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(S, \mathcal{B}(S))\) of probability measures on a topological space \(S\) is called tight if for every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists a compact set \(K_\epsilon \subseteq S\) such that: \[\mu(K_\epsilon) \ge 1 - \epsilon \quad \forall \mu \in \mathcal{A}\]
Thus, a sequence \(\{\mu_n\}\) is tight exactly when, for every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists a compact set \(K_\epsilon\) such that \(\inf_n \mu_n(K_\epsilon) \ge 1 - \epsilon\).


The key word is uniformity: the same compact set \(K_\epsilon\) must work for all measures in the family \(\mathcal{A}\) for a given \(\epsilon\). So the probability mass of every measure in the family is concentrated, up to an arbitrarily small amount, inside a common compact set.


Example 48.2 (Examples of Tightness)  

Weakly Convergent Sequences: If \(\mu_n \implies \mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), we proved in Lemma 49.1 that \(\lim_{R\to\infty} \inf_n \mu_n(\bar{B}_R) = 1\). Taking \(K_\epsilon = \bar{B}_R\) for large enough \(R\) demonstrates that every weakly convergent sequence is tight. Thus, weak convergence implies tightness.
Fleeing Sequence: The sequence \(\mu_n =\frac{1}{2}\delta_0 + \frac{1}{2}\delta_n\) is not tight. For any compact set \(K \subset \mathbb{R}\), there exists \(N\) such that \(n > N\) implies \(n \notin K\). Then \(\mu_n(K) \le 1/2 < 1 - \epsilon\) for \(\epsilon < 1/2\), showing that no compact set can capture at least \(1 - \epsilon\) of the mass for all \(n\).

title: 48  Lecture 23.1: Vague Convergence
section: 48.4 Characterization of Weak Convergence via Tightness
text:
48.4 Characterization of Weak Convergence via Tightness

Theorem 48.2 (Equivalence of Weak Convergence and Tight Vague Limits) Let \(\mu_n \in \mathcal{P}\left(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\right)\) and let \(\mu\) be a positive Radon measure on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) such that \(\mu_n \xrightarrow{v} \mu\). Then \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) = 1\) if and only if the sequence \(\{\mu_n\}\) is tight. In that case, \(\mu\) is a probability measure and \(\mu_n \implies \mu\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 48.2). 

\((\implies)\): Suppose \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) = 1\), so \(\mu\) is a probability measure. Since \(\mu_n \xrightarrow{v} \mu\) means \(\int f \, d\mu_n \to \int f \, d\mu\) for all \(f \in C_c(\mathbb{R}^d)\), and both \(\mu_n\) and \(\mu\) are probability measures, the \(C_c\) characterization of weak convergence (Theorem 49.1) gives \(\mu_n \implies \mu\). By Lemma 49.1 (proved in the previous lecture), every weakly convergent sequence on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is tight.
\((\impliedby)\): Assume \(\{\mu_n\}\) is tight. Fix \(\epsilon > 0\). By tightness, choose a compact set \(K_\epsilon \subset \mathbb{R}^d\) such that \(\mu_n(K_\epsilon) \ge 1 - \epsilon\) for all \(n\). Define \(f(x)=\max\{1-\operatorname{dist}(x,K_\epsilon),0\}\). Then \(f \in C_c(\mathbb{R}^d)\) because the closed unit neighborhood of the compact set \(K_\epsilon\) is compact, and \(\mathbf{1}_{K_\epsilon} \le f \le 1\).
Since \(f \ge \mathbf{1}_{K_\epsilon}\), we have \(\int f \, d\mu_n \ge \mu_n(K_\epsilon) \ge 1 - \epsilon\) for all \(n\). Using \(f \in C_c\) and vague convergence: \[\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) \ge \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \, d\mu = \lim_{n\to\infty} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \, d\mu_n \ge \liminf_{n\to\infty} \mu_n(K_\epsilon) \ge 1 - \epsilon.\]
Since \(\epsilon > 0\) was arbitrary, \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) \ge 1\). Combined with Theorem 48.1 (\(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) \le 1\)), we conclude \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) = 1\), so \(\mu\) is a probability measure. Since \(\mu_n \xrightarrow{v} \mu\) already gives \(\int f \, d\mu_n \to \int f \, d\mu\) for all \(f \in C_c(\mathbb{R}^d)\), and both \(\mu_n\) and \(\mu\) are probability measures, the \(C_c\) characterization (Theorem 49.1) yields \(\mu_n \implies \mu\).



Example 48.3 Let \(\mu_n=\delta_n\), where \(\delta_n\) is the point mass at \(n\in\mathbb R\): \(\delta_n(A)=\mathbf 1\{n\in A\}\). Consider the sequence \(\delta_1,\delta_2,\delta_3,\ldots\). For any compact set \(K\subset\mathbb R\), there exists \(M<\infty\) such that \(K\subset[-M,M]\). For every \(n>M\), \(\delta_n(K)=0\). Thus, for example, if \(\epsilon=1/2\), there is no compact \(K\) such that \[
\delta_n(K)\geq1-\epsilon=\frac12 \qquad\text{for every }n.
\] Hence \(\{\delta_n\}_{n\ge 1}\) is not tight.
Take any \(f\in C_c(\mathbb R)\). Because \(f\) has compact support, there exists \(M<\infty\) such that \(f(x)=0\) whenever \(|x|>M\). Therefore, for all \(n>M\), \[
\int f\,d\delta_n=f(n)=0.
\] Consequently, \(\int f\,d\delta_n\longrightarrow0\). Thus \[
\delta_n\xrightarrow{v}0,
\] where \(0\) denotes the zero measure. The limiting measure has mass \(0(\mathbb R)=0\). So the mass has completely escaped to infinity.
The theorem says that if \(\mu_n\xrightarrow{v}\mu\) and the sequence \(\{\mu_n\}\) is tight, then necessarily \(\mu(\mathbb R)=1\) and therefore \(\mu_n\implies\mu\). Here, the sequence is not tight, and indeed the vague limit has mass \(0\), not \(1\). In particular, there cannot be weak convergence: \(\delta_n\not\implies0\), because \(0\) is not a probability measure.

title: 48  Lecture 23.1: Vague Convergence
section: 48.5 Vague Convergence via Interval Differences on \(\mathbb{R}\)
text:
48.5 Vague Convergence via Interval Differences on \(\mathbb{R}\)

Theorem 48.3 (Characterization by CDF Differences) Let \(\mu_n \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) and let \(\mu\) be a finite Borel measure on \(\mathbb{R}\). Define the CDFs \(F_n(t) = \mu_n((-\infty, t])\) and the cumulative mass function \(F(t) = \mu((-\infty, t])\); unlike a probability CDF, \(F\) satisfies \(F(+\infty)=\mu(\mathbb{R})\), which need not equal \(1\). Then \(\mu_n \xrightarrow{v} \mu\) if and only if \[
F_n(b) - F_n(a) \longrightarrow F(b) - F(a) \quad \forall a, b \in \text{Cont}(F) \text{ with } a < b.
\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 48.3). First observe that, for \(a<b\), \[
F_n(b)-F_n(a)=\mu_n((a,b])
\quad\text{and}\quad
F(b)-F(a)=\mu((a,b]).
\] Moreover, \(t\in\operatorname{Cont}(F)\) if and only if \(\mu(\{t\})=0\). Indeed, \[
F(t)-F(t^-)=\mu(\{t\}).
\]

\((\implies)\): Suppose that \(\mu_n\xrightarrow{v}\mu\), and fix \(a,b\in\operatorname{Cont}(F)\) with \(a<b\). For \(0<\delta<(b-a)/2\), choose functions \(\ell_\delta,u_\delta\in C_c(\mathbb R)\) as follows:

\(\ell_\delta\) is \(0\) outside \((a,b)\), is \(1\) on \([a+\delta,b-\delta]\), is linear on the two intervening intervals, and satisfies \(0\leq\ell_\delta\leq1\);
\(u_\delta\) is \(1\) on \([a,b]\), is \(0\) outside \((a-\delta,b+\delta)\), is linear on the two intervening intervals, and satisfies \(0\leq u_\delta\leq1\).

These functions satisfy \[
\ell_\delta\leq\mathbf 1_{(a,b]}\leq u_\delta.
\] Therefore, \[
\int \ell_\delta\,d\mu_n
\leq \mu_n((a,b])
\leq \int u_\delta\,d\mu_n.
\] Vague convergence applies to both cutoff functions, so \[
\int \ell_\delta\,d\mu
\leq \liminf_{n\to\infty}\mu_n((a,b])
\leq \limsup_{n\to\infty}\mu_n((a,b])
\leq \int u_\delta\,d\mu.
\] As \(\delta\downarrow0\), the lower cutoffs converge pointwise to \(\mathbf 1_{(a,b)}\), while the upper cutoffs converge pointwise to \(\mathbf 1_{[a,b]}\). All these functions are bounded by the indicator of a fixed compact interval once \(\delta\) is restricted, and \(\mu\) is finite on compact sets. Hence dominated convergence gives \[
\int \ell_\delta\,d\mu\longrightarrow\mu((a,b)),
\qquad
\int u_\delta\,d\mu\longrightarrow\mu([a,b]).
\] Since \(a,b\in\operatorname{Cont}(F)\), we have \(\mu(\{a\})=\mu(\{b\})=0\), and consequently \[
\mu((a,b))=\mu((a,b])=\mu([a,b]).
\] Letting \(\delta\downarrow0\) in the preceding bounds yields \[
\mu_n((a,b])\longrightarrow\mu((a,b]),
\] which is exactly \[
F_n(b)-F_n(a)\longrightarrow F(b)-F(a).
\]
\((\impliedby)\): Conversely, suppose that \[
\mu_n((a,b])\longrightarrow\mu((a,b])
\qquad\text{for every }a,b\in\operatorname{Cont}(F),\ a<b.
\] Because \(F\) is nondecreasing, it has at most countably many discontinuities. Thus \(\operatorname{Cont}(F)\) is dense in \(\mathbb R\).
Let \(f\in C_c(\mathbb R)\). Choose \(A<B\) such that \(\operatorname{supp}(f)\subseteq[A,B]\). Given \(\eta>0\), uniform continuity of \(f\) gives \(\rho>0\) such that \[
|x-y|<\rho\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |f(x)-f(y)|<\eta.
\] Using the density of \(\operatorname{Cont}(F)\), choose a finite partition \[
x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_k,
\] all of whose points belong to \(\operatorname{Cont}(F)\), such that \(x_0<A\), \(x_k>B\), and \(x_j-x_{j-1}<\rho\) for every \(j\). Define \[
f_\pi(x)=\sum_{j=1}^k f(x_j)\mathbf 1_{(x_{j-1},x_j]}(x).
\] Since \(f\) vanishes outside \([A,B]\) and every interval of the partition has length less than \(\rho\), we have \[
\lVert f-f_\pi\rVert_\infty\leq\eta.
\] The assumed interval convergence and finiteness of the sum imply \[
\begin{aligned}
\int f_\pi\,d\mu_n
&=\sum_{j=1}^k f(x_j)\mu_n((x_{j-1},x_j])\\
&\longrightarrow
\sum_{j=1}^k f(x_j)\mu((x_{j-1},x_j])
=\int f_\pi\,d\mu.
\end{aligned}
\] Because each \(\mu_n\) is a probability measure and \(\mu\) is finite, \[
\begin{aligned}
\left|\int f\,d\mu_n-\int f\,d\mu\right|
&\leq \left|\int(f-f_\pi)\,d\mu_n\right|
+\left|\int f_\pi\,d\mu_n-\int f_\pi\,d\mu\right|\\
&\quad+\left|\int(f_\pi-f)\,d\mu\right|\\
&\leq \eta+\left|\int f_\pi\,d\mu_n-\int f_\pi\,d\mu\right|
+\eta\mu(\mathbb R).
\end{aligned}
\] Taking \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}\) gives \[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\left|\int f\,d\mu_n-\int f\,d\mu\right|
\leq \eta\bigl(1+\mu(\mathbb R)\bigr).
\] Since \(\eta>0\) is arbitrary, the left-hand side is \(0\). Therefore \[
\int f\,d\mu_n\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu
\qquad\forall f\in C_c(\mathbb R),
\] which proves \(\mu_n\xrightarrow{v}\mu\).



Example 48.4 (Symmetric Split Mass) Consider the sequence of measures \(\mu_n = \frac{1}{2}(\delta_n + \delta_{-n})\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). For any test function \(f \in C_c(\mathbb{R})\) supported on \([-R, R]\): \[\int_{\mathbb{R}} f \, d\mu_n = \frac{1}{2}(f(n) + f(-n)) = 0 \quad \forall n > R\]
Thus \(\mu_n \xrightarrow{v} \mathbf{0}\), where \(\mathbf{0}\) is the zero measure. Evaluating the CDFs of \(\mu_n\): \[F_n(t) = \begin{cases} 0, & t < -n \\ 1/2, & -n \le t < n \\ 1, & t \ge n \end{cases}\]
For every fixed \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), eventually \(-n < t < n\), so \(F_n(t) \to 1/2\) pointwise. However, the vague limit is \(\mu = \mathbf{0}\), whose CDF is \(F(t) = \mu((-\infty,t]) = 0\) for all \(t\). The pointwise limit of \(F_n\) (which is \(1/2\)) is therefore not the CDF of the vague limit — this discrepancy is precisely the mass-loss phenomenon.
To verify the CDF-difference criterion in Theorem 48.3 consistently with the vague convergence already established above, note that for any \(a < b\) and all \(n > \max(|a|, |b|)\), \(F_n(a) = F_n(b) = 1/2\), so: \[F_n(b) - F_n(a) = 0 \longrightarrow 0 = F(b) - F(a),\] confirming vague convergence to the zero measure. Both halves of the probability mass escaped to opposite infinities.

title: 48  Lecture 23.1: Vague Convergence
text:
48.6 Takeaways

Vague convergence is \(C_c\)-convergence for general measures.
\(\mu_n \xrightarrow{v} \mu\) means \(\int f \, d\mu_n \to \int f \, d\mu\) for all \(f \in C_c(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Unlike weak convergence, the limit \(\mu\) need not be a probability measure — mass can escape to infinity and be lost. Vague convergence is the natural notion for sequences of measures that may not remain tight.
Mass can only be lost, never gained, under vague convergence.
By Theorem 48.1, if \(\mu_n\) are probability measures and \(\mu_n \xrightarrow{v} \mu\), then \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) \le 1\). The proof constructs a test function \(f \in C_c\) with \(\mathbf{1}_{B_R} \le f \le 1\) and uses vague convergence to derive a contradiction if \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) > 1\). By contrast, mass can strictly decrease: the fleeing example \(\mu_n = \frac{1}{2}\delta_0 + \frac{1}{2}\delta_{n e_1}\) gives \(\mu_n \xrightarrow{v} \frac{1}{2}\delta_0\) with only half the mass preserved.
Tightness bridges vague and weak convergence.
By Theorem 48.2, if \(\mu_n \xrightarrow{v} \mu\) (with \(\mu_n\) probability measures), then \(\mu_n \implies \mu\) (i.e., \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) = 1\) and vague convergence upgrades to weak convergence) if and only if \(\{\mu_n\}\) is tight. The key directions are:

Tight \(\Rightarrow\) weak: tightness gives a cutoff function \(f \ge \mathbf{1}_{K_\epsilon}\) that forces \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) \ge 1 - \epsilon\); since \(\epsilon\) is arbitrary, \(\mu(\mathbb{R}^d) = 1\), and the \(C_c\) characterization (Theorem 22.2) then gives \(\mu_n \implies \mu\).
Weak \(\Rightarrow\) tight: weak convergence implies \(\lim_{R\to\infty} \inf_n \mu_n(\bar{B}_R) = 1\) (Lemma 22.2).

Vague convergence on \(\mathbb{R}\) is characterized by differences of CDFs.
By Theorem 48.3, \(\mu_n \xrightarrow{v} \mu\) iff \(F_n(b) - F_n(a) \to F(b) - F(a)\) for all continuity points \(a < b\) of \(F\), where \(F\) is the CDF of \(\mu\). Note that CDF differences (not pointwise CDF values) are the correct quantity: the pointwise limit of \(F_n\) need not equal the CDF of the vague limit.
The pointwise limit of CDFs need not be the CDF of the vague limit.
The example \(\mu_n = \frac{1}{2}(\delta_n + \delta_{-n}) \xrightarrow{v} \mathbf{0}\) illustrates this: \(F_n(t) \to 1/2\) pointwise for every finite \(t\), yet the CDF of \(\mathbf{0}\) is \(F \equiv 0\). The CDF differences \(F_n(b) - F_n(a) = 0 \to 0 = F(b) - F(a)\) correctly capture vague convergence, even though the pointwise limits of \(F_n\) are not meaningful for the limit measure.

title: 80  Lecture 37.1: Markov Processes
text:
80.1 Foundations of Markov Processes
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space and let \(T \subseteq [0, \infty)\) or \(T \subseteq \mathbb{Z}\) be the parameter set (time domain).

title: 80  Lecture 37.1: Markov Processes
text:
A filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \in T}\) is a family of sub-\(\sigma\)-algebras of \(\mathcal{F}\) with \(\mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t\) whenever \(s \le t\). Let \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be a measurable state space, and write \(\mathcal{B}_b(S) = \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) for the bounded \(\mathcal{B}\)-measurable functions \(S \to \mathbb{R}\).
A probability kernel on \((S, \mathcal{B})\) is a map \(q : S \times \mathcal{B} \to [0, 1]\) such that \(q(x, \cdot)\) is a probability measure on \((S, \mathcal{B})\) for every \(x \in S\), and \(x \mapsto q(x, B)\) is \(\mathcal{B}\)-measurable for every \(B \in \mathcal{B}\).
Its associated operator acts on \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\) by \[
(Qf)(x) = \int_S f(y) \, q(x, dy),
\] and \(Qf \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\) with \(\|Qf\|_\infty \le \|f\|_\infty\).
The composition of two kernels is the probability kernel \((q q')(x, B) = \int_S q(x, dy) \, q'(y, B)\), whose operator is \(Q Q'\).


Definition 80.1 (Adapted Process) A stochastic process \(X = \{X_t\}_{t \in T}\) defined on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) taking values in \((S, \mathcal{B})\) is said to be adapted to the filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \in T}\) if \(X_t : \Omega \to S\) is \((\mathcal{F}_t, \mathcal{B})\)-measurable for each \(t \in T\).


Definition 80.2 (Markov Property) An adapted stochastic process \(X = \{X_t\}_{t \in T}\) on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \in T}, \mathbb{P})\) satisfies the Markov property (with respect to \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\)) if, for every \(s, t \in T\) with \(s < t\) and every \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\), we have: \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] \quad \mathbb{P}\text{-almost surely.}
\tag{80.1}\]


Suppose that \((S, \mathcal{B})\) is a standard Borel space (e.g., a Polish space equipped with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra). Then, for all \(s < t\) in \(T\), there exists a regular conditional distribution of \(X_t\) given \(X_s\), i.e. a probability kernel \(q_{s,t}\) on \((S, \mathcal{B})\) such that \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] = \int_S f(y) \, q_{s,t}(X_s, dy) = (Q_{s,t} f)(X_s) \quad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}
\tag{80.2}\] for all \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\), where \(Q_{s,t}\) is the operator of \(q_{s,t}\).
So \(Q_{s,t}\) is the operator that takes a function of the future state \(X_t\) and produces its conditional expectation as a function of the current state \(X_s\): \[
\boxed{ \mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid X_s] = (Q_{s,t}f)(X_s). }
\]
Existence holds for any random element \(X_t\) with values in a standard Borel space (the Markov property is not needed), and the kernel is unique only up to \(\mu_{X_s}\)-null sets, where \(\mu_{X_s} = \text{Law}(X_s)\). Throughout, “the” kernel \(q_{s,t}\) means a fixed choice of such a version.

title: 80  Lecture 37.1: Markov Processes
section: 80.2 Derivation of Transition Operators and the Chapman–Kolmogorov Property
text:
80.2 Derivation of Transition Operators and the Chapman–Kolmogorov Property
We now investigate the properties of the transition operators \(Q_{s,t}\).

Proposition 80.1 (Chapman–Kolmogorov Equations Hold Almost Everywhere) Let \(X\) be adapted and satisfy the Markov property, let \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be standard Borel, and let \(q_{s,t}\) (\(s < t\)) be regular conditional distributions as in Equation 80.2. Then for all \(r < s < t\) in \(T\) and every \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\), \[
Q_{r,t} f = Q_{r,s} (Q_{s,t} f) \quad \mu_{X_r}\text{-almost everywhere.}
\tag{80.3}\] Moreover, there is a \(\mu_{X_r}\)-null set \(N\) (depending on \(r,s,t\) but not on \(B\)) such that \[
q_{r,t}(x, B) = \int_S q_{r,s}(x, dy) \, q_{s,t}(y, B),
\tag{80.4}\] for all \(x \in S \setminus N\) and all \(B \in \mathcal{B}\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 80.1). Since \(X\) is adapted and the filtration is increasing, \(\sigma(X_r) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_r \subseteq \mathcal{F}_s\). The function \(Q_{s,t} f\) is bounded and measurable, so by the tower property, the Markov property, and Equation 80.2 applied to \(f\) at times \((s,t)\) and to \(Q_{s,t}f\) at times \((r,s)\): \[
\begin{aligned}
(Q_{r,t} f)(X_r) &= \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_r] \\
&= \mathbb{E} \Big[ \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] \;\Big|\; X_r \Big] \\
&= \mathbb{E} \Big[ \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] \;\Big|\; X_r \Big] \\
&= \mathbb{E} \Big[ (Q_{s,t} f)(X_s) \;\Big|\; X_r \Big] \\
&= \big(Q_{r,s}(Q_{s,t} f)\big)(X_r) \quad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}
\end{aligned}
\tag{80.5}\] Put \(h = Q_{r,t} f - Q_{r,s}(Q_{s,t} f)\), a bounded measurable function on \(S\). Then \(\mu_{X_r}(h \neq 0) = \mathbb{P}(h(X_r) \neq 0) = 0\), which is Equation 80.3.
(The left-hand side does not depend on the version chosen for \(Q_{s,t}f\): since \(\mu_{X_s} = \mu_{X_r} q_{r,s}\), two versions that agree \(\mu_{X_s}\)-a.e. have images under \(Q_{r,s}\) that agree \(\mu_{X_r}\)-a.e.)
For the kernel form, the difficulty is that Equation 80.3 only gives, for each fixed \(B\), a null set \(N_B\) outside of which equality holds for that \(B\); since \(\mathcal{B}\) is uncountable, naively taking \(N = \bigcup_{B \in \mathcal{B}} N_B\) could fail to be null. The standard Borel hypothesis repairs this, by letting us reduce to countably many \(B\)’s before taking the union, and then use Dynkin’s theorem to recover all of \(\mathcal B\).

A countable generating \(\pi\)-system. Since \((S,\mathcal{B})\) is standard Borel, it is Borel-isomorphic to a Polish space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, which has a countable base \(\{U_n\}_{n \ge 1}\) of open sets. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be the collection of all finite intersections \(U_{n_1} \cap \cdots \cap U_{n_k}\) together with \(S\) itself. Then \(\mathcal{C}\) is countable, closed under finite intersections (a \(\pi\)-system), and \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}) = \mathcal{B}\).
One null set per \(B \in \mathcal{C}\), then a countable union. For each \(B \in \mathcal{C}\), apply Equation 80.3 with \(f = \mathbf{1}_B\): by Remark 80.1 this produces a \(\mu_{X_r}\)-null set \(N_B\) such that \(q_{r,t}(x,B) = (q_{r,s}q_{s,t})(x,B)\) for all \(x \notin N_B\). Set \[
N := \bigcup_{B \in \mathcal{C}} N_B.
\] Because \(\mathcal{C}\) is countable, \(N\) is a countable union of \(\mu_{X_r}\)-null sets, so \(\mu_{X_r}(N) \le \sum_{B \in \mathcal{C}} \mu_{X_r}(N_B) = 0\). Crucially, \(N\) was built by exhausting all of \(\mathcal{C}\) in advance, so it no longer depends on \(B\).
Agreement on \(\mathcal{C}\), for a fixed \(x\). Fix any \(x \in S \setminus N\). Since \(N = \bigcup_{B \in \mathcal{C}} N_B\), this single \(x\) avoids every \(N_B\) simultaneously, so \[
q_{r,t}(x,B) = (q_{r,s}q_{s,t})(x,B) \qquad \text{for all } B \in \mathcal{C}.
\] (This is the key swap of quantifiers: having fixed \(x\) first, we now let \(B\) range over all of \(\mathcal{C}\), rather than fixing \(B\) first and asking for a.e. \(x\).)
Extension from \(\mathcal{C}\) to \(\mathcal{B}\) via Dynkin. For this fixed \(x\), the set functions \(\nu_1(B) := q_{r,t}(x,B)\) and \(\nu_2(B) := (q_{r,s}q_{s,t})(x,B) = \int_S q_{s,t}(y,B)\,q_{r,s}(x,dy)\) are both probability measures on \((S,\mathcal{B})\): \(\nu_1\) because \(q_{r,t}(x,\cdot)\) is a probability measure, and \(\nu_2\) because \(q_{s,t}(y,\cdot)\) is countably additive in \(B\) for each \(y\) with total mass \(1\), so integrating term by term against \(q_{r,s}(x,dy)\) (monotone convergence) shows \(\nu_2\) is countably additive with \(\nu_2(S) = 1\). Since \(\nu_1 = \nu_2\) on the \(\pi\)-system \(\mathcal{C}\) and both are finite measures, Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem gives \(\nu_1 = \nu_2\) on \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}) = \mathcal{B}\), i.e. \[
q_{r,t}(x,B) = (q_{r,s}q_{s,t})(x,B) \qquad \text{for all } B \in \mathcal{B}.
\]

As \(x \in S \setminus N\) was arbitrary, this is Equation 80.4, with \(N\) depending only on \(r,s,t\) and not on \(B\).


Remark 80.1. For \(f=\mathbf 1_B\), \[
Q_{r,t}\mathbf 1_B(x) = q_{r,t}(x,B),
\] while \[
\begin{aligned}
Q_{r,s}(Q_{s,t}\mathbf 1_B)(x) &= \int_S Q_{s,t}\mathbf 1_B(y)\,q_{r,s}(x,dy)\\
&= \int_S q_{s,t}(y,B)\,q_{r,s}(x,dy)\\
&=(q_{r,s}q_{s,t})(x,B).
\end{aligned}
\] Thus, \(Q_{r,t}\mathbf 1_B = Q_{r,s} (Q_{s,t} \mathbf 1_B)\) gives \(q_{r,t}(x,B) = (q_{r,s}q_{s,t})(x,B)\) for \(\mu_{X_r}\)-a.e. \(x\), for each fixed \(B\).
The standard Borel assumption allows this conclusion to be strengthened: there exists a single \(\mu_{X_r}\)-null set \(N\) such that the equality holds for every \(x\notin N\) and every \(B\in\mathcal B\). Indeed, choose a countable generating \(\pi\)-system for \(\mathcal B\), take the union of the corresponding null sets, and use Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem to extend the equality from the generating \(\pi\)-system to all of \(\mathcal B\).

Integrating Equation 80.3 against \(\mu_{X_r}\) gives only the weaker identity \(\int Q_{r,t} f \, d\mu_{X_r} = \int Q_{r,s} Q_{s,t} f \, d\mu_{X_r}\) (equality of the laws of \(X_t\) computed via both kernels), which does not characterize Equation 80.4: with \(S = \{0,1\}\), \(\mu\) uniform, \(q_{r,t} = I\) and \(q_{r,s} q_{s,t}\) equal to the swap matrix, both sides agree for all \(f\) although the kernels differ everywhere. The correct joint-law version tests against functions of both coordinates: for all bounded measurable \(g, f\), \[
\int_S g(x) \, (Q_{r,t} f)(x) \, \mu_{X_r}(dx) = \int_S g(x) \, \big(Q_{r,s} Q_{s,t} f\big)(x) \, \mu_{X_r}(dx),
\tag{80.6}\] i.e. \(\mu_{X_r} \otimes q_{r,t} = \mu_{X_r} \otimes (q_{r,s} q_{s,t})\) as measures on \(S \times S\).

Remark 80.2 (The Chapman–Kolmogorov Equation). The key idea is that to calculate the probability of being in \(B\) at time \(t\), given the state \(x\) at time \(r\), you can condition on the intermediate state at time \(s\) and average over all possible intermediate states. The Chapman–Kolmogorov equation expresses this idea mathematically: \[
q_{r,t}(x,B)=\int_S q_{s,t}(y,B)\,q_{r,s}(x,dy).
\]

Left-hand side: \(q_{r,t}(x,B)\) is the probability of being in \(B\) at time \(t\), starting from state \(x\) at time \(r\).
First kernel on the right: \(q_{r,s}(x,dy)\) is the distribution of the intermediate state \(X_s\), given \(X_r=x\).
Second kernel on the right: \(q_{s,t}(y,B)\) is the probability of reaching \(B\) at time \(t\), starting from state \(y\) at time \(s\).

The integral averages the last quantity over the distribution of the intermediate state \(y\).

Intuitively, Proposition 80.1 says something very simple: If \(X\) is Markov, then predicting the future from the present can be done in stages: first predict the intermediate state, and then predict the later state from that intermediate state. Suppose \(r<s<t\). Think of the process as \(X_r \longrightarrow X_s \longrightarrow X_t\).
The kernel \(q_{r,t}(x,\cdot)\) describes the distribution of \(X_t\) when the process is currently at \(x\) at time \(r\). The Chapman–Kolmogorov result says that this distribution can be obtained by:
Move from \(x\) at time \(r\) to the possible states \(y\) at time \(s\) according to \(q_{r,s}(x,dy)\). From each such \(y\), move to the possible states at time \(t\) according to \(q_{s,t}(y,dz)\). Average over all possible intermediate states \(y\). In symbols, \[
q_{r,t}(x,C) = \int_S q_{s,t}(y,C)\,q_{r,s}(x,dy),
\] for \(\mu_{X_r}\)-almost every \(x\).
Why is this a Markov property? The crucial idea is that once we know \(X_s\), the earlier state \(X_r\) contains no additional information about \(X_t\). Schematically, \(X_r \quad\longrightarrow\quad X_s \quad\longrightarrow\quad X_t\). Thus, to predict \(X_t\) from \(X_r\), we do not need to carry the entire history from \(r\) to \(s\). We can simply pass through the intermediate state \(X_s\). For a function \(f\), the same idea appears even more clearly: \[
\boxed{ Q_{r,t}f = Q_{r,s}(Q_{s,t}f) \qquad \mu_{X_r}\text{-a.e.} }
\] Here \(Q_{s,t}f(y)\) is the expected value of \(f(X_t)\) if the process is at \(y\) at time \(s\). Then \(Q_{r,s}\) averages those conditional expectations over the possible values of \(X_s\) given \(X_r=x\). So it is essentially the tower property combined with the Markov property: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid X_r] &= \mathbb E\left[ \mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid X_s] \mid X_r \right]\\ &= \mathbb E\left[ (Q_{s,t}f)(X_s) \mid X_r \right]\\ &= (Q_{r,s}Q_{s,t}f)(X_r).
\end{aligned}
\] A useful interpretation of the operators is the following. You can think of \(Q_{r,t}\) as a prediction operator: \[
f \quad\xrightarrow{\quad Q_{r,t}\quad}\quad \text{expected value of }f(X_t)\text{ given }X_r.
\] Then Chapman–Kolmogorov says that prediction over a long interval is equivalent to successive prediction over shorter intervals: \[
\boxed{ \text{prediction from }r\text{ to }t = \text{prediction from }r\text{ to }s \;\circ\; \text{prediction from }s\text{ to }t. }
\] That is the fundamental intuition behind the semigroup/transition-operator viewpoint. One subtlety the proposition captures especially well is that, because regular conditional distributions are only defined up to null sets, this equality is initially an almost-everywhere statement, rather than necessarily a pointwise statement for every \(x\in S\).

title: 80  Lecture 37.1: Markov Processes
section: 80.3 Markov Transition Kernels and Markov Processes
text:
80.3 Markov Transition Kernels and Markov Processes

Definition 80.3 (Markov Transition Kernels and Operators) A collection of probability kernels \(\{q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t,\; s,t \in T}\) on \((S, \mathcal{B})\) (with corresponding operators \(\{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}\) acting on \(\mathcal{B}_b(S)\)) is called a family of Markov transition kernels (operators) if:

For all \(s \in T\) and all \(x \in S\), \(q_{s,s}(x, \cdot) = \delta_x(\cdot)\) (or \(Q_{s,s} = \text{Id}\)).
For all \(r \le s \le t\) in \(T\) and all \(x \in S\), the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations hold pointwise: \[
Q_{r,t} = Q_{r,s} Q_{s,t},
\tag{80.7}\] which is explicitly written in kernel form as: \[
q_{r,t}(x, B) = \int_S q_{r,s}(x, dy) \, q_{s,t}(y, B) \quad \forall B \in \mathcal{B}, \, \forall x \in S.
\tag{80.8}\]


(The operator and kernel forms are equivalent by the standard monotone class argument: kernels are determined by their action on indicators, and operators by their action on \(\mathcal{B}_b(S)\).)

Definition 80.4 (Markov Process) Given a filtered probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \in T}, \mathbb{P})\) and a state space \((S, \mathcal{B})\), an adapted stochastic process \(X = \{X_t\}_{t \in T}\) is a Markov process (with respect to \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\)) if it satisfies the Markov property (Equation 80.1) and there exists a family of Markov transition operators \(\{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}\) in the sense of Definition 80.3 such that: \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] = (Q_{s,t} f)(X_s) \quad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.} \quad \forall s \le t \text{ in } T, \, \forall f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S).
\tag{80.9}\]

(For \(s = t\), Equation 80.9 is trivial since \(f(X_s)\) is \(\sigma(X_s)\)-measurable.)

Example 80.1 (Why Both Clauses of Definition 80.4 Are Needed) Let \(Z_0, Z_1\) be i.i.d. uniform on \(\{0,1\}\), set \(Z_2 = Z_0 \oplus Z_1\) (addition modulo \(2\)), and put \(X_0 = Z_0\), \(X_1 = Z_1\), \(X_2 = Z_2\) on \(T = \{0,1,2\}\) with \(\mathcal{F}_t = \sigma(X_0, \dots, X_t)\). Then \((Z_0, Z_1, Z_2)\) are pairwise independent, so in particular \(X_1\) is independent of \(X_0\), and, given \(X_1 = y\), \(X_2 = Z_0 \oplus y\) with \(Z_0\) independent of \(X_1\).
Take \(q_{0,1}(x, \cdot)\) to be uniform on \(\{0,1\}\) (not depending on \(x\)) and \(q_{1,2}(y, \{z\}) = \tfrac12\) for \(z \in \{0,1\}\) (not depending on \(y\)). Both reproduce Equation 80.9: \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_1) \mid X_0] = \tfrac12(f(0)+f(1)) = (Q_{0,1}f)(X_0)\) since \(X_1 \perp X_0\), and \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_2) \mid X_1] = \tfrac12(f(0)+f(1)) = (Q_{1,2}f)(X_1)\) since \(X_2 = X_1 \oplus Z_0\) with \(Z_0 \perp X_1\) uniform. Composing, \((q_{0,1}q_{1,2})(x, \cdot)\) is again uniform on \(\{0,1\}\) for every \(x\), which coincides with \(q_{0,2}(x,\cdot) := \mathrm{Law}(X_2 \mid X_0 = x)\) (also uniform on \(\{0,1\}\), since \(X_2 = X_0 \oplus Z_1\) with \(Z_1 \perp X_0\) uniform). So Chapman–Kolmogorov holds pointwise, and this family satisfies Equation 80.9 at every pair \((s,t)\).
Yet \(X\) is not Markov: \(X_2 = X_0 \oplus X_1\) is a deterministic, non-constant function of \(\mathcal{F}_1 = \sigma(X_0, X_1)\), so \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_2) \mid \mathcal{F}_1] = f(X_0 \oplus X_1)\) depends on \(X_0\) for non-constant \(f\), whereas \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_2) \mid X_1] = \tfrac12(f(0)+f(1))\) does not; these disagree, so Equation 80.1 fails at \((s,t) = (1,2)\). Hence a Chapman–Kolmogorov-consistent transition family satisfying Equation 80.9 is not enough to make \(X\) a Markov process — Definition 80.4 imposes the Markov property as a genuinely separate requirement.

title: 80  Lecture 37.1: Markov Processes
text:
80.4 Independent Increment Processes
In this section \(S = \mathbb{R}^d\) with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra (more generally, a measurable group), so that addition and subtraction are measurable.

Definition 80.5 (Independent Increment Process) Let \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\) be a filtration. An adapted process \(X = \{X_t\}_{t \in T}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) has independent increments (with respect to \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\)) if, for all \(s < t\) in \(T\), the increment \(X_t - X_s\) is independent of \(\mathcal{F}_s\). When no filtration is mentioned, \(\mathcal{F}_t = \mathcal{F}_t^X = \sigma(X_u : u \le t)\).


Remark 80.3 (On the Definition). In particular, for \(t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_n\) the increments \(X_{t_1} - X_{t_0}, \dots, X_{t_n} - X_{t_{n-1}}\) are independent. This weaker property alone is not sufficient for the Markov property, because it says nothing about the initial value: with \(T = \{0,1\}\), \(X_0 = \pm 1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each, and \(X_1 = 2X_0\), there is a single increment \(X_1 - X_0 = X_0\), which is trivially “independent”, yet it is not independent of \(\mathcal{F}_0^X = \sigma(X_0)\).
If \(T\) has a least element \(t_*\), the definition above is equivalent to: for all \(t_* < t_1 < \dots < t_n\) the random variables \(X_{t_*}, X_{t_1} - X_{t_*}, X_{t_2} - X_{t_1}, \dots, X_{t_n} - X_{t_{n-1}}\) are independent. Thus random walks require \(X_0\) independent of the steps, and Poisson processes (with \(X_0 = 0\)) are examples.


Proposition 80.2 (Independent Increment Processes are Markovian) Let \(X = \{X_t\}_{t \in T}\) be an \(\mathbb{R}^d\)-valued process with independent increments with respect to \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\). Then \(X\) is a Markov process with respect to \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\), and the transition kernel is given by: \[
q_{s,t}(x, B) = \mathbb{P}\left( x + X_t - X_s \in B \right), \, s \le t, \; x \in \mathbb{R}^d, \, B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d),
\] and this family satisfies the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations at every \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 80.2). 

Step 0 (a \(\sigma\)-algebra form of the freezing lemma). We will repeatedly use the following generalization of Proposition 71.2: if \(Z\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, \(W\) is independent of \(\mathcal{G}\) (not merely of \(Z\)), and \(\phi \in \mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d)\), then \[
\mathbb{E}[\phi(Z,W) \mid \mathcal{G}] = \psi(Z) \text{ a.s.}, \qquad \psi(z) := \mathbb{E}[\phi(z,W)],
\] and consequently, taking total expectation, \(\mathbb{E}[\phi(Z,W)] = \mathbb{E}[\psi(Z)]\). Indeed, for any bounded \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable \(h\), the pair \((Z,h)\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, hence independent of \(W\) (since \(W \perp \mathcal{G}\)); applying Fubini–Tonelli to the product measure \(\mu_{(Z,h)} \otimes \mu_W\), exactly as in the proof of Proposition 71.2 but with \(h\) in place of the test function there, gives \(\mathbb{E}[\phi(Z,W) h] = \mathbb{E}[\psi(Z) h]\) for every such \(h\), which is the defining property of \(\mathbb{E}[\phi(Z,W) \mid \mathcal{G}] = \psi(Z)\).
Step 1 (the kernel is well defined and measurable). Fix \(s \le t\), let \(\Delta = X_t - X_s\) with law \(\mu_\Delta\), and fix \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Then \(q_{s,t}(x,B) = \mathbb{P}(x + \Delta \in B) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \mathbf{1}_B(x+z) \, \mu_\Delta(dz)\). For fixed \(x\), \(B \mapsto q_{s,t}(x,B)\) is the law of \(x + \Delta\), hence a probability measure. For fixed \(B\), the map \((x,z) \mapsto \mathbf{1}_B(x+z)\) is the indicator of the preimage of \(B\) under the continuous (hence Borel) addition map, so it is jointly measurable and nonnegative; by Tonelli’s theorem, \(x \mapsto \int \mathbf{1}_B(x+z)\,\mu_\Delta(dz) = q_{s,t}(x,B)\) is Borel measurable. So \(q_{s,t}\) is a probability kernel.
Step 2 (Markov property and Equation 80.9). Fix \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{R}^d)\) and \(s \le t\), and let \(\Delta = X_t - X_s\), so \(X_t = X_s + \Delta\) with \(X_s\) being \(\mathcal{F}_s\)-measurable (as \(X\) is adapted). If \(s = t\), then \(\Delta = 0\) a.s., so \(H(x) := \mathbb{E}[f(x+\Delta)] = f(x)\), and since \(f(X_t) = f(X_s)\) is already \(\sigma(X_s)\)-measurable, \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = f(X_s) = H(X_s)\) trivially — no independence is needed in this degenerate case. If \(s < t\), then by definition of independent increments \(\Delta\) is independent of \(\mathcal{F}_s\); the map \(\phi(x,z) = f(x+z)\) is bounded and jointly measurable (addition is continuous, \(f\) is Borel), so Step 0 with \(\mathcal{G} = \mathcal{F}_s\), \(Z = X_s\), \(W = \Delta\) gives \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = H(X_s), \qquad H(x) = \mathbb{E}[f(x+\Delta)] = \int f(y) \, q_{s,t}(x,dy).
\] In either case \(H(X_s)\) is \(\sigma(X_s)\)-measurable, and \(\sigma(X_s) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_s\), so the tower property gives \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] \mid X_s] = \mathbb{E}[H(X_s) \mid X_s] = H(X_s)\). Comparing the two displays, \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t)\mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s]\), which is Equation 80.1, and \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] = H(X_s) = (Q_{s,t}f)(X_s)\), which is Equation 80.9.
Step 3 (Definition 80.3, part 1). Taking \(s=t\) in Step 1, \(\Delta = X_s - X_s = 0\) a.s., so \(q_{s,s}(x,B) = \mathbb{P}(x \in B) = \mathbf{1}_B(x)\), i.e. \(q_{s,s}(x,\cdot) = \delta_x\).
Step 4 (Definition 80.3, part 2: pointwise Chapman–Kolmogorov). Fix \(r \le s \le t\), \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\), \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Let \(Y := x + (X_s - X_r)\) and \(\Delta_2 := X_t - X_s\); by Step 1 applied to \((r,s)\), \(Y\) has law \(q_{r,s}(x,\cdot)\). Since \(X\) is adapted and \(\mathcal{F}_r \subseteq \mathcal{F}_s\), both \(X_r\) and \(X_s\) (hence \(X_s - X_r\), and hence \(Y\)) are \(\mathcal{F}_s\)-measurable; and \(\Delta_2\) is independent of \(\mathcal{F}_s\) (trivially if \(s=t\), as in Step 2; by definition of independent increments if \(s < t\)). By Step 1 applied to \((s,t)\), \(y \mapsto q_{s,t}(y,B)\) is bounded and measurable, so by the change-of-variables formula (law of the unconscious statistician) applied to the law \(q_{r,s}(x,\cdot)\) of \(Y\), \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} q_{r,s}(x,dy)\, q_{s,t}(y,B) = \mathbb{E}[q_{s,t}(Y,B)].
\] Now apply Step 0, in its total-expectation form, with \(\mathcal{G} = \mathcal{F}_s\), \(Z = Y\), \(W = \Delta_2\), \(\phi(y,w) = \mathbf{1}_B(y+w)\): since \(q_{s,t}(Y,B) = \psi(Y)\) with \(\psi(y) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_B(y+\Delta_2)]\), \[
\mathbb{E}[q_{s,t}(Y,B)] = \mathbb{E}[\psi(Y)] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_B(Y + \Delta_2)] = \mathbb{P}(Y + \Delta_2 \in B).
\] Since \(Y + \Delta_2 = x + (X_s - X_r) + (X_t - X_s) = x + (X_t - X_r)\), this equals \(\mathbb{P}(x + (X_t-X_r) \in B) = q_{r,t}(x,B)\). Hence \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} q_{r,s}(x,dy)\, q_{s,t}(y,B) = q_{r,t}(x,B)
\] for every \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\) and every \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\) — i.e. Equation 80.8 holds pointwise, not merely \(\mu_{X_r}\)-almost everywhere as in the general setting of Proposition 80.1.

title: 80  Lecture 37.1: Markov Processes
section: 80.5 Discrete-Time Parameterization and Discrete State Spaces
text:
80.5 Discrete-Time Parameterization and Discrete State Spaces
Let us now focus on discrete time \(T = \mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\). The family of transition operators is \(\{Q_{m,n} : 0 \le m \le n < \infty\}\).
By the (pointwise) Chapman–Kolmogorov equations and induction on \(n - m\): \[
Q_{m,n} = Q_{m,m+1} Q_{m+1,m+2} \cdots Q_{n-1,n}.
\tag{80.10}\]
Hence, in discrete time, a transition family is determined by the one-step operators \(\{Q_{m,m+1} : m \in \mathbb{N}\}\). Conversely, any sequence of probability kernels \(\{q_{m,m+1}\}_{m \in \mathbb{N}}\), together with \(q_{m,m} = \delta_x\) and \(q_{m,n}\) defined by composition, satisfies Definition 80.3. In particular, in discrete time the pointwise requirement of Definition 80.3 is automatic once the one-step kernels are chosen (for \(S\) standard Borel, with one-step kernels taken as regular conditional distributions).

title: 80  Lecture 37.1: Markov Processes
text:
80.6 Discrete State Space
If \(S\) is countable (equipped with the discrete \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B} = 2^S\)), write \(q_{m,n}(x, y) := q_{m,n}(x, \{y\})\), so that \[
q_{m,m+1}(x, B) = \sum_{y \in B} q_{m,m+1}(x, y),
\tag{80.11}\] where \(q_{m,m+1}(x, y)\) is a regular conditional distribution of \(X_{m+1}\) given \(X_m\), characterized by \[
\begin{aligned}
q_{m,m+1}(x, y) &= \mathbb{P}(X_{m+1} = y \mid X_m = x) \\
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}(X_{m+1} = y, X_m = x)}{\mathbb{P}(X_m = x)},
\end{aligned}
\tag{80.12}\] whenever \(\mathbb{P}(X_m = x) > 0\). For \(x\) with \(\mathbb{P}(X_m = x) = 0\) the row \(q_{m,m+1}(x, \cdot)\) is not determined by the process; it may be any probability vector, and the pointwise convention of Definition 80.3 simply fixes one such choice.
In this framework, for \(n \ge m + 2\) the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation represents a sum over intermediate states (“sum over paths”): \[
\begin{aligned}
&q_{m,n}(x, y) = \sum_{x_{m+1} \in S} \sum_{x_{m+2} \in S} \dots \\
&\sum_{x_{n-1} \in S} q_{m,m+1}(x, x_{m+1}) q_{m+1,m+2}(x_{m+1}, x_{m+2}) \cdots q_{n-1,n}(x_{n-1}, y).
\end{aligned}
\tag{80.13}\] (For \(n = m+1\) there are no intermediate sums, and for \(n = m\) one has \(q_{m,m}(x,y) = \mathbf{1}_{\{x = y\}}\).) The order of the countable sums is immaterial since all terms are nonnegative.

title: 80  Lecture 37.1: Markov Processes
text:
80.7 Finite-Dimensional Distributions
Let \((X_t)_{t \in T}\) be a Markov process (in the sense of Definition 80.4) with transition kernels \(\{q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}\). Fix arbitrary ordered time points \(t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_n\) in \(T\), and let \(\nu_0 = \text{Law}(X_{t_0})\) be the initial law. We write \(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_0}[h] := \int_S h \, d\nu_0\) for \(h \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\).
The measure on the right of Equation 80.14 below is the probability measure on \((S^{n+1}, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes(n+1)})\) defined by iterated integration of the kernels: \[
A \mapsto \int \nu_0(dx_0) \int q_{t_0,t_1}(x_0, dx_1) \cdots \int q_{t_{n-1},t_n}(x_{n-1}, dx_n) \, \mathbf{1}_A(x_0, \dots, x_n).
\]

Proposition 80.3 (Finite-Dimensional Distributions) The joint distribution \(\text{Law}(X_{t_0}, X_{t_1}, \dots, X_{t_n})\) on \(S^{n+1}\) is given by: \[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Law}(X_{t_0}, X_{t_1}, \dots, X_{t_n})(dx_0, dx_1, \dots, dx_n) \\
&= \nu_0(dx_0) q_{t_0, t_1}(x_0, dx_1) q_{t_1, t_2}(x_1, dx_2) \cdots q_{t_{n-1}, t_n}(x_{n-1}, dx_n).
\end{aligned}
\tag{80.14}\] Equivalently, for all bounded measurable functions \(f_0, f_1, \dots, f_n \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\): \[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{E}\left[ \prod_{i=0}^n f_i(X_{t_i}) \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{\nu_0} \left[ f_0 Q_{t_0, t_1} \left( f_1 Q_{t_1, t_2} \left( \cdots (f_{n-1} Q_{t_{n-1}, t_n} f_n) \cdots \right) \right) \right],
\end{aligned}
\tag{80.15}\] where for \(n = 0\) the right-hand side is read as \(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_0}[f_0]\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 80.3). We prove Equation 80.15 by induction on \(n\), simultaneously for all time points \(t_0 < \dots < t_n\) and all bounded measurable \(f_0, \dots, f_n\).
Base Case (\(n=0\)): \(\mathbb{E}[f_0(X_{t_0})] = \int_S f_0 \, d\nu_0 = \mathbb{E}_{\nu_0}[f_0]\) by definition of \(\nu_0\).
Inductive Step: Assume Equation 80.15 holds for \(n\) (all tuples of \(n+1\) times and all bounded measurable functions). Consider \(n+2\) time points \(t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_n < t_{n+1}\). Since \(X\) is adapted and the filtration is increasing, \(\prod_{i=0}^n f_i(X_{t_i})\) is bounded and \(\mathcal{F}_{t_n}\)-measurable, so by the tower property and “taking out what is known”: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E} \left[ \prod_{i=0}^{n+1} f_i(X_{t_i}) \right] &= \mathbb{E} \left[ \mathbb{E} \left[ \prod_{i=0}^{n+1} f_i(X_{t_i}) \;\middle|\; \mathcal{F}_{t_n} \right] \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E} \left[ \left( \prod_{i=0}^n f_i(X_{t_i}) \right) \mathbb{E} \left[ f_{n+1}(X_{t_{n+1}}) \;\middle|\; \mathcal{F}_{t_n} \right] \right].
\end{aligned}
\]
By the Markov property at \((t_n, t_{n+1})\) and Equation 80.9: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[f_{n+1}(X_{t_{n+1}}) \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_n}] &= \mathbb{E}[f_{n+1}(X_{t_{n+1}}) \mid X_{t_n}] \\
&= (Q_{t_n, t_{n+1}} f_{n+1})(X_{t_n}) \quad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}
\end{aligned}
\tag{80.16}\]
Define \(g_n \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\) as: \[
g_n(x) := f_n(x) \cdot (Q_{t_n, t_{n+1}} f_{n+1})(x).
\tag{80.17}\]
Substituting Equation 80.16 and Equation 80.17 gives: \[
\mathbb{E} \left[ \prod_{i=0}^{n+1} f_i(X_{t_i}) \right] = \mathbb{E} \left[ \left( \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} f_i(X_{t_i}) \right) g_n(X_{t_n}) \right]
\tag{80.18}\] (for \(n = 0\) the empty product is \(1\)). By the induction hypothesis applied to the \(n+1\) times \(t_0 < \dots < t_n\) and the functions \(f_0, \dots, f_{n-1}, g_n\), the right-hand side equals \[
\mathbb{E}_{\nu_0} \left[ f_0 Q_{t_0, t_1} \left( f_1 Q_{t_1, t_2} \left( \cdots (f_{n-1} Q_{t_{n-1}, t_n} g_n) \cdots \right) \right) \right].
\] Replacing \(g_n\) with \(f_n Q_{t_n, t_{n+1}} f_{n+1}\) yields \[
\mathbb{E}_{\nu_0} \left[ f_0 Q_{t_0, t_1} \left( f_1 Q_{t_1, t_2} \left( \cdots \Big( f_{n-1} Q_{t_{n-1}, t_n} (f_n Q_{t_n, t_{n+1}} f_{n+1}) \Big) \cdots \right) \right) \right],
\] which is Equation 80.15 for \(n+1\).
From Equation 80.15 to Equation 80.14: Unwinding the nested expression by iterated integration of the kernels shows that its right-hand side equals \(\int \prod_i f_i \, d\pi\), where \(\pi\) is the iterated-kernel measure defined before the proposition. Taking \(f_i = \mathbf{1}_{B_i}\), the laws \(\text{Law}(X_{t_0}, \dots, X_{t_n})\) and \(\pi\) agree on measurable rectangles \(B_0 \times \dots \times B_n\). These form a \(\pi\)-system generating \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes(n+1)}\), so the two probability measures coincide by Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem. \(\blacksquare\)

The proof uses only the Markov property and Equation 80.9; it does not depend on which version of the kernels is used, since different versions differ only on null sets of the relevant marginal laws.

title: 81  Lecture 37.2: Kolmogorov Extension Theorem
text:
81.1 Introduction and Conceptual Context
In the foundational theory of Markov processes, a process defined on a standard Borel space \((S, \mathcal{B})\) comes equipped with a family of transition operators \(\{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}\) acting on \(\mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\). These operators satisfy the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations: \[
Q_{r,t} = Q_{r,s} Q_{s,t}, \quad Q_{t,t} = \text{Id} \quad \text{for all } r \le s \le t \text{ in } T.
\tag{81.1}\]
This setup is directly analogous to the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) setting: an i.i.d. sequence \(\{X_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\) comes with a sequence of joint laws \(\mu_n \in \mathcal{P}(S^n)\) satisfying the multiplicativity property \(\mu_n \otimes \mu_m = \mu_{n+m}\) — a special case of the (weaker, and operative) projective-consistency condition defined in Definition 81.2 below, which only requires compatibility of marginals rather than this full tensor-factorization property.
The fundamental reverse problem asks: given a family of consistent finite-dimensional marginal distributions, can we construct an actual stochastic process on a canonical probability space having these exact joint distributions? For i.i.d. random variables, the existence of such a process on \(S^{\mathbb{N}}\) is established via Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem. Here, we extend this framework to construct general continuous- or discrete-time Markov processes on product spaces \(S^T\).

title: 81  Lecture 37.2: Kolmogorov Extension Theorem
text:
81.2 Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem
Let \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be a standard Borel space (a space homeomorphic to a Borel subset of a complete separable metric space) and let \(T\) be an arbitrary index set (e.g., \(T = \mathbb{R}_+\), \(T = \mathbb{N}\), or an uncountably infinite set).

Definition 81.1 (Canonical Product Space and Cylinder Sets) The product space \(S^T := \{\omega : T \to S\}\) consists of all paths/functions from \(T\) to \(S\). For each \(t \in T\), the coordinate projection map \(\pi_t : S^T \to S\) is defined by: \[
\pi_t(\omega) = \omega(t).
\tag{81.2}\]
For a finite subset \(\Lambda = \{t_1, \dots, t_n\} \subseteq T\) (listed in the order induced by \(T\)), the finite-dimensional projection \(\pi_\Lambda : S^T \to S^\Lambda\) is: \[
\pi_\Lambda(\omega) = \big(\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_n)\big),
\tag{81.3}\] where we identify \(S^\Lambda\) (functions \(\Lambda \to S\)) with \(S^n\) via this ordering; the product \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes \Lambda}\) is transported along the same identification. This identification is used silently throughout the rest of this chapter.
The product \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\) is generated by all individual coordinate projections: \[
\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T} := \sigma(\pi_t : t \in T) = \sigma \left( \bigcup_{\Lambda \subseteq T, \, |\Lambda| < \infty} \sigma(\pi_\Lambda) \right).
\tag{81.4}\] (The two expressions on the right agree because \(\sigma(\pi_t) \subseteq \sigma(\pi_\Lambda)\) whenever \(t \in \Lambda\), giving “\(\subseteq\)”; and \(\sigma(\pi_\Lambda) \subseteq \sigma(\pi_t : t \in T)\) for every finite \(\Lambda\), since \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes\Lambda}\) is generated by rectangles and \(\pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B_1\times\cdots\times B_n) = \bigcap_i \pi_{t_i}^{-1}(B_i)\), giving “\(\supseteq\)”.)
A subset \(A \subseteq S^T\) is called a cylinder set if \(A = \pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B)\) for some finite subset \(\Lambda \subseteq T\) and \(B \in \mathcal{B}^{\otimes \Lambda}\); every cylinder set belongs to \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\), by the displayed equality above.


Remark 81.1 (Remark on Cylinder Sets). Let \(\Lambda=\{t_1,\ldots,t_n\}\subseteq T\) be a finite set of time points, and define the coordinate map \(\pi_\Lambda:\Omega\to S^\Lambda\) and \(\pi_\Lambda(\omega)=(\omega(t_1),\ldots,\omega(t_n))\). For \(B\in\mathcal B^{\otimes\Lambda}\), a cylinder set is a set of the form \[
A=\pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B)
=\{\omega\in\Omega:\pi_\Lambda(\omega)\in B\}.
\] In other words, a path belongs to \(A\) if its values at the selected finite set of times satisfy the condition specified by \(B\). The path’s values at all other times are irrelevant to membership in \(A\).
For example, take \(S=\mathbb R\), \(T=[0,\infty)\), and \(\Lambda=\{1,2\}\). Let \(B=\{(x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb R^2:x_1\leq 0,\ x_2>1\}\). The corresponding cylinder set is \(A=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega(1)\leq 0,\ \omega(2)>1\}\). This set contains every path whose value at time \(1\) is nonpositive and whose value at time \(2\) exceeds \(1\), regardless of what the path does at any other time.
Basic Properties of Cylinder Sets

Every cylinder set is measurable: By definition of the product \(\sigma\)-algebra, \(A=\pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F\). Thus, every cylinder set is an event in the canonical measurable space.
Cylinder sets are closed under finite intersections: Suppose \(A_1=\pi_{\Lambda_1}^{-1}(B_1)\) and \(A_2=\pi_{\Lambda_2}^{-1}(B_2)\). Then \(A_1\cap A_2=\pi_{\Lambda_1\cup\Lambda_2}^{-1}(C)\), where \(C\) imposes both conditions \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) on their respective coordinates. Since \(\Lambda_1\cup\Lambda_2\) is finite, the intersection is again a cylinder set. More generally, a finite intersection of cylinder sets is a cylinder set.
The complement of a cylinder set is a cylinder set: If \(A=\pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B)\), then \(A^c=\pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B^c)\), where \(B^c=S^\Lambda\setminus B\). Hence \(A^c\) is a cylinder set.
Cylinder sets are closed under finite unions: For cylinder sets \(A_1\) and \(A_2\), their union can be represented as a cylinder set based on \(\Lambda_1\cup\Lambda_2\), just as for intersections. Therefore, finite unions of cylinder sets are cylinder sets.
Cylinder sets generate the product \(\sigma\)-algebra: The product \(\sigma\)-algebra is precisely \(\mathcal B^{\otimes T} = \sigma(\mathcal C)\), where \(\mathcal C\) denotes the collection of all cylinder sets. This means that every set in the product \(\sigma\)-algebra can be obtained from cylinder sets by taking countable unions, countable intersections, and complements.
Important: Cylinder sets themselves are generally not closed under countable unions or countable intersections. They form an algebra of sets, not necessarily a \(\sigma\)-algebra.
Cylinder sets depend on finitely many coordinates: If two paths \(\omega,\omega'\in\Omega\) agree on \(\Lambda\), then \(\pi_\Lambda(\omega)=\pi_\Lambda(\omega')\).Consequently, \(\omega\in A\iff\omega'\in A\) for every cylinder set \(A=\pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B)\).


The goal is to construct a probability measure on the entire path space \(S^T\), where a path specifies the process’s values at every time point. We begin by specifying distributions for finite collections of coordinates. But these distributions cannot be chosen independently: they must be compatible. Projective consistency is precisely this compatibility requirement. In short, projective consistency means that reducing a joint distribution to fewer coordinates must give the distribution already specified for those coordinates.

Definition 81.2 (Consistency Condition) A family of probability measures \(\{\mu_\Lambda \in \mathcal{P}(S^\Lambda, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes \Lambda}) : \Lambda \subseteq T, \, |\Lambda| < \infty\}\) is called projectively consistent if, for all finite index sets \(\Lambda' \subseteq \Lambda \subseteq T\), we have: \[
(\pi_{\Lambda' \mid S^\Lambda})^* \mu_\Lambda = \mu_{\Lambda'},
\tag{81.5}\] where \(\pi_{\Lambda' \mid S^\Lambda} : S^\Lambda \to S^{\Lambda'}\) is the natural restriction map between finite Cartesian products, and \(f^*\mu\) denotes the pushforward of a measure \(\mu\) along a measurable map \(f\) (i.e. \((f^*\mu)(B) := \mu(f^{-1}(B))\)); we use this superscript-star convention for pushforwards throughout. Explicitly, for all \(B' \in \mathcal{B}^{\otimes \Lambda'}\): \[
\mu_\Lambda \big( B' \times S^{\Lambda \setminus \Lambda'} \big) = \mu_{\Lambda'}(B').
\tag{81.6}\]


Theorem 81.1 (Kolmogorov’s (Extended) Extension Theorem) Let \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be a standard Borel space and let \(T\) be an arbitrary set. Suppose \(\{\mu_\Lambda\}_{\Lambda \subseteq T, \, |\Lambda| < \infty}\) is a projectively consistent family of probability measures. Then there exists a unique probability measure \(\mathbb{P} \in \mathcal{P}(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\) such that: \[
\pi_\Lambda^* \mathbb{P} = \mu_\Lambda \quad \text{for all finite subsets } \Lambda \subseteq T.
\tag{81.7}\]


Remark 81.2 (Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem). The theorem provides the mathematical foundation for constructing a stochastic process from its finite-dimensional distributions.

Input: A probability distribution for every finite collection of time points, with all these distributions satisfying projective consistency.
Output: A probability measure \(\mathbb P\) on the entire path space \(S^T\) that reproduces every specified finite-dimensional distribution.

The existence part says that the finite-dimensional distributions can be realized jointly on a common path space. The uniqueness part says that there is only one such probability measure on the product \(\sigma\)-algebra.

title: 81  Lecture 37.2: Kolmogorov Extension Theorem
text:
81.3 Proof Construction
We structure the proof in two main steps: pre-measure construction on an algebra, followed by verification of countable additivity.

81.3.1 Step 1: Definition on the Cylinder Algebra
Define the collection of cylinder sets: \[
\mathcal{A} := \bigcup_{\Lambda \subseteq T, \, |\Lambda| < \infty} \sigma(\pi_\Lambda) = \left\{ \pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B) : \Lambda \subseteq T \text{ finite}, \, B \in \mathcal{B}^{\otimes \Lambda} \right\}.
\tag{81.8}\]
We will repeatedly use the following elementary fact. For finite \(\Lambda \subseteq \Lambda' \subseteq T\), write \(p_\Lambda^{\Lambda'} : S^{\Lambda'} \to S^\Lambda\) for the natural restriction map; then \(\pi_\Lambda = p_\Lambda^{\Lambda'} \circ \pi_{\Lambda'}\), so for \(C \subseteq S^\Lambda\), \[
\pi_\Lambda^{-1}(C) = \pi_{\Lambda'}^{-1}\big( (p_\Lambda^{\Lambda'})^{-1}(C) \big).
\tag{81.9}\] Moreover, since \(S \ne \emptyset\) (implicit throughout, as each \(\mu_\Lambda\) with \(\Lambda \ne \emptyset\) is a genuine probability measure on \(S^\Lambda\)), every projection \(\pi_\Lambda : S^T \to S^\Lambda\) and every restriction map \(p_\Lambda^{\Lambda'}\) is surjective (any partial assignment extends to \(S^T\), resp. \(S^{\Lambda'}\), by filling in arbitrary values of \(S\) elsewhere). Consequently, for surjective \(f\), \(f^{-1}(C_1) \subseteq f^{-1}(C_2) \iff C_1 \subseteq C_2\) (so in particular \(f^{-1}(C_1)=f^{-1}(C_2) \iff C_1=C_2\), and \(f^{-1}\) commutes with the resulting set operations, including monotone limits). We refer to this as the cylinder-factorization lemma; it is used below to pass between a cylinder set on \(S^T\) and any of its finite-dimensional representations.
Using Equation 81.9 and surjectivity of the restriction maps, \(\mathcal{A}\) is closed under complementation (\((\pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B))^c = \pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B^c)\)) and finite unions (lift two cylinders \(\pi_{\Lambda_1}^{-1}(B_1), \pi_{\Lambda_2}^{-1}(B_2)\) to the common index set \(\Lambda_1 \cup \Lambda_2\) via Equation 81.9, then take the union of the lifted base sets in \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes(\Lambda_1\cup\Lambda_2)}\)); together with \(S^T \in \mathcal A\), this shows \(\mathcal{A}\) forms a Boolean algebra of subsets of \(S^T\). Also \(\sigma(\mathcal{A}) = \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\), by Equation 81.4.
Define a set function \(\mathbb{P} : \mathcal{A} \to [0, 1]\) by setting, for \(A = \pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B)\): \[
\mathbb{P}(A) := \mu_\Lambda(B).
\tag{81.10}\]
To verify that \(\mathbb{P}\) is well-defined, suppose \(A \in \mathcal{A}\) has two representations: \(A = \pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B)\) and \(A = \pi_{\Lambda'}^{-1}(B')\). Let \(\Lambda'' = \Lambda \cup \Lambda'\). By Equation 81.9, \(A = \pi_{\Lambda''}^{-1}(B \times S^{\Lambda''\setminus\Lambda}) = \pi_{\Lambda''}^{-1}(B' \times S^{\Lambda''\setminus\Lambda'})\), and surjectivity of \(\pi_{\Lambda''}\) then forces the literal set equality \(B \times S^{\Lambda''\setminus\Lambda} = B' \times S^{\Lambda''\setminus\Lambda'}\) in \(S^{\Lambda''}\) (cylinder-factorization lemma). Hence, by the projective consistency condition Equation 81.6: \[
\mu_\Lambda(B) = \mu_{\Lambda''}(B \times S^{\Lambda'' \setminus \Lambda}) = \mu_{\Lambda''}(B' \times S^{\Lambda'' \setminus \Lambda'}) = \mu_{\Lambda'}(B'),
\] where the middle equality now holds because both sides are the \(\mu_{\Lambda''}\)-measure of the same set. Thus, \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) does not depend on the choice of cylinder representation.
Furthermore, \(\mathbb{P}(S^T) = \mu_\Lambda(S^\Lambda) = 1\). Finite additivity follows directly: if \(A_1, \dots, A_n \in \mathcal{A}\) are disjoint cylinder sets, we represent them over a joint index set \(\Lambda = \bigcup_{j=1}^n \Lambda_j\) as \(A_j = \pi_\Lambda^{-1}(B_j')\) (via Equation 81.9) with \(B_j' \in \mathcal{B}^{\otimes \Lambda}\) pairwise disjoint — disjointness of the \(B_j'\) follows from disjointness of the \(A_j\) and surjectivity of \(\pi_\Lambda\), again by the cylinder-factorization lemma. By finite additivity of \(\mu_\Lambda\): \[
\mathbb{P}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^n A_j\right) = \mu_\Lambda\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^n B_j'\right) = \sum_{j=1}^n \mu_\Lambda(B_j') = \sum_{j=1}^n \mathbb{P}(A_j).
\tag{81.11}\]


81.3.2 Step 2: Verification of Countable Additivity
To extend \(\mathbb{P}\) from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\) via the Carathéodory Extension Theorem (Theorem 8.1), it suffices to prove that \(\mathbb{P}\) is countably additive on \(\mathcal{A}\), or equivalently (since \(\mathcal{A}\) is an algebra and \(\mathbb{P}\) is finite with \(\mathbb{P}(S^T)=1\)), that if \(A_n \downarrow \emptyset\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(\mathbb{P}(A_n) \to 0\).
Let \(A_n = \pi_{\Lambda_n}^{-1}(B_n) \in \mathcal{A}\) with \(A_n \downarrow \emptyset\). Each \(A_n\) depends on a finite coordinate set \(\Lambda_n \subseteq T\). Define the countable collection of involved time points: \[
L := \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \Lambda_n \subseteq T.
\tag{81.12}\]
Consider the countable product space \((S^L, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes L})\). Since \(L\) is countable, fix a bijection between \(L\) and \(\mathbb{N}\) (or an initial segment of \(\mathbb{N}\), if \(L\) is finite); under this relabeling, \(\{\mu_\Lambda\}_{\Lambda \subseteq L, \,|\Lambda|<\infty}\) is exactly a projectively consistent family of finite-dimensional measures indexed by initial segments of \(\mathbb{N}\), in the sense of Corollary 35.2. That theorem — proved independently in Lecture 16.2 via tightness of Borel probability measures on a Polish space (and extended there, in Remark 35.2, from \(S = \mathbb{R}\) to an arbitrary standard Borel state space) — is a logically prior result, not a special case of the theorem we are currently proving; invoking it here for the countable index set \(L\) therefore involves no circularity. It guarantees the existence of a unique probability measure \(\mathbb{P}_L \in \mathcal{P}(S^L, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes L})\) satisfying \(\pi_{\Lambda_n \mid S^L}^* \mathbb{P}_L = \mu_{\Lambda_n}\) for every \(n\).
Define \(\tilde{B}_n := (\pi_{\Lambda_n \mid S^L})^{-1}(B_n) \subseteq S^L\). Then: \[
\mathbb{P}(A_n) = \mu_{\Lambda_n}(B_n) = \mathbb{P}_L(\tilde{B}_n).
\tag{81.13}\]
Since \(A_n \downarrow \emptyset\) on \(S^T\), and \(A_n = \pi_L^{-1}(\tilde B_n)\) by Equation 81.9 (as \(\Lambda_n \subseteq L\)), surjectivity of \(\pi_L : S^T \to S^L\) (cylinder-factorization lemma) transfers both the monotonicity and the empty intersection through the projection, so \(\tilde{B}_n \downarrow \emptyset\) in \(S^L\). By the countable additivity of the probability measure \(\mathbb{P}_L\) on \((S^L, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes L})\): \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}(A_n) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_L(\tilde{B}_n) = \mathbb{P}_L(\emptyset) = 0.
\tag{81.14}\]
Thus, \(\mathbb{P}\) is countably additive on \(\mathcal{A}\), i.e. \(\mathbb{P}\) is a (finite) premeasure on the algebra \(\mathcal{A}\). By the Carathéodory Extension Theorem (Theorem 8.1), \(\mathbb{P}\) extends to a probability measure on \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T} = \sigma(\mathcal{A})\), and since \(\mathbb{P}(S^T) = 1 < \infty\), this extension is unique by the uniqueness theorem for finite premeasures (Theorem 10.1). \(\blacksquare\)

title: 81  Lecture 37.2: Kolmogorov Extension Theorem
text:
81.4 Canonical Construction of Markov Processes
The following theorem provides a canonical construction of Markov processes using the Kolmogorov Extension Theorem.

Theorem 81.2 (Existence of Canonical Markov Measure) Let \(T\) be a totally ordered index set with a least element, denoted \(0\) (e.g. \(T \subseteq [0,\infty)\) or \(T = \mathbb{N}\), as in Lecture 37.1), and let \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be a standard Borel space. Let \(
u \in \mathcal{P}(S, \mathcal{B})\) be an initial distribution, and let \(\{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}\) be a family of Markov transition operators on \((S, \mathcal{B})\) satisfying the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations.
Then there exists a unique probability measure \(\mathbb{P}^
u \in \mathcal{P}(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\) on the product space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}) = (S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\) such that the coordinate process \(X_t(\omega) := \omega(t)\) is a Markov process relative to its natural filtration \(\mathcal{F}_t^X = \sigma(X_s : s \le t)\), with initial law \(	ext{Law}_{\mathbb{P}^
u}(X_0) = 
u\) and transition operators \(\{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}\). We write \(\mathbb{E}^
u[\cdot]\) for expectation with respect to \(\mathbb{P}^
u\).

title: 81  Lecture 37.2: Kolmogorov Extension Theorem
text:
81.5 Proof
The proof proceeds in two main steps: defining finite-dimensional distributions and checking consistency, followed by verifying the Markov property.

81.5.1 Step 1: Definition of Finite-Dimensional Marginals and Consistency
For any finite ordered set of times \(\Lambda = \{t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_n\} \subseteq T\), write \(\nu_{t_0} := \nu Q_{0,t_0}\) for the pushforward of \(\nu\) along the transition operator from \(0\) to \(t_0\) (so \(\nu_{t_0} = \nu\) when \(t_0 = 0\), since \(Q_{0,0} = \text{Id}\)), and define the finite-dimensional measure \(\mu_\Lambda \in \mathcal{P}(S^{n+1})\) by: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_\Lambda(dx_0, dx_1, \dots, dx_n) &:= \nu_{t_0}(dx_0) \, q_{t_0, t_1}(x_0, dx_1) \, q_{t_1, t_2}(x_1, dx_2)\\
&\quad \cdots q_{t_{n-1}, t_n}(x_{n-1}, dx_n).
\end{aligned}
\tag{81.15}\] (When \(0 \in \Lambda\), i.e. \(t_0 = 0\), this reduces to the familiar \(\nu(dx_0) q_{0,t_1}(x_0,dx_1)\cdots\); the role of \(\nu_{t_0}\) is to supply the correct marginal law of \(X_{t_0}\) at the smallest element of \(\Lambda\) when \(\Lambda\) does not contain \(0\) — using \(\nu\) itself in that case would be incorrect in general, since it would force \(\nu\) to be invariant under the transition kernels, which is not assumed.)
We verify projective consistency by checking that deleting a single point from \(\Lambda\) reproduces the corresponding smaller measure; full consistency for arbitrary \(\Lambda' \subseteq \Lambda\) then follows by induction on \(|\Lambda \setminus \Lambda'|\). There are three cases, according to whether the deleted point is interior, the largest point of \(\Lambda\), or the smallest point of \(\Lambda\).
Interior point. Let \(\Lambda = \{t_0 < t_1 < t_2\}\) and \(\Lambda' = \{t_0 < t_2\}\) (deleting \(t_1\)). Integrating over the intermediate state \(x_1 \in S\): \[
\begin{aligned}
&\mu_\Lambda(B_0 \times S \times B_2) = \int_{B_0} \nu_{t_0}(dx_0) \int_S q_{t_0, t_1}(x_0, dx_1) \int_{B_2} q_{t_1, t_2}(x_1, dx_2) \\
&= \int_{B_0} \nu_{t_0}(dx_0) \int_{B_2} \left( \int_S q_{t_0, t_1}(x_0, dx_1) \, q_{t_1, t_2}(x_1, dx_2) \right) \\
&= \int_{B_0} \nu_{t_0}(dx_0) \int_{B_2} q_{t_0, t_2}(x_0, dx_2) \quad \text{(by Chapman–Kolmogorov)} \\
&= \mu_{\Lambda'}(B_0 \times B_2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{81.16}\] (The inner reordering of the two integrals is Tonelli’s theorem, valid since all integrands are nonnegative.) The same computation, with an arbitrary number of untouched factors carried along on either side of \(t_1\), handles deletion of any interior point of \(\Lambda\).
Largest point. Deleting \(t_n\) from \(\Lambda\) is immediate: since \(q_{t_{n-1},t_n}(x_{n-1}, \cdot)\) is a probability measure, \(\int_S q_{t_{n-1},t_n}(x_{n-1}, dx_n) = 1\), so integrating the last factor of Equation 81.15 over \(S\) gives \(\mu_\Lambda(B_0\times\cdots\times B_{n-1}\times S) = \mu_{\Lambda \setminus \{t_n\}}(B_0 \times \cdots \times B_{n-1})\).
Smallest point. This is the case not covered by the two above, and the one for which the correction \(\nu_{t_0} = \nu Q_{0,t_0}\) (rather than \(\nu\) itself) is essential. Let \(\Lambda = \{t_0 < t_1\}\) and \(\Lambda' = \{t_1\}\) (deleting \(t_0\)). Integrating over \(x_0 \in S\) and using associativity of kernel composition together with the Chapman–Kolmogorov identity \(Q_{0,t_0}Q_{t_0,t_1} = Q_{0,t_1}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_\Lambda(S \times B_1) &= \int_S \nu_{t_0}(dx_0) \int_{B_1} q_{t_0,t_1}(x_0,dx_1) \\
&= \int_{B_1} \big( (\nu Q_{0,t_0}) Q_{t_0,t_1} \big)(dx_1) \\
&= \int_{B_1} (\nu Q_{0,t_1})(dx_1) \\
&= \nu_{t_1}(B_1) \\
&= \mu_{\Lambda'}(B_1).
\end{aligned}
\tag{81.17}\] (With \(\nu\) in place of \(\nu_{t_0}\), this computation would instead require \(\nu Q_{t_0,t_1} = \nu\) for every \(t_0 < t_1\) — i.e. \(\nu\) invariant under the whole transition semigroup — which is not assumed; this is exactly why the plain formula \(\nu(dx_0)q_{t_0,t_1}(x_0,dx_1)\cdots\) fails to be projectively consistent when \(\Lambda\) does not contain \(0\).)
Together, these three cases show that the family \(\{\mu_\Lambda\}_{\Lambda \subseteq T, \, |\Lambda| < \infty}\) satisfies projective consistency for all finite subsets.
Applying Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (Theorem 81.1), there exists a unique probability measure \(\mathbb{P}^\nu \in \mathcal{P}(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\) such that \(\pi_\Lambda^* \mathbb{P}^\nu = \mu_\Lambda\). Taking \(\Lambda = \{0\}\) gives \(\nu_0 = \nu Q_{0,0} = \nu\), so under \(\mathbb{P}^\nu\), the coordinate process \(X_t(\omega) = \omega(t)\) has initial law \(\nu\) and the target finite-dimensional distributions.


81.5.2 Step 2: Verification of the Markov Property
Fix \(t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_{n-1} = s < t = t_n\) in \(T\) (not necessarily including \(0\)). Let \(g \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\) and let \(h \in \mathcal{B}_b(S^n)\) be a bounded test function. Compute the joint expectation under \(\mathbb{P}^\nu\), using Equation 81.15 with leading factor \(\nu_{t_0} = \nu Q_{0,t_0}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{E}^\nu \left[ h(X_{t_0}, \dots, X_{t_{n-1}}) \, g(X_{t_n}) \right] = \int_{S^{n+1}} h(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \, g(x_n) \, \nu_{t_0}(dx_0) \prod_{i=1}^n q_{t_{i-1}, t_i}(x_{i-1}, dx_i) \\
&= \int_{S^n} h(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \left( \int_S g(x_n) \, q_{t_{n-1}, t_n}(x_{n-1}, dx_n) \right) \nu_{t_0}(dx_0) \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} q_{t_{i-1}, t_i}(x_{i-1}, dx_i) \\
&= \int_{S^n} h(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \, (Q_{s,t} g)(x_{n-1}) \, \nu_{t_0}(dx_0) \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} q_{t_{i-1}, t_i}(x_{i-1}, dx_i) \\
&= \mathbb{E}^\nu \left[ h(X_{t_0}, \dots, X_{t_{n-1}}) \, (Q_{s,t} g)(X_s) \right].
\end{aligned}
\tag{81.18}\]
Thus, for any cylinder random variable \(Y = h(X_{t_0}, \dots, X_{t_{n-1}})\) with \(t_{n-1} = s\): \[
\mathbb{E}^\nu \left[ g(X_t) \, Y \right] = \mathbb{E}^\nu \left[ (Q_{s,t} g)(X_s) \, Y \right].
\tag{81.19}\]
By Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) Theorem (uniqueness of measures agreeing on a generating \(\pi\)-system; cf. Lemma 32.1) — or standard monotone class arguments — identity Equation 81.19 extends from the generating class of finite-dimensional cylinder functions \(Y = h(X_{t_0},\dots,X_{t_{n-1}})\), \(t_0 < \dots < t_{n-1} \le s\) arbitrary, to all bounded \(\mathcal{F}_s^X\)-measurable random variables \(Y \in \mathcal{B}_b(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_s^X)\).
By definition of conditional expectation: \[
\mathbb{E}^\nu \left[ g(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s^X \right] = (Q_{s,t} g)(X_s) = \mathbb{E}^\nu \left[ g(X_t) \mid X_s \right] \quad \mathbb{P}^\nu\text{-a.s.}
\tag{81.20}\]
This proves that \(X_t\) is a Markov process relative to \(\mathcal{F}_t^X\) with transition operators \(\{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}\). \(\blacksquare\)
