title: 82  Lecture 38.1: Path Space
text:
82.1 Introduction and the Path Space Framework
Given a totally ordered index set \(T\) with least element \(0\), an initial probability measure \(
u \in \mathcal{P}(S, \mathcal{B})\), and a family of Markov transition operators \(\{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}\) satisfying the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations on a standard Borel space \((S, \mathcal{B})\) (Theorem 81.2, Lecture 37.2), the Kolmogorov Extension Theorem constructs a canonical probability measure \(\mathbb{P}^
u \in \mathcal{P}(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\) on the infinite product space \(S^T = \{\omega : T 	o S\}\). Under \(\mathbb{P}^
u\), the coordinate process \(X_t(\omega) = \omega(t)\) is a Markov process matching the specified finite-dimensional distributions.
However, not every Markov process associated with the data \((
u, \{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t})\) “is” literally this coordinate process on \(S^T\). In general, any stochastic process \(X = \{X_t\}_{t \in T}\) defined on an arbitrary probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) induces a pushforward measure \(P_X\) on the path space \((S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\):

title: 82  Lecture 38.1: Path Space
text:
Definition 82.1 (Law of a Stochastic Process / Path Measure) Let \(X = \{X_t\}_{t \in T}\) be an \(S\)-valued stochastic process defined on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\). The law of the process \(X\), denoted by \(P_X \in \mathcal{P}(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\), is the pushforward measure under the path map \(\omega \mapsto (t \mapsto X_t(\omega))\): \[
P_X(E) := \mathbb{P} \Big( \big\{ \omega \in \Omega : (t \mapsto X_t(\omega))_{t \in T} \in E \big\} \Big) \quad \text{for } E \in \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}.
\tag{82.1}\] This is well defined: since \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T} = \sigma(\pi_t : t \in T)\) and \(\pi_t \circ (t \mapsto X_t(\omega)) = X_t\) is \((\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{B})\)-measurable for every \(t \in T\), the path map \(\omega \mapsto (t \mapsto X_t(\omega))\) is \((\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\)-measurable, so \(P_X\) is a genuine probability measure on \((S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\).

title: 82  Lecture 38.1: Path Space
text:
82.2 Limitations of the Product \(\sigma\)-Algebra
The product \(\sigma\)-algebra allows us to describe events determined by countably many coordinates, but it cannot capture every property of an entire path when the time index set is uncountable. A central measure-theoretic challenge arises when evaluating path properties (e.g., continuity, right-continuity, boundedness) directly on \((S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\).

Remark 82.1 (Smallness of \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\)). Recall that the product \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T} := \sigma(\pi_t : t \in T)\) is generated by individual coordinate projections. Consequently (a standard fact about product \(\sigma\)-algebras, provable by a monotone-class argument: the collection of sets depending on only countably many coordinates is itself a \(\sigma\)-algebra containing every cylinder set, hence all of \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\)), every set \(E \in \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\) depends on at most a countable subset of time coordinates \(T_0 \subseteq T\), i.e. \(E = \pi_{T_0}^{-1}(E')\) for some \(E' \in \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T_0}\) and some countable \(T_0 \subseteq T\).
When \(T = [0, \infty)\), this countable-dependence property shows that path properties genuinely depending on uncountably many time coordinates are not measurable with respect to \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\). For example, the space of continuous paths \(C([0, \infty), \mathbb{R})\) is not an element of \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})^{\otimes [0, \infty)}\): if it were, it would depend only on the coordinates in some countable \(T_0 \subseteq [0,\infty)\), i.e. membership in \(C([0,\infty),\mathbb{R})\) would be determined by \((\omega(t))_{t \in T_0}\) alone. But any \(\omega \in C([0,\infty),\mathbb{R})\) can be modified at a single point \(t^* \notin T_0\) (which exists since \(T_0\) is countable and \([0,\infty)\) is not) to destroy continuity at \(t^*\) while leaving all \(T_0\)-coordinates unchanged — contradicting that membership in \(C([0,\infty),\mathbb{R})\) depends only on \(T_0\).

text: 82.3 Construction of Continuous-Time Markov Processes

title: 82  Lecture 38.1: Path Space
text:
82.4 Brownian Motion

Definition 82.2 (Standard Brownian Motion) An adapted stochastic process \(B = \{B_t\}_{t \ge 0}\) defined on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \ge 0}, \mathbb{P})\) is a standard Brownian motion if:

Standard Start: \(B_0 = 0\) \(\mathbb{P}\)-almost surely.
Independent Increments: For all \(0 \le s < t\), \(B_t - B_s\) is independent of \(\mathcal{F}_s\) (in the sense of Definition 80.5, Lecture 37.1). (If \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\) is the natural filtration \(\mathcal{F}_t^B = \sigma(B_u : u \le t)\), this is equivalent, via Remark 80.3 together with \(B_0 = 0\), to the weaker-looking statement that for any \(0 \le t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_n\) the increments \(B_{t_1}-B_{t_0},\dots,B_{t_n}-B_{t_{n-1}}\) are mutually independent; for a general, possibly strictly larger, filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\) the two need not coincide, and it is independence from \(\mathcal{F}_s\) that is required for the Markov property.)
Gaussian Increments: \(B_t - B_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t-s)\) for all \(0 \le s < t\).
Continuous Sample Paths: The map \(t \mapsto B_t(\omega)\) is continuous \(\mathbb{P}\)-almost surely.


Using Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem, one can readily construct a Markov process \(X = \{X_t\}_{t \ge 0}\) satisfying conditions (0)–(2) via the Gaussian transition kernel \[
q_{s,t}(x, B) := \int_B \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi(t-s)}} \exp \left( -\frac{(y-x)^2}{2(t-s)} \right) dy,
\tag{82.2}\] for \(0 \le s \le t\), \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) together with \(\nu = \delta_0\) as initial law, applying Theorem 81.2 (Lecture 37.2). Once a process \(B\) with this law is in hand, Equation 82.2 indeed coincides with \[
q_{s,t}(x,B) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_B(x+B_t-B_s)]= \mathbb{P}(x + B_t - B_s \in B),
\] since \(x + B_t - B_s \sim \mathcal{N}(x,\, t-s)\).
The corresponding transition operators \(Q_{s,t} f = \gamma_{t-s} * f\) (where \(\gamma_\tau\) denotes the centered Gaussian density with variance \(\tau\)) satisfy the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations by convolution properties of independent normal distributions: \[
\gamma_{s-r} * \gamma_{t-s} = \gamma_{t-r}, \quad \text{which gives} \quad Q_{r,s} Q_{s,t} = Q_{r,t}.
\tag{82.3}\]
Moreover, because the kernel is translation-invariant (\(q_{s,t}(x,\cdot)\) is the law of \(x + Z_{s,t}\) for \(Z_{s,t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,t-s)\) not depending on \(x\) beyond this translation), the resulting finite-dimensional law of \((X_{t_0}, X_{t_1}, \dots, X_{t_n})\) factors, via the change of variables \(z_i = x_i - x_{i-1}\) (exactly as in the arrival-time computation of Proposition 82.1 below), into a product of the marginal law of \(X_{t_0}\) and independent \(\mathcal{N}(0, t_i - t_{i-1})\) laws for the increments \(z_i = X_{t_i}-X_{t_{i-1}}\). This confirms that \(X\) constructed this way indeed also satisfies condition (1), i.e. has independent increments relative to its own natural filtration.
Property 3 asserts that the sample paths of \(B\) are continuous almost surely: \[
\mathbb{P}\!\Big(\big\{\omega \in \Omega : t \mapsto B_t(\omega) \text{ is continuous on } [0,\infty)\big\}\Big) = 1.
\] Equivalently, there exists \(\Omega' \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(\mathbb{P}(\Omega') = 1\) such that for every \(\omega \in \Omega'\) and every \(t_0 \ge 0\), \(\lim_{t \to t_0} B_t(\omega) = B_{t_0}(\omega)\).
For this statement to make sense, the set \(\{\omega : t \mapsto B_t(\omega) \text{ is continuous}\}\) must belong to \(\mathcal{F}\). This is where the lecture’s remark bites: the set of continuous paths \(C([0,\infty), \mathbb{R})\) is not a member of the product \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})^{\otimes [0,\infty)}\), as shown there — continuity genuinely depends on uncountably many coordinates simultaneously, so it lies outside what the product \(\sigma\)-algebra can see.
However, incorporating path continuity (Property 3) requires substantial further analysis (e.g., Kolmogorov’s Continuity Theorem or explicit series expansions). An explicit constructive representation using i.i.d. \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) random variables \(\{\xi_n\}_{n=0}^\infty\) on \(t \in [0, 1]\) is given by the Paley–Wiener / Fourier series: \[
B_t = \xi_0 \, t + \sqrt{2} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \xi_n \, \frac{\sin(n \pi t)}{n \pi}, \qquad t \in [0,1],
\] (or standard Haar/Lévy–Ciesielski series expansions), where the series converges uniformly in \(t\) almost surely, which is what yields the a.s. continuity of \(t \mapsto B_t\).

title: 82  Lecture 38.1: Path Space
section: 82.5 The Poisson Process and Jump Timings
text:
82.5 The Poisson Process and Jump Timings

Definition 82.3 (Poisson Process) An adapted process \(N = \{N_t\}_{t \ge 0}\) defined on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \ge 0}, \mathbb{P})\) and taking values in \(\mathbb{N}_0 = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\) is a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda > 0\) if:

Standard Start: \(N_0 = 0\) \(\mathbb{P}\)-almost surely.
Independent Increments: For all \(0 \le s < t\), \(N_t - N_s\) is independent of \(\mathcal{F}_s\); equivalently (given \(N_0=0\)), increments over disjoint intervals are mutually independent.
Poisson Increments: \(N_t - N_s \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s))\) for all \(0 \le s < t\).
Cadlag / Right-Continuous Paths: \(t \mapsto N_t(\omega)\) is non-decreasing and right-continuous \(\mathbb{P}\)-a.s., with jumps of size exactly \(1\).


Property 3 is not redundant: it is a genuine regularity condition on sample paths that is not implied by properties 0–2 alone (Remark 82.2 below spells this out), and it is exactly what makes \(N\) a bona fide counting process whose jump times can be read off from the path. (That the jumps automatically have size \(1\), given right-continuity and monotonicity, follows from \(\mathbb{P}(N_{t+h}-N_t \ge 2) = O(h^2)\) as \(h \downarrow 0\) together with a standard dyadic-partition/Borel–Cantelli argument; we take it as part of the definition here rather than re-derive it.)
We explicitly construct \(N_t\) from jump arrival times \(X_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \xi_k\) (with \(X_0 := 0\)), where \(\{\xi_k\}_{k=1}^\infty \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \text{Exp}(\lambda)\): \[
N_t(\omega) := \sup \left\{ n \in \mathbb{N}_0 : X_n(\omega) \le t \right\}.
\tag{82.4}\]
The transition kernel on the discrete state space \(S = \mathbb{N}_0\) is given by: \[
\begin{aligned}
q_{s,t}(n, m) &= \mathbb{P}(n + N_t - N_s = m)\\
& = e^{-\lambda(t-s)} \frac{\big(\lambda(t-s)\big)^{m-n}}{(m-n)!} \quad \text{for } m \ge n.
\end{aligned}
\tag{82.5}\]
Convolution of independent Poisson variables confirms that \(\{q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}\) satisfies the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations.

Proposition 82.1 (Characterization of Jump Times) Let \(N = \{N_t\}_{t \ge 0}\) satisfy properties (0)–(3) of Definition 82.3 (so, in particular, \(N_0 = 0\) a.s. and \(N\) has non-decreasing, right-continuous paths with unit jumps, in addition to independent and Poisson increments). Define the sequence of jump arrival times by \(X_n := \inf \{ t \ge 0 : N_t = n\}\) for \(n \in \mathbb{N}_0\), and the inter-arrival times \(\xi_n := X_n - X_{n-1}\) for \(n \ge 1\). Then \(\{\xi_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are i.i.d. \(\text{Exp}(\lambda)\) random variables.
(Properties 0 and 3 are essential, not merely convenient: they are what make \(X_n\) the literal \(n\)-th jump time of the path \(t \mapsto N_t(\omega)\), so that \(\{X_n \in J_n\}\) can be read off from the values of \(N\) at the endpoints of \(J_n\). Properties (1)–(2) alone, without path regularity, do not suffice for this conclusion — see Remark 82.2.)


Proof 82.1 (Proof). Fix \(n \ge 1\). Partition \([0, t_n]\) into alternating disjoint intervals: \[
\begin{aligned}
&K_1 = (0, s_1], \; J_1 = (s_1, t_1], \; K_2 = (t_1, s_2], \; J_2 = (s_2, t_2],\\
& \dots, \; K_n = (t_{n-1}, s_n], \; J_n = (s_n, t_n],
\end{aligned}
\] where \(0 < s_1 < t_1 < s_2 < t_2 < \dots < s_n < t_n\). Denote \(N(s, t) := N_t - N_s\).
Since \(N_0 = 0\) and \(N\) is non-decreasing, right-continuous, with unit jumps (property 3), the path \(t\mapsto N_t(\omega)\) passes through every integer value it ever reaches, one at a time, so for each \(n\) there is a.s. a well-defined, finite, strictly increasing sequence of jump times \(X_1(\omega) < X_2(\omega) < \dots\) with \(N_t(\omega) = \#\{k \ge 1 : X_k(\omega) \le t\}\). In particular, \(X_j \in (s_j, t_j]\) holds if and only if no jump has occurred by time \(s_j\) beyond the \((j-1)\)-th (i.e. \(N_{s_j} \le j-1\)) and the \(j\)-th jump has occurred by time \(t_j\) (i.e. \(N_{t_j} \ge j\)); this is what licenses translating the event \(\{X_1 \in J_1, \dots, X_n \in J_n\}\) into the disjoint increment conditions below. The event \(\{X_1 \in J_1, X_2 \in J_2, \dots, X_n \in J_n\}\) corresponds to: \[
\begin{aligned}
&\{X_1 \in J_1, \dots, X_n \in J_n\} \\
&= \left\{ \bigcap_{j=1}^n \{N(K_j) = 0\} \right\} \cap \left\{ \bigcap_{j=1}^{n-1} \{N(J_j) = 1\} \right\} \cap \{N(J_n) \ge 1\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{82.6}\]
Because \(N\) has independent increments over disjoint intervals \(K_1, J_1, \dots, K_n, J_n\), these \(2n\) events are independent. Recalling that \(\mathbb{P}(N(J) = k) = e^{-\lambda|J|} \frac{(\lambda|J|)^k}{k!}\) and \(\mathbb{P}(N(J) \ge 1) = 1 - e^{-\lambda|J|}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X_1 \in J_1, \dots, X_n \in J_n) &= \left( \prod_{j=1}^n e^{-\lambda |K_j|} \right) \left( \prod_{j=1}^{n-1} \lambda |J_j| e^{-\lambda |J_j|} \right) \left( 1 - e^{-\lambda |J_n|} \right) \\
&= \lambda^{n-1} \left( \prod_{j=1}^{n-1} |J_j| \right) e^{-\lambda s_n} \left( 1 - e^{-\lambda(t_n - s_n)} \right) \\
&= \lambda^{n-1} \left( \prod_{j=1}^{n-1} |J_j| \right) \left( e^{-\lambda s_n} - e^{-\lambda t_n} \right) \\
&= \int_{J_1} \dots \int_{J_n} \lambda^n e^{-\lambda x_n} \, dx_1 dx_2 \dots dx_n.
\end{aligned}
\tag{82.7}\]
By Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) Theorem, the joint distribution of \((X_1, \dots, X_n)\) on \(\Delta_n = \{0 < x_1 < x_2 < \dots < x_n\}\) has joint density: \[
f_{X_1, \dots, X_n}(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \lambda^n e^{-\lambda x_n} \mathbf{1}_{\{0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n\}}.
\tag{82.8}\]
Applying the change of variables transformation \(\xi_k = X_k - X_{k-1}\) (with \(X_0 = 0\)), the Jacobian determinant is \(1\), yielding joint density: \[
\begin{aligned}
f_{\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n}(u_1, \dots, u_n) &= \lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum_{k=1}^n u_k} \mathbf{1}_{\{u_1 > 0, \dots, u_n > 0\}} \\
&= \prod_{k=1}^n \left( \lambda e^{-\lambda u_k} \mathbf{1}_{\{u_k > 0\}} \right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{82.9}\]
This proves that \(\{\xi_k\}_{k=1}^n\) are i.i.d. \(\text{Exp}(\lambda)\) random variables. \(\blacksquare\)

title: 82  Lecture 38.1: Path Space
section: 82.6 Insufficiency of Transition Kernels for Path Properties
text:
82.6 Insufficiency of Transition Kernels for Path Properties

Remark 82.2 (Moral: Path Properties Lie Outside Transition Kernels). Property 3 (right-continuity of \(t \mapsto N_t\)) does not follow from the finite-dimensional distributions or transition kernels alone — nor, as noted above, does it follow from properties (0)–(2).
To demonstrate this, consider the modified process defined using the arrival times \(X_n\) (not the inter-arrival times \(\xi_n\)): \[
M_t(\omega) := \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{[0, t)}(X_n(\omega)) = N_{t-}(\omega).
\tag{82.10}\] Because each \(X_n\) has a continuous (atomless) law, \(\mathbb{P}(X_n = t) = 0\) for every fixed \(t \ge 0\), so \(\mathbb{P}(M_t \ne N_t) = 0\) at each fixed \(t\), and in fact \(\mathbb{P}(M_{t_1} \ne N_{t_1}, \dots, \text{or } M_{t_k} \ne N_{t_k}) = 0\) for every finite set of times \(t_1, \dots, t_k\) (a finite union of null events is null). Hence \(\{M_t\}_{t \ge 0}\) has the exact same finite-dimensional distributions as \(\{N_t\}_{t \ge 0}\), but its paths are left-continuous instead of right-continuous (it is the left-limit process \(N_{t-}\)).
Key Takeaway: Transition kernels \(\{q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}\) uniquely specify finite-dimensional distributions on \((S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\), but they do not dictate sample path properties (such as continuity, cadlag paths, or measurability of path functionals). Sample path regularity requires selecting an appropriate separable modification or constructing the process on a restricted path space (such as \(D([0, \infty), S)\) or \(C([0, \infty), S)\)).

title: 82  Lecture 38.1: Path Space
text:
82.7 Editorial & Reconstruction Notes

Explicit Joint Density Integration: Restructured the abbreviated handwritten proof for the Poisson jump times into a step-by-step density integration[cite: 3]. Explicitly evaluated the product of exponential increments and presented the change-of-variables step from \((X_1, \dots, X_n)\) to \((\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n)\)[cite: 3].
Clarification on Path Regularity: Expanded Remark Remark 82.2 to explicitly state why product \(\sigma\)-algebras fail for non-countable events and why separable modifications or Skorokhod spaces (\(D[0,\infty)\)) are required[cite: 3].

title: 82  Lecture 38.1: Path Space
text:

title: 49  Lecture 23.2: Prokhorov’s Compactness Theorem
text:
WarningCounterexample: Mass Escape to Infinity



Consider the sequence of Dirac measures on \(\mathbb{R}\): \[
\mu_n=\delta_n.
\] For any compact set \(K\subset\mathbb{R}\), there exists \(M>0\) such that \(K\subset[-M,M]\). Hence, for all sufficiently large \(n\), \[
\mu_n(K)=\delta_n(K)=0.
\] Thus, for every compact set \(K\), \[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mu_n(K)=0.
\] Consequently, \((\mu_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) is not tight, and neither is any subsequence. Since weak convergence of probability measures implies tightness, \((\mu_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) has no weakly convergent subsequence.
Intuitively, the entire probability mass moves farther and farther away from every fixed compact set; the mass escapes to infinity.

title: 49  Lecture 23.2: Prokhorov’s Compactness Theorem
text:
49.2 Main Statements

Theorem 49.1 (Prokhorov’s Compactness Theorem) Let \(S\) be a separable metric space. If \(\{\mu_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} \subset \text{Prob}(S, \mathcal{B}(S))\), then there exists a vaguely convergent subsequence.


Corollary 49.1 (Weak Convergence via Tightness) If \(\{\mu_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) is also tight, then there exists a weakly convergent subsequence \(\{\mu_{n_k}\}_{k=1}^\infty\) whose limit \(\mu\) is a proper probability measure (i.e., \(\mu(S) = 1\)).

In these notes, we present the classic proof for the foundational baseline case where \(S = \mathbb{R}\), using Helly’s Selection Theorem.

title: 49  Lecture 23.2: Prokhorov’s Compactness Theorem
text:
49.3 Proof of Helly’s Selection Theorem (\(S = \mathbb{R}\))
Let \(F_n(x) = \mu_n((-\infty, x])\) be the sequence of Cumulative Distribution Functions (CDFs) associated with the probability measures \(\mu_n\).

title: 49  Lecture 23.2: Prokhorov’s Compactness Theorem
text:
49.6 Verification of CDF Properties for \(F(x)\)

49.6.1 Property 1: Non-decreasing
Let \(x < y\). If \(q \in \mathbb{Q}\) satisfies \(q > y\), then automatically \(q > x\). Thus: \[
\{G(q) : q \in \mathbb{Q}, q > y\} \subseteq \{G(q) : q \in \mathbb{Q}, q > x\}
\] Taking the infimum over a larger set yields a smaller or equal value: \[
F(y) = \inf \{G(q) : q \in \mathbb{Q}, q > y\} \ge \inf \{G(q) : q \in \mathbb{Q}, q > x\} = F(x)
\]


49.6.2 Property 2: Right-Continuous
Let \(x_n \downarrow x\) as \(n \to \infty\). Since \(F\) is non-decreasing, the sequence \(F(x_n)\) is non-increasing, so \(\lim_{n\to\infty} F(x_n) = \inf_n F(x_n)\).
Evaluating the nested infima: \[
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{n \to \infty} F(x_n) &= \inf_{n} F(x_n) \\
&= \inf_{n} \left( \inf \{G(q) : q \in \mathbb{Q}, q > x_n\} \right) \\
&= \inf \{G(q) : q \in \mathbb{Q}, \exists n \text{ s.t. } q > x_n\} \\
&= \inf \{G(q) : q \in \mathbb{Q}, q > x\} \\
&= F(x)
\end{aligned}
\] Thus, \(F(x)\) is right-continuous, making it a valid generalized CDF of a sub-probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}\).

title: 49  Lecture 23.2: Prokhorov’s Compactness Theorem
text:
49.8 Takeaways






NoteSummary



1. Helly’s Selection Theorem (the \(S = \mathbb{R}\) engine). Every sequence of probability measures on \(\mathbb{R}\) has a subsequence that converges vaguely to a sub-probability measure \(\mu\) with \(\mu(\mathbb{R}) \le 1\). The proof has three layers:

Cantor’s diagonal (Step 1): Bolzano–Weierstrass + diagonal extraction yields a subsequence \(\{F_{n_k}\}\) that converges pointwise on \(\mathbb{Q}\) to a non-decreasing limit \(G\).
Infimum extension (Step 2): Setting \(F(x) = \inf\{G(q): q \in \mathbb{Q},\, q > x\}\) produces a non-decreasing, right-continuous function — a valid sub-CDF — automatically, without any additional extraction.
Continuity-point convergence (Step 3): A two-sided squeeze argument shows \(F_{n_k}(x) \to F(x)\) at every continuity point of \(F\): the upper bound uses \(G(r_j) \downarrow F(x)\) (non-decreasingness of \(G\) plus the infimum definition), and the lower bound uses \(G(q_j) \uparrow F(x)\) (which requires continuity of \(F\) at \(x\) to match the left limit \(F(x^-)\) to \(F(x)\)).

2. Vague \(\neq\) Weak. The sub-CDF \(F\) may satisfy \(F(+\infty) < 1\) or \(F(-\infty) > 0\) when probability mass escapes to \(\pm\infty\) (cf.~the \(\delta_n\) counterexample). The associated measure \(\mu\) is then a strict sub-probability measure, and convergence is only vague, not weak.
3. Prokhorov’s Theorem: tightness upgrades vague to weak. A family \(\{\mu_n\}\) is tight if \[
\forall\,\varepsilon > 0,\ \exists\,\text{compact } K:\quad \inf_n \mu_n(K) \ge 1 - \varepsilon.
\] Tightness is exactly what prevents mass escape:

If \(\{\mu_n\}\) is tight, any vaguely convergent subsequence \(\mu_{n_k}\) converges weakly and its limit is a proper probability measure (\(\mu(S) = 1\)).
Conversely, every weakly convergent sequence of probability measures is tight.
On a Polish (separable, completely metrizable) space, tightness \(\Leftrightarrow\) relative sequential compactness in the weak topology.

4. A practical tightness criterion. For random variables \(\{X_n\}\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), a sufficient condition for tightness is \[
\sup_n \mathbf{E}[|X_n|^p] < \infty \quad \text{for some } p > 0.
\] By Markov’s inequality, \(\mu_n([-M,M]^c) \le M^{-p}\,\mathbf{E}[|X_n|^p] \to 0\) uniformly in \(n\) as \(M \to \infty\), which is precisely the tightness condition.

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
50.7 Takeaways
1. The Quantile Construction. For any CDF \(F\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), the left-continuous inverse \(F^\leftarrow(u) = \sup\{y : F(y) < u\}\) is finite for each \(u \in (0,1)\) and defines a Borel map on \(\left((0,1),\lambda\right)\) whose pushforward is \(\mu\). This is the inverse transform sampling principle and is the key building block of the theorem.
2. Skorohod’s Representation Theorem. If \(\mu_n \Rightarrow \mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), the explicit Skorohod coupling is \(Y_n = F_n^\leftarrow\) and \(Y = F^\leftarrow\) on the same Lebesgue space \(\left((0,1),\lambda\right)\). The a.s. convergence \(Y_n \to Y\) is proved by a two-sided squeeze: - Lower bound: for \(y < Y(u)\), Property 3 gives \(F(y) < u\); weak convergence then forces \(F_n(y) < u\) eventually, so \(Y_n(u) \ge y\). - Upper bound: for \(y > Y(u)\) (using \(u \notin E\), so \(F^\leftarrow = F^\rightarrow\)), the fact that \(\{z: F(z)>u\}\) is upward-closed gives \(F(y)>u\); weak convergence forces \(F_n(y)>u\) eventually, and non-decreasingness of \(F_n\) then gives \(Y_n(u) \le y\).
Both limiting arguments are legitimate because \(\text{Cont}(F)\) is dense in \(\mathbb{R}\), a monotone bounded \(F\) having at most countably many discontinuities.
3. Why \(u \notin E\) is required. The set \(E = \{u : F^\leftarrow(u) < F^\rightarrow(u)\}\) collects the heights of the flat spots of \(F\). The upper bound argument uses \(F^\leftarrow(u) = F^\rightarrow(u)\), which fails on \(E\); the lower bound argument needs no such restriction. Since flat spots of \(F\) correspond to disjoint open intervals in \(\mathbb{R}\), \(E\) is countable, so \(\lambda(E) = 0\) and the a.s. conclusion holds.
4. The Continuous Mapping Theorem. Skorohod’s theorem reduces CMT to a pointwise statement: since \(Y_n \to Y\) a.s. and \(g \circ f\) is continuous at \(Y(\omega)\) for \(\lambda\)-a.e. \(\omega\) (because \(\mathcal{L}(Y) = \mu_X\), \(\mu_X(\text{Disc}(f)) = 0\), and \(\text{Disc}(g \circ f) \subseteq \text{Disc}(f)\)), we get \((g\circ f)(Y_n) \to (g\circ f)(Y)\) a.s., and DCT finishes the argument. For bounded \(f\) one argues the same way, but on the set \(\Omega_f\) where \(f\) itself is continuous at \(Y(\omega)\): the set built for a fixed test function \(g\) will not do, since \(\text{Disc}(g \circ f)\) can be much smaller than \(\text{Disc}(f)\).
5. Scope and Limitations. The explicit CDF-inversion proof is special to \(\mathbb{R}\). For a general separable metric space \(S\) — completeness is not needed — the coupling is obtained by constructing a suitable joint measure on an auxiliary space (via nested partitions or probability kernels), not a product of the marginals; the conclusion, and all applications including CMT, remain the same. That general statement is quoted here as a standard result and is not proved in this chapter. Importantly, Skorohod’s theorem does not assert that \(X_n \to X\) a.s. on the original probability space; it only provides an equivalent coupling on a new space.

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
Theorem 50.1 (Skorohod’s Representation Theorem) Let \((S, d)\) be a separable metric space, and let \(\mu_n, \mu \in \text{Prob}(S,\mathcal{B}(S))\). If \(\mu_n \Rightarrow \mu\) weakly as \(n \to \infty\), then there exists a common probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) and random variables \(Y_n, Y: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (S, \mathcal{B}(S))\) such that:

\(Y_{n*} P = \mu_{Y_n} = \mu_n\) for all \(n \ge 1\),
\(Y_{*} P = \mu_Y = \mu\),
\(Y_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} Y\) as \(n \to \infty\).



Recall that \(Y_{n*} P= P \circ Y_n^{-1} = \mu_{Y_n}\) is the pushforward measure of \(P\) under \(Y_n\), which is the same as the distribution of \(Y_n\). Similarly, \(Y_{*} P = \mu_Y\) is the distribution of \(Y\).
On the hypotheses. Separability of \((S,d)\) is enough; completeness is not required, so we do not need \(S\) to be Polish. (It suffices that the limit law \(\mu\) have separable support.) Polishness is often assumed in textbook statements only because it supplies convenient tightness and standard-Borel machinery.
On the scope of these notes. Theorem 50.1 is quoted here as a standard result in this generality. What we prove below is the case \(S = \mathbb{R}\); the general separable case is not proved in this chapter.


Example 50.1 (Skorohod Representation for Converging Normal Distributions) Consider the sequence of probability measures \(\mu_n = N\left(\frac{1}{n},1\right)\) for \(n\geq 1\) and let \(\mu=N(0,1)\). We first observe that \(\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\). Indeed, the CDF of \(\mu_n\) is \(F_n(x)=\Phi\left(x-\frac{1}{n}\right)\), where \(\Phi\) is the CDF of the standard normal distribution. Since \(x-\frac{1}{n}\longrightarrow x\) and \(\Phi\) is continuous, \(F_n(x) = \Phi\left(x-\frac{1}{n}\right) \longrightarrow \Phi(x) = F(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). Hence \(\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\).
Skorohod’s Representation Theorem tells us that there exists a common probability space on which random variables with these distributions can be constructed so that they converge almost surely. We now construct such random variables explicitly.

50.1.0.1 Step 1: Start with a uniform random variable
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)=\bigl((0,1),\mathcal{B}((0,1)),\lambda\bigr)\), where \(\lambda\) denotes Lebesgue measure, and define \(U(\omega)=\omega\). Then \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\).
We work on the open interval \((0,1)\), not on \([0,1]\). The reason is that \(\Phi^{-1}(0)=-\infty\) and \(\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty\), so on \([0,1]\) the variables defined below would fail to be \(\mathbb{R}\)-valued at the two endpoints, and the difference \(Y_n-Y\) would be the undefined expression \(\infty-\infty\) there. On \((0,1)\) every value is finite.


50.1.0.2 Step 2: Transform the uniform random variable
Define \(Y=\Phi^{-1}(U)\) and, for each \(n\geq1\), \(Y_n=\frac{1}{n}+\Phi^{-1}(U)\). The important feature of this construction is that the same random variable \(U\) is used for every \(Y_n\) and for \(Y\).


50.1.0.3 Step 3: Verify the distribution of \(Y\)
We first show that \(Y\sim N(0,1)\). For any \(y\in\mathbb{R}\), \[
\begin{aligned}
P(Y\leq y)
&=
P\left(\Phi^{-1}(U)\leq y\right)\\
&=
P\left(U\leq\Phi(y)\right).
\end{aligned}
\] The second equality follows because \(\Phi\) is a continuous, strictly increasing bijection from \(\mathbb{R}\) onto \((0,1)\); hence \(\Phi^{-1}:(0,1)\to\mathbb{R}\) is well defined and \(\Phi^{-1}(u)\leq y\Longleftrightarrow u\leq\Phi(y)\). (Strict increase alone would not suffice; see the warning in the next section.) Since \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) and \(\Phi(y)\in(0,1)\), \(P\left(U\leq\Phi(y)\right)=\Phi(y)\). Therefore, \(P(Y\leq y)=\Phi(y)\). Thus the CDF of \(Y\) is \(\Phi\), so \(Y\sim N(0,1)=\mu\).


50.1.0.4 Step 4: Verify the distribution of \(Y_n\)
We now show that \(Y_n\sim N\left(\frac1n,1\right)=\mu_n\). For any \(y\in\mathbb{R}\), \[
\begin{aligned}
P(Y_n\leq y)
&=
P\left(\frac1n+\Phi^{-1}(U)\leq y\right)\\
&=
P\left(\Phi^{-1}(U)\leq y-\frac1n\right)\\
&=
P\left(U\leq
\Phi\left(y-\frac1n\right)\right)\\
&=
\Phi\left(y-\frac1n\right).
\end{aligned}
\] But \(F_n(y)=\Phi\left(y-\frac1n\right)\) is the CDF of \(N(1/n,1)\). Hence \(Y_n\sim N\left(\frac1n,1\right)=\mu_n\). Thus the construction preserves all the required marginal distributions: \[
P\circ Y_n^{-1}=\mu_n,
\qquad
P\circ Y^{-1}=\mu.
\]


50.1.0.5 Step 5: Verify almost-sure convergence
The construction makes the convergence particularly simple. We have \[
Y_n-Y
=\left(\frac1n+\Phi^{-1}(U)\right)-\Phi^{-1}(U)
=\frac1n.
\] Both terms are finite at every \(\omega\in\Omega=(0,1)\), so the subtraction is legitimate pointwise. Therefore, for every \(\omega\in\Omega\), \(|Y_n(\omega)-Y(\omega)|=\frac1n\longrightarrow0\). Hence \(Y_n\longrightarrow Y\) everywhere on \(\Omega\), which is in particular the almost sure convergence asserted by Theorem 50.1.








NoteNote on the General Metric Space Proof



The proof for a general separable metric space is quite involved. The canonical probability space can be constructed on \(\Omega = (0, 1) \times S^{\mathbb{N}}\), with \(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{B}((0, 1) \times S^{\mathbb{N}})\), and \(P\) taken to be a suitable joint coupling measure (built, for instance, from nested partitions of \(S\), or from probability kernels). It is essential that \(P\) is in general not the product of the marginal laws: a product measure would make the coordinates independent, whereas the entire purpose of the construction is to introduce precise dependence between the \(Y_n\)’s.
In these notes, we present the complete proof for the foundational case where \(S = \mathbb{R}\) by explicitly inverting the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF).

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
50.2 Inverting the CDF & Generalized Inverses
Suppose \(F: \mathbb{R} \to [0, 1]\) is the CDF of a probability measure \(\mu \in \text{Prob}\left(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\right)\), i.e., \(F = F_\mu\).
Suppose for a moment that \(F\) is continuous and strictly increasing. Strict increase means \(F(a) < F(b)\) whenever \(a<b\), which (since \(F(b)-F(a) = \mu((a,b])\)) is equivalent to \(\mu\left((a,b)\right) > 0\) for all \(a<b\). Combined with \(\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0\), \(\lim_{x\to+\infty}F(x)=1\) and the intermediate value theorem, continuity and strict increase make \(F\) a bijection from \(\mathbb{R}\) onto \((0,1)\). We may then set \(Y := F^{-1}: (0, 1) \to \mathbb{R}\). Equipping \((0, 1)\) with the Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\), the distribution function of \(Y\) satisfies: \[
\begin{aligned}
F_Y(t) &= \lambda\left(Y^{-1}\left((-\infty, t]\right)\right)
= \lambda\left(\left\{ u \in (0,1) : F^{-1}(u) \le t \right\}\right) \\
&= \lambda\left(\left(0, F(t)\right]\right) = F(t),
\end{aligned}
\] hence \(\mu_Y = \mu\).






WarningStrict increase alone is not enough



Continuity cannot be dropped. A strictly increasing CDF may still have jumps, in which case its range omits an interval and \(F^{-1}\) is not defined on all of \((0,1)\). For example, take \[
\mu = \tfrac12 \delta_0 + \tfrac12 N(0,1),
\qquad
F(x) = \tfrac12 \Phi(x) + \tfrac12 \mathbf{1}_{\{x \ge 0\}}.
\] The normal component forces \(\mu\left((a,b)\right)>0\) for all \(a<b\), so \(F\) is strictly increasing. But \(F\) jumps by \(\tfrac12\) at \(x=0\), and its range omits \(\left(\tfrac14,\tfrac34\right)\). Hence \(F^{-1}(u)\) is undefined in the ordinary sense for every \(u \in \left(\tfrac14,\tfrac34\right)\). This is precisely the defect the generalized inverses below repair.


To handle general CDFs (which may have flat spots or jump discontinuities), we define generalized lower and upper inverses.

Definition 50.1 (Generalized CDF Inverses) Let \(F: \mathbb{R} \to [0, 1]\) be a CDF. For \(u \in (0, 1)\), define:

Left-continuous Inverse (Lower Quantile Function): \[
F^\leftarrow(u) := \sup \{ x \in \mathbb{R} : F(x) < u \}
\]
Right-continuous Inverse (Upper Quantile Function): \[
F^\rightarrow(u) := \inf \{ x \in \mathbb{R} : F(x) > u \}
\]


Finiteness. Both quantities are finite real numbers for every \(u \in (0,1)\), so that \(F^\leftarrow, F^\rightarrow : (0,1) \to \mathbb{R}\). Indeed, fix \(u \in (0,1)\). Since \(F(x) \to 0\) as \(x \to -\infty\), there is \(m\) with \(F(m) < u\), so \(\{F < u\} \ne \emptyset\). Since \(F(x) \to 1\) as \(x \to +\infty\), there is \(M\) with \(F(M) > u\); then \(F(x) < u\) forces \(x \le M\) by monotonicity, so \(\{F<u\}\) is bounded above. Hence \(F^\leftarrow(u) = \sup\{F<u\}\) is finite, and a symmetric argument applies to \(F^\rightarrow(u) = \inf\{F>u\}\). This is what makes the expression \(F\left(F^\leftarrow(u)\right)\) meaningful and makes the quantile transform an \(\mathbb{R}\)-valued random variable.

Example 50.2 Suppose \(P(X=0)=0.3\), \(P(X=1)=0.4\), and \(P(X=2)=0.3\). Then the CDF is \[
F(y)=
\begin{cases} 0, & y<0,\\
0.3, & 0\leq y<1,\\ 0.7, & 1\leq y<2,\\
1, & y\geq2.
\end{cases}
\] Now take \(u=0.5\). We want \(F^\leftarrow(0.5) = \sup\{y:F(y)<0.5\}\). Since \(F(y)<0.5\) whenever \(y<1\), \(\{y:F(y)<0.5\}=(-\infty,1)\). Therefore, \(F^\leftarrow(0.5) = 1\).
Now consider the upper quantile: \(F^\rightarrow(0.5) = \inf\{y:F(y)>0.5\}\). We need to find all \(y\) for which \(F(y)>0.5\). From the CDF, \(F(y)=0.7>0.5\) for \(y\ge1\). Therefore, \(\{y:F(y)>0.5\}=[1,\infty)\) and hence \(F^\rightarrow(0.5)=1\).
Consider \(u=0.7\). Now we see the difference. For the lower quantile, \(F^\leftarrow(0.7) = \sup\{y:F(y)<0.7\}\). Since \(F(y)<0.7\) for \(y<1\), \(F^\leftarrow(0.7)=1\). But for the upper quantile, \(F^\rightarrow(0.7) = \inf\{y:F(y)>0.7\}\). At \(y=1\), we have \(F(1)=0.7\), which is not strictly greater than \(0.7\). We therefore have to move to the next jump: \(F(y)>0.7 \Longleftrightarrow y\ge2\). Thus, \(F^\rightarrow(0.7)=2\). So here \[
F^\leftarrow(0.7)=1, \qquad F^\rightarrow(0.7)=2.
\]

The lower quantile asks: what is the supremum (right endpoint) of the set on which the CDF is strictly below \(0.7\)? Answer: 1. Observe that this supremum is not attained: \(\{y:F(y)<0.7\}=(-\infty,1)\) has no largest element. This is exactly why the definition takes a supremum rather than a maximum.
The upper quantile asks: what is the infimum (left endpoint) of the set on which the CDF is strictly greater than \(0.7\)? Answer: 2. Here the infimum is attained, since \(\{y:F(y)>0.7\}=[2,\infty)\).

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
50.4 Construction of the Random Variable

Lemma 50.1 (Quantile Transformation) Let \(\mu \in \text{Prob}\left(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\right)\) with CDF \(F_\mu = F\). Define \(Y: (0, 1) \to \mathbb{R}\) by: \[
Y(u) := F^\leftarrow(u) = \sup \{ y \in \mathbb{R} : F(y) < u \}.
\] Equip \(\left((0, 1), \mathcal{B}((0, 1))\right)\) with the Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\). Then \(Y\) is a Borel-measurable random variable, and: \[
Y_* \lambda = \lambda \circ Y^{-1} = \mu_Y = \mu.
\]


Proof (Proof of Lemma 50.1). First note that \(Y\) is real-valued at every \(u \in (0,1)\), by the finiteness remark following Definition 50.1. For any \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), we claim the fundamental equivalence: \[
\{ u \in (0, 1) : Y(u) \le t \} = (0, 1) \cap (0, F(t)].
\]

\((\subseteq)\): Suppose \(Y(u) \le t\). By the right-hand inequality of Property 3, applied at level \(u\), we have \(u \le F\left(F^\leftarrow(u)\right)\). Since \(F^\leftarrow(u) = Y(u) \le t\), monotonicity gives \(F\left(F^\leftarrow(u)\right) \le F(t)\). Combining, \(u \le F(t)\), so \(u \in (0,1) \cap (0, F(t)]\).
\((\supseteq)\): If \(u \le F(t)\), then every \(y\) with \(F(y) < u\) satisfies \(y \le t\): if \(y > t\), then non-decreasingness of \(F\) gives \(F(y) \ge F(t) \ge u\), contradicting \(F(y) < u\). Thus \(t\) is an upper bound for \(\{y : F(y) < u\}\), so \(Y(u) = \sup\{y : F(y) < u\} \le t\).

Measurability. The displayed identity shows that \(\{Y \le t\} \in \mathcal{B}((0,1))\) for every \(t \in \mathbb{R}\). Since the sets \(\{(-\infty, t] : t \in \mathbb{R}\}\) generate \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\), it follows that \(Y\) is Borel measurable.
Distribution. Taking the Lebesgue measure of the above set gives, for every \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), \[
\lambda\left(\{ u \in (0, 1) : Y(u) \le t \}\right) = \lambda\left((0,1) \cap (0, F(t)]\right) = F(t) = F_\mu(t).
\] The middle equality also covers the degenerate cases: if \(F(t) = 0\) the set is empty, and if \(F(t) = 1\) it equals \((0,1)\). Since two probability measures on \(\mathbb{R}\) with the same CDF coincide, \(\mu_Y = \mu\). \(\blacksquare\)


Corollary 50.1 (Inverse Transform Sampling) Let \(\mu \in \text{Prob}\left(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\right)\) have CDF \(F\), and let \(U \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1)\) be defined on some probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\). Since \(P(U \in (0,1)) = 1\), the composition \(F^\leftarrow(U)\) is defined almost surely, and \[
F^\leftarrow(U) \sim \mu.
\]

This is immediate from Lemma 50.1: the law of \(U\) is \(\lambda\) on \((0,1)\), and pushing forward once more along the Borel map \(F^\leftarrow\) gives \(\left(F^\leftarrow\right)_* \lambda = \mu\).

Proof (Proof of Corollary 50.1). Set \(Y=F^\leftarrow(U)\). For any \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), the generalized inverse satisfies \[
F^\leftarrow(u)\leq x
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
u\leq F(x),
\qquad u\in(0,1).
\] Therefore, \[
\begin{aligned}
P(Y\leq x)
&=P\left(F^\leftarrow(U)\leq x\right)\\
&=P\left(U\leq F(x)\right).
\end{aligned}
\] Since \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(F(x)\in[0,1]\), \(P\left(U\leq F(x)\right)=F(x)\). Hence, \(P(Y\leq x)=F(x)=F_\mu(x)\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). Thus \(Y\) and \(\mu\) have the same CDF. Therefore, \(F_Y=F_\mu\), and consequently \(Y\sim\mu\). That is, \(F^\leftarrow(U)\sim\mu\).


Example 50.3 Suppose we want to generate a random variable \(X\) with \(P(X=1)=0.2\), \(P(X=2)=0.5\), \(P(X=4)=0.3\). Its CDF is \[
F(x)=
\begin{cases} 0, & x<1,\\
0.2, & 1\le x<2,\\
0.7, & 2\le x<4,\\
1, & x\ge4.
\end{cases}
\] The generalized inverse is \(F^\leftarrow(u)=\sup\{x:F(x)<u\}\). We can determine it interval by interval: \[
F^\leftarrow(u)=
\begin{cases} 1, & 0<u\le0.2,\\
2, & 0.2<u\le0.7,\\
4, & 0.7<u<1.
\end{cases}
\] Now let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and define \(Y=F^\leftarrow(U)\). Then: \[
\begin{aligned}
&P(Y=1) = P(0<U\le0.2) =0.2, \\
&P(Y=2) = P(0.2<U\le0.7) =0.5, \\
&P(Y=4) = P(0.7<U<1) =0.3.
\end{aligned}
\] Therefore, \(Y\sim\mu\), exactly as the corollary states.

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
50.6 Proof of Skorokhod’s Theorem (\(S = \mathbb{R}\))
Let \(\mu_n, \mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})\) with \(\mu_n \Rightarrow \mu\). Let \(F_n = F_{\mu_n}\) and \(F = F_\mu\) be their corresponding CDFs.
Define our probability space as \(\Omega = (0, 1)\), \(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{B}(0, 1)\), and \(P = \lambda\) (Lebesgue measure). Define the sequence of random variables: \[
Y_n(x) := F_n^\leftarrow(x), \quad Y(x) := F^\leftarrow(x), \quad \forall x \in (0, 1).
\]
By the Lemma above, \(Y_n \overset{d}{=} \mu_n\) and \(Y \overset{d}{=} \mu\). To complete the proof, it remains to show that \(Y_n(x) \to Y(x)\) for all \(x \notin E\), where: \[
E = \{ t \in (0, 1) : F^\leftarrow(t) < F^\rightarrow(t) \}.
\] Since \(E\) is countable, \(\lambda(E) = 0\), which proves \(Y_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} Y\).

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
50.6 Application: The Continuous Mapping Theorem
Skorohod’s representation theorem allows us to easily transfer continuous functional properties to weak limit theorems.

Corollary 50.2 (Continuous Mapping Theorem) Let \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a Borel-measurable function, and let \(X_n\) (\(n \ge 1\)) and \(X\) be real-valued random variables, not necessarily defined on a common probability space. Write \(\text{Disc}(f)\) for the set of discontinuity points of \(f\), and \(\mu_X\) for the law of \(X\). Suppose \[
X_n \xrightarrow{d} X
\quad (\text{i.e., } \mu_{X_n} \Rightarrow \mu_X),
\qquad
\mu_X\left(\text{Disc}(f)\right) = 0.
\]

Weak Convergence: \(f(X_n) \xrightarrow{d} f(X)\).
Expectation Limit: If \(f\) is additionally bounded, then \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_n)] \to \mathbb{E}[f(X)]\).


Two remarks on the hypotheses:

First, the condition \(\mu_X\left(\text{Disc}(f)\right) = 0\) is meaningful because \(\text{Disc}(f)\) is always a Borel set: it is the \(F_\sigma\) set \(\bigcup_{k \ge 1}\left\{x : \operatorname{osc} f(x) \ge 1/k\right\}\), and each oscillation set is closed.
Second, the hypothesis is intrinsic to the law of \(X\), which is why the \(X_n\) and \(X\) need not share a probability space. Borel measurability of \(f\) ensures that \(f(X_n)\) and \(f(X)\) are themselves random variables, so that all expectations below are defined.


Proof (Proof of Corollary 50.2). Step 0: Skorohod Coupling:
Since \(X_n \xrightarrow{d} X\), Skorohod’s Representation Theorem provides a common probability space \(((0, 1), \mathcal{B}(0,1), \lambda)\) and random variables \((Y_n, Y)\) satisfying: \[
Y_n \overset{d}{=} X_n \quad \forall n, \qquad Y \overset{d}{=} X, \qquad \text{and} \qquad Y_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} Y.
\] That is, there exists a set \(\Omega_1 \subset (0,1)\) with \(\lambda(\Omega_1) = 1\) such that \(Y_n(\omega) \to Y(\omega)\) for all \(\omega \in \Omega_1\).
Step 1: The Composition \(g \circ f\) is Continuous \(\lambda\)-a.s. at \(Y\):
Let \(g \in C_b(\mathbb{R})\) be any bounded continuous test function. Since \(g\) is everywhere continuous, any point of continuity of \(f\) is also a point of continuity of \(g \circ f\): \[
x \in \text{Cont}(f) \implies g \circ f \text{ is continuous at } x \implies x \notin \text{Disc}(g \circ f).
\] Taking complements: \(\text{Disc}(g \circ f) \subseteq \text{Disc}(f)\). Therefore: \[
\lambda\left(Y^{-1}\left(\text{Disc}(g \circ f)\right)\right) = \mu_X\left(\text{Disc}(g \circ f)\right) \le \mu_X\left(\text{Disc}(f)\right) = 0,
\] where the first equality holds because \(\mathcal{L}(Y) = \mu_X\). So there exists \(\Omega_2 \subset (0,1)\) with \(\lambda(\Omega_2) = 1\) and \(Y(\omega) \notin \text{Disc}(g \circ f)\) for all \(\omega \in \Omega_2\). Note that \(\Omega_2\) depends on the chosen \(g\); this is harmless for Part 1, in which \(g\) stays fixed throughout Steps 1–5.
Step 2: Pointwise A.S. Convergence of \(g \circ f\):
The set \(\Omega^* := \Omega_1 \cap \Omega_2\) satisfies \(\lambda(\Omega^*) = 1\). Fix any \(\omega \in \Omega^*\):

\(Y_n(\omega) \to Y(\omega)\) (since \(\omega \in \Omega_1\)).
\(g \circ f\) is continuous at \(Y(\omega)\) (since \(\omega \in \Omega_2\)).

By the definition of continuity, \(y_n \to y\) and \(h\) continuous at \(y\) implies \(h(y_n) \to h(y)\). Applying this with \(y_n = Y_n(\omega)\), \(y = Y(\omega)\), \(h = g \circ f\): \[(g \circ f)(Y_n(\omega)) \longrightarrow (g \circ f)(Y(\omega)).\] Since this holds for all \(\omega \in \Omega^*\): \[
(g \circ f)(Y_n) \xrightarrow{a.s.} (g \circ f)(Y).
\]
Step 3: Dominated Convergence:
Since \(g \in C_b(\mathbb{R})\), there exists \(M < \infty\) with \(|g(y)| \le M\) for all \(y\). Thus: \[
|(g \circ f)(Y_n(\omega))| \le M \quad \text{for all } n \text{ and all } \omega \in (0,1).
\] The constant function \(M\) is integrable on \(((0,1), \lambda)\). By the Dominated Convergence Theorem: \[
\mathbb{E}_\lambda[(g \circ f)(Y_n)] \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}_\lambda[(g \circ f)(Y)].\]
Step 4: Transfer Back to \((X_n, X)\):
Since \(Y_n \overset{d}{=} X_n\), for any bounded Borel-measurable function \(h\): \[
\mathbb{E}_\lambda[h(Y_n)] = \int_{\mathbb{R}} h \, d\mu_{Y_n} = \int_{\mathbb{R}} h \, d\mu_{X_n} = \mathbb{E}[h(X_n)],
\] and similarly \(\mathbb{E}_\lambda[h(Y)] = \mathbb{E}[h(X)]\). Here \(\mathbb{E}_\lambda\) denotes expectation on the coupling space \(\left((0,1), \mathcal{B}((0,1)), \lambda\right)\), whereas \(\mathbb{E}\) denotes expectation on whichever space carries \(X_n\) (respectively \(X\)); the two are linked only through equality of laws. Applying this with \(h = g \circ f\), which is bounded and Borel: \[
\mathbb{E}[g(f(X_n))] = \mathbb{E}_\lambda[(g \circ f)(Y_n)] \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}_\lambda[(g \circ f)(Y)] = \mathbb{E}[g(f(X))].
\]
Step 5: Conclusion of Part 1:
Since \(g \in C_b(\mathbb{R})\) was arbitrary and \(\mathbb{E}[g(f(X_n))] \to \mathbb{E}[g(f(X))]\) for every such \(g\), the definition of weak convergence gives \(f(X_n) \xrightarrow{d} f(X)\).
Step 6: Part 2 — Bounded \(f\) Implies \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_n)] \to \mathbb{E}[f(X)]\):
Suppose \(|f| \le M\) for some \(M < \infty\). We must not reuse the set \(\Omega^*\) of Step 2: that set was built to make \(g \circ f\) continuous at \(Y(\omega)\), which does not imply that \(f\) itself is continuous there (see the warning below). Instead, define a new full-measure set directly from the hypothesis: \[
\Omega_f := \Omega_1 \cap \left\{ \omega \in (0,1) : Y(\omega) \notin \text{Disc}(f) \right\}.
\] Since \(\mathcal{L}(Y) = \mu_X\) and \(\mu_X\left(\text{Disc}(f)\right) = 0\), the second set has \(\lambda\)-measure \(1\); hence \(\lambda(\Omega_f) = 1\).
For every \(\omega \in \Omega_f\) we have \(Y_n(\omega) \to Y(\omega)\) and \(f\) is continuous at \(Y(\omega)\), so \(f(Y_n(\omega)) \to f(Y(\omega))\). Hence: \[
f(Y_n) \xrightarrow{a.s.} f(Y).
\] The uniform bound \(|f(Y_n)| \le M\) provides a dominating function, integrable because \(\lambda\) is a probability measure, so by DCT: \[
\mathbb{E}_\lambda[f(Y_n)] \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}_\lambda[f(Y)].
\] Transferring back via Step 4 (with \(h = f\), which is bounded Borel): \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_n)] = \mathbb{E}_\lambda[f(Y_n)] \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}_\lambda[f(Y)] = \mathbb{E}[f(X)].
\]







WarningWhy Part 2 needs its own full-measure set



The inclusion established in Step 1 is \[
\text{Disc}(g \circ f) \subseteq \text{Disc}(f),
\] and it runs in the wrong direction for deducing continuity of \(f\) from continuity of \(g \circ f\). The inclusion can be strict in the extreme: if \(g \equiv c\) is constant, then \(g \circ f\) is continuous everywhere, so \(\text{Disc}(g \circ f) = \emptyset\) and \(\Omega_2 = (0,1)\), no matter how badly discontinuous \(f\) may be. Nor can one simply take \(g = \text{id}\), since \(\text{id} \notin C_b(\mathbb{R})\) — and boundedness of \(g\) is exactly what supplied the dominating constant in Step 3. This is why Part 2 is proved using \(\Omega_f\), which invokes the hypothesis \(\mu_X\left(\text{Disc}(f)\right) = 0\) directly.



Example 50.4 (Absolute deviation around a threshold) Suppose \(X_n\sim N\left(c_n,1\right)\), where \(c_n=1+\frac1n\) so that \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\), where \(X\sim N(1,1)\). Consider the function \[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
(x-1)^2, & x\leq 1,\\
2(x-1)^2+1, & x>1.
\end{cases}
\] This function is discontinuous at \(x=1\) because \[
\lim_{x\uparrow1}f(x)=0, \qquad \lim_{x\downarrow1}f(x)=1.
\] Thus \(\operatorname{Disc}(f)=\{1\}\). But the limiting random variable \(X\sim N(1,1)\) has a continuous distribution, so \(P(X=1)=0\). Consequently, \(\mu_X(\operatorname{Disc}(f))=0\). The Continuous Mapping Theorem therefore gives \(f(X_n)\xrightarrow{d}f(X)\).
What does the transformed distribution look like? The transformation is \[
f(X_n) = (X_n-1)^2\mathbf 1\{X_n\leq1\} + \left[2(X_n-1)^2+1\right]\mathbf 1\{X_n>1\}.
\] The transformation treats observations differently depending on whether they fall below or above the threshold 1. Nevertheless, \(X_n\xrightarrow d X\) is enough to conclude that the entire transformed random variable converges in distribution: \[
\begin{aligned}
&(X_n-1)^2\mathbf 1\{X_n\leq1\} + [2(X_n-1)^2+1]\mathbf 1\{X_n>1\} \\
&\xrightarrow d
(X-1)^2\mathbf 1\{X\leq1\} + [2(X-1)^2+1]\mathbf 1\{X>1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 83  Lecture 38.2: Time-Homogeneous Markov Processes
text:
83.1 Introduction and Motivation
In time-homogeneous processes, transition kernels depend on time \(s\) and \(t\) only through the time elapsed \(t - s\). We illustrate this via two standard motivating examples before formalizing operator semigroups and transition dynamics.

title: 83  Lecture 38.2: Time-Homogeneous Markov Processes
text:
Example 83.1 (Poisson Process Transition Kernel) Consider a Poisson process \((N_t)_{t \ge 0}\) with intensity parameter \(\lambda > 0\). The transition kernel \(q_{s,t}(n, B)\) for \(s \le t\), \(n \in \mathbb{N}_0\), and \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{N}_0)\) is given by \[
q_{s,t}(n, B) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbf{1}_B(n + N_t - N_s) \right] = \sum_{m \in B} \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda(t - s))(\{m - n\}).
\] Since the distribution of \(N_t - N_s\) is \(\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda(t - s))\), \(q_{s,t}\) depends on \(s\) and \(t\) solely through the difference \(t - s\), so \(q_{s,t} = q_{0, t-s}\).


Example 83.2 ((Pre-) Brownian Motion Transition Kernel) Consider a (pre-) Brownian motion \((B_t)_{t \ge 0}\). Its transition kernel \(q_{s,t}(x, A)\) for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) is \[
q_{s,t}(x, A) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbf{1}_A(x + B_t - B_s) \right].
\] Because \(B_t - B_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t - s)\), the transition kernel \(q_{s,t}\) depends on \(s, t\) only through \(t - s\).

title: 83  Lecture 38.2: Time-Homogeneous Markov Processes
text:
83.2 Time Homogeneity and One-Parameter Semigroups
Throughout, \(T\) denotes the totally ordered index set with least element \(0\) fixed in Lecture 38.1 (e.g. \(T = [0,\infty)\) or \(T = \mathbb{N}_0\)), so that for \(s \le t \in T\) the difference \(t - s\) and, for \(s,t\ge0\), the sum \(s+t\) again lie in \(T\). We also recall from Lectures 37.1–38.1 that any family of Markov transition operators \(\{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t \in T}\) on \((S,\mathcal{B}(S))\) is assumed to satisfy the (general, not-yet-homogeneous) Chapman-Kolmogorov equations \[
Q_{r,s} Q_{s,t} = Q_{r,t}, \quad \forall r \le s \le t \in T.
\tag{83.1}\]

Definition 83.1 (Time-Homogeneous Markov Transition Operators) Let \(\{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t \in T}\) be a collection of Markov transition operators on \((S, \mathcal{B}(S))\) satisfying Equation 83.1. The collection is called time-homogeneous if \[
Q_{s,t} = Q_{0, t-s} =: Q_{t-s}, \quad \forall s \le t \in T.
\tag{83.2}\]

Under time homogeneity, the general Chapman-Kolmogorov equation Equation 83.1 forces the single-index family \((Q_r)_{r\ge0}\) to satisfy the semigroup law: substituting \(Q_{r,s}=Q_{s-r}\), \(Q_{s,t}=Q_{t-s}\), and \(Q_{r,t}=Q_{t-r}\) into Equation 83.1 gives \[
Q_{s-r} Q_{t-s} = Q_{r,s} Q_{s,t} \overset{\text{(CK)}}{=} Q_{r,t} = Q_{t-r} = Q_{(s-r) + (t-s)},
\] where (CK) marks the use of the general Chapman-Kolmogorov equation Equation 83.1 — the only non-notational step in the chain, since the remaining equalities are either the time-homogeneity substitution or the trivial arithmetic identity \((s-r)+(t-s)=t-r\). Writing \(a := s-r \ge 0\) and \(b := t - s \ge 0\) (which range over all of \(T\cap[0,\infty)\) as \(r,s,t\) vary), we obtain \(Q_a Q_b = Q_{a+b}\). In other words, time homogeneity together with the general Chapman-Kolmogorov equations implies (rather than merely relabels) the one-parameter semigroup property defined next.

Definition 83.2 (One-Parameter Transition Semigroup) A collection \((Q_t)_{t \in T, t \ge 0}\) of Markov transition operators on \(\mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}(S))\) (i.e. bounded linear operators with \(Q_t f \ge 0\) whenever \(f \ge 0\), and \(Q_t \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}\)) satisfying \[
Q_s Q_t = Q_{s+t} \quad \text{and} \quad Q_0 = \mathrm{Id}
\tag{83.3}\] is called a 1-parameter (transition) semigroup.


Definition 83.3 (Time-Homogeneous Markov Process) A Markov process \((X_t)_{t \in T}\) with transition operators \(\{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t \in T}\) is called a time-homogeneous Markov process if \(\{Q_{s,t}\}\) is time-homogeneous in the sense of Definition 83.1. By the computation above, the induced single-index family \((Q_t)_{t \ge 0} := (Q_{0,t})_{t \ge 0}\) then automatically forms a 1-parameter semigroup in the sense of Definition 83.2, which we call the transition semigroup of the process.


Remark 83.1 (Intuitive Interpretation). By definition of the transition operators (Lecture 38.1) together with time homogeneity, for every \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\) and \(s \le t \in T\) we have the exact identity \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = (Q_{t-s} f)(X_s),
\] or equivalently, shifting by \(s\): \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X_{s+t}) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = (Q_t f)(X_s).
\] (Theorem 83.1 below gives the rigorous generalization of this identity to arbitrary bounded measurable functionals of the whole future path, not just single-time functionals \(f(X_t)\).) Informally, \(Q_t\) determines the state distribution at time \(t\) given \(X_0\). For \(X_{t+s}\) given \(X_0\), the evolution decomposes via \(Q_tQ_s=Q_sQ_t\) (the two operators commute since \(Q_aQ_b=Q_{a+b}=Q_bQ_a\)), corresponding to evaluating a new process \(\tilde{X}_t\) given \(X_s\).

title: 83  Lecture 38.2: Time-Homogeneous Markov Processes
section: 83.3 Canonical Process Notation and Measures on Path Space
text:
83.3 Canonical Process Notation and Measures on Path Space
For any time-homogeneous Markov process, all finite-dimensional distributions are uniquely determined by:

The initial distribution \(\nu = \mathrm{Law}(X_0) \in \mathcal{P}(S, \mathcal{B})\);
The transition semigroup \((Q_t)_{t \in T}\).

Thinking of the process as a measure on the path space \(S^T\), we fix the transition semigroup \((Q_t)_{t \in T}\) and consider the family of probability measures \(\{\mathbb{P}^\nu\}_{\nu \in \mathcal{P}(S,\mathcal{B})}\) corresponding to different starting distributions \(\nu\).
Notation:

Let \(X_\cdot = (X_t)_{t \in T}\) denote the canonical process ensemble.
For a bounded, measurable functional \(F \in \mathcal{B}_b(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\), \(\mathbb{E}^\nu[F(X_\cdot)]\) denotes the expected value of \(F(X_\cdot)\) under the law where \(X_0 \sim \nu\).
In the Dirac case where \(\nu = \delta_x\) for \(x \in S\), we write \(\mathbb{E}^x\) and \(\mathbb{P}^x\). \(\mathbb{P}^x\) is the law of the process started at \(x\). The superscript \(x\) in \(\mathbb{E}^x\) specifies the initial condition: under \(\mathbb{P}^x = \mathbb{P}^{\delta_x}\), the process begins at \(x\) with certainty (\(X_0 = x\) almost surely).
\(g(x) = \mathbb{E}^x[F(X_\cdot)]\) is simply: start the process at \(x\), run it forward in time, apply \(F\) to the resulting path, and take the expected value. Doing this for every \(x \in S\) produces a function \(g : S \to \mathbb{R}\). It tells you, for each possible starting state, how large \(F\) is expected to be along the path.
Before you can write “\(g(X_t)\)” in the following theorem, we need \(g\) to be a measurable function \(S \to \mathbb{R}\). Otherwise, composing \(g\) with the random variable \(X_t\) doesn’t produce a well-defined random variable. Statement 1 in Theorem 83.1 guarantees exactly this.
Statement 2 of the following theorem is: \(\mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}[F(X_{t+\cdot}) \mid X_t] = g(X_t), \quad \mathbb{P}^{\nu_0}\text{-a.s.}\) This should be read as: to compute the conditional expectation of any path functional of the future trajectory, you don’t need to know the full past — you just evaluate \(g\) at the current state. The entire job of the conditional expectation is done by the single function \(g\) evaluated at one point.

title: 83  Lecture 38.2: Time-Homogeneous Markov Processes
section: 83.4 Main Shift-Invariance and Conditional Expectation Theorem
text:
83.4 Main Shift-Invariance and Conditional Expectation Theorem

Theorem 83.1 (Shift Property and Measurability of Markov Expectations) Let \(X_\cdot\) be a time-homogeneous Markov process taking values in a measurable state space \((S, \mathcal{B}(S))\) with transition semigroup \((Q_t)_{t \ge 0}\). Let \(F \in \mathcal{B}_b(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\). Then:

The mapping \(S \ni x \mapsto \mathbb{E}^x[F(X_\cdot)]\) is \(\mathcal{B}(S) / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\)-measurable.
For all \(t \ge 0\) and any initial distribution \(\nu_0 \in \mathcal{P}(S, \mathcal{B}(S))\), \[
\mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}\left[ F(X_{t+\cdot}) \mid \mathcal{F}_t \right] = \mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}\left[ F(X_{t+\cdot}) \mid X_t \right] = \mathbb{E}^{X_t}[F(X_\cdot)], \quad \mathbb{P}^{\nu_0}\text{-a.s.}
\tag{83.4}\] where \(g(x) := \mathbb{E}^x[F(X_\cdot)]\) and \(g(X_t) = \mathbb{E}^{X_t}[F(X_\cdot)]\).



Remark 83.2 (What the theorem actually says). 

At the level of a single observable \(f(X_{s+t})\), time homogeneity already gives you the familiar identity \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_{s+t}) \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = (Q_t f)(X_s)\). The shift property theorem lifts this to the entire future path at once: instead of just \(f(X_{s+t})\), you can take any bounded measurable functional \(F\) of the whole future trajectory \((X_{t+s})_{s \geq 0}\) — say, the supremum of the path, a stopping-time functional, a running integral — and the identity still holds. The conclusion is: \[
\mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}\!\left[F(X_{t+\cdot}) \mid \mathcal{F}_t\right] = \mathbb{E}^{X_t}[F(X_\cdot)], \quad \mathbb{P}^{\nu_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]
Statement 1 (measurability) is a prerequisite, not just a bonus. Before you can write \(\mathbb{E}^{X_t}[F(X_\cdot)]\) — i.e., evaluate the map \(x \mapsto \mathbb{E}^x[F(X_\cdot)]\) at the random variable \(X_t\) — you need to know that this map is measurable, otherwise the composition isn’t a well-defined random variable. The theorem guarantees this first, making the right-hand side of the equation meaningful. Notice also that measurability holds for any measurable transition kernel family and does not itself require time homogeneity.
Statement 2 is where time homogeneity plays its role. The first equality (conditioning on \(\mathcal{F}_t\) is the same as conditioning on \(X_t\)) is just the Markov property. The second equality — that the conditional expectation equals \(\mathbb{E}^{X_t}[F(X_\cdot)]\) — is genuinely using time homogeneity. Because the transition kernels from time \(t\) onward coincide with those of a fresh process started at \(X_t\) from time \(0\), the law of the future path \((X_{t+s})_{s \geq 0}\) given \(X_t = x\) is exactly the same as the law of \((X_s)_{s \geq 0}\) under \(\mathbb{P}^x\).
The restart interpretation: The theorem is the rigorous statement of: a time-homogeneous Markov process restarts from scratch at any fixed time \(t\), with the current state \(X_t\) as the new initial condition, and this holds not just for observations at a single future time, but for the entire future path at once. \(\mathbb{E}^{X_t}[F(X_\cdot)]\) should literally be read as “run a fresh copy of the process starting at \(X_t\), and apply \(F\) to that copy’s trajectory.” The theorem says this equals the conditional expectation of \(F\) applied to the actual time-shifted path.

title: 83  Lecture 38.2: Time-Homogeneous Markov Processes
text:
83.5 Proof of the Main Theorem

Proof (Step 1: Reduction to Local \(\sigma\)-Algebras). Recall \(\mathcal{F}_t\) denotes a filtration to which \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) is adapted and Markov, and \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge t}^X := \sigma(X_u : u \ge t)\) denotes the future \(\sigma\)-algebra from time \(t\) onward (Lecture 36.1). Observe that \(F(X_{t+\cdot}) \in \mathcal{B}(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_{\ge t}^X)\), since \(F(X_{t+\cdot})\) is a (pointwise) limit of functions depending only on finitely many coordinates \(X_u\), \(u \ge t\). As established in Theorem 78.1 (Lecture 36.1), if \(Y\) is a bounded \(\mathcal{F}_{\ge t}^X\)-measurable random variable, then by the Markov property: \[
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X_t].
\] Applying this to \(Y = F(X_{t+\cdot})\) directly yields the first equality in Equation 83.4: \[
\mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}\left[ F(X_{t+\cdot}) \mid \mathcal{F}_t \right] = \mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}\left[ F(X_{t+\cdot}) \mid X_t \right].
\]

83.5.1 Step 2: Proof for Cylinder Functions
It remains to prove the second equality in Equation 83.4, \(\mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}[F(X_{t+\cdot}) \mid X_t] = \mathbb{E}^{X_t}[F(X_\cdot)]\), together with statement 1, for general \(F \in \mathcal{B}_b(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\). We reduce to cylinder functions via Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem (Theorem 29.1, Lecture 14.1), exactly as in the proof of Theorem 78.1 (Lecture 36.1):

Let \(\mathbb{M}\) be the collection of functions \[
F(w) = f_0(w(t_0)) f_1(w(t_1)) \cdots f_n(w(t_n)),
\tag{83.5}\] where \(0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_n\) and \(f_j \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) for \(j = 0, \dots, n\). As in Lemma 78.1 (Lecture 36.1), \(\mathbb{M}\) is closed under pointwise products (merge coincident time points and multiply the corresponding factors) and \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) = \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\): taking \(n=0\) recovers every generator \(\{X_0 \in A\}\), and padding with \(f_0 \equiv 1\) recovers every generator \(\{X_t \in A\}\) for \(t > 0\), \(A \in \mathcal{B}\). Hence \(\mathbb{M}\) is a multiplicative system generating \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\).
Let \(\mathbb{H} := \{F \in \mathcal{B}_b(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}) : \text{statements 1 and 2 hold for } F\}\). \(\mathbb{H}\) is a vector space (both statements are linear in \(F\)) containing the constant function \(1\) (both sides of statement 2 reduce to \(1\), and \(x \mapsto 1\) is trivially measurable). \(\mathbb{H}\) is closed under bounded convergence: if \(F_k \in \mathbb{H}\), \(|F_k| \le C\), and \(F_k \to F\) pointwise, then for each fixed \(x\), \(g_k(x) := \mathbb{E}^x[F_k(X_\cdot)] \to \mathbb{E}^x[F(X_\cdot)] =: g(x)\) by (ordinary) bounded convergence under \(\mathbb{P}^x\), so \(g\) is measurable as a pointwise limit of measurable functions (statement 1), and \(g_k(X_t) \to g(X_t)\) everywhere on \(\Omega\); combined with the Conditional Dominated Convergence Theorem applied to \(F_k(X_{t+\cdot}) \to F(X_{t+\cdot})\) (boundedly), the identities \(\mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}[F_k(X_{t+\cdot}) \mid X_t] = g_k(X_t)\) pass to the limit to give \(\mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}[F(X_{t+\cdot}) \mid X_t] = g(X_t)\) a.s. (statement 2).

By Theorem 29.1, if \(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}\) then \(\mathbb{H} = \mathcal{B}_b(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\). It therefore suffices to establish statements 1 and 2 for cylinder functions \(F \in \mathbb{M}\) of the form Equation 83.5.

83.5.1.1 Proof of Statement 1 (Measurability)
For \(F\) given by Equation 83.5: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}^x[F(X_\cdot)] &= \mathbb{E}^x\left[ f_0(X_{t_0}) f_1(X_{t_1}) \cdots f_n(X_{t_n}) \right] \\
&= \int \delta_x(\mathrm{d}x_0) \int q_{t_0, t_1}(x_0, \mathrm{d}x_1) \cdots \int q_{t_{n-1}, t_n}(x_{n-1}, \mathrm{d}x_n) f_0(x_0) \cdots f_n(x_n) \\
&= f_0(x) \left( Q_{t_0, t_1} \left( f_1 \cdots Q_{t_{n-1}, t_n} f_n \right) \right)(x).
\end{aligned}
\] Because transition operators map bounded measurable functions to bounded measurable functions, \(x \mapsto \mathbb{E}^x[F(X_\cdot)]\) is a composition of measurable functions, hence \(\mathcal{B}(S)/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\)-measurable. \(\checkmark\)


83.5.1.2 Proof of Statement 2 (Conditional Shift Property)
We wish to show that \(\mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}[F(X_{t+\cdot}) \mid X_t] = g(X_t)\) \(\mathbb{P}^{\nu_0}\)-a.s., where \(g(x) := \mathbb{E}^x[F(X_\cdot)]\).
For \(F(X_{t+\cdot}) = f_0(X_t) f_1(X_{t + t_1}) \cdots f_n(X_{t + t_n})\), let \(h \in \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B})\) be an arbitrary test function. Evaluating the joint expectation yields: \[
\begin{aligned}
I &:= \mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}\left[ h(X_t) F(X_{t+\cdot}) \right] = \mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}\left[ h(X_t) f_0(X_t) f_1(X_{t+t_1}) \cdots f_n(X_{t+t_n}) \right] \\
&= \int \nu_0(\mathrm{d}x_{-1}) \int q_{0, t}(x_{-1}, \mathrm{d}x_0) \int q_{t, t+t_1}(x_0, \mathrm{d}x_1) \cdots \\
& \quad \quad \cdots \int q_{t+t_{n-1}, t+t_n}(x_{n-1}, \mathrm{d}x_n) h(x_0) f_0(x_0) f_1(x_1) \cdots f_n(x_n).
\end{aligned}
\]
By time homogeneity (the initial kernel \(q_{0,t} = q_t\), and \(q_{t+t_{j-1}, t+t_j} = q_{0, t_j - t_{j-1}} = q_{t_j - t_{j-1}}\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n\)) and using the marginal distribution \(\nu_t(\mathrm{d}x_0) := \int \nu_0(\mathrm{d}x_{-1}) q_t(x_{-1}, \mathrm{d}x_0) = \mathrm{Law}(X_t)\), we rewrite \(I\) as: \[
\begin{aligned}
I &= \int \nu_t(\mathrm{d}x_0) h(x_0) f_0(x_0) \int q_{t_1}(x_0, \mathrm{d}x_1) \cdots \int q_{t_n - t_{n-1}}(x_{n-1}, \mathrm{d}x_n) f_1(x_1) \cdots f_n(x_n) \\
&= \int \nu_t(\mathrm{d}x_0) h(x_0) \underbrace{\mathbb{E}^{x_0}\left[ f_0(X_0) f_1(X_{t_1}) \cdots f_n(X_{t_n}) \right]}_{= \mathbb{E}^{x_0}[F(X_\cdot)] = g(x_0)} \\
&= \int \nu_t(\mathrm{d}x_0) h(x_0) g(x_0) \\
&= \mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}\left[ h(X_t) \mathbb{E}^{X_t}[F(X_\cdot)] \right].
\end{aligned}
\] Since \(\mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}[h(X_t) F(X_{t+\cdot})] = \mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}[h(X_t) g(X_t)]\) holds for all bounded measurable test functions \(h\), and \(g(X_t)\) is \(\sigma(X_t)\)-measurable, by definition of conditional expectation we conclude: \[
\mathbb{E}^{\nu_0}\left[ F(X_{t+\cdot}) \mid X_t \right] = g(X_t) = \mathbb{E}^{X_t}[F(X_\cdot)], \quad \mathbb{P}^{\nu_0}\text{-a.s.} \quad \blacksquare
\]

83.6 Items Requiring Verification

Dummy Variable Indexing in Proof Step 2: In the handwritten integration, the initial measure step uses \(x_{-1}\) and \(x_0\) to cleanly separate the integral producing \(\nu_t(\mathrm{d}x_0)\). This notation has been rendered rigorously above.

title: 84  Lecture 39.1: Markov Matrix
text:
84.1 Discrete-Time Homogeneous Markov Processes
We consider discrete time parameter spaces \(T = \mathbb{N}_0 = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\).
In discrete time, the Chapman-Kolmogorov equations simplify to operator iteration: \[
Q_{n+m} = Q_n Q_m, \quad \forall n, m \in \mathbb{N}_0.
\tag{84.1}\]
By induction (with base case \(Q_0 = \mathrm{Id} = Q_1^0\), recall Lecture 38.2), for any \(n \in \mathbb{N}_0\), the \(n\)-step transition operator \(Q_n\) is the \(n\)-fold composition of the single 1-step transition operator \(Q_1\): \[
Q_n = Q_1 Q_{n-1} = Q_1 Q_1 Q_{n-2} = \dots = Q_1^n.
\tag{84.2}\]
Thus, the entire discrete-time homogeneous dynamics is governed by iterating a single transition operator: \[
Q_1 : \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}) \to \mathcal{B}_b(S, \mathcal{B}).
\tag{84.3}\]

title: 84  Lecture 39.1: Markov Matrix
text:
Example 84.1 (Discrete Random Walk) Let \((\xi_k)_{k=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with common distribution \(\mu_{\xi_1} = \mathrm{Law}(\xi_1)\). Define the random walk \(X_0 = 0\) and \[
X_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \xi_k, \quad n \ge 1.
\tag{84.4}\]
For any bounded measurable function \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{R}^d)\), the 1-step operator \(Q_1\) acts as (using that the increment \(\xi_1\) is independent of the starting point, i.e. translation invariance of the walk): \[
\begin{aligned}
(Q_1 f)(x) &= \mathbb{E}[f(x + X_1 - X_0)] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[f(x + \xi_1)] \\
&= \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(x + y) \, \mu_{\xi_1}(\mathrm{d}y).
\end{aligned}
\tag{84.5}\]
Special Case (Simple Random Walk on \(\mathbb{Z}\)): If \(S = \mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mu_{\xi_1} = p \delta_1 + (1-p) \delta_{-1}\) with \(p \in (0, 1)\), then: \[
(Q_1 f)(x) = p f(x + 1) + (1 - p) f(x - 1).
\tag{84.6}\] This walk is symmetric precisely when \(p = 1/2\) (cf. Lecture 18.2); for \(p \ne 1/2\) it has nonzero drift \(\mathbb{E}[\xi_1] = 2p - 1 \ne 0\) and is transient.

title: 84  Lecture 39.1: Markov Matrix
text:
84.2 Discrete State Space: Markov Chains
When the state space \(S\) is countable (or finite), equipped with the discrete \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B} = 2^S\), the transition kernel simplifies to transition probabilities: \[
q_{n,m}(x, B) = \sum_{y \in B} q_{n,m}(x, y), \quad x \in S, \, B \subseteq S.
\tag{84.7}\]
For \(n < m\), the multi-step transition probability \(q_{n,m}(x, y) = \mathbb{P}(X_m = y \mid X_n = x)\) expands across intermediate paths \(y_{n+1}, \dots, y_{m-1} \in S\) as: \[
q_{n,m}(x, y) = \sum_{y_{n+1}, \dots, y_{m-1} \in S} q_{n, n+1}(x, y_{n+1}) q_{n+1, n+2}(y_{n+1}, y_{n+2}) \dots q_{m-1, m}(y_{m-1}, y),
\tag{84.8}\] with the convention that the (empty) sum is omitted when \(m = n+1\), so that Equation 84.8 reduces to \(q_{n,n+1}(x,y)\) in that case.

Example 84.2 (Ehrenfest Urn Model) Consider an urn containing \(N\) total particles separated by a semipermeable membrane. Let \(X_n \in S = \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\) represent the number of particles on the left side of the urn at time \(n\).
At each step \(n \to n+1\), a particle is selected uniformly at random from the entire urn and moved to the opposite side of the membrane.
We model \((X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0}\) as a time-homogeneous Markov process. The 1-step transition kernel \(q_1(i, j) = q_{n, n+1}(i, j) = \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i)\) is: \[
q_1(i, j) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{i}{N}, & \text{if } j = i - 1, \\[1ex]
1 - \dfrac{i}{N}, & \text{if } j = i + 1, \\[1ex]
0, & \text{if } |i - j| \ne 1.
\end{cases}
\tag{84.9}\]


Remark 84.1 (Terminological Conventions). If \((X_t)_{t \in T}\) is a Markov process taking values in a discrete state space \(S\), it is typically called a Markov Chain.

Some authors define a discrete-time process \((X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0}\) as a Markov Chain regardless of whether the state space is discrete or continuous.
By standard convention, a continuous-time process \((X_t)_{t \ge 0}\) with continuous state space is usually called a continuous Markov process rather than a Markov chain.

title: 84  Lecture 39.1: Markov Matrix
text:
84.3 Transition Matrices and Finite-Dimensional Distributions
For discrete state spaces \(S\), let \(\nu_k\) denote the probability mass function (PMF) of \(X_k\), represented as a row vector \(\boldsymbol{\nu}_k\): \[
\nu_k(i) = \mathbb{P}(X_k = i), \quad i \in S.
\tag{84.10}\]
The 1-step transition probabilities define an \(S \times S\) matrix \(P = (P_{ij})_{i, j \in S}\) where: \[
P_{ij} = q_1(i, j) = \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i).
\tag{84.11}\]
The \(n\)-step transition probability \(q_n(i, j) = \mathbb{P}(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i)\) corresponds to matrix multiplication: \[
q_n(i, j) = \sum_{k_1, k_2, \dots, k_{n-1} \in S} P_{i, k_1} P_{k_1, k_2} \dots P_{k_{n-1}, j} = [P^n]_{ij}.
\tag{84.12}\]
Consequently, the marginal distribution at step \(n\) is obtained via row-vector matrix multiplication: \[
\nu_n(j) = \sum_{i \in S} \nu_0(i) \mathbb{P}(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i) = [\boldsymbol{\nu}_0 P^n]_j.
\tag{84.13}\]

Remark 84.2 (Beyond Marginal Distributions). Marginal distributions \(\boldsymbol{\nu}_n = \boldsymbol{\nu}_0 P^n\) capture only part of the Markov chain structure. Multi-time joint distributions (finite-dimensional distributions) utilize the Markov property explicitly. For example, for \(n < m\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X_n = j, X_m = k) &= \mathbb{P}(X_m = k \mid X_n = j) \mathbb{P}(X_n = j) \\
&= [\boldsymbol{\nu}_0 P^n]_j [P^{m-n}]_{jk}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{84.14}\]

title: 84  Lecture 39.1: Markov Matrix
text:
84.4 Stochastic Matrices and Graph Representation

Definition 84.1 (Stochastic Matrix) Let \(S\) be countable (or finite), as fixed in the preceding section. A matrix \(P = (P_{ij})_{i,j \in S}\) is called a stochastic matrix (or Markov matrix) if:

\(P_{ij} \ge 0\) for all \(i, j \in S\);
\(\sum_{j \in S} P_{ij} = 1\) for all \(i \in S\) (rows sum to 1).

Conversely, every stochastic matrix \(P\) arises as the transition matrix of some discrete-time Markov chain: given any initial distribution \(\nu_0\) on \(S\), the formulas Equation 84.12 and Equation 84.13 define a consistent family of finite-dimensional distributions on \(S^{\mathbb{N}_0}\), so the Kolmogorov extension theorem (Lecture 16 / 37.2) yields a probability measure on \(S^{\mathbb{N}_0}\) under which the coordinate process \((X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0}\) is a Markov chain with transition matrix \(P\) and \(\mathrm{Law}(X_0) = \nu_0\).

In the finite state space setting, the transition dynamics can be visualized as a directed, weighted (looped) graph \(G = (V, E)\) where vertices \(V = S\) represent states, and directed edges \((i, j) \in E\) bear weights \(P_{ij} = \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i)\).

Remark 84.3. In the time-homogeneous setting, edge labels \(P_{ij}\) remain constant across all time steps \(n \to n + 1\). In a time-inhomogeneous setting, arrow labels would depend on \(n\).

These have been rendered as a standard ASCII structural graph.
