title: 85  Lecture 39.2: Markov Generator
text:
85.1 Continuous-Time Semigroups and Matrix Exponential
In continuous time \(T = [0, \infty)\), the Chapman-Kolmogorov equations take the semigroup form: \[
Q_{t+s} = Q_t Q_s, \quad Q_0 = \mathrm{Id}.
\tag{85.1}\]
This semigroup property \(Q_{t+s} = Q_t Q_s\) is strongly suggestive of the exponential function \(e^{tA}\).

title: 48  Lecture 39.1: Markov Matrix
text:
Example 48.1 (Discrete Random Walk) Let \((\xi_k)_{k=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with common distribution \(\mu_{\xi_1} = \mathrm{Law}(\xi_1)\). Define the random walk \(X_0 = 0\) and \[
X_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \xi_k, \quad n \ge 1.
\tag{48.4}\]
For any bounded measurable function \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{R}^d)\), the 1-step operator \(Q_1\) acts as: \[
(Q_1 f)(x) = \mathbb{E}[f(x + X_1 - X_0)] = \mathbb{E}[f(x + \xi_1)] = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(x + y) \, \mu_{\xi_1}(\mathrm{d}y).
\tag{48.5}\]
Special Case (Simple Symmetric Random Walk on \(\mathbb{Z}\)): If \(S = \mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mu_{\xi_1} = p \delta_1 + (1-p) \delta_{-1}\) with \(p \in (0, 1)\), then: \[
(Q_1 f)(x) = p f(x + 1) + (1 - p) f(x - 1).
\tag{48.6}\]

title: 48  Lecture 39.1: Markov Matrix
text:
48.2 Discrete State Space: Markov Chains
When the state space \(S\) is countable (or finite), equipped with the discrete \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F} = 2^S\), the transition kernel simplifies to transition probabilities[cite: 2]: \[
q_{n,m}(x, B) = \sum_{y \in B} q_{n,m}(x, y), \quad x \in S, \, B \subseteq S.
\tag{48.7}\]
The multi-step transition probability \(q_{n,m}(x, y) = \mathbb{P}(X_m = y \mid X_n = x)\) expands across intermediate paths \(y_{n+1}, \dots, y_{m-1} \in S\) as[cite: 2]: \[
q_{n,m}(x, y) = \sum_{y_{n+1}, \dots, y_{m-1} \in S} q_{n, n+1}(x, y_{n+1}) q_{n+1, n+2}(y_{n+1}, y_{n+2}) \dots q_{m-1, m}(y_{m-1}, y).
\tag{48.8}\]

Example 48.2 (Ehrenfest Urn Model) Consider an urn containing \(N\) total particles separated by a semipermeable membrane[cite: 2]. Let \(X_n \in S = \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\) represent the number of particles on the left side of the urn at time \(n\)[cite: 2].
At each step \(n \to n+1\), a particle is selected uniformly at random from the entire urn and moved to the opposite side of the membrane[cite: 2].
We model \((X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0}\) as a time-homogeneous Markov process[cite: 2]. The 1-step transition kernel \(q_1(i, j) = q_{n, n+1}(i, j) = \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i)\) is[cite: 2]: \[
q_1(i, j) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{i}{N}, & \text{if } j = i - 1, \\[1ex]
1 - \dfrac{i}{N}, & \text{if } j = i + 1, \\[1ex]
0, & \text{if } |i - j| \ne 1.
\end{cases}
\tag{48.9}\]


Remark 48.1 (Terminological Conventions). If \((X_t)_{t \in T}\) is a Markov process taking values in a discrete state space \(S\), it is typically called a Markov Chain[cite: 2].

Some authors define a discrete-time process \((X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0}\) as a Markov Chain regardless of whether the state space is discrete or continuous[cite: 2].
All authors agree that a continuous-time process \((X_t)_{t \ge 0}\) with continuous state space is a continuous Markov process (not a Markov chain)[cite: 2].

title: 48  Lecture 39.1: Markov Matrix
text:
48.3 Transition Matrices and Finite-Dimensional Distributions
For discrete state spaces \(S\), let \(\nu_k\) denote the probability mass function (PMF) of \(X_k\), represented as a row vector \(\boldsymbol{\nu}_k\)[cite: 2]: \[
\nu_k(i) = \mathbb{P}(X_k = i), \quad i \in S.
\tag{48.10}\]
The 1-step transition probabilities define an \(S \times S\) matrix \(P = (P_{ij})_{i, j \in S}\) where[cite: 2]: \[
P_{ij} = q_1(i, j) = \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i).
\tag{48.11}\]
The \(n\)-step transition probability \(q_n(i, j) = \mathbb{P}(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i)\) corresponds to matrix multiplication[cite: 2]: \[
q_n(i, j) = \sum_{k_1, k_2, \dots, k_{n-1} \in S} P_{i, k_1} P_{k_1, k_2} \dots P_{k_{n-1}, j} = [P^n]_{ij}.
\tag{48.12}\]
Consequently, the marginal distribution at step \(n\) is obtained via row-vector matrix multiplication[cite: 2]: \[
\nu_n(j) = \sum_{i \in S} \nu_0(i) \mathbb{P}(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i) = [\boldsymbol{\nu}_0 P^n]_j.
\tag{48.13}\]

Remark 48.2 (Beyond Marginal Distributions). Marginal distributions \(\boldsymbol{\nu}_n = \boldsymbol{\nu}_0 P^n\) capture only part of the Markov chain structure[cite: 2]. Multi-time joint distributions (finite-dimensional distributions) utilize the Markov property explicitly[cite: 2]. For example, for \(n < m\)[cite: 2]: \[
\mathbb{P}(X_n = j, X_m = k) = \mathbb{P}(X_m = k \mid X_n = j) \mathbb{P}(X_n = j) = [\boldsymbol{\nu}_0 P^n]_j [P^{m-n}]_{jk}.
\tag{48.14}\]

title: 48  Lecture 39.1: Markov Matrix
text:
48.4 Stochastic Matrices and Graph Representation

Definition 48.1 (Stochastic Matrix) A matrix \(P = (P_{ij})_{i,j \in S}\) is called a stochastic matrix (or Markov matrix) if[cite: 2]: 1. \(P_{ij} \ge 0\) for all \(i, j \in S\); 2. \(\sum_{j \in S} P_{ij} = 1\) for all \(i \in S\) (rows sum to 1)[cite: 2].
Every stochastic matrix serves as the transition matrix of a discrete-time Markov chain[cite: 2].

In the finite state space setting, the transition dynamics can be visualized as a directed, weighted (looped) graph \(G = (V, E)\) where vertices \(V = S\) represent states, and directed edges \((i, j) \in E\) bear weights \(P_{ij} = \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i)\)[cite: 2].

Remark 48.3. In the time-homogeneous setting, edge labels \(P_{ij}\) remain constant across all time steps \(n \to n + 1\)[cite: 2]. In a time-inhomogeneous setting, arrow labels would depend on \(n\)[cite: 2].

title: 85  Lecture 39.2: Markov Generator
text:
85.8 Items Requiring Verification

Shift Operator Representation: The shift operator notation \(T f(k) = f(k+1)\) was used to evaluate \(e^{tA} = e^{-\lambda t} e^{\lambda t T}\) via power series expansion, confirming \(A = \lambda(T - \mathrm{Id})\)[cite: 3].
Poisson Series Convergence: Differentiating the Poisson power series term-by-term is justified by \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{N}_0)\) guaranteeing uniform convergence on compact \(t\)-intervals[cite: 3].

title: 85  Lecture 39.2: Markov Generator
text:
85.2 Finite State Space
Let the state space be finite, \(S = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\). If there exists an \(n \times n\) matrix \(A \in \mathbb{M}_{n \times n}(\mathbb{R})\) such that \(Q_t = e^{tA} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{t^k A^k}{k!}\), then:

\(Q_0 = e^{0 \cdot A} = \mathrm{Id}\);
\(Q_{t+s} = e^{(t+s)A} = e^{tA} e^{sA} = Q_t Q_s\) (since \(tA\) and \(sA\) commute).

The matrix \(A\) is called the infinitesimal generator of the transition semigroup \((Q_t)_{t \ge 0}\).
If \(A\) exists, it can be recovered via the time derivative at \(t = 0\): \[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} Q_t = A e^{tA} = e^{tA} A\\
&\implies A = \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} Q_t \right|_{t=0} = \lim_{t \downarrow 0} \frac{Q_t - \mathrm{Id}}{t}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{85.2}\]
Because \(q_t(i, j) = \mathbb{P}(X_t = j \mid X_0 = i)\) denotes the scalar entries of the transition kernel of \(Q_t\) on \(S\) (so that \(Q_t = (q_t(i,j))_{i,j\in S}\), matching the operator/matrix-entry convention of Lecture 39.1), \(q_t\) satisfies: \[
q_t(i, j) \ge 0 \quad \forall i, j \in S, \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{j=1}^n q_t(i, j) = 1 \quad \forall i \in S.
\tag{85.3}\]

Proposition 85.1 (Characterization of Finite Generator Matrices) Let \(A \in \mathbb{M}_{n \times n}(\mathbb{R})\). Then \(Q_t = e^{tA}\) is a time-homogeneous Markov transition operator for all \(t \ge 0\) if and only if \(A\) is an intensity matrix (or \(Q\)-matrix), meaning:

\(A_{ij} \ge 0\) for all \(i \ne j\);
\(\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij} = 0\) for all \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) (implying \(A_{ii} = -\sum_{j \ne i} A_{ij} \le 0\)).



Proof. \((\implies)\) Since \(q_t(i, j) \ge 0\) for all \(t > 0\), taking off-diagonal entries \(i \ne j\) gives: \[
A_{ij} = \lim_{t \downarrow 0} \frac{q_t(i, j) - q_0(i, j)}{t} = \lim_{t \downarrow 0} \frac{q_t(i, j)}{t} \ge 0.
\] Furthermore, since \(\sum_{j=1}^n q_t(i, j) = 1\) for all \(t \ge 0\), differentiating with respect to \(t\) at \(t = 0\) yields: \[
\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij} = \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \sum_{j=1}^n q_t(i, j) \right|_{t=0} = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(1) = 0.
\]
\((\impliedby)\) Suppose \(A\) satisfies conditions 1–2. Let \(c := \max_{i} (-A_{ii}) = \max_i \sum_{j \ne i} A_{ij} < \infty\) (finite since \(S\) is finite), and set \(B := A + cI\). Then \(B_{ij} = A_{ij} \ge 0\) for \(i \ne j\), and \(B_{ii} = A_{ii} + c \ge 0\) by the choice of \(c\); so \(B\) has all entries \(\ge 0\). Since \(B\) and \(cI\) commute, \[
Q_t = e^{tA} = e^{t(B - cI)} = e^{-ct} e^{tB} = e^{-ct} \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{t^k B^k}{k!}.
\] For \(t \ge 0\), every term \(\frac{t^k}{k!} B^k\) has non-negative entries (a product, and hence any power, of entrywise non-negative matrices is entrywise non-negative), so the convergent series \(\sum_k \frac{t^kB^k}{k!}\) has non-negative entries; multiplying by the positive scalar \(e^{-ct}\) preserves this, giving \(q_t(i,j) \ge 0\) for all \(i,j\).
For the row sums, condition 2 says \(A\mathbf{1} = 0\) where \(\mathbf{1} = (1,\dots,1)^\top\), so by induction \(A^k\mathbf{1} = A^{k-1}(A\mathbf{1}) = 0\) for every \(k \ge 1\). Hence \[
Q_t \mathbf{1} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{t^k}{k!} A^k \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1} + \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{t^k}{k!}\cdot 0 = \mathbf{1},
\] i.e. \(\sum_{j=1}^n q_t(i,j) = 1\) for every \(i \in S\) and every \(t \ge 0\). Together with \(Q_0 = \mathrm{Id}\) and the semigroup property already verified, \((Q_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a time-homogeneous Markov transition semigroup.

title: 85  Lecture 39.2: Markov Generator
text:
85.3 Characterization of Finite Generator Matrices
Let \(A \in \mathbb{M}_{n \times n}(\mathbb{R})\). Then \(Q_t = e^{tA}\) is a time-homogeneous Markov transition operator for all \(t \ge 0\) if and only if \(A\) is an intensity matrix (or \(Q\)-matrix), meaning:

\(A_{ij} \ge 0\) for all \(i \ne j\);
\(\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij} = 0\) for all \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) (implying \(A_{ii} = -\sum_{j \ne i} A_{ij} \le 0\)).

title: 85  Lecture 39.2: Markov Generator
text:
85.7 Infinitesimal Generator of Brownian Motion
If \(f \in C_b^2(\mathbb{R})\) (bounded, with bounded continuous first and second derivatives), then \((Q_t f)(x)\) satisfies the Kolmogorov forward/backward equations: \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} (Q_t f)(x) = A (Q_t f)(x) = Q_t (A f)(x),
\tag{85.9}\] where the generator operator \(A\) on \(C_b^2(\mathbb{R})\) is given by: \[
A f(x) = \frac{1}{2} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 f}{\mathrm{d}x^2}(x) = \frac{1}{2} f''(x).
\tag{85.10}\]

text:

title: 85  Lecture 39.2: Markov Generator
text:
85.4 Generator of the Poisson Process
Consider a Poisson process \((N_t)_{t \ge 0}\) with intensity \(\lambda > 0\) on state space \(S = \mathbb{N}_0 = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\).
The transition kernel is: \[
\begin{aligned}
q_{s,t}(m, n) &= \mathbb{P}(N_t = n \mid N_s = m) \\
&= \mathbb{P}(N_t - N_s+N_s  = n\mid N_s = m) \\
&= \mathbb{P}(N_t - N_s + m = n \mid N_s = m) \\
&= \mathbb{P}(N_t - N_s = n - m) \\
&= e^{-\lambda(t-s)} \frac{(\lambda(t-s))^{n-m}}{(n-m)!} \mathbf{1}_{\{n \ge m\}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For any \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{N}_0)\), the operator \(Q_t\) acts on \(f\) as: \[
\begin{aligned}
(Q_t f)(k) &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty q_t(k, k+n) f(k+n)\\
&= e^{-\lambda t} \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!} f(k+n).
\end{aligned}
\tag{85.4}\] Notice that \((Q_t f)(k)\) is simply \((Q_tf)(k)=\mathbb E[f(k+N_t)]\). This representation makes the probabilistic interpretation particularly transparent: starting from state \(k\), the process moves to state \(k+N_t\). Differentiating \((Q_t f)(k)\) with respect to \(t\) using power series term-by-term differentiation (valid since \(f\) is bounded): \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} (Q_t f)(k) &= -\lambda e^{-\lambda t} \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!} f(k+n) + e^{-\lambda t} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \lambda \frac{n (\lambda t)^{n-1}}{n!} f(k+n) \\
&= -\lambda (Q_t f)(k) + \lambda e^{-\lambda t} \sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{(\lambda t)^m}{m!} f(k+m+1) \quad (\text{setting } m = n-1) \\
&= -\lambda (Q_t f)(k) + \lambda Q_t f(k+1) \\
&= \lambda \left[ (Q_t f)(k+1) - (Q_t f)(k) \right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Defining the operator \(A\) by: \[
(A f)(k) := \lambda [f(k+1) - f(k)],
\tag{85.5}\] the computation above shows \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} Q_t f = A Q_t f\). The companion identity \(A Q_t f = Q_t A f\) follows from the translation-invariance of the Poisson kernel, \(q_t(k, k+n) = q_t(k+1, k+1+n)\) for every \(n \ge 0\) (both sides equal \(e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^n/n!\)): reindexing, \[
\begin{aligned}
(Q_t A f)(k) &= \lambda \sum_{n=0}^\infty q_t(k,k+n)\big[f(k+n+1) - f(k+n)\big] \\
&= \lambda\big[(Q_tf)(k+1) - (Q_tf)(k)\big] = (AQ_tf)(k),
\end{aligned}
\] where we use \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_n q_t(k,k+n) f(k+n+1) &= \sum_n q_t(k+1,(k+1)+n) f((k+1)+n) \\
&= (Q_tf)(k+1).
\end{aligned}
\] Hence, we obtain the differential equation \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} Q_t f = Q_t A f = A Q_t f\).

Theorem 85.1 (Exponential Representation for Poisson Generator) Let \(A = \lambda (T - \mathrm{Id})\) where \(T f(k) = f(k+1)\) is the forward shift operator on \(\mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{N}_0)\). Then \(A\) is a bounded operator on \((\mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{N}_0), \|\cdot\|_\infty)\) with \(\|A\| \le 2\lambda\).
Consequently, the operator exponential series \(e^{tA} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^n A^n}{n!}\) converges uniformly, and: \[
\begin{aligned}
e^{tA} &= e^{t \lambda (T - \mathrm{Id})} \\
&= e^{-\lambda t \mathrm{Id}} e^{\lambda t T} \\
&= e^{-\lambda t} \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!} T^n \\
&= Q_t.
\end{aligned}
\tag{85.6}\] Thus, \(A = \lambda (T - \mathrm{Id})\) is the explicit infinitesimal generator of the Poisson process.


Proof (Proof of Theorem 85.1). Let \(T:\mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{N}_0)\to\mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{N}_0)\) be the forward shift \(Tf(k)=f(k+1)\), and set \(A=\lambda(T-\mathrm{Id})\). Then:

\(A\) is a bounded operator with \(\|A\|\le 2\lambda\).
The series \(e^{tA}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^n A^n}{n!}\) converges in operator norm for every \(t\ge 0\).
\(e^{tA} = Q_t\), i.e. \((e^{tA}f)(k) = e^{-\lambda t}\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!}f(k+n)\).

Step 1: Boundedness of \(T\) and \(A\): The shift \(T\) is an isometry: for any \(f\in\mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{N}_0)\), \[
\|Tf\|_\infty = \sup_{k\in\mathbb{N}_0}|f(k+1)| = \sup_{k\in\mathbb{N}_0}|f(k)| = \|f\|_\infty,
\] so \(\|T\|=1\). Since \(\|\mathrm{Id}\|=1\) as well, the triangle inequality gives \[
\|Af\|_\infty = \lambda\|(T-\mathrm{Id})f\|_\infty \le \lambda\bigl(\|Tf\|_\infty + \|f\|_\infty\bigr) = 2\lambda\|f\|_\infty.
\] Hence \(A\) is bounded with \(\|A\|\le 2\lambda\).
Step 2: Norm convergence of \(e^{tA}\): Because \(\|A^n\|\le\|A\|^n\le(2\lambda)^n\) (operator norm is submultiplicative), the series of operator norms satisfies \[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^n\|A^n\|}{n!} \le \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(2\lambda t)^n}{n!} = e^{2\lambda t} < \infty.
\] Absolute convergence in operator norm implies the series \(e^{tA}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^nA^n}{n!}\) converges to a well-defined bounded operator.
Step 3: Splitting \(e^{tA}=e^{-\lambda t}e^{\lambda tT}\): Write \(A = \lambda T - \lambda\,\mathrm{Id}\), so \(tA = (\lambda t T) + (-\lambda t\,\mathrm{Id})\). The two summands commute because \(\mathrm{Id}\) commutes with every operator. For commuting bounded operators \(B\) and \(C\) (meaning \(BC=CB\)), the identity \(e^{B+C}=e^Be^C\) holds. To see why, use the binomial theorem (valid since \(B\) and \(C\) commute): \[
(B+C)^n = \sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}B^k C^{n-k},
\] so \[
e^{B+C} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}B^kC^{n-k} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty\sum_{j=0}^\infty\frac{B^k}{k!}\frac{C^j}{j!} = e^Be^C,
\] where the double series rearrangement is justified by absolute convergence (both \(B\) and \(C\) are bounded). Applying this with \(B=-\lambda t\,\mathrm{Id}\) and \(C=\lambda tT\): \[
e^{tA} = e^{-\lambda t\,\mathrm{Id}}\,e^{\lambda tT}.
\] Since \((\alpha\,\mathrm{Id})^n=\alpha^n\mathrm{Id}\), the series for \(e^{-\lambda t\,\mathrm{Id}}\) gives simply the scalar \(e^{-\lambda t}\) times the identity, so \[
e^{tA} = e^{-\lambda t}\,e^{\lambda tT}.
\]
Step 4: Computing \(T^n\) and the series for \(e^{\lambda tT}\): Applying the shift \(n\) times: \(T^n f(k) = T^{n-1}(Tf)(k) = T^{n-1}f(k+1) = \cdots = f(k+n)\). Therefore \[
(e^{\lambda tT}f)(k) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!}(T^nf)(k) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!}f(k+n).
\] This series converges for every \(k\) since \(f\) is bounded: \[
\left|\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!}f(k+n)\right| \le \|f\|_\infty\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!} = e^{\lambda t}\|f\|_\infty < \infty.
\]
Step 5: Conclusion \(e^{tA}=Q_t\): Combining Steps 3 and 4: \[
(e^{tA}f)(k) = e^{-\lambda t}(e^{\lambda tT}f)(k) = e^{-\lambda t}\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!}f(k+n).
\] This is exactly \((Q_tf)(k)\) from the file. Hence \(e^{tA}=Q_t\) as operators on \(\mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{N}_0)\), and \(A=\lambda(T-\mathrm{Id})\) is the infinitesimal generator of the Poisson semigroup.

title: 85  Lecture 39.2: Markov Generator
text:
85.5 Generator of Brownian Motion
Consider standard Brownian motion \((B_t)_{t \ge 0}\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Its transition density is the Gaussian heat kernel: \[
q_t(x, y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}} e^{-\frac{|x-y|^2}{2t}}, \quad t > 0, \, x, y \in \mathbb{R}.
\tag{85.7}\]
By definition, \((Q_t f)(x) = \mathbb{E}[f(B_t) \mid B_0 = x]\). Given \(B_0 = x\), the random variable \(B_t\) has distribution \(\mathcal{N}(x, t)\), whose density is exactly \(q_t(x, y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}e^{-\frac{(y-x)^2}{2t}}\). Writing the expectation as an integral against this density: \[
\begin{aligned}
(Q_t f)(x) &= \mathbb{E}[f(B_t)\mid B_0=x] \\
& = \int_\mathbb{R} f(y)\, q_t(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y\\
& = (q_t * f)(x).
\end{aligned}
\tag{85.8}\]

Remark 85.1. A convolution \((g * f)(x) = \int_\mathbb{R} g(x-y)f(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\) only makes sense when the kernel depends on \(x\) and \(y\) solely through their difference \(x - y\). The heat kernel has exactly this structure: since \(|x-y|^2 = |y-x|^2\), the kernel satisfies \[
q_t(x,y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}e^{-\frac{(y-x)^2}{2t}} = p_t(y-x),
\] where \(p_t(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}e^{-z^2/2t}\) is a function of the single variable \(z = y - x\) only. Because \(p_t\) is even (\(p_t(-z) = p_t(z)\), since the Gaussian is symmetric), we also have \(p_t(y-x) = p_t(x-y)\), so \[
\int_\mathbb{R} f(y)\,q_t(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y = \int_\mathbb{R} p_t(x-y)f(y)\,\mathrm{d}y = (p_t * f)(x).
\] We write this as \((q_t * f)(x)\), using \(q_t\) to also denote the one-variable function \(p_t\) — a slight abuse of notation, but standard in this context.


Proposition 85.2 (Infinitesimal Generator of Brownian Motion) If \(f \in C_b^2(\mathbb{R})\) (bounded, with bounded continuous first and second derivatives), then \((Q_t f)(x)\) satisfies the Kolmogorov forward/backward equations: \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} (Q_t f)(x) = A (Q_t f)(x) = Q_t (A f)(x),
\tag{85.9}\] where the generator operator \(A\) on \(C_b^2(\mathbb{R})\) is given by: \[
A f(x) = \frac{1}{2} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 f}{\mathrm{d}x^2}(x) = \frac{1}{2} f''(x).
\tag{85.10}\]


Proof. Step 1: \(A f(x) = \frac12 f''(x)\) at \(t=0\). Fix \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) and write \((Q_tf)(x) = \mathbb{E}[f(x+B_t)]\) (using \(B_0=0\) and the translation structure of Equation 85.8). By Taylor’s theorem with Lagrange remainder, for each realization of \(B_t\) there is \(\xi\) between \(x\) and \(x+B_t\) with \[
f(x+B_t) = f(x) + f'(x)B_t + \tfrac12 f''(x) B_t^2 + \tfrac12\big[f''(\xi) - f''(x)\big]B_t^2.
\] Taking expectations and using \(\mathbb{E}[B_t]=0\), \(\mathbb{E}[B_t^2]=t\): \[
\frac{(Q_tf)(x) - f(x)}{t} = \tfrac12 f''(x) + \tfrac12\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\big(f''(\xi)-f''(x)\big)\frac{B_t^2}{t}\right].
\] We next show that the remainder \(\to 0\) as \(t\downarrow 0\). This is where dominated convergence does the heavy lifting. Write \(B_t = \sqrt{t}\,Z\) with \(Z\sim N(0,1)\). Then \(B_t^2/t = Z^2\), and the remainder becomes \[
\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[(f''(\xi)-f''(x))\,Z^2\right].
\] Now check the two hypotheses for DCT:

Domination: since \(f''\) is bounded, \(|f''(\xi)-f''(x)| \le 2\|f''\|_\infty\), so the integrand is dominated by \(2\|f''\|_\infty Z^2\), which has finite expectation \(2\|f''\|_\infty \cdot \mathbb{E}[Z^2] = 2\|f''\|_\infty\).
Pointwise convergence: as \(t\downarrow 0\), \(B_t = \sqrt{t}\,Z \to 0\) almost surely, which forces \(\xi \to x\) almost surely (since \(\xi\) is squeezed between \(x\) and \(x+B_t\)). By continuity of \(f''\) at \(x\), we get \(f''(\xi)\to f''(x)\) a.s., so the integrand goes to \(0\) pointwise.

By DCT, the remainder expectation \(\to 0\). Putting it together: \[
Af(x) = \lim_{t\downarrow 0}\frac{(Q_tf)(x)-f(x)}{t} = \frac{1}{2}f''(x).
\]
Step 2: extension to all \(t \ge 0\). The heat kernel Equation 85.7 is \(C^\infty\) in \(x\) with all \(x\)-derivatives bounded by integrable functions of \(y\) uniformly for \(x\) in compacts (Gaussian tails dominate any polynomial prefactor), so differentiation under the integral sign in Equation 85.8 is justified and \(Q_tf \in C_b^2(\mathbb{R})\) for every \(t>0\) and every \(f\in\mathcal B_b(\mathbb R)\), in particular for \(f \in C_b^2(\mathbb{R})\). Using the semigroup property \(Q_{t+h}=Q_tQ_h=Q_hQ_t\) (Equation 85.1), \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(Q_tf)(x) = \lim_{h\downarrow0}\frac{(Q_h(Q_tf))(x) - (Q_tf)(x)}{h} = A(Q_tf)(x)
\] by Step 1 applied to \(Q_tf \in C_b^2(\mathbb{R})\) in place of \(f\); and, since \(Q_t\) is a bounded operator (\(\|Q_tg\|_\infty \le \|g\|_\infty\)) and hence continuous, \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(Q_tf)(x) &= \lim_{h\downarrow0}\frac{(Q_t(Q_hf))(x) - (Q_t f)(x)}{h} \\
&= Q_t\!\left(\lim_{h\downarrow0}\frac{Q_hf - f}{h}\right)\!(x) = Q_t(Af)(x),
\end{aligned}
\] where passing the limit inside \(Q_t\) uses boundedness/linearity of \(Q_t\) together with Step 1 applied at the point \(x\) after convolving. This proves Equation 85.9.


Remark 85.2. 

The generator of Brownian motion is the half-Laplacian. The most concrete output is the formula \(Af = \frac{1}{2}f''\). Recall that the generator is defined as \(Af(x) = \lim_{t\downarrow 0}\frac{(Q_tf)(x)-f(x)}{t}\), the “instantaneous rate of change” of the semigroup. The proof shows this limit equals \(\frac{1}{2}f''(x)\) by a second-order Taylor expansion of \(f(x+B_t)\): the mean-zero symmetry of \(B_t\) kills the first-order term \(f'(x)\mathbb{E}[B_t] = 0\), and the second-order term contributes \(\frac{1}{2}f''(x)\cdot\frac{\mathbb{E}[B_t^2]}{t} = \frac{1}{2}f''(x)\). So the curvature of \(f\), measured by \(f''\), is what the Brownian semigroup “sees” instantaneously.
The evolution equation is the heat equation. Setting \(u(t,x) := (Q_tf)(x)\), the equation \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}Q_tf = A\,Q_tf\) becomes \[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}(t,x) = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}(t,x),
\] which is the classical heat equation with initial condition \(u(0,x) = f(x)\). The proposition is therefore saying that Brownian motion solves the heat equation: \((Q_tf)(x) = \mathbb{E}[f(x+B_t)]\) is the unique solution starting from \(f\).



Remark 85.3 (Domain Restrictions and Feller Processes). Unlike the Poisson generator \(A = \lambda(T - \mathrm{Id})\), which is bounded on all of \(\mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{N}_0)\), the Laplacian operator \(A = \frac{1}{2} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}x^2}\) is unbounded.
It cannot be defined on all of \(\mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{R})\) because discontinuous or non-differentiable functions (such as \(f = \mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}\)) cannot be differentiated twice in the classical sense. Sequences \(\psi_n \in C_c^2(\mathbb{R})\) approximating \(\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}\) pointwise have unbounded second derivatives \(\|\psi_n''\|_\infty \to \infty\).
This domain issue motivates the theory of Feller semigroups and Feller processes, where the domain of \(A\) is restricted to continuous functions vanishing at infinity, \(\mathcal{D}(A) \subset C_0(\mathbb{R})\).


Example 85.2 An operator \(A: X \to X\) on a normed space \((X, \|\cdot\|)\) is bounded if there is a constant \(C < \infty\) such that \(\|Af\| \leq C\|f\|\) for all \(f\) in the domain. Work with the sup-norm \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) and consider the sequence of functions \[
f_n(x) = \sin(nx), \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots
\] Each \(f_n \in C_b^2(\mathbb{R})\), and they all have the same sup-norm: \(\|f_n\|_\infty = 1 \quad \text{for all } n\). But applying the generator: \[
Af_n(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}f_n''(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}(-n^2)\sin(nx) = -\tfrac{n^2}{2}\sin(nx),
\] so \(\|Af_n\|_\infty = \frac{n^2}{2} \to \infty \text{ as } n\to\infty\). A bounded operator would need \(\|Af_n\|_\infty \leq C\|f_n\|_\infty = C\) for some fixed \(C\). No such \(C\) exists here, so \(A\) is unbounded. This is ultimately why the Brownian motion generator requires a restricted domain \(C_b^2(\mathbb{R})\) and cannot be extended to all of \(\mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{R})\), motivating the Feller semigroup framework.

title: 3  Lecture 1.2: Sigma Algebra
text:
3.6 Takeaways






NoteSummary



1. Fields vs. \(\sigma\)-Fields. A field requires closure under finite unions; a \(\sigma\)-field strengthens this to countable unions. The difference matters in measure theory: probability can only be assigned consistently to countably many events at once, making \(\sigma\)-fields the right domain.
2. Closure under intersections is free. Neither definition explicitly requires closure under intersections, but it follows immediately from closure under complements and unions via De Morgan’s law. The same holds for countable intersections in a \(\sigma\)-field.
3. The countable-cocountable \(\sigma\)-field. On an uncountable \(\Omega\), the collection of sets that are either countable or have countable complement is a \(\sigma\)-field. The key to the union closure proof is the two-case split: if every set is countable the union is countable; if any one set has countable complement then De Morgan forces the complement of the union to be even smaller, hence countable.
4. \(\sigma\)-Fields are closed under arbitrary intersections. This is what makes the generated \(\sigma\)-field \(\sigma(\mathcal{E})\) well-defined: take the intersection of all \(\sigma\)-fields containing \(\mathcal{E}\). The resulting object is itself a \(\sigma\)-field (by the intersection lemma) and is the smallest one containing \(\mathcal{E}\).
5. Comparing generated \(\sigma\)-fields. \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}_1) = \sigma(\mathcal{E}_2)\) if and only if each generating class is contained in the \(\sigma\)-field generated by the other. This is the standard two-sided inclusion argument and is the main tool for showing two different descriptions generate the same \(\sigma\)-field.
6. The Borel \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\). Generated by the open sets of \(\mathbb{R}\), it can equivalently be generated by open intervals, half-open intervals, or rays \((-\infty, a]\). The equivalence follows from the exercise above: each class generates the other because every open set is a countable union of such intervals. The ray generator \(\sigma(\{(-\infty,a]: a\in\mathbb{R}\})\) is especially convenient in probability since CDFs are defined pointwise on these sets. In \(\mathbb{R}^d\), separability (density of \(\mathbb{Q}^d\)) reduces the generator to a countable collection of rational balls.

title: 4  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
4.6 Takeaways






NoteSummary



1. What a measure is. A measure on a measurable space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F})\) is a set function \(\mu:\mathcal{F}\to[0,\infty]\) satisfying \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) and countable additivity. The empty-set condition is independent of countable additivity for general (infinite) measures and must be stated as a separate axiom.
2. Finite additivity is a consequence. Applying countable additivity to a two-set disjoint union padded with empty sets (using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\)) gives \(\mu(A\cup B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\) whenever \(A\cap B=\emptyset\). All “finite additivity” steps in the Properties proof rely on this.
3. The Dirac measure. \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is the simplest non-trivial probability measure: it places unit mass at a single point. Countable additivity holds because a point can belong to at most one member of a disjoint family.
4. Building new measures by linear combination. Non-negative countable linear combinations \(\mu = \sum_j c_j\mu_j\) are again measures. The key step is interchanging the order of two non-negative summations, which is always valid (Tonelli). Normalization (\(\mu(\Omega)=1\)) is then checked separately, giving the class of discrete probability measures.
5. Derived properties from the axioms.

Monotonicity: \(A\subseteq B\implies\mu(A)\le\mu(B)\), via the disjoint decomposition \(B=A\cup(B\setminus A)\).
Inclusion-exclusion: \(\mu(A\cup B)+\mu(A\cap B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\); rearranges the same two disjoint decompositions.
Sub-additivity (Boole’s inequality): \(\mu(\bigcup B_n)\le\sum\mu(B_n)\) for arbitrary (not necessarily disjoint) sets, proved by the disjointification \(A_n=B_n\setminus\bigcup_{j<n}B_j\) which reduces to countable additivity followed by monotonicity \(\mu(A_n)\le\mu(B_n)\).

title: 5  Lecture 2.2: Finitely Additive Measures
text:
5.1 Introduction
Genuine measures (defined on full \(\sigma\)-algebras) are often difficult to construct directly, owing to the complex collection of sets in a \(\sigma\)-algebra. To approach this problem, we start with weaker notions of measure defined on simpler algebraic structures (algebras or semi-algebras) and later extend them to the full \(\sigma\)-algebra.

title: 5  Lecture 2.2: Finitely Additive Measures
text:
5.2 Premeasures and Finitely-Additive Measures

Definition 5.1 (Premeasurable Space and Premeasure) Let \(\Omega\) be a non-empty set.

A pair \((\Omega, \mathcal{A})\) is called a premeasurable space if \(\mathcal{A}\) is a field (algebra) over \(\Omega\).
A function \(\mu: \mathcal{A} \to [0, \infty]\) is called a premeasure if it is countably additive; that is, if \(\{E_i\}_{i=1}^\infty \subset \mathcal{A}\) is a sequence of pairwise disjoint sets such that \(\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty E_i \in \mathcal{A}\), then \[
\mu\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty E_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^\infty \mu(E_i).
\]
If \(\mu: \mathcal{A} \to [0, \infty]\) is only finitely additive (i.e., \(\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B)\) for all disjoint \(A, B \in \mathcal{A}\)), then \(\mu\) is called a finitely-additive measure.



Note that algebras are closed under finite unions and intersections, but not necessarily under countable unions. Therefore, finitely-additive measures are weaker than premeasures, which require countable additivity.
That is also the reason why we assume that the union of the disjoint sets \(\{E_i\}_{i=1}^\infty\) belongs to \(\mathcal{A}\) in the definition of premeasure.


Proposition 5.1 (Subadditivity Inequality for Finitely-Additive Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finitely-additive measure space. If \(\{A_i\}_{i=1}^\infty \subset \mathcal{A}\) is a collection of pairwise disjoint sets such that \(A := \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i \in \mathcal{A}\), then \[
\mu(A) \ge \sum_{i=1}^\infty \mu(A_i).
\tag{5.1}\]
The inequality in Equation 5.1 can be strict.


Proof (Proof of Equation 5.1). Finitely-additive measures are monotone: if \(E, F \in \mathcal{A}\) with \(E \subseteq F\), then since \(F = E \cup (F \setminus E)\) with \(E \cap (F \setminus E) = \emptyset\) and \(F \setminus E \in \mathcal{A}\), finite additivity yields \[
\mu(F) = \mu(E) + \mu(F \setminus E) \ge \mu(E).
\] Fix \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). Since \(\{A_i\}_{i=1}^\infty\) are pairwise disjoint and belong to the algebra \(\mathcal{A}\), the finite union \(\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i\) belongs to \(\mathcal{A}\). Moreover, \(\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i \subseteq A\). By monotonicity and finite additivity, \[
\mu(A) \ge \mu\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mu(A_i).
\] Taking the limit as \(n \to \infty\) on the right-hand side yields \[
\mu(A) \ge \sum_{i=1}^\infty \mu(A_i).
\]

title: 5  Lecture 2.2: Finitely Additive Measures
text:
5.3 Generating Fields on \(\mathbb{R}\)
Among the natural generating sets for the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) is the collection of left-open, right-closed intervals: \[
\mathcal{S}_{(]} := \{(a, b]: -\infty \le a \le b \le \infty\},
\tag{5.2}\] where by convention \((a, b] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : a < x \le b\}\), \((a, a] = \emptyset\), and \((a, \infty] = (a, \infty)\).
To study the field generated by these intervals, denoted \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\), we introduce the notion of a semi-algebra.

title: 5  Lecture 2.2: Finitely Additive Measures
text:
5.4 Semi-Algebras of Sets

Definition 5.2 (Semi-Algebra (Elementary Class)) A collection of subsets \(\mathcal{S} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) is called a semi-algebra (or an elementary class) over \(\Omega\) if:

\(\emptyset \in \mathcal{S}\);
\(\mathcal{S}\) is closed under finite intersections: if \(A, B \in \mathcal{S}\), then \(A \cap B \in \mathcal{S}\);
If \(A \in \mathcal{S}\), then its complement \(A^c = \Omega \setminus A\) can be expressed as a finite disjoint union of elements from \(\mathcal{S}\): \[
A^c = \bigcup_{j=1}^k C_j, \quad \text{where } C_j \in \mathcal{S} \text{ are pairwise disjoint.}
\]



The following proposition characterizes the field generated by a semi-algebra. This result is useful because it allows us to construct finitely-additive measures on the field generated by a semi-algebra, which can then be extended to a premeasure on the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by the semi-algebra.
The field generated by a semi-algebra is the smallest field containing the semi-algebra, and it can be described explicitly as the collection of all finite disjoint unions of elements from the semi-algebra.


Proposition 5.2 (Structure of the Generated Field) If \(\mathcal{S}\) is a semi-algebra over \(\Omega\), then the field \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\) generated by \(\mathcal{S}\) is equal to the set of all finite disjoint unions of elements from \(\mathcal{S}\): \[
\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}) = \text{DU}(\mathcal{S}) := \left\{ \bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i : n \in \mathbb{N}, \, A_i \in \mathcal{S} \text{ pairwise disjoint} \right\}.
\tag{5.3}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 5.2). Clearly, \(\mathcal{S} \subseteq \text{DU}(\mathcal{S}) \subseteq \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\). To prove equality, it suffices to show that \(\text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\) is a field.

Empty Set and Universe: Since \(\emptyset \in \mathcal{S}\), \(\emptyset \in \text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\). By Property (3) of semi-algebras, \(\Omega = \emptyset^c\) is a finite disjoint union of elements in \(\mathcal{S}\), so \(\Omega \in \text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\).
Closure under Finite Intersections: Let \(D = \bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i \in \text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\) and \(E = \bigcup_{j=1}^m B_j \in \text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\), where \(\{A_i\}\) and \(\{B_j\}\) are finite disjoint collections from \(\mathcal{S}\). Then \[
D \cap E = \bigcup_{i=1}^n \bigcup_{j=1}^m (A_i \cap B_j).
\] Since \(\mathcal{S}\) is closed under intersection, \(A_i \cap B_j \in \mathcal{S}\). Furthermore, for \((i, j) \neq (i', j')\), the sets \((A_i \cap B_j)\) and \((A_{i'} \cap B_{j'})\) are disjoint: if \(i \neq i'\) then \((A_i \cap B_j) \cap (A_{i'} \cap B_{j'}) \subseteq A_i \cap A_{i'} = \emptyset\); if \(j \neq j'\) then \((A_i \cap B_j) \cap (A_{i'} \cap B_{j'}) \subseteq B_j \cap B_{j'} = \emptyset\). Thus, \(D \cap E\) is a finite disjoint union of sets from \(\mathcal{S}\), so \(D \cap E \in \text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\).
Closure under Complement: Let \(D = \bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i \in \text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\) with \(A_i \in \mathcal{S}\) pairwise disjoint. Then \[
D^c = \bigcap_{i=1}^n A_i^c.
\] For each \(i\), \(A_i^c \in \text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\) by definition of a semi-algebra. Since \(\text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\) is closed under finite intersections (as established above), it follows that \(D^c \in \text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\).

Thus, \(\text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\) is a field containing \(\mathcal{S}\), which implies \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}) = \text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\).

title: 5  Lecture 2.2: Finitely Additive Measures
text:
5.5 Finitely Additive Measures on Semi-Algebras
Once we have a finitely-additive measure defined on a semi-algebra, we can extend it to the field generated by that semi-algebra. This is a crucial step in constructing measures on more complex structures.

Proposition 5.3 (Extension to Generated Field) Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a semi-algebra over \(\Omega\). Let \(\mu: \mathcal{S} \to [0, \infty]\) be finitely additive on \(\mathcal{S}\); that is, whenever \(A \in \mathcal{S}\) is the disjoint union of finitely many sets \(A = \bigsqcup_{i=1}^n A_i\) with \(A_i \in \mathcal{S}\), we have \(\mu(A) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mu(A_i)\).
Then \(\mu\) extends uniquely to a finitely-additive measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\), defined for \(A = \bigcup_{i=1}^n E_i \in \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\) (with \(\{E_i\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathcal{S}\) pairwise disjoint) by: \[
\mu(A) := \sum_{i=1}^n \mu(E_i).
\tag{5.4}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 5.3). If \(\mu\) is to be a finitely additive measure on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\), formula Equation 5.4 must hold, which guarantees uniqueness.
To show that \(\mu\) is well-defined, suppose \(A \in \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\) has two finite disjoint representations: \[
A = \bigcup_{i=1}^n E_i = \bigcup_{j=1}^m F_j, \quad \text{where } E_i, F_j \in \mathcal{S}.
\] For each fixed \(i\), \(E_i = E_i \cap A = \bigcup_{j=1}^m (E_i \cap F_j)\) is a finite disjoint union of elements in \(\mathcal{S}\). By finite additivity on \(\mathcal{S}\), \[
\mu(E_i) = \sum_{j=1}^m \mu(E_i \cap F_j).
\] Summing over \(i=1, \dots, n\) gives: \[
\sum_{i=1}^n \mu(E_i) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m \mu(E_i \cap F_j) = \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{i=1}^n \mu(E_i \cap F_j) = \sum_{j=1}^m \mu(F_j).
\] Thus, the value assigned to \(\mu(A)\) is independent of the choice of disjoint decomposition, so \(\mu\) is well-defined.
It remains to verify finite additivity on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\). Let \(A, B \in \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\) be disjoint, with representations \[
A = \bigcup_{i=1}^n E_i, \qquad B = \bigcup_{j=1}^m F_j,
\] where \(\{E_i\}_{i=1}^n, \{F_j\}_{j=1}^m \subset \mathcal{S}\) are each pairwise disjoint. Since \(A \cap B = \emptyset\), the full collection \(\{E_1, \dots, E_n, F_1, \dots, F_m\}\) is pairwise disjoint. Therefore, \[
A \cup B = \bigcup_{i=1}^n E_i \;\cup\; \bigcup_{j=1}^m F_j
\] is a finite disjoint union of elements of \(\mathcal{S}\), so \(A \cup B \in \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\). By definition Equation 5.4 applied to this representation, \[
\mu(A \cup B) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mu(E_i) + \sum_{j=1}^m \mu(F_j) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\] By induction, \(\mu\) is finitely additive on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\).

title: 5  Lecture 2.2: Finitely Additive Measures
text:
5.6 Stieltjes (Pre)Measures on \(\mathcal{S}_{(]}\)
The Stieltjes measure is a classical example of a finitely-additive measure defined on the semi-algebra of left-open, right-closed intervals. It is constructed from a non-decreasing function \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\), and it can be extended to a premeasure on the field generated by \(\mathcal{S}_{(]}\).
The Stieltjes measure is particularly important in probability theory, as it provides a way to define measures corresponding to cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of random variables.

Definition 5.3 (Stieltjes Set Function) Let \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a non-decreasing function. On the semi-algebra \(\mathcal{S}_{(]} = \{(a, b]: -\infty \le a \le b \le \infty\}\), define: \[
\mu_F((a, b]) := F(b) - F(a) \ge 0.
\tag{5.5}\]


Proposition 5.4 (Additivity on Interval Semi-Algebra) The set function \(\mu_F\) is additive on \(\mathcal{S}_{(]}\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 5.4). Suppose \((a, b] = \bigsqcup_{k=1}^n (c_k, d_k]\) is a finite disjoint covering of \((a,b]\) by elements of \(\mathcal{S}_{(]}\). We verify the hypothesis of Proposition 5.3 by showing \(\sum_{k=1}^n \mu_F((c_k, d_k]) = \mu_F((a,b])\).
The intervals are pairwise disjoint subsets of \((a, b]\), so \(c_k \ge a\) and \(d_k \le b\) for all \(k\). After sorting by left endpoint (reindexing so that \(c_1 \le c_2 \le \cdots \le c_n\)), the covering condition forces:

\(c_1 = a\): any point \(a + \varepsilon \in (a, b]\) must lie in some interval \((c_k, d_k]\), so \(c_k < a + \varepsilon\); letting \(\varepsilon \to 0\) gives \(c_k \le a\), and combined with \(c_k \ge a\) gives \(c_k = a\).
\(d_k = c_{k+1}\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, n-1\): if \(d_k < c_{k+1}\), the point \((d_k + c_{k+1})/2\) would belong to \((a,b]\) but to no interval.
\(d_n = b\): otherwise \(b\) itself is uncovered.

Hence \(a = c_1 < d_1 = c_2 < \cdots < d_{n-1} = c_n < d_n = b\), and the sum telescopes: \[
\sum_{k=1}^n \mu_F((c_k, d_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \bigl(F(d_k) - F(c_k)\bigr) = F(b) - F(a) = \mu_F((a, b]).
\] By Proposition 5.3, \(\mu_F\) extends uniquely to a finitely-additive measure on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\).

title: 5  Lecture 2.2: Finitely Additive Measures
text:
5.7 Counterexample: When \(\mu_F\) Fails Countable Additivity
A fundamental question is: Is \(\mu_F\) always a premeasure (countably additive) on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\)?
Consider a non-decreasing function \(F\) that is not right-continuous at \(a \in \mathbb{R}\). Take the interval \((a, a+1] \in \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\). We can decompose this interval into a countable disjoint union: \[
(a, a+1] = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \left(a + \frac{1}{n+1}, a + \frac{1}{n}\right].
\]
Evaluating \(\mu_F\) on the whole set gives: \[
\mu_F((a, a+1]) = F(a+1) - F(a).
\]
On the other hand, summing the series of measures of the individual disjoint pieces: \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu_F\left(\left(a + \frac{1}{n+1}, a + \frac{1}{n}\right]\right) &= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left( F\left(a + \frac{1}{n}\right) - F\left(a + \frac{1}{n+1}\right) \right) \\
&= \lim_{m \to \infty} \sum_{n=1}^m \left( F\left(a + \frac{1}{n}\right) - F\left(a + \frac{1}{n+1}\right) \right) \\
&= \lim_{m \to \infty} \left( F(a+1) - F\left(a + \frac{1}{m+1}\right) \right) \\
&= F(a+1) - F(a+),
\end{aligned}
\] where \(F(a+) := \lim_{\epsilon \downarrow 0} F(a + \epsilon)\).
If \(F\) is discontinuous from the right at \(a\), then \(F(a+) \neq F(a)\), which implies \[
\begin{align*}
\mu_F((a, a+1]) &= F(a+1) - F(a) \neq F(a+1) - F(a+)\\
&= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu_F\left(\left(a + \frac{1}{n+1}, a + \frac{1}{n}\right]\right).
\end{align*}
\]
Thus, \(\mu_F\) is not countably additive (and hence not a premeasure) if \(F\) is not right-continuous.

title: 5  Lecture 2.2: Finitely Additive Measures
text:
5.8 Reconstructions, Corrections, and Interpretations

Notation Standardization: Standardized measure-theoretic notation throughout (e.g., replaced variable handwriting symbols like \(\chi\) / \(\mu\) with consistent measure notation \(\mu_F\) and \(\mu\), and script \(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}\)).
Semi-Algebra Definition: In Condition (3) of the semi-algebra definition, the original manuscript abbreviated \(A^c\) as a finite disjoint union without explicitly naming the elements \(C_j \in \mathcal{S}\); this was made fully explicit.
Proof Extensions: In the proof that \(\text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\) is closed under complementation, the manuscript noted \(D^c = \bigcap A_i^c\); the step showing that each \(A_i^c \in \text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\) and that \(\text{DU}(\mathcal{S})\) is closed under finite intersections was expanded to ensure logical completeness.

title: 5  Lecture 2.2: Finitely Additive Measures
text:
5.9 Mathematical Gaps & Verification Items

5.9.1 Mathematical Analysis & Gaps

Right-Continuity Requirement: The counterexample correctly demonstrates that right-continuity (\(F(a+) = F(a)\)) is a necessary condition for \(\mu_F\) to be countably additive on \(\mathcal{S}_{(]}\). (It can further be proved that right-continuity is also sufficient for countable additivity via a compactness argument).



5.9.2 Items Requiring Verification

Interval Semi-Algebra Notation: Verify if \(\mathcal{S}_{(]}\) or \(\mathcal{J}_{(]}\) is your preferred macro/symbol across the rest of your course notes for the semi-algebra of left-open, right-closed intervals.

title: 6  Lecture 3.1: Stieltjes Premeasures
text:
6.1 Characterization of Stieltjes Premeasures
Let \(\mathcal{S}_{(]} = \{(a, b]: -\infty \le a \le b \le \infty\}\) be the canonical semi-algebra of left-open, right-closed intervals in \(\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]}) = \mathcal{B}_{\text{el}}(\mathbb{R})\) denote the generated elementary field of finite disjoint unions of such intervals.
For a non-decreasing function \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\), the set function \(\mu_F((a, b]) = F(b) - F(a)\) defines a well-defined finitely-additive measure \(\mu_F\) on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\).
As established previously, if \(F\) fails to be right-continuous at any point, \(\mu_F\) fails to be countably additive. The converse also holds, yielding a full characterization.
To prove this theorem, we first establish a general criterion for countable additivity of a finitely-additive measure on a field generated by a semi-algebra.

title: 6  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
Definition 6.1 (Measure and Measure Space) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and \(\mathcal{F}\) be a \(\sigma\)-field (\(\sigma\)-algebra) over \(\Omega\). The pair \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) is called a measurable space, and elements \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) are called measurable sets (or events).
A set function \(\mu: \mathcal{F} \to [0, \infty]\) is called a measure if it satisfies the following two conditions:

Empty Set: \(\mu(\emptyset) = 0\).
Countable Additivity (\(\sigma\)-additivity): For any countable sequence of pairwise disjoint sets \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (i.e., \(E_i \cap E_j = \emptyset\) for all \(i \neq j\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu(E_j).
\tag{6.1}\]







Note



The condition \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) is independent of countable additivity for general measures: without it, the constant function \(\mu \equiv \infty\) satisfies countable additivity but violates the empty-set condition. For finite measures \(\mu(\Omega)<\infty\), the condition can be derived by applying countable additivity to \(\Omega = \Omega \cup \emptyset \cup \emptyset \cup \cdots\).


The triple \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called a measure space.


Definition 6.2 (Finite and Probability Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

\(\mu\) is a finite measure if \(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\).
\(\mu\) is a probability measure if \(\mu(\Omega) = 1\). In this case, \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called a probability space.

title: 6  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
6.2 Canonical Examples of Measures

6.2.1 Trivial Measure
On any measurable space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), the constant zero function \(\mu(E) \equiv 0\) for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is trivially a valid measure.


6.2.2 Point Mass (Dirac Measure)

Definition 6.3 (Dirac / Point Mass Measure) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space and fix a point \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\). The Dirac measure (or point mass) at \(\omega_0\), denoted by \(\delta_{\omega_0}: \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]\), is defined by: \[
\delta_{\omega_0}(E) := \begin{cases}  1 & \text{if } \omega_0 \in E, \\  0 & \text{if } \omega_0 \notin E.  \end{cases}
\tag{6.2}\]


Proposition 6.1 (Validity of Dirac Measure) For any \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\), \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 16.1). First, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(\Omega) = 1\) since \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\).
Next, let \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a countable sequence of pairwise disjoint measurable sets. Since the sets are disjoint, the point \(\omega_0\) can belong to at most one set \(E_k\):

Case 1: There exists a unique index \(k \ge 1\) such that \(\omega_0 \in E_k\). Then \(\omega_0 \in \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 1\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) = 1\) and \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \neq k\). Thus: \[\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = \delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) + \sum_{j \neq k} 0 = 1 + 0 = 1.\]
Case 2: \(\omega_0 \notin E_j\) for all \(j \ge 1\). Then \(\omega_0 \notin \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 0\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \ge 1\), yielding \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\).

In both cases, \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j)\), proving countable additivity.

title: 6  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
section: 6.3 Constructing New Measures from Existing Measures
text:
6.3 Constructing New Measures from Existing Measures

Theorem 6.1 (Linear Combinations and Sums of Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space.

Scalar Multiplication: If \(\mu\) is a measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(a \in (0, \infty)\), then \(a\mu\) defined by \((a\mu)(E) := a \cdot \mu(E)\) is a valid measure.
Countable Linear Combinations: If \(\{\mu_j\}_{j=1}^\infty\) is a countable collection of measures on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(\{c_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, \infty)\), then the set function: \[
\mu := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j
\tag{6.3}\] defined by \(\mu(E) := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E)\) for \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is a valid measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).



Proof (Proof of Theorem 16.1). Because all terms \(c_j \mu_j(E)\) are non-negative (\(c_j \mu_j(E) \in [0, \infty]\)), all infinite sums consist of non-negative real/extended terms, which guarantees that sums are well-defined and order of summation can be interchanged by Tonelli’s theorem for series.
Let \(\{E_k\}_{k=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be pairwise disjoint events. Using countable additivity of each individual measure \(\mu_j\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \left( \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu_j(E_k) \right) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E_k) \quad \text{(interchanging non-negative double summation)} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu(E_k).
\end{aligned}
\] Hence, \(\mu\) is countably additive and constitutes a valid measure.

title: 6  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
6.4 Discrete Probability Measures

Corollary 6.1 (Discrete Probability Measures) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and let \(\{\omega_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \Omega\) be a countable sequence of points. Let \(\{p_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, 1]\) be weights satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j = 1\).
Then \(\mu := \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j \delta_{\omega_j}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 16.1). By Theorem 16.1, \(\mu\) is a valid measure. Evaluating \(\mu\) on the entire space \(\Omega\) gives: \[
\mu(\Omega) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j \delta_{\omega_j}(\Omega) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j (1) = 1.
\] Thus, \(\mu\) is a normalized probability measure.

title: 6  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
6.5 Basic Properties of Measures
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

Proposition 6.2 (Fundamental Properties of Measures)  

Monotonicity: If \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(A \subseteq B\), then: \[
\mu(A) \le \mu(B).
\tag{6.4}\] If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), then \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion Rule (Addition Rule): For any \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\): \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\tag{6.5}\] When \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), this is written as \(\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\).
Countable Sub-Additivity (Boole’s Inequality): For any countable sequence of measurable sets \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (not necessarily disjoint): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\tag{6.6}\]



Proof (Proof of Proposition 16.2). 

Monotonicity: Decompose \(B\) into the disjoint union \(B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\). By countable additivity (applied to the two-set partition, using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) to pad with empty sets): \[
\mu(B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] Since \(\mu(B \setminus A) \ge 0\), it immediately follows that \(\mu(A) \le \mu(B)\). If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), subtracting \(\mu(A)\) from both sides gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion: Decompose \(A \cup B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint) and \(B = (A \cap B) \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint). By countable additivity applied to each two-set partition: \[
\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A), \quad \text{and} \quad \mu(B) = \mu(A \cap B) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] The second equation gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\) (valid when \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), which is the stated hypothesis). Substituting into the first: \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\]
Countable Sub-additivity: Disjointify the sequence \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) by defining: \[
A_1 := B_1, \quad A_n := B_n \setminus \left( \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1} B_j \right) \quad \text{for } n \ge 2.
\tag{6.7}\] By construction, \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are pairwise disjoint measurable sets, \(A_n \subseteq B_n\) for all \(n\), and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\). Applying countable additivity and monotonicity (\(A_n \subseteq B_n \implies \mu(A_n) \le \mu(B_n)\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\]

title: 6  Lecture 3.1: Stieltjes Premeasures
text:
6.5 Takeaways

The Stieltjes premeasure \(\mu_F\) is countably additive on the field \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\) if and only if \(F\) is right-continuous.
The Lebesgue premeasure \(\mu\) is translation-invariant on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\).
The Lebesgue premeasure \(\mu\) is the unique translation-invariant premeasure on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\) satisfying \(\mu((0, 1]) = 1\).
The Lebesgue premeasure \(\mu\) can be extended to a complete measure on the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\), known as the Lebesgue measure.
The Lebesgue measure is the unique translation-invariant measure on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) satisfying \(\mu((0, 1]) = 1\).

title: 7  Lecture 3.2: Outer Measure
text:
7.1 The Measure Extension Problem
Historically, the extension result for premeasures is associated primarily with Constantin Carathéodory and his development of the outer-measure construction. Starting from a premeasure on an algebra of sets, Carathéodory’s method constructs an outer measure and then identifies a \(\sigma\)-algebra of measurable sets on which the outer measure becomes a measure extending the original premeasure. The corresponding Carathéodory Extension Theorem is now a fundamental result in measure theory; under a suitable \(\sigma\)-finiteness condition, the extension is also unique.
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a premeasure space, where \(\mathcal{A}\) is a field over \(\Omega\) and \(\mu: \mathcal{A} \to [0, \infty]\) is a countably additive set function (a premeasure).
Our goal is to extend \(\mu\) to a genuine measure \(\bar{\mu}\) defined on the generated \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\). Specifically, we seek a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\Omega\) with \(\sigma(\mathcal{A}) \subseteq \mathcal{F} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) and a measure \(\bar{\mu}: \mathcal{F} \to [0, \infty]\) such that: \[
\bar{\mu}\vert{}_{\mathcal{A}} = \mu.
\tag{7.1}\]

title: 7  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
Definition 7.1 (Measure and Measure Space) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and \(\mathcal{F}\) be a \(\sigma\)-field (\(\sigma\)-algebra) over \(\Omega\). The pair \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) is called a measurable space, and elements \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) are called measurable sets (or events).
A set function \(\mu: \mathcal{F} \to [0, \infty]\) is called a measure if it satisfies the following two conditions:

Empty Set: \(\mu(\emptyset) = 0\).
Countable Additivity (\(\sigma\)-additivity): For any countable sequence of pairwise disjoint sets \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (i.e., \(E_i \cap E_j = \emptyset\) for all \(i \neq j\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu(E_j).
\tag{7.1}\]







Note



The condition \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) is independent of countable additivity for general measures: without it, the constant function \(\mu \equiv \infty\) satisfies countable additivity but violates the empty-set condition. For finite measures \(\mu(\Omega)<\infty\), the condition can be derived by applying countable additivity to \(\Omega = \Omega \cup \emptyset \cup \emptyset \cup \cdots\).


The triple \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called a measure space.


Definition 7.2 (Finite and Probability Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

\(\mu\) is a finite measure if \(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\).
\(\mu\) is a probability measure if \(\mu(\Omega) = 1\). In this case, \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called a probability space.

title: 7  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
7.2 Canonical Examples of Measures

7.2.1 Trivial Measure
On any measurable space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), the constant zero function \(\mu(E) \equiv 0\) for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is trivially a valid measure.


7.2.2 Point Mass (Dirac Measure)

Definition 7.3 (Dirac / Point Mass Measure) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space and fix a point \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\). The Dirac measure (or point mass) at \(\omega_0\), denoted by \(\delta_{\omega_0}: \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]\), is defined by: \[
\delta_{\omega_0}(E) := \begin{cases}  1 & \text{if } \omega_0 \in E, \\  0 & \text{if } \omega_0 \notin E.  \end{cases}
\tag{7.2}\]


Proposition 7.1 (Validity of Dirac Measure) For any \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\), \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 16.1). First, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(\Omega) = 1\) since \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\).
Next, let \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a countable sequence of pairwise disjoint measurable sets. Since the sets are disjoint, the point \(\omega_0\) can belong to at most one set \(E_k\):

Case 1: There exists a unique index \(k \ge 1\) such that \(\omega_0 \in E_k\). Then \(\omega_0 \in \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 1\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) = 1\) and \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \neq k\). Thus: \[\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = \delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) + \sum_{j \neq k} 0 = 1 + 0 = 1.\]
Case 2: \(\omega_0 \notin E_j\) for all \(j \ge 1\). Then \(\omega_0 \notin \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 0\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \ge 1\), yielding \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\).

In both cases, \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j)\), proving countable additivity.

title: 7  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
section: 7.3 Constructing New Measures from Existing Measures
text:
7.3 Constructing New Measures from Existing Measures

Theorem 7.1 (Linear Combinations and Sums of Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space.

Scalar Multiplication: If \(\mu\) is a measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(a \in (0, \infty)\), then \(a\mu\) defined by \((a\mu)(E) := a \cdot \mu(E)\) is a valid measure.
Countable Linear Combinations: If \(\{\mu_j\}_{j=1}^\infty\) is a countable collection of measures on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(\{c_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, \infty)\), then the set function: \[
\mu := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j
\tag{7.3}\] defined by \(\mu(E) := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E)\) for \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is a valid measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).



Proof (Proof of Theorem 16.1). Because all terms \(c_j \mu_j(E)\) are non-negative (\(c_j \mu_j(E) \in [0, \infty]\)), all infinite sums consist of non-negative real/extended terms, which guarantees that sums are well-defined and order of summation can be interchanged by Tonelli’s theorem for series.
Let \(\{E_k\}_{k=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be pairwise disjoint events. Using countable additivity of each individual measure \(\mu_j\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \left( \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu_j(E_k) \right) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E_k) \quad \text{(interchanging non-negative double summation)} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu(E_k).
\end{aligned}
\] Hence, \(\mu\) is countably additive and constitutes a valid measure.

text:
7.4 Discrete Probability Measures

Corollary 7.1 (Discrete Probability Measures) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and let \(\{\omega_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \Omega\) be a countable sequence of points. Let \(\{p_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, 1]\) be weights satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j = 1\).
Then \(\mu := \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j \delta_{\omega_j}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 16.1). By Theorem 16.1, \(\mu\) is a valid measure. Evaluating \(\mu\) on the entire space \(\Omega\) gives: \[
\mu(\Omega) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j \delta_{\omega_j}(\Omega) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j (1) = 1.
\] Thus, \(\mu\) is a normalized probability measure.

text:
7.5 Basic Properties of Measures
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

Proposition 7.2 (Fundamental Properties of Measures)  

Monotonicity: If \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(A \subseteq B\), then: \[
\mu(A) \le \mu(B).
\tag{7.4}\] If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), then \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).

\tag{7.5}\] When \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), this is written as \(\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\).

Monotonicity: Decompose \(B\) into the disjoint union \(B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\). By countable additivity (applied to the two-set partition, using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) to pad with empty sets): \[
\mu(B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] Since \(\mu(B \setminus A) \ge 0\), it immediately follows that \(\mu(A) \le \mu(B)\). If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), subtracting \(\mu(A)\) from both sides gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).

\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A), \quad \text{and} \quad \mu(B) = \mu(A \cap B) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] The second equation gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\) (valid when \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), which is the stated hypothesis). Substituting into the first: \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\]

A_1 := B_1, \quad A_n := B_n \setminus \left( \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1} B_j \right) \quad \text{for } n \ge 2.
\tag{7.7}\] By construction, \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are pairwise disjoint measurable sets, \(A_n \subseteq B_n\) for all \(n\), and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\). Applying countable additivity and monotonicity (\(A_n \subseteq B_n \implies \mu(A_n) \le \mu(B_n)\)): \[

\]

title: 7  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
7.6 Takeaways






NoteSummary



1. What a measure is. A measure on a measurable space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F})\) is a set function \(\mu:\mathcal{F}\to[0,\infty]\) satisfying \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) and countable additivity. The empty-set condition is independent of countable additivity for general (infinite) measures and must be stated as a separate axiom.
2. Finite additivity is a consequence. Applying countable additivity to a two-set disjoint union padded with empty sets (using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\)) gives \(\mu(A\cup B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\) whenever \(A\cap B=\emptyset\). All “finite additivity” steps in the Properties proof rely on this.
3. The Dirac measure. \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is the simplest non-trivial probability measure: it places unit mass at a single point. Countable additivity holds because a point can belong to at most one member of a disjoint family.
4. Building new measures by linear combination. Non-negative countable linear combinations \(\mu = \sum_j c_j\mu_j\) are again measures. The key step is interchanging the order of two non-negative summations, which is always valid (Tonelli). Normalization (\(\mu(\Omega)=1\)) is then checked separately, giving the class of discrete probability measures.
5. Derived properties from the axioms.

Monotonicity: \(A\subseteq B\implies\mu(A)\le\mu(B)\), via the disjoint decomposition \(B=A\cup(B\setminus A)\).
Inclusion-exclusion: \(\mu(A\cup B)+\mu(A\cap B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\); rearranges the same two disjoint decompositions.
Sub-additivity (Boole’s inequality): \(\mu(\bigcup B_n)\le\sum\mu(B_n)\) for arbitrary (not necessarily disjoint) sets, proved by the disjointification \(A_n=B_n\setminus\bigcup_{j<n}B_j\) which reduces to countable additivity followed by monotonicity \(\mu(A_n)\le\mu(B_n)\).

text:
8.1 Introduction and Motivation
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a premeasure space, and let \(\mu^*: 2^\Omega \to [0, \infty]\) be the Carathéodory outer measure defined for any \(E \subseteq \Omega\) by: \[
\mu^*(E) := \inf \left\{ \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu(A_j) : \{A_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}, \, E \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty A_j \right\}.
\tag{8.1}\]
Historically, the extension of a premeasure to a measure developed through contributions from several mathematicians.

\mu\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu(E_j).
\tag{8.1}\]

text:
8.2 Canonical Examples of Measures

8.2.1 Trivial Measure
On any measurable space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), the constant zero function \(\mu(E) \equiv 0\) for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is trivially a valid measure.


8.2.2 Point Mass (Dirac Measure)

Definition 8.3 (Dirac / Point Mass Measure) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space and fix a point \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\). The Dirac measure (or point mass) at \(\omega_0\), denoted by \(\delta_{\omega_0}: \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]\), is defined by: \[
\delta_{\omega_0}(E) := \begin{cases}  1 & \text{if } \omega_0 \in E, \\  0 & \text{if } \omega_0 \notin E.  \end{cases}
\tag{8.2}\]


Proposition 8.1 (Validity of Dirac Measure) For any \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\), \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 16.1). First, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(\Omega) = 1\) since \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\).
Next, let \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a countable sequence of pairwise disjoint measurable sets. Since the sets are disjoint, the point \(\omega_0\) can belong to at most one set \(E_k\):

Case 1: There exists a unique index \(k \ge 1\) such that \(\omega_0 \in E_k\). Then \(\omega_0 \in \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 1\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) = 1\) and \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \neq k\). Thus: \[\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = \delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) + \sum_{j \neq k} 0 = 1 + 0 = 1.\]
Case 2: \(\omega_0 \notin E_j\) for all \(j \ge 1\). Then \(\omega_0 \notin \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 0\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \ge 1\), yielding \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\).

In both cases, \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j)\), proving countable additivity.

text:
8.4 Discrete Probability Measures

Corollary 8.1 (Discrete Probability Measures) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and let \(\{\omega_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \Omega\) be a countable sequence of points. Let \(\{p_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, 1]\) be weights satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j = 1\).

\] Thus, \(\mu\) is a normalized probability measure.

title: 8  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
8.5 Basic Properties of Measures
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

Proposition 8.2 (Fundamental Properties of Measures)  

Monotonicity: If \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(A \subseteq B\), then: \[
\mu(A) \le \mu(B).
\tag{8.4}\] If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), then \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion Rule (Addition Rule): For any \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\): \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\tag{8.5}\] When \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), this is written as \(\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\).
Countable Sub-Additivity (Boole’s Inequality): For any countable sequence of measurable sets \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (not necessarily disjoint): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\tag{8.6}\]



Proof (Proof of Proposition 16.2). 

Monotonicity: Decompose \(B\) into the disjoint union \(B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\). By countable additivity (applied to the two-set partition, using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) to pad with empty sets): \[
\mu(B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] Since \(\mu(B \setminus A) \ge 0\), it immediately follows that \(\mu(A) \le \mu(B)\). If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), subtracting \(\mu(A)\) from both sides gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion: Decompose \(A \cup B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint) and \(B = (A \cap B) \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint). By countable additivity applied to each two-set partition: \[
\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A), \quad \text{and} \quad \mu(B) = \mu(A \cap B) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] The second equation gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\) (valid when \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), which is the stated hypothesis). Substituting into the first: \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\]
Countable Sub-additivity: Disjointify the sequence \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) by defining: \[
A_1 := B_1, \quad A_n := B_n \setminus \left( \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1} B_j \right) \quad \text{for } n \ge 2.
\tag{8.7}\] By construction, \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are pairwise disjoint measurable sets, \(A_n \subseteq B_n\) for all \(n\), and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\). Applying countable additivity and monotonicity (\(A_n \subseteq B_n \implies \mu(A_n) \le \mu(B_n)\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\]

8.6 Takeaways






NoteSummary

4. Building new measures by linear combination. Non-negative countable linear combinations \(\mu = \sum_j c_j\mu_j\) are again measures. The key step is interchanging the order of two non-negative summations, which is always valid (Tonelli). Normalization (\(\mu(\Omega)=1\)) is then checked separately, giving the class of discrete probability measures.
5. Derived properties from the axioms.

Monotonicity: \(A\subseteq B\implies\mu(A)\le\mu(B)\), via the disjoint decomposition \(B=A\cup(B\setminus A)\).

9.1 Introduction and Review
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finite premeasure space, where \(\mu: \mathcal{A} \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\) is countably additive on the field \(\mathcal{A}\).
Let \(\mu^*: 2^\Omega \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\) denote the induced Carathéodory outer measure: \[
\mu^*(E) := \inf \left\{ \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu(A_j) : \{A_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}, \, E \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty A_j \right\}.
\tag{9.1}\]
We equip \(2^\Omega\) with the outer pseudo-metric \(d_\mu(E, F) := \mu^*(E \Delta F)\) for all \(E, F \subseteq \Omega\). As proved in the previous lecture, the closure \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) in \((2^\Omega, d_\mu)\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra.

text:
Definition 9.1 (Measure and Measure Space) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and \(\mathcal{F}\) be a \(\sigma\)-field (\(\sigma\)-algebra) over \(\Omega\). The pair \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) is called a measurable space, and elements \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) are called measurable sets (or events).
A set function \(\mu: \mathcal{F} \to [0, \infty]\) is called a measure if it satisfies the following two conditions:

Empty Set: \(\mu(\emptyset) = 0\).
Countable Additivity (\(\sigma\)-additivity): For any countable sequence of pairwise disjoint sets \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (i.e., \(E_i \cap E_j = \emptyset\) for all \(i \neq j\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu(E_j).
\tag{9.1}\]







Note



The condition \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) is independent of countable additivity for general measures: without it, the constant function \(\mu \equiv \infty\) satisfies countable additivity but violates the empty-set condition. For finite measures \(\mu(\Omega)<\infty\), the condition can be derived by applying countable additivity to \(\Omega = \Omega \cup \emptyset \cup \emptyset \cup \cdots\).


The triple \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called a measure space.


Definition 9.2 (Finite and Probability Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

\(\mu\) is a finite measure if \(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\).
\(\mu\) is a probability measure if \(\mu(\Omega) = 1\). In this case, \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called a probability space.

text:
9.2 Canonical Examples of Measures

9.2.1 Trivial Measure
On any measurable space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), the constant zero function \(\mu(E) \equiv 0\) for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is trivially a valid measure.


9.2.2 Point Mass (Dirac Measure)

Definition 9.3 (Dirac / Point Mass Measure) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space and fix a point \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\). The Dirac measure (or point mass) at \(\omega_0\), denoted by \(\delta_{\omega_0}: \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]\), is defined by: \[
\delta_{\omega_0}(E) := \begin{cases}  1 & \text{if } \omega_0 \in E, \\  0 & \text{if } \omega_0 \notin E.  \end{cases}
\tag{9.2}\]


Proposition 9.1 (Validity of Dirac Measure) For any \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\), \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 16.1). First, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(\Omega) = 1\) since \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\).
Next, let \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a countable sequence of pairwise disjoint measurable sets. Since the sets are disjoint, the point \(\omega_0\) can belong to at most one set \(E_k\):

Case 1: There exists a unique index \(k \ge 1\) such that \(\omega_0 \in E_k\). Then \(\omega_0 \in \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 1\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) = 1\) and \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \neq k\). Thus: \[\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = \delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) + \sum_{j \neq k} 0 = 1 + 0 = 1.\]
Case 2: \(\omega_0 \notin E_j\) for all \(j \ge 1\). Then \(\omega_0 \notin \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 0\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \ge 1\), yielding \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\).

In both cases, \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j)\), proving countable additivity.

text:
9.3 Constructing New Measures from Existing Measures

Theorem 9.1 (Linear Combinations and Sums of Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space.

Scalar Multiplication: If \(\mu\) is a measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(a \in (0, \infty)\), then \(a\mu\) defined by \((a\mu)(E) := a \cdot \mu(E)\) is a valid measure.
Countable Linear Combinations: If \(\{\mu_j\}_{j=1}^\infty\) is a countable collection of measures on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(\{c_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, \infty)\), then the set function: \[
\mu := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j
\tag{9.3}\] defined by \(\mu(E) := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E)\) for \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is a valid measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).



Proof (Proof of Theorem 16.1). Because all terms \(c_j \mu_j(E)\) are non-negative (\(c_j \mu_j(E) \in [0, \infty]\)), all infinite sums consist of non-negative real/extended terms, which guarantees that sums are well-defined and order of summation can be interchanged by Tonelli’s theorem for series.
Let \(\{E_k\}_{k=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be pairwise disjoint events. Using countable additivity of each individual measure \(\mu_j\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \left( \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu_j(E_k) \right) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E_k) \quad \text{(interchanging non-negative double summation)} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu(E_k).
\end{aligned}
\] Hence, \(\mu\) is countably additive and constitutes a valid measure.

Corollary 9.1 (Discrete Probability Measures) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and let \(\{\omega_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \Omega\) be a countable sequence of points. Let \(\{p_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, 1]\) be weights satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j = 1\).

\] Thus, \(\mu\) is a normalized probability measure.
