text:
10.5 Basic Properties of Measures
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

Proposition 10.2 (Fundamental Properties of Measures)  

Monotonicity: If \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(A \subseteq B\), then: \[
\mu(A) \le \mu(B).
\tag{10.4}\] If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), then \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion Rule (Addition Rule): For any \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\): \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\tag{10.5}\] When \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), this is written as \(\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\).
Countable Sub-Additivity (Boole’s Inequality): For any countable sequence of measurable sets \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (not necessarily disjoint): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\tag{10.6}\]



Proof (Proof of Proposition 16.2). 

Monotonicity: Decompose \(B\) into the disjoint union \(B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\). By countable additivity (applied to the two-set partition, using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) to pad with empty sets): \[
\mu(B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] Since \(\mu(B \setminus A) \ge 0\), it immediately follows that \(\mu(A) \le \mu(B)\). If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), subtracting \(\mu(A)\) from both sides gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion: Decompose \(A \cup B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint) and \(B = (A \cap B) \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint). By countable additivity applied to each two-set partition: \[
\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A), \quad \text{and} \quad \mu(B) = \mu(A \cap B) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] The second equation gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\) (valid when \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), which is the stated hypothesis). Substituting into the first: \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\]
Countable Sub-additivity: Disjointify the sequence \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) by defining: \[
A_1 := B_1, \quad A_n := B_n \setminus \left( \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1} B_j \right) \quad \text{for } n \ge 2.
\tag{10.7}\] By construction, \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are pairwise disjoint measurable sets, \(A_n \subseteq B_n\) for all \(n\), and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\). Applying countable additivity and monotonicity (\(A_n \subseteq B_n \implies \mu(A_n) \le \mu(B_n)\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\]

10.6 Takeaways






NoteSummary



1. What a measure is. A measure on a measurable space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F})\) is a set function \(\mu:\mathcal{F}\to[0,\infty]\) satisfying \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) and countable additivity. 2. Finite additivity is a consequence. Applying countable additivity to a two-set disjoint union padded with empty sets (using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\)) gives \(\mu(A\cup B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\) whenever \(A\cap B=\emptyset\). All “finite additivity” steps in the Properties proof rely on this.
3. The Dirac measure. \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is the simplest non-trivial probability measure: it places unit mass at a single point. Countable additivity holds because a point can belong to at most one member of a disjoint family.
4. Building new measures by linear combination. Non-negative countable linear combinations \(\mu = \sum_j c_j\mu_j\) are again measures. The key step is interchanging the order of two non-negative summations, which is always valid (Tonelli). Definition 11.1 (Measure and Measure Space) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and \(\mathcal{F}\) be a \(\sigma\)-field (\(\sigma\)-algebra) over \(\Omega\). The pair \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) is called a measurable space, and elements \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) are called measurable sets (or events).

\mu\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu(E_j).
\tag{11.1}\]







Note



The condition \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) is independent of countable additivity for general measures: without it, the constant function \(\mu \equiv \infty\) satisfies countable additivity but violates the empty-set condition. For finite measures \(\mu(\Omega)<\infty\), the condition can be derived by applying countable additivity to \(\Omega = \Omega \cup \emptyset \cup \emptyset \cup \cdots\).

11.2 Canonical Examples of Measures

11.2.1 Trivial Measure
On any measurable space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), the constant zero function \(\mu(E) \equiv 0\) for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is trivially a valid measure.


11.2.2 Point Mass (Dirac Measure)

Definition 11.3 (Dirac / Point Mass Measure) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space and fix a point \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\). The Dirac measure (or point mass) at \(\omega_0\), denoted by \(\delta_{\omega_0}: \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]\), is defined by: \[
\delta_{\omega_0}(E) := \begin{cases}  1 & \text{if } \omega_0 \in E, \\  0 & \text{if } \omega_0 \notin E.  \end{cases}
\tag{11.2}\]


Proposition 11.1 (Validity of Dirac Measure) For any \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\), \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 16.1). First, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(\Omega) = 1\) since \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\).
Next, let \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a countable sequence of pairwise disjoint measurable sets. Since the sets are disjoint, the point \(\omega_0\) can belong to at most one set \(E_k\):

Case 1: There exists a unique index \(k \ge 1\) such that \(\omega_0 \in E_k\). Then \(\omega_0 \in \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 1\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) = 1\) and \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \neq k\). Thus: \[\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = \delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) + \sum_{j \neq k} 0 = 1 + 0 = 1.\]
Case 2: \(\omega_0 \notin E_j\) for all \(j \ge 1\). Then \(\omega_0 \notin \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 0\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \ge 1\), yielding \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\).

In both cases, \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j)\), proving countable additivity.

11.3 Constructing New Measures from Existing Measures

Theorem 11.1 (Linear Combinations and Sums of Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space.

Scalar Multiplication: If \(\mu\) is a measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(a \in (0, \infty)\), then \(a\mu\) defined by \((a\mu)(E) := a \cdot \mu(E)\) is a valid measure.
Countable Linear Combinations: If \(\{\mu_j\}_{j=1}^\infty\) is a countable collection of measures on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(\{c_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, \infty)\), then the set function: \[
\mu := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j
\tag{11.3}\] defined by \(\mu(E) := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E)\) for \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is a valid measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).



Proof (Proof of Theorem 16.1). Because all terms \(c_j \mu_j(E)\) are non-negative (\(c_j \mu_j(E) \in [0, \infty]\)), all infinite sums consist of non-negative real/extended terms, which guarantees that sums are well-defined and order of summation can be interchanged by Tonelli’s theorem for series.
Let \(\{E_k\}_{k=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be pairwise disjoint events. Using countable additivity of each individual measure \(\mu_j\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \left( \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu_j(E_k) \right) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E_k) \quad \text{(interchanging non-negative double summation)} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu(E_k).
\end{aligned}
\] Hence, \(\mu\) is countably additive and constitutes a valid measure.

11.4 Discrete Probability Measures

Corollary 11.1 (Discrete Probability Measures) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and let \(\{\omega_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \Omega\) be a countable sequence of points. Let \(\{p_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, 1]\) be weights satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j = 1\).

\mu(\Omega) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j \delta_{\omega_j}(\Omega) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j (1) = 1.
\] Thus, \(\mu\) is a normalized probability measure.

\] Since \(\mu(B \setminus A) \ge 0\), it immediately follows that \(\mu(A) \le \mu(B)\). If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), subtracting \(\mu(A)\) from both sides gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion: Decompose \(A \cup B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint) and \(B = (A \cap B) \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint). By countable additivity applied to each two-set partition: \[
\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A), \quad \text{and} \quad \mu(B) = \mu(A \cap B) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] The second equation gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\) (valid when \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), which is the stated hypothesis). Substituting into the first: \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\]
Countable Sub-additivity: Disjointify the sequence \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) by defining: \[
A_1 := B_1, \quad A_n := B_n \setminus \left( \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1} B_j \right) \quad \text{for } n \ge 2.
\tag{12.7}\] By construction, \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are pairwise disjoint measurable sets, \(A_n \subseteq B_n\) for all \(n\), and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\). Applying countable additivity and monotonicity (\(A_n \subseteq B_n \implies \mu(A_n) \le \mu(B_n)\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\]

text:
12.6 Takeaways






NoteSummary



1. What a measure is. A measure on a measurable space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F})\) is a set function \(\mu:\mathcal{F}\to[0,\infty]\) satisfying \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) and countable additivity. The empty-set condition is independent of countable additivity for general (infinite) measures and must be stated as a separate axiom.
2. Finite additivity is a consequence. Applying countable additivity to a two-set disjoint union padded with empty sets (using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\)) gives \(\mu(A\cup B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\) whenever \(A\cap B=\emptyset\). All “finite additivity” steps in the Properties proof rely on this.
3. The Dirac measure. \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is the simplest non-trivial probability measure: it places unit mass at a single point. Countable additivity holds because a point can belong to at most one member of a disjoint family.
4. Building new measures by linear combination. Non-negative countable linear combinations \(\mu = \sum_j c_j\mu_j\) are again measures. The key step is interchanging the order of two non-negative summations, which is always valid (Tonelli). Normalization (\(\mu(\Omega)=1\)) is then checked separately, giving the class of discrete probability measures.
5. Derived properties from the axioms.

Monotonicity: \(A\subseteq B\implies\mu(A)\le\mu(B)\), via the disjoint decomposition \(B=A\cup(B\setminus A)\).
Inclusion-exclusion: \(\mu(A\cup B)+\mu(A\cap B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\); rearranges the same two disjoint decompositions.

title: 13  Lecture 6.1: Random Variables Motivation
text:
13.1 Random Variables: Motivation
We begin with informal “experiments” to motivate our formal measure-theoretic framework.
In general, each experiment has an outcome \(\omega\), belonging to the set of all possible outcomes called the sample space, denoted by \(\Omega\).
Probability is a measure of the likelihood of an event \(E \subseteq \Omega\), which is a set of outcomes.
Outcomes                   Measurements
   ω ∈ Ω      ─────── X ───────>   ℝ
(Inaccessible)               (Observable)
The underlying sample space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) is often “inaccessible” directly:
A function \(X: \Omega \to S\) maps the inaccessible sample space to a manageable “state space” \(S\).
To perform probability calculations, we need to be able to compute probabilities of sets formed by conditions on \(X\), such as: \[
\{X \le 1\} := \{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le 1\}.
\]

title: 13  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
Definition 13.1 (Measure and Measure Space) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and \(\mathcal{F}\) be a \(\sigma\)-field (\(\sigma\)-algebra) over \(\Omega\). The pair \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) is called a measurable space, and elements \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) are called measurable sets (or events).
A set function \(\mu: \mathcal{F} \to [0, \infty]\) is called a measure if it satisfies the following two conditions:

Empty Set: \(\mu(\emptyset) = 0\).
Countable Additivity (\(\sigma\)-additivity): For any countable sequence of pairwise disjoint sets \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (i.e., \(E_i \cap E_j = \emptyset\) for all \(i \neq j\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu(E_j).
\tag{13.1}\]







Note



The condition \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) is independent of countable additivity for general measures: without it, the constant function \(\mu \equiv \infty\) satisfies countable additivity but violates the empty-set condition. For finite measures \(\mu(\Omega)<\infty\), the condition can be derived by applying countable additivity to \(\Omega = \Omega \cup \emptyset \cup \emptyset \cup \cdots\).


The triple \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called a measure space.


Definition 13.2 (Finite and Probability Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

\(\mu\) is a finite measure if \(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\).
\(\mu\) is a probability measure if \(\mu(\Omega) = 1\). In this case, \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called a probability space.

title: 13  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
13.2 Canonical Examples of Measures

13.2.1 Trivial Measure
On any measurable space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), the constant zero function \(\mu(E) \equiv 0\) for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is trivially a valid measure.


13.2.2 Point Mass (Dirac Measure)

Definition 13.3 (Dirac / Point Mass Measure) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space and fix a point \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\). The Dirac measure (or point mass) at \(\omega_0\), denoted by \(\delta_{\omega_0}: \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]\), is defined by: \[
\delta_{\omega_0}(E) := \begin{cases}  1 & \text{if } \omega_0 \in E, \\  0 & \text{if } \omega_0 \notin E.  \end{cases}
\tag{13.2}\]


Proposition 13.1 (Validity of Dirac Measure) For any \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\), \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 16.1). First, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(\Omega) = 1\) since \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\).
Next, let \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a countable sequence of pairwise disjoint measurable sets. Since the sets are disjoint, the point \(\omega_0\) can belong to at most one set \(E_k\):

Case 1: There exists a unique index \(k \ge 1\) such that \(\omega_0 \in E_k\). Then \(\omega_0 \in \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 1\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) = 1\) and \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \neq k\). Thus: \[\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = \delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) + \sum_{j \neq k} 0 = 1 + 0 = 1.\]
Case 2: \(\omega_0 \notin E_j\) for all \(j \ge 1\). Then \(\omega_0 \notin \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 0\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \ge 1\), yielding \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\).

In both cases, \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j)\), proving countable additivity.

title: 13  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
section: 13.3 Constructing New Measures from Existing Measures
text:
13.3 Constructing New Measures from Existing Measures

Theorem 13.1 (Linear Combinations and Sums of Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space.

Scalar Multiplication: If \(\mu\) is a measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(a \in (0, \infty)\), then \(a\mu\) defined by \((a\mu)(E) := a \cdot \mu(E)\) is a valid measure.
Countable Linear Combinations: If \(\{\mu_j\}_{j=1}^\infty\) is a countable collection of measures on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(\{c_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, \infty)\), then the set function: \[
\mu := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j
\tag{13.3}\] defined by \(\mu(E) := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E)\) for \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is a valid measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).



Proof (Proof of Theorem 16.1). Because all terms \(c_j \mu_j(E)\) are non-negative (\(c_j \mu_j(E) \in [0, \infty]\)), all infinite sums consist of non-negative real/extended terms, which guarantees that sums are well-defined and order of summation can be interchanged by Tonelli’s theorem for series.
Let \(\{E_k\}_{k=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be pairwise disjoint events. Using countable additivity of each individual measure \(\mu_j\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \left( \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu_j(E_k) \right) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E_k) \quad \text{(interchanging non-negative double summation)} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu(E_k).
\end{aligned}
\] Hence, \(\mu\) is countably additive and constitutes a valid measure.

title: 13  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
13.4 Discrete Probability Measures

Corollary 13.1 (Discrete Probability Measures) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and let \(\{\omega_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \Omega\) be a countable sequence of points. Let \(\{p_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, 1]\) be weights satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j = 1\).
Then \(\mu := \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j \delta_{\omega_j}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 16.1). By Theorem 16.1, \(\mu\) is a valid measure. Evaluating \(\mu\) on the entire space \(\Omega\) gives: \[
\mu(\Omega) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j \delta_{\omega_j}(\Omega) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j (1) = 1.
\] Thus, \(\mu\) is a normalized probability measure.

title: 13  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
13.5 Basic Properties of Measures
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

Proposition 13.2 (Fundamental Properties of Measures)  

Monotonicity: If \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(A \subseteq B\), then: \[
\mu(A) \le \mu(B).
\tag{13.4}\] If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), then \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion Rule (Addition Rule): For any \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\): \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\tag{13.5}\] When \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), this is written as \(\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\).
Countable Sub-Additivity (Boole’s Inequality): For any countable sequence of measurable sets \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (not necessarily disjoint): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\tag{13.6}\]



Proof (Proof of Proposition 16.2). 

Monotonicity: Decompose \(B\) into the disjoint union \(B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\). By countable additivity (applied to the two-set partition, using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) to pad with empty sets): \[
\mu(B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] Since \(\mu(B \setminus A) \ge 0\), it immediately follows that \(\mu(A) \le \mu(B)\). If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), subtracting \(\mu(A)\) from both sides gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion: Decompose \(A \cup B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint) and \(B = (A \cap B) \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint). By countable additivity applied to each two-set partition: \[
\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A), \quad \text{and} \quad \mu(B) = \mu(A \cap B) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] The second equation gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\) (valid when \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), which is the stated hypothesis). Substituting into the first: \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\]
Countable Sub-additivity: Disjointify the sequence \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) by defining: \[
A_1 := B_1, \quad A_n := B_n \setminus \left( \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1} B_j \right) \quad \text{for } n \ge 2.
\tag{13.7}\] By construction, \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are pairwise disjoint measurable sets, \(A_n \subseteq B_n\) for all \(n\), and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\). Applying countable additivity and monotonicity (\(A_n \subseteq B_n \implies \mu(A_n) \le \mu(B_n)\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\]

title: 14  Lecture 6.2: Measurable Functions
text:
14.1 Preimages vs. Images
Let \(f: \Omega \to S\) be a function between two arbitrary sets.
The function \(f\) naturally induces two set maps:
The image set map is not well-behaved with respect to set operations: one always has \(f(A \cap B) \subseteq f(A) \cap f(B)\), but the inclusion may be strict unless \(f\) is injective. By contrast, the preimage map \(E \mapsto f^{-1}(E)\) preserves all standard set operations: for any family \(\{E_\alpha\} \subseteq 2^S\) and any \(E \subseteq S\), \[
\begin{align*}
&f^{-1}\left( \bigcup_\alpha E_\alpha \right) = \bigcup_\alpha f^{-1}(E_\alpha), \\
&f^{-1}\left( \bigcap_\alpha E_\alpha \right) = \bigcap_\alpha f^{-1}(E_\alpha),\\
&f^{-1}(S \setminus E) = \Omega \setminus f^{-1}(E).
\end{align*}
\]

\tag{14.2}\]

Monotonicity: Decompose \(B\) into the disjoint union \(B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\). By countable additivity (applied to the two-set partition, using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) to pad with empty sets): \[
\mu(B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] Since \(\mu(B \setminus A) \ge 0\), it immediately follows that \(\mu(A) \le \mu(B)\). If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), subtracting \(\mu(A)\) from both sides gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion: Decompose \(A \cup B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint) and \(B = (A \cap B) \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint). By countable additivity applied to each two-set partition: \[
\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A), \quad \text{and} \quad \mu(B) = \mu(A \cap B) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] The second equation gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\) (valid when \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), which is the stated hypothesis). Substituting into the first: \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\]
Countable Sub-additivity: Disjointify the sequence \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) by defining: \[
A_1 := B_1, \quad A_n := B_n \setminus \left( \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1} B_j \right) \quad \text{for } n \ge 2.
\tag{14.7}\] By construction, \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are pairwise disjoint measurable sets, \(A_n \subseteq B_n\) for all \(n\), and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\). Applying countable additivity and monotonicity (\(A_n \subseteq B_n \implies \mu(A_n) \le \mu(B_n)\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\]

text:
14.6 Takeaways






NoteSummary



1. What a measure is. A measure on a measurable space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F})\) is a set function \(\mu:\mathcal{F}\to[0,\infty]\) satisfying \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) and countable additivity. The empty-set condition is independent of countable additivity for general (infinite) measures and must be stated as a separate axiom.
2. Finite additivity is a consequence. Applying countable additivity to a two-set disjoint union padded with empty sets (using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\)) gives \(\mu(A\cup B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\) whenever \(A\cap B=\emptyset\). All “finite additivity” steps in the Properties proof rely on this.
3. The Dirac measure. \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is the simplest non-trivial probability measure: it places unit mass at a single point. Countable additivity holds because a point can belong to at most one member of a disjoint family.
4. Building new measures by linear combination. Non-negative countable linear combinations \(\mu = \sum_j c_j\mu_j\) are again measures. The key step is interchanging the order of two non-negative summations, which is always valid (Tonelli). Normalization (\(\mu(\Omega)=1\)) is then checked separately, giving the class of discrete probability measures.
5. Derived properties from the axioms.

Monotonicity: \(A\subseteq B\implies\mu(A)\le\mu(B)\), via the disjoint decomposition \(B=A\cup(B\setminus A)\).
Inclusion-exclusion: \(\mu(A\cup B)+\mu(A\cap B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\); rearranges the same two disjoint decompositions.

Definition 15.1 (Measure and Measure Space) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and \(\mathcal{F}\) be a \(\sigma\)-field (\(\sigma\)-algebra) over \(\Omega\). The pair \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) is called a measurable space, and elements \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) are called measurable sets (or events).
A set function \(\mu: \mathcal{F} \to [0, \infty]\) is called a measure if it satisfies the following two conditions:

Empty Set: \(\mu(\emptyset) = 0\).
Countable Additivity (\(\sigma\)-additivity): For any countable sequence of pairwise disjoint sets \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (i.e., \(E_i \cap E_j = \emptyset\) for all \(i \neq j\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu(E_j).
\tag{15.1}\]







Note



The condition \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) is independent of countable additivity for general measures: without it, the constant function \(\mu \equiv \infty\) satisfies countable additivity but violates the empty-set condition. For finite measures \(\mu(\Omega)<\infty\), the condition can be derived by applying countable additivity to \(\Omega = \Omega \cup \emptyset \cup \emptyset \cup \cdots\).


The triple \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called a measure space.


Definition 15.2 (Finite and Probability Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

\(\mu\) is a finite measure if \(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\).
\(\mu\) is a probability measure if \(\mu(\Omega) = 1\). In this case, \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called a probability space.

title: 15  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
15.2 Canonical Examples of Measures

15.2.1 Trivial Measure
On any measurable space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), the constant zero function \(\mu(E) \equiv 0\) for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is trivially a valid measure.


15.2.2 Point Mass (Dirac Measure)

Definition 15.3 (Dirac / Point Mass Measure) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space and fix a point \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\). The Dirac measure (or point mass) at \(\omega_0\), denoted by \(\delta_{\omega_0}: \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]\), is defined by: \[
\delta_{\omega_0}(E) := \begin{cases}  1 & \text{if } \omega_0 \in E, \\  0 & \text{if } \omega_0 \notin E.  \end{cases}
\tag{15.2}\]


Proposition 15.1 (Validity of Dirac Measure) For any \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\), \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 16.1). First, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(\Omega) = 1\) since \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\).
Next, let \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a countable sequence of pairwise disjoint measurable sets. Since the sets are disjoint, the point \(\omega_0\) can belong to at most one set \(E_k\):

Case 1: There exists a unique index \(k \ge 1\) such that \(\omega_0 \in E_k\). Then \(\omega_0 \in \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 1\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) = 1\) and \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \neq k\). Thus: \[\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = \delta_{\omega_0}(E_k) + \sum_{j \neq k} 0 = 1 + 0 = 1.\]
Case 2: \(\omega_0 \notin E_j\) for all \(j \ge 1\). Then \(\omega_0 \notin \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\), so \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = 0\). On the sum side, \(\delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\) for all \(j \ge 1\), yielding \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j) = 0\).

In both cases, \(\delta_{\omega_0}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\right) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_{\omega_0}(E_j)\), proving countable additivity.

text:
15.3 Constructing New Measures from Existing Measures

Theorem 15.1 (Linear Combinations and Sums of Measures) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space.

Scalar Multiplication: If \(\mu\) is a measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(a \in (0, \infty)\), then \(a\mu\) defined by \((a\mu)(E) := a \cdot \mu(E)\) is a valid measure.
Countable Linear Combinations: If \(\{\mu_j\}_{j=1}^\infty\) is a countable collection of measures on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \(\{c_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, \infty)\), then the set function: \[
\mu := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j
\tag{15.3}\] defined by \(\mu(E) := \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E)\) for \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is a valid measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).



Proof (Proof of Theorem 16.1). Because all terms \(c_j \mu_j(E)\) are non-negative (\(c_j \mu_j(E) \in [0, \infty]\)), all infinite sums consist of non-negative real/extended terms, which guarantees that sums are well-defined and order of summation can be interchanged by Tonelli’s theorem for series.
Let \(\{E_k\}_{k=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be pairwise disjoint events. Using countable additivity of each individual measure \(\mu_j\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k \right) \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \left( \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu_j(E_k) \right) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j \mu_j(E_k) \quad \text{(interchanging non-negative double summation)} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu(E_k).
\end{aligned}
\] Hence, \(\mu\) is countably additive and constitutes a valid measure.

title: 15  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
15.4 Discrete Probability Measures

Corollary 15.1 (Discrete Probability Measures) Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space and let \(\{\omega_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \Omega\) be a countable sequence of points. Let \(\{p_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq [0, 1]\) be weights satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j = 1\).
Then \(\mu := \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j \delta_{\omega_j}\) is a valid probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 16.1). By Theorem 16.1, \(\mu\) is a valid measure. Evaluating \(\mu\) on the entire space \(\Omega\) gives: \[
\mu(\Omega) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j \delta_{\omega_j}(\Omega) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j (1) = 1.
\] Thus, \(\mu\) is a normalized probability measure.

text:
15.5 Basic Properties of Measures
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.

Proposition 15.2 (Fundamental Properties of Measures)  

Monotonicity: If \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(A \subseteq B\), then: \[
\mu(A) \le \mu(B).
\tag{15.4}\] If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), then \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion Rule (Addition Rule): For any \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\): \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\tag{15.5}\] When \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), this is written as \(\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\).
Countable Sub-Additivity (Boole’s Inequality): For any countable sequence of measurable sets \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) (not necessarily disjoint): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\tag{15.6}\]



Proof (Proof of Proposition 16.2). 

Monotonicity: Decompose \(B\) into the disjoint union \(B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\). By countable additivity (applied to the two-set partition, using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) to pad with empty sets): \[
\mu(B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] Since \(\mu(B \setminus A) \ge 0\), it immediately follows that \(\mu(A) \le \mu(B)\). If \(\mu(A) < \infty\), subtracting \(\mu(A)\) from both sides gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\).
Inclusion-Exclusion: Decompose \(A \cup B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint) and \(B = (A \cap B) \cup (B \setminus A)\) (disjoint). By countable additivity applied to each two-set partition: \[
\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A), \quad \text{and} \quad \mu(B) = \mu(A \cap B) + \mu(B \setminus A).
\] The second equation gives \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A \cap B)\) (valid when \(\mu(A \cap B) < \infty\), which is the stated hypothesis). Substituting into the first: \[
\mu(A \cup B) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B \setminus A) + \mu(A \cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B).
\]
Countable Sub-additivity: Disjointify the sequence \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) by defining: \[
A_1 := B_1, \quad A_n := B_n \setminus \left( \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1} B_j \right) \quad \text{for } n \ge 2.
\tag{15.7}\] By construction, \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are pairwise disjoint measurable sets, \(A_n \subseteq B_n\) for all \(n\), and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\). Applying countable additivity and monotonicity (\(A_n \subseteq B_n \implies \mu(A_n) \le \mu(B_n)\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\]

Countable Sub-additivity: Disjointify the sequence \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) by defining: \[
A_1 := B_1, \quad A_n := B_n \setminus \left( \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1} B_j \right) \quad \text{for } n \ge 2.
\tag{16.7}\] By construction, \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are pairwise disjoint measurable sets, \(A_n \subseteq B_n\) for all \(n\), and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\). Applying countable additivity and monotonicity (\(A_n \subseteq B_n \implies \mu(A_n) \le \mu(B_n)\)): \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\]

title: 16  Lecture 2.1: Measures, Definition, Examples
text:
16.6 Takeaways






NoteSummary



1. What a measure is. A measure on a measurable space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F})\) is a set function \(\mu:\mathcal{F}\to[0,\infty]\) satisfying \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) and countable additivity. The empty-set condition is independent of countable additivity for general (infinite) measures and must be stated as a separate axiom.
2. Finite additivity is a consequence. Applying countable additivity to a two-set disjoint union padded with empty sets (using \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\)) gives \(\mu(A\cup B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\) whenever \(A\cap B=\emptyset\). All “finite additivity” steps in the Properties proof rely on this.
3. The Dirac measure. \(\delta_{\omega_0}\) is the simplest non-trivial probability measure: it places unit mass at a single point. Countable additivity holds because a point can belong to at most one member of a disjoint family.
4. Building new measures by linear combination. Non-negative countable linear combinations \(\mu = \sum_j c_j\mu_j\) are again measures. The key step is interchanging the order of two non-negative summations, which is always valid (Tonelli). Normalization (\(\mu(\Omega)=1\)) is then checked separately, giving the class of discrete probability measures.
5. Derived properties from the axioms.

Monotonicity: \(A\subseteq B\implies\mu(A)\le\mu(B)\), via the disjoint decomposition \(B=A\cup(B\setminus A)\).
Inclusion-exclusion: \(\mu(A\cup B)+\mu(A\cap B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\); rearranges the same two disjoint decompositions.
Sub-additivity (Boole’s inequality): \(\mu(\bigcup B_n)\le\sum\mu(B_n)\) for arbitrary (not necessarily disjoint) sets, proved by the disjointification \(A_n=B_n\setminus\bigcup_{j<n}B_j\) which reduces to countable additivity followed by monotonicity \(\mu(A_n)\le\mu(B_n)\).

title: 6  Lecture 3.1: Stieltjes Premeasures
text:
Theorem 6.1 (Stieltjes Premeasure Theorem) The finitely-additive measure \(\mu_F\) is a premeasure (i.e., countably additive) on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\) if and only if \(F\) is right-continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\): \[
\lim_{\delta \downarrow 0} F(x + \delta) = F(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R}.
\tag{6.1}\]

title: 6  Lecture 3.1: Stieltjes Premeasures
text:
6.2 Countable Subadditivity Criterion on Semi-Algebras
Recall that a finitely-additive measure \(\mu\) on a field \(\mathcal{A}\) is countably superadditive; that is, for any countable collection of disjoint sets \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathcal{A}\) with \(A = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \in \mathcal{A}\), we have: \[
\mu(A) \ge \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n).
\] The following proposition shows that, for a finitely additive set function defined on the field generated by a semi-algebra, it is enough to verify countable subadditivity on the semi-algebra to obtain countable additivity on the entire field.

Proposition 6.1 (Countable Subadditivity Criterion) Let \(\mathcal{S} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) be a semi-algebra over \(\Omega\), and let \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\) be the generated field. A finitely-additive measure \(\mu: \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}) \to [0, \infty]\) is a premeasure (countably additive) if and only if \(\mu\) is countably subadditive on \(\mathcal{S}\); that is, whenever \(E = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E_n\) with \(E, E_n \in \mathcal{S}\), we have: \[
\mu(E) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(E_n).
\tag{6.2}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 6.1). \((\Rightarrow)\) If \(\mu\) is a premeasure on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\), it is countably additive on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\), which directly implies countable subadditivity on \(\mathcal{S}\).
\((\Leftarrow)\) Finitely-additive measures are always countably superadditive on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\). Thus, to establish countable additivity, it suffices to prove that \(\mu\) is countably subadditive on the entire field \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\).
Let \(A = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\) where \(A, A_n \in \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\). By Proposition 5.2, any set in \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\) is a finite disjoint union of elements from \(\mathcal{S}\). Thus, we can write: \[
A = \bigcup_{j=1}^N E_j \quad \text{and} \quad A_n = \bigcup_{i=1}^{N_n} E_i^n,
\] where \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^N \subset \mathcal{S}\) are pairwise disjoint, and for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(\{E_i^n\}_{i=1}^{N_n} \subset \mathcal{S}\) are pairwise disjoint.
For each fixed \(j \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), since \(E_j \subseteq A = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\), we have: \[
E_j = E_j \cap A = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty (A_n \cap E_j) = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \bigcup_{i=1}^{N_n} (E_i^n \cap E_j).
\]
Since \(\mathcal{S}\) is a semi-algebra, \(E_i^n \cap E_j \in \mathcal{S}\). Applying countable subadditivity on \(\mathcal{S}\) yields: \[
\mu(E_j) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{i=1}^{N_n} \mu(E_i^n \cap E_j).
\]
Summing over \(j = 1, \dots, N\) and using finite additivity on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\) gives: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu(A) = \sum_{j=1}^N \mu(E_j) &\le \sum_{j=1}^N \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{i=1}^{N_n} \mu(E_i^n \cap E_j) \\
&= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{i=1}^{N_n} \sum_{j=1}^N \mu(E_i^n \cap E_j) \\
&= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{i=1}^{N_n} \mu\left( E_i^n \cap \bigcup_{j=1}^N E_j \right) \\
&= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{i=1}^{N_n} \mu(E_i^n \cap A) \\
&\le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{i=1}^{N_n} \mu(E_i^n) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, \(\mu(A) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n)\), proving that \(\mu\) is countably subadditive and hence a premeasure on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\).

title: 6  Lecture 3.1: Stieltjes Premeasures
section: 6.3 Proof of the Stieltjes Premeasure Theorem
text:
6.3 Proof of the Stieltjes Premeasure Theorem
We now prove Theorem 6.1 by verifying countable subadditivity of \(\mu_F\) on the semi-algebra \(\mathcal{S}_{(]}\) using a Heine-Borel compactness argument.

Proof (Proof of Theorem 6.1). Assume \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is right-continuous. By Proposition 6.1, it suffices to prove that \(\mu_F\) is countably subadditive on \(\mathcal{S}_{(]}\).
Suppose \((a, b] \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty (a_j, b_j]\) with \((a, b], (a_j, b_j] \in \mathcal{S}_{(]}\). If \(a = b\) or \(a > b\), \((a, b] = \emptyset\) and subadditivity holds trivially. Assume \(-\infty < a < b < \infty\).
Fix \(\epsilon > 0\) and \(\delta > 0\) such that \(a + \delta < b\).

Open Cover Construction: The compact interval \([a + \delta, b]\) is contained in \((a, b]\): \[
[a + \delta, b] \subset (a, b] \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty (a_j, b_j].
\] By right-continuity of \(F\), for each \(j \ge 1\), we can choose \(\delta_j > 0\) such that: \[
F(b_j + \delta_j) - F(b_j) < \frac{\epsilon}{2^j}.
\tag{6.3}\] Then \([a + \delta, b] \subset \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty (a_j, b_j + \delta_j)\).
Compactness Argument: Since \([a + \delta, b]\) is compact and \(\{(a_j, b_j + \delta_j)\}_{j=1}^\infty\) is an open cover of \([a + \delta, b]\), there exists a finite subcover \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that: \[
[a + \delta, b] \subset \bigcup_{j=1}^N (a_j, b_j + \delta_j).
\] This implies the interval cover \((a + \delta, b] \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^N (a_j, b_j + \delta_j]\).
Finite Subadditivity and Limit Bounds: By finite subadditivity of \(\mu_F\) on interval unions, we have: \[
\mu_F((a + \delta, b]) \le \sum_{j=1}^N \mu_F((a_j, b_j + \delta_j]).
\] Using additivity \(\mu_F((a_j, b_j + \delta_j]) = \mu_F((a_j, b_j]) + \mu_F((b_j, b_j + \delta_j])\), we obtain: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_F((a + \delta, b]) &\le \sum_{j=1}^N \left( \mu_F((a_j, b_j]) + \mu_F((b_j, b_j + \delta_j]) \right) \\
&\le \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu_F((a_j, b_j]) + \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu_F((b_j, b_j + \delta_j]).
\end{aligned}
\] Applying bound Equation 6.3: \[
\mu_F((a + \delta, b]) \le \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu_F((a_j, b_j]) + \sum_{j=1}^\infty \frac{\epsilon}{2^j} = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu_F((a_j, b_j]) + \epsilon.
\]
Evaluating the left-hand side: \(\mu_F((a + \delta, b]) = F(b) - F(a + \delta)\). Taking \(\delta \downarrow 0\), right-continuity of \(F\) at \(a\) implies \(F(a + \delta) \to F(a)\), yielding: \[
\mu_F((a, b]) = F(b) - F(a) \le \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu_F((a_j, b_j]) + \epsilon.
\] Since \(\epsilon > 0\) was arbitrary, letting \(\epsilon \to 0\) gives: \[
\mu_F((a, b]) \le \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu_F((a_j, b_j]).
\]

Extending to unbounded intervals (\(a = -\infty\) or \(b = \infty\)) follows by taking limits. Thus \(\mu_F\) is a premeasure on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: 6  Lecture 3.1: Stieltjes Premeasures
text:
6.4 Lebesgue Premeasure and Translation Invariance

Definition 6.1 (Lebesgue Premeasure) When \(F(x) = x\), the associated Stieltjes premeasure \(\mu: \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]}) \to [0, \infty]\) is called the Lebesgue premeasure, satisfying: \[
\mu((a, b]) = b - a.
\tag{6.4}\]


Proposition 6.2 (Translation Invariance of Lebesgue Premeasure) The Lebesgue premeasure \(\mu\) is translation-invariant on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\). Specifically, for any \(E \in \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\) and \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\), if \(E + \alpha := \{x + \alpha : x \in E\}\), then \(E + \alpha \in \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\) and: \[
\mu(E + \alpha) = \mu(E).
\tag{6.5}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 6.2). Any set \(E \in \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\) can be expressed as a finite disjoint union \(E = \bigcup_{j=1}^n (a_j, b_j]\). Then \(E + \alpha = \bigcup_{j=1}^n (a_j + \alpha, b_j + \alpha]\), which is also a finite disjoint union of elements in \(\mathcal{S}_{(]}\).
By definition and finite additivity: \[
\begin{align*}
\mu(E + \alpha) &= \sum_{j=1}^n \mu((a_j + \alpha, b_j + \alpha])\\
& = \sum_{j=1}^n ((b_j + \alpha) - (a_j + \alpha)) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^n (b_j - a_j) = \sum_{j=1}^n \mu((a_j, b_j]) \\
&= \mu(E).
\end{align*}
\]

title: 6  Lecture 3.1: Stieltjes Premeasures
text:
6.5 Reconstructions, Corrections, and Interpretations

Subadditivity Proof Expansion: In Proposition 6.1, the original handwritten proof sketched the double sum manipulation over \(E_i^n \cap E_j\); the intermediate step evaluating \(E_i^n \cap \bigcup_{j=1}^N E_j = E_i^n \cap A\) was explicitly added for logical completeness.
Compactness Subcover Boundary: In the Heine-Borel step of Theorem 6.1, the original text noted \([a+\delta, b] \subset \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty (a_j, b_j + \delta_j)\); the finite subcover step to \(N\) and its extension to intervals \((a_j, b_j + \delta_j]\) was made step-by-step explicit.
Notation Standardization: Standardized the notation for the elementary field \(\mathcal{B}_{\text{el}}(\mathbb{R}) = \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\) and the translation operator \(E + \alpha\) across all sections.

title: 6  Lecture 3.1: Stieltjes Premeasures
text:
6.6 Mathematical Gaps & Verification Items

6.6.1 Mathematical Analysis & Gaps

Infinite Interval Cases: The compactness argument directly applies to finite intervals \((a, b]\) where \(-\infty < a < b < \infty\). For unbounded intervals (e.g., \((a, \infty)\) or \((-\infty, b]\)), the result follows by taking limits of truncated finite intervals \(\lim_{M \to \infty} (-M, b]\) or \(\lim_{M \to \infty} (a, M]\).



6.6.2 Items Requiring Verification

Field Symbol Variant: In page 1 of the manuscript, the generated field is written alternatively as \(\mathcal{B}_{\text{el}}(\mathbb{R})\) and \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\). Both are preserved as equivalent in the Quarto text.

title: 7  Lecture 3.2: Outer Measure
text:
Theorem 7.1 (Fréchet Extension Theorem (1924)) Every premeasure \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) extends to a measure on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\). The extension \(\bar{\mu}\) is unique if the premeasure \(\mu\) is \(\sigma\)-finite on \(\mathcal{A}\); that is, if there exists a sequence \(\{A_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) such that \[
\Omega = \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty A_j \quad \text{and} \quad \mu(A_j) < \infty \quad \text{for all } j \in \mathbb{N}.
\tag{7.2}\]

title: 7  Lecture 3.2: Outer Measure
text:
7.2 Counterexample: Non-Uniqueness of Measure Extensions
If \(\mu\) is not \(\sigma\)-finite, the extension to \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\) need not be unique.
Consider \(\Omega = \mathbb{R}\) and let \(\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{B}_{\text{el}}(\mathbb{R})\) be the elementary field generated by half-open intervals. Define the premeasure \(\mu: \mathcal{A} \to [0, \infty]\) by: \[
\mu(A) =
\begin{cases}  
0 & \text{if } A = \emptyset, \\
\infty & \text{if } A \neq \emptyset.
\end{cases}
\tag{7.3}\]
We can extend \(\mu\) to \(\sigma(\mathcal{A}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) in multiple ways:

First extension (\(\bar{\mu}\)): Define \(\bar{\mu}(A) = \infty\) for all non-empty \(A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\), with \(\bar{\mu}(\emptyset) = 0\). This is a valid measure on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) extending \(\mu\).
Second extension (\(\tilde{\mu}\)): Define \(\tilde{\mu}\) as the counting measure on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\): \[    
\tilde{\mu}(A) = \# A.    
\tag{7.4}\] For any non-empty interval \((a, b] \in \mathcal{A}\), \(\#(a, b] = \infty\), so \(\tilde{\mu}(A) = \mu(A) = \infty\) for all non-empty \(A \in \mathcal{A}\), and \(\tilde{\mu}(\emptyset) = 0\).

Both \(\bar{\mu}\) and \(\tilde{\mu}\) are valid measures on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) extending \(\mu\), but \(\bar{\mu} \neq \tilde{\mu}\) (for instance, on singletons \(\{x\} \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\), \(\bar{\mu}(\{x\}) = \infty\) whereas \(\tilde{\mu}(\{x\}) = 1\)).

title: 7  Lecture 3.2: Outer Measure
text:
7.3 Carathéodory Outer Measure Construction
We now describe Carathéodory’s method for constructing an outer measure from a premeasure. This construction is fundamental in measure theory and provides a systematic way to extend premeasures to measures on \(\sigma\)-algebras. It has the following features:

It is defined on all subsets of \(\Omega\) (\(2^\Omega\)), not just on the algebra \(\mathcal{A}\).
It assigns zero to the empty set and is monotone and countably subadditive.


Definition 7.1 (Outer Measure) Let \(\Omega\) be a non-empty set. A function \(\mu^*: 2^\Omega \to [0, \infty]\) is called an outer measure if it satisfies the following three conditions:

Empty Set: \(\mu^*(\emptyset) = 0\).
Monotonicity: If \(A \subseteq B \subseteq \Omega\), then \(\mu^*(A) \le \mu^*(B)\).
Countable Subadditivity: For any sequence of sets \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq 2^\Omega\), \[
\mu^*\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu^*(A_n).
\tag{7.5}\]


To construct an outer measure from a set function defined on a collection of subsets \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq 2^\Omega\), we use Carathéodory’s method.

Definition 7.2 (Carathéodory Outer Measure Induced by a Set Function) Let \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) be a collection of subsets containing \(\emptyset\) and \(\Omega\), and let \(\rho: \mathcal{E} \to [0, \infty]\) be a set function with \(\rho(\emptyset) = 0\). The outer measure induced by \(\rho\), denoted \(\rho^*: 2^\Omega \to [0, \infty]\), is defined for any \(A \subseteq \Omega\) by: \[
\rho^*(A) := \inf \left\{ \sum_{j=1}^\infty \rho(E_j) : E_j \in \mathcal{E} \text{ for all } j \ge 1 \text{ and } A \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j \right\}.
\tag{7.6}\]


Proposition 7.1 (Outer Measure Properties of \(\rho^*\)) For any collection \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) containing \(\emptyset\) and \(\Omega\) and any set function \(\rho: \mathcal{E} \to [0, \infty]\) with \(\rho(\emptyset) = 0\), the induced function \(\rho^*: 2^\Omega \to [0, \infty]\) is a valid outer measure on \(2^\Omega\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 7.1). We verify the three defining properties of an outer measure:

Empty set: Since \(\emptyset \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty \emptyset\) with \(\emptyset \in \mathcal{E}\), we have \(0 \le \rho^*(\emptyset) \le \sum_{j=1}^\infty \rho(\emptyset) = 0\), so \(\rho^*(\emptyset) = 0\).
Monotonicity: Let \(A \subseteq B \subseteq \Omega\). If \(\{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{E}\) is a countable cover for \(B\) (i.e., \(B \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\)), then \(A \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\). Thus, any cover of \(B\) by elements of \(\mathcal{E}\) is also a valid cover of \(A\). Taking the infimum over all such covers yields \(\rho^*(A) \le \rho^*(B)\).
Countable subadditivity: Let \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq 2^\Omega\). If \(\rho^*(A_n) = \infty\) for some \(n\), then the inequality \(\rho^*(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \rho^*(A_n)\) holds trivially. Assume \(\rho^*(A_n) < \infty\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).
Fix \(\epsilon > 0\). By the definition of infimum, for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), there exists a countable cover \(\{E_j^n\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{E}\) such that \(A_n \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j^n\) and: \[
\sum_{j=1}^\infty \rho(E_j^n) \le \rho^*(A_n) + \frac{\epsilon}{2^n}.
\tag{7.7}\]
Notice that \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \subseteq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j^n\). Since \(\{E_j^n\}_{n,j=1}^\infty\) is a countable collection of sets in \(\mathcal{E}\) covering \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\), definition Equation 7.6 implies: \[
\rho^*\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{j=1}^\infty \rho(E_j^n) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left( \rho^*(A_n) + \frac{\epsilon}{2^n} \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \rho^*(A_n) + \epsilon.
\] Since \(\epsilon > 0\) was arbitrary, letting \(\epsilon \downarrow 0\) yields: \[
\rho^*\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \rho^*(A_n).
\] Thus, \(\rho^*\) is an outer measure.

title: 7  Lecture 3.2: Outer Measure
section: 7.4 Properties of Outer Measures and Premeasure Extensions
text:
7.4 Properties of Outer Measures and Premeasure Extensions
Carathéodory’s outer measure construction provides a theoretical tool to distinguish premeasures from purely finitely-additive measures.

Lemma 7.1 (Outer Measure Minimal Extension Property) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a premeasure space, and let \((\Omega, \sigma(\mathcal{A}), \nu)\) be any measure space extending \(\mu\) (i.e., \(\nu(A) = \mu(A)\) for all \(A \in \mathcal{A}\)). Then \(\nu\) is bounded above by the induced outer measure \(\mu^*\) on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\): \[
\nu(B) \le \mu^*(B) \quad \text{for all } B \in \sigma(\mathcal{A}).
\tag{7.8}\]


Proof (Proof of Lemma 7.1). Fix \(B \in \sigma(\mathcal{A})\). Let \(\{E_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) be any countable cover of \(B\), so \(B \subseteq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E_n\). Since \(\nu\) is a measure on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\), it is countably subadditive. Furthermore, because \(\nu\vert{}_{ \mathcal{A}} = \mu\), we have: \[
\nu(B) \le \nu\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E_n\right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \nu(E_n) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(E_n).
\]
Taking the infimum over all countable covers \(\{E_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) of \(B\) gives: \[
\nu(B) \le \inf \left\{ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(E_n) : E_n \in \mathcal{A}, \, B \subseteq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E_n \right\} = \mu^*(B).
\]


Proposition 7.2 (Premeasure Characterization via Outer Measure) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finitely-additive measure space. Let \(\mu^*: 2^\Omega \to [0, \infty]\) be the outer measure induced by \(\mu\) on \(\mathcal{A}\).

\(\mu^* \le \mu\) on \(\mathcal{A}\).
\(\mu^* = \mu\) on \(\mathcal{A}\) if and only if \(\mu\) is a premeasure (countably additive) on \(\mathcal{A}\).



Proof (Proof of Proposition 7.2). Part 1 (\(\mu^* \le \mu\) on \(\mathcal{A}\)): Let \(A \in \mathcal{A}\). We can cover \(A\) using the sequence \(E_1 = A\) and \(E_n = \emptyset\) for \(n \ge 2\), where \(E_n \in \mathcal{A}\) for all \(n\). Since \(A \subseteq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E_n\), the definition of infimum implies: \[
\mu^*(A) \le \mu(A) + \sum_{n=2}^\infty \mu(\emptyset) = \mu(A) + 0 = \mu(A).
\]
Part 2 (\(\Leftarrow\): Assume \(\mu\) is a premeasure): Let \(A \in \mathcal{A}\). Let \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) be any countable cover of \(A\), i.e., \(A \subseteq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\).
Define \(B_n := A_n \cap A \in \mathcal{A}\) for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), so \(A = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\). Disjointify \(\{B_n\}\) by setting: \[
\tilde{B}_1 := B_1, \quad \text{and} \quad \tilde{B}_n := B_n \setminus \left( \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1} B_j \right) \subseteq B_n \quad \text{for } n \ge 2.
\] Since \(\mathcal{A}\) is a field, \(\tilde{B}_n \in \mathcal{A}\) for all \(n\), and \(\{\tilde{B}_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) is a collection of pairwise disjoint sets whose union is \(A = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \tilde{B}_n\). Since \(\mu\) is countably additive on \(\mathcal{A}\): \[
\mu(A) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(\tilde{B}_n).
\] Using monotonicity of finitely-additive measures (\(\tilde{B}_n \subseteq B_n \subseteq A_n \implies \mu(\tilde{B}_n) \le \mu(A_n)\)), we get: \[
\mu(A) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(\tilde{B}_n) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n).
\] Taking the infimum over all countable covers \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) of \(A\) yields \(\mu(A) \le \mu^*(A)\). Combining this with Part 1 gives \(\mu^*(A) = \mu(A)\) for all \(A \in \mathcal{A}\).
Part 2 (\(\Rightarrow\): Assume \(\mu^* = \mu\) on \(\mathcal{A}\)): Let \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) be a sequence of pairwise disjoint sets in \(\mathcal{A}\) such that \(A := \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \in \mathcal{A}\).
Since \(\mu^*\) is an outer measure (hence countably subadditive) and \(\mu^* = \mu\) on \(\mathcal{A}\), we have: \[
\mu(A) = \mu^*(A) = \mu^*\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu^*(A_n) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n).
\] On the other hand, for any finite \(N \in \mathbb{N}\), since \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^N \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) are disjoint and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^N A_n \subseteq A\), finite additivity and monotonicity yield: \[
\sum_{n=1}^N \mu(A_n) = \mu\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^N A_n\right) \le \mu(A).
\] Taking the limit as \(N \to \infty\) gives: \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) \le \mu(A).
\]
Combining both inequalities yields \(\mu(A) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n)\), proving that \(\mu\) is countably additive (a premeasure) on \(\mathcal{A}\). \(\blacksquare\)

7.6.1 Mathematical Analysis & Gaps

Fréchet Theorem Context: The manuscript references Fréchet (1924). In modern measure theory literature, the extension of a premeasure on an algebra via an outer measure to a full measure on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\) is most commonly termed the Carathéodory Extension Theorem.

These have been unified to \(\rho\) for general functions, \(\mu\) for premeasures, and \(\mu^*\) for outer measures. Please verify if this standardized notation aligns with your preference.

title: 8  Lecture 4.1: Outer Pseudo-Metric
text:
Theorem 8.1 (Measure Extension Theorem (Fréchet, Carathéodory, Hopf, Kolmogorov, 1920s)) There exists a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{M} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) containing \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\) such that \(\mu^*\vert{}_{\mathcal{M}}\) is a measure extending \(\mu\).



Carathéodory provided the fundamental outer-measure construction that underlies the modern extension theorem: starting from a premeasure on an algebra, his method constructs an outer measure whose restriction to the Carathéodory measurable sets is a complete measure extending the original premeasure.
Fréchet made important early contributions to the abstract theory of measure and extension problems, while Hopf and Kolmogorov contributed to the subsequent development and abstraction of measure theory and its applications to probability.
Although these contributions are historically connected, the extension theorem in the outer-measure form used here is most appropriately attributed to Carathéodory.

title: 8  Lecture 4.1: Outer Pseudo-Metric
text:
8.3 Pseudo-Metric Spaces and Extension Preliminaries

Definition 8.1 (Pseudo-Metric Space) A function \(d: X \times X \to [0, \infty)\) is called a pseudo-metric on a set \(X\) if for all \(x, y, z \in X\):

\(d(x, x) = 0\) (note that \(d(x, y) = 0\) does not necessarily imply \(x = y\)),
Symmetry: \(d(x, y) = d(y, x)\),
Triangle Inequality: \(d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)\).



Definition 8.2 (Sequential Limits, Closure, and Lipschitz Extensions) Let \((X, d)\) be a pseudo-metric space.

A sequence \((x_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq X\) converges to a limit \(x \in X\) (denoted \(x_n \xrightarrow{d} x\)) if \(\lim_{n \to \infty} d(x_n, x) = 0\).
For \(V \subseteq X\), its closure \(\overline{V}\) is the set of all sequential limits of sequences in \(V\): \[
\overline{V} := \{x \in X : \exists (x_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq V \text{ such that } d(x_n, x) \to 0\}.
\]
A function \(f: V \to \mathbb{R}\) is \(K\)-Lipschitz if there exists \(K \in (0, \infty)\) such that \(\vert{}f(x) - f(y)\vert{} \le K d(x, y)\) for all \(x, y \in V\).



Proposition 8.1 (Unique Extension of Lipschitz Functions) If \(f: V \to \mathbb{R}\) is Lipschitz on a non-empty subset \(V \subseteq X\), then \(f\) extends uniquely to a continuous function \(\overline{f}: \overline{V} \to \mathbb{R}\) preserving the Lipschitz constant \(K\).

title: 8  Lecture 4.1: Outer Pseudo-Metric
text:
8.4 The Outer Pseudo-Metric \(d_\mu\)
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finite premeasure space (so \(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\)), and let \(\mu^*: 2^\Omega \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\) be the Carathéodory outer measure induced by \(\mu\).

Definition 8.3 (Outer Pseudo-Metric) Define \(d_\mu: 2^\Omega \times 2^\Omega \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\) by: \[
d_\mu(E, F) := \mu^*(E \Delta F),
\tag{8.3}\] where \(E \Delta F = (E \setminus F) \cup (F \setminus E)\) denotes the symmetric difference between \(E\) and \(F\).


Proposition 8.2 (Verification of Pseudo-Metric Axioms) The set function \(d_\mu\) is a valid pseudo-metric on \(2^\Omega\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 8.2). 

Non-negativity and Zero Distance: \(d_\mu(E, E) = \mu^*(E \Delta E) = \mu^*(\emptyset) = 0\).
Symmetry: Since \(E \Delta F = F \Delta E\), we have \(d_\mu(E, F) = \mu^*(E \Delta F) = \mu^*(F \Delta E) = d_\mu(F, E)\).
Triangle Inequality: For any \(E, F, G \in 2^\Omega\), we have the set inclusion \(E \Delta G \subseteq (E \Delta F) \cup (F \Delta G)\). By monotonicity and countable subadditivity of \(\mu^*\): \[
\begin{align*}
d_\mu(E, G) &= \mu^*(E \Delta G) \\
&\le \mu^*((E \Delta F) \cup (F \Delta G))\\
& \le \mu^*(E \Delta F) + \mu^*(F \Delta G)\\
& = d_\mu(E, F) + d_\mu(F, G).
\end{align*}
\] Thus \(d_\mu\) is a pseudo-metric on \(2^\Omega\).

title: 8  Lecture 4.1: Outer Pseudo-Metric
text:
8.5 Key Algebraic Properties of \(d_\mu\)

Proposition 8.3 (Fundamental Set-Operation Inequalities) For any \(A, B, A_n, B_n \in 2^\Omega\):

Complements: \(d_\mu(A, B) = d_\mu(A^c, B^c)\).
Countable Unions: \[
d_\mu\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n, \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty d_\mu(A_n, B_n).
\tag{8.4}\]
Countable Intersections: \[
d_\mu\left(\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A_n, \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty B_n\right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty d_\mu(A_n, B_n).
\tag{8.5}\]



Proof (Proof of Proposition 8.3). 

Complements: Note that \(A^c \Delta B^c = (A^c \setminus B^c) \cup (B^c \setminus A^c) = (B \setminus A) \cup (A \setminus B) = B \Delta A = A \Delta B\). Thus: \[
d_\mu(A^c, B^c) = \mu^*(A^c \Delta B^c) = \mu^*(A \Delta B) = d_\mu(A, B).
\]
Countable Unions: Using the set identity \(\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\right) \Delta \left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\right) \subseteq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty (A_n \Delta B_n)\), subadditivity of \(\mu^*\) yields: \[
\begin{align*}
d_\mu\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n, \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\right) &= \mu^*\left( \left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\right) \Delta \left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\right) \right)\\
& \le \mu^*\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty (A_n \Delta B_n) \right) \\
& \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu^*(A_n \Delta B_n)\\
& = \sum_{n=1}^\infty d_\mu(A_n, B_n).
\end{align*}
\]
Countable Intersections: By De Morgan’s Laws combined with Parts 1 and 2: \[
\begin{align*}
d_\mu\left(\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A_n, \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty B_n\right) &= d_\mu\left(\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n^c\right)^c, \left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n^c\right)^c\right)\\
&= d_\mu\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n^c, \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n^c\right)\\
& \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty d_\mu(A_n^c, B_n^c) \\
&= \sum_{n=1}^\infty d_\mu(A_n, B_n).
\end{align*}
\]

title: 8  Lecture 4.1: Outer Pseudo-Metric
section: 8.6 Distance Convergence for Incremental Disjoint Unions
text:
8.6 Distance Convergence for Incremental Disjoint Unions

Lemma 8.1 (Approximation Lemma) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finite premeasure space. If \(\{D_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) is a sequence of pairwise disjoint sets in \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(A = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty D_n\), let \(A_N := \bigcup_{n=1}^N D_n \in \mathcal{A}\). Then \(A_N \uparrow A\) and: \[
d_\mu(A_N, A) = \mu^*(A) - \mu(A_N) \xrightarrow{N \to \infty} 0.
\tag{8.6}\]


Proof (Proof of Lemma 8.1). By definition of the outer measure \(\mu^*\) on \(A = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty D_n\): \[
\begin{align*}
\mu^*(A) &\le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(D_n)\\
& = \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=1}^N \mu(D_n)\\
& = \lim_{N \to \infty} \mu\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^N D_n\right) \\
&= \lim_{N \to \infty} \mu(A_N).
\end{align*}
\]
Conversely, since \(A_N \in \mathcal{A}\) and \(A_N \subseteq A\), monotonicity of \(\mu^*\) gives \(\mu(A_N) = \mu^*(A_N) \le \mu^*(A)\) for all \(N \in \mathbb{N}\). Taking limits yields \(\lim_{N \to \infty} \mu(A_N) = \mu^*(A)\).
Now fix \(N \in \mathbb{N}\). Note that \(A \setminus A_N = \bigcup_{n=N+1}^\infty D_n\). Thus: \[
\begin{align*}
d_\mu(A, A_N) &= \mu^*(A \Delta A_N) \\
&= \mu^*(A \setminus A_N) \\
&\le \sum_{n=N+1}^\infty \mu(D_n) \\
&= \mu^*(A) - \mu(A_N) \xrightarrow{N \to \infty} 0.
\end{align*}
\]


Corollary 8.1 (Disjoint Union Belongs to Closure) If \(\{D_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) are pairwise disjoint, then \(A = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty D_n \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\).

title: 8  Lecture 4.1: Outer Pseudo-Metric
text:
8.7 Proving that \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\) is a \(\sigma\)-Algebra

Theorem 8.2 (Structure of \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\)) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finite premeasure space. The closure \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\) of the field \(\mathcal{A}\) in the pseudo-metric space \((2^\Omega, d_\mu)\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra.


Proof (Proof of Theorem 8.2). We verify the three axioms of a \(\sigma\)-algebra:

Empty Set: \(\emptyset \in \mathcal{A} \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{A}}\).
Closure under Complement: Let \(B \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\). By definition of closure, there exists a sequence \((A_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) such that \(d_\mu(A_n, B) \to 0\). By Property 1 of Proposition 8.3: \[
d_\mu(A_n^c, B^c) = d_\mu(A_n, B) \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0.
\]
Since \(\mathcal{A}\) is a field, \(A_n^c \in \mathcal{A}\) for all \(n\). Thus \(B^c\) is the limit of a sequence in \(\mathcal{A}\), so \(B^c \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\).
Closure under Countable Unions: Let \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{A}}\). We need to show that \(B := \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\).
Fix \(\epsilon > 0\). For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), since \(B_n \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\), there exists a set \(A_n \in \mathcal{A}\) such that: \[
d_\mu(A_n, B_n) < \frac{\epsilon}{2^{n+1}}.
\tag{8.7}\]
By Property 2 of Proposition 8.3: \[
d_\mu\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n, \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty d_\mu(A_n, B_n) < \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\epsilon}{2^{n+1}} = \frac{\epsilon}{2}.
\tag{8.8}\]
Now consider \(A := \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\). Although each \(A_n \in \mathcal{A}\), the infinite union \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\) is not guaranteed to be in \(\mathcal{A}\). However, we can disjointify \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) by setting \(D_1 = A_1\) and \(D_n = A_n \setminus (\bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1} A_j) \in \mathcal{A}\) for \(n \ge 2\). Then \(A = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty D_n\) with \(\{D_n\} \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) pairwise disjoint.
By Lemma 8.1, setting \(A^{(N)} := \bigcup_{n=1}^N D_n = \bigcup_{n=1}^N A_n \in \mathcal{A}\), we can pick \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) sufficiently large such that: \[
d_\mu\left( A^{(N)}, \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) < \frac{\epsilon}{2}.
\tag{8.9}\]
Combining Equation 8.8 and Equation 8.9 via the triangle inequality: \[
\begin{align*}
d_\mu\left( A^{(N)}, \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) &\le d_\mu\left( A^{(N)}, \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) + d_\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n, \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) \\
&< \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon.
\end{align*}
\] Since \(A^{(N)} \in \mathcal{A}\) and \(\epsilon > 0\) was arbitrary, \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\) lies in the closure \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\).

Hence, \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra. \(\blacksquare\)
