text: 8.9 Mathematical Gaps & Verification Items

title: 9  Lecture 4.2: Extension Theorem
section: 9.2 Lipschitz Continuity of \(\mu\) and Extension to \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\)
text:
9.2 Lipschitz Continuity of \(\mu\) and Extension to \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\)
We first show that \(\mu\) is 1-Lipschitz continuous on \((\mathcal{A}, d_\mu)\) and therefore extends uniquely to \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\).

Proposition 9.1 (1-Lipschitz Continuity of \(\mu\)) For any \(A, B \in \mathcal{A}\), we have \(\mu^*\vert{}_{ \mathcal{A}} = \mu\). Furthermore, \(\mu\) satisfies: \[
\vert{}\mu(A) - \mu(B)\vert{} \le d_\mu(A, B).
\tag{9.2}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 9.1). For \(A, B \in \mathcal{A}\), by finite additivity on \(\mathcal{A}\): \[
\mu(A) = \mu(A \setminus B) + \mu(A \cap B) \le \mu(A \Delta B) + \mu(B) = d_\mu(A, B) + \mu(B).
\] Rearranging yields \(\mu(A) - \mu(B) \le d_\mu(A, B)\). Reversing the roles of \(A\) and \(B\) gives \(\mu(B) - \mu(A) \le d_\mu(A, B)\). Combining both inequalities yields: \[
\vert{}\mu(A) - \mu(B)\vert{} \le d_\mu(A, B).
\]


Proposition 9.2 (Unique Extension \(\overline{\mu}\)) Since \(\mu\) is 1-Lipschitz on the non-empty set \(\mathcal{A}\) in the pseudo-metric space \((2^\Omega, d_\mu)\), it extends uniquely to a continuous 1-Lipschitz function \(\overline{\mu}: \overline{\mathcal{A}} \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\) such that \(\overline{\mu}\vert{}_{\mathcal{A}} = \mu\).

title: 9  Lecture 4.2: Extension Theorem
text:
9.3 \(\sigma\)-Invariance and Monotone Sequence Convergence

Definition 9.1 (Countable Unions Collection \(\mathcal{E}_\sigma\)) For any collection \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq 2^\Omega\), define \(\mathcal{E}_\sigma\) as the collection of all countable unions of elements in \(\mathcal{E}\): \[
\mathcal{E}_\sigma := \left\{ \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E_n : \{E_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{E} \right\}.
\tag{9.3}\]
Note: \(\mathcal{E}_\sigma\) is automatically closed under countable unions. If \(\mathcal{E}\) is closed under finite intersections, then \(\mathcal{E}_\sigma\) is also closed under finite intersections: \[
\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty E_i\right) \cap \left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty F_j\right) = \bigcup_{i,j=1}^\infty (E_i \cap F_j) \in \mathcal{E}_\sigma.
\]


Lemma 9.1 (Closure Invariance under Countable Unions) For a finite premeasure space \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\), we have \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}_\sigma = \overline{\mathcal{A}}\). Furthermore, \(\overline{\mu} = \mu^*\) on \(\mathcal{A}_\sigma\).


Proof (Proof of Lemma 9.1). Let \(A \in \mathcal{A}_\sigma\), so \(A = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\) with \(B_n \in \mathcal{A}\). Define \(A_n := \bigcup_{j=1}^n B_j \in \mathcal{A}\). Then \(A_n \uparrow A\).
By the Approximation Lemma (from the previous lecture), \(d_\mu(A_n, A) = \mu^*(A) - \mu(A_n) \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\). Thus, \(A\) is the sequential limit of \((A_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\), which implies \(A \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\). Hence \(\mathcal{A}_\sigma \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{A}}\).
By continuity of the extension \(\overline{\mu}\), we have \(\mu^*(A) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \mu(A_n) = \overline{\mu}(A)\) for all \(A \in \mathcal{A}_\sigma\).
Finally, since \(\mathcal{A} \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{A}}\) and \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra (hence closed under countable unions), we have: \[
\overline{\mathcal{A}} \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{A}}_\sigma \subseteq \overline{\overline{\mathcal{A}}} = \overline{\mathcal{A}},
\]
which yields \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}_\sigma = \overline{\mathcal{A}}\).

title: 9  Lecture 4.2: Extension Theorem
text:
9.4 Characterization of Sets in \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\)

Theorem 9.1 (Outer Approximation Characterization) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finite premeasure space, and let \(B \in 2^\Omega\). The following statements are equivalent:

\(B \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\).
For every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists a set \(C \in \mathcal{A}_\sigma\) such that \(B \subseteq C\) and \[
\mu^*(C \setminus B) = d_\mu(B, C) < \epsilon.
\tag{9.4}\]



Proof (Proof of Theorem 9.1). (2) \(\Rightarrow\) (1): Assume Condition (2) holds. For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), select \(C_n \in \mathcal{A}_\sigma\) such that \(B \subseteq C_n\) and \(d_\mu(B, C_n) < \frac{1}{n}\). Then \(d_\mu(C_n, B) \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\), so \(B \in \overline{\mathcal{A}_\sigma}\). Since \(\overline{\mathcal{A}_\sigma} = \overline{\mathcal{A}}\), it follows that \(B \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\).
(1) \(\Rightarrow\) (2): Fix \(\epsilon > 0\). By (1), \(B \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\), so there exists \(G \in \mathcal{A}\) such that: \[
d_\mu(B, G) = \mu^*(B \Delta G) < \frac{\epsilon}{2}.
\]
By definition of outer measure as an infimum, since \(\mu^*(B \Delta G) < \frac{\epsilon}{2}\), there exists a sequence \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) covering \(B \Delta G\) (i.e., \(B \Delta G \subseteq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\)) such that: \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) < \frac{\epsilon}{2}.
\]
Define \(C := G \cup \left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\right) \in \mathcal{A}_\sigma\).

Containment (\(B \subseteq C\)): \[
B \subseteq (B \setminus G) \cup G \subseteq (B \Delta G) \cup G \subseteq \left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\right) \cup G = C.
\]
Difference Bound (\(\mu^*(C \setminus B) < \epsilon\)): \[
\begin{align*}
C \setminus B &= \left( G \cup \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) \setminus B \\
&= (G \setminus B) \cup \left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \setminus B \right) \\
&\subseteq (B \Delta G) \cup \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \\
&\subseteq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n.
\end{align*}
\]
By monotonicity and subadditivity of \(\mu^*\): \[
\mu^*(C \setminus B) \le \mu^*\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\right) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) < \frac{\epsilon}{2} < \epsilon.
\]

This establishes Condition (2).

title: 9  Lecture 4.2: Extension Theorem
text:
9.5 Identity of \(\mu^*\) and \(\overline{\mu}\) on \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\)

Corollary 9.1 (Coincidence of Outer Measure and Extended Measure) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finite premeasure space. Then: \[
\mu^* = \overline{\mu} \quad \text{on } \overline{\mathcal{A}}.
\tag{9.5}\]


Proof (Proof of Corollary 9.1). Let \(B \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\).

Upper Bound (\(\overline{\mu}(B) \le \mu^*(B)\)): Since \(\overline{\mu}\) is 1-Lipschitz and \(\overline{\mu}(\emptyset) = 0\): \[
\vert{}\overline{\mu}(B)\vert{} = \vert{}\overline{\mu}(B) - \overline{\mu}(\emptyset)\vert{} \le d_\mu(B, \emptyset) = \mu^*(B \Delta \emptyset) = \mu^*(B).
\]
Thus \(\overline{\mu}(B) \le \mu^*(B)\).
Lower Bound (\(\mu^*(B) \le \overline{\mu}(B)\)): Fix \(\epsilon > 0\). By Theorem 9.1, select \(C \in \mathcal{A}_\sigma\) such that \(B \subseteq C\) and \(d_\mu(B, C) = \mu^*(C \setminus B) < \epsilon\). By 1-Lipschitz continuity of \(\overline{\mu}\): \[
\vert{}\overline{\mu}(B) - \overline{\mu}(C)\vert{} \le d_\mu(B, C) < \epsilon \implies \overline{\mu}(C) \le \overline{\mu}(B) + \epsilon.
\]
Since \(C \in \mathcal{A}_\sigma\), Lemma 9.1 implies \(\overline{\mu}(C) = \mu^*(C)\). By monotonicity of outer measure (\(B \subseteq C \implies \mu^*(B) \le \mu^*(C)\)): \[
\mu^*(B) \le \mu^*(C) = \overline{\mu}(C) \le \overline{\mu}(B) + \epsilon.
\]
Taking \(\epsilon \downarrow 0\) yields \(\mu^*(B) \le \overline{\mu}(B)\).

Combining both bounds yields \(\overline{\mu}(B) = \mu^*(B)\) for all \(B \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\).

title: 9  Lecture 4.2: Extension Theorem
text:
9.6 Proof that \(\overline{\mu}\) is a Measure

Theorem 9.2 (Measure Extension Main Theorem) If \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) is a finite premeasure space, then the unique extension \(\overline{\mu}: \overline{\mathcal{A}} \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\) is a measure on the \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 9.2). We show that \(\overline{\mu}\) is finitely additive on \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\).
Let \(A, B \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\). By definition of closure, choose sequences \((A_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) and \((B_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) such that \(d_\mu(A_n, A) \to 0\) and \(d_\mu(B_n, B) \to 0\).
By Property 2 of \(d_\mu\), we have: \[
d_\mu(A_n \cup B_n, A \cup B) \le d_\mu(A_n, A) + d_\mu(B_n, B) \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0,
\]
and similarly \(d_\mu(A_n \cap B_n, A \cap B) \to 0\).
By inclusion-exclusion on the algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\): \[
\mu(A_n \cup B_n) + \mu(A_n \cap B_n) = \mu(A_n) + \mu(B_n).
\tag{9.6}\]
Taking limits as \(n \to \infty\) and using continuity of \(\overline{\mu}\): \[
\begin{align*}
\overline{\mu}(A \cup B) + \overline{\mu}(A \cap B) &= \lim_{n \to \infty} [\mu(A_n \cup B_n) + \mu(A_n \cap B_n)] \\
&= \lim_{n \to \infty} [\mu(A_n) + \mu(B_n)] \\
&= \overline{\mu}(A) + \overline{\mu}(B).
\end{align*}
\]
If \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint (\(A \cap B = \emptyset\)), then \(\overline{\mu}(A \cap B) = \overline{\mu}(\emptyset) = 0\), yielding finite additivity: \[
\overline{\mu}(A \cup B) = \overline{\mu}(A) + \overline{\mu}(B).
\]
Thus, \(\overline{\mu}\) is a finitely-additive measure on the \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\), which implies \(\overline{\mu}\) is countably superadditive.
On the other hand, Corollary 9.1 establishes that \(\overline{\mu} = \mu^*\) on \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\). Since the outer measure \(\mu^*\) is countably subadditive on \(2^\Omega\), \(\overline{\mu}\) is countably subadditive on \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\).
Combining countable superadditivity and countable subadditivity proves that \(\overline{\mu}\) is countably additive on \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\). Since \(\overline{\mu}(\emptyset) = 0\), \(\overline{\mu}\) is a measure.

title: 9  Lecture 4.2: Extension Theorem
text:
9.7 Reconstructions, Corrections, and Interpretations

Inclusion-Exclusion Limit Justification: In Theorem 9.2, the manuscript noted \(\mu(A_n \cup B_n) + \mu(A_n \cap B_n) = \mu(A_n) + \mu(B_n)\) and took limits; the joint convergence \(d_\mu(A_n \cup B_n, A \cup B) \to 0\) and \(d_\mu(A_n \cap B_n, A \cap B) \to 0\) was explicitly detailed to justify applying continuity of \(\overline{\mu}\).
\(\mathcal{A}_\sigma\) Intersection Closure: In Definition 9.1, the distributive identity \((\bigcup A_i) \cap (\bigcup B_j) = \bigcup (A_i \cap B_j)\) was added to explicitly justify why \(\mathcal{A}_\sigma\) is closed under finite intersections when \(\mathcal{A}\) is a field.
Notation Consistency: Standardized notation across all parts of the extension proof (\(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\) for the closure \(\sigma\)-algebra, \(\overline{\mu}\) for the continuous extension, and \(\mu^*\) for the outer measure).

title: 9  Lecture 4.2: Extension Theorem
text:
9.8 Mathematical Gaps & Verification Items

9.8.1 Mathematical Analysis & Gaps

Countable Superadditivity vs Subadditivity: The proof elegantly concludes countable additivity of \(\overline{\mu}\) by sandwiching it between finite additivity (which yields countable superadditivity on non-negative set functions) and outer measure countable subadditivity (\(\mu^* = \overline{\mu}\)).



9.8.2 Items Requiring Verification

Extension from Finite to \(\sigma\)-Finite Case: The manuscript covers the extension proof for finite premeasures (\(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\)). If your course notes continue into the standard \(\sigma\)-finite extension via partition sequence \(\Omega = \bigcup \Omega_k\), verify if that should be appended to this chapter or structured as a standalone following section.

title: 10  Lecture 4.3: Uniqueness of Sigma-Finite Extension
text:
Carathéodory Outer Measure: Define \(\mu^*: 2^\Omega \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\) by: \[
\mu^*(E) := \inf \left\{ \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mu(A_j) : \{A_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}, \, E \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty A_j \right\}.
\tag{10.1}\]

The function \(\mu^*\) is monotone and countably subadditive.
If \(\nu\) is any measure on a \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{F} \supseteq \mathcal{A}\) extending \(\mu\), then \(\nu \le \mu^*\) on \(\mathcal{F}\).
If \(\nu\) is a finitely additive measure, then \(\nu^* \le \nu\), and \(\nu = \nu^*\) if and only if \(\nu\) is countably additive.

Outer Pseudo-Metric: The set function \(d_\mu: 2^\Omega \times 2^\Omega \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\) given by \(d_\mu(E, F) := \mu^*(E \Delta F)\) defines a well-behaved pseudo-metric with respect to unions, intersections, and complements.
Lipschitz Extension: \(\mu: \mathcal{A} \to \mathbb{R}\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz on \((\mathcal{A}, d_\mu)\), and therefore extends uniquely to a continuous \(1\)-Lipschitz function \(\overline{\mu}: \overline{\mathcal{A}} \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\).
Invariance of the Closure: Let \(\mathcal{A}_\sigma := \left\{ \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n : \{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A} \right\}\) denote the collection of countable unions of sets in \(\mathcal{A}\). In \((2^\Omega, d_\mu)\), we have \(\overline{\mathcal{A}_\sigma} = \overline{\mathcal{A}}\), and \(\overline{\mu} = \mu^*\) on \(\mathcal{A}_\sigma\).
Structure of \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\): The closure \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\) in \((2^\Omega, d_\mu)\) is a \(\sigma\)-field.
Outer Approximation: For any \(B \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\) and \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists \(C \in \mathcal{A}_\sigma\) such that \(B \subseteq C\) and \(\mu^*(C \setminus B) = d_\mu(B, C) < \epsilon\). Using this together with \(\overline{\mu} = \mu^*\) on \(\mathcal{A}_\sigma\), we deduce \(\mu^* = \overline{\mu}\) on \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\).
Countable Additivity: The extension \(\overline{\mu}\) is a countably additive measure on \(\overline{\mathcal{A}} \supseteq \sigma(\mathcal{A})\).

section: 10.2 Uniqueness Theorem in the Finite Case
text:
10.2 Uniqueness Theorem in the Finite Case

Theorem 10.1 (Uniqueness of Extension) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finite premeasure space. If \(\mathcal{F}\) is a \(\sigma\)-field satisfying \(\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{F} \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{A}}\), and \(
u\) is a measure on \(\mathcal{F}\) extending \(\mu\) (i.e., \(
u\vert{}_{\mathcal{A}} = \mu\)), then: \[

u = \overline{\mu} ig\vert{}_{\mathcal{F}}.
	ag{10.2}\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 10.1). Let \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\). By finite additivity and monotonicity of \(
u\) on \(\mathcal{F}\): \[
u(B) \le 
u(A \cup B) = 
u(A) + 
u(B \setminus A) \le 
u(A) + 
u(A \Delta B),\] which implies \(
u(B) - 
u(A) \le 
u(A \Delta B)\). Reversing the roles of \(A\) and \(B\) yields: \[
\vert{}
u(B) - 
u(A)\vert{} \le 
u(A \Delta B) \le \mu^*(A \Delta B) = d_\mu(A, B).
	ag{10.3}\] Thus, \(
u: \mathcal{F} 	o \mathbb{R}\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz continuous with respect to \(d_\mu\).
Now let \(E \in \mathcal{F} \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{A}}\). By definition of the closure \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\), there exists a sequence \((A_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) such that \(d_\mu(A_n, E) 	o 0\) as \(n 	o \infty\). By \(1\)-Lipschitz continuity of both \(
u\) and \(\overline{\mu}\): \[

u(E) = \lim_{n 	o \infty} 
u(A_n) = \lim_{n 	o \infty} \mu(A_n) = \overline{\mu}(E). 	ag{10.4}\] Hence \(
u = \overline{\mu} ig\vert{}_{\mathcal{F}}\).

title: 10  Lecture 4.3: Uniqueness of Sigma-Finite Extension
text:
10.3 Extension to \(\sigma\)-Finite Premeasure Spaces

Definition 10.1 (\(\sigma\)-Finite Premeasure Space) A premeasure space \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) is called \(\sigma\)-finite if there exists a sequence \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) such that \(\Omega = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\) and \(\mu(A_n) < \infty\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).

By defining \(\Omega_1 := A_1\) and \(\Omega_n := A_n \setminus A_{n-1} \in \mathcal{A}\) for \(n \ge 2\), we obtain a pairwise disjoint sequence \(\{\Omega_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) such that \(\Omega = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \Omega_n\) and \(\mu(\Omega_n) \le \mu(A_n) < \infty\).
For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), define the localized premeasure \(\mu_n: \mathcal{A} \to [0, \infty)\) by: \[
\mu_n(A) := \mu(A \cap \Omega_n).
\tag{10.5}\] Then \((\Omega_n, \mathcal{A}, \mu_n)\) is a finite premeasure space. By the finite extension theorem, each \(\mu_n\) extends uniquely to a finite measure \(\overline{\mu}_n\) on \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}^n \supseteq \sigma(\mathcal{A})\).

Theorem 10.2 (\(\sigma\)-Finite Measure Extension Theorem) The set function \(\overline{\mu} := \sum_{n=1}^\infty \overline{\mu}_n\) is the unique measure on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\) that extends \(\mu\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 10.2). 

Countable Additivity of \(\overline{\mu}\): Since each \(\overline{\mu}_n\) is a countably additive measure on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\), the countable sum of measures \(\overline{\mu} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \overline{\mu}_n\) is automatically a countably additive measure on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\). Moreover, for any \(A \in \mathcal{A}\): \[
\overline{\mu}(A) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \overline{\mu}_n(A) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A \cap \Omega_n) = \mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty (A \cap \Omega_n) \right) = \mu(A),
\]
so \(\overline{\mu}\) extends \(\mu\) on \(\mathcal{A}\).
Uniqueness: Suppose \(\nu\) is any measure on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\) such that \(\nu\vert{}_{\mathcal{A}} = \mu\). For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), define the localized measure \(\nu_n\) on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\) by: \[
\nu_n(E) := \nu(E \cap \Omega_n) \quad \text{for } E \in \sigma(\mathcal{A}).
\tag{10.6}\] For any \(A \in \mathcal{A}\), since \(A \cap \Omega_n \in \mathcal{A}\), we have: \[
\nu_n(A) = \nu(A \cap \Omega_n) = \mu(A \cap \Omega_n) = \mu_n(A).
\]
Thus, \(\nu_n\) is a finite measure on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\) extending the finite premeasure \(\mu_n\) on \(\mathcal{A}\). By uniqueness in the finite case (Theorem 10.1), we must have: \[
\nu_n = \overline{\mu}_n\big\vert{}_{\sigma(\mathcal{A})} \quad \text{for all } n \in \mathbb{N}.
\tag{10.7}\]
Finally, for any \(E \in \sigma(\mathcal{A})\), since \(E = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty (E \cap \Omega_n)\) as a disjoint union, countable additivity of \(\nu\) yields: \[
\nu(E) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \nu(E \cap \Omega_n) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \nu_n(E) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \overline{\mu}_n(E) = \overline{\mu}(E).
\tag{10.8}\]

Hence, \(\nu = \overline{\mu}\) on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\).

title: 10  Lecture 4.3: Uniqueness of Sigma-Finite Extension
text:
10.4 Approximation Properties on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\)

Proposition 10.1 (Outer and Algebra Approximation Characterizations) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite premeasure space, and let \(\overline{\mu}\) denote the extended measure on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\).

Outer Measure Coincidence: \(\overline{\mu} = \mu^*\) on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\).
Outer Approximation by \(\mathcal{A}_\sigma\): If \(B \in \sigma(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists \(C \in \mathcal{A}_\sigma\) such that \(B \subseteq C\) and: \[
\overline{\mu}(C \setminus B) < \epsilon.
\tag{10.9}\]
Approximation by Algebra Elements: Moreover, if \(\overline{\mu}(B) < \infty\), then for every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists \(A \in \mathcal{A}\) such that: \[
\overline{\mu}(A \Delta B) < \epsilon.
\tag{10.10}\]



Proof. Proof of Part 3. Fix \(\epsilon > 0\) and assume \(\overline{\mu}(B) < \infty\).
By Part 2, choose \(C \in \mathcal{A}_\sigma\) such that \(B \subseteq C\) and \(\overline{\mu}(C \setminus B) < \frac{\epsilon}{2}\).
Since \(C \in \mathcal{A}_\sigma\), there exists an increasing sequence of algebra sets \((A_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) such that \(A_n \uparrow C\). Note that: \[
\overline{\mu}(C) \le \overline{\mu}(C \setminus B) + \overline{\mu}(B) < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \overline{\mu}(B) < \infty.
\tag{10.11}\]
Since \(\overline{\mu}(C) < \infty\) and \(A_n \uparrow C\), continuity of measure from below implies: \[
\overline{\mu}(C \setminus A_n) = \overline{\mu}(C) - \overline{\mu}(A_n) \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0.
\tag{10.12}\] Choose \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) large enough such that \(\overline{\mu}(C \setminus A_n) < \frac{\epsilon}{2}\).
Set \(A := A_n \in \mathcal{A}\). Observing the set inclusion \(A \Delta B \subseteq (C \setminus B) \cup (C \setminus A)\): \[
\overline{\mu}(A \Delta B) \le \overline{\mu}(C \setminus B) + \overline{\mu}(C \setminus A) < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon.
\tag{10.13}\]
This completes the proof.

title: 11  Lecture 5.1. Radon Measure
text:
Definition 11.1 (Borel and Radon Measures) If \(\Omega\) is a topological space, any measure defined on the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(\Omega)\) is called a Borel measure.
A Borel measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) is called a Radon measure if it assigns finite measure to all bounded intervals: \[
\mu((a, b]) < \infty \quad \text{for all } -\infty < a < b < \infty.
\tag{11.1}\]
(More generally, a Radon measure on a Hausdorff topological space is a locally finite Borel measure that is inner regular with respect to compact sets; on \(\mathbb{R}\), this simplifies to finiteness on compact sets \(\mu(K) < \infty\).)

title: 11  Lecture 5.1. Radon Measure
text:
11.2 Stieltjes Premeasures and Correspondence
Recall that for any non-decreasing, right-continuous function \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\), the associated Stieltjes set function \(\mu_F((a, b]) = F(b) - F(a)\) defines a premeasure on the algebra of finite disjoint unions of half-open intervals \(\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{R}}\).
The next result shows that every Radon measure on \(\mathbb{R}\) arises from a unique (up to an additive constant) Stieltjes premeasure.

Theorem 11.1 (Characterization of Radon Measures on \(\mathbb{R}\)) If \(\mu\) is a Radon measure on \(\mathbb{R}\), then there exists a non-decreasing, right-continuous function \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) (unique up to an additive constant) such that: \[
\mu((a, b]) = F(b) - F(a) \quad \text{for all } -\infty < a \le b < \infty.
\tag{11.2}\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 11.1). 

Uniqueness: If \(G: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is another non-decreasing right-continuous function satisfying \(\mu((a, b]) = G(b) - G(a)\), then for all \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\): \[G(b) - G(a) = F(b) - F(a) \implies G(b) = F(b) + [G(0) - F(0)].\]
Setting \(C = G(0) - F(0)\), we have \(G(x) = F(x) + C\), establishing uniqueness up to a constant \(C \in \mathbb{R}\).
Existence: Define \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) centered at \(0\) by: \[
F(x) :=
\begin{cases}   
\mu((0, x]), & x \ge 0, \\    
-\mu((x, 0]), & x < 0.    
\end{cases}
\tag{11.3}\]

Interval Measure Identity: For any \(a < b\), set additive subtraction yields \(\mu((a, b]) = F(b) - F(a)\).
Monotonicity: For \(x \le y\), set inclusion \((0, x] \subseteq (0, y]\) (or \((y, 0] \subseteq (x, 0]\) for negative values) together with monotonicity of \(\mu\) implies \(F(x) \le F(y)\).
Right-Continuity: Fix \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) and let \(x_n \downarrow x\) with \(x_n > x\). Then \((x, x_1] \setminus (x_n, x_1] = (x, x_n] \downarrow \emptyset\). By continuity of measure from above for finite measure sets: \[
F(x_n) - F(x) = \mu((x, x_n]) \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0.
\]
Thus, \(F(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} F(x_n)\), proving right-continuity.

title: 11  Lecture 5.1. Radon Measure
text:
11.3 Premeasure Continuity Equivalences

Proposition 11.1 (Equivalences for Premeasures (Driver, Prop. 6.3)) Let \(\mu\) be a finitely additive set function on an algebra \(\mathcal{A}\). The following conditions are equivalent:

\(\mu\) is a premeasure (countably additive) on \(\mathcal{A}\).
Monotone Increasing Continuity: If \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) with \(A_n \uparrow A \in \mathcal{A}\), then \(\mu(A_n) \uparrow \mu(A)\) as \(n \to \infty\).

Moreover, if \(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\), these are also equivalent to:

Monotone Decreasing Continuity: If \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) with \(A_n \downarrow A \in \mathcal{A}\), then \(\mu(A_n) \downarrow \mu(A)\) as \(n \to \infty\).
Continuity at Empty Set from Above: If \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) with \(A_n \downarrow \emptyset\), then \(\mu(A_n) \downarrow 0\).



Proof (Proof of Proposition 11.1). 

(1) \(\Rightarrow\) (2): Let \(A_n \uparrow A \in \mathcal{A}\). Set \(B_1 = A_1\) and \(B_n = A_n \setminus A_{n-1} \in \mathcal{A}\) for \(n \ge 2\). The sequence \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) is pairwise disjoint with \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n = A\) and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^N B_n = A_N\). By countable additivity: \[
\mu(A) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=1}^N \mu(B_n) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \mu(A_N).
\]
(2) \(\Rightarrow\) (1): Let \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) be pairwise disjoint with \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n = B \in \mathcal{A}\). Define \(A_N := \bigcup_{n=1}^N B_n \in \mathcal{A}\). Then \(A_N \uparrow B\). Applying (2): \[
\mu(B) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \mu(A_N) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=1}^N \mu(B_n) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\]
Equivalence of (3)–(4) for Finite Measures: Follows directly by complementary set subtraction: \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\) whenever \(A \subseteq B\) and \(\mu(B) < \infty\).

title: 11  Lecture 5.1. Radon Measure
text:
11.4 Cumulative Distribution Functions (CDFs)

Definition 11.2 (Cumulative Distribution Function) Let \(\mu\) be a Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb{R}\) (so \(\mu(\mathbb{R}) = 1\)). The Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of \(\mu\) is the function \(F_\mu: \mathbb{R} \to [0, 1]\) defined by: \[
F_\mu(x) := \mu((-\infty, x]).
\tag{11.4}\]


Corollary 11.1 (Characterization of Probability CDFs) A function \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is the CDF of a unique Borel probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) if and only if it satisfies:

Monotonicity: \(F\) is non-decreasing;
Right-Continuity: \(F(x^+) = \lim_{y \downarrow x} F(y) = F(x)\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\);
Asymptotic Limits: \[
\lim_{x \to -\infty} F(x) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x \to +\infty} F(x) = 1.
\tag{11.5}\]

title: 11  Lecture 5.1. Radon Measure
section: 11.5 Classification of Borel Probability Measures on \(\mathbb{R}\)
text:
11.5 Classification of Borel Probability Measures on \(\mathbb{R}\)
Every CDF \(F\) can be decomposed into three standard types of behavior: Absolutely Continuous, Purely Discrete, and Singular Continuous.

11.5.1 Absolutely Continuous Measures
A measure \(\mu\) is continuous/absolutely continuous if \(F_\mu\) is continuous everywhere. In this case, singletons have zero measure: \[
\mu(\{x_0\}) = \lim_{x \uparrow x_0} \mu((x, x_0]) = \lim_{x \uparrow x_0} (F_\mu(x_0) - F_\mu(x)) = 0.
\tag{11.6}\]
Example (Uniform Distribution): \[
F(x) = \begin{cases}  0, & x \le 0, \\ x, & 0 \le x \le 1, \\ 1, & x \ge 1. \end{cases}
\tag{11.7}\]
In the following, we use Python to visualize the CDF of the uniform distribution on \([0, 1]\).

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(-0.5, 1.5, 500)

F = np.piecewise(
    x,
    [x < 0, (x >= 0) & (x < 1), x >= 1],
    [0, lambda x: x, 1]
)

plt.figure(figsize=(4, 3))
plt.plot(x, F)
plt.xlabel(r'$x$')
plt.ylabel(r'$F(x)$')
#plt.title('CDF of Uniform Distribution on [0, 1]')
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()







Figure 11.1: CDF of Uniform Distribution on [0, 1]







11.5.2 Purely Discrete / Point Mass Measures
A measure \(\mu\) is purely discrete if its CDF \(F_\mu\) is a step function supported on a countable set of point masses \(\{x_k\}\).
Example (Discrete Jump Measure): \[
\mu = \frac{1}{3}\delta_0 + \frac{1}{9}\delta_1 + \frac{5}{9}\delta_2.
\tag{11.8}\]
Note that the CDF \(F_\mu\) is discontinuous at the points \(x_0 = 0\), \(x_1 = 1\), and \(x_2 = 2\), with jump sizes equal to the corresponding point masses: \[
F_\mu(x) =
\begin{cases}  
0, & x < 0, \\
1/3, & 0 \le x < 1, \\
4/9, & 1 \le x < 2, \\
1, & x \ge 2.
\end{cases}
\tag{11.9}\]
In the following, we use Python to visualize the CDF of this discrete measure.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Jump locations and CDF values
x = np.array([-0.5, 0, 1, 2, 2.5])
F = np.array([0, 1/3, 4/9, 1, 1])

plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3.5))

# Horizontal pieces
plt.hlines(0, -0.5, 0, linewidth=1.5)
plt.hlines(1/3, 0, 1, linewidth=1.5)
plt.hlines(4/9, 1, 2, linewidth=1.5)
plt.hlines(1, 2, 2.5, linewidth=1.5)

# Vertical jumps
plt.vlines(0, 0, 1/3, linewidth=1.5)
plt.vlines(1, 1/3, 4/9, linewidth=1.5)
plt.vlines(2, 4/9, 1, linewidth=1.5)

# Filled circles: F(x), showing right-continuity
plt.plot([0, 1, 2], [1/3, 4/9, 1], 'o')

# Open circles: F(x-), showing failure of left-continuity
plt.plot([0, 1, 2], [0, 1/3, 4/9], 'o',
         markerfacecolor='white')

plt.xlabel(r'$x$')
plt.ylabel(r'$F(x)$')
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()







Figure 11.2: CDF of Discrete Jump Measure







11.5.3 Singular Continuous Measures (The Devil’s Staircase / Cantor Measure)
A measure \(\mu_{\text{Cantor}}\) can be continuous everywhere (\(F\) has no jump discontinuities), yet completely singular with respect to Lebesgue measure (\(\mu_{\text{Cantor}}\) is concentrated entirely on a set of Lebesgue measure zero).
Construction (Cantor Function): Let \(C_n\) denote the \(n\)-th stage in the construction of the middle-thirds Cantor set \(C = \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty C_n \subset [0, 1]\).






Figure 11.3: Cantor Set



Define the density functions and sequence of CDFs: \[
F_n(x) := \int_0^x \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^n \mathbf{1}_{C_n}(t) \, dt.
\tag{11.10}\]

Uniform Limit: \(F_n \to F_{\text{Cantor}}\) uniformly on \([0, 1]\).
Properties of \(F_{\text{Cantor}}\):

\(F(0) = 0\) and \(F(1) = 1\);
\(F\) is continuous and non-decreasing;
\(F'(x) = 0\) almost everywhere with respect to Lebesgue measure (since \(F\) is constant on each open interval removed during the Cantor construction);
\(\mu_{\text{Cantor}}(\{x\}) = 0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\);
\(\mu_{\text{Cantor}}(C) = 1\), even though \(m(C) = 0\) (where \(m\) is Lebesgue measure).

title: 11  Lecture 5.1. Radon Measure
text:
11.6 Reconstructions, Corrections, and Interpretations

Uniqueness Constant in Radon Theorem: In Theorem 11.1, the manuscript proves that \(G(b) - F(b) = G(a) - F(a)\) for all \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\). Setting \(a = 0\) explicitly yields \(G(x) = F(x) + [G(0) - F(0)]\), clarifying the constant shift \(C = G(0) - F(0)\).
Subtle Distinctions in Monotone Limits: In Proposition 11.1, condition (2) requires \(A_n \uparrow A\) with \(A \in \mathcal{A}\). If \(A = \bigcup A_n \notin \mathcal{A}\), the set \(A\) is not in the domain of \(\mu\), which is precisely why the premeasure condition must be checked against countable unions that remain within the algebra.
Cantor Density Factor: In the Devil’s staircase sequence \(F_n(x) = \int_0^x (3/2)^n \mathbf{1}_{C_n}(t) \, dt\), the total measure of \(C_n\) is \((2/3)^n\). Multiplying by the normalization factor \((3/2)^n\) ensures that \(\int_0^1 (3/2)^n \mathbf{1}_{C_n}(t) \, dt = 1\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).

title: 11  Lecture 5.1. Radon Measure
text:
11.7 Mathematical Gaps & Verification Items

11.7.1 Mathematical Analysis & Gaps

Lebesgue-Radon-Nikodym Decomposition Preview: The breakdown into discrete, absolutely continuous, and singular continuous components previews the general Lebesgue Decomposition Theorem (\(d\mu = d\mu_{\text{ac}} + d\mu_{\text{pp}} + d\mu_{\text{sing}}\)).



11.7.2 Items Requiring Verification

General Topological Definition vs Real Line Definition: On general locally compact Hausdorff (LCH) spaces, Radon measures require inner regularity (\(\mu(E) = \sup\{\mu(K) : K \subseteq E, K \text{ compact}\}\)). On \(\mathbb{R}\), second countability ensures that all locally finite Borel measures are automatically Radon (inner regular). Verify if your course explicitly proves this automatic regularity step.

title: 12  Lecture 5.2: Lebesgue Measure
text:
Definition 12.1 (Lebesgue Measure) The unique Radon measure \(\lambda\) on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) satisfying: \[
\lambda((a, b]) = b - a \quad \text{for all } -\infty < a < b < \infty
\tag{12.1}\] is called Lebesgue measure.

title: 12  Lecture 5.2: Lebesgue Measure
text:
12.3 Characterization and Scaling Properties

Theorem 12.1 (Uniqueness of Translation-Invariant Borel Measures) Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\) is the unique translation-invariant Borel measure on \(\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(\lambda((0, 1]) = 1\). If \(\mu\) is any other translation-invariant Borel measure on \(\mathbb{R}\), then \(\mu = \alpha \lambda\) for some constant \(\alpha \ge 0\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 12.1). 

Existence/Base Case: Since \(\lambda\) is constructed from the translation-invariant premeasure on half-open intervals, \(\lambda\) (and its outer measure \(\lambda^*\)) is translation-invariant with \(\lambda((0, 1]) = 1 - 0 = 1\).
Uniqueness for \(\mu((0, 1]) = 1\): Suppose \(\mu\) is a translation-invariant Borel measure with \(\mu((0, 1]) = 1\). For any \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), partition \((0, 1]\) into \(n\) equal disjoint intervals: \[
(0, 1] = \bigcup_{k=0}^{n-1} \left( \frac{k}{n}, \frac{k+1}{n} \right] = \bigcup_{k=0}^{n-1} \left( \frac{k}{n} + \left(0, \frac{1}{n}\right] \right).
\tag{12.3}\] By countable additivity and translation invariance of \(\mu\): \[
\begin{align*}
&1 = \mu((0, 1]) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \mu\left( \frac{k}{n} + \left(0, \frac{1}{n}\right] \right) = n \cdot \mu\left( \left(0, \frac{1}{n}\right] \right)\\
&\implies \mu\left( \left(0, \frac{1}{n}\right] \right) = \frac{1}{n}.
\end{align*}
\tag{12.4}\] By additivity across \(m\) disjoint copies, for any rational \(r = \frac{m}{n} > 0\): \[
\mu((0, r]) = \mu\left( \left(0, \frac{m}{n}\right] \right) = m \cdot \mu\left( \left(0, \frac{1}{n}\right] \right) = \frac{m}{n} = r.
\tag{12.5}\] Thus \(F_\mu(r) - F_\mu(0) = r\) for all \(r \in \mathbb{Q}^+\). By right-continuity of CDFs, \(F_\mu(x) - F_\mu(0) = x\) for all \(x \ge 0\). Hence, \(\mu((a, b]) = b - a = \lambda((a, b])\), so \(\mu = \lambda\) on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\).
General Scaling Constant \(\alpha\): If \(\mu(\mathbb{R}) = 0\), then \(\alpha = 0\). If \(\mu((0, 1]) = \alpha > 0\), define \(\nu := \frac{1}{\alpha} \mu\). Then \(\nu\) is translation-invariant and \(\nu((0, 1]) = 1\). By Step 2, \(\nu = \lambda \implies \mu = \alpha \lambda\).



Theorem 12.2 (Scaling Invariance Property) For any scale factor \(\gamma \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\): \[
\lambda(\gamma \cdot B) = \vert{}\gamma\vert{} \cdot \lambda(B).
\tag{12.6}\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 12.2). If \(\gamma = 0\), then \(\lambda(\{0\}) = 0 = 0 \cdot \lambda(B)\).
For \(\gamma \ne 0\), set \(\gamma \cdot B = \{\gamma x : x \in B\}\). Define the set function \(\mu(B) := \frac{1}{\vert{}\gamma\vert{}} \lambda(\gamma \cdot B)\).

\(\mu\) is a translation-invariant Borel measure on \(\mathbb{R}\).
Check its value on \((0, 1]\):

If \(\gamma > 0\), then \(\gamma \cdot (0, 1] = (0, \gamma]\), so \(\mu((0, 1]) = \frac{1}{\gamma} \lambda((0, \gamma]) = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma} = 1\).
If \(\gamma < 0\), then \(\gamma \cdot (0, 1] = [\gamma, 0)\), so \(\mu((0, 1]) = \frac{1}{\vert{}\gamma\vert{}} \lambda([\gamma, 0)) = \frac{\vert{}\gamma\vert{}}{\vert{}\gamma\vert{}} = 1\).


Since \(\mu\) is translation-invariant and \(\mu((0, 1]) = 1\), Theorem 12.1 yields \(\mu = \lambda\). Therefore, \(\lambda(\gamma \cdot B) = \vert{}\gamma\vert{} \lambda(B)\).

title: 12  Lecture 5.2: Lebesgue Measure
text:
12.4 Null Sets and Sub-Sets

Definition 12.2 (Null Set) In a measure space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), a set \(N \in \mathcal{F}\) is called a null set if \(\mu(N) = 0\).


12.4.1 Examples of Lebesgue Null Sets

Countable Sets: Every countable set \(X = \{x_1, x_2, \dots\} \subset \mathbb{R}\) is Lebesgue null (\(\lambda(X) = 0\)). Cover each \(x_n\) by \((x_n - \frac{\epsilon}{2^n}, x_n]\) for any \(\epsilon > 0\): \[
\begin{align*}
&\lambda(X) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \lambda\left( \left(x_n - \frac{\epsilon}{2^n}, x_n\right] \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\epsilon}{2^n} = \epsilon\\
& \implies \lambda(X) = 0.
\end{align*}
\tag{12.7}\]
Uncountable Null Sets (Cantor Set): The middle-thirds Cantor set \(C = \bigcap_{n=0}^\infty C_n\) is uncountable. Since \(C_n\) consists of \(2^n\) closed intervals each of length \(3^{-n}\), \(\lambda(C_n) = (2/3)^n\). By monotonicity: \[
\lambda(C) \le \lambda(C_n) = \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0 \implies \lambda(C) = 0.
\tag{12.8}\]

title: 12  Lecture 5.2: Lebesgue Measure
text:
12.5 Completion of Measure Spaces
The Measurability Problem: Subsets of null sets are not guaranteed to be measurable in \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\). For example, there exist non-Borel subsets \(\Lambda \subseteq C\) contained inside the Borel null set \(C \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\).

Definition 12.3 (Null Complete Measure Space) A measure space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called (null) complete if for every \(N \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(\mu(N) = 0\), every subset \(\Lambda \subseteq N\) belongs to \(\mathcal{F}\) (and satisfies \(\mu(\Lambda) = 0\)).


Theorem 12.3 (Completion Theorem) For any measure space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), there exists a minimal complete extension \((\Omega, \tilde{\mathcal{F}}, \tilde{\mu})\) where \(\mathcal{F} \subseteq \tilde{\mathcal{F}}\) and \(\tilde{\mu}\big\vert{}_{\mathcal{F}} = \mu\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 12.3). Define the candidate collection and extended measure by: \[
\tilde{\mathcal{F}} := \{ A \cup \Lambda : A \in \mathcal{F}, \, \Lambda \subseteq N \text{ for some } N \in \mathcal{F} \text{ with } \mu(N) = 0 \},
\tag{12.9}\] \[
\tilde{\mu}(A \cup \Lambda) := \mu(A).
\tag{12.10}\]

\(\tilde{\mathcal{F}}\) is a \(\sigma\)-field:

Complements: Let \(E = A \cup \Lambda \in \tilde{\mathcal{F}}\) with \(\Lambda \subseteq N\) and \(\mu(N) = 0\). Then: \[
E^c = (A \cup \Lambda)^c = A^c \cap \Lambda^c = (A^c \cap (N \setminus \Lambda)) \cup (A^c \cap N^c).
\tag{12.11}\] Set \(A' := A^c \cap N^c \in \mathcal{F}\) and \(\Lambda' := A^c \cap (N \setminus \Lambda) \subseteq N\). Thus \(E^c = A' \cup \Lambda' \in \tilde{\mathcal{F}}\).
Countable Unions: Let \(E_n = A_n \cup \Lambda_n \in \tilde{\mathcal{F}}\) with \(\Lambda_n \subseteq N_n\) and \(\mu(N_n) = 0\). Then: \[
\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E_n = \left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \right) \cup \left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \Lambda_n \right).
\tag{12.12}\] Here \(\bigcup A_n \in \mathcal{F}\) and \(\bigcup \Lambda_n \subseteq \bigcup N_n \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(\mu(\bigcup N_n) \le \sum \mu(N_n) = 0\). Thus \(\bigcup E_n \in \tilde{\mathcal{F}}\).

Well-Definedness of \(\tilde{\mu}\): Suppose \(A_1 \cup \Lambda_1 = A_2 \cup \Lambda_2\) with \(\Lambda_1 \subseteq N_1, \Lambda_2 \subseteq N_2\) and \(\mu(N_1) = \mu(N_2) = 0\). Then: \[
\begin{align*}
&A_1 \subseteq A_1 \cup \Lambda_1 = A_2 \cup \Lambda_2 \subseteq A_2 \cup N_2 \\
&\implies \mu(A_1) \le \mu(A_2) + \mu(N_2) = \mu(A_2).
\end{align*}
\tag{12.13}\] By symmetry, \(\mu(A_2) \le \mu(A_1)\), so \(\mu(A_1) = \mu(A_2)\).
Countable Additivity: Follows directly from the disjointness of base sets \(A_n \in \mathcal{F}\) and sub-null terms \(\Lambda_n\). Completion is established by construction. \(\blacksquare\)

title: 12  Lecture 5.2: Lebesgue Measure
text:
12.6 The Lebesgue \(\sigma\)-Algebra \(\mathcal{M}\)
When defined via Carathéodory’s criterion, the Lebesgue \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{M}\) is defined as: \[
\mathcal{M} := \{ E \subseteq \mathbb{R} : \lambda^*(A) = \lambda^*(A \cap E) + \lambda^*(A \cap E^c) \quad \forall A \subseteq \mathbb{R} \}.
\tag{12.14}\]

Properties: \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) \subsetneq \mathcal{M}\). \(\mathcal{M}\) is complete and represents the formal completion of \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) under \(\lambda\).
Course Convention: Throughout this course, Lebesgue measure is treated as a Borel measure on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) unless completion is explicitly invoked.

title: 12  Lecture 5.2: Lebesgue Measure
text:
12.7 Remark (Driver, Prop. 7.11)
In a finite (pre)measure space \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\), the Carathéodory measurable \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{M}_\mu\) coincides with \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\), the closure of the algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) under the pseudo-metric \(d_\mu(E, F) = \mu^*(E \Delta F)\).

title: 12  Lecture 5.2: Lebesgue Measure
text:
12.7 Reconstructions, Corrections, and Interpretations

Rational Base Partition Step: In Theorem 12.1, the decomposition \((0, 1] = \bigcup_{k=0}^{n-1} \left( \frac{k}{n} + (0, \frac{1}{n}] \right)\) was expanded to highlight why translation invariance forces \(\mu((0, 1/n]) = 1/n\) without assuming continuity beforehand.
Complement Verification in Completion: In Theorem 12.3, the set-theoretic identity \((A \cup \Lambda)^c = (A^c \cap N^c) \cup (A^c \cap (N \setminus \Lambda))\) explicitly confirms that the complement remains in \(\tilde{\mathcal{F}}\).

title: 12  Lecture 5.2: Lebesgue Measure
text:
12.8 Mathematical Gaps & Verification Items

12.8.1 Mathematical Analysis & Gaps

Non-Measurable Sets (Vitali Sets): The manuscript notes that \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) \subsetneq \mathcal{M} \subsetneq 2^\mathbb{R}\). The existence of non-Lebesgue-measurable sets requires the Axiom of Choice (e.g., Vitali construction).



12.8.2 Items Requiring Verification

Linear Transformation Invariance on \(\mathbb{R}^d\): On \(\mathbb{R}^d\), the scaling theorem generalizes to \(\lambda(T(B)) = \vert{}\det T\vert{} \lambda(B)\) for any linear operator \(T \in \text{GL}_d(\mathbb{R})\). Check if your upcoming module extends Lebesgue measure to multidimensional spaces.

title: 5  Lecture 2.2: Finitely Additive Measures
text:
5.8 Takeaways

Premeasures vs finitely-additive measures. A premeasure on an algebra is countably additive (whenever the countable disjoint union lies in the algebra); a finitely-additive measure is only finitely additive. The two notions coincide for finite unions but diverge in general.
Subadditivity for finitely-additive measures (Proposition 5.1). If \(\{A_i\}_{i=1}^\infty\) are pairwise disjoint in \(\mathcal{A}\) with \(\bigcup_i A_i \in \mathcal{A}\), then \(\mu\!\left(\bigcup_i A_i\right) \ge \sum_i \mu(A_i)\), and the inequality can be strict. A premeasure would give equality; the gap measures the failure of countable additivity.
Structure of the generated field (Proposition 5.2). The field generated by a semi-algebra \(\mathcal{S}\) is exactly \(\operatorname{DU}(\mathcal{S})\), the collection of all finite disjoint unions of elements of \(\mathcal{S}\). This explicit description is the key to extending measures from \(\mathcal{S}\).
Unique extension from semi-algebras (Proposition 5.3). Any finitely-additive measure \(\mu\) on a semi-algebra \(\mathcal{S}\) extends uniquely to a finitely-additive measure on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\) via \(\mu\!\left(\bigsqcup_i E_i\right) := \sum_i \mu(E_i)\). Uniqueness is forced by the formula; well-definedness requires showing the value is independent of the chosen \(\mathcal{S}\)-decomposition, which follows from the common-refinement identity \(\mu(E_i) = \sum_j \mu(E_i \cap F_j)\).
Stieltjes measure (Proposition 5.4). Every non-decreasing \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) defines a finitely-additive Stieltjes measure \(\mu_F((a,b]) = F(b) - F(a)\) on \(\mathcal{S}_{(]}\), which extends uniquely to \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{(]})\). Additivity on \(\mathcal{S}_{(]}\) follows from the telescoping identity for ordered partitions of an interval.
Right-continuity is necessary for countable additivity. \(\mu_F\) is a premeasure only if \(F\) is right-continuous: a right-discontinuity at \(a\) causes \(\mu_F((a,a+1]) > \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu_F\!\left(\!\left(a+\tfrac{1}{n+1}, a+\tfrac{1}{n}\right]\right)\). Right-continuity is also sufficient, as shown in Lecture 3.1 via the Carathéodory extension theorem.

title: 13  Lecture 6.1: Random Variables Motivation
text:
13.2 The Intuitive Picture
We begin with informal “experiments” to motivate our formal measure-theoretic framework.

Example 13.1 Coin Tossing. Consider tossing a fair coin \(N\) times. The individual outcomes are sequences of heads (\(H\)) and tails (\(T\)), such as \(HTHH\). We might be interested in a summary numerical measurement, such as \(X = \text{\# heads}\). In this specific outcome, \(X = 3\). We can then consider events defined by conditions on \(X\), such as \(\{X \le 3\}\) or \(\{X \ge 2\}\).


Example 13.2 Dart Board. Consider throwing a dart at a circular dartboard of radius \(R\). The point where the dart lands can be represented in polar coordinates as \((r, \theta)\). A natural summary quantity is \(R\), the distance from the center. An outcome might be \((r, \theta) = \left(0.15, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) (or \((0.15, 0)\)), yielding \(R = 0.15\). We are then interested in events such as \(\{R \le 0.25\}\).

In general, each experiment has an outcome \(\omega\), belonging to the set of all possible outcomes called the sample space, denoted by \(\Omega\).
Probability is a measure of the likelihood of an event \(E \subseteq \Omega\), which is a set of outcomes.

Outcomes                   Measurements
   ω ∈ Ω      ─────── X ───────>   ℝ
(Inaccessible)               (Observable)

The underlying sample space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) is often “inaccessible” directly:

Outcomes are elements \(\omega \in \Omega\).
Events are measurable subsets of \(\Omega\), i.e., elements of \(\mathcal{F}\).

A function \(X: \Omega \to S\) maps the inaccessible sample space to a manageable “state space” \(S\).

The state space \(S\) could be \(\mathbb{C}\).
\(S\) is usually \(\mathbb{R}\).
If \(S = \mathbb{R}^d\), we usually call \(X\) a random vector.


Remark 13.1 (Random Variable versus Random Function). The term “random variable” is a misnomer. A random variable is not a variable in the sense of algebra, but rather a function. It is a function that takes an outcome \(\omega \in \Omega\) and returns a real number \(X(\omega) \in \mathbb{R}\). The “random” part refers to the fact that the outcome \(\omega\) is random, and thus \(X(\omega)\) is also random. Historically, we should perhaps call them “random functions,” but the very old “variable” terminology has stuck since its usage by Laplace in the early 19th century.

To perform probability calculations, we need to be able to compute probabilities of sets formed by conditions on \(X\), such as: \[
\{X \le 1\} := \{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le 1\}.
\]

title: 13  Lecture 6.1: Random Variables Motivation
section: 13.2 Formal Definition of a Random Variable
text:
13.2 Formal Definition of a Random Variable

Definition 13.1 (Random Variable) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space. A function \(X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is a random variable if it is \(\mathcal{F}\)-measurable; that is, for every \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), \[
\{X \le t\} := \{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le t\} \in \mathcal{F}.
\]


Note that the definition of a random variable depends on the underlying probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\). A random variable is not just a function from \(\Omega\) to \(\mathbb{R}\); it must also be measurable with respect to the sigma-algebra \(\mathcal{F}\).
The measurability condition ensures that we can assign probabilities to events defined by the random variable, such as \(\{X \le t\}\), using the probability measure \(\mathbb{P}\).
We can also denote \(\{X \le t\}\) as \[
\{X \le t\} = X^{-1}((-\infty, t]) = \{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \in (-\infty, t]\}.
\]

title: 13  Lecture 6.1: Random Variables Motivation
text:
13.3 Cumulative Distribution Functions (CDFs)

Definition 13.2 (Cumulative Distribution Function) Let \(X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) be a random variable on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\). The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of \(X\) is the function \(F_X: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by: \[
F_X(t) := \mathbb{P}(X \le t) = \mathbb{P}\bigl(\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le t\}\bigr).
\]


Proposition 13.1 (Properties of the CDF) The function \(F_X: \mathbb{R} \to [0, 1]\) satisfies the following properties:

\(F_X\) is non-decreasing: if \(s \le t\), then \(F_X(s) \le F_X(t)\).
\(F_X\) is right-continuous: for all \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\lim_{n \to \infty} F_X(t_n) = F_X(t)\) for any sequence \(t_n \downarrow t\).
Limits at infinity: \[
\lim_{t \to -\infty} F_X(t) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{t \to +\infty} F_X(t) = 1.
\]



Proof (Proof of Proposition 13.1). We establish each property using continuity of the probability measure \(\mathbb{P}\):

Non-decreasing: Let \(s \le t\). Then \(\{\omega : X(\omega) \le s\} \subseteq \{\omega : X(\omega) \le t\}\). By monotonicity of measure \(\mathbb{P}\): \[
F_X(s) = \mathbb{P}(X \le s) \le \mathbb{P}(X \le t) = F_X(t).
\]
Right-continuity: Let \(t_n \downarrow t\) (i.e., \(t_1 \ge t_2 \ge \dots \to t\)). Define \(A_n = \{X \le t_n\}\). The sequence of events \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) is non-increasing (\(A_n \supseteq A_{n+1}\)) and satisfies: \[
\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A_n = \{X \le t\}.
\] By continuity of measure from above (since \(\mathbb{P}(A_1) \le 1 < \infty\)): \[
F_X(t_n) = \mathbb{P}(X \le t_n) \downarrow \mathbb{P}(X \le t) = F_X(t).
\]
Limits at infinity:

Consider \(b_n \downarrow -\infty\). The events \(B_n = \{X \le b_n\}\) satisfy \(B_n \supseteq B_{n+1}\) and \(\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty B_n = \emptyset\). Thus: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} F_X(b_n) = \mathbb{P}(\emptyset) = 0.
\]
Consider \(c_n \uparrow +\infty\). The events \(C_n = \{X \le c_n\}\) satisfy \(C_n \subseteq C_{n+1}\) and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty C_n = \Omega\). By continuity of measure from below: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} F_X(c_n) = \mathbb{P}(\Omega) = 1.
\]



By the Carathéodory Extension Theorem, \(F_X\) uniquely determines a Borel probability measure \(\mu_X\) on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\), defined on intervals by \(\mu_X((a, b]) = F_X(b) - F_X(a)\).

Definition 13.3 (Probability Distribution / Law) The measure \(\mu_X\) is called the probability distribution (or law) of \(X\).


Remark 13.2. 

Note that the probability distribution \(\mu_X\) is a measure on the Borel sigma-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\), which is generated by intervals of the form \((a, b]\). On the other hand, \(\mathbb{P}\) is a measure on the sigma-algebra \(\mathcal{F}\) of the sample space \(\Omega\).
Consider \(\mu_X((a, b])\): \[
\begin{align*}
\mu_X((a, b]) &= F_X(b) - F_X(a)\\
&= \mathbb{P}(X \le b) - \mathbb{P}(X \le a)\\
&= \mathbb{P}(\{\omega : X(\omega) \le b\}) - \mathbb{P}(\{\omega : X(\omega) \le a\})\\
&= \mathbb{P}(\{\omega : a < X(\omega) \le b\})\\
&= \mathbb{P}(X^{-1}((a, b]))\\
&= \mathbb{P}\circ X^{-1}((a, b]).
\end{align*}
\]
Often \(\mu_X\) is all we will really know about \(X\). And even more often, we won’t even know \(\mu_X\), but will only have some limited clues about it.

title: 13  Lecture 6.1: Random Variables Motivation
text: 13.4 (Great) Expectations

title: 13  Lecture 6.1: Random Variables Motivation
text:
13.5 Finite and Countable Sample Spaces
Can we get a “snapshot” number that tells us something about this distribution?

Definition 13.4 (Expectation on Finite Sample Spaces) Let \(\Omega = \{\omega_1, \omega_2, \dots, \omega_N\}\) be a finite sample space, and set \(\mathcal{F} = 2^\Omega\). The probability of any event \(E \subseteq \Omega\) is given by: \[
\mathbb{P}(E) = \sum_{\omega \in E} \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) = \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} \mathbf{1}_{E}(\omega) \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}),
\] where \(\mathbf{1}_A(\omega)\) is the indicator function: \[
\mathbf{1}_A(\omega) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \omega \in A, \\ 0 & \text{if } \omega \notin A. \end{cases}
\]
If \(X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is a random variable, its CDF is: \[
F_X(t) = \mathbb{P}(X \le t) = \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} \mathbf{1}_{\{X(\omega) \le t\}} \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}).
\]
We define the expected value (or weighted average) of \(X\) as: \[
\mathbb{E}(X) := \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} X(\omega) \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}). \tag{$\star$}
\]


Example 13.3 Three Coin Tosses. Toss a fair coin 3 times, and let \(X = \text{\# Heads}\). The sample space is: \[
\Omega = \{HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT\},
\] with \(\mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) = \frac{1}{8}\) for all \(\omega \in \Omega\).
The values of \(X(\omega)\) are:

\(X(HHH) = 3\) (1 outcome)
\(X(HHT) = X(HTH) = X(THH) = 2\) (3 outcomes)
\(X(HTT) = X(THT) = X(TTH) = 1\) (3 outcomes)
\(X(TTT) = 0\) (1 outcome)

Applying formula \((\star)\): \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}(X) &= \frac{1}{8} \left( 3 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 3 + 0 \cdot 1 \right) \\
&= \frac{1}{8}(3 + 6 + 3 + 0) = \frac{12}{8} = \frac{3}{2} = 1.5.
\end{align*}
\]

title: 13  Lecture 6.1: Random Variables Motivation
text:
13.6 Limitations and Generalizations
The definition \((\star)\) makes perfect sense if \(\Omega\) is finite. It is also okay if \(\Omega\) is countably infinite.
However, formula \((\star)\) will not help us if \(\mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) = 0\) for all \(\omega \in \Omega\), which is typical for continuous sample spaces (e.g., throwing a dart).

13.6.1 The Undergraduate Probability Approach
In introductory probability, one grouping transformation is performed: \[
\begin{align*}
\sum_{\omega \in \Omega} X(\omega) \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) &= \sum_{t} \sum_{\omega : X(\omega) = t} X(\omega) \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) \\
&= \sum_{t} t \sum_{\omega : X(\omega) = t} \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) \\
&= \sum_{t} t \, \mathbb{P}(X = t).
\end{align*}
\]
One then attempts to find an analogue of this sum in the “continuous” setting by replacing sums with integrals: \(\sum_t t \, \mathbb{P}(X=t) \rightsquigarrow \int t f_X(t) \, dt\).
Problems with this approach: There are many. For instance, proving fundamental structural properties like linearity \(\mathbb{E}(X + Y) = \mathbb{E}(X) + \mathbb{E}(Y)\) becomes cumbersome or requires separating discrete and continuous cases.


13.6.2 The Measure-Theoretic Solution
We will develop the right generalization of \((\star)\) to work in any general probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\): the Lebesgue Integral.
\[
\mathbb{E}(X) = \int_{\Omega} X \, d\mathbb{P}.
\]

title: 14  Lecture 6.2: Measurable Functions
text:
14.2 Pull-Back and Push-Forward \(\sigma\)-Algebras
Pull-back and push-forward \(\sigma\)-algebras are two fundamental constructions in measure theory that allow us to transfer \(\sigma\)-algebra structures between different measurable spaces via a function.

Definition 14.1 (Pull-Back and Push-Forward \(\sigma\)-Algebras) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be measurable spaces, and let \(f: \Omega \to S\) be a function.

The pull-back of \(\mathcal{B}\) to \(\Omega\) by \(f\) is: \[
f^* \mathcal{B} := \{ f^{-1}(B) \subseteq \Omega : B \in \mathcal{B} \} \subseteq 2^\Omega.
\]
The push-forward of \(\mathcal{F}\) to \(S\) by \(f\) is: \[
f_* \mathcal{F} := \{ E \subseteq S : f^{-1}(E) \in \mathcal{F} \} \subseteq 2^S.
\]



Proposition 14.1 (Both Constructions Yield \(\sigma\)-Algebras) In the setting of Definition 14.1, \(f^* \mathcal{B}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) and \(f_* \mathcal{F}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(S\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 14.1). Both claims follow from the fact that preimages commute with complements and countable unions.
For \(f^* \mathcal{B}\): we have \(\Omega = f^{-1}(S) \in f^* \mathcal{B}\); if \(A = f^{-1}(B)\) with \(B \in \mathcal{B}\), then \(\Omega \setminus A = f^{-1}(S \setminus B) \in f^* \mathcal{B}\); and if \(A_n = f^{-1}(B_n)\) with \(B_n \in \mathcal{B}\), then \(\bigcup_{n} A_n = f^{-1}\left( \bigcup_{n} B_n \right) \in f^* \mathcal{B}\).
For \(f_* \mathcal{F}\): we have \(f^{-1}(S) = \Omega \in \mathcal{F}\), so \(S \in f_* \mathcal{F}\); if \(f^{-1}(E) \in \mathcal{F}\), then \(f^{-1}(S \setminus E) = \Omega \setminus f^{-1}(E) \in \mathcal{F}\); and if \(f^{-1}(E_n) \in \mathcal{F}\) for all \(n\), then \(f^{-1}\left( \bigcup_{n} E_n \right) = \bigcup_{n} f^{-1}(E_n) \in \mathcal{F}\).

Some Remarks:

The pull-back \(\sigma\)-algebra \(f^* \mathcal{B}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) formed by taking the preimages of all sets in \(\mathcal{B}\).
The push-forward \(\sigma\)-algebra \(f_* \mathcal{F}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(S\) consisting of all subsets of \(S\) whose preimages under \(f\) are in \(\mathcal{F}\).












(a) Pull-back











(b) Push-forward







Figure 14.1: Pull-Back and Push-Forward \(\sigma\)-Algebras




Example 14.1 Let \(\Omega=\mathbb R\), \(\mathcal F=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\), \(S=[0,\infty)\), and \(\mathcal B=\mathcal B([0,\infty))\). Define \(f:\mathbb{R} \to [0,\infty)\) by \(f(x) = x^2\).
Take a Borel set \(B\subseteq[0,\infty)\). Its pull-back is \[
f^{-1}(B) = \{x\in\mathbb R:x^2\in B\}.
\] For example, take \(B=[0,1]\). Then \[
f^{-1}([0,1]) = \{x:x^2\leq1\} = [-1,1].
\] Thus \([-1,1] \in f^* \mathcal{B}\). If \(B=(1,4]\), then its pull-back is \[
f^{-1}((1,4]) = \{x:1<x^2\leq4\} = [-2,-1)\cup(1,2].
\] Therefore, \([-2,-1)\cup(1,2] \in f^* \mathcal{B}\).
Now start with \(\mathcal F=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\) and push it forward to \(S=[0,\infty)\): \[
f_*\mathcal F = \{E\subseteq[0,\infty): f^{-1}(E)\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}.
\] Take any Borel set \(E\in\mathcal B([0,\infty))\). Because \(f(x)=x^2\) is continuous, \(f^{-1}(E)\) is Borel in \(\mathbb R\). Therefore, \(E\in f_*\mathcal F\). Thus \[
\mathcal B([0,\infty)) \subseteq f_*\mathcal F.
\] But in fact we have equality: \[
f_* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) = \mathcal{B}([0,\infty)).
\]

More generally, for any collection of subsets \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq 2^S\), we can define the pull-back collection: \[
f^* \mathcal{E} := \{ f^{-1}(E) \subseteq \Omega : E \in \mathcal{E} \} \subseteq 2^\Omega.
\]

Lemma 14.1 (Pull-Back and \(\sigma\)-Algebra Generation) Let \(\Omega\) and \(S\) be arbitrary sets, let \(f: \Omega \to S\) be an arbitrary map, and let \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq 2^S\) be a family of subsets. Then: \[
\sigma(f^* \mathcal{E}) = f^* \left( \sigma(\mathcal{E}) \right).
\] No measurability assumption on \(f\) is required; this is what makes the lemma applicable before measurability is known.


Proof (Proof of Lemma 14.1). We prove two-way inclusion:

Inclusion \((\subseteq)\): By Proposition 14.1, \(f^*(\sigma(\mathcal{E}))\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\). Since \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E})\), we have: \[
f^* \mathcal{E} \subseteq f^*(\sigma(\mathcal{E})).
\] Since \(\sigma(f^* \mathcal{E})\) is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra containing \(f^* \mathcal{E}\), it follows that: \[
\sigma(f^* \mathcal{E}) \subseteq f^*(\sigma(\mathcal{E})).
\]
Inclusion \((\supseteq)\): Define the set collection: \[
\mathcal{G} := \{ B \in \sigma(\mathcal{E}) : f^{-1}(B) \in \sigma(f^* \mathcal{E}) \}.
\] We show that \(\mathcal{G}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(S\):

\(S \in \mathcal{G}\) since \(f^{-1}(S) = \Omega \in \sigma(f^* \mathcal{E})\).
If \(B \in \mathcal{G}\), then \(f^{-1}(B^c) = (f^{-1}(B))^c \in \sigma(f^* \mathcal{E})\), so \(B^c \in \mathcal{G}\).
If \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{G}\), then \(f^{-1}\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty f^{-1}(B_n) \in \sigma(f^* \mathcal{E})\), so \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \in \mathcal{G}\).

Moreover \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{G}\): for every \(E \in \mathcal{E}\) we have \(E \in \sigma(\mathcal{E})\), and \(f^{-1}(E) \in f^* \mathcal{E} \subseteq \sigma(f^* \mathcal{E})\).
Thus \(\mathcal{G}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(S\) containing \(\mathcal{E}\). Therefore, by minimality of the generated \(\sigma\)-algebra, \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}) \subseteq \mathcal{G}\), which implies that for every \(B \in \sigma(\mathcal{E})\), \(f^{-1}(B) \in \sigma(f^* \mathcal{E})\). Consequently: \[
f^*(\sigma(\mathcal{E})) \subseteq \sigma(f^* \mathcal{E}).
\] Both inclusions yield equality.

title: 14  Lecture 6.2: Measurable Functions
text:
14.3 Measurable Functions

Definition 14.2 (Measurable Function) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be measurable spaces. A function \(f: \Omega \to S\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B})\)-measurable if: \[
f^* \mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{F}, \quad \text{i.e., } \forall B \in \mathcal{B}, \; f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{F}.
\]

Some Remarks:

A measurable function is one for which the preimage of every measurable set in \(S\) is a measurable set in \(\Omega\).
If \(f:(\Omega,f^*\mathcal{B})\to (S,\mathcal{B})\) then, by definition, \(f\) is measurable. In this sense, the pull-back \(\sigma\)-algebra \(f^*\mathcal{B}\) is the “smallest” \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) that makes \(f\) measurable.
If \(f:(\Omega,\mathcal{F})\to (S,f_*\mathcal{F})\) then, by definition, \(f\) is measurable. In this sense, the push-forward \(\sigma\)-algebra \(f_*\mathcal{F}\) is the largest \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(S\) with respect to inclusion that makes \(f\) measurable: every other such \(\sigma\)-algebra is contained in \(f_*\mathcal{F}\).


Example 14.2 Indicator Functions. Let \(A \subseteq \Omega\) and consider the indicator function \(\mathbf{1}_A: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\). Then \(\mathbf{1}_A\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable if and only if \(A \in \mathcal{F}\).
Proof. For any \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) the preimage \((\mathbf{1}_A)^{-1}(B)\) depends only on \(B \cap \{0, 1\}\), and the four resulting cases are exhaustive and mutually exclusive: \[
(\mathbf{1}_A)^{-1}(B) = \begin{cases}
\Omega & \text{if } 0 \in B \text{ and } 1 \in B, \\
A & \text{if } 1 \in B \text{ and } 0 \notin B, \\
A^c & \text{if } 0 \in B \text{ and } 1 \notin B, \\
\emptyset & \text{if } 0 \notin B \text{ and } 1 \notin B.
\end{cases}
\] If \(A \in \mathcal{F}\), then each of \(\Omega, A, A^c, \emptyset\) lies in \(\mathcal{F}\), so every preimage is in \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathbf{1}_A\) is measurable. Conversely, if \(\mathbf{1}_A\) is measurable, then taking \(B = \{1\} \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) gives \(A = (\mathbf{1}_A)^{-1}(\{1\}) \in \mathcal{F}\).


Proposition 14.2 (Criterion for Measurability on Generators) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) and \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be measurable spaces, and let \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq 2^S\) be a collection of subsets such that \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}) = \mathcal{B}\). A function \(f: \Omega \to S\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B})\)-measurable if and only if \(f^* \mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 14.2). 

(\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(f\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B})\)-measurable, then \(f^* \mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\). Since \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{B}\), it immediately follows that \(f^* \mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) Assume \(f^* \mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\). Since \(\mathcal{F}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra containing \(f^* \mathcal{E}\), minimality of the generated \(\sigma\)-algebra gives \(\sigma(f^* \mathcal{E}) \subseteq \mathcal{F}\). By Lemma 14.1: \[
f^* \mathcal{B} = f^*(\sigma(\mathcal{E})) = \sigma(f^* \mathcal{E}) \subseteq \mathcal{F}.
\] Hence \(f\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B})\)-measurable.

title: 14  Lecture 6.2: Measurable Functions
section: 14.4 Real-Valued Measurable Functions and Random Variables
text:
14.4 Real-Valued Measurable Functions and Random Variables

Example 14.3 Important Characterizations on \(\mathbb{R}\). A function \(X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable if and only if any one of the following equivalent conditions holds:

\(X^{-1}((-\infty, t]) = \{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le t\} = \{X \le t\} \in \mathcal{F}\) for all \(t \in \mathbb{R}\);
\(X^{-1}((a, b]) = \{a < X \le b\} \in \mathcal{F}\) for all \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\) with \(a < b\);
\(X^{-1}((a, \infty)) = \{X > a\} \in \mathcal{F}\) for all \(a \in \mathbb{R}\).

These are equivalent by Proposition 14.2, because each of the three displayed collections generates \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\). For the first two this is Proposition 3.2. For the third, \((a, \infty) = \mathbb{R} \setminus (-\infty, a]\), so the two collections generate the same \(\sigma\)-algebra: \[
\sigma(\{(a, \infty) : a \in \mathbb{R}\}) = \sigma(\{(-\infty, a] : a \in \mathbb{R}\}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}).
\]


Definition 14.3 (Borel Random Variable) Given a probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\), a (Borel) random variable is an \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable function \(X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\).

title: 14  Lecture 6.2: Measurable Functions
text:
14.5 Compositions and Continuous Functions

Proposition 14.3 (Composition of Measurable Functions) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), \((S, \mathcal{B})\), and \((T, \mathcal{C})\) be measurable spaces. If \(f: \Omega \to S\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B})\)-measurable and \(g: S \to T\) is \((\mathcal{B}/\mathcal{C})\)-measurable, then the composition \(g \circ f: \Omega \to T\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{C})\)-measurable.


Proof (Proof of Proposition 14.3). For any \(C \in \mathcal{C}\), using the preimage composition property: \[
(g \circ f)^{-1}(C) = f^{-1}(g^{-1}(C)).
\] Since \(g\) is \((\mathcal{B}/\mathcal{C})\)-measurable, \(g^{-1}(C) \in \mathcal{B}\). Since \(f\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B})\)-measurable, \(f^{-1}(g^{-1}(C)) \in \mathcal{F}\). Thus \((g \circ f)^{-1}(C) \in \mathcal{F}\).


Corollary 14.1 (Continuous Transformations of Random Variables) Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_d\) be random variables on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\). If \(f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) is Borel measurable (in particular, if it is continuous), then \(Y = f(X_1, \dots, X_d)\) is a random variable.
(Examples: \(X_1 + X_2\), \(X_1 X_2\), \(\max(X_1, X_2)\), etc.)


Proof (Proof of Corollary 14.1). If \(f\) is assumed Borel measurable, its \((\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurability is part of the hypothesis. If \(f\) is continuous, then \(f^{-1}((-\infty, t])\) is closed, because \((-\infty, t]\) is closed, and closed sets are Borel; since \(\{(-\infty, t] : t \in \mathbb{R}\}\) generates \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) by Proposition 3.2, Proposition 14.2 shows that \(f\) is \((\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable.
Define the joint map \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \dots, X_d): \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^d\) and let \[
\mathcal{E} := \left\{ \prod_{j=1}^d (a_j, b_j) \;:\; a_j, b_j \in \mathbb{Q}, \; a_j < b_j \right\}
\] be the countable collection of open boxes with rational vertices. Exactly as in Proposition 3.2, \(\mathcal{E}\) is a base for the topology of \(\mathbb{R}^d\): every open \(U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) is the union of those members of \(\mathcal{E}\) contained in \(U\), and that union is countable because \(\mathcal{E}\) is countable. Hence \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E})\), and since every box is open the reverse inclusion also holds, so \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\).
Each \(X_j\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable, so for every box in \(\mathcal{E}\), \[
\mathbf{X}^{-1}\left( \prod_{j=1}^d (a_j, b_j) \right) = \bigcap_{j=1}^d X_j^{-1}((a_j, b_j)) \in \mathcal{F},
\] being a finite intersection of sets in \(\mathcal{F}\). By Proposition 14.2, \(\mathbf{X}\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\)-measurable. Since \(Y = f \circ \mathbf{X}\), by Proposition 14.3, \(Y\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable, so \(Y\) is a random variable.

title: 14  Lecture 6.2: Measurable Functions
text:
14.6 Information and Push-Forward Distributions
In the “background” (inaccessible) probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\), we observe random variables \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_d\). What is actually knowable?
Two primary structures emerge:

14.6.1 Current Information (\(\sigma\)-Algebra Generated by Random Variables)

Definition 14.4 (Generated \(\sigma\)-Algebra) The \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by a collection of random variables \(\{X_j\}_{j=1}^d\) on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) is: \[
\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) := \sigma\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^d X_j^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) \right) \subseteq \mathcal{F},
\] where the inclusion holds because each \(X_j\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable, so that \(\bigcup_{j=1}^d X_j^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) \subseteq \mathcal{F}\).
This is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) with respect to which \(X_1, \dots, X_d\) are all measurable: a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{G}\) on \(\Omega\) makes every \(X_j\) measurable if and only if \(X_j^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) \subseteq \mathcal{G}\) for each \(j\), i.e. if and only if \(\mathcal{G} \supseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^d X_j^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\), and the smallest such \(\sigma\)-algebra is by definition the one generated by that union.

Equivalent and very useful characterizations:
\[
\begin{align*}
\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) &= \sigma\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^d \{X^{-1}_j(B): B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\}\right)\\
&=  \sigma\left(\{X^{-1}_j(B): B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}), j = 1, \dots, d\}\right)\\
&=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^d \{X^{-1}_j((-\infty, t]): t \in \mathbb{R}\}\right)\\
&=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^d \{\{X_j \le t\}: t \in \mathbb{R}\}\right).
\end{align*}
\]
The first two lines merely rewrite the same collection of sets. The passage to the third line is not a rewriting and uses Lemma 14.1. Put \(\mathcal{E} := \{(-\infty, t] : t \in \mathbb{R}\}\), \(\mathcal{A} := \bigcup_{j=1}^d X_j^* \mathcal{E}\) and \(\mathcal{C} := \bigcup_{j=1}^d X_j^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\). Since \(\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{C}\), we get \(\sigma(\mathcal{A}) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{C})\). Conversely, for each \(j\), \[
X_j^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) = X_j^*\left( \sigma(\mathcal{E}) \right) = \sigma\left( X_j^* \mathcal{E} \right) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{A}),
\] using \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) from Proposition 3.2 and Lemma 14.1 for the middle equality. Hence \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{A})\), so \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{A})\) and the two \(\sigma\)-algebras agree.
Note that the outer \(\sigma(\cdot)\) cannot be dropped: \(\bigcup_{j=1}^d \sigma\left( X_j^* \mathcal{E} \right)\) is in general not a \(\sigma\)-algebra.



14.6.2 Push-Forward Measure (Distribution)
The next natural question is: what is the probability distribution of the random vector \((X_1, \dots, X_d)\)? This is captured by the push-forward measure. It is the probability measure on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) induced by the random vector \((X_1, \dots, X_d)\).

Proposition 14.4 (Push-Forward Probability Measure) If \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) is a probability space and \(f: \Omega \to S\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B})\)-measurable, then \(f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{F}\) for every \(B \in \mathcal{B}\), and the map \(\mu_f: \mathcal{B} \to [0, 1]\) defined by: \[
\mu_f(B) := (f_*\mathbb{P})(B) = \mathbb{P}(f^{-1}(B)) = \mathbb{P}(\{f \in B\})
\] is a probability measure on \((S, \mathcal{B})\) (also written as \(\mathbb{P} \circ f^{-1}\)). The notation \(f_*\mathbb{P}\) distinguishes this push-forward measure from the pull-back operation \(f^*\) on sets.


Proof (Proof of Proposition 14.4). We verify the axioms of a probability measure. Note first that \(\mu_f\) is well defined and non-negative: \(f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{F}\) for every \(B \in \mathcal{B}\) by measurability, and \(\mathbb{P} \ge 0\).

Null empty set: \[
\mu_f(\emptyset) = \mathbb{P}(f^{-1}(\emptyset)) = \mathbb{P}(\emptyset) = 0.
\]
Normalization: \[
\mu_f(S) = \mathbb{P}(f^{-1}(S)) = \mathbb{P}(\Omega) = 1.
\]
Countable Additivity: Let \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{B}\) be a sequence of pairwise disjoint measurable sets. Since preimages preserve disjoint unions: \[
f^{-1}\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty f^{-1}(B_n), \quad \text{with } f^{-1}(B_i) \cap f^{-1}(B_j) = \emptyset \text{ for } i \neq j.
\] By the countable additivity of \(\mathbb{P}\): \[
\mu_f\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \mathbb{P}\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty f^{-1}(B_n) \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb{P}(f^{-1}(B_n)) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu_f(B_n).
\]



Remark 14.1 (The Law of a Random Vector). Taking \((S, \mathcal{B}) = (\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) and \(f = \mathbf{X} = (X_1, \dots, X_d)\), which is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\)-measurable by the proof of Corollary 14.1, Proposition 14.4 yields the joint law \(\mu_{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{X}_* \mathbb{P}\) of the random vector. It is a probability measure on \((\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) with \[
\mu_{\mathbf{X}}(B) = \mathbb{P}\left( (X_1, \dots, X_d) \in B \right), \qquad B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d).
\]


Remark 14.2 (Special Case for Real Random Variables). When \((S, \mathcal{B}) = (\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) and \(f = X\) is a real random variable, \(\mu_X = \mathbb{P} \circ X^{-1}\) is the law/distribution of \(X\), and \(\mu_X(B) = \mathbb{P}(X \in B)\).
The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of \(X\) is defined by \(F_X(t) := \mathbb{P}(X \le t)\) for \(t \in \mathbb{R}\). Evaluating the law on the rays \((-\infty, t]\) recovers it: \[
\mu_X((-\infty, t]) = \mathbb{P}(X \le t) = F_X(t).
\]

14.7 Current Information (\(\sigma\)-Algebra Generated by Random Variables)

Definition 14.4 (Generated \(\sigma\)-Algebra) The \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by a collection of random variables \(\{X_j\}_{j=1}^d\) is: \[
\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) := \sigma\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^d X_j^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) \right) \subseteq \mathcal{F}.
\] This is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) with respect to which \(X_1, \dots, X_d\) are all measurable.

Equivalent and very useful characterizations:
\[
\begin{align*}
\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) &= \sigma\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^d \{X^{-1}_j(B): B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\}\right)\\
&=  \sigma\left(\{X^{-1}_j(B): B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}), j = 1, \dots, d\}\right)\\
&=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^d \{X^{-1}_j((-\infty, t]): t \in \mathbb{R}\}\right)\\
&=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^d \{\{X_j \le t\}: t \in \mathbb{R}\}\right).
\end{align*}
\]

title: 14  Lecture 6.2: Measurable Functions
text:
14.8 Push-Forward Measure (Distribution)
The next natural question is: what is the probability distribution of the random vector \((X_1, \dots, X_d)\)? This is captured by the push-forward measure. It is the probability measure on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) induced by the random vector \((X_1, \dots, X_d)\).

Proposition 14.3 (Push-Forward Probability Measure) If \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) is a probability space and \(f: \Omega \to S\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B})\)-measurable, then \(f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{F}\) for every \(B \in \mathcal{B}\), and the map \(\mu_f: \mathcal{B} \to [0, 1]\) defined by: \[
\mu_f(B) := (f_*\mathbb{P})(B) = \mathbb{P}(f^{-1}(B)) = \mathbb{P}(\{f \in B\})
\] is a probability measure on \((S, \mathcal{B})\) (also written as \(\mathbb{P} \circ f^{-1}\)). The notation \(f_*\mathbb{P}\) distinguishes this push-forward measure from the pull-back operation \(f^*\) on sets.


Proof (Proof of Proposition 14.3). We verify the axioms of a probability measure:

Normalization: \[
\mu_f(S) = \mathbb{P}(f^{-1}(S)) = \mathbb{P}(\Omega) = 1.
\]
Countable Additivity: Let \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{B}\) be a sequence of pairwise disjoint measurable sets. Since preimages preserve disjoint unions: \[
f^{-1}\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty f^{-1}(B_n), \quad \text{with } f^{-1}(B_i) \cap f^{-1}(B_j) = \emptyset \text{ for } i \neq j.
\] By the countable additivity of \(\mathbb{P}\): \[
\mu_f\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \right) = \mathbb{P}\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty f^{-1}(B_n) \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb{P}(f^{-1}(B_n)) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu_f(B_n).
\]



Remark 14.1 (Special Case for Real Random Variables). When \((S, \mathcal{B}) = (\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) and \(f = X\) is a real random variable, \(\mu_X = \mathbb{P} \circ X^{-1}\) is the law/distribution of \(X\), and \(\mu_X(B) = \mathbb{P}(X \in B)\).
In particular, evaluated on rays \((-\infty, t]\), we recover the cumulative distribution function (CDF): \[
\mu_X((-\infty, t]) = \mathbb{P}(X \le t) = F_X(t).
\]
