title: 15  Lecture 7.1: Robustness and Measurability
text:
15.2 Continuous and Discontinuous Transformations
We showed previously that if \(f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) is \((\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable and \(X_1, \dots, X_d\) are \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable random variables on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\), then \(Y = f(X_1, \dots, X_d)\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable.
This property applies in particular to continuous functions \(f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\).

Example 15.1 (Continuous Transformations: Maximum, Minimum, and Absolute Value) The maps \((x, y) \mapsto \max(x, y) = x \vee y=\frac{x+y+|x-y|}{2}\) and \((x, y) \mapsto \min(x, y) = x \wedge y=\frac{x+y-|x-y|}{2}\) are continuous on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and thus Borel measurable.
For any real random variable \(X\), we define its positive and negative parts by: \[
X_+ := \max(X, 0) = X \vee 0, \quad X_- := -\min(X, 0) = (-X) \vee 0.
\] Then

\(X_+\) and \(X_-\) are measurable random variables.
Consequently, \(X = X_+ - X_-\) and \(|X| = X_+ + X_-\) are measurable, and
\(X\) is measurable if and only if both \(X_+\) and \(X_-\) are measurable.


The general result for \((\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable maps is also useful when dealing with discontinuous functions of random variables.

Example 15.2 (The Generalized Reciprocal Map) For any fixed parameter \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\), define the modified inversion function \(i_\alpha: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) by: \[
i_\alpha(x) := \begin{cases} \frac{1}{x} & \text{if } x \neq 0, \\ \alpha & \text{if } x = 0. \end{cases}
\]
To verify that \(i_\alpha\) is \((\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable, consider first \(\alpha = 0\). For any \(x > 0\): \[
i_0^{-1}((x, \infty)) = \left(0, \frac{1}{x}\right) \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}),
\] and for any \(x < 0\): \[
i_0^{-1}((x, \infty)) = [0, \infty) \cup \left(-\infty, \frac{1}{x}\right) \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}).
\] Thus \(i_0\) is Borel measurable. In general, for any \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\), we can decompose \(i_\alpha\) as: \[
i_\alpha(x) = i_0(x) \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}}(x) + \alpha \mathbf{1}_{\{0\}}(x),
\] which is a sum and product of Borel measurable functions and is therefore Borel measurable.
Consequently, if \(f: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable, then the function \((i_\alpha \circ f): \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) given by: \[
(i_\alpha \circ f)(\omega) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{f(\omega)} & \text{if } f(\omega) \neq 0, \\ \alpha & \text{if } f(\omega) = 0 \end{cases}
\] is also \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable.

title: 15  Lecture 7.1: Robustness and Measurability
text:
15.3 Measurability Under Pointwise Limits
Let \(\overline{\mathbb{R}} = [-\infty, \infty]\) denote the extended real numbers equipped with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})\).

Proposition 15.1 (Measurability of Limits and Extrema) Let \(f_n: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (\overline{\mathbb{R}}, \mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}}))\) be a sequence of measurable functions for \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). Then the following functions are also \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}}))\)-measurable: \[
\sup_{n \ge 1} f_n, \quad \inf_{n \ge 1} f_n, \quad \limsup_{n \to \infty} f_n, \quad \liminf_{n \to \infty} f_n.
\] (Note: An analogous closure property under pointwise limits is false in general for continuous functions \(C(\mathbb{R})\).)


Proof (Proof of Proposition 15.1). We evaluate the preimages under generators of \(\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})\):

Supremum: For any \(t \in \mathbb{R}\): \[
\begin{align*}
\left( \sup_{n \ge 1} f_n \right)^{-1}([-\infty, t]) &= \left\{ \omega \in \Omega : \sup_{n \ge 1} f_n(\omega) \le t \right\} \\
&= \left\{ \omega \in \Omega : f_n(\omega) \le t \text{ for all } n \ge 1 \right\}.
\end{align*}
\] This yields the countable intersection: \[
\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty \{ \omega \in \Omega : f_n(\omega) \le t \} = \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty f_n^{-1}([-\infty, t]) \in \mathcal{F}.
\]
Infimum: Using \(\inf_{n} f_n = -\sup_{n} (-f_n)\) (or directly observing \(\{ \inf_n f_n \ge t \} = \bigcap_n \{ f_n \ge t \}\)), \(\inf_n f_n\) is measurable.
Limit Superior and Inferior: By definition of limit superior and limit inferior: \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} f_n = \inf_{n \ge 1} \left( \sup_{j \ge n} f_j \right), \quad \liminf_{n \to \infty} f_n = \sup_{n \ge 1} \left( \inf_{j \ge n} f_j \right).
\] Since \(g_n = \sup_{j \ge n} f_j\) is measurable for each \(n\), its infimum \(\inf_{n \ge 1} g_n = \limsup_{n \to \infty} f_n\) is measurable. Similarly, \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} f_n\) is measurable.

If \(f(\omega) = \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(\omega)\) exists pointwise, then \(f = \limsup_{n \to \infty} f_n = \liminf_{n \to \infty} f_n\), so \(f\) is measurable.

title: 15  Lecture 7.1: Robustness and Measurability
text:
15.4 Simple Functions and Approximations

Definition 15.1 (Simple Function) A function \(\varphi: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is called a simple function if its range \(\varphi(\Omega) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) is a finite set.


Example 15.3 (Canonical Representation of Simple Functions) Let \(\varphi(\Omega) = \{\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots, \alpha_n\}\) be the distinct values taken by \(\varphi\). Define \(A_j := \varphi^{-1}(\{\alpha_j\}) \subseteq \Omega\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n\).
The sets \(A_1, \dots, A_n\) form a finite partition of \(\Omega\) (i.e., they are pairwise disjoint and \(\bigcup_{j=1}^n A_j = \Omega\)). The function \(\varphi\) can be written uniquely in canonical form as: \[
\varphi(\omega) = \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \mathbf{1}_{A_j}(\omega).
\] Special case: For a single indicator function \(\varphi = \alpha \mathbf{1}_A\), \(\varphi\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable if and only if \(A \in \mathcal{F}\).


Lemma 15.1 (Measurability Criterion for Simple Functions) A simple function \(\varphi = \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \mathbf{1}_{A_j}\) with distinct non-zero values \(\{\alpha_j\}_{j=1}^n\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable if and only if \(A_j = \varphi^{-1}(\{\alpha_j\}) \in \mathcal{F}\) for every \(j = 1, \dots, n\).

title: 15  Lecture 7.1: Robustness and Measurability
text:
15.5 Simple Approximation Theorem

Theorem 15.1 (Simple Approximation Theorem) If \(f: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) is measurable, then there exists a sequence of simple measurable functions \(\{\varphi_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) such that: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \varphi_n(\omega) = f(\omega) \quad \text{for all } \omega \in \Omega.
\] Moreover:

If \(f \ge 0\), the sequence can be chosen to be non-decreasing (\(0 \le \varphi_1 \le \varphi_2 \le \dots \le f\)).
If \(f\) is bounded on \(M \subseteq \Omega\), then \(\varphi_n \to f\) uniformly on \(M\).








Figure 15.1: Simple Function Approximation




Proof (Proof of Theorem 15.1). It suffices to prove the result for \(f \ge 0\); for a general real-valued function \(f\), we apply the construction separately to \(f_+\) and \(f_-\), setting \(\varphi_n = \varphi_n^+ - \varphi_n^-\).
Assume \(f \ge 0\). For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), partition \([0, 2^n]\) into \(2^{2n}\) dyadic intervals of length \(2^{-n}\), and define: \[
\varphi_n(\omega) := \sum_{k=0}^{2^{2n}-1} \frac{k}{2^n} \mathbf{1}_{\left\{ \frac{k}{2^n} < f \le \frac{k+1}{2^n} \right\}}(\omega) + 2^n \mathbf{1}_{\{f > 2^n\}}(\omega).
\] Equivalently, \[
\varphi_n(\omega) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{k}{2^n} & \text{if } \frac{k}{2^n} < f(\omega) \le \frac{k+1}{2^n}, \quad k = 0, 1, \dots, 2^{2n}-1, \\
2^n & \text{if } f(\omega) > 2^n.
\end{cases}
\] Thus \(\varphi_n\) is essentially obtained by rounding \(f\) down to the nearest multiple of \(2^{-n}\), while truncating values above \(2^n\). The function \(\varphi_n\) takes only finitely many values: \[
0, 2^{-n}, 2 \cdot 2^{-n}, \dots, (2^{2n}-1) \cdot 2^{-n}, 2^n.
\]

Measurability: Each set \(\left\{ \omega \in \Omega : \frac{k}{2^n} < f(\omega) \le \frac{k+1}{2^n} \right\} = f^{-1}\left( \left(\frac{k}{2^n}, \frac{k+1}{2^n}\right] \right) \in \mathcal{F}\) and \(\{f > 2^n\} = f^{-1}((2^n, \infty)) \in \mathcal{F}\) by measurability of \(f\). Thus \(\varphi_n\) is a simple measurable function.
Monotonicity: By construction, refining from \(n\) to \(n+1\) splits each interval of length \(2^{-n}\) into two sub-intervals of length \(2^{-(n+1)}\), yielding \(\varphi_n \le \varphi_{n+1} \le f\).
Convergence: For any \(\omega \in \Omega\), choose \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) large enough such that \(f(\omega) \le 2^N\). Then for all \(n \ge N\): \[
0 \le f(\omega) - \varphi_n(\omega) \le 2^{-n}.
\] Taking \(n \to \infty\) gives pointwise convergence \(\varphi_n(\omega) \to f(\omega)\). If \(f\) is bounded on \(M\), \(N\) can be chosen independently of \(\omega\), yielding uniform convergence on \(M\).

title: 15  Lecture 7.1: Robustness and Measurability
text:
15.7 Characterization of Generated \(\sigma\)-Algebras

Definition 15.2 (Generated \(\sigma\)-Algebra) The \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by a collection of random variables \(\{X_j\}_{j=1}^d\) is: \[
\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) := \sigma\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^d X_j^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) \right) \subseteq \mathcal{F}.
\] This is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) with respect to which \(X_1, \dots, X_d\) are all measurable.

Equivalent and very useful characterizations:
\[
\begin{align*}
\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) &= \sigma\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^d \{X^{-1}_j(B): B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\}\right)\\
&=  \sigma\left(\{X^{-1}_j(B): B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}), j = 1, \dots, d\}\right)\\
&=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^d \{X^{-1}_j((-\infty, t]): t \in \mathbb{R}\}\right)\\
&=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^d \{X_j \le t\}: t \in \mathbb{R}\right).
\end{align*}
\]
Let \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \dots, X_d)^T : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^d\) be a random vector formed by \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable random variables \(X_1, \dots, X_d\).

Lemma 15.2 (Structure of \(\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d)\)) Let \(\mathbf{X}: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^d\) be defined by \(\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_1(\omega), \dots, X_d(\omega))^T\). Then: \[
\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) = \mathbf{X}^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \{ \mathbf{X}^{-1}(B) \subseteq \Omega : B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \}.
\] This is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) with respect to which \(X_1, \dots, X_d\) are measurable.


Proof (Proof of Lemma 15.2). To establish the equality \(\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) = \mathbf{X}^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\), we show inclusion in both directions.

15.7.1 Step 1: Proof that \(\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) \subseteq \mathbf{X}^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\)
Recall that the individual generated \(\sigma\)-algebra is defined as: \[
\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) = \sigma\left( \bigcup_{i=1}^d \{ X_i^{-1}(A) : A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) \} \right).
\]
For each coordinate index \(i \in \{1, \dots, d\}\), consider the coordinate projection map \(\pi_i : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(\pi_i(x_1, \dots, x_d) = x_i\).

Measurability of \(\pi_i\): The projection map \(\pi_i\) is continuous under the standard Euclidean topology, which implies it is \((\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable.
Composition: Notice that \(X_i = \pi_i \circ \mathbf{X}\). For any Borel set \(A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\), taking preimages gives: \[
X_i^{-1}(A) = (\pi_i \circ \mathbf{X})^{-1}(A) = \mathbf{X}^{-1}\left( \pi_i^{-1}(A) \right).
\]
Inclusion of Generators: Since \(\pi_i\) is measurable, \(\pi_i^{-1}(A) \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Thus, by definition of the pull-back \(\sigma\)-algebra: \[
X_i^{-1}(A) \in \mathbf{X}^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \quad \forall A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}), \; \forall i \in \{1, \dots, d\}.
\]

Because \(\mathbf{X}^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\) is a valid \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) that contains all generator sets of \(\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d)\), the minimal property of generated \(\sigma\)-algebras implies: \[
\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) \subseteq \mathbf{X}^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d).
\]



15.7.2 Step 2: Proof that \(\mathbf{X}^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \subseteq \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d)\)
Consider the collection of open hyper-rectangles in \(\mathbb{R}^d\): \[
\mathcal{C} = \left\{ \prod_{i=1}^d (a_i, b_i) \subset \mathbb{R}^d : a_i, b_i \in \mathbb{R}, \; a_i < b_i \right\}.
\] It is a standard result of measure theory that \(\mathcal{C}\) generates the \(d\)-dimensional Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, i.e., \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \sigma(\mathcal{C})\).

Preimages of Generators: Take any open rectangle \(I = \prod_{i=1}^d (a_i, b_i) \in \mathcal{C}\). Using the properties of preimages: \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbf{X}^{-1}(I) &= \mathbf{X}^{-1}\left( \bigcap_{i=1}^d \pi_i^{-1}((a_i, b_i)) \right)\\
& = \bigcap_{i=1}^d \mathbf{X}^{-1}\left( \pi_i^{-1}((a_i, b_i)) \right)\\
& = \bigcap_{i=1}^d X_i^{-1}((a_i, b_i)).
\end{align*}
\] Since \(X_i^{-1}((a_i, b_i)) \in \sigma(X_i) \subseteq \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d)\) for each \(i\), and \(\sigma\)-algebras are closed under finite intersections, we have: \[
\mathbf{X}^{-1}(I) \in \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) \quad \forall I \in \mathcal{C}.
\]
Good Sets Argument: Define the collection of sets in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) whose preimage under \(\mathbf{X}\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d)\): \[
\mathcal{M} = \left\{ B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) : \mathbf{X}^{-1}(B) \in \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) \right\}.
\] We verify that \(\mathcal{M}\) forms a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\mathbb{R}^d\):

Entire space: \(\mathbf{X}^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \Omega \in \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d)\), so \(\mathbb{R}^d \in \mathcal{M}\).
Complements: If \(B \in \mathcal{M}\), then \(\mathbf{X}^{-1}(B^c) = (\mathbf{X}^{-1}(B))^c \in \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d)\) because \(\sigma\)-algebras are closed under complementation. Thus \(B^c \in \mathcal{M}\).
Countable Unions: If \((B_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{M}\), then \(\mathbf{X}^{-1}\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n\right) = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \mathbf{X}^{-1}(B_n) \in \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d)\) by countable closure. Thus \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n \in \mathcal{M}\).

Conclusion: Since \(\mathcal{M}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) and contains \(\mathcal{C}\), it must contain the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by \(\mathcal{C}\): \[
\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \sigma(\mathcal{C}) \subseteq \mathcal{M}.
\] By definition of \(\mathcal{M}\), this implies that for every \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\), \(\mathbf{X}^{-1}(B) \in \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d)\), which proves: \[
\mathbf{X}^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \subseteq \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d).
\]

Combining Step 1 and Step 2 yields \(\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) = \mathbf{X}^* \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\), completing the proof.

title: 15  Lecture 7.1: Robustness and Measurability
text:
15.8 The Doob–Dynkin Representation Theorem

Theorem 15.2 (Doob–Dynkin Representation Theorem) Let \(X_1, \dots, X_d\) be \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable random variables, and let \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \dots, X_d): \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^d\).
A random variable \(Y: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is \((\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d) / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable if and only if there exists a Borel measurable function \(f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) such that: \[
Y = f(X_1, \dots, X_d) = f \circ \mathbf{X}.
\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 15.2). 

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Assume that \(Y = f \circ \mathbf{X}\) with \(f\) Borel measurable. Recall that \(\mathbf{X}\) is \(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\)-measurable. Indeed, since each \(X_j\) is measurable, the vector-valued map \(\mathbf{X}\) is measurable. Therefore, by composition of measurable functions, \(Y=f \circ \mathbf{X}\) is \(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal {B}(\mathbb{R})\)-measurable. More importantly, for every \(B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\), \[
Y^{-1}(B) = (f\circ\mathbf{X})^{-1}(B) = \mathbf{X}^{-1}\bigl(f^{-1}(B)\bigr).
\] Since \(f\) is Borel measurable, \(f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Hence \[
Y^{-1}(B) \in \{\mathbf{X}^{-1}(A): A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\}
= \sigma(\mathbf{X}).
\] Thus \(Y:\bigl(\Omega,\sigma(\mathbf X)\bigr) \to \bigl(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\bigr)\) is measurable. Therefore, \(Y\) is \(\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_d)/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\)-measurable. ​
(\(\Rightarrow\)) We prove existence of \(f\) via standard machine induction on the structure of \(Y\):
Step 1: Indicator Functions. Suppose \(Y = \mathbf{1}_A\) for some \(A \in \sigma(X_1, \dots, X_d)\). By Lemma 15.2, \(A = \mathbf{X}^{-1}(B)\) for some \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Define \(f = \mathbf{1}_B: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\), which is Borel measurable. Then: \[
f(\mathbf{X}(\omega)) = \mathbf{1}_B(\mathbf{X}(\omega)) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{X}^{-1}(B)}(\omega) = \mathbf{1}_A(\omega) = Y(\omega).
\] Therefore \(Y=f\circ\mathbf X\). Thus, the result holds for indicator functions.
Step 2: Simple Functions. Suppose \(Y = \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \mathbf{1}_{A_j}\) is simple and \((\sigma(\mathbf{X})/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable. Then \(A_j \in \sigma(\mathbf{X})\) for each \(j\), so \(A_j = \mathbf{X}^{-1}(B_j)\) for some \(B_j \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Define \(f = \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \mathbf{1}_{B_j}\), which is Borel measurable. Then: \[
f \circ \mathbf{X} = \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \mathbf{1}_{B_j} \circ \mathbf{X} = \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{X}^{-1}(B_j)} = \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \mathbf{1}_{A_j} = Y.
\] Thus the result holds for simple measurable functions.
Step 3: General Measurable Functions. Let \(Y\) be an arbitrary \((\sigma(\mathbf{X})/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\)-measurable random variable. By Theorem 15.1, there exists a sequence of simple \(\sigma(\mathbf{X})\)-measurable functions \(\{Y_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) such that \(Y_n(\omega) \to Y(\omega)\) pointwise for all \(\omega \in \Omega\).
By Step 2, for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), there exists a Borel measurable function \(g_n: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) such that \(Y_n = g_n \circ \mathbf{X}\). Define \(f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) by: \[
f(x) := \limsup_{n \to \infty} g_n(x).
\] By Proposition 15.1, \(f\) is Borel measurable. Moreover, for every \(\omega \in \Omega\): \[
f(\mathbf{X}(\omega)) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} g_n(\mathbf{X}(\omega)) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} Y_n(\omega) = \lim_{n \to \infty} Y_n(\omega) = Y(\omega).
\] Hence \(Y = f(\mathbf{X}) = f(X_1, \dots, X_d)\).

title: 16  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
text:
16.2 The Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
To see why a new integration theory is necessary, we first review the classic Riemann–Stieltjes integral on \(\mathbb{R}\).

Definition 16.1 (Lebesgue–Stieltjes Measure) Let \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a non-decreasing, right-continuous function. The function \(F\) uniquely determines a Radon measure \(\mu_F\) on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) defined on half-open intervals by: \[
\mu_F((a, b]) := F(b) - F(a) \quad \text{for all } a < b.
\]


Definition 16.2 (Riemann–Stieltjes Upper and Lower Sums) Let \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\) be a compact interval and let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function. Consider a partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\): \[
\pi = \{a = t_0 < t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_{n-1} < t_n = b\}.
\]
We define the upper Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\overline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) and lower Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\underline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) with respect to \(\pi\) by: \[
\begin{align*}
\overline{S}_\pi(f, F) &:= \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) \\
&= \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})),
\end{align*}
\] \[
\begin{align*}
\underline{S}_\pi(f, F) &:= \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) \\
&= \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})).
\end{align*}
\]
The upper and lower Darboux integrals are defined by taking infima and suprema over all finite partitions \(\mathcal{P}([a, b])\): \[
\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \inf_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \overline{S}_\pi(f, F), \quad \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \sup_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \underline{S}_\pi(f, F).
\] If \(\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF = \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF\), we say \(f\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable with respect to \(F\) on \([a, b]\), and we write \(\int_a^b f(x) \, dF(x)\) or \(\int_a^b f \, d\mu_F\) for this common value.

title: 16  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
section: 16.3 Limitations and Defects of the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
text:
16.3 Limitations and Defects of the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
While simple and intuitive, the Riemann–Stieltjes integral suffers from severe structural limitations when applied to modern probability and analysis:

Domain Constraint: It is fundamentally defined only on compact intervals \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\).
Boundedness Constraint: It requires the integrand \(f\) to be bounded.
Weak Limit Properties: It lacks good limit theorems (e.g., dominated convergence) and handles only finite additivity naturally.
Failure on Simple Functions: It fails to integrate basic functions that oscillate rapidly on small scales.


Example 16.1 (Failure on the Dirichlet Function) Consider the indicator function of the rational numbers on \([a, b]\), \(f(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\). For any interval \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\) with \(t_{k-1} < t_k\), density of \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}\) implies: \[
\sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 1, \quad \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 0.
\]
Thus, for any partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\): \[
\overline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 1 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = F(b) - F(a),
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 0 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = 0.
\]
Hence \(\overline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = F(b) - F(a)\) and \(\underline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = 0\). Therefore, \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if \(F(b) = F(a)\) (i.e., \(F\) is constant on \([a, b]\)).

title: 16  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
text:
16.4 Characterization of Riemann Integrability

Theorem 16.1 (Lebesgue Criterion for Riemann Integrability) Let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function, and let \(F(x) = x\) (so that \(\mu_F = \lambda\), the Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}\)).
The function \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if the set of discontinuity points of \(f\), \[
D_f := \{x \in [a, b] : f \text{ is discontinuous at } x\},
\] has Lebesgue measure zero (i.e., \(\bar{\lambda}(D_f) = 0\), where \(\bar{\lambda}\) denotes the outer measure/completion).

title: 16  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
section: 16.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?
text:
16.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?

16.5.1 The Problem
The Riemann–Stieltjes integral is designed for functions that are well-adapted to an interval partition of the domain. It works well if preimages \(f^{-1}((s, t))\) are nice unions of intervals for any \(s < t\) (such as continuous functions).
However, functions like \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) oscillate rapidly on all scales, making domain interval partitions completely ineffective.


16.5.2 The Fix: Partition the Range, Not the Domain
Instead of partitioning the domain \([a, b]\) into subintervals \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\), we partition the range (target space \(\mathbb{R}\)) into intervals \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\).
For each range interval \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\), we look at its preimage under \(f\): \[
E_k := f^{-1}((y_{k-1}, y_k]) = \{\omega \in \Omega : y_{k-1} < f(\omega) \le y_k\}.
\]

The set \(E_k \subseteq \Omega\) is not necessarily an interval, but if \(f\) is measurable, \(E_k \in \mathcal{F}\) is a measurable set.
We know how to measure \(E_k\) using the measure \(\mu(E_k)\)!

This leads directly to simple function approximations of the form \(\sum_k y_k \, \mu(E_k)\) and establishes the foundation for the Lebesgue Integral.

title: 8  Lecture 4.1: Outer Pseudo-Metric
text:
8.2 Comparison of Proof Strategies

Standard Approach (Carathéodory Split Condition): Define the class of measurable sets as: \[
\mathcal{M} := \left\{ E \subseteq \Omega : \mu^*(T) = \mu^*(T \cap E) + \mu^*(T \cap E^c) \text{ for all } T \subseteq \Omega \right\}.
\tag{8.2}\]

Advantages: Works directly for arbitrary (including infinite) premeasures.
Disadvantages: Finicky, highly technical, and unmotivated (“too clever by half”). Proving that \(\mathcal{M}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra containing \(\mathcal{A}\) typically requires the Monotone Class Theorem or Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) Theorem.

Driver’s Topological Approach (For Finite Premeasures): Restricting first to finite premeasures \(\mu: \mathcal{A} \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\):

Equip \(2^\Omega\) with a natural pseudo-metric \(d_\mu\) induced by \(\mu^*\).
Define \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\) as the closure of the field \(\mathcal{A}\) under \(d_\mu\).
Show that \(\mu: \mathcal{A} \to [0, \infty)\) is uniformly continuous (Lipschitz) on \(\mathcal{A}\) and extends uniquely to \(\overline{\mu} = \mu^*\) on \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\).
Use metric and topological tools to prove that \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra and \(\overline{\mu}\) is a measure.

title: 17  Lecture 8.1: Simple Integration
text:
17.1 Introduction and Definitions
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space.
We denote the space of all simple \(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\)-measurable functions by: \[
\mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}} := \{ f: \Omega \to \mathbb{R} \mid f \text{ is a simple } \mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\text{-measurable function} \}
\]

title: 17  Lecture 8.1: Simple Integration
text:
Definition 17.1 (Simple Function) A function \(f: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is called a simple \(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\)-measurable function if it takes on only finitely many distinct real values. That is, \(f(\Omega) = \{\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots, \alpha_n\} \subset \mathbb{R}\) for some \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).
Equivalently, \(f\) can be written in its canonical representation as: \[
f = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_j \mathbf{1}_{A_j}
\tag{17.1}\] where \(A_j = \{w \in \Omega : f(w) = \alpha_j\} = f^{-1}(\{\alpha_j\}) \in \mathcal{F}\) are pairwise disjoint measurable sets partitioning \(\Omega\), and \(\mathbf{1}_{A_j}\) denotes the indicator function of the set \(A_j\).



Definition 17.2 (Integral of a Simple Function) For any simple function \(f \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) with representation \(f = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_j \mathbf{1}_{A_j}\) (where \(A_j \in \mathcal{F}\) and \(\alpha_j \in \mathbb{R}\)), the integral of \(f\) with respect to \(\mu\) is defined as: \[
\int f \, d\mu := \sum_{t \in \mathbb{R}} t \cdot \mu(\{f = t\}) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_j \mu(A_j)
\tag{17.2}\] where \(\{f = t\} := \{\omega \in \Omega : f(\omega) = t\}\).
If \(\mu = \mathbb{P}\) is a probability measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), the integral is often denoted as the expectation: \[
\mathbb{E}(f) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}(f) := \int f \, d\mathbb{P}= \sum_{t \in \mathbb{R}} t \cdot \mathbb{P}(\{f = t\}) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_j \mathbb{P}(A_j).
\]


Example 17.1 Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space and let \(A \in \mathcal{F}\). The expectation of the indicator function \(\mathbf{1}_A\) is given by: \[
\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{1}_A) = 0 \cdot \mathbb{P}(A^c) + 1 \cdot \mathbb{P}(A) = \mathbb{P}(A)
\]

title: 17  Lecture 8.1: Simple Integration
text:
17.2 Algebraic Properties of the Integral

Proposition 17.1 (Properties of Simple Functions and Integration (Driver [5.27])) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space and let \(\mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) be the set of simple \(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\)-measurable functions.

\(\mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) is a real vector space.
The mapping \(\int \cdot \, d\mu : \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}} \to \mathbb{R}\) is a positive linear functional. That is:

Linearity: For all \(f, g \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) and \(\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\alpha f + \beta g \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) and: \[
\int (\alpha f + \beta g) \, d\mu = \alpha \int f \, d\mu + \beta \int g \, d\mu
\tag{17.3}\]
Monotonicity (Positivity): If \(f, g \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) and \(f \le g\) pointwise, then: \[
\int f \, d\mu \le \int g \, d\mu
\tag{17.4}\] In particular, if \(f \ge 0\), then \(\int f \, d\mu \ge 0\).




Proof (Proof of Proposition 17.1). We prove each property systematically.

17.2.1 Step 1: Scalar Multiplication
Let \(f \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) and \(\beta \in \mathbb{R}\). If \(f = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_j \mathbf{1}_{A_j}\), then \((\beta f)(\omega) = \beta f(\omega) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} (\beta \alpha_j) \mathbf{1}_{A_j}(\omega)\). Since \(\beta f\) assumes at most \(n\) distinct finite values, \(\beta f \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\).
By definition of the integral: \[
\int \beta f \, d\mu = \sum_{j=1}^{n} (\beta \alpha_j) \mu(A_j) = \beta \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_j \mu(A_j) = \beta \int f \, d\mu
\]


17.2.2 Step 2: Closure Under Addition
Let \(f, g \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\). The range of \(f + g\) is contained in \(\{x + y : x \in f(\Omega), y \in g(\Omega)\}\). Since \(f(\Omega)\) and \(g(\Omega)\) are finite sets, the sum of their ranges is also finite.
Furthermore, for any \(t \in \mathbb{R}\): \[
\{f + g = t\} = \bigcup_{\substack{x, y \in \mathbb{R} \\ x + y = t}} \left( \{f = x\} \cap \{g = y\} \right)
\] Because \(\{f = x\}\) and \(\{g = y\}\) are empty for all but finitely many pairs \((x, y)\), this is a finite union of measurable sets, hence \(\{f + g = t\} \in \mathcal{F}\). Thus, \(f + g \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\).


17.2.3 Step 3: Additivity of Integral
Using the partition property, we compute: \[
\begin{aligned}
&\int (f + g) \, d\mu = \sum_{t \in \mathbb{R}} t \cdot \mu(\{f + g = t\}) \\
&= \sum_{t \in \mathbb{R}} \sum_{\substack{x, y \in \mathbb{R} \\ x + y = t}} t \cdot \mu(\{f = x\} \cap \{g = y\}) \\
&= \sum_{x, y \in \mathbb{R}} (x + y) \mu(\{f = x\} \cap \{g = y\}) \\
&= \sum_{x, y \in \mathbb{R}} x \, \mu(\{f = x\} \cap \{g = y\}) + \sum_{x, y \in \mathbb{R}} y \, \mu(\{f = x\} \cap \{g = y\}) \\
&= \sum_{x \in \mathbb{R}} x \sum_{y \in \mathbb{R}} \mu(\{f = x\} \cap \{g = y\}) + \sum_{y \in \mathbb{R}} y \sum_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \mu(\{f = x\} \cap \{g = y\})
\end{aligned}
\]
By countable additivity over the disjoint partitions \(\bigcup_{y \in \mathbb{R}} \{g = y\} = \Omega\) and \(\bigcup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \{f = x\} = \Omega\): \[
\begin{align*}
\sum_{y \in \mathbb{R}} \mu(\{f = x\} \cap \{g = y\}) &= \mu(\{f = x\}), \quad \text{and} \quad \\
\sum_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \mu(\{f = x\} \cap \{g = y\}) &= \mu(\{g = y\})
\end{align*}
\]
Substituting these back gives: \[
\int (f + g) \, d\mu = \sum_{x \in \mathbb{R}} x \, \mu(\{f = x\}) + \sum_{y \in \mathbb{R}} y \, \mu(\{g = y\}) = \int f \, d\mu + \int g \, d\mu
\]
Combining Steps 1, 2, and 3 establishes that \(\mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) is a real vector space and \(\int \cdot \, d\mu\) is a linear functional on \(\mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\).


17.2.4 Step 4: Positivity and Monotonicity
If \(f \ge 0\), all non-zero values \(t\) in the image of \(f\) satisfy \(t > 0\). Thus: \[
\int f \, d\mu = \sum_{t \ge 0} t \cdot \mu(\{f = t\}) \ge 0
\]
If \(f \le g\), then \(g - f \ge 0\). By linearity and positivity: \[
\int g \, d\mu - \int f \, d\mu = \int (g - f) \, d\mu \ge \int 0 \, d\mu = 0 \implies \int f \, d\mu \le \int g \, d\mu
\]



Corollary 17.1 (Triangle Inequality for Simple Integrals) For any \(f \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\): \[
\left| \int f \, d\mu \right| \le \int |f| \, d\mu
\tag{17.5}\]


Proof (Proof of Corollary 17.1). Using the discrete definition of the integral and the classical triangle inequality on \(\mathbb{R}\): \[
\left| \int f \, d\mu \right| = \left| \sum_{t \in \mathbb{R}} t \cdot \mu(\{f = t\}) \right| \le \sum_{t \in \mathbb{R}} |t| \cdot \mu(\{f = t\}) = \int |f| \, d\mu
\]

text: 17.3 Applications

title: 17  Lecture 8.1: Simple Integration
text:
17.4 The Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space and \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(\mu(A_i) < \infty\) for all \(i\). Note that for any events \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\), \(\mathbf{1}_{A \cap B} = \mathbf{1}_A \cdot \mathbf{1}_B\).

Theorem 17.1 (Inclusion-Exclusion Principle) Let \(A = \bigcup_{j=1}^{n} A_j\). Then: \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{j=1}^{n} A_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} (-1)^{j+1} \sum_{1 \le k_1 < \dots < k_j \le n} \mu(A_{k_1} \cap \dots \cap A_{k_j})
\tag{17.6}\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 17.1). Consider the complement \(A^c = \bigcap_{j=1}^{n} A_j^c\). In terms of indicator functions: \[
\mathbf{1}_{A^c} = \prod_{j=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}_{A_j^c} = \prod_{j=1}^{n} (1 - \mathbf{1}_{A_j})
\]
Since \(\mathbf{1}_{A^c} = 1 - \mathbf{1}_A\), we expand the algebraic product: \[
\begin{align*}
1 - \mathbf{1}_A &= \sum_{j=0}^{n} \sum_{1 \le k_1 < \dots < k_j \le n} (-1)^j \mathbf{1}_{A_{k_1}} \cdots \mathbf{1}_{A_{k_j}}\\
&= 1 + \sum_{j=1}^{n} (-1)^j \sum_{1 \le k_1 < \dots < k_j \le n} \mathbf{1}_{A_{k_1} \cap \dots \cap A_{k_j}}
\end{align*}
\]
Subtracting \(1\) and multiplying by \(-1\) gives the indicator identity: \[
\mathbf{1}_A = \sum_{j=1}^{n} (-1)^{j+1} \sum_{1 \le k_1 < \dots < k_j \le n} \mathbf{1}_{A_{k_1} \cap \dots \cap A_{k_j}}
\]
Integrating both sides with respect to \(\mu\) and applying linearity yields Equation 17.6.


Example 17.2  

For \(n = 2\): \[
\mu(A_1 \cup A_2) = \mu(A_1) + \mu(A_2) - \mu(A_1 \cap A_2)
\]
For \(n = 3\): \[
\begin{align*}
\mu(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3) &= \mu(A_1) + \mu(A_2) + \mu(A_3) - \mu(A_1 \cap A_2)\\
& - \mu(A_1 \cap A_3) - \mu(A_2 \cap A_3) + \mu(A_1 \cap A_2 \cap A_3)
\end{align*}
\]

title: 17  Lecture 8.1: Simple Integration
text:
17.5 The Derangement Problem (Matching Cards)

Example 17.3 Shuffle a deck of \(n\) cards.

What is the probability that at least one card remains in its original position?
What is the expected number of unmoved cards?


Model Formalization: Let \(\Omega = S_n\) be the symmetric group of all \(n!\) permutations of \(\{1, 2, \dots, n\}\), equipped with the power set \(\mathcal{F} = 2^\Omega\) and the uniform probability measure \(\mathbb{P}(A) = \frac{\# A}{n!}\).
Let \(A_i = \{\omega \in S_n : \omega(i) = i\}\) be the event that the \(i\)-th card is fixed. The event that at least one card remains unmoved is \(B = \bigcup_{i=1}^{n} A_i\).

17.5.1 Probability of At Least One Fixed Point
For any subset \(\{k_1, \dots, k_j\} \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\) of distinct indices, the intersection \(A_{k_1} \cap \dots \cap A_{k_j} = \{\omega \in S_n : \omega(k_1) = k_1, \dots, \omega(k_j) = k_j\}\) consists of permutations fixing \(j\) specified elements. The remaining \(n-j\) elements can be permuted arbitrarily, so: \[
\#(A_{k_1} \cap \dots \cap A_{k_j}) = (n - j)! \implies \mathbb{P}(A_{k_1} \cap \dots \cap A_{k_j}) = \frac{(n - j)!}{n!}
\]
By Inclusion-Exclusion (Theorem 17.1): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(B) &= \sum_{j=1}^{n} (-1)^{j+1} \sum_{1 \le k_1 < \dots < k_j \le n} \mathbb{P}(A_{k_1} \cap \dots \cap A_{k_j}) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} (-1)^{j+1} \binom{n}{j} \frac{(n - j)!}{n!} \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} (-1)^{j+1} \frac{n!}{j!(n-j)!} \frac{(n - j)!}{n!} = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{(-1)^{j+1}}{j!} = 1 - \sum_{j=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^j}{j!}
\end{aligned}
\]
As \(n \to \infty\): \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}(B) = 1 - e^{-1} \approx 63.2\%
\]


17.5.2 Expected Number of Unmoved Cards
Let \(X\) be the random variable counting the total number of fixed cards: \[
X = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}_{A_i}
\]
Using linearity of expectation: \[
\mathbb{E}(X) = \mathbb{E}\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}_{A_i} \right) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}(\mathbf{1}_{A_i}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{P}(A_i)
\]
Since \(\mathbb{P}(A_i) = \frac{(n - 1)!}{n!} = \frac{1}{n}\) for each \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\): \[
\mathbb{E}(X) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{n} = 1
\]

18.2 The Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
To see why a new integration theory is necessary, we first review the classic Riemann–Stieltjes integral on \(\mathbb{R}\).

Definition 18.1 (Lebesgue–Stieltjes Measure) Let \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a non-decreasing, right-continuous function. The function \(F\) uniquely determines a Radon measure \(\mu_F\) on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) defined on half-open intervals by: \[
\mu_F((a, b]) := F(b) - F(a) \quad \text{for all } a < b.
\]


Definition 18.2 (Riemann–Stieltjes Upper and Lower Sums) Let \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\) be a compact interval and let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function. Consider a partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\pi = \{a = t_0 < t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_{n-1} < t_n = b\}[cite: 4].
\]
We define the upper Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\overline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) and lower Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\underline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) with respect to \(\pi\) by[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4].
\]
The upper and lower Darboux integrals are defined by taking infima and suprema over all finite partitions \(\mathcal{P}([a, b])\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \inf_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \overline{S}_\pi(f, F), \quad \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \sup_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \underline{S}_\pi(f, F)[cite: 4].
\] If \(\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF = \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF\), we say \(f\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable with respect to \(F\) on \([a, b]\), and we write \(\int_a^b f(x) \, dF(x)\) or \(\int_a^b f \, d\mu_F\) for this common value[cite: 4].

18.3 Limitations and Defects of the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
While simple and intuitive, the Riemann–Stieltjes integral suffers from severe structural limitations when applied to modern probability and analysis[cite: 4]:

Domain Constraint: It is fundamentally defined only on compact intervals \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\)[cite: 4].
Boundedness Constraint: It requires the integrand \(f\) to be bounded[cite: 4].
Weak Limit Properties: It lacks good limit theorems (e.g., dominated convergence) and handles only finite additivity naturally[cite: 4].
Failure on Simple Functions: It fails to integrate basic functions that oscillate rapidly on small scales[cite: 4].


Example 18.1 (Failure on the Dirichlet Function) Consider the indicator function of the rational numbers on \([a, b]\), \(f(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\)[cite: 4]. For any interval \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\) with \(t_{k-1} < t_k\), density of \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}\) implies[cite: 4]: \[
\sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 1, \quad \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Thus, for any partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 1 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = F(b) - F(a)[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 0 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Hence \(\overline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = F(b) - F(a)\) and \(\underline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = 0\)[cite: 4]. Therefore, \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if \(F(b) = F(a)\) (i.e., \(F\) is constant on \([a, b]\))[cite: 4].

text:
18.4 Characterization of Riemann Integrability

Theorem 18.1 (Lebesgue Criterion for Riemann Integrability) Let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function, and let \(F(x) = x\) (so that \(\mu_F = \lambda\), the Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}\))[cite: 4].
The function \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if the set of discontinuity points of \(f\), \[
D_f := \{x \in [a, b] : f \text{ is discontinuous at } x\},
\] has Lebesgue measure zero (i.e., \(\bar{\lambda}(D_f) = 0\), where \(\bar{\lambda}\) denotes the outer measure/completion)[cite: 4].

title: 18  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
section: 18.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?
text:
18.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?

18.5.1 The Problem
The Riemann–Stieltjes integral is designed for functions that are well-adapted to an interval partition of the domain[cite: 4]. It works well if preimages \(f^{-1}((s, t))\) are nice unions of intervals for any \(s < t\) (such as continuous functions)[cite: 4].
However, functions like \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) oscillate rapidly on all scales, making domain interval partitions completely ineffective[cite: 4].


18.5.2 The Fix: Partition the Range, Not the Domain
Instead of partitioning the domain \([a, b]\) into subintervals \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\), we partition the range (target space \(\mathbb{R}\)) into intervals \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\)[cite: 4].
For each range interval \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\), we look at its preimage under \(f\)[cite: 4]: \[
E_k := f^{-1}((y_{k-1}, y_k]) = \{\omega \in \Omega : y_{k-1} < f(\omega) \le y_k\}[cite: 4].
\]

The set \(E_k \subseteq \Omega\) is not necessarily an interval, but if \(f\) is measurable, \(E_k \in \mathcal{F}\) is a measurable set[cite: 4].
We know how to measure \(E_k\) using the measure \(\mu(E_k)\)[cite: 4]!

This leads directly to simple function approximations of the form \(\sum_k y_k \, \mu(E_k)\) and establishes the foundation for the Lebesgue Integral[cite: 4].

21.1 1-Parameter Families and Leibniz’s Integral Rule
In probability theory and measure-theoretic analysis, we frequently encounter 1-parameter families of random variables or integrands \(\{X_t : t \in (a, b)\}\) defined on a measure space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\). A central problem is establishing conditions under which differentiation and integration can be interchanged.

title: 21  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
text:
21.2 The Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
To see why a new integration theory is necessary, we first review the classic Riemann–Stieltjes integral on \(\mathbb{R}\).

Definition 21.1 (Lebesgue–Stieltjes Measure) Let \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a non-decreasing, right-continuous function. The function \(F\) uniquely determines a Radon measure \(\mu_F\) on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) defined on half-open intervals by: \[
\mu_F((a, b]) := F(b) - F(a) \quad \text{for all } a < b.
\]


Definition 21.2 (Riemann–Stieltjes Upper and Lower Sums) Let \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\) be a compact interval and let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function. Consider a partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\pi = \{a = t_0 < t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_{n-1} < t_n = b\}[cite: 4].
\]
We define the upper Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\overline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) and lower Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\underline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) with respect to \(\pi\) by[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4].
\]
The upper and lower Darboux integrals are defined by taking infima and suprema over all finite partitions \(\mathcal{P}([a, b])\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \inf_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \overline{S}_\pi(f, F), \quad \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \sup_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \underline{S}_\pi(f, F)[cite: 4].
\] If \(\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF = \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF\), we say \(f\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable with respect to \(F\) on \([a, b]\), and we write \(\int_a^b f(x) \, dF(x)\) or \(\int_a^b f \, d\mu_F\) for this common value[cite: 4].

title: 21  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
section: 21.3 Limitations and Defects of the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
text:
21.3 Limitations and Defects of the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
While simple and intuitive, the Riemann–Stieltjes integral suffers from severe structural limitations when applied to modern probability and analysis[cite: 4]:

Domain Constraint: It is fundamentally defined only on compact intervals \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\)[cite: 4].
Boundedness Constraint: It requires the integrand \(f\) to be bounded[cite: 4].
Weak Limit Properties: It lacks good limit theorems (e.g., dominated convergence) and handles only finite additivity naturally[cite: 4].
Failure on Simple Functions: It fails to integrate basic functions that oscillate rapidly on small scales[cite: 4].


Example 21.1 (Failure on the Dirichlet Function) Consider the indicator function of the rational numbers on \([a, b]\), \(f(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\)[cite: 4]. For any interval \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\) with \(t_{k-1} < t_k\), density of \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}\) implies[cite: 4]: \[
\sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 1, \quad \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Thus, for any partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 1 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = F(b) - F(a)[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 0 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Hence \(\overline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = F(b) - F(a)\) and \(\underline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = 0\)[cite: 4]. Therefore, \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if \(F(b) = F(a)\) (i.e., \(F\) is constant on \([a, b]\))[cite: 4].

title: 21  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
text:
21.4 Characterization of Riemann Integrability

Theorem 21.1 (Lebesgue Criterion for Riemann Integrability) Let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function, and let \(F(x) = x\) (so that \(\mu_F = \lambda\), the Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}\))[cite: 4].
The function \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if the set of discontinuity points of \(f\), \[
D_f := \{x \in [a, b] : f \text{ is discontinuous at } x\},
\] has Lebesgue measure zero (i.e., \(\bar{\lambda}(D_f) = 0\), where \(\bar{\lambda}\) denotes the outer measure/completion)[cite: 4].

title: 21  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
section: 21.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?
text:
21.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?

21.5.1 The Problem
The Riemann–Stieltjes integral is designed for functions that are well-adapted to an interval partition of the domain[cite: 4]. It works well if preimages \(f^{-1}((s, t))\) are nice unions of intervals for any \(s < t\) (such as continuous functions)[cite: 4].
However, functions like \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) oscillate rapidly on all scales, making domain interval partitions completely ineffective[cite: 4].


21.5.2 The Fix: Partition the Range, Not the Domain
Instead of partitioning the domain \([a, b]\) into subintervals \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\), we partition the range (target space \(\mathbb{R}\)) into intervals \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\)[cite: 4].
For each range interval \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\), we look at its preimage under \(f\)[cite: 4]: \[
E_k := f^{-1}((y_{k-1}, y_k]) = \{\omega \in \Omega : y_{k-1} < f(\omega) \le y_k\}[cite: 4].
\]

The set \(E_k \subseteq \Omega\) is not necessarily an interval, but if \(f\) is measurable, \(E_k \in \mathcal{F}\) is a measurable set[cite: 4].
We know how to measure \(E_k\) using the measure \(\mu(E_k)\)[cite: 4]!

This leads directly to simple function approximations of the form \(\sum_k y_k \, \mu(E_k)\) and establishes the foundation for the Lebesgue Integral[cite: 4].

title: 22  Lecture 10.2: Lebesgue vs. Riemann
text:
22.1 Lebesgue Integration vs. Riemann Integration
The Lebesgue integral extends integration to a much broader class of functions than the classical Riemann integral. A canonical example of a function that is Lebesgue integrable but not Riemann integrable is the Dirichlet function on \([0, 1]\): \[
f(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q} \cap [0, 1]}(x)
\]
Since \(\mathbb{Q} \cap [0, 1]\) is countable, \(\lambda(\mathbb{Q} \cap [0, 1]) = 0\). Thus, \(f = 0\) a.e. \([\lambda]\), giving: \[
\int_{[0, 1]} f \, d\lambda = \lambda(\mathbb{Q} \cap [0, 1]) = 0
\] However, \(f\) is nowhere continuous on \([0, 1]\), so its upper and lower Riemann integrals disagree (\(\overline{\int}_0^1 f(x) dx = 1 \ne 0 = \underline{\int}_0^1 f(x) dx\)), making it Riemann non-integrable.

title: 23  Lecture 11.1: Radon-Nikodym
text:
23.1 Absolute Continuity and Densities
When working with two measures \(\mu\) and \(
u\) on the same measurable space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), a natural question arises: under what conditions can \(
u\) be expressed via a density function \(ho \ge 0\) with respect to \(\mu\) such that \(
u(A) = \int_A ho \, d\mu\) for all \(A \in \mathcal{F}\)?
This condition is strictly necessary for the existence of a density. Indeed, if \(
u(A) = \int_A ho \, d\mu\) for some \(ho \in L^+(\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), then \(\mu(A) = 0\) implies \(
u(A) = \int_A ho \, d\mu = 0\), since the Lebesgue integral of any non-negative measurable function over a \(\mu\)-null set is zero: \(\int_A ho\,d\mu \le \|ho\|_\infty \mu(A) = 0\), or more generally \(\int_A ho\,d\mu = 0\) follows directly from the definition of the integral and \(\mu(A) = 0\).
Geometric Interpretation on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (special case \(\mu = \lambda\)): When \(\mu = \lambda\) is the Lebesgue measure and \(
u \ll \lambda\) with \(d
u = ho\,d\lambda\), the Lebesgue Differentiation Theorem gives: \[
 rac{d
u}{d\lambda}(x) = ho(x) = \lim_{\epsilon \downarrow 0}  rac{
u(B_\epsilon(x))}{\lambda(B_\epsilon(x))} \quad \lambda	ext{-a.e. } x.
	ag{23.4}\] This formula is specific to \(\mu = \lambda\); for a general \(\sigma\)-finite reference measure \(\mu\), the Radon-Nikodym derivative need not equal this ball-ratio limit.

title: 24  Lecture 11.2: Laws Revisited
text:
24.1 Motivation and Finite Setup
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space. If \(\Omega\) is a finite sample space and \(X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is a finite-valued random variable, the expectation of \(X\) is defined as: \[
\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} X(\omega) \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) = \int_{\Omega} X \, d\mathbb{P}.
\]
If \(g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is a measurable function, then \(g \circ X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is also a random variable. Assuming \(X\) takes finitely many distinct values \(\{t_1, t_2, \dots, t_n\} \subset \mathbb{R}\), we can compute the expectation of \(g(X)\) by partitioning \(\Omega\) according to the level sets \(X^{-1}(\{t_j\})\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[g(X)] &= \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} g(X(\omega)) \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} \sum_{\omega \in X^{-1}(\{t_j\})} g(X(\omega)) \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} g(t_j) \sum_{\omega \in X^{-1}(\{t_j\})} \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} g(t_j) \mathbb{P}\bigl(\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) = t_j\}\bigr) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} g(t_j) \mathbb{P}\bigl(X^{-1}(\{t_j\})\bigr) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} g(t_j) \mu_X(\{t_j\}) \\
&= \int_{\mathbb{R}} g \, d\mu_X,
\end{aligned}
\] where \(\mu_X \triangleq X_{*} \mathbb{P} = \mathbb{P} \circ X^{-1}\) denotes the push-forward measure (law/distribution) of \(X\) under \(\mathbb{P}\).

24.2 The Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
To see why a new integration theory is necessary, we first review the classic Riemann–Stieltjes integral on \(\mathbb{R}\).

Definition 24.1 (Lebesgue–Stieltjes Measure) Let \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a non-decreasing, right-continuous function. The function \(F\) uniquely determines a Radon measure \(\mu_F\) on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) defined on half-open intervals by: \[
\mu_F((a, b]) := F(b) - F(a) \quad \text{for all } a < b.
\]


Definition 24.2 (Riemann–Stieltjes Upper and Lower Sums) Let \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\) be a compact interval and let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function. Consider a partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\pi = \{a = t_0 < t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_{n-1} < t_n = b\}[cite: 4].
\]
We define the upper Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\overline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) and lower Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\underline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) with respect to \(\pi\) by[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4].
\]
The upper and lower Darboux integrals are defined by taking infima and suprema over all finite partitions \(\mathcal{P}([a, b])\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \inf_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \overline{S}_\pi(f, F), \quad \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \sup_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \underline{S}_\pi(f, F)[cite: 4].
\] If \(\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF = \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF\), we say \(f\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable with respect to \(F\) on \([a, b]\), and we write \(\int_a^b f(x) \, dF(x)\) or \(\int_a^b f \, d\mu_F\) for this common value[cite: 4].

title: 24  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
section: 24.3 Limitations and Defects of the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
text:
24.3 Limitations and Defects of the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
While simple and intuitive, the Riemann–Stieltjes integral suffers from severe structural limitations when applied to modern probability and analysis[cite: 4]:

Domain Constraint: It is fundamentally defined only on compact intervals \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\)[cite: 4].
Boundedness Constraint: It requires the integrand \(f\) to be bounded[cite: 4].
Weak Limit Properties: It lacks good limit theorems (e.g., dominated convergence) and handles only finite additivity naturally[cite: 4].
Failure on Simple Functions: It fails to integrate basic functions that oscillate rapidly on small scales[cite: 4].


Example 24.1 (Failure on the Dirichlet Function) Consider the indicator function of the rational numbers on \([a, b]\), \(f(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\)[cite: 4]. For any interval \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\) with \(t_{k-1} < t_k\), density of \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}\) implies[cite: 4]: \[
\sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 1, \quad \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Thus, for any partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 1 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = F(b) - F(a)[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 0 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Hence \(\overline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = F(b) - F(a)\) and \(\underline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = 0\)[cite: 4]. Therefore, \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if \(F(b) = F(a)\) (i.e., \(F\) is constant on \([a, b]\))[cite: 4].

title: 24  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
text:
24.4 Characterization of Riemann Integrability

Theorem 24.1 (Lebesgue Criterion for Riemann Integrability) Let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function, and let \(F(x) = x\) (so that \(\mu_F = \lambda\), the Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}\))[cite: 4].
The function \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if the set of discontinuity points of \(f\), \[
D_f := \{x \in [a, b] : f \text{ is discontinuous at } x\},
\] has Lebesgue measure zero (i.e., \(\bar{\lambda}(D_f) = 0\), where \(\bar{\lambda}\) denotes the outer measure/completion)[cite: 4].

title: 24  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
section: 24.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?
text:
24.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?

24.5.1 The Problem
The Riemann–Stieltjes integral is designed for functions that are well-adapted to an interval partition of the domain[cite: 4]. It works well if preimages \(f^{-1}((s, t))\) are nice unions of intervals for any \(s < t\) (such as continuous functions)[cite: 4].
However, functions like \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) oscillate rapidly on all scales, making domain interval partitions completely ineffective[cite: 4].


24.5.2 The Fix: Partition the Range, Not the Domain
Instead of partitioning the domain \([a, b]\) into subintervals \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\), we partition the range (target space \(\mathbb{R}\)) into intervals \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\)[cite: 4].
For each range interval \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\), we look at its preimage under \(f\)[cite: 4]: \[
E_k := f^{-1}((y_{k-1}, y_k]) = \{\omega \in \Omega : y_{k-1} < f(\omega) \le y_k\}[cite: 4].
\]

The set \(E_k \subseteq \Omega\) is not necessarily an interval, but if \(f\) is measurable, \(E_k \in \mathcal{F}\) is a measurable set[cite: 4].
We know how to measure \(E_k\) using the measure \(\mu(E_k)\)[cite: 4]!

This leads directly to simple function approximations of the form \(\sum_k y_k \, \mu(E_k)\) and establishes the foundation for the Lebesgue Integral[cite: 4].

\]

\overline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4],
\] \[

27.3 Limitations and Defects of the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
While simple and intuitive, the Riemann–Stieltjes integral suffers from severe structural limitations when applied to modern probability and analysis[cite: 4]:

Domain Constraint: It is fundamentally defined only on compact intervals \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\)[cite: 4].
Boundedness Constraint: It requires the integrand \(f\) to be bounded[cite: 4].
Weak Limit Properties: It lacks good limit theorems (e.g., dominated convergence) and handles only finite additivity naturally[cite: 4].
Failure on Simple Functions: It fails to integrate basic functions that oscillate rapidly on small scales[cite: 4].


Example 27.1 (Failure on the Dirichlet Function) Consider the indicator function of the rational numbers on \([a, b]\), \(f(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\)[cite: 4]. For any interval \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\) with \(t_{k-1} < t_k\), density of \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}\) implies[cite: 4]: \[
\sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 1, \quad \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Thus, for any partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 1 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = F(b) - F(a)[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 0 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Hence \(\overline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = F(b) - F(a)\) and \(\underline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = 0\)[cite: 4]. Therefore, \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if \(F(b) = F(a)\) (i.e., \(F\) is constant on \([a, b]\))[cite: 4].

27.4 Characterization of Riemann Integrability

Theorem 27.1 (Lebesgue Criterion for Riemann Integrability) Let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function, and let \(F(x) = x\) (so that \(\mu_F = \lambda\), the Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}\))[cite: 4].
The function \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if the set of discontinuity points of \(f\), \[
D_f := \{x \in [a, b] : f \text{ is discontinuous at } x\},
\] has Lebesgue measure zero (i.e., \(\bar{\lambda}(D_f) = 0\), where \(\bar{\lambda}\) denotes the outer measure/completion)[cite: 4].

27.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?

27.5.1 The Problem
The Riemann–Stieltjes integral is designed for functions that are well-adapted to an interval partition of the domain[cite: 4]. It works well if preimages \(f^{-1}((s, t))\) are nice unions of intervals for any \(s < t\) (such as continuous functions)[cite: 4].
However, functions like \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) oscillate rapidly on all scales, making domain interval partitions completely ineffective[cite: 4].


27.5.2 The Fix: Partition the Range, Not the Domain
Instead of partitioning the domain \([a, b]\) into subintervals \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\), we partition the range (target space \(\mathbb{R}\)) into intervals \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\)[cite: 4].
For each range interval \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\), we look at its preimage under \(f\)[cite: 4]: \[
E_k := f^{-1}((y_{k-1}, y_k]) = \{\omega \in \Omega : y_{k-1} < f(\omega) \le y_k\}[cite: 4].
\]

The set \(E_k \subseteq \Omega\) is not necessarily an interval, but if \(f\) is measurable, \(E_k \in \mathcal{F}\) is a measurable set[cite: 4].
We know how to measure \(E_k\) using the measure \(\mu(E_k)\)[cite: 4]!

This leads directly to simple function approximations of the form \(\sum_k y_k \, \mu(E_k)\) and establishes the foundation for the Lebesgue Integral[cite: 4].

While simple and intuitive, the Riemann–Stieltjes integral suffers from severe structural limitations when applied to modern probability and analysis[cite: 4]:

Domain Constraint: It is fundamentally defined only on compact intervals \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\)[cite: 4].
Boundedness Constraint: It requires the integrand \(f\) to be bounded[cite: 4].
Weak Limit Properties: It lacks good limit theorems (e.g., dominated convergence) and handles only finite additivity naturally[cite: 4].
Failure on Simple Functions: It fails to integrate basic functions that oscillate rapidly on small scales[cite: 4].


Example 30.1 (Failure on the Dirichlet Function) Consider the indicator function of the rational numbers on \([a, b]\), \(f(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\)[cite: 4]. For any interval \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\) with \(t_{k-1} < t_k\), density of \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}\) implies[cite: 4]: \[
\sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 1, \quad \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Thus, for any partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 1 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = F(b) - F(a)[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 0 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = 0[cite: 4].
\]

30.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?

30.5.1 The Problem
The Riemann–Stieltjes integral is designed for functions that are well-adapted to an interval partition of the domain[cite: 4]. It works well if preimages \(f^{-1}((s, t))\) are nice unions of intervals for any \(s < t\) (such as continuous functions)[cite: 4].
However, functions like \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) oscillate rapidly on all scales, making domain interval partitions completely ineffective[cite: 4].


30.5.2 The Fix: Partition the Range, Not the Domain
Instead of partitioning the domain \([a, b]\) into subintervals \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\), we partition the range (target space \(\mathbb{R}\)) into intervals \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\)[cite: 4].
For each range interval \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\), we look at its preimage under \(f\)[cite: 4]: \[
E_k := f^{-1}((y_{k-1}, y_k]) = \{\omega \in \Omega : y_{k-1} < f(\omega) \le y_k\}[cite: 4].
\]

The set \(E_k \subseteq \Omega\) is not necessarily an interval, but if \(f\) is measurable, \(E_k \in \mathcal{F}\) is a measurable set[cite: 4].
We know how to measure \(E_k\) using the measure \(\mu(E_k)\)[cite: 4]!

This leads directly to simple function approximations of the form \(\sum_k y_k \, \mu(E_k)\) and establishes the foundation for the Lebesgue Integral[cite: 4].

31.2 The Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
To see why a new integration theory is necessary, we first review the classic Riemann–Stieltjes integral on \(\mathbb{R}\).

Definition 31.1 (Lebesgue–Stieltjes Measure) Let \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a non-decreasing, right-continuous function. The function \(F\) uniquely determines a Radon measure \(\mu_F\) on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) defined on half-open intervals by: \[
\mu_F((a, b]) := F(b) - F(a) \quad \text{for all } a < b.
\]


Definition 31.2 (Riemann–Stieltjes Upper and Lower Sums) Let \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\) be a compact interval and let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function. Consider a partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\pi = \{a = t_0 < t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_{n-1} < t_n = b\}[cite: 4].
\]
We define the upper Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\overline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) and lower Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\underline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) with respect to \(\pi\) by[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4].
\]
The upper and lower Darboux integrals are defined by taking infima and suprema over all finite partitions \(\mathcal{P}([a, b])\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \inf_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \overline{S}_\pi(f, F), \quad \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \sup_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \underline{S}_\pi(f, F)[cite: 4].
\] If \(\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF = \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF\), we say \(f\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable with respect to \(F\) on \([a, b]\), and we write \(\int_a^b f(x) \, dF(x)\) or \(\int_a^b f \, d\mu_F\) for this common value[cite: 4].

33.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?

34.2 The Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
To see why a new integration theory is necessary, we first review the classic Riemann–Stieltjes integral on \(\mathbb{R}\).

Definition 34.1 (Lebesgue–Stieltjes Measure) Let \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a non-decreasing, right-continuous function. The function \(F\) uniquely determines a Radon measure \(\mu_F\) on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) defined on half-open intervals by: \[
\mu_F((a, b]) := F(b) - F(a) \quad \text{for all } a < b.
\]


Definition 34.2 (Riemann–Stieltjes Upper and Lower Sums) Let \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\) be a compact interval and let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function. Consider a partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\pi = \{a = t_0 < t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_{n-1} < t_n = b\}[cite: 4].
\]
We define the upper Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\overline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) and lower Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\underline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) with respect to \(\pi\) by[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4].
\]
The upper and lower Darboux integrals are defined by taking infima and suprema over all finite partitions \(\mathcal{P}([a, b])\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \inf_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \overline{S}_\pi(f, F), \quad \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \sup_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \underline{S}_\pi(f, F)[cite: 4].
\] If \(\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF = \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF\), we say \(f\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable with respect to \(F\) on \([a, b]\), and we write \(\int_a^b f(x) \, dF(x)\) or \(\int_a^b f \, d\mu_F\) for this common value[cite: 4].

34.3 Limitations and Defects of the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
While simple and intuitive, the Riemann–Stieltjes integral suffers from severe structural limitations when applied to modern probability and analysis[cite: 4]:

Domain Constraint: It is fundamentally defined only on compact intervals \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\)[cite: 4].
Boundedness Constraint: It requires the integrand \(f\) to be bounded[cite: 4].
Weak Limit Properties: It lacks good limit theorems (e.g., dominated convergence) and handles only finite additivity naturally[cite: 4].
Failure on Simple Functions: It fails to integrate basic functions that oscillate rapidly on small scales[cite: 4].


Example 34.1 (Failure on the Dirichlet Function) Consider the indicator function of the rational numbers on \([a, b]\), \(f(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\)[cite: 4]. For any interval \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\) with \(t_{k-1} < t_k\), density of \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}\) implies[cite: 4]: \[
\sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 1, \quad \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Thus, for any partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 1 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = F(b) - F(a)[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 0 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Hence \(\overline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = F(b) - F(a)\) and \(\underline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = 0\)[cite: 4]. Therefore, \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if \(F(b) = F(a)\) (i.e., \(F\) is constant on \([a, b]\))[cite: 4].

To see why a new integration theory is necessary, we first review the classic Riemann–Stieltjes integral on \(\mathbb{R}\).

Definition 37.1 (Lebesgue–Stieltjes Measure) Let \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a non-decreasing, right-continuous function. The function \(F\) uniquely determines a Radon measure \(\mu_F\) on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) defined on half-open intervals by: \[
\mu_F((a, b]) := F(b) - F(a) \quad \text{for all } a < b.
\]


Definition 37.2 (Riemann–Stieltjes Upper and Lower Sums) Let \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\) be a compact interval and let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function. Consider a partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\pi = \{a = t_0 < t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_{n-1} < t_n = b\}[cite: 4].
\]
We define the upper Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\overline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) and lower Riemann–Stieltjes sum \(\underline{S}_\pi(f, F)\) with respect to \(\pi\) by[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4].
\]

\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \inf_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \overline{S}_\pi(f, F), \quad \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \sup_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \underline{S}_\pi(f, F)[cite: 4].
\] If \(\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF = \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF\), we say \(f\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable with respect to \(F\) on \([a, b]\), and we write \(\int_a^b f(x) \, dF(x)\) or \(\int_a^b f \, d\mu_F\) for this common value[cite: 4].

37.3 Limitations and Defects of the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
While simple and intuitive, the Riemann–Stieltjes integral suffers from severe structural limitations when applied to modern probability and analysis[cite: 4]:

Domain Constraint: It is fundamentally defined only on compact intervals \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\)[cite: 4].
Boundedness Constraint: It requires the integrand \(f\) to be bounded[cite: 4].
Weak Limit Properties: It lacks good limit theorems (e.g., dominated convergence) and handles only finite additivity naturally[cite: 4].
Failure on Simple Functions: It fails to integrate basic functions that oscillate rapidly on small scales[cite: 4].


Example 37.1 (Failure on the Dirichlet Function) Consider the indicator function of the rational numbers on \([a, b]\), \(f(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\)[cite: 4]. For any interval \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\) with \(t_{k-1} < t_k\), density of \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}\) implies[cite: 4]: \[
\sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 1, \quad \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Thus, for any partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 1 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = F(b) - F(a)[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 0 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Hence \(\overline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = F(b) - F(a)\) and \(\underline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = 0\)[cite: 4]. Therefore, \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if \(F(b) = F(a)\) (i.e., \(F\) is constant on \([a, b]\))[cite: 4].

37.4 Characterization of Riemann Integrability

Theorem 37.1 (Lebesgue Criterion for Riemann Integrability) Let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function, and let \(F(x) = x\) (so that \(\mu_F = \lambda\), the Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}\))[cite: 4].
The function \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if the set of discontinuity points of \(f\), \[
D_f := \{x \in [a, b] : f \text{ is discontinuous at } x\},
\] has Lebesgue measure zero (i.e., \(\bar{\lambda}(D_f) = 0\), where \(\bar{\lambda}\) denotes the outer measure/completion)[cite: 4].

37.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?

37.5.1 The Problem
The Riemann–Stieltjes integral is designed for functions that are well-adapted to an interval partition of the domain[cite: 4]. It works well if preimages \(f^{-1}((s, t))\) are nice unions of intervals for any \(s < t\) (such as continuous functions)[cite: 4].
However, functions like \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) oscillate rapidly on all scales, making domain interval partitions completely ineffective[cite: 4].


37.5.2 The Fix: Partition the Range, Not the Domain
Instead of partitioning the domain \([a, b]\) into subintervals \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\), we partition the range (target space \(\mathbb{R}\)) into intervals \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\)[cite: 4].
For each range interval \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\), we look at its preimage under \(f\)[cite: 4]: \[
E_k := f^{-1}((y_{k-1}, y_k]) = \{\omega \in \Omega : y_{k-1} < f(\omega) \le y_k\}[cite: 4].
\]

The set \(E_k \subseteq \Omega\) is not necessarily an interval, but if \(f\) is measurable, \(E_k \in \mathcal{F}\) is a measurable set[cite: 4].
We know how to measure \(E_k\) using the measure \(\mu(E_k)\)[cite: 4]!

This leads directly to simple function approximations of the form \(\sum_k y_k \, \mu(E_k)\) and establishes the foundation for the Lebesgue Integral[cite: 4].

title: 39  Lecture 18.2: Kolmogorov Convergence Criterion
text:
39.1 \(L^2\) Convergence of Uncorrelated Sums
Let \(\{Y_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of uncorrelated random variables in \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), meaning \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_n, Y_m) = 0\) for all \(n \neq m\). Define \(\dot{Y}_n \triangleq Y_n - \mathbb{E}[Y_n]\), so that \(\{\dot{Y}_n\}\) forms an orthogonal sequence in the Hilbert space \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\).
Orthogonal sums in \(L^2\) generally fail to converge almost surely without additional independence structure. To bridge \(L^2\) convergence to almost sure convergence, we require Kolmogorov’s Maximal Inequality.

text:
41.1 Frequentist Interpretation of Probability
The Strong Law of Large Numbers (SLLN) provides mathematical justification for the frequentist interpretation of probability. Given an event \(A \in \mathcal{F}\), let \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be an i.i.d. sequence of indicator random variables \(X_n \triangleq \mathbf{1}_A^{(n)}\) representing independent trials. Since \(E[X_1] = E[\mathbf{1}_A] = P(A)\), SLLN establishes: \[
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n X_k \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} P(A) \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
\tag{41.1}\]
