\underline{S}_\pi(f, F) := \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) \mu_F((t_{k-1}, t_k]) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} f(t) \right) (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1}))[cite: 4].
\]
The upper and lower Darboux integrals are defined by taking infima and suprema over all finite partitions \(\mathcal{P}([a, b])\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \inf_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \overline{S}_\pi(f, F), \quad \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF := \sup_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}([a, b])} \underline{S}_\pi(f, F)[cite: 4].
\] If \(\overline{\int_a^b} f \, dF = \underline{\int_a^b} f \, dF\), we say \(f\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable with respect to \(F\) on \([a, b]\), and we write \(\int_a^b f(x) \, dF(x)\) or \(\int_a^b f \, d\mu_F\) for this common value[cite: 4].

title: 40  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
section: 40.3 Limitations and Defects of the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
text:
40.3 Limitations and Defects of the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
While simple and intuitive, the Riemann–Stieltjes integral suffers from severe structural limitations when applied to modern probability and analysis[cite: 4]:

Domain Constraint: It is fundamentally defined only on compact intervals \([a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}\)[cite: 4].
Boundedness Constraint: It requires the integrand \(f\) to be bounded[cite: 4].
Weak Limit Properties: It lacks good limit theorems (e.g., dominated convergence) and handles only finite additivity naturally[cite: 4].
Failure on Simple Functions: It fails to integrate basic functions that oscillate rapidly on small scales[cite: 4].


Example 40.1 (Failure on the Dirichlet Function) Consider the indicator function of the rational numbers on \([a, b]\), \(f(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\)[cite: 4]. For any interval \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\) with \(t_{k-1} < t_k\), density of \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}\) implies[cite: 4]: \[
\sup_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 1, \quad \inf_{t \in [t_{k-1}, t_k]} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(t) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Thus, for any partition \(\pi\) of \([a, b]\)[cite: 4]: \[
\overline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 1 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = F(b) - F(a)[cite: 4],
\] \[
\underline{S}_\pi(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}, F) = \sum_{k=1}^n 0 \cdot (F(t_k) - F(t_{k-1})) = 0[cite: 4].
\]
Hence \(\overline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = F(b) - F(a)\) and \(\underline{\int_a^b} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} \, dF = 0\)[cite: 4]. Therefore, \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if \(F(b) = F(a)\) (i.e., \(F\) is constant on \([a, b]\))[cite: 4].

title: 40  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
text:
40.4 Characterization of Riemann Integrability

Theorem 40.1 (Lebesgue Criterion for Riemann Integrability) Let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a bounded function, and let \(F(x) = x\) (so that \(\mu_F = \lambda\), the Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}\))[cite: 4].
The function \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a, b]\) if and only if the set of discontinuity points of \(f\), \[
D_f := \{x \in [a, b] : f \text{ is discontinuous at } x\},
\] has Lebesgue measure zero (i.e., \(\bar{\lambda}(D_f) = 0\), where \(\bar{\lambda}\) denotes the outer measure/completion)[cite: 4].

title: 40  Lecture 7.2: Riemann-Stieltjes Integration
section: 40.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?
text:
40.5 What is the Fundamental Problem and What is the Fix?

40.5.1 The Problem
The Riemann–Stieltjes integral is designed for functions that are well-adapted to an interval partition of the domain[cite: 4]. It works well if preimages \(f^{-1}((s, t))\) are nice unions of intervals for any \(s < t\) (such as continuous functions)[cite: 4].
However, functions like \(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}\) oscillate rapidly on all scales, making domain interval partitions completely ineffective[cite: 4].


40.5.2 The Fix: Partition the Range, Not the Domain
Instead of partitioning the domain \([a, b]\) into subintervals \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\), we partition the range (target space \(\mathbb{R}\)) into intervals \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\)[cite: 4].
For each range interval \((y_{k-1}, y_k]\), we look at its preimage under \(f\)[cite: 4]: \[
E_k := f^{-1}((y_{k-1}, y_k]) = \{\omega \in \Omega : y_{k-1} < f(\omega) \le y_k\}[cite: 4].
\]

The set \(E_k \subseteq \Omega\) is not necessarily an interval, but if \(f\) is measurable, \(E_k \in \mathcal{F}\) is a measurable set[cite: 4].
We know how to measure \(E_k\) using the measure \(\mu(E_k)\)[cite: 4]!

This leads directly to simple function approximations of the form \(\sum_k y_k \, \mu(E_k)\) and establishes the foundation for the Lebesgue Integral[cite: 4].

title: 18  Lecture 8.2: The Lebesgue Integral and the MC Theorem
text:
Definition 18.1 (Lebesgue Integral for Non-Negative Functions) For any \(f \in L^+\), the Lebesgue integral of \(f\) with respect to \(\mu\) is defined by: \[
\begin{align*}
\int f \, d\mu &= \int_{\Omega} f(\omega) \, \mu(d\omega) \\
&:= \sup \left\{ \int \varphi \, d\mu \mid \varphi \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}, \, 0 \le \varphi \le f \right\}
\end{align*}
\tag{18.2}\] where \(\mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) is the space of simple \(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\)-measurable functions.
If \(\mu = \mathbb{P}\) is a probability measure, the integral is also denoted as the expectation: \[
\mathbb{E}[f] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[f] := \int f \, d\mathbb{P}
\]


Remark 18.1. The integral \(\int f \, d\mu\) takes values in \([0, \infty]\). If \(f = 0\) pointwise, then the only simple function \(0 \le \varphi \le 0\) is \(\varphi = 0\), giving \(\int 0 \, d\mu = 0\).


Proposition 18.1 (Basic Properties of the Integral on \(L^+\)) Let \(f, g \in L^+\) and \(\alpha \ge 0\).

Homogeneity: \(\int \alpha f \, d\mu = \alpha \int f \, d\mu\) (with the convention \(0 \cdot \infty = 0\)).
Additivity: \(\int (f + g) \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu + \int g \, d\mu\).
Monotonicity: If \(f \le g\) pointwise, then \(\int f \, d\mu \le \int g \, d\mu\).



Proof (Proof of Proposition 18.1). We prove Properties 1 and 3 first, postponing Property 2 until after establishing the Monotone Convergence Theorem.

18.1.1 Proof of Property 1 (Homogeneity)
Case \(\alpha = 0\): If \(\alpha = 0\), then \(\alpha f = 0\) pointwise. Thus \(\int 0 \cdot f \, d\mu = \int 0 \, d\mu = 0 = 0 \cdot \int f \, d\mu\).
Case \(\alpha > 0\): By definition of the Lebesgue integral: \[
\begin{aligned}
\int \alpha f \, d\mu &= \sup \left\{ \int \varphi \, d\mu \mid \varphi \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}, \, 0 \le \varphi \le \alpha f \right\} \\
&= \sup \left\{ \int \alpha \psi \, d\mu \mid \psi \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}, \, 0 \le \psi \le f \right\} \quad (\text{setting } \psi = \alpha^{-1} \varphi) \\
&= \alpha \cdot \sup \left\{ \int \psi \, d\mu \mid \psi \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}, \, 0 \le \psi \le f \right\} \\
&= \alpha \int f \, d\mu
\end{aligned}
\]


18.1.2 Proof of Property 3 (Monotonicity)
Assume \(0 \le f \le g\) pointwise. If \(\varphi \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) satisfies \(0 \le \varphi \le f\), then by transitivity \(0 \le \varphi \le g\).
Hence, the set of simple functions bounded by \(f\) is a subset of those bounded by \(g\): \[
\{ \varphi \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}} \mid 0 \le \varphi \le f \} \subseteq \{ \varphi \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}} \mid 0 \le \varphi \le g \}
\] Taking the supremum over both sets yields: \[
\int f \, d\mu = \sup_{\varphi \le f} \int \varphi \, d\mu \le \sup_{\varphi \le g} \int \varphi \, d\mu = \int g \, d\mu
\]

title: 18  Lecture 8.2: The Lebesgue Integral and the MC Theorem
text:
18.2 The Monotone Convergence Theorem
To establish full additivity and compute limits for general non-negative measurable functions, we require a foundational convergence result.

Theorem 18.1 (Monotone Convergence Theorem) Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset L^+\) be a non-decreasing sequence of functions, i.e., \(0 \le f_1 \le f_2 \le \dots \le f_n \le \dots\) pointwise. Define \(f(\omega) := \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(\omega)\) for all \(\omega \in \Omega\). Then \(f \in L^+\) and: \[
\int f_n \, d\mu \uparrow \int f \, d\mu \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
\tag{18.3}\] That is, \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu = \int \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n \, d\mu=\int f \, d\mu\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 18.1). We divide the proof into two directional inequalities.

18.2.1 Step 1: Upper Bound (\(\lim_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu \le \int f \, d\mu\))
Since \(f_n \le f_{n+1} \le f\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), monotonicity (Property 3) implies that \((\int f_n \, d\mu)_{n=1}^\infty\) is a non-decreasing sequence in \([0, \infty]\) bounded above by \(\int f \, d\mu\).
Therefore, the limit exists in \([0, \infty]\) and satisfies: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu \le \int f \, d\mu
\tag{18.4}\]


18.2.2 Step 2: Lower Bound (\(\lim_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu \ge \int f \, d\mu\))
Fix an arbitrary simple function \(\varphi \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) such that \(0 \le \varphi \le f\), and fix a constant parameter \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\). Define the sequence of sets: \[
\Omega_n := \{ \omega \in \Omega \mid f_n(\omega) \ge \alpha \varphi(\omega) \} = (f_n - \alpha \varphi)^{-1}([0, \infty]) \in \mathcal{F}
\tag{18.5}\]
We observe two critical properties of \(\Omega_n\):

Monotonicity: Since \(f_n \le f_{n+1}\), we have \(\Omega_n \subseteq \Omega_{n+1}\) for all \(n\).
Exhaustion of \(\Omega\): Fix \(\omega \in \Omega\). If \(\varphi(\omega) = 0\), then \(\alpha \varphi(\omega) = 0 \le f_1(\omega)\), so \(\omega \in \Omega_1\). If \(\varphi(\omega) > 0\), then \(\alpha \varphi(\omega) < \varphi(\omega) \le f(\omega) = \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(\omega)\). Thus, there exists \(n(\omega) \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \(f_n(\omega) \ge \alpha \varphi(\omega)\) for all \(n \ge n(\omega)\), implying \(\omega \in \Omega_n\). Hence, \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \Omega_n = \Omega\).

For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), since \(f_n \ge f_n \mathbf{1}_{\Omega_n} \ge \alpha \mathbf{1}_{\Omega_n} \varphi \ge 0\), monotonicity gives: \[
\int f_n \, d\mu \ge \int \alpha \mathbf{1}_{\Omega_n} \varphi \, d\mu = \alpha \int \mathbf{1}_{\Omega_n} \varphi \, d\mu
\tag{18.6}\]
Since \(\varphi\) is a simple function, we represent it as \(\varphi = \sum_{t > 0} t \mathbf{1}_{\{\varphi = t\}}\). Then: \[
\int \mathbf{1}_{\Omega_n} \varphi \, d\mu = \sum_{t > 0} t \, \mu(\{\varphi = t\} \cap \Omega_n)
\]
Taking the limit as \(n \to \infty\), continuity of the measure \(\mu\) from below on the expanding sequence \((\{\varphi = t\} \cap \Omega_n)_{n=1}^\infty \uparrow \{\varphi = t\}\) yields: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \mu(\{\varphi = t\} \cap \Omega_n) = \mu(\{\varphi = t\})
\]
Substituting this back into Equation 18.6 gives: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu \ge \alpha \sum_{t > 0} t \, \mu(\{\varphi = t\}) = \alpha \int \varphi \, d\mu
\]
Since this holds for any \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\), taking \(\alpha \uparrow 1\) yields: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu \ge \int \varphi \, d\mu
\]
Finally, taking the supremum over all simple functions \(0 \le \varphi \le f\) gives: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu \ge \sup_{0 \le \varphi \le f} \int \varphi \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu
\tag{18.7}\]
Combining Equation 18.4 and Equation 18.7 completes the proof.

title: 18  Lecture 8.2: The Lebesgue Integral and the MC Theorem
text:
18.3 Explicit Standard Approximation & Additivity
Using the Monotone Convergence Theorem, we can construct an explicit simple-function approximation sequence for any \(f \in L^+\).

Proposition 18.2 (Standard Approximation Sequence) For \(f \in L^+\), define the sequence \((\varphi_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) by: \[
\varphi_n := \sum_{k=0}^{2^{2n}-1} \frac{k}{2^n} \mathbf{1}_{\left\{ \frac{k}{2^n} < f \le \frac{k+1}{2^n} \right\}} + 2^n \mathbf{1}_{\{f > 2^n\}}
\tag{18.8}\]
Then \(\varphi_n \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\), \(0 \le \varphi_n \uparrow f\) pointwise as \(n \to \infty\), and: \[
\begin{align*}
\int f \, d\mu &= \lim_{n \to \infty} \int \varphi_n \, d\mu \\
&= \lim_{n \to \infty} \left[ \sum_{k=0}^{2^{2n}-1} \frac{k}{2^n} \mu\left( \left\{ \frac{k}{2^n} < f \le \frac{k+1}{2^n} \right\} \right) + 2^n \mu(\{f > 2^n\}) \right]
\end{align*}
\tag{18.9}\] (Note: This limit always exists in \([0, \infty]\) as a non-decreasing sequence.)


Corollary 18.1 (Additivity of the Lebesgue Integral on \(L^+\)) For any \(f, g \in L^+\): \[
\int (f + g) \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu + \int g \, d\mu
\tag{18.10}\]


Proof. Let \((\psi_n)_{n=1}^\infty, (\varphi_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) be standard approximation sequences such that \(0 \le \psi_n \uparrow f\) and \(0 \le \varphi_n \uparrow g\). Then \((\psi_n + \varphi_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) satisfies \(0 \le (\psi_n + \varphi_n) \uparrow (f + g)\).
By linearity of simple integrals (Equation 17.3) and the Monotone Convergence Theorem (Theorem 18.1): \[
\begin{align*}
\int (f + g) \, d\mu &= \lim_{n \to \infty} \int (\psi_n + \varphi_n) \, d\mu\\
&= \lim_{n \to \infty} \int \psi_n \, d\mu + \lim_{n \to \infty} \int \varphi_n \, d\mu \\
&= \int f \, d\mu + \int g \, d\mu.
\end{align*}
\]


Corollary 18.2 (Integration of Infinite Series in \(L^+\)) Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset L^+\). Then: \[
\int \left( \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n \right) d\mu = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \int f_n \, d\mu
\tag{18.11}\]


Proof. Let \(g_N := \sum_{n=1}^{N} f_n \in L^+\). Since \(f_n \ge 0\), the partial sums satisfy \(0 \le g_N \uparrow g := \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n\) pointwise.
By finite additivity (Corollary 18.1) and the Monotone Convergence Theorem (Theorem 18.1): \[
\begin{align*}
\int \left( \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n \right) d\mu &= \int \lim_{N \to \infty} g_N \, d\mu\\
& = \lim_{N \to \infty} \int g_N \, d\mu \\
&= \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \int f_n \, d\mu \\
&= \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \int f_n \, d\mu
\end{align*}
\]

text:
18.4 Application: Integration with Respect to Discrete Measures

Example 18.1 Let \(\Omega\) be a countable set and let \(\rho: \Omega \to [0, \infty]\) be a weight function. Define a measure \(\mu\) on \((\Omega, 2^\Omega)\) by: \[
\mu = \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} \rho(\omega) \delta_\omega \implies \mu(A) = \sum_{\omega \in A} \rho(\omega), \quad \forall A \subseteq \Omega
\tag{18.12}\]
(For example, if \(\Omega = \{\omega_1, \omega_2, \dots\}\), \(0 \le \rho_n \le 1\), and \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \rho_n = 1\), then \(\mu\) is a discrete probability measure.)
Then for any \(f \in L^+\), the integral reduces to a weighted sum: \[
\int f \, d\mu = \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} f(\omega) \rho(\omega)
\tag{18.13}\]


Proof (Proof of Example 18.1). We prove Equation 18.13 by showing two inequalities.

18.4.1 Lower Inequality (\(\int f \, d\mu \le \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} f(\omega) \rho(\omega)\))
First assume \(\varphi \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) is a non-negative simple function \(\varphi = \sum_{t > 0} t \mathbf{1}_{\{\varphi = t\}}\). Then: \[
\begin{aligned}
\int \varphi \, d\mu &= \sum_{t > 0} t \, \mu(\{\varphi = t\}) = \sum_{t > 0} t \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} \rho(\omega) \mathbf{1}_{\{\varphi(\omega) = t\}} \\
&= \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} \rho(\omega) \sum_{t > 0} t \mathbf{1}_{\{\varphi(\omega) = t\}} = \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} \varphi(\omega) \rho(\omega)
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(0 \le \varphi \le f\), then \(\varphi(\omega) \rho(\omega) \le f(\omega) \rho(\omega)\) for all \(\omega \in \Omega\). Taking the supremum over all simple \(0 \le \varphi \le f\) gives: \[
\int f \, d\mu = \sup_{0 \le \varphi \le f} \int \varphi \, d\mu \le \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} f(\omega) \rho(\omega)
\]


18.4.2 Upper Inequality (\(\int f \, d\mu \ge \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} f(\omega) \rho(\omega)\))
Fix an arbitrary finite subset \(\Lambda \subseteq \Omega\) and a constant \(N \in \mathbb{N}\). Define the truncated simple function: \[
\varphi_{N, \Lambda} := \mathbf{1}_{\Lambda} \min\{f, N\} \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}
\]
Since \(0 \le \varphi_{N, \Lambda} \le f\) pointwise: \[
\int f \, d\mu \ge \int \varphi_{N, \Lambda} \, d\mu = \sum_{\omega \in \Lambda} \min\{f(\omega), N\} \rho(\omega)
\]
Taking \(N \to \infty\) via Monotone Convergence on the finite sum yields \(\sum_{\omega \in \Lambda} f(\omega) \rho(\omega) \le \int f \, d\mu\). Finally, taking the supremum over all finite subsets \(\Lambda \subseteq \Omega\) yields: \[
\sum_{\omega \in \Omega} f(\omega) \rho(\omega) \le \int f \, d\mu
\]
Combining both inequalities establishes Equation 18.13.

18.5 Reconstructions and Corrections

Standard Approximation Upper Sum Bound: In the handwritten manuscript, the upper bound index in \(\varphi_n\) was transcribed as \(\sum_{k=0}^{2^n-1}\); this has been mathematically corrected to \(\sum_{k=0}^{2^{2n}-1}\) (or \(\sum_{k=0}^{n 2^n - 1}\)) to ensure that the truncation range up to \(2^n\) is properly partitioned into steps of width \(2^{-n}\).
Exhaustion Proof in MCT: Expanded the justification for \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \Omega_n = \Omega\) by explicitly partitioning into cases where \(\varphi(\omega) = 0\) and \(\varphi(\omega) > 0\).

title: 19  Lecture 9.1: Fatou and Borel-Cantelli
text:
Definition 19.1 (Null Sets and Almost Everywhere Convergence) A set \(N \in \mathcal{F}\) is called a null set (or measure zero set) if \(\mu(N) = 0\).
A statement \(P(\omega)\) depending on \(\omega \in \Omega\) is said to hold almost everywhere (a.e.) with respect to \(\mu\) (or almost surely (a.s.) if \(\mu = \mathbb{P}\) is a probability measure) if there exists a null set \(N \in \mathcal{F}\) such that: \[
\{\omega \in \Omega \mid P(\omega) \text{ is false}\} \subseteq N
\]


Lemma 19.1 (Integration over Null Sets) Let \(\varphi \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}^+\) be a non-negative simple function and let \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(\mu(E) = 0\). Then: \[
\int_E \varphi \, d\mu := \int_{\Omega} \varphi \mathbf{1}_E \, d\mu = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \int_{\Omega} \varphi \, d\mu = \int_{E^c} \varphi \, d\mu
\tag{19.1}\]


Proof (Proof of Lemma 19.1). Let \(\varphi = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_j \mathbf{1}_{A_j}\) with \(\alpha_j \ge 0\) and \(A_j \in \mathcal{F}\). Then \(\varphi \mathbf{1}_E = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_j \mathbf{1}_{A_j \cap E}\).
By definition of simple integrals: \[
\int_E \varphi \, d\mu = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_j \mu(A_j \cap E)
\]
Since \(A_j \cap E \subseteq E\) and \(\mu(E) = 0\), monotonicity of measure gives \(\mu(A_j \cap E) = 0\) for all \(j \in \{1, \dots, n\}\). Hence \(\int_E \varphi \, d\mu = 0\).
Using the disjoint identity \(\mathbf{1}_{\Omega} = \mathbf{1}_E + \mathbf{1}_{E^c}\) and additivity: \[
\int_{\Omega} \varphi \, d\mu = \int_{\Omega} \varphi \mathbf{1}_E \, d\mu + \int_{\Omega} \varphi \mathbf{1}_{E^c} \, d\mu = 0 + \int_{E^c} \varphi \, d\mu = \int_{E^c} \varphi \, d\mu
\]



Proposition 19.1 (Almost Everywhere Properties of \(L^+\) Integrals) Let \(f, g \in L^+(\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).

Monotonicity: If \(f \le g\) a.e., then \(\int f \, d\mu \le \int g \, d\mu\).
Equivalence: If \(f = g\) a.e., then \(\int f \, d\mu = \int g \, d\mu\).
Vanishing Integral: \(\int f \, d\mu = 0 \iff f = 0\) a.e.



Proof (Proof of Proposition 19.1). We prove each assertion step-by-step.

19.1.1 Proof of Part 1
Let \(E = \{\omega \in \Omega \mid f(\omega) > g(\omega)\} \in \mathcal{F}\). By assumption, \(\mu(E) = 0\). For any simple function \(\varphi \in \mathbb{S}_{\mathcal{F}}\) with \(0 \le \varphi \le f\), we have \(\mathbf{1}_{E^c} \varphi \le \mathbf{1}_{E^c} f \le \mathbf{1}_{E^c} g \le g\).
By Lemma 19.1 and monotonicity on simple functions: \[
\int \varphi \, d\mu = \int_{E^c} \varphi \, d\mu \le \int g \, d\mu
\] Taking the supremum over all simple \(0 \le \varphi \le f\) gives \(\int f \, d\mu \le \int g \, d\mu\).


19.1.2 Proof of Part 2
If \(f = g\) a.e., then \(f \le g\) a.e. and \(g \le f\) a.e.. Applying Part 1 twice yields \(\int f \, d\mu \le \int g \, d\mu\) and \(\int g \, d\mu \le \int f \, d\mu\), so \(\int f \, d\mu = \int g \, d\mu\).


19.1.3 Proof of Part 3
\((\Leftarrow)\) If \(f = 0\) a.e., then by Part 2, \(\int f \, d\mu = \int 0 \, d\mu = 0\).
\((\Rightarrow)\) Assume \(\int f \, d\mu = 0\). For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), the pointwise bound \(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge 1/n\}} \le f\) together with monotonicity of integration gives: \[
\frac{1}{n}\,\mu\!\left(\left\{f \ge \frac{1}{n}\right\}\right) = \int \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge 1/n\}} \, d\mu \le \int f \, d\mu = 0 \implies \mu\!\left(\left\{f \ge \frac{1}{n}\right\}\right) = 0
\]
Notice that \(\{f > 0\} = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\{f \ge \frac{1}{n}\right\}\). By countable subadditivity of measure: \[
\mu(\{f > 0\}) \le \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mu\left(\left\{f \ge \frac{1}{n}\right\}\right) = 0 \implies f = 0 \text{ a.e.}
\]




Corollary 19.1 (Monotone Convergence Theorem (a.e. Version)) If \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset L^+\) satisfies \(f_n \uparrow f\) a.e. as \(n \to \infty\), then: \[
\int f_n \, d\mu \uparrow \int f \, d\mu
\tag{19.2}\]


Proof (Proof of Corollary 19.1). Let \(E = \{\omega \in \Omega \mid f_n(\omega) \uparrow f(\omega) \text{ fails}\} \in \mathcal{F}\), so \(\mu(E) = 0\). Then \(f_n \mathbf{1}_{E^c} \uparrow f \mathbf{1}_{E^c}\) pointwise everywhere on \(\Omega\).
Applying the pointwise Monotone Convergence Theorem and Lemma 19.1: \[
\int f_n \, d\mu = \int f_n \mathbf{1}_{E^c} \, d\mu \uparrow \int f \mathbf{1}_{E^c} \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu
\]

title: 19  Lecture 9.1: Fatou and Borel-Cantelli
text:
19.2 Markov’s Inequality & Fatou’s Lemma

Markov’s inequality shows that the measure of the set where a non-negative function exceeds a threshold is bounded by the integral of the function.
Fatou’s lemma provides a lower bound for the integral of the limit inferior of a sequence of non-negative functions.


Theorem 19.1 (Markov’s Inequality) Let \(f \in L^+\), \(\epsilon > 0\), and \(p > 0\). Then: \[
\mu(\{f \ge \epsilon\}) \le \frac{1}{\epsilon^p} \int f^p \, d\mu.
\tag{19.3}\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 19.1). Observe the indicator pointwise inequality: \[
\mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge \epsilon\}} \le \left( \frac{f}{\epsilon} \right)^p \mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge \epsilon\}} \le \left( \frac{f}{\epsilon} \right)^p.
\]
Integrating both sides with respect to \(\mu\) and using monotonicity: \[
\mu(\{f \ge \epsilon\}) = \int \mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge \epsilon\}} \, d\mu \le \int \left( \frac{f}{\epsilon} \right)^p \, d\mu = \frac{1}{\epsilon^p} \int f^p \, d\mu.
\]


Theorem 19.2 (Fatou’s Lemma) Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset L^+\) be any sequence of non-negative measurable functions. Then: \[
\int \liminf_{n \to \infty} f_n \, d\mu \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu.
\tag{19.4}\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 19.2). For each \(k \in \mathbb{N}\), define the pointwise infimum sequence \(g_k := \inf_{n \ge k} f_n \in L^+\).

Monotonicity: As \(k\) increases, the infimum is taken over smaller sets, so \(g_k \le g_{k+1}\) for all \(k\).
Pointwise Limit: By definition of limit inferior, \(g_k \uparrow \liminf_{n \to \infty} f_n\) pointwise as \(k \to \infty\).

Applying the Monotone Convergence Theorem to the non-decreasing sequence \((g_k)_{k=1}^\infty\): \[
\int \liminf_{n \to \infty} f_n \, d\mu = \int \lim_{k \to \infty} g_k \, d\mu = \lim_{k \to \infty} \int g_k \, d\mu
\tag{19.5}\]
For any fixed \(n \ge k\), \(g_k \le f_n\) pointwise. Monotonicity gives \(\int g_k \, d\mu \le \int f_n \, d\mu\) for all \(n \ge k\). Taking the infimum over \(n \ge k\) on the right side yields: \[
\int g_k \, d\mu \le \inf_{n \ge k} \int f_n \, d\mu.
\tag{19.6}\]
Taking the limit as \(k \to \infty\) on both sides of Equation 19.6 and combining with Equation 19.5: \[
\int \liminf_{n \to \infty} f_n \, d\mu = \lim_{k \to \infty} \int g_k \, d\mu \le \lim_{k \to \infty} \left( \inf_{n \ge k} \int f_n \, d\mu \right) = \liminf_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu.
\]

19.4 Almost Disjoint Additivity

The following proposition shows that the additivity property of measures extends to sequences of events that are disjoint almost everywhere.


Proposition 19.2 Let \((A_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathcal{F}\) be a sequence of events that are disjoint a.e., meaning \(\mu(A_n \cap A_m) = 0\) for all \(n \ne m\). Then: \[
\mu\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n \right) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mu(A_n)
\tag{19.7}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 19.2). Step 1: Construct the null set. Define \(N = \bigcup_{n \ne m} (A_n \cap A_m) \in \mathcal{F}\). By countable subadditivity: \[
\mu(N) \le \sum_{n \ne m} \mu(A_n \cap A_m) = 0,
\] so \(\mu(N) = 0\).
Step 2: Establish the pointwise identity on \(N^c\). The sets \((A_n \cap N^c)_{n \ge 1}\) are pairwise disjoint: if \(\omega \in (A_n \cap N^c) \cap (A_m \cap N^c)\) for some \(n \ne m\), then \(\omega \in A_n \cap A_m \subseteq N\), contradicting \(\omega \in N^c\). Therefore each \(\omega \in N^c\) belongs to at most one \(A_n\), so: \[
\mathbf{1}_{\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n}(\omega) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{A_n}(\omega) \quad \text{for all } \omega \in N^c.
\tag{19.8}\]
Step 3: Reduce the indicator integral to \(N^c\). Since \(\mathbf{1}_{\bigcup A_n}\) is a simple function and \(\mu(N) = 0\), Lemma 19.1 gives: \[
\int_\Omega \mathbf{1}_{\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n} \, d\mu = \int_{N^c} \mathbf{1}_{\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n} \, d\mu.
\tag{19.9}\]
Step 4: Reduce the series integral to \(N^c\). For each \(n\), monotonicity of measure gives \(\mu(A_n \cap N) \le \mu(N) = 0\). Applying Corollary 18.2: \[
\int_N \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{A_n} \, d\mu = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n \cap N) = 0,
\] so \(\int_\Omega \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{A_n} \, d\mu = \int_{N^c} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{A_n} \, d\mu\).
Step 5: Conclude. Combining Equation 19.9, the pointwise identity Equation 19.8 on \(N^c\), Corollary 18.2, and \(\mu(A_n \cap N) = 0\): \[
\begin{align*}
\mu\!\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n\right)
&= \int_{N^c} \mathbf{1}_{\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n} \, d\mu = \int_{N^c} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathbf{1}_{A_n} \, d\mu \\
&= \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \int_{N^c} \mathbf{1}_{A_n} \, d\mu = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mu(A_n \cap N^c)\\
&= \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mu(A_n).
\end{align*}
\]

title: 19  Lecture 9.1: Fatou and Borel-Cantelli
text:
19.5 The First Borel-Cantelli Lemma

Definition 19.2 (Infinitely Often (\(i.o.\)) / Limit Superior of Events) For a sequence of events \((A_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathcal{F}\), we define \(\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\}\) (read “\(A_n\) infinitely often”) as: \[
\begin{align*}
\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\} &:= \{\omega \in \Omega \mid \omega \in A_n \text{ for infinitely many } n\} \\
&= \bigcap_{N=1}^{\infty} \bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty} A_n = \limsup_{n \to \infty} A_n
\end{align*}
\tag{19.10}\]


Theorem 19.3 (First Borel-Cantelli Lemma) Let \((A_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathcal{F}\) be a sequence of events. If \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mu(A_n) < \infty\), then: \[
\mu(\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\}) = 0
\tag{19.11}\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 19.3). Step 1: Reformulate using \(Y\). Define \(Y := \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathbf{1}_{A_n} \in L^+\). Since each \(\mathbf{1}_{A_n}(\omega) \in \{0,1\}\), the value \(Y(\omega)\) is exactly the number of sets \(A_n\) that contain \(\omega\). Therefore: \[
\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\} = \{\omega \in \Omega \mid \omega \in A_n \text{ for infinitely many } n\} = \{Y = \infty\}.
\]
Step 2: Compute \(\int Y \, d\mu\). By Corollary 18.2: \[
\int_{\Omega} Y \, d\mu = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \int_{\Omega} \mathbf{1}_{A_n} \, d\mu = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mu(A_n) < \infty.
\tag{19.12}\]
Step 3: Bound \(\mu(\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\})\) via Markov’s inequality. For each \(k \in \mathbb{N}\), the inclusion \(\{Y = \infty\} \subseteq \{Y \ge k\}\) and monotonicity of measure give: \[
\mu(\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\}) = \mu(\{Y = \infty\}) \le \mu(\{Y \ge k\}).
\] Applying Theorem 19.1 with \(\epsilon = k\) and \(p = 1\): \[
\mu(\{Y \ge k\}) \le \frac{1}{k} \int_{\Omega} Y \, d\mu = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mu(A_n).
\]
Step 4: Conclude. Combining Steps 3 and Equation 19.12: \[
0 \le \mu(\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\}) \le \frac{1}{k} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mu(A_n) \quad \text{for all } k \in \mathbb{N}.
\] Since \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mu(A_n) < \infty\) is a fixed finite constant, taking \(k \to \infty\) gives \(\mu(\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\}) = 0\).


Example 19.1 Consider an infinite sequence of independent coin tosses where \(X_n = 1\) if the \(n\)-th toss is heads and \(X_n = 0\) otherwise, with \(\mathbb{P}(X_n = 1) = p_n\).

Case \(p_n = \frac{1}{n^2}\): Since \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} p_n = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6} < \infty\), the First Borel-Cantelli Lemma implies \(\mathbb{P}(X_n = 1 \text{ i.o.}) = 0\). Thus, with probability 1, only finitely many heads occur (eventually, heads never appear again).
Case \(p_n = \frac{1}{n}\): Here \(p_n \to 0\), but \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} p_n = \infty\). The First Borel-Cantelli Lemma does not apply; determining \(\mathbb{P}(X_n = 1 \text{ i.o.})\) requires the Second Borel-Cantelli Lemma (for independent events).

\(|f| = f_{+} + f_{-}\), and
\(f_{+}, f_{-} \in L^+(\Omega, \mathcal{F})\).


Definition 20.1 (Integrability and Space \(\mathcal{L}^1\)) A measurable function \(f: \Omega \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is called \(\mu\)-integrable if: \[
\int_{\Omega} f_{+} \, d\mu < \infty \quad \text{and} \quad \int_{\Omega} f_{-} \, d\mu < \infty.
\tag{20.3}\]
The space of all integrable functions is denoted by \(\mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\). For any \(f \in \mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), its Lebesgue integral is defined as: \[
\int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu := \int_{\Omega} f_{+} \, d\mu - \int_{\Omega} f_{-} \, d\mu.
\tag{20.4}\]


Since \(|f| = f_{+} + f_{-}\), we can equivalently define \(\mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) as \[
\mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu) := \{f: \Omega \to \overline{\mathbb{R}} \text{ measurable s.t. } \int_{\Omega} |f| \, d\mu < \infty\}.
\]


Remark 20.1. Note that \[
f \in \mathcal{L}^1 \implies \int_{\Omega} |f| \, d\mu = \int_{\Omega} f_{+} \, d\mu + \int_{\Omega} f_{-} \, d\mu < \infty.
\] Thus, it follows that \(|f| < \infty\) almost everywhere. Thus, by modifying \(f\) on a null set, we can assume without loss of generality that \(f\) is strictly real-valued (\(f: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\)).

title: 20  Lecture 9.2: \(L^1\) and the Dominated Convergence Theorem
text:
20.2 Properties of \(\mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\)
In the following proposition, we summarize some important properties of the space \(\mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) and the Lebesgue integral.

Proposition 20.1 (Linearity and Monotonicity of \(\mathcal{L}^1\))  

\(\mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is a real vector space.
The integral operator \(\int \cdot \, d\mu : \mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu) \to \mathbb{R}\) is a linear functional: \[
\int (a f + b g) \, d\mu = a \int f \, d\mu + b \int g \, d\mu \quad \forall a, b \in \mathbb{R}, \, f, g \in \mathcal{L}^1.
\tag{20.5}\]
Monotonicity: If \(f, g \in \mathcal{L}^1\) and \(f \le g\) a.e., then: \[
\int f \, d\mu \le \int g \, d\mu
\tag{20.6}\]
Triangle Inequality: For any \(f \in \mathcal{L}^1\): \[
\left| \int f \, d\mu \right| \le \int |f| \, d\mu.
\tag{20.7}\]



Proof (Proof of Proposition 20.1). We prove each property systematically.

20.2.1 Proof of Step 1 & Vector Space Structure
Let \(f, g \in \mathcal{L}^1\) and \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\). By the point-wise triangle inequality: \[
|a f + b g| \le |a| |f| + |b| |g|.
\] Integrating both sides and using \(L^+\) linearity (Corollary 18.1 and Proposition 18.1): \[
\int |a f + b g| \, d\mu \le |a| \int |f| \, d\mu + |b| \int |g| \, d\mu < \infty.
\] Hence, \(a f + b g \in \mathcal{L}^1\), proving \(\mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is a vector space.


20.2.2 Proof of Step 2 (Linearity)
Scalar Multiplication: If \(a \ge 0\), \((af)_{+} = a f_{+}\) and \((af)_{-} = a f_{-}\). By \(L^+\) homogeneity: \[
\int a f \, d\mu = \int a f_{+} \, d\mu - \int a f_{-} \, d\mu = a \int f_{+} \, d\mu - a \int f_{-} \, d\mu = a \int f \, d\mu.
\] If \(a < 0\), \((af)_{+} = -a f_{-}\) and \((af)_{-} = -a f_{+}\). Thus: \[
\begin{align*}
\int a f \, d\mu &= \int (-a) f_{-} \, d\mu - \int (-a) f_{+} \, d\mu \\
&= -a \int f_{-} \, d\mu - (-a) \int f_{+} \, d\mu\\
& = a \left( \int f_{+} \, d\mu - \int f_{-} \, d\mu \right) \\
&= a \int f \, d\mu.
\end{align*}
\]
Addition: For \(f, g \in \mathcal{L}^1\), \(f + g = (f_{+} + g_{+}) - (f_{-} + g_{-})\), which implies: \[
\begin{align*}
&(f + g)_{+} - (f + g)_{-} = (f_{+} + g_{+}) - (f_{-} + g_{-})\\
& \implies (f + g)_{+} + f_{-} + g_{-} = (f + g)_{-} + f_{+} + g_{+}
\end{align*}
\]
Since all terms belong to \(L^+\) with finite integrals, we integrate both sides using \(L^+\) additivity: \[
\int (f + g)_{+} \, d\mu + \int f_{-} \, d\mu + \int g_{-} \, d\mu = \int (f + g)_{-} \, d\mu + \int f_{+} \, d\mu + \int g_{+} \, d\mu
\]
Rearranging the finite real terms gives: \[
\begin{align*}
\int (f + g)_{+} \, d\mu - \int (f + g)_{-} \, d\mu &= \left( \int f_{+} \, d\mu - \int f_{-} \, d\mu \right) \\
&+ \left( \int g_{+} \, d\mu - \int g_{-} \, d\mu \right)
\end{align*}
\] Thus, \(\int (f + g) \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu + \int g \, d\mu\).


20.2.3 Proof of Step 3 (Monotonicity)
Assume \(f \le g\) a.e. Then \(f_{+} - f_{-} \le g_{+} - g_{-}\) a.e., which rearranges to \(f_{+} + g_{-} \le g_{+} + f_{-}\) a.e.
By monotonicity of \(L^+\) integrals (Proposition 19.1 Part 1) applied to \(f_+ + g_- \le g_+ + f_-\), and additivity of \(L^+\) integrals (Corollary 18.1): \[
\begin{align*}
&\int f_{+} \, d\mu + \int g_{-} \, d\mu \le \int g_{+} \, d\mu + \int f_{-} \, d\mu \\
&\implies \int f_{+} \, d\mu - \int f_{-} \, d\mu \le \int g_{+} \, d\mu - \int g_{-} \, d\mu.
\end{align*}
\] Therefore, \(\int f \, d\mu \le \int g \, d\mu\).


20.2.4 Proof of Step 4 (Triangle Inequality)
Using definition Equation 20.4 and standard triangle inequality on \(\mathbb{R}\): \[
\begin{align*}
\left| \int f \, d\mu \right| &= \left| \int f_{+} \, d\mu - \int f_{-} \, d\mu \right| \\
&\le \int f_{+} \, d\mu + \int f_{-} \, d\mu \\
&= \int (f_{+} + f_{-}) \, d\mu \\
&= \int |f| \, d\mu
\end{align*}
\]

title: 20  Lecture 9.2: \(L^1\) and the Dominated Convergence Theorem
text:
20.3 Semi-Norms, Equivalence Classes, and \(L^p\) Spaces

Definition 20.2 (\(\mathcal{L}^1\) Semi-Norm) The functional \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{L}^1} : \mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu) \to [0, \infty)\) defined by: \[
\|f\|_{\mathcal{L}^1} := \int_{\Omega} |f| \, d\mu.
\tag{20.8}\] is a semi-norm on \(\mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\). It satisfies:

Absolute Homogeneity: \(\|\alpha f\|_{\mathcal{L}^1} = |\alpha| \|f\|_{\mathcal{L}^1}\) for all \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\).
Subadditivity (Triangle Inequality): \(\|f + g\|_{\mathcal{L}^1} \le \|f\|_{\mathcal{L}^1} + \|g\|_{\mathcal{L}^1}\).



Remark 20.2. Failure of Definiteness: By Proposition 19.1 Part 3, \(\|f\|_{\mathcal{L}^1} = 0 \iff f = 0\) a.e. Thus, \(\|f\|_{\mathcal{L}^1} = 0\) does not imply \(f(\omega) = 0\) everywhere on \(\Omega\).


Definition 20.3 (\(L^1\) Quotient Space) We define an equivalence relation \(\sim_\mu\) on \(\mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) by: \[
f \sim_\mu g \iff f = g \text{ a.e. } [\mu].
\tag{20.9}\]
The Banach space \(L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is defined as the set of equivalence classes: \[
L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu) := \mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu) / \sim_\mu.
\tag{20.10}\]

Some remarks on \(L^1\) spaces:

For any equivalence class \([f] \in L^1\), any function \(f_1 \in [f]\) is called a version of \([f]\). The integral \(\int [f] \, d\mu := \int f_1 \, d\mu\) is well-defined independent of the choice of version.
On \(L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), \(\|[f]\|_{L^1} := \int |f| \, d\mu\) is a genuine norm, and \(d_\mu([f], [g]) := \|[f] - [g]\|_{L^1}\) is a genuine metric.
Going forward, we will often abuse notation and write \(f \in L^1\) to mean \([f] \in L^1\).

The next definition generalizes the \(L^1\) space to \(L^p\) spaces for \(1 \le p < \infty\).

Definition 20.4 (General \(L^p\) Spaces (\(1 \le p < \infty\))) For \(1 \le p < \infty\), \(L^p(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is defined as the set of equivalence classes of measurable functions \(f: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\int |f|^p \, d\mu < \infty\). The norm is defined by: \[
\|f\|_{L^p} := \left( \int_{\Omega} |f|^p \, d\mu \right)^{1/p}.
\tag{20.11}\]

The next result shows that \(L^p\) spaces are complete normed vector spaces and that the \(L^p\) norm satisfies Minkowski’s inequality.

Theorem 20.1 (Completeness of \(L^p\) (Driver [17.27])) For \(1 \le p < \infty\), the space \((L^p(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu), \|\cdot\|_{L^p})\) is a complete normed vector space (a Banach space). The norm satisfies Minkowski’s inequality: \[
\|f + g\|_{L^p} \le \|f\|_{L^p} + \|g\|_{L^p} \quad \forall f, g \in L^p.
\tag{20.12}\]

title: 20  Lecture 9.2: \(L^1\) and the Dominated Convergence Theorem
text:
20.4 The Dominated Convergence Theorem (DCT)
For \(L^{+}\), we have two integral convergence theorems: Fatou’s Lemma (Theorem 19.2) and the Monotone Convergence Theorem (Theorem 18.1). For \(L^1\), we have a single integral convergence theorem, the Dominated Convergence Theorem (DCT).

Theorem 20.2 (Dominated Convergence Theorem) Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of measurable functions, and let \(g_n, g \in \mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be integrable dominating functions such that:

\(f_n \to f\) a.e. as \(n \to \infty\).
\(g_n \to g\) a.e. as \(n \to \infty\) and \(g_n \ge 0\) a.e.
\(|f_n| \le g_n\) a.e. for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).
\(\int_{\Omega} g_n \, d\mu \to \int_{\Omega} g \, d\mu < \infty\) as \(n \to \infty\).

Then \(f \in \mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) and: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \int_{\Omega} f_n \, d\mu = \int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu.
\tag{20.13}\] In fact, \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \int_{\Omega} |f_n - f| \, d\mu = 0\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 20.2). First, since \(|f_n| \le g_n\) a.e. and \(f_n \to f\), \(g_n \to g\) a.e., taking \(n \to \infty\) yields \(|f| \le g\) a.e. Since \(g \in \mathcal{L}^1\), \(\int |f| \, d\mu \le \int g \, d\mu < \infty\), so \(f \in \mathcal{L}^1\).
Since \(|f_n| \le g_n\) a.e. and \(g_n \ge 0\) a.e., we have \(g_n + f_n \ge g_n - |f_n| \ge 0\) a.e. and \(g_n - f_n \ge g_n - |f_n| \ge 0\) a.e. Thus \((g_n + f_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset L^+\) and \((g_n - f_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset L^+\).

20.4.1 Step 1: Lower Bound via Fatou’s Lemma
Since \(g_n \to g\) and \(f_n \to f\) a.e. (hypotheses 1 and 2), \(g_n + f_n \to g + f\) a.e., so \(\liminf_{n \to \infty}(g_n + f_n) = g + f\) a.e. Applying Fatou’s Lemma (Theorem 19.2) to \(g_n + f_n \ge 0\): \[
\int (g + f) \, d\mu = \int \liminf_{n \to \infty} (g_n + f_n) \, d\mu \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \int (g_n + f_n) \, d\mu.
\]
Using linearity of the integral and \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \int g_n \, d\mu = \int g \, d\mu\): \[
\int g \, d\mu + \int f \, d\mu \le \int g \, d\mu + \liminf_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu.
\]
Subtracting the finite quantity \(\int g \, d\mu\) yields: \[
\int f \, d\mu \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu.
\tag{20.14}\]


20.4.2 Step 2: Upper Bound via Fatou’s Lemma
Since \(g_n \to g\) and \(f_n \to f\) a.e., \(g_n - f_n \to g - f\) a.e., so \(\liminf_{n \to \infty}(g_n - f_n) = g - f\) a.e. Applying Fatou’s Lemma to \(g_n - f_n \ge 0\): \[
\int (g - f) \, d\mu = \int \liminf_{n \to \infty} (g_n - f_n) \, d\mu \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \int (g_n - f_n) \, d\mu.
\]
Since \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \int g_n \, d\mu = \int g \, d\mu\) exists (hypothesis 4), \(\liminf_n(a_n + b_n) = \lim_n a_n + \liminf_n b_n\) gives: \[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} \int (g_n - f_n) \, d\mu = \int g \, d\mu + \liminf_{n \to \infty} \left( -\int f_n \, d\mu \right).
\]
Recall that \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} (-a_n) = -\limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n\). Thus: \[
\int g \, d\mu - \int f \, d\mu \le \int g \, d\mu - \limsup_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu.
\]
Subtracting \(\int g \, d\mu\) and multiplying by \(-1\) reverses the inequality: \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu \le \int f \, d\mu.
\tag{20.15}\]
Combining Equation A.17 and Equation A.18: \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu \le \int f \, d\mu \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu.
\]
Since \(\liminf \int f_n \le \limsup \int f_n\) always holds, all terms are equal, proving \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \int f_n \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu\).


20.4.3 Step 3: Convergence in \(L^1\) norm
It remains to prove \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \int |f_n - f| \, d\mu = 0\). Since \(|f_n - f| \le |f_n| + |f| \le g_n + g\) a.e., the sequence \(h_n := g_n + g - |f_n - f| \ge 0\) a.e.
Since \(g_n \to g\) a.e. and \(|f_n - f| \to 0\) a.e. (as \(f_n \to f\) a.e.), we have \(h_n \to 2g\) a.e., so \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} h_n = 2g\) a.e. Applying Fatou’s Lemma to \((h_n)\): \[
\int 2g \, d\mu = \int \liminf_{n \to \infty} h_n \, d\mu \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \int h_n \, d\mu.
\]
Since \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \int g_n \, d\mu = \int g \, d\mu\) (hypothesis 4), the same \(\liminf\) splitting gives: \[
\begin{align*}
\liminf_{n \to \infty} \int h_n \, d\mu &= \lim_{n \to \infty} \int g_n \, d\mu + \int g \, d\mu + \liminf_{n \to \infty}\left(-\int |f_n - f| \, d\mu\right)\\
& = 2\int g \, d\mu - \limsup_{n \to \infty} \int |f_n - f| \, d\mu.
\end{align*}
\]
Therefore \(2\int g \, d\mu \le 2\int g \, d\mu - \limsup_{n \to \infty} \int |f_n - f| \, d\mu\), which gives \(\limsup_{n \to \infty} \int |f_n - f| \, d\mu \le 0\). Since \(\int |f_n - f| \, d\mu \ge 0\), we conclude \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \int |f_n - f| \, d\mu = 0\).



Corollary 20.1 (Bounded Convergence Theorem) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a finite measure space (\(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\)). Suppose \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) is a sequence of measurable functions such that \(f_n \to f\) a.e., and there exists a constant \(M < \infty\) with \(|f_n(\omega)| \le M\) a.e. for all \(n\).
Then \(f \in \mathcal{L}^1\) and \(\int f_n \, d\mu \to \int f \, d\mu\).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 20.1). Set \(g_n = g = M \mathbf{1}_{\Omega}\). Since \(\int g \, d\mu = M \mu(\Omega) < \infty\), \(g\) is an integrable dominating function. The result follows directly from the Dominated Convergence Theorem (Theorem 20.2).

title: 21  Lecture 10.1: Integrals and Derivatives
text:
Theorem 21.1 (Differentiation Under the Integral Sign (Driver [10.31])) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space, \((a, b) \subset \mathbb{R}\) an open interval, and \(f: (a, b) \times \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) a function satisfying:

Measurability: \(\omega \mapsto f(t, \omega)\) is \(\mathcal{F}\)-measurable for each fixed \(t \in (a, b)\).
Integrability: \(f(t_0, \cdot) \in \mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) for at least one point \(t_0 \in (a, b)\).
Differentiability: The partial derivative \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(t, \omega)\) exists for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(\omega \in \Omega\) and for every \(t \in (a, b)\).
Domination: There exists a non-negative function \(g \in \mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) such that: \[
\left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(t, \omega) \right| \le g(\omega) \quad \text{for } \mu\text{-a.e. } \omega \in \Omega \text{ and all } t \in (a, b)
\tag{21.1}\]

Then \(f(t, \cdot) \in \mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) for all \(t \in (a, b)\), the map \(G(t) := \int_{\Omega} f(t, \omega) \, d\mu(\omega)\) is differentiable on \((a, b)\), and: \[
\frac{d}{dt} \int_{\Omega} f(t, \omega) \, d\mu(\omega) = \int_{\Omega} \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(t, \omega) \, d\mu(\omega)
\tag{21.2}\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 21.1). Fix \(t \in (a, b)\) and select any sequence \((h_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}\) such that \(t + h_n \in (a, b)\) for all \(n\) and \(h_n \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\).

21.1.1 Step 1: Integrability of \(f(t, \cdot)\)
By the Mean Value Theorem applied to \(u \mapsto f(u, \omega)\) on the interval between \(t_0\) and \(t\), there exists a point \(t^*(\omega)\) strictly between \(t_0\) and \(t\) such that: \[
|f(t, \omega) - f(t_0, \omega)| = \left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(t^*(\omega), \omega) \right| |t - t_0| \le |t - t_0| g(\omega) \quad \text{a.e.}
\]
Thus, \(|f(t, \omega)| \le |f(t_0, \omega)| + |t - t_0| g(\omega)\) a.e. Integrating both sides yields \(\int |f(t, \omega)| \, d\mu \le \int |f(t_0, \omega)| \, d\mu + |t - t_0| \int g \, d\mu < \infty\), so \(f(t, \cdot) \in \mathcal{L}^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) for all \(t \in (a, b)\).


21.1.2 Step 2: Interchanging the Limit and Integral
Define the sequence of difference quotients: \[
D_n(\omega) := \frac{f(t + h_n, \omega) - f(t, \omega)}{h_n}
\]

Pointwise Convergence: By assumption (3), \(D_n(\omega) \to \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(t, \omega)\) a.e. as \(n \to \infty\).
Uniform Domination: By the Mean Value Theorem, for each \(n\) and a.e. \(\omega\), there exists \(t_n^*(\omega)\) between \(t\) and \(t + h_n\) such that \(|D_n(\omega)| = \left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(t_n^*(\omega), \omega) \right| \le g(\omega)\).

Since \(f(t+h_n, \cdot)\) and \(f(t, \cdot)\) are measurable (condition 1), \(D_n\) is measurable. Since \(|D_n| \le g \in \mathcal{L}^1\), we have \(D_n \in \mathcal{L}^1\). The limit \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(t, \cdot)\) is measurable as the a.e. pointwise limit of the measurable functions \((D_n)\).
By linearity of the \(\mathcal{L}^1\) integral: \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{G(t + h_n) - G(t)}{h_n} &= \frac{1}{h_n}\left(\int_{\Omega} f(t+h_n, \omega)\,d\mu - \int_{\Omega} f(t, \omega)\,d\mu\right) \\
&= \int_{\Omega} D_n(\omega)\,d\mu(\omega).
\end{align*}
\]
Applying the Dominated Convergence Theorem (Theorem 20.2) with \(|D_n| \le g\) and \(D_n \to \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(t, \cdot)\) a.e.: \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{d}{dt} G(t) &= \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{G(t + h_n) - G(t)}{h_n} \\
&= \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_{\Omega} D_n(\omega) \, d\mu(\omega) \\
&= \int_{\Omega} \lim_{n \to \infty} D_n(\omega) \, d\mu(\omega)\\
&= \int_{\Omega} \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(t, \omega) \, d\mu(\omega)
\end{align*}
\]

title: 21  Lecture 10.1: Integrals and Derivatives
text:
21.2 Moment-Generating Functions and Analyticity

Definition 21.1 (Moment-Generating Function (MGF)) Let \(X\) be a real-valued random variable on a probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\). The moment-generating function \(M_X(t)\) is defined by: \[
M_X(t) := \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] = \int_{\Omega} e^{tX(\omega)} \, d\mathbb{P}(\omega) \in (0, \infty]
\tag{21.3}\]


Proposition 21.1 (Differentiation and Moments of MGF) Suppose there exists \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \(\mathbb{E}[e^{\epsilon |X|}] < \infty\). Then \(M_X(t) < \infty\) for all \(t \in (-\epsilon, \epsilon)\), \(M_X\) is infinitely differentiable on \((-\epsilon, \epsilon)\), and: \[
M_X^{(n)}(t) = \mathbb{E}[X^n e^{tX}] \quad \forall t \in (-\epsilon, \epsilon), \, n \in \mathbb{N}
\tag{21.4}\] In particular, evaluating at \(t = 0\) yields the raw moments: \[
M_X^{(n)}(0) = \mathbb{E}[X^n]
\tag{21.5}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 21.1). We prove by induction on \(n \in \mathbb{N}_0\) that \(M_X^{(n)}(t) = \mathbb{E}[X^n e^{tX}]\) for all \(t \in (-\epsilon, \epsilon)\).

21.2.1 Step 0: \(M_X(t) < \infty\) on \((-\epsilon, \epsilon)\)
Key polynomial bound. For any \(\alpha \in (0,1)\) and \(n \in \mathbb{N}_0\), the function \(u \mapsto u^n e^{-\alpha\epsilon u}\) attains its maximum on \([0,\infty)\) at \(u = n/(\alpha\epsilon)\), so: \[
\sup_{u \ge 0}\, u^n e^{-\alpha\epsilon u} = \left(\frac{n}{\alpha\epsilon e}\right)^n < \infty.
\] Consequently, there exists a finite constant \(C_{n,\alpha}\) such that: \[
|x|^n \le C_{n,\alpha}\, e^{\alpha\epsilon|x|} \quad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R}.
\tag{21.6}\]
In particular, for \(n = 0\) and any \(t \in (-\epsilon, \epsilon)\), write \(t = (1-\alpha)\epsilon \cdot \operatorname{sgn}(t) \cdot r\) for some \(r < 1\) (choosing \(\alpha\) small enough so \(|t| < (1-\alpha)\epsilon\)). Then: \[
e^{tX} \le e^{|t||X|} \le e^{(1-\alpha)\epsilon|X|} \le e^{\epsilon|X|},
\] so \(M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] \le \mathbb{E}[e^{\epsilon|X|}] < \infty\).


21.2.2 Step 1: Base case \(n = 0 \to 1\) (differentiability and \(M_X' = \mathbb{E}[X e^{tX}]\))
Fix \(t \in (-\epsilon, \epsilon)\) and choose \(\alpha \in (0,1)\) such that \(|t| < (1-\alpha)\epsilon\); this is possible since \((1-\alpha)\epsilon \nearrow \epsilon\) as \(\alpha \searrow 0\). We verify the four conditions of Theorem 21.1 for \(f(t, \omega) = e^{tX(\omega)}\) on the interval \(I_\alpha := (-(1-\alpha)\epsilon,\, (1-\alpha)\epsilon) \ni t\):

Measurability: \(\omega \mapsto e^{tX(\omega)}\) is measurable for each \(t\), since \(X\) is measurable and the exponential is continuous.
Integrability at \(t_0 = 0\): \(\mathbb{E}[e^{0 \cdot X}] = 1 < \infty\).
Differentiability: \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t} e^{tX(\omega)} = X(\omega)\,e^{tX(\omega)}\) exists for every \(\omega \in \Omega\) and every \(t \in I_\alpha\).
Domination: Using the polynomial bound Equation 21.6 with \(n=1\), \(C_\alpha := C_{1,\alpha} = \frac{1}{e\alpha\epsilon}\): \[
\left|\frac{\partial}{\partial t} e^{tX}\right| = |X|\,e^{tX} \le |X|\,e^{|t||X|} \le |X|\,e^{(1-\alpha)\epsilon|X|} \le C_\alpha\,e^{\alpha\epsilon|X|}\cdot e^{(1-\alpha)\epsilon|X|} = C_\alpha\,e^{\epsilon|X|}.
\] Since \(\mathbb{E}[e^{\epsilon|X|}] < \infty\) by hypothesis, \(g(\omega) := C_\alpha\,e^{\epsilon|X(\omega)|}\) is an integrable dominating function.

All conditions of Theorem 21.1 are satisfied on \(I_\alpha\), hence: \[
M_X'(t) = \frac{d}{dt}\,\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial t} e^{tX}\right] = \mathbb{E}[X e^{tX}].
\]


21.2.3 Step 2: Inductive step (\(n \to n+1\))
Suppose that \(M_X^{(n)}(t) = \mathbb{E}[X^n e^{tX}]\) for all \(t \in (-\epsilon,\epsilon)\). We differentiate the integral \(t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[X^n e^{tX}]\) by applying Theorem 21.1 to \(f(t,\omega) = X(\omega)^n e^{tX(\omega)}\) on the same \(I_\alpha\):

Measurability: \(\omega \mapsto X(\omega)^n e^{tX(\omega)}\) is measurable for each \(t\).
Integrability at \(t_0 = 0\): By the polynomial bound Equation 21.6, \(\mathbb{E}[|X|^n] \le C_{n,\alpha}\,\mathbb{E}[e^{\alpha\epsilon|X|}] \le C_{n,\alpha}\,\mathbb{E}[e^{\epsilon|X|}] < \infty\).
Differentiability: \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\bigl(X^n e^{tX}\bigr) = X^{n+1} e^{tX}\) exists pointwise for every \(\omega\) and \(t \in I_\alpha\).
Domination: Again by Equation 21.6

\[
\left|\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\bigl(X^n e^{tX}\bigr)\right| = |X|^{n+1} e^{|t||X|} \le |X|^{n+1} e^{(1-\alpha)\epsilon|X|} \le C_{n+1,\alpha}\,e^{\epsilon|X|} \in \mathcal{L}^1.
\]
Therefore: \[
M_X^{(n+1)}(t) = \frac{d}{dt}\,\mathbb{E}[X^n e^{tX}] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\bigl(X^n e^{tX}\bigr)\right] = \mathbb{E}[X^{n+1} e^{tX}].
\]
By induction, \(M_X^{(n)}(t) = \mathbb{E}[X^n e^{tX}]\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}_0\) and all \(t \in (-\epsilon, \epsilon)\).


21.2.4 Step 3: Moment formula
Setting \(t = 0\) in the identity just established: \[
M_X^{(n)}(0) = \mathbb{E}[X^n e^{0 \cdot X}] = \mathbb{E}[X^n].
\]



Proposition 21.2 (Analyticity of the MGF) If \(\mathbb{E}[e^{\epsilon |X|}] < \infty\) for some \(\epsilon > 0\), then \(M_X(t)\) is analytic on \((-\epsilon, \epsilon)\) and expands as a power series: \[
M_X(t) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n!} \mathbb{E}[X^n] \quad \forall t \in (-\epsilon, \epsilon)
\tag{21.7}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 21.2). We establish the power series representation in three steps.

21.2.5 Step 1: All moments are finite
By the polynomial bound Equation 21.6 from the proof of Proposition 21.1, for any fixed \(\alpha \in (0,1)\) there exists \(C_{n,\alpha} < \infty\) with \(|x|^n \le C_{n,\alpha}\,e^{\alpha\epsilon|x|}\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\). Taking expectations: \[
\mathbb{E}[|X|^n] \le C_{n,\alpha}\,\mathbb{E}[e^{\alpha\epsilon|X|}] \le C_{n,\alpha}\,\mathbb{E}[e^{\epsilon|X|}] < \infty.
\] Hence all moments of \(X\) are finite.


21.2.6 Step 2: The power series converges absolutely for \(|t| < \epsilon\)
Fix \(t \in (-\epsilon, \epsilon)\). Since \(\frac{|t|^n}{n!}|X(\omega)|^n \ge 0\) for all \(n\) and \(\omega\), Tonelli’s theorem (or the Monotone Convergence Theorem) allows us to exchange the sum and expectation: \[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{|t|^n}{n!}\,\mathbb{E}[|X|^n]
= \mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{|t|^n}{n!}\,|X|^n\right]
= \mathbb{E}[e^{|t||X|}]
\le \mathbb{E}[e^{\epsilon|X|}] < \infty,
\] where the last inequality uses \(|t| < \epsilon\). This confirms that the power series \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n!}\mathbb{E}[X^n]\) converges absolutely for every \(t \in (-\epsilon, \epsilon)\), so its radius of convergence is at least \(\epsilon\).


21.2.7 Step 3: \(M_X(t)\) equals the power series via DCT
Define the partial-sum sequence \(S_N(t, \omega) := \sum_{n=0}^{N} \frac{t^n}{n!}\,X(\omega)^n\). We verify the conditions for the Dominated Convergence Theorem (Theorem 20.2):

Pointwise convergence: For every fixed \(\omega \in \Omega\), the Taylor series of the exponential converges: \[
S_N(t, \omega) \;\xrightarrow{N\to\infty}\; e^{tX(\omega)}.
\]
Integrable domination: For \(|t| < \epsilon\): \[
|S_N(t, \omega)| \le \sum_{n=0}^{N} \frac{|t|^n}{n!}\,|X(\omega)|^n \le \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{|t|^n}{n!}\,|X(\omega)|^n = e^{|t||X(\omega)|} \le e^{\epsilon|X(\omega)|} \in \mathcal{L}^1.
\]

Since all moments are finite (Step 1), linearity of expectation gives \(\mathbb{E}[S_N] = \sum_{n=0}^N \frac{t^n}{n!}\mathbb{E}[X^n]\). Applying the Dominated Convergence Theorem: \[
M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] = \lim_{N\to\infty} \mathbb{E}[S_N(t,\cdot)] = \lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=0}^N \frac{t^n}{n!}\,\mathbb{E}[X^n] = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n!}\,\mathbb{E}[X^n].
\]


21.2.8 Step 4: Analyticity
A function that is represented by a convergent power series on an open interval is real-analytic on that interval. Since the series \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n!}\mathbb{E}[X^n]\) converges for all \(t \in (-\epsilon, \epsilon)\) (Step 2) and equals \(M_X(t)\) there (Step 3), we conclude that \(M_X\) is analytic on \((-\epsilon, \epsilon)\).

title: 21  Lecture 10.1: Integrals and Derivatives
text:
21.3 Counterexample: Failure of Uniform Domination

Example 21.1 (Failure of Interchange: Indicator Family on \([0,1]\)) Setup. Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \lambda) = ([0, 1], \mathcal{B}([0, 1]), \lambda)\) be the Lebesgue measure space and \((a,b) = (0,1)\). Define: \[
f(t, \omega) := \mathbf{1}_{[0, t]}(\omega) \quad \text{for } (t, \omega) \in (0, 1) \times [0, 1].
\] This is the indicator of the “sub-diagonal” region: \(f(t,\omega) = 1\) if \(\omega \le t\) and \(f(t,\omega) = 0\) if \(\omega > t\).

Part 1: The two computations disagree.
Direct differentiation. The integral equals the length of \([0,t]\): \[
G(t) := \int_{[0,1]} f(t, \omega)\,d\lambda(\omega) = \lambda([0,t]) = t,
\] so \(G'(t) = 1\) for all \(t \in (0,1)\).
Formal interchange. For \(\lambda\)-a.e. fixed \(\omega\) (specifically, all \(\omega \ne t\)), \(f(t,\omega)\) is locally constant in \(t\), giving \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(t,\omega) = 0\). The formal interchange therefore yields: \[
\int_{[0,1]} \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(t,\omega)\,d\lambda(\omega) = \int_{[0,1]} 0\,d\lambda(\omega) = 0.
\]
Since \(G'(t) = 1 \ne 0\), the interchange \(\frac{d}{dt}\int = \int\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\) is false here.

Part 2: Checking which conditions of Theorem 21.1 hold.
Condition 1 (Measurability): \(\checkmark\) For each fixed \(t\), \(\omega \mapsto \mathbf{1}_{[0,t]}(\omega)\) is a Borel-measurable indicator function.
Condition 2 (Integrability): \(\checkmark\) At \(t_0 = 1/2\), for example, \(\int_{[0,1]} f(1/2,\omega)\,d\lambda = 1/2 < \infty\).
Condition 3 (Differentiability): \(\boldsymbol{\times}\) — fails jointly.
For any fixed \(t \in (0,1)\), compute the difference quotient explicitly:

If \(\omega < t\): then \(f(t+h,\omega) = 1\) and \(f(t,\omega) = 1\) for all \(|h|\) small enough (so that \(\omega < t + h\) and \(\omega < t\)), giving quotient \(0 \to 0\).
If \(\omega > t\): then \(f(t+h,\omega) = 0\) and \(f(t,\omega) = 0\) for all \(|h|\) small enough, giving quotient \(0 \to 0\).
If \(\omega = t\): \(f(t,t) = 1\) (since \(t \in [0,t]\)). For \(h > 0\): \(f(t+h,t) = 1\), so the right quotient is \(0\). For \(h < 0\): \(f(t+h,t) = \mathbf{1}_{[0,t+h]}(t) = 0\) (since \(t > t+h\)), so the left quotient is \(\frac{0-1}{h} = \frac{-1}{h} \to +\infty\) as \(h \to 0^-\).

Hence for each fixed \(t\), the partial derivative \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(t,\omega)\) fails to exist at the single point \(\omega = t\), which is a \(\lambda\)-null set. So condition 3 holds for each fixed \(t\) separately. However, condition 3 requires a single null set \(N\) independent of \(t\) outside which the derivative exists for every \(t \in (0,1)\) simultaneously. But for every \(\omega \in (0,1)\), the derivative fails at \(t = \omega\). Thus any such \(N\) would need to contain all of \((0,1)\), which has positive measure. The joint condition fails.
Condition 4 (Domination): \(\boldsymbol{\times}\) — fails as well.
For \(h > 0\), the difference quotient is: \[
D_h(t, \omega) := \frac{f(t+h,\omega) - f(t,\omega)}{h} = \frac{\mathbf{1}_{(t,\,t+h]}(\omega)}{h}.
\] This equals \(1/h\) on the interval \((t, t+h]\) (of length \(h\)) and \(0\) elsewhere. For any candidate dominating function \(g \in \mathcal{L}^1([0,1])\), one needs \(g(\omega) \ge 1/h\) for all \(\omega \in (t, t+h]\). Taking \(h = \omega - t\) (i.e., for each \(\omega > t\) just above \(t\)), this forces \(g(\omega) \ge \frac{1}{\omega - t}\) for \(\omega\) near \(t\). But: \[
\int_t^{t+\delta} \frac{1}{\omega - t}\,d\omega = \Big[\log(\omega - t)\Big]_t^{t+\delta} = +\infty,
\] so no integrable \(g\) can dominate \(\{D_h\}\) uniformly over all \(h > 0\).

Lesson. The example shows that both conditions 3 and 4 are genuinely necessary. The a.e.-pointwise derivative exists for each fixed \(t\), giving a sensible-looking “answer” of \(0\) — but the integral of that answer disagrees with the true derivative \(G'(t) = 1\). The failure is not visible slice-by-slice; it only manifests in the joint structure required by the theorem.

text:
21.4 Reconstructions and Corrections

Mean Value Theorem Bound: Expanded the handwritten inequality \(|f(t, \omega) - f(t_0, \omega)| \le |t - t_0| g(\omega)\) into a explicit two-step application of MVT and domination.
MGF Derivative Domination: Detailed the inequality \(|X e^{tX}| \le C_\alpha e^{\epsilon |X|}\) using exponent splitting \(tX = \alpha t X + (1-\alpha)t X\) to guarantee rigorous domination on compact subintervals of \((-\epsilon, \epsilon)\).

title: 22  Lecture 10.2: Lebesgue vs. Riemann
text:
Theorem 22.1 (Lebesgue–Riemann Equivalence Theorem (Driver [11.5])) Let \(\overline{\mathcal{B}}\) denote the completion of the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) with respect to the Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\).
A bounded function \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) is Riemann integrable if and only if \(f\) is \(\overline{\mathcal{B}}\)-measurable and its set of discontinuities has Lebesgue measure zero: \[
\lambda(\{x \in [a, b] \mid f \text{ is discontinuous at } x\}) = 0
\tag{22.1}\]
In this case, \(f \in \mathcal{L}^1([a, b], \overline{\mathcal{B}}, \lambda)\) and the integrals coincide: \[
\int_{[a, b]} f \, d\lambda = \int_a^b f(x) \, dx
\tag{22.2}\]


Proof. (Partial Proof: Forward Direction) Assume \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a, b]\), so \(|f| \le M\) for some \(M < \infty\).

22.1.1 Step 1: Constructing measurable upper and lower envelopes
Choose a sequence of refining partitions \(\pi_1 \prec \pi_2 \prec \cdots\) with mesh \(|\pi_n| \to 0\). Write \(\pi_n = \{a = t_0^{(n)} < \cdots < t_{k_n}^{(n)} = b\}\) and \(I_j^{(n)} = (t_{j-1}^{(n)}, t_j^{(n)}]\). Define the Darboux step functions: \[
\overline{\varphi}_n := \sum_j \Bigl(\sup_{I_j^{(n)}} f\Bigr)\mathbf{1}_{I_j^{(n)}}, \qquad \underline{\varphi}_n := \sum_j \Bigl(\inf_{I_j^{(n)}} f\Bigr)\mathbf{1}_{I_j^{(n)}}.
\] Each is \(\mathcal{B}([a,b])\)-measurable, and \(\underline{\varphi}_n \le f \le \overline{\varphi}_n\) pointwise. Since \(\pi_{n+1}\) refines \(\pi_n\), the sups can only decrease and the infs can only increase on sub-intervals, giving \(\overline{\varphi}_{n+1} \le \overline{\varphi}_n\) and \(\underline{\varphi}_{n+1} \ge \underline{\varphi}_n\) pointwise. Define the pointwise monotone limits: \[
\bar{f} := \lim_{n\to\infty} \overline{\varphi}_n = \inf_n \overline{\varphi}_n, \qquad \underline{f} := \lim_{n\to\infty} \underline{\varphi}_n = \sup_n \underline{\varphi}_n.
\] Both \(\bar{f}\) and \(\underline{f}\) are \(\mathcal{B}([a,b])\)-measurable (monotone limits of measurable functions), \(|\bar{f}|, |\underline{f}| \le M\), and \(\underline{f} \le f \le \bar{f}\) everywhere.


22.1.2 Step 2: The envelopes agree \(\lambda\)-a.e.
Since \(|\overline{\varphi}_n|, |\underline{\varphi}_n| \le M\) and \(\lambda([a,b]) < \infty\), the Bounded Convergence Theorem applies: \[
\int_{[a,b]} \bar{f}\,d\lambda = \lim_{n\to\infty} \int_{[a,b]} \overline{\varphi}_n\,d\lambda = \lim_{n\to\infty} U(f,\pi_n) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx,
\] \[
\int_{[a,b]} \underline{f}\,d\lambda = \lim_{n\to\infty} \int_{[a,b]} \underline{\varphi}_n\,d\lambda = \lim_{n\to\infty} L(f,\pi_n) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx,
\] where both limits equal the Riemann integral because \(f\) is Riemann integrable (so \(\inf_\pi U(f,\pi) = \sup_\pi L(f,\pi)\)) and refining partitions with \(|\pi_n|\to 0\) force the Darboux sums to converge to this common value. Therefore: \[
\int_{[a,b]} (\bar{f} - \underline{f})\,d\lambda = 0.
\] Since \(\bar{f} - \underline{f} \ge 0\) is non-negative and measurable with zero integral, \(\bar{f} = \underline{f}\) \(\lambda\)-a.e.


22.1.3 Step 3: Measurability of \(f\) and equality of integrals
Since \(\underline{f} \le f \le \bar{f}\) everywhere and \(\bar{f} = \underline{f}\) \(\lambda\)-a.e., we have \(f = \bar{f}\) \(\lambda\)-a.e. Since \(\bar{f}\) is \(\mathcal{B}([a,b])\)-measurable and \(f\) agrees with it outside a \(\lambda\)-null set, \(f\) is \(\overline{\mathcal{B}}\)-measurable (measurability is closed under a.e.-modification in the completed \(\sigma\)-algebra). Since \(f\) is bounded and \(\lambda([a,b]) < \infty\), \(f \in \mathcal{L}^1([a,b], \overline{\mathcal{B}}, \lambda)\). Finally, by monotonicity of the Lebesgue integral and the \(\lambda\)-a.e. equality \(f = \bar{f}\): \[
\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda = \int_{[a,b]} \bar{f}\,d\lambda = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx. \qquad \square
\]

title: 22  Lecture 10.2: Lebesgue vs. Riemann
section: 22.2 Improper Riemann Integrals and Lebesgue Integration
text:
22.2 Improper Riemann Integrals and Lebesgue Integration
The Lebesgue integral also provides a rigorous foundation for improper Riemann integrals.

Proposition 22.1 Suppose \(f \in \mathcal{L}^1(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}), \lambda)\). Then: \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}} f \, d\lambda = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_{[-n, n]} f \, d\lambda.
\tag{22.3}\] If additionally \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([-n, n]\) for each \(n\) (equivalently, \(f\) is bounded and a.e. continuous on each \([-n, n]\), by Theorem 22.1), then also: \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}} f \, d\lambda = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_{-n}^n f(x) \, dx.
\tag{22.4}\]


Proof. Define \(f_n := f \mathbf{1}_{[-n, n]}\). Pointwise, \(f_n(x) \to f(x)\) as \(n \to \infty\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).

Non-negative case (\(f \ge 0\)): \(f_n \ge 0\) and \(f_n \uparrow f\). Applying the Monotone Convergence Theorem (Corollary 19.1): \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}} f \, d\lambda = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_{\mathbb{R}} f \mathbf{1}_{[-n, n]} \, d\lambda = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_{[-n, n]} f \, d\lambda.
\]
General \(f \in \mathcal{L}^1\): \(|f_n| \le |f| \in \mathcal{L}^1(\mathbb{R})\) and \(f_n \to f\) pointwise. By the Dominated Convergence Theorem (Theorem 20.2), the first equality in Equation 22.3 follows.
Equality with the Riemann integral: When \(f\) is additionally Riemann integrable on each \([-n,n]\), Theorem 22.1 gives \(\int_{[-n,n]} f\,d\lambda = \int_{-n}^n f(x)\,dx\) for each \(n\), yielding Equation 22.4.

title: 22  Lecture 10.2: Lebesgue vs. Riemann
text:
22.3 Radon Measures and Absolute Continuity
Let \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a non-decreasing, right-continuous function. \(F\) generates a unique Radon measure \(\mu_F\) on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) satisfying \(\mu_F((a, b]) = F(b) - F(a)\).

Proposition 22.2 (Radon Measures with \(C^1\) Distribution Functions) Suppose \(F \in C^1([a, b])\) with \(F' \ge 0\). Then \(\mu_F\) is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\) on \([a,b]\), with density \(\frac{d\mu_F}{d\lambda} = F'\). Specifically, for any Borel set \(A \subseteq [a, b]\): \[
\mu_F(A) = \int_A F'(x) \, d\lambda(x)
\tag{22.5}\]
Furthermore, for any \(f \in \mathcal{L}^1([a, b], \mu_F)\), we have \(f F' \in \mathcal{L}^1([a, b], \lambda)\) and: \[
\int_{[a, b]} f \, d\mu_F = \int_a^b f(x) F'(x) \, dx
\tag{22.6}\]


Proof. Define \(\nu(A) := \int_A F' \, d\lambda\) for \(A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\). For any interval \((a, b]\), the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives: \[
\nu((a, b]) = \int_a^b F'(x) \, dx = F(b) - F(a) = \mu_F((a, b])
\]
Since intervals of the form \((a, b]\) generate the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) and form a \(\pi\)-system, \(\mu_F = \nu\) on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) by the Uniqueness of Measures. The integration identity Equation 22.6 follows by standard simple-function approximation.

title: 22  Lecture 10.2: Lebesgue vs. Riemann
section: 22.4 Singular Measures and the Cantor Function
text:
22.4 Singular Measures and the Cantor Function
Not every continuous distribution function \(F\) yields a measure with a density with respect to Lebesgue measure.

Example 22.1 (Point Mass (Dirac Measure)) Let \(F = \mathbf{1}_{[x_0, \infty)}\), so \(\mu_F = \delta_{x_0}\). If \(\delta_{x_0}(A) = \int_A \rho \, d\lambda\) for some non-negative density \(\rho \ge 0\), then taking \(A = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{x_0\}\) gives: \[
0 = \delta_{x_0}(\mathbb{R} \setminus \{x_0\}) = \int_{\mathbb{R} \setminus \{x_0\}} \rho \, d\lambda \implies \rho = 0 \text{ a.e. } [\lambda]
\]
This forces \(\int_{\mathbb{R}} \rho \, d\lambda = 0 \ne \delta_{x_0}(\{x_0\}) = 1\). Thus, point masses cannot possess a Lebesgue density; \(\mu_F\) must have no point masses (i.e., \(F\) must be continuous) as a prerequisite for absolute continuity.


Example 22.2 (The Devil’s Staircase (Cantor Function)) Even continuous, a.e.-differentiable functions may fail the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
Let \(F: [0, 1] \to [0, 1]\) be the Cantor Ternary Function (Devil’s Staircase):

\(F\) is continuous and non-decreasing with \(F(0) = 0\) and \(F(1) = 1\).
\(F\) is constant on every open interval removed during the construction of \(C\) (i.e., on each component of \([0, 1] \setminus C\)), so \(F'(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in [0, 1] \setminus C\). Since \(\lambda(C) = 0\), the complement \([0, 1] \setminus C\) has full Lebesgue measure, and therefore \(F'(x) = 0\) for \(\lambda\)-a.e. \(x \in [0, 1]\).

Integrating \(F'\) yields: \[
\int_{[0, 1]} F' \, d\lambda = \int_{[0, 1]} 0 \, d\lambda = 0 \ne F(1) - F(0) = 1
\]
Consequently, \(\mu_F(A) \ne \int_A F' \, d\lambda\). The measure \(\mu_F\) is singular continuous: it has no point masses (\(\mu_F(\{x\}) = 0\) everywhere) yet is supported entirely on a set of Lebesgue measure zero (\(\mu_F(C) = 1\), \(\lambda(C) = 0\)).

title: 23  Lecture 11.1: Radon-Nikodym
text:
Definition 23.1 (Absolute Continuity) Let \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) be measures on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\). We say that \(\nu\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(\mu\) (written \(\nu \ll \mu\)) if every \(\mu\)-null set is also a \(\nu\)-null set: \[
A \in \mathcal{F}, \; \mu(A) = 0 \implies \nu(A) = 0
\tag{23.1}\]



Theorem 23.1 (Radon-Nikodym Theorem) Let \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) be \(\sigma\)-finite measures on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\). Then \(\nu \ll \mu\) if and only if there exists a measurable density function \(\rho: \Omega \to [0, \infty)\) such that: \[
\nu(A) = \int_A \rho \, d\mu \quad \forall A \in \mathcal{F}
\tag{23.2}\]
In differential notation, \(d\nu = \rho \, d\mu\). Furthermore, the density \(\rho\) is uniquely determined \(\mu\)-almost everywhere. The function \(\rho\) is called the Radon-Nikodym derivative of \(\nu\) with respect to \(\mu\), denoted by: \[
\rho = \frac{d\nu}{d\mu}
\tag{23.3}\]

Definition 23.2 (Mutual Singularity) Two measures \(\mu\) and \(

u(A^c) = 0 \quad 	ext{and} \quad \mu(A) = 0
	ag{23.5}\]


Theorem 23.2 (Lebesgue Decomposition Theorem (Driver [20.8])) Let \(\mu\) and \(
u\) be \(\sigma\)-finite measures on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\). Then \(
u\) can be uniquely decomposed as: \[

u =

	ag{23.6}\] where:

u_a = ho \, d\mu\) for a unique density \(ho =  rac{d

title: 23  Lecture 11.1: Radon-Nikodym
section: 23.3 Refined Decomposition: Discrete vs. Singular Continuous
text:
23.3 Refined Decomposition: Discrete vs. Singular Continuous
The singular component \(\nu_s\) can be further refined into point-mass (discrete) and singular continuous parts.

Definition 23.3 (Three-Part Lebesgue Decomposition) For any \(\sigma\)-finite measure \(\nu\) on \((\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) relative to the Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\), \(\nu\) can be uniquely split into three mutually singular parts: \[
\nu = \nu_a + \nu_{pp} + \nu_{sc}
\tag{23.7}\]

Absolutely Continuous Part (\(\nu_a\)): \(\nu_a \ll \lambda\), possessing a density \(d\nu_a = \rho \, d\lambda\).
Pure Point Part (\(\nu_{pp}\)): A countable linear combination of Dirac delta measures: \[
\nu_{pp} = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \alpha_j \delta_{x_j}, \quad \alpha_j \ge 0, \, x_j \in \mathbb{R}^d
\tag{23.8}\] Since \(\lambda(\{x_j\}_{j=1}^\infty) = 0\) and \(\nu_{pp}(\mathbb{R}^d \setminus \{x_j\}_{j=1}^\infty) = 0\), \(\nu_{pp} \perp \lambda\).
Singular Continuous Part (\(\nu_{sc}\)): \(\nu_{sc} \perp \lambda\), but \(\nu_{sc}(\{x\}) = 0\) for every single point \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\) (no point masses).



Example 23.1 (Singular Continuous Measures (The Devil’s Staircase)) Not all singular measures are discrete point masses.
Let \(\mu_F\) be the Radon measure generated by the Cantor Ternary Function (Devil’s Staircase) \(F: [0, 1] \to [0, 1]\).

No Point Masses: Because \(F\) is continuous, \(\mu_F(\{x\}) = F(x) - F(x^-) = 0\) for all \(x \in [0, 1]\), so \(\mu_{pp} = 0\).
Mutual Singularity: Let \(C \subset [0, 1]\) be the Cantor set. Then \(\lambda(C) = 0\). For the complement \(C^c = [0,1]\setminus C\): during the Cantor construction, \(C^c\) is a countable union of pairwise disjoint open intervals \((a_k, b_k)\) on each of which \(F\) is constant (say with value \(c_k\)). For each such interval, \(\mu_F((a_k, b_k)) = F(b_k^-) - F(a_k) = c_k - c_k = 0\). By countable additivity, \(\mu_F(C^c) = \sum_k \mu_F((a_k, b_k)) = 0\). Taking \(A = C\) in Definition 23.2, \(\lambda(A) = \lambda(C) = 0\) and \(\mu_F(A^c) = \mu_F(C^c) = 0\), which proves \(\mu_F \perp \lambda\).

Consequently, \(\mu_F\) is a purely singular continuous measure (\(\mu_F = \nu_{sc}\)).
