title: 24  Lecture 11.2: Laws Revisited
text:
24.2 Motivation and Finite Setup
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space. If \(\Omega\) is a finite sample space and \(X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is a finite-valued random variable, the expectation of \(X\) is defined as: \[
\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} X(\omega) \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) = \int_{\Omega} X \, d\mathbb{P}.
\]
If \(g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is a measurable function, then \(g \circ X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is also a random variable. Assuming \(X\) takes finitely many distinct values \(\{t_1, t_2, \dots, t_n\} \subset \mathbb{R}\), we can compute the expectation of \(g(X)\) by partitioning \(\Omega\) according to the level sets \(X^{-1}(\{t_j\})\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[g(X)] &= \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} g(X(\omega)) \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} \sum_{\omega \in X^{-1}(\{t_j\})} g(X(\omega)) \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} g(t_j) \sum_{\omega \in X^{-1}(\{t_j\})} \mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} g(t_j) \mathbb{P}\bigl(\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) = t_j\}\bigr) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} g(t_j) \mathbb{P}\bigl(X^{-1}(\{t_j\})\bigr) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} g(t_j) \mu_X(\{t_j\}) \\
&= \int_{\mathbb{R}} g \, d\mu_X,
\end{aligned}
\] where \(\mu_X \triangleq X_{*} \mathbb{P} = \mathbb{P} \circ X^{-1}\) denotes the push-forward measure (law/distribution) of \(X\) under \(\mathbb{P}\).

title: 24  Lecture 11.2: Laws Revisited
text:
24.2 Abstract Change of Variables

The identity above generalizes to arbitrary measure spaces and measurable mappings via the abstract Change of Variables Theorem.
The change of variables formula is a special case of the Radon-Nikodym Theorem when the push-forward measure is absolutely continuous with respect to a reference measure. It allows us to compute expectations of functions of random variables in terms of their distribution (law) without reference to the underlying probability space.


Proposition 24.1 (Abstract Change of Variables) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space, \((S, \mathcal{S})\) be a measurable space, and \(X: \Omega \to S\) be an \((\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{S})\)-measurable function. Define the push-forward measure \(\nu \triangleq X_* \mu\) on \((S, \mathcal{S})\) by \(\nu(B) = \mu(X^{-1}(B))\) for all \(B \in \mathcal{S}\).
A measurable function \(g: S \to \mathbb{R}\) is in \(L^1(S, \mathcal{S}, \nu)\) if and only if \(g \circ X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is in \(L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\). In either case, \[
\int_{S} g \, d(X_* \mu) = \int_{S} g \, d\nu = \int_{\Omega} (g \circ X) \, d\mu.
\tag{24.1}\]

Some Remarks:

The important conceptual point is that integration with respect to the distribution/push-forward of \(X\) is equivalent to integration over the original space after composing with \(X\).
The push-forward measure \(\nu=X_*\mu\) simply records how much \(\mu\)-mass gets transported to each part of \(S\): \(\nu(B) = \mu\{\omega:X(\omega)\in B\}\). So \(\nu\) tells us how much mass \(X\) assigns to each set of values in \(S\).
Now suppose we want to calculate \(\int_\Omega g(X(\omega))\,d\mu(\omega)\). Although this integral is formally over \(\Omega\), the quantity \(g(X(\omega))\) depends on \(\omega\) only through the value \(X(\omega)\). Therefore, we don’t really need to keep track of the individual \(\omega\)’s. We can instead group together all \(\omega\)’s that produce the same region of \(S\). The push-forward measure \(\nu\) does exactly this grouping. Thus, \[
\int_\Omega g(X(\omega))\,d\mu(\omega) = \int_S g(x)\,d\nu(x).
\]


Proof (Proof of Equation 24.1). The proof follows the standard measure-theoretic induction: indicators \(\to\) simple functions \(\to\) non-negative measurables \(\to\) general \(L^1\).

24.2.1 Step 1: Indicator functions
Let \(g = \mathbf{1}_B\) for \(B \in \mathcal{S}\). Using the key identity \(\mathbf{1}_B \circ X = \mathbf{1}_{X^{-1}(B)}\) (since \((\mathbf{1}_B \circ X)(\omega) = 1 \iff X(\omega) \in B \iff \omega \in X^{-1}(B)\)) and the definition of the push-forward \(\nu(B) = \mu(X^{-1}(B))\): \[
\int_S \mathbf{1}_B \, d\nu = \nu(B) = \mu\bigl(X^{-1}(B)\bigr) = \int_{\Omega} \mathbf{1}_{X^{-1}(B)} \, d\mu = \int_{\Omega} (\mathbf{1}_B \circ X) \, d\mu.
\]


24.2.2 Step 2: Non-negative simple functions
Let \(g = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i \mathbf{1}_{B_i}\) with \(c_i \ge 0\) and \(B_i \in \mathcal{S}\) pairwise disjoint. Then \(g \circ X = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \mathbf{1}_{X^{-1}(B_i)}\). By linearity of the integral and Step 1: \[
\begin{align*}
\int_S g \, d\nu &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i \, \nu(B_i) \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i \, \mu\bigl(X^{-1}(B_i)\bigr)\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i \,\int_{\Omega} (\mathbf{1}_{X^{-1}(B_i)}) \, d\mu\\
&= \int_{\Omega} \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i\ \mathbf{1}_{X^{-1}(B_i)} \, d\mu \\
&= \int_{\Omega} (g \circ X) \, d\mu.
\end{align*}
\]


24.2.3 Step 3: Non-negative measurable functions
Let \(g: S \to [0, \infty)\) be measurable. By the simple-function approximation theorem, there exist non-negative simple functions \(0 \le s_n \uparrow g\) pointwise on \(S\). Then \(0 \le s_n \circ X \uparrow g \circ X\) pointwise on \(\Omega\). Applying the Monotone Convergence Theorem (Corollary 19.1) twice and using Step 2: \[
\int_S g \, d\nu = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_S s_n \, d\nu = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_{\Omega} (s_n \circ X) \, d\mu = \int_{\Omega} (g \circ X) \, d\mu.
\]


24.2.4 Step 4: \(L^1\) equivalence and general signed functions
For general measurable \(g\), write \(g = g^+ - g^-\) where \(g^+ = \max(g, 0)\) and \(g^- = \max(-g, 0)\). Note that \((g \circ X)^+ = g^+ \circ X\) and \((g \circ X)^- = g^- \circ X\) pointwise. Applying Step 3 to \(|g| = g^+ + g^-\): \[
\int_S |g| \, d\nu = \int_{\Omega} (|g| \circ X) \, d\mu = \int_{\Omega} |g \circ X| \, d\mu.
\] This establishes the \(L^1\) equivalence: \(g \in L^1(S, \mathcal{S}, \nu) \iff g \circ X \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\). When either (hence both) conditions hold, both \(\int_S g^\pm \, d\nu\) and \(\int_\Omega (g^\pm \circ X)\,d\mu\) are finite, and: \[
\begin{align*}
\int_S g \, d\nu &= \int_S g^+ \, d\nu - \int_S g^- \, d\nu \\
&= \int_{\Omega} (g^+ \circ X) \, d\mu - \int_{\Omega} (g^- \circ X) \, d\mu\\
&= \int_{\Omega} (g \circ X) \, d\mu.
\end{align*}
\]


Step 3 of the preceding proof is used often enough on its own to be recorded separately. Note that it needs no integrability hypothesis, and that it extends verbatim to integrands taking the value \(+\infty\).

Corollary 24.1 (Change of Variables for Non-Negative Integrands) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space, \((S, \mathcal{S})\) a measurable space, \(X: \Omega \to S\) an \((\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{S})\)-measurable map, and \(\nu \triangleq X_* \mu\). Then for every \(\mathcal{S}/\mathcal{B}([0,\infty])\)-measurable \(g: S \to [0, \infty]\), \[
\int_S g \, d\nu = \int_\Omega (g \circ X) \, d\mu \qquad \text{in } [0, \infty].
\tag{24.2}\]


Proof (Proof of Corollary 24.1). For \(g\) with values in \([0, \infty)\) this is Step 3 of the proof of Proposition 24.1. For general \(g: S \to [0, \infty]\), set \(g_n \triangleq \min(g, n)\), so that \(g_n: S \to [0, \infty)\) is measurable and \(g_n \uparrow g\) pointwise on \(S\). Then \(g_n \circ X \uparrow g \circ X\) pointwise on \(\Omega\), and applying Theorem 18.1 on both spaces together with the finite-valued case gives \[
\int_S g \, d\nu = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_S g_n \, d\nu = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_\Omega (g_n \circ X) \, d\mu = \int_\Omega (g \circ X) \, d\mu .
\]

title: 24  Lecture 11.2: Laws Revisited
text:
24.5 Example: Moments and Tail Behavior
For \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), the \(n\)-th moment of \(X\) is: \[
\mathbb{E}[X^n] = \int_{\mathbb{R}} t^n \, \mu_X(dt).
\]

Proposition 24.2 (Moment Hierarchy) Let \(X\) be a real-valued random variable and \(0 \le q < p\). If \(\mathbb{E}[|X|^p] < \infty\), then \(\mathbb{E}[|X|^q] < \infty\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 24.2). Split the integral at \(|t| = 1\): \[
\mathbb{E}[|X|^q] = \int_{|t| < 1} |t|^q \, \mu_X(dt) + \int_{|t| \ge 1} |t|^q \, \mu_X(dt).
\]
For the first term, \(|t|^q \le 1\) on \(\{|t| < 1\}\), so: \[
\int_{|t| < 1} |t|^q \, \mu_X(dt) \le \mu_X(\mathbb{R}) = 1 < \infty.
\]
For the second term, \(|t|^q \le |t|^p\) on \(\{|t| \ge 1\}\) (since \(p > q\)), so: \[
\int_{|t| \ge 1} |t|^q \, \mu_X(dt) \le \int_{|t| \ge 1} |t|^p \, \mu_X(dt) \le \mathbb{E}[|X|^p] < \infty.
\]
Combining both terms gives \(\mathbb{E}[|X|^q] < \infty\).

Thus, if a random variable has a finite \(p\)-th absolute moment, then it has finite absolute moments of every order \(q\in[0,p)\).

title: 24  Lecture 11.2: Laws Revisited
text: 24.5 Standard Continuous and Discrete Distributions

title: 24  Lecture 11.2: Laws Revisited
text:
24.5 Normal (Gaussian) Distributions
Let \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(t > 0\). The normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(\alpha, t)\) has probability density function: \[
f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}} e^{-\frac{(x - \alpha)^2}{2t}}, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}.
\]

Proposition 24.3 If \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha, t)\) and \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\), then \(X \overset{d}{=} \sqrt{t} Z + \alpha\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 24.3). Note that since \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), its law \(\mu_Z\) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure and has density \(\phi(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/2}\). Therefore \(\mu_Z(dx) = \phi(x) dx\).
For any non-negative measurable function \(g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\): \[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(\sqrt{t}Z + \alpha)\bigr] = \int_{\mathbb{R}} g(\sqrt{t}x + \alpha) \, \mu_Z(dx) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} g(\sqrt{t}x + \alpha) \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/2} \, dx.
\]
Applying the substitution \(u = \sqrt{t}x + \alpha\), so that \(x = \frac{u - \alpha}{\sqrt{t}}\) and \(dx = \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} du\): \[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(\sqrt{t}Z + \alpha)\bigr] = \int_{\mathbb{R}} g(u) \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}} e^{-\frac{(u - \alpha)^2}{2t}} \, du = \mathbb{E}[g(X)].
\] Choosing \(g = \mathbf{1}_{(a, b]}\), we obtain: \[
\mathbb{P}(X \in (a, b]) = \mathbb{P}\bigl(\sqrt{t}Z + \alpha \in (a, b]\bigr) \implies \mu_X = \mu_{\sqrt{t}Z + \alpha}.
\]

Let \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\).

First Moment: By symmetry: \[
\mathbb{E}[Z] = \int_{\mathbb{R}} x \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/2} \, dx = \lim_{r \to \infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-r}^{r} x e^{-x^2/2} \, dx = 0.
\]
Second Moment: Using integration by parts: \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[Z^2] &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \lim_{r \to \infty} \int_{-r}^{r} x \cdot \left(x e^{-x^2/2}\right) dx \\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \left( \lim_{r \to \infty} \left[ -x e^{-x^2/2} \right]_{-r}^{r} + \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2/2} \, dx \right) \\
&= 0 + 1 = 1.
\end{align*}
\]
Expectation of \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha, t)\): \[
\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[\sqrt{t}Z + \alpha] = \sqrt{t} \mathbb{E}[Z] + \alpha = \alpha.
\]

For higher moments of the standard normal distribution, we can use Gaussian integration by parts. The following proposition formalizes this technique.

Proposition 24.4 Let \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\). For any continuously differentiable function \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\mathbb{E}[|f'(Z)|] < \infty\) and boundary terms vanish at infinity: \[
\mathbb{E}[Z f(Z)] = \mathbb{E}[f'(Z)].
\tag{24.4}\]

Applying Equation 24.4 with \(f(z) = z^{n+1}\) yields the recurrence relation: \[
\mathbb{E}[Z^{n+2}] = \mathbb{E}[Z \cdot Z^{n+1}] = (n + 1) \mathbb{E}[Z^n].
\]
By induction, for \(n \in \mathbb{N}_0\): \[
\mathbb{E}[Z^n] = \begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd,} \\
(n - 1)!! = (n - 1)(n - 3) \cdots 3 \cdot 1 & \text{if } n \text{ is even.}
\end{cases}
\]

Remark 24.1. For even \(n\), \((n-1)!!\) represents the number of distinct pairings (matchings) of \(n\) distinct objects.

title: 24  Lecture 11.2: Laws Revisited
text:
24.6 Exponential Distributions

Definition 24.1 A random variable \(T\) follows an exponential distribution with parameter \(\alpha > 0\), written \(T \sim \text{Exp}(\alpha)\), if its CDF is given by: \[
F_T(t) = (1 - e^{-\alpha t}) \mathbf{1}_{\{t \ge 0\}}.
\]

Differentiating \(F_T\) with respect to \(t\) yields the density function: \[
f_T(t) = F_T'(t) = \alpha e^{-\alpha t} \mathbf{1}_{[0, \infty)}(t).
\]
The exponential distribution frequently models waiting times, with tail probability: \[
\mathbb{P}(T > t) = 1 - F_T(t) = e^{-\alpha t}, \quad t \ge 0.
\]
Using the density \(f_T\), we can calculate the expectation of \(T\) as: \[
\mathbb{E}[T] = \int_{0}^{\infty} t \cdot \alpha e^{-\alpha t} \, dt.
\]
Since \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} e^{-\alpha t} = -t e^{-\alpha t}\), we have \(\alpha t e^{-\alpha t} = -\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} e^{-\alpha t}\). The interchange of differentiation and integration is justified by the Dominated Convergence Theorem: for any fixed \(\alpha_0 > 0\) and all \(\alpha \ge \alpha_0\), the dominating function \(t e^{-\alpha_0 t}\) is integrable on \([0, \infty)\). Therefore: \[
\mathbb{E}[T] = -\alpha \frac{d}{d\alpha} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-\alpha t} \, dt = -\alpha \frac{d}{d\alpha} \left( \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) = -\alpha \left( -\frac{1}{\alpha^2} \right) = \frac{1}{\alpha}.
\]

title: 24  Lecture 11.2: Laws Revisited
text:
24.7 Poisson Distribution

Definition 24.2 A discrete random variable \(N: \Omega \to \mathbb{N}_0\) follows a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\alpha > 0\), written \(N \sim \text{Pois}(\alpha)\), if: \[
\mathbb{P}(N = k) = e^{-\alpha} \frac{\alpha^k}{k!}, \quad k \in \mathbb{N}_0.
\]

The Poisson distribution models the number of events occurring within a fixed time interval. Note that it defines a valid probability distribution since: \[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(N = k) = e^{-\alpha} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{\alpha^k}{k!} = e^{-\alpha} e^{\alpha} = 1.
\]
The \(k=0\) term contributes nothing, so: \[
\mathbb{E}[N] = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k \, e^{-\alpha} \frac{\alpha^k}{k!} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} e^{-\alpha} \frac{\alpha^k}{(k-1)!}.
\]
Substituting \(j = k - 1\): \[
\mathbb{E}[N] = \alpha e^{-\alpha} \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{\alpha^j}{j!} = \alpha e^{-\alpha} e^{\alpha} = \alpha.
\]

title: 24  Lecture 11.2: Laws Revisited
text:
24.8 Uniform Random Variables and Vectors
Let \(\lambda\) denote \(d\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Let \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\) with \(0 < \lambda(B) < \infty\).

Definition 24.3 A random vector \(\mathbf{X}\) is uniformly distributed on \(B\), written \(\mathbf{X} \sim \text{Unif}(B)\), if for any \(A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\): \[
\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X} \in A) = \frac{\lambda(A \cap B)}{\lambda(B)} = \frac{1}{\lambda(B)} \int_{A} \mathbf{1}_B \, d\lambda.
\]

The density function of \(\mathbf{X}\) with respect to Lebesgue measure is \(f_{\mathbf{X}} = \frac{1}{\lambda(B)} \mathbf{1}_B\).
For \(U \sim \text{Unif}([a, b])\) with \(a < b\), \(f_U(x) = \frac{1}{b - a} \mathbf{1}_{[a, b]}(x)\). The expectation is: \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[U] &= \int_{\mathbb{R}} x \frac{1}{b - a} \mathbf{1}_{[a, b]}(x) \, dx \\
&= \frac{1}{b - a} \int_{a}^{b} x \, dx = \frac{1}{b - a} \left[ \frac{b^2 - a^2}{2} \right] = \frac{a + b}{2}.
\end{align*}
\]

title: 25  Lecture 12.1: \(L^2\) and Covariance
25  Lecture 12.1: \(L^2\) and Covariance
text:
25.2 Inclusions and Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
The following proposition shows that the product of two \(L^2\) functions is integrable, which is a key fact in defining covariance and correlation.

Proposition 25.1 If \(f, g \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), then \(fg \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 25.1). For any \(f, g \in \mathbb{R}\), expanding \(0 \le (|f| - |g|)^2 = f^2 - 2|fg| + g^2\) yields the elementary point-wise inequality: \[
|fg| \le \frac{1}{2} \left( f^2 + g^2 \right).
\tag{25.1}\]
Integrating Equation 25.1 over \(\Omega\) with respect to \(\mu\): \[
\int_{\Omega} |fg| \, d\mu \le \frac{1}{2} \int_{\Omega} f^2 \, d\mu + \frac{1}{2} \int_{\Omega} g^2 \, d\mu < \infty.
\]
Thus, \(fg \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\).

This result implies the following corollary, which shows that \(L^2\) functions are also \(L^1\) functions when the measure is finite.

Corollary 25.1 If \(\mu\) is a finite measure (\(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\)), then \(L^2(\mu) \subseteq L^1(\mu)\).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 25.1). Let \(f \in L^2(\mu)\). Taking \(g = \mathbf{1}_{\Omega} \in L^2(\mu)\), we have \(\int_{\Omega} \mathbf{1}_{\Omega}^2 \, d\mu = \mu(\Omega) < \infty\). By Proposition 25.1, \(f \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\Omega} = f \in L^1(\mu)\).

title: 25  Lecture 12.1: \(L^2\) and Covariance
text:
25.3 Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
For \(f, g \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), define the inner product and norm: \[
\langle f, g \rangle_{L^2} \triangleq \int_{\Omega} fg \, d\mu, \quad \|f\|_{L^2} \triangleq \left( \int_{\Omega} f^2 \, d\mu \right)^{1/2}.
\tag{25.2}\]

Theorem 25.1 (Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality) If \(f, g \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), then: \[
\left| \int_{\Omega} fg \, d\mu \right| \le \int_{\Omega} |fg| \, d\mu \le \|f\|_{L^2} \|g\|_{L^2}.
\tag{25.3}\]


Proof (Proof of Equation 25.3). The inequality \(\left|\int_{\Omega} fg \, d\mu\right| \le \int_{\Omega} |fg| \, d\mu\) is standard. To establish the second inequality, define the quadratic polynomial for \(t \in \mathbb{R}\): \[
p(t) \triangleq \int_{\Omega} (|f| - t|g|)^2 \, d\mu \ge 0.
\]
Expanding the integrand: \[
\begin{aligned}
p(t) &= \int_{\Omega} f^2 \, d\mu - 2t \int_{\Omega} |fg| \, d\mu + t^2 \int_{\Omega} g^2 \, d\mu \\
&= \|f\|_{L^2}^2 - 2t \int_{\Omega} |fg| \, d\mu + t^2 \|g\|_{L^2}^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(p(t) \ge 0\) for all \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), its discriminant \(\Delta\) must be non-positive: \[
\Delta = \left( -2 \int_{\Omega} |fg| \, d\mu \right)^2 - 4 \|f\|_{L^2}^2 \|g\|_{L^2}^2 \le 0.
\]
\[
4 \left( \int_{\Omega} |fg| \, d\mu \right)^2 \le 4 \|f\|_{L^2}^2 \|g\|_{L^2}^2 \implies \int_{\Omega} |fg| \, d\mu \le \|f\|_{L^2} \|g\|_{L^2}.
\]

title: 25  Lecture 12.1: \(L^2\) and Covariance
text:
25.4 Vector Space Structure of \(L^2\)

Corollary 25.2 \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is a vector space, and \(\|\cdot\|_{L^2}\) defines a norm on it (up to \(\mu\)-almost sure equivalence classes).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 25.2). We verify the norm axioms:

Homogeneity: For \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(f \in L^2\), \(\|\alpha f\|_{L^2}^2 = \int_{\Omega} (\alpha f)^2 \, d\mu = \alpha^2 \int_{\Omega} f^2 \, d\mu = \alpha^2 \|f\|_{L^2}^2\), so \(\|\alpha f\|_{L^2} = |\alpha| \|f\|_{L^2}\).
Positive Definiteness: \(\|f\|_{L^2} = 0 \implies \int_{\Omega} f^2 \, d\mu = 0 \implies f^2 = 0 \quad \mu\text{-a.s.} \implies f = 0 \quad \mu\text{-a.s.}\)
Triangle Inequality (Minkowski’s Inequality): For \(f, g \in L^2\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\|f + g\|_{L^2}^2 &= \int_{\Omega} (f + g)^2 \, d\mu = \int_{\Omega} f^2 \, d\mu + 2 \int_{\Omega} fg \, d\mu + \int_{\Omega} g^2 \, d\mu \\
&\le \|f\|_{L^2}^2 + 2 \|f\|_{L^2} \|g\|_{L^2} + \|g\|_{L^2}^2 = \left( \|f\|_{L^2} + \|g\|_{L^2} \right)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Taking square roots yields \(\|f + g\|_{L^2} \le \|f\|_{L^2} + \|g\|_{L^2} < \infty\).


Remark 25.1. \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is a Hilbert space under the inner product \[
\langle f, g \rangle_{L^2} = \int fg \, d\mu.
\] It is Cauchy complete. That is, if \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset L^2\) is Cauchy (\(\|f_n - f_m\|_{L^2} \to 0\) as \(n, m \to \infty\)), there exists \(f \in L^2\) such that \(\|f_n - f\|_{L^2} \to 0\). Completeness holds in general \(L^p\) spaces for \(1 \le p \le \infty\) and plays a crucial role in constructing conditional expectations.

title: 25  Lecture 12.1: \(L^2\) and Covariance
text:
25.5 Covariance, Variance, and Correlation
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space. Because \(\mathbb{P}(\Omega) = 1 < \infty\), \(L^2(\mathbb{P}) \subseteq L^1(\mathbb{P})\). In particular: \[
\begin{aligned}
\|X\|_{L^1} &= \int_{\Omega} |X| \, d\mathbb{P} = \int_{\Omega} |X \cdot 1| \, d\mathbb{P} \\
&\le \|X\|_{L^2} \|1\|_{L^2} = \|X\|_{L^2} = \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X^2]}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{25.4}\]
Thus, \(|\mathbb{E}[X]| \le \mathbb{E}[|X|] \le \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X^2]}\).
For \(X, Y \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\), define the centered random variables: \[
\dot{X} \triangleq X - \mathbb{E}[X], \quad \dot{Y} \triangleq Y - \mathbb{E}[Y]
\tag{25.5}\]

Definition 25.2  

Covariance: \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Cov}(X, Y) &\triangleq \mathbb{E}[\dot{X} \dot{Y}] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y].
\end{aligned}
\]
Variance: \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Var}(X) &\triangleq \text{Cov}(X, X) = \mathbb{E}[\dot{X}^2] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 \ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]



Lemma 25.1 If \(X \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) and \(\text{Var}(X) = 0\), then \(X = \mathbb{E}[X]\) \(\mathbb{P}\)-almost surely (i.e., \(X\) is constant a.s.).


Proof (Proof of Lemma 25.1). \(0 = \text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\dot{X}^2] = \int_{\Omega} \dot{X}^2 \, d\mathbb{P}\). Since \(\dot{X}^2 \ge 0\), \(\dot{X}^2 = 0\) \(\mathbb{P}\)-a.s., which implies \(\dot{X} = 0 \implies X = \mathbb{E}[X]\) \(\mathbb{P}\)-a.s.

title: 25  Lecture 12.1: \(L^2\) and Covariance
text:
25.6 Definitions
For \(X, Y \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\), define the centered random variables: \[
\dot{X} \triangleq X - \mathbb{E}[X], \quad \dot{Y} \triangleq Y - \mathbb{E}[Y]
\tag{25.5}\]

Definition 25.2  

Covariance: \[
\text{Cov}(X, Y) \triangleq \mathbb{E}[\dot{X} \dot{Y}] = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])] = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y].
\tag{25.6}\]
Variance: \[
\text{Var}(X) \triangleq \text{Cov}(X, X) = \mathbb{E}[\dot{X}^2] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 \ge 0.
\tag{25.7}\]



Lemma 25.1 If \(X \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) and \(\text{Var}(X) = 0\), then \(X = \mathbb{E}[X]\) \(\mathbb{P}\)-almost surely (i.e., \(X\) is constant a.s.).


Proof (Proof of Lemma 25.1). \(0 = \text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\dot{X}^2] = \int_{\Omega} \dot{X}^2 \, d\mathbb{P}\). Since \(\dot{X}^2 \ge 0\), \(\dot{X}^2 = 0\) \(\mathbb{P}\)-a.s., which implies \(\dot{X} = 0 \implies X = \mathbb{E}[X]\) \(\mathbb{P}\)-a.s.

title: 25  Lecture 12.1: \(L^2\) and Covariance
text:
25.6 Variance Examples

Normal Distribution \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha, t)\): Since \(X \overset{d}{=} \sqrt{t} Z + \alpha\) with \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\), we have \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \alpha\) (computed in Lecture 11.2), so \(X - \mathbb{E}[X] = \sqrt{t}\,Z\). Therefore: \[
\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[(X - \alpha)^2\bigr] = \mathbb{E}\bigl[(\sqrt{t}\,Z)^2\bigr] = t\,\mathbb{E}[Z^2] = t \cdot 1 = t.
\]
Exponential Distribution \(T \sim \text{Exp}(\alpha)\): We use \(\text{Var}(T) = \mathbb{E}[T^2] - (\mathbb{E}[T])^2\) and compute \(\mathbb{E}[T^2]\) by differentiating the Laplace integral twice. Since \(\frac{d^2}{d\alpha^2}e^{-\alpha t} = t^2 e^{-\alpha t}\), the interchange with integration is justified by DCT (the dominator \(t^2 e^{-\alpha_0 t}\) is integrable for any fixed \(\alpha_0 > 0\)): \[
\int_{0}^{\infty} t^2 e^{-\alpha t} \, dt = \frac{d^2}{d\alpha^2} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-\alpha t} \, dt = \frac{d^2}{d\alpha^2}\!\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\right) = \frac{2}{\alpha^3}.
\] Therefore \(\mathbb{E}[T^2] = \alpha \cdot \dfrac{2}{\alpha^3} = \dfrac{2}{\alpha^2}\), and: \[
\text{Var}(T) = \mathbb{E}[T^2] - \bigl(\mathbb{E}[T]\bigr)^2 = \frac{2}{\alpha^2} - \frac{1}{\alpha^2} = \frac{1}{\alpha^2}.
\]
Poisson Distribution \(N \sim \text{Pois}(\alpha)\): We use \(\text{Var}(N) = \mathbb{E}[N(N-1)] + \mathbb{E}[N] - (\mathbb{E}[N])^2\). The \(k=0\) and \(k=1\) terms vanish, so: \[
\mathbb{E}[N(N-1)] = \sum_{k=2}^{\infty} k(k-1)\, e^{-\alpha} \frac{\alpha^k}{k!} = \sum_{k=2}^{\infty} e^{-\alpha} \frac{\alpha^k}{(k-2)!}.
\] Substituting \(j = k - 2\): \[
\mathbb{E}[N(N-1)] = \alpha^2 e^{-\alpha} \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{\alpha^j}{j!} = \alpha^2 e^{-\alpha} e^{\alpha} = \alpha^2.
\] Therefore: \[
\text{Var}(N) = \mathbb{E}[N(N-1)] + \mathbb{E}[N] - \bigl(\mathbb{E}[N]\bigr)^2 = \alpha^2 + \alpha - \alpha^2 = \alpha.
\]

title: 25  Lecture 12.1: \(L^2\) and Covariance
text:
25.7 Correlation and Uncorrelated Variables

Definition 25.3 Two random variables \(X, Y \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) are uncorrelated if \(\text{Cov}(X, Y) = 0\).
Their correlation is defined as: \[
\text{Corr}(X, Y) \triangleq \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)\text{Var}(Y)}} = \frac{\langle \dot{X}, \dot{Y} \rangle_{L^2}}{\|\dot{X}\|_{L^2} \|\dot{Y}\|_{L^2}}.
\tag{25.6}\]
By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, \(|\text{Corr}(X, Y)| \le 1\).


Proposition 25.2  

For any \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\text{Cov}(X + \alpha, Y) = \text{Cov}(X, Y)\).
If \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n \in L^2\) are pairwise uncorrelated, then: \[
\text{Var}(X_1 + X_2 + \dots + X_n) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \text{Var}(X_j).
\tag{25.7}\]



Proof (Proof of Proposition 25.2). Observe that \(\dot{(X + \alpha)} = (X + \alpha) - \mathbb{E}[X + \alpha] = X - \mathbb{E}[X] = \dot{X}\).
For the sum of random variables: \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Var}\left( \sum_{j=1}^{n} X_j \right) &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \left( \sum_{j=1}^{n} \dot{X}_j \right)^2 \right] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{j=1}^{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \dot{X}_j \dot{X}_k \right] = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}[\dot{X}_j \dot{X}_k] \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \text{Cov}(X_j, X_k).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\text{Cov}(X_j, X_k) = 0\) for \(j \neq k\), only terms with \(j = k\) remain: \[
\text{Var}\left( \sum_{j=1}^{n} X_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \text{Cov}(X_j, X_j) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \text{Var}(X_j).
\]

title: 25  Lecture 12.1: \(L^2\) and Covariance
text: 25.9 Interpretation of Covariance

title: 25  Lecture 12.1: \(L^2\) and Covariance
text:
25.8 Indicator Functions and Independence
Let \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\), and consider \(X = \mathbf{1}_A\) and \(Y = \mathbf{1}_B\). \(X\) and \(Y\) are Bernoulli random variables with \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_A] = \mathbb{P}(A)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_B] = \mathbb{P}(B)\).
Since \(\mathbf{1}_A \mathbf{1}_B = \mathbf{1}_{A \cap B}\): \[
\text{Cov}(\mathbf{1}_A, \mathbf{1}_B) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_{A \cap B}] - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_A]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_B] = \mathbb{P}(A \cap B) - \mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B).
\]
Therefore, \(\text{Cov}(\mathbf{1}_A, \mathbf{1}_B) = 0\) if and only if \(A\) and \(B\) are independent events.

title: 25  Lecture 12.1: \(L^2\) and Covariance
text:
25.9 Example: Coin Tossing Sequence
Consider tossing a fair coin \(n\) times.

Sample Space: \(\Omega = \{ (\omega_1, \dots, \omega_n) \mid \omega_j \in \{0, 1\} \}\), so \(|\Omega| = 2^n\), where \(1 = \text{Heads}\) and \(0 = \text{Tails}\).
\(\sigma\)-algebra: \(\mathcal{F} = 2^{\Omega}\).
Probability Measure: Uniform measure \(\mathbb{P}(A) = \frac{|A|}{2^n}\) for \(A \subseteq \Omega\).
Coordinate Random Variables: \(X_j(\omega) = \omega_j \in \{0,1\}\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n\). Since each \(X_j\) is bounded, \(X_j \in L^2(\mathbb{P})\).


Exercise 25.1 Show that \(\text{Cov}(X_j, X_k) = \frac{1}{4} \delta_{jk}\), where \(\delta_{jk}\) is the Kronecker delta.


Solution. Step 1: Mean. For each \(j\), exactly half of the \(2^n\) outcomes have \(\omega_j = 1\): \[
\mathbb{E}[X_j] = \mathbb{P}(X_j = 1) = \frac{2^{n-1}}{2^n} = \frac{1}{2}.
\]
Step 2: Second moment. Since \(X_j \in \{0,1\}\), we have \(X_j^2 = X_j\), so \(\mathbb{E}[X_j^2] = \mathbb{E}[X_j] = \frac{1}{2}\).
Step 3: Diagonal case \(j = k\). By the shortcut formula: \[
\text{Cov}(X_j, X_j) = \text{Var}(X_j) = \mathbb{E}[X_j^2] - \bigl(\mathbb{E}[X_j]\bigr)^2 = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{4}.
\]
Step 4: Off-diagonal case \(j \neq k\). The product \(X_j X_k = 1\) if and only if \(\omega_j = 1\) and \(\omega_k = 1\). For \(j \neq k\), the remaining \(n-2\) coordinates are free, giving \(2^{n-2}\) such outcomes: \[
\mathbb{E}[X_j X_k] = \mathbb{P}(X_j = 1,\, X_k = 1) = \frac{2^{n-2}}{2^n} = \frac{1}{4}.
\] Therefore: \[
\text{Cov}(X_j, X_k) = \mathbb{E}[X_j X_k] - \mathbb{E}[X_j]\mathbb{E}[X_k] = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 0.
\]
Conclusion. Combining both cases: \[
\text{Cov}(X_j, X_k) = \frac{1}{4}\,\delta_{jk}. \qquad \square
\]

title: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers
text:
26.2 Markov’s Inequality
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space. Recall Markov’s inequality: if \(f \ge 0\) is a non-negative measurable function and \(\epsilon > 0, p > 0\), then: \[
\mu(\{f \ge \epsilon\}) \le \frac{1}{\epsilon^p} \int_{\Omega} f^p \, d\mu
\tag{26.1}\]
crumbs: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers

title: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers
text:
26.3 Chebyshev’s Inequality
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space and let \(X \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\).
Setting \(p = 2\) and applying Markov’s inequality to the non-negative random variable \(f = |\dot{X}| = |X - \mathbb{E}[X]|\), we obtain Chebyshev’s inequality:

Theorem 26.1 (Chebyshev’s Inequality) Let \(X \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\). For any \(\epsilon > 0\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}\left(|X - \mathbb{E}[X]| \ge \epsilon\right) &= \mathbb{P}\left(|\dot{X}|\ge \epsilon\right) \\
&\le \frac{1}{\epsilon^2} \mathbb{E}\left[|\dot{X}|^2\right] = \frac{\text{Var}(X)}{\epsilon^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.2}\]


Proof. By definition of expectation and non-negativity of \(|\dot{X}|^2\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Var}(X) &= \mathbb{E}\left[|\dot{X}|^2\right] = \int_{\Omega} |\dot{X}|^2 \, d\mathbb{P}\\
& \ge \int_{\{|\dot{X}| \ge \epsilon\}} |\dot{X}|^2 \, d\mathbb{P} \ge \epsilon^2 \int_{\{|\dot{X}| \ge \epsilon\}} \, d\mathbb{P} = \epsilon^2 \mathbb{P}(|\dot{X}| \ge \epsilon).
\end{aligned}
\]
Dividing both sides by \(\epsilon^2 > 0\) completes the proof.

Alternative Form (Standard Deviation Units):
Let \(\sigma(X) \triangleq \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}\) denote the standard deviation of \(X\). Setting \(\epsilon = k \sigma(X)\) for \(k > 0\) in Equation 26.2 yields: \[
\mathbb{P}\left(|X - \mathbb{E}[X]| \ge k \sigma(X)\right) \le \frac{\text{Var}(X)}{(k \sigma(X))^2} = \frac{1}{k^2}
\tag{26.3}\]
crumbs: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers

title: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers
section: 26.4 Interpretation of Expectation and the Empirical Mean
text:
26.4 Interpretation of Expectation and the Empirical Mean
Consider tossing a fair coin \(n\) times:

Sample Space: \(\Omega = \{ \omega = (\omega_1, \dots, \omega_n) \mid \omega_j \in \{0, 1\} \}\).
\(\sigma\)-algebra: \(\mathcal{F} = 2^{\Omega}\).
Probability Measure: \(\mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) = 2^{-n}\) for each elementary outcome \(\omega \in \Omega\).
Indicator Random Variables: \(X_j(\omega) = \omega_j \in \{0, 1\}\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n\).

Each coordinate \(X_j\) takes value 1 for \(2^{n-1}\) outcomes and 0 for \(2^{n-1}\) outcomes, giving: \[
\mathbb{E}[X_j] = \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} X_j(\omega) \mathbb{P}(\omega) = \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} \omega_j 2^{-n} = \frac{1}{2}
\]
crumbs: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers

title: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers
crumbs: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers

title: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers
text:
26.6 Proportion of Heads
Consider the sample mean \(\frac{S_n}{n}\). Its expectation is \(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{S_n}{n}\right] = \frac{1}{2}\).
Since the \(X_j\) are pairwise uncorrelated (shown in Lecture 12.1, with \(\text{Var}(X_j) = \frac{1}{4}\)), Bienaymé’s identity gives: \[
\text{Var}(S_n) = \sum_{j=1}^n \text{Var}(X_j) = n \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{n}{4}.
\]
Using \(\text{Var}(cX) = c^2 \text{Var}(X)\) with \(c = 1/n\): \[
\text{Var}\!\left(\frac{S_n}{n}\right) = \frac{1}{n^2} \text{Var}(S_n) = \frac{n/4}{n^2} = \frac{1}{4n}.
\]
Applying Chebyshev’s inequality to \(\frac{S_n}{n}\): \[
\mathbb{P}\left(\left| \frac{S_n}{n} - \frac{1}{2} \right| \ge \epsilon\right) \le \frac{\text{Var}(S_n/n)}{\epsilon^2} = \frac{1}{4n\epsilon^2} = \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{n}\right).
\]
This concentration property is not restricted to binomial distributions; it holds because \(S_n = \sum_{j=1}^n X_j\) is a sum of uncorrelated random variables normalized by \(n\).
crumbs: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers

title: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers
section: 26.7 The Weak Law of Large Numbers (WLLN)
text:
26.7 The Weak Law of Large Numbers (WLLN)

Theorem 26.2 (Weak Law of Large Numbers (Uncorrelated \(L^2\) Case)) Let \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be a sequence of \(L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) random variables on a common probability space. Suppose \(\{X_n\}\) are pairwise uncorrelated: \[
\text{Cov}(X_n, X_m) = 0 \quad \text{for } n \neq m,
\]
and share a common mean \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\) and common variance \(t > 0\): \[
\mathbb{E}[X_n] = \alpha, \quad \text{Var}(X_n) = t \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{N}.
\]
Let \(S_n \triangleq \sum_{j=1}^n X_j\). Then for any \(\epsilon > 0\): \[
\mathbb{P}\left(\left| \frac{S_n}{n} - \alpha \right| \ge \epsilon\right) \le \frac{t}{n \epsilon^2} = \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0.
\tag{26.4}\]


Proof (Proof of Equation 26.4). By linearity of expectation: \[
\mathbb{E}[S_n] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{j=1}^n X_j \right] = \sum_{j=1}^n \mathbb{E}[X_j] = n \alpha \implies \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{S_n}{n} \right] = \alpha
\]
Because the \(\{X_j\}\) are pairwise uncorrelated, Bienaymé’s identity applies: \[
\text{Var}(S_n) = \text{Var}\left( \sum_{j=1}^n X_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^n \text{Var}(X_j) = n t
\]
Therefore, the variance of the sample average is: \[
\text{Var}\left( \frac{S_n}{n} \right) = \frac{1}{n^2} \text{Var}(S_n) = \frac{n t}{n^2} = \frac{t}{n}
\]
Applying Chebyshev’s inequality to \(\frac{S_n}{n}\) yields: \[
\mathbb{P}\left(\left| \frac{S_n}{n} - \alpha \right| \ge \epsilon\right) \le \frac{\text{Var}(S_n/n)}{\epsilon^2} = \frac{t}{n \epsilon^2}
\]
Taking \(n \to \infty\) proves the assertion.
crumbs: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers

title: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers
section: 26.8 Convergence Modes: Convergence in Probability vs. Almost Sure Convergence
text:
26.8 Convergence Modes: Convergence in Probability vs. Almost Sure Convergence
The convergence established by the Weak Law of Large Numbers: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}\left(\left| \frac{S_n}{n} - \alpha \right| \ge \epsilon\right) = 0 \quad \forall \epsilon > 0
\]
is called convergence in probability, written \(\frac{S_n}{n} \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} \alpha\).
crumbs: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers

title: 26  Lecture 12.2: The Weak Law of Large Numbers
section: 26.9 Question: Does Convergence in Probability Imply Almost Sure Convergence?
text:
26.9 Question: Does Convergence in Probability Imply Almost Sure Convergence?
Does \(\frac{S_n}{n} \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} \alpha\) imply that \(\frac{S_n}{n} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} \alpha\), i.e., \(\mathbb{P}\left(\left\{ \omega \in \Omega \mid \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{S_n(\omega)}{n} = \alpha \right\}\right) = 1\)?

Example 26.1 Consider an independent sequence of indicator random variables \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) such that: \[
\mathbb{P}(X_n = 1) = \frac{1}{n}, \quad \mathbb{P}(X_n = 0) = 1 - \frac{1}{n}
\]

Convergence in Probability: Since \(X_n \in \{0, 1\}\), for any \(\epsilon > 0\):

If \(\epsilon > 1\): \(\{|X_n| \ge \epsilon\} = \emptyset\), so \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n| \ge \epsilon) = 0\).
If \(0 < \epsilon \le 1\): \(\{|X_n| \ge \epsilon\} = \{X_n = 1\}\), so \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n| \ge \epsilon) = \frac{1}{n}\).

In both cases \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n - 0| \ge \epsilon) \le \dfrac{1}{n} \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0\), so \(X_n \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} 0\).
Almost Sure Behavior: Summing the probabilities: \[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(X_n = 1) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n} = \infty
\]
Since \(\{X_n\}\) are independent, the second Borel-Cantelli Lemma (which requires independence) implies: \[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(X_n = 1 \text{ infinitely often (i.o.)}\bigr) = 1.
\]
Consequently, \(X_n(\omega)\) does not converge to \(0\) almost surely, because \(X_n(\omega) = 1\) infinitely many times for almost every \(\omega \in \Omega\).

title: 27  Lecture 13.1: Convergence in Measure
text:
Definition 27.1 Let \(f, f_1, f_2, \dots\) be \(\mathcal{F}\)-measurable functions mapping \(\Omega\) to \(\mathbb{R}\). We say that \(f_n\) converges in measure to \(f\), denoted \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\), if for every \(\epsilon > 0\): \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \mu\left( \{ \omega \in \Omega \mid |f_n(\omega) - f(\omega)| \ge \epsilon \} \right) = 0.
\tag{27.1}\]
When \(\mu = \mathbb{P}\) is a probability measure, convergence in measure is called convergence in probability, denoted \(X_n \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} X\).

title: 27  Lecture 13.1: Convergence in Measure
text:
27.2 The “Typewriter Sequence” Example
Consider the Lebesgue measure space \(([0, 1], \mathcal{B}([0, 1]), \lambda)\). We construct a sequence of indicator functions \(\{f_n\}\) whose interval support shrinks to zero width while repeatedly sweeping across \([0, 1]\).
For any \(n \in \mathbb{N}_0\), write \(j = 2^n + k\) where \(0 \le k \le 2^n - 1\). Define: \[
f_{2^n + k} \triangleq \mathbf{1}_{\left[ \frac{k}{2^n}, \frac{k+1}{2^n} \right]}.
\tag{27.2}\]

Visualizing the Sequence:

\(f_1 = \mathbf{1}_{[0, 1]}\)
\(f_2 = \mathbf{1}_{[0, 1/2]}\), \(f_3 = \mathbf{1}_{[1/2, 1]}\)
\(f_4 = \mathbf{1}_{[0, 1/4]}\), \(f_5 = \mathbf{1}_{[1/4, 1/2]}\), \(f_6 = \mathbf{1}_{[1/2, 3/4]}\), \(f_7 = \mathbf{1}_{[3/4, 1]}\)

Convergence in Measure: For any \(0 < \epsilon \le 1\): \[
\lambda\left( \{ |f_{2^n + k} - 0| \ge \epsilon \} \right) = \lambda\left( \left[ \frac{k-1}{2^n}, \frac{k}{2^n} \right] \right) = \frac{1}{2^n} \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0.
\] Thus, \(f_j \xrightarrow{\lambda} 0\).
Failure of Pointwise Convergence: For every \(x \in [0, 1]\), \(f_j(x) = 1\) for infinitely many \(j\) and \(f_j(x) = 0\) for infinitely many \(j\). Hence, \(\lim_{j \to \infty} f_j(x)\) does not exist anywhere in \([0, 1]\).

title: 27  Lecture 13.1: Convergence in Measure
text:
27.3 Metrization of Convergence in Measure
Convergence is generally defined with respect to a metric topology.

title: 27  Lecture 13.1: Convergence in Measure
text:
27.4 Pseudo-Metric Attempt and Triangle Inequality
Consider \(d_\epsilon(f, g) \triangleq \mu(\{|f - g| \ge \epsilon\})\) for a fixed \(\epsilon > 0\). This does not define a metric or pseudo-metric because it fails the standard triangle inequality. However, an adjusted version holds:

Lemma 27.1 For any \(f, g, h \in L^0(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) and \(\epsilon > 0\): \[
d_\epsilon(f, h) \le d_{\epsilon/2}(f, g) + d_{\epsilon/2}(g, h).
\tag{27.3}\]


Proof (Proof Lemma 27.1). By point-wise triangle inequality, \(|f - h| \le |f - g| + |g - h|\). If \(|f(\omega) - h(\omega)| \ge \epsilon\), then either \(|f(\omega) - g(\omega)| \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2}\) or \(|g(\omega) - h(\omega)| \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2}\). Thus: \[
\{ |f - h| \ge \epsilon \} \subseteq \left\{ |f - g| \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2} \right\} \cup \left\{ |g - h| \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2} \right\}.
\]
Applying monotonicity and subadditivity of \(\mu\): \[
\begin{align*}
\mu(\{|f - h| \ge \epsilon\}) &\le \mu\left(\left\{|f - g| \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2}\right\}\right) + \mu\left(\left\{|g - h| \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2}\right\}\right) \\
&= d_{\epsilon/2}(f, g) + d_{\epsilon/2}(g, h).
\end{align*}
\]

title: 27  Lecture 13.1: Convergence in Measure
text:
27.5 The \(d_0\) Metric for \(L^0(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\)

Definition 27.2 Define the space \(L^0(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) as the set of all equivalence classes of measurable functions \(f: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) under \(\mu\)-almost sure equality.


Theorem 27.1 The function \(d_0: L^0 \times L^0 \to [0, \infty)\) defined by: \[
d_0(f, g) \triangleq \inf_{\epsilon > 0} \left( \mu(\{|f - g| \ge \epsilon\}) + \epsilon \right),
\tag{27.4}\] defines a metric on \(L^0(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\). Moreover, \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\) if and only if \(d_0(f_n, f) \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\).


Remark 27.1. On a probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\), alternative metrics characterize convergence in probability, such as \(d(X, Y) \triangleq \mathbb{E}[\min(|X - Y|, 1)]\).

title: 27  Lecture 13.1: Convergence in Measure
text:
27.6 Properties and Completeness of \(L^0\)

Definition 27.3 A sequence \(\{f_n\} \subset L^0(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is Cauchy in measure (or \(L^0\)-Cauchy) if for every \(\epsilon > 0\): \[
\lim_{n, m \to \infty} \mu(\{|f_n - f_m| \ge \epsilon\}) = 0.
\tag{27.5}\]

title: 27  Lecture 13.1: Convergence in Measure
text:
27.7 Basic Limit Properties

Theorem 27.2 Let \(f_n, g_n, f, g \in L^0(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\).

Uniqueness of Limits: If \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\) and \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} g\), then \(f = g\) \(\mu\)-a.s.
Linearity: If \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\), \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\), and \(g_n \xrightarrow{\mu} g\), then \(a f_n + b g_n \xrightarrow{\mu} a f + b g\).
Cauchy Property: If \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\), then \(\{f_n\}\) is Cauchy in measure.



Proof (Proof of Theorem 27.2). Property 1 (Uniqueness of Limits). Suppose \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\) and \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} g\). We show \(\mu(\{f \neq g\}) = 0\). Write: \[
\{f \neq g\} = \bigcup_{m=1}^{\infty} \left\{ |f - g| \ge \tfrac{1}{m} \right\}.
\] By countable subadditivity it suffices to show \(\mu(\{|f - g| \ge \epsilon\}) = 0\) for every fixed \(\epsilon > 0\). By the pointwise triangle inequality \(|f - g| \le |f - f_n| + |f_n - g|\), so: \[
\left\{ |f - g| \ge \epsilon \right\} \subseteq \left\{ |f_n - f| \ge \tfrac{\epsilon}{2} \right\} \cup \left\{ |f_n - g| \ge \tfrac{\epsilon}{2} \right\}.
\] Applying subadditivity of \(\mu\): \[
\mu\!\left(\left\{ |f - g| \ge \epsilon \right\}\right) \le \mu\!\left(\left\{|f_n - f| \ge \tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\right\}\right) + \mu\!\left(\left\{|f_n - g| \ge \tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\right\}\right).
\] Both terms tend to \(0\) as \(n \to \infty\) by assumption. Since the left side is a fixed non-negative number independent of \(n\), we conclude \(\mu(\{|f - g| \ge \epsilon\}) = 0\), and hence \(\mu(\{f \neq g\}) = 0\).

Property 2 (Linearity). Let \(\epsilon > 0\). The pointwise bound \[
|(af_n + bg_n) - (af + bg)| = |a(f_n - f) + b(g_n - g)| \le |a|\,|f_n - f| + |b|\,|g_n - g|
\] implies that if the left side is \(\ge \epsilon\), then at least one of \(|a|\,|f_n - f| \ge \epsilon/2\) or \(|b|\,|g_n - g| \ge \epsilon/2\) must hold. Therefore: \[
\left\{ |(af_n + bg_n) - (af + bg)| \ge \epsilon \right\} \subseteq \left\{|f_n - f| \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2|a|}\right\} \cup \left\{|g_n - g| \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2|b|}\right\}
\] when \(a, b \neq 0\) (if \(a = 0\) the first set is empty and the argument reduces to the \(b \neq 0\) case, and vice versa). Applying subadditivity: \[
\mu\!\left(\left\{|(af_n+bg_n)-(af+bg)| \ge \epsilon\right\}\right) \le \mu\!\left(\left\{|f_n - f| \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2|a|}\right\}\right) + \mu\!\left(\left\{|g_n - g| \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2|b|}\right\}\right) \to 0
\] as \(n \to \infty\), since \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\) and \(g_n \xrightarrow{\mu} g\).

Property 3 (Cauchy Property). By the triangle inequality \(|f_n - f_m| \le |f_n - f| + |f_m - f|\): \[
\begin{align*}
\mu(\{|f_n - f_m| \ge \epsilon\}) &\le \mu\!\left(\left\{|f_n - f| \ge \tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\right\}\right) + \mu\!\left(\left\{|f_m - f| \ge \tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\right\}\right) \xrightarrow{n, m \to \infty} 0.
\end{align*}
\]

title: 27  Lecture 13.1: Convergence in Measure
section: 27.8 Completeness of \(L^0\) and Almost Sure Subsequences
text:
27.8 Completeness of \(L^0\) and Almost Sure Subsequences

Theorem 27.3 If \(\{f_n\}\) is an \(L^0\)-Cauchy sequence in measure, there exists \(f \in L^0\) such that \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\). Furthermore, there exists a subsequence \(\{f_{n_k}\}\) that converges to \(f\) \(\mu\)-almost surely.


Proof (Proof of Theorem 27.3). Step 1: Constructing the Subsequence. Since \(\{f_n\}\) is Cauchy in measure, for each \(k \in \mathbb{N}\), choose an index \(n_k\) with \(n_{k+1} > n_k\) such that: \[
\mu\left( \left\{ |f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k}| \ge 2^{-k} \right\} \right) \le 2^{-k}.
\]
Define \(A_k \triangleq \left\{ |f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k}| \ge 2^{-k} \right\}\). Since \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \mu(A_k) \le \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 1 < \infty\), the First Borel-Cantelli Lemma implies: \[
\mu(E) = 0 \quad \text{where } E \triangleq \{A_k \text{ i.o.}\} = \bigcap_{N=1}^\infty \bigcup_{k=N}^\infty A_k.
\]
Step 2: Pointwise Convergence on \(E^c\). On \(E^c\), there exists \(K(\omega)\) such that for all \(k \ge K(\omega)\), \(|f_{n_{k+1}}(\omega) - f_{n_k}(\omega)| < 2^{-k}\). The series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty (f_{n_{k+1}}(\omega) - f_{n_k}(\omega))\) converges absolutely by comparison with \(\sum 2^{-k}\).
Define \(f: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) by: \[
f(\omega) \triangleq \begin{cases}
f_{n_1}(\omega) + \sum_{k=1}^\infty \left( f_{n_{k+1}}(\omega) - f_{n_k}(\omega) \right) & \text{for } \omega \in E^c, \\
0 & \text{for } \omega \in E.
\end{cases}
\]
Because \(f_{n_j} = f_{n_1} + \sum_{k=1}^{j-1} (f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k})\), \(f_{n_k}(\omega) \to f(\omega)\) pointwise on \(E^c\), so \(f_{n_k} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} f\).
Step 3: Convergence of \(f_{n_k} \xrightarrow{\mu} f\). For any \(\omega \in E^c \setminus \bigcup_{k=l}^\infty A_k\), we have \(|f_{n_{k+1}}(\omega) - f_{n_k}(\omega)| < 2^{-k}\) for every \(k \ge l\), so: \[
|f(\omega) - f_{n_l}(\omega)| = \left| \sum_{k=l}^\infty (f_{n_{k+1}}(\omega) - f_{n_k}(\omega)) \right| \le \sum_{k=l}^\infty 2^{-k} = 2^{-l+1}.
\]
Therefore \(\left\{ |f - f_{n_l}| \ge 2^{-l+1} \right\} \subseteq E \cup \bigcup_{k=l}^\infty A_k\), and since \(\mu(E) = 0\): \[
\mu\left( \left\{ |f - f_{n_l}| \ge 2^{-l+1} \right\} \right) \le \sum_{k=l}^\infty \mu(A_k) \le \sum_{k=l}^\infty 2^{-k} = 2^{-l+1} \xrightarrow{l \to \infty} 0.
\]
Step 4: Convergence of Full Sequence \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\). For any \(\epsilon > 0\): \[
\mu(\{|f_n - f| \ge \epsilon\}) \le \mu\left(\left\{|f_n - f_{n_l}| \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2}\right\}\right) + \mu\left(\left\{|f_{n_l} - f| \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2}\right\}\right)
\]
Choosing \(l\) sufficiently large so that \(\mu(\{|f_{n_l} - f| \ge \epsilon/2\}) < \epsilon/2\) and \(n, n_l\) sufficiently large so that \(\mu(\{|f_n - f_{n_l}| \ge \epsilon/2\}) < \epsilon/2\) establishes \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\).

title: 27  Lecture 13.1: Convergence in Measure
section: 27.9 Almost Sure Convergence Implies Convergence in Measure (Finite Measure Case)
text:
27.9 Almost Sure Convergence Implies Convergence in Measure (Finite Measure Case)

Theorem 27.4 Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a finite measure space (\(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\)). If \(f_n \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} f\), then \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\).


Proof. Let \(\epsilon > 0\) and define \(A_n \triangleq \{ |f_n - f| \ge \epsilon \}\). Since \(f_n \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} f\), the set where \(f_n \not\to f\) has measure zero: \[
\mu(\{ A_n \text{ i.o.} \}) = \mu\left( \bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty} \bigcup_{n=k}^{\infty} A_n \right) = 0
\]
Define \(B_k \triangleq \bigcup_{n=k}^{\infty} A_n\). The sequence of sets \(\{B_k\}\) is non-increasing (\(B_{k+1} \subseteq B_k\)) and \(\mu(B_1) \le \mu(\Omega) < \infty\). By continuity of measure from above: \[
\lim_{k \to \infty} \mu(B_k) = \mu\left( \bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty} B_k \right) = 0
\]
Since \(A_k \subseteq B_k = \bigcup_{n=k}^{\infty} A_n\), monotonicity implies: \[
\mu(A_k) \le \mu(B_k) \xrightarrow{k \to \infty} 0 \implies \mu(\{|f_k - f| \ge \epsilon\}) \to 0
\]
Thus, \(f_k \xrightarrow{\mu} f\).

text:
28.2 \(L^p\) Convergence vs. Convergence in Measure

Lemma 28.1 Let \(1 \le p < \infty\) and \(f, f_1, f_2, \dots \in L^p(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\). If \(\|f_n - f\|_{L^p} \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\), then \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\).


Proof (Proof of Lemma 28.1). By Markov’s inequality applied to \(|f_n - f|^p\), for any fixed \(\epsilon > 0\): \[
\begin{aligned}
&\mu\left( \{ \omega \in \Omega \mid |f_n(\omega) - f(\omega)| \ge \epsilon \} \right) \\
&\le \frac{1}{\epsilon^p} \int_{\Omega} |f_n - f|^p \, d\mu = \frac{1}{\epsilon^p} \|f_n - f\|_{L^p}^p \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\).

title: 28  Lecture 13.2: \(L^p\) is Complete
text:
28.3 Counterexample: The Converse Is False
Convergence in measure does not imply \(L^p\) convergence.

Example 28.1 Consider the Lebesgue measure space \(([0, 1], \mathcal{B}([0, 1]), \lambda)\). Define the sequence: \[
f_n \triangleq n \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\left[0, \frac{1}{n}\right]}, \quad n \in \mathbb{N}
\tag{28.4}\] We can express \(f_n\) explicitly as: \[
f_n(x) =
\begin{cases}
n & \text{if } 0 \le x \le \frac{1}{n}, \\
0 & \text{if } \frac{1}{n} < x \le 1.
\end{cases}
\]
Consider the set \(\{x \in [0,1]: |f_n(x)| \ge \epsilon\}\) for any \(\epsilon > 0\). On the interval \([0, 1/n]\), \(|f_n(x)| = n \ge \epsilon\). On the interval \((1/n, 1]\), \(|f_n(x)| = 0 < \epsilon\). Therefore, \(\{x \in [0,1]: |f_n(x)| \ge \epsilon\}= [0, 1/n]\).

Convergence in Measure: For any \(\epsilon > 0\), taking \(n > \epsilon\) yields: \[
\lambda\left( \{ |f_n - 0| \ge \epsilon \} \right) =\lambda\left( \left[0, \frac{1}{n}\right] \right) = \frac{1}{n} \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0
\] Therefore, \(f_n \xrightarrow{\lambda} 0\).
\(L^p\) Norm Evaluation: For \(1 \le p < \infty\): \[
\|f_n - 0\|_{L^p}^p = \int_{[0, 1]} |f_n|^p \, d\lambda = \int_{0}^{1/n} n^p \, d\lambda = \frac{1}{n} \cdot n^p = n^{p-1}
\]
Taking the \(p\)-th root: \[
\|f_n - 0\|_{L^p} = n^{1 - \frac{1}{p}} = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } p = 1, \\
\to \infty & \text{if } p > 1.
\end{cases}
\]
In either case, \(\|f_n - 0\|_{L^p} \not\to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\).

title: 28  Lecture 13.2: \(L^p\) is Complete
text:
28.4 Completeness of \(L^p\) Spaces (Riesz-Fischer Theorem)

Theorem 28.2 (Riesz-Fischer Theorem) For \(1 \le p < \infty\), the space \(L^p(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is Cauchy complete (i.e., a Banach space). Namely, if \(\{f_n\} \subset L^p\) is an \(L^p\)-Cauchy sequence (\(\|f_n - f_m\|_{L^p} \to 0\) as \(n, m \to \infty\)), there exists \(f \in L^p\) such that \(\|f_n - f\|_{L^p} \to 0\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 28.2). Step 1: Extracting an Almost Sure Convergent Subsequence. By Lemma 28.1, every \(L^p\)-Cauchy sequence is \(L^0\)-Cauchy in measure: \[
\mu(\{|f_n - f_m| \ge \epsilon\}) \le \frac{1}{\epsilon^p} \|f_n - f_m\|_{L^p}^p \xrightarrow{n, m \to \infty} 0
\]
By \(L^0\) completeness, there exists a subsequence \(\{f_{n_k}\}\) and a measurable function \(f \in L^0\) such that \(f_{n_k} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} f\) as \(k \to \infty\).
Step 2: \(L^p\) Limit Identification via Fatou’s Lemma. Note that \(|f_{n_k} - f_{n_j}|^p \to |f_{n_k} - f|^p\) a.s. as \(j \to \infty\). Then, applying Fatou’s Lemma to the non-negative sequence \(|f_{n_k} - f_{n_j}|^p\) as \(j \to \infty\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\|f_{n_k} - f\|_{L^p}^p &= \int_{\Omega} \lim_{j \to \infty} |f_{n_k} - f_{n_j}|^p \, d\mu \\
&\le \liminf_{j \to \infty} \int_{\Omega} |f_{n_k} - f_{n_j}|^p \, d\mu \\
&= \liminf_{j \to \infty} \|f_{n_k} - f_{n_j}\|_{L^p}^p
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(\{f_n\}\) is \(L^p\)-Cauchy, for any \(\epsilon > 0\), choosing \(k, j\) sufficiently large makes \(\|f_{n_k} - f_{n_j}\|_{L^p}^p < \epsilon\). Thus: \[
\|f_{n_k} - f\|_{L^p}^p \le \epsilon \implies \lim_{k \to \infty} \|f_{n_k} - f\|_{L^p} = 0
\]
By Minkowski’s inequality, \(\|f\|_{L^p} \le \|f - f_{n_k}\|_{L^p} + \|f_{n_k}\|_{L^p} < \infty\), so \(f \in L^p\).
Step 3: Convergence of Full Sequence. By triangle inequality: \[
\|f_n - f\|_{L^p} \le \|f_n - f_{n_k}\|_{L^p} + \|f_{n_k} - f\|_{L^p} \xrightarrow{n, k \to \infty} 0
\]

28.5 Summary of Modes of Convergence and Relationships
The logical connections between the primary modes of convergence are summarized in the following structural map:

\(L^p\) Convergence (\(1 \le p < \infty\)): Implies convergence in measure (\(L^0\) convergence) via Markov’s inequality.
Almost Sure Convergence: Implies convergence in measure on finite measure spaces.
Convergence in Measure (\(L^0\) Convergence): Implies almost sure convergence of a suitable subsequence.

text:
28.6 General \(L^0\)-\(L^1\) Dominated Convergence Theorem
The following theorem generalizes the classical Dominated Convergence Theorem to the setting where the limit function is only assumed to be in \(L^0\) (measurable) rather than \(L^1\).

Theorem 28.3 (\(L^0\)-\(L^1\) Generalized Dominated Convergence Theorem) Let \(\{f_n\}, \{g_n\} \subset L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), \(g \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), and \(f \in L^0(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\). Suppose that:

\(|f_n| \le g_n\) \(\mu\)-a.s. for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\);
\(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\) and \(g_n \xrightarrow{\mu} g\);
\(\int_{\Omega} g_n \, d\mu \to \int_{\Omega} g \, d\mu\) as \(n \to \infty\).

Then \(f \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) and \(\|f_n - f\|_{L^1} \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\). In particular, \(\int_{\Omega} f_n \, d\mu \to \int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 28.3). Step 1: Dominating Function and Pointwise Subsequences. Because \(f_n \xrightarrow{\mu} f\) and \(g_n \xrightarrow{\mu} g\), we can extract a sub-subsequence \(\{n_k\}\) along which \(f_{n_k} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} f\) and \(g_{n_k} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} g\).
Taking pointwise limits on the inequality \(|f_{n_k}| \le g_{n_k}\) yields \(|f| = \lim_{k \to \infty} |f_{n_k}| \le \lim_{k \to \infty} g_{n_k} = g\) \(\mu\)-a.s. Since \(g \in L^1\), \(f \in L^1\).
Step 2: Subsequence Criterion for \(L^1\) Convergence. Suppose \(\|f_n - f\|_{L^1} \not\to 0\). Then there exists \(\epsilon > 0\) and a subsequence \(\{f_{n_k}\}\) such that \(\|f_{n_k} - f\|_{L^1} \ge \epsilon\) for all \(k\).
However, passing to a further sub-subsequence \(\{n_{k_j}\}\) such that \(f_{n_{k_j}} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} f\) and \(g_{n_{k_j}} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} g\), the classical Generalized Dominated Convergence Theorem applies to \(f_{n_{k_j}}\) dominated by \(g_{n_{k_j}}\). This guarantees \(\|f_{n_{k_j}} - f\|_{L^1} \to 0\), contradicting \(\|f_{n_k} - f\|_{L^1} \ge \epsilon\).
Step 3: Integral Convergence. By triangle inequality: \[
\begin{aligned}
\left| \int_{\Omega} f_n \, d\mu - \int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu \right| &= \left| \int_{\Omega} (f_n - f) \, d\mu \right| \\
&\le \int_{\Omega} |f_n - f| \, d\mu \\
&= \|f_n - f\|_{L^1} \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 29  Lecture 14.1: Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem
text:
29.2 Trapezoidal Approximation in \(C_c(\mathbb{R})\)
To demonstrate why \(C_c(\mathbb{R})\) is not closed under bounded convergence, approximate the indicator function \(\mathbf{1}_{(a, b]}\) by a sequence of trapezoidal continuous functions \(\psi_n \in C_c(\mathbb{R})\):
\[
\psi_n(x) \triangleq \begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } x \le a \text{ or } x \ge b + \frac{1}{n}, \\
n(x - a) & \text{if } a \le x \le a + \frac{1}{n}, \\
1 & \text{if } a + \frac{1}{n} \le x \le b, \\
1 - n\left(x - b\right) & \text{if } b \le x \le b + \frac{1}{n}.
\end{cases}
\tag{29.1}\]

29.2.1 Properties of the Sequence

Continuity: For each fixed \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(\psi_n \in C_c(\mathbb{R})\). At \(x = b\), the left-hand limit is \(\lim_{x \to b^-} \psi_n(x) = 1\) and the right-hand limit is \(\lim_{x \to b^+} (1 - n(x - b)) = 1\), matching \(\psi_n(b) = 1\).
Uniform Boundedness: \(|\psi_n(x)| \le 1\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) and all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).



29.2.2 Proof of Pointwise Convergence \(\psi_n(x) \to \mathbf{1}_{(a, b]}(x)\)
We verify \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \psi_n(x) = \mathbf{1}_{(a, b]}(x)\) by partitioning \(\mathbb{R}\) into four cases:

Case 1 (\(x \le a\)): For all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(\psi_n(x) = 0\). Thus, \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \psi_n(x) = 0 = \mathbf{1}_{(a, b]}(x)\).
Case 2 (\(x \in (a, b)\)): Since \(x - a > 0\), by the Archimedean property choose \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \(\frac{1}{N} < x - a\). For all \(n \ge N\), \(a + \frac{1}{n} < x \le b\), so \(\psi_n(x) = 1\). Thus, \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \psi_n(x) = 1 = \mathbf{1}_{(a, b]}(x)\).
Case 3 (\(x = b\)): For all \(n\) sufficiently large such that \(\frac{1}{n} \le b - a\), \(a + \frac{1}{n} \le b\), so \(\psi_n(b) = 1\). Thus, \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \psi_n(b) = 1 = \mathbf{1}_{(a, b]}(b)\).
Case 4 (\(x > b\)): Since \(x - b > 0\), choose \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \(\frac{1}{N} < x - b\). For all \(n \ge N\), \(x > b + \frac{1}{n}\), so \(\psi_n(x) = 0\). Thus, \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \psi_n(x) = 0 = \mathbf{1}_{(a, b]}(x)\).

Since the pointwise limit \(\mathbf{1}_{(a, b]}\) has jump discontinuities at \(x = a\) and \(x = b\), \(\mathbf{1}_{(a, b]} \notin C_c(\mathbb{R})\), establishing that \(C_c(\mathbb{R})\) is not closed under bounded convergence.

title: 29  Lecture 14.1: Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem
text:
29.3 Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem

Definition 29.2 A collection \(\mathbb{M}\) of \(\mathbb{R}\)-valued bounded functions on \(\Omega\) is a multiplicative system if: \[
f, g \in \mathbb{M} \implies f \cdot g \in \mathbb{M}
\tag{29.2}\]


Notation: If \(\mathbb{M}\) is any subset of \(\mathbb{B}(\Omega,2^\Omega,\mathbb{R})\), let \(\mathbb{H}(\mathbb{M})\) denote the smallest subspace of bounded functions on \(\Omega\) which contains \(\mathbb{M}\cup \{1\}\), and is closed under bounded convergence.


Theorem 29.1 (Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem) Let \(\mathbb{H} \subseteq \mathbb{B}(\Omega,2^\Omega,\mathbb{R})\) be a vector subspace containing the constant function \(1\) and closed under bounded convergence. Let \(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}\) be a multiplicative system. Then \(\mathbb{H}\) contains all bounded \(\sigma(\mathbb{M})\)-measurable functions: \[
\mathbb{B}(\Omega, \sigma(\mathbb{M}), \mathbb{R}) \subseteq \mathbb{H}
\tag{29.3}\]
In particular, \(\mathbb{H}(\mathbb{M}) = \mathbb{B}(\Omega, \sigma(\mathbb{M}), \mathbb{R})\).
crumbs: 29  Lecture 14.1: Dynkin's Multiplicative Systems Theorem

title: 29  Lecture 14.1: Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem
text:
29.4 Applications and Corollaries

Corollary 29.1 Let \(\mathbb{H}(C_c(\mathbb{R}))\) denote the smallest subspace closed under bounded convergence containing \(C_c(\mathbb{R}) \cup \{1\}\). The bounded convergence closure of \(C_c(\mathbb{R}) \cup \{1\}\) equals the set of all bounded Borel-measurable functions: \[
\mathbb{H}(C_c(\mathbb{R})) = \mathbb{B}(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}), \mathbb{R})
\tag{29.4}\]


Proof (Proof of Corollary 29.1). 

\(C_c(\mathbb{R})\) is a multiplicative system because the product of two continuous compactly supported functions is continuous and compactly supported.
Continuous functions generate the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra: \(\sigma(C_c(\mathbb{R})) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) because interval indicators \(\mathbf{1}_{(a, b]}\) can be obtained via pointwise limits of \(\psi_n \in C_c(\mathbb{R})\).
Applying Dynkin’s Theorem to \(\mathbb{M} = C_c(\mathbb{R})\) yields \(\mathbb{H}(C_c(\mathbb{R})) = \mathbb{B}(\mathbb{R}, \sigma(C_c(\mathbb{R})), \mathbb{R}) = \mathbb{B}(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}), \mathbb{R})\).



Corollary 29.2 Let \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) be Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb{R}\). If \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}} f \, d\mu = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f \, d\nu \quad \forall f \in C_c(\mathbb{R})
\tag{29.5}\] then \(\mu = \nu\) on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 29.2). Define \(\mathbb{H} \triangleq \left\{ g \in \mathbb{B}(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}), \mathbb{R}) \;\middle|\; \int_{\mathbb{R}} g \, d\mu = \int_{\mathbb{R}} g \, d\nu \right\}\).

\(\mathbb{H}\) is a linear subspace containing \(1\) (since \(\mu(\mathbb{R}) = \nu(\mathbb{R}) = 1\)).
By the Dominated Convergence Theorem, \(\mathbb{H}\) is closed under bounded convergence.
Since \(\mathbb{M} = C_c(\mathbb{R}) \subseteq \mathbb{H}\) is a multiplicative system, Dynkin’s Theorem implies \(\mathbb{H} \supseteq \mathbb{B}(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}), \mathbb{R})\).
Taking \(g = \mathbf{1}_B\) for any \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) gives \(\mu(B) = \nu(B)\).

title: 29  Lecture 14.1: Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem
section: 29.5 Proof of Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem
text:
29.5 Proof of Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem
Without loss of generality, assume \(\mathbb{H} = \mathbb{H}(\mathbb{M})\).

29.5.1 Step 1: \(\mathbb{H}\) Is an Algebra of Functions
\(\mathbb{H}\) is already a vector space containing \(1\); we must show it is closed under pointwise multiplication. For any \(f \in \mathbb{H}\), define: \[
\mathbb{H}^f \triangleq \{ g \in \mathbb{H} \mid f \cdot g \in \mathbb{H} \}
\tag{29.6}\]

\(\mathbb{H}^f \subseteq \mathbb{H}\) is a linear subspace.
\(\mathbb{H}^f\) is closed under bounded convergence: if \(g_n \in \mathbb{H}^f\) with \(|g_n| \le M\) and \(g_n \to g\), then \(f \cdot g_n \to f \cdot g\) boundedly, so \(f \cdot g \in \mathbb{H} \implies g \in \mathbb{H}^f\).
If \(f \in \mathbb{M}\), then \(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}^f\) (since \(\mathbb{M}\) is a multiplicative system). Thus \(\mathbb{H}(\mathbb{M}) \subseteq \mathbb{H}^f \subseteq \mathbb{H}\), which implies \(\mathbb{H}^f = \mathbb{H}\) for all \(f \in \mathbb{M}\).
Repeating the argument for an arbitrary \(f \in \mathbb{H}\), we conclude \(\mathbb{H}^f = \mathbb{H}\) for all \(f \in \mathbb{H}\). Hence \(\mathbb{H}\) is an algebra.



29.5.2 Step 2: Collection of Sets \(\mathcal{F}_0\) Forms a \(\sigma\)-Algebra
Define \(\mathcal{F}_0 \triangleq \{ A \subseteq \Omega \mid \mathbf{1}_A \in \mathbb{H} \}\).

Empty Set and Whole Space: \(\mathbf{1}_\emptyset = 0 \in \mathbb{H}\) and \(\mathbf{1}_\Omega = 1 \in \mathbb{H} \implies \emptyset, \Omega \in \mathcal{F}_0\).
Complements: If \(A \in \mathcal{F}_0\), then \(\mathbf{1}_{A^c} = 1 - \mathbf{1}_A \in \mathbb{H} \implies A^c \in \mathcal{F}_0\).
Intersections: If \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}_0\), then \(\mathbf{1}_{A \cap B} = \mathbf{1}_A \cdot \mathbf{1}_B \in \mathbb{H}\) (since \(\mathbb{H}\) is an algebra) \(\implies A \cap B \in \mathcal{F}_0\).
Countable Unions: If \(A_n \in \mathcal{F}_0\) with \(A_n \uparrow A\), then \(\mathbf{1}_{A_n} \to \mathbf{1}_A\) boundedly \(\implies \mathbf{1}_A \in \mathbb{H} \implies A \in \mathcal{F}_0\).

Because \(\mathcal{F}_0\) is an algebra of sets that is closed under countable increasing unions, \(\mathcal{F}_0\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra.



29.5.3 Step 3: \(\mathbb{B}(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_0) \subseteq \mathbb{H}\)
Since \(\mathcal{F}_0\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra, every simple \(\mathcal{F}_0\)-measurable function \(\varphi = \sum_{j=1}^k c_j \mathbf{1}_{A_j}\) (\(A_j \in \mathcal{F}_0\)) belongs to \(\mathbb{H}\).
For any non-negative bounded \(\mathcal{F}_0\)-measurable function \(f\), there exists a sequence of simple functions \(\varphi_n \uparrow f\) boundedly. Since \(\mathbb{H}\) is closed under bounded convergence, \(f \in \mathbb{H}\). Splitting general \(f = f^+ - f^-\) shows \(\mathbb{B}(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_0) \subseteq \mathbb{H}\).



29.5.4 Step 4: \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_0\)
We have \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) = \sigma\left( \bigcup_{f \in \mathbb{M}} f^{-1}((a, \infty)) \right)\). It suffices to show that for any \(f \in \mathbb{M}\) and \(a \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\{ f > a \} \in \mathcal{F}_0\), i.e., \(\mathbf{1}_{\{f > a\}} \in \mathbb{H}\).
Let \(f \in \mathbb{M}\). Since \(f\) is bounded, choose \(K < \infty\) such that \(f(\Omega) \subseteq [-K, K]\).

For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), define the continuous cut-off function \(\psi_n: [-K, K] \to [0, 1]\) by: \[
\psi_n(x) \triangleq 0 \vee \big(n(x - a) \wedge 1\big)
\]
By the Stone-Weierstrass Theorem, \(\psi_n\) can be uniformly approximated on \([-K, K]\) by polynomial functions. That is, for each \(n\), there exists a sequence of polynomials \(\{p_{n, k}\}_{k=1}^\infty\) such that \(p_{n, k} \to \psi_n\) uniformly on \([-K, K]\) as \(k \to \infty\).
Since \(\mathbb{H}\) is an algebra containing \(1\), \(p_{n, k}(f) \in \mathbb{H}\) for all \(k\).
Uniform convergence implies \(p_{n, k}(f(\omega)) \to \psi_n(f(\omega))\) boundedly on \(\Omega\) as \(k \to \infty\). Since \(\mathbb{H}\) is closed under bounded convergence, \(\psi_n(f) \in \mathbb{H}\) for every \(n\).
As \(n \to \infty\), \(\psi_n(x) \to \mathbf{1}_{(a, \infty)}(x)\) pointwise for all \(x \in [-K, K]\). Thus, \(\psi_n(f(\omega)) \to \mathbf{1}_{\{f > a\}}(\omega)\) pointwise and boundedly on \(\Omega\).
Since \(\mathbb{H}\) is closed under bounded convergence, \(\mathbf{1}_{\{f > a\}} \in \mathbb{H}\), which implies \(\{f > a\} \in \mathcal{F}_0\).

Since sets of the form \(\{f > a\}\) generate \(\sigma(\mathbb{M})\), it follows that \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_0\).



29.5.5 Step 5: Conclusion
From Step 4, \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_0\), so \(\mathbb{B}(\Omega, \sigma(\mathbb{M})) \subseteq \mathbb{B}(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_0)\). Combining with Step 3: \[
\mathbb{B}(\Omega, \sigma(\mathbb{M})) \subseteq \mathbb{B}(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_0) \subseteq \mathbb{H}(\mathbb{M})
\]
Conversely, \(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{B}(\Omega, \sigma(\mathbb{M}))\) and \(\mathbb{B}(\Omega, \sigma(\mathbb{M}))\) is closed under bounded convergence, so \(\mathbb{H}(\mathbb{M}) \subseteq \mathbb{B}(\Omega, \sigma(\mathbb{M}))\). Hence \(\mathbb{H}(\mathbb{M}) = \mathbb{B}(\Omega, \sigma(\mathbb{M}))\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: 29  Lecture 14.1: Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem
section: 29.6 Step 1: \(H\) Is an Algebra of Functions
text:
29.6 Step 1: \(H\) Is an Algebra of Functions
\(H\) is already a vector space containing \(1\); we must show it is closed under pointwise multiplication. For any \(f \in H\), define: \[
H^f \triangleq \{ g \in H \mid f \cdot g \in H \}
\tag{29.6}\]

\(H^f \subseteq H\) is a linear subspace.
\(H^f\) is closed under bounded convergence: if \(g_n \in H^f\) with \(|g_n| \le M\) and \(g_n \to g\), then \(f \cdot g_n \to f \cdot g\) boundedly, so \(f \cdot g \in H \implies g \in H^f\).
If \(f \in M\), then \(M \subseteq H^f\) (since \(M\) is a multiplicative system). Thus \(H(M) \subseteq H^f \subseteq H\), which implies \(H^f = H\) for all \(f \in M\).
Repeating the argument for an arbitrary \(f \in H\), we conclude \(H^f = H\) for all \(f \in H\). Hence \(H\) is an algebra.

title: 29  Lecture 14.1: Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem
section: 29.7 Step 2: Collection of Sets \(\mathcal{F}_0\) Forms a \(\sigma\)-Algebra
text:
29.7 Step 2: Collection of Sets \(\mathcal{F}_0\) Forms a \(\sigma\)-Algebra
Define \(\mathcal{F}_0 \triangleq \{ A \subseteq \Omega \mid \mathbf{1}_A \in H \}\).

Empty Set and Whole Space: \(\mathbf{1}_\emptyset = 0 \in H\) and \(\mathbf{1}_\Omega = 1 \in H \implies \emptyset, \Omega \in \mathcal{F}_0\).
Complements: If \(A \in \mathcal{F}_0\), then \(\mathbf{1}_{A^c} = 1 - \mathbf{1}_A \in H \implies A^c \in \mathcal{F}_0\).
Intersections: If \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}_0\), then \(\mathbf{1}_{A \cap B} = \mathbf{1}_A \cdot \mathbf{1}_B \in H\) (since \(H\) is an algebra) \(\implies A \cap B \in \mathcal{F}_0\).
Countable Unions: If \(A_n \in \mathcal{F}_0\) with \(A_n \uparrow A\), then \(\mathbf{1}_{A_n} \to \mathbf{1}_A\) boundedly \(\implies \mathbf{1}_A \in H \implies A \in \mathcal{F}_0\).

Thus, \(\mathcal{F}_0\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra.

title: 29  Lecture 14.1: Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem
text:
29.8 Step 3: \(B(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_0) \subseteq H\)
Since \(\mathcal{F}_0\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra, every simple \(\mathcal{F}_0\)-measurable function \(\varphi = \sum_{j=1}^k c_j \mathbf{1}_{A_j}\) (\(A_j \in \mathcal{F}_0\)) belongs to \(H\).
For any non-negative bounded \(\mathcal{F}_0\)-measurable function \(f\), there exists a sequence of simple functions \(\varphi_n \uparrow f\) boundedly. Since \(H\) is closed under bounded convergence, \(f \in H\). Splitting general \(f = f^+ - f^-\) shows \(B(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_0) \subseteq H\).

title: 29  Lecture 14.1: Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem
text:
29.9 Step 4: \(\sigma(M) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_0\)
We have \(\sigma(M) = \sigma\left( \bigcup_{f \in M} f^{-1}((a, \infty)) \right)\). It suffices to show that for any \(f \in M\) and \(a \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\{ f > a \} \in \mathcal{F}_0\), i.e., \(\mathbf{1}_{\{f > a\}} \in H\).
Since \(f \in M \subseteq B(\Omega)\), let \(\|f\|_\infty \le K < \infty\). By the Stone-Weierstrass theorem, the discontinuous threshold function \(h_a(x) = \mathbf{1}_{(a, \infty)}(x)\) on \([-K, K]\) can be approximated pointwise by continuous functions \(\psi_n\), which in turn are uniformly approximated by polynomials \(p_{n, k}(x)\).
Since \(H\) is an algebra containing \(1\), \(p_{n, k}(f) \in H\). Taking sequential bounded limits yields \(\psi_n(f) \in H\), and taking \(n \to \infty\) gives \(\mathbf{1}_{\{f > a\}} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \psi_n(f) \in H\). Thus \(\{f > a\} \in \mathcal{F}_0\).

title: 29  Lecture 14.1: Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem
text:
29.10 Step 5: Conclusion
From Step 4, \(\sigma(M) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_0\), so \(B(\Omega, \sigma(M)) \subseteq B(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_0)\). Combining with Step 3: \[
B(\Omega, \sigma(M)) \subseteq B(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_0) \subseteq H(M)
\]
Conversely, \(M \subseteq B(\Omega, \sigma(M))\) and \(B(\Omega, \sigma(M))\) is closed under bounded convergence, so \(H(M) \subseteq B(\Omega, \sigma(M))\). Hence \(H(M) = B(\Omega, \sigma(M))\). \(\blacksquare\)
