title: 30  Lecture 14.2: Product Measure
text:
Definition 30.1 The product \(\sigma\)-algebra, denoted \(\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2\), is the \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2\) generated by product sets (rectangles) \(A_1 \times A_2\) with \(A_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1\) and \(A_2 \in \mathcal{F}_2\): \[
\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2 \triangleq \sigma(\{ A_1 \times A_2 \mid A_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1, A_2 \in \mathcal{F}_2 \})
\tag{30.1}\]
More generally, for a finite family of measurable spaces \(\{(\Omega_j, \mathcal{F}_j)\}_{j=1}^d\): \[
\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j \triangleq \sigma\left( \left\{ \prod_{j=1}^d B_j \;\middle|\; B_j \in \mathcal{F}_j \text{ for } 1 \le j \le d \right\} \right)
\tag{30.2}\]


Canonical Projections: For an arbitrary index set \(J\) and measurable spaces \(\{(\Omega_j,\mathcal{F}_j)\}_{j \in J}\), let \(\pi_k: \prod_{j \in J} \Omega_j \to \Omega_k\) be the coordinate map \(\pi_k\big((\omega_j)_{j \in J}\big) = \omega_k\). When \(J = \{1,\dots,d\}\) we write \(\pi_k(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_d) = \omega_k\).


Example 30.1 (Two-dimensional product space) Let \(\Omega=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\) and consider the first and second coordinate maps \(\pi_1(x,y)=x\) and \(\pi_2(x,y)=y\). Take \(A=(0,1]\). Then \[
\pi_1^{-1}(A) = \{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:x\in(0,1]\}.
\] Equivalently, \(\pi_1^{-1}((0,1]) = (0,1]\times\mathbb R\). Geometrically, this is a vertical strip in \(\mathbb R^2\).
Take \(B=[2,5]\). Under the second coordinate projection, we have \[
\pi_2^{-1}([2,5]) = \{(x,y):y\in[2,5]\}.
\] Therefore, \(\pi_2^{-1}([2,5])=\mathbb{R}\times[2,5]\).
Finally, note that the intersection of cylinder sets is again a cylinder set. For example, \[
\pi_1^{-1}((0,1]) \cap \pi_2^{-1}([2,5]) = (0,1] \times [2,5],
\] which restricts both the first and second coordinates.



Definition 30.2 (Cylinder Sets) A cylinder set in the product \(\Omega = \prod_{j\in J}\Omega_j\) is a set of the form \(\prod_{j\in J}B_j\) with \(B_j\in\mathcal F_j\) for every \(j\in J\) and \(B_j=\Omega_j\) for all but finitely many \(j\). In particular, a cylinder that restricts only the \(j\)-th coordinate is of the form \(\pi_j^{-1}(B_j)=\prod_{k\in J}B_k\), where \[
B_k=
\begin{cases}
B_j,&k=j,\\
\Omega_k,&k\neq j.
\end{cases}
\]


For a product space \(\Omega=S_1\times\cdots\times S_N\), the inverse image of a set under the \(n\)th coordinate map has the form \[
\pi_n^{-1}(A) = S_1\times\cdots\times S_{n-1} \times A\times S_{n+1}\times\cdots\times S_N.
\] This is called a cylinder set: we restrict one coordinate and leave all the other coordinates unrestricted.


Example 30.2 (A cylinder set in \(\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}\)) Consider the product space \(\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}} = \{(x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots):x_j\in\mathbb R\}\). Define \[
C = [0,1]\times[2,3]\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\cdots.
\] This is a cylinder set because \(B_1=[0,1]\), \(B_2=[2,3]\), and \(B_j=\mathbb R\quad(j\ge3)\), so only finitely many coordinates are restricted. Equivalently, \[
C = \left\{ x\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}: x_1\in[0,1],\ x_2\in[2,3] \right\}.
\] In terms of coordinate projections, we have \[
\begin{aligned}
&\pi_1^{-1}([0,1])=\{ x\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}: x_1\in[0,1] \} = [0,1]\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\cdots,\\
&\pi_2^{-1}([2,3])=\{ x\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}: x_2\in[2,3] \}= \mathbb R\times[2,3]\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\cdots.
\end{aligned}
\] Then, \[
\begin{aligned}
C &= [0,1]\times[2,3]\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\cdots\\
&= \pi_1^{-1}([0,1]) \cap \pi_2^{-1}([2,3]).
\end{aligned}
\]


Example 30.3 (Cylinder events for an infinite sequence of coin tosses) Consider the sample space \(\Omega=\{H,T\}^{\mathbb N}\), where an element \(\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\ldots)\) represents an infinite sequence of coin tosses. Define the cylinder set \[
C=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega_1=H,\ \omega_3=T,\ \omega_7=H\}.
\] In product notation, \[
\begin{aligned}
C &= \{H\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{T\} \times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\\
&\times\{H\} \times\prod_{j=8}^{\infty}\{H,T\}.
\end{aligned}
\] This is a cylinder set because only three coordinates are restricted: 1, 3, and 7. All other coordinates are unrestricted. Equivalently, if \(\pi_j(\omega)=\omega_j\) denotes the \(j\)-th coordinate projection, then \[
\begin{aligned}
&\pi_1^{-1}(\{H\})=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega_1=H\} = \{H\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\cdots\\
&\pi_3^{-1}(\{T\})=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega_3=T\} = \{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\cdots\\
&\pi_7^{-1}(\{H\})=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega_7=H\} = \{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\\
&\times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{H\}\times\cdots
\end{aligned}
\] Then, we can express \(C\) as the intersection of these cylinder sets: \[
C = \pi_1^{-1}(\{H\}) \cap \pi_3^{-1}(\{T\}) \cap \pi_7^{-1}(\{H\}).
\] This illustrates the fundamental idea of a cylinder set: A cylinder event specifies finitely many observations and ignores the rest.



Definition 30.3 (Product \(\sigma\)-Algebra for an Arbitrary Index Set) Let \(J\) be an arbitrary index set and let \(\{(\Omega_j,\mathcal{F}_j)\}_{j \in J}\) be measurable spaces. Set \(\Omega \triangleq \prod_{j \in J}\Omega_j\). The product \(\sigma\)-algebra is the \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) generated by the cylinder sets: \[
\bigotimes_{j \in J} \mathcal{F}_j \triangleq \sigma\left( \left\{ \pi_j^{-1}(B_j) \;\middle|\; j \in J,\ B_j \in \mathcal{F}_j \right\} \right),
\tag{30.3}\] equivalently the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by those products \(\prod_{j \in J} B_j\) with \(B_j \in \mathcal{F}_j\) for every \(j\) and \(B_j = \Omega_j\) for all but finitely many \(j\).


Notation (\(\sigma\)-algebra generated by a family of maps): Given maps \(g_i : \Omega \to \Omega_i'\) into measurable spaces \((\Omega_i', \mathcal{F}_i')\), \(i \in I\), define \[
\sigma(\{g_i \mid i \in I\}) \triangleq \sigma\left( \bigcup_{i \in I} g_i^{-1}(\mathcal{F}_i') \right).
\tag{30.4}\] This is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) making every \(g_i\) measurable: a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) on \(\Omega\) renders every \(g_i\) measurable iff \(g_i^{-1}(\mathcal{F}_i') \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) for all \(i \in I\), iff \(\mathcal{A} \supseteq \sigma(\{g_i \mid i \in I\})\). With this notation, Equation 30.3 reads \(\bigotimes_{j \in J}\mathcal{F}_j = \sigma(\{\pi_j \mid j \in J\})\).


Remark 30.1 (The Rectangle Definition Does Not Extend to Uncountable \(J\)). For countable \(J\) the cylinder definition Equation 30.3 agrees with the naive rectangle definition, because then \[
\prod_{j \in J} B_j = \bigcap_{j \in J} \pi_j^{-1}(B_j)
\] is a countable intersection of cylinders. For uncountable \(J\) the two differ, and \(\sigma\big(\{\prod_{j \in J}B_j\}\big)\) is strictly larger than \(\bigotimes_{j \in J}\mathcal{F}_j\).


Lemma 30.1 Let \(J\) be an arbitrary index set and \(\{(\Omega_j,\mathcal{F}_j)\}_{j \in J}\) measurable spaces. Each canonical projection \(\pi_k : \prod_{j \in J}\Omega_j \to \Omega_k\), \(k \in J\), is \(\bigotimes_{j \in J}\mathcal{F}_j \,/\, \mathcal{F}_k\)-measurable.


Proof (Proof of Lemma 30.1). To prove that \(\pi_k\) is measurable, we must show that \(\pi_k^{-1}(A)\in \bigotimes_{j \in J}\mathcal{F}_j\) for every \(A\in\mathcal{F}_k\). Take an arbitrary \(A\in\mathcal{F}_k\). By Definition 30.3, \(\pi_k^{-1}(A)\) is one of the generating cylinder sets of \(\bigotimes_{j \in J}\mathcal{F}_j\), hence lies in it.
In the finite case \(J = \{1,\dots,d\}\) one can argue directly from Definition 30.1. By the definition of \(\pi_k\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_k^{-1}(A) &= \left\{\omega \in \prod_{j=1}^d \Omega_j \mid \pi_k(\omega) \in A \right\}= \left\{\omega \in \prod_{j=1}^d \Omega_j \mid \omega_k \in A \right\}.
\end{aligned}
\] This set can be written as the rectangle \[
\pi_k^{-1}(A) = \Omega_1 \times \dots \times \Omega_{k-1} \times A \times \Omega_{k+1} \times \dots \times \Omega_d.
\] Since \(\Omega_j \in \mathcal{F}_j\) for all \(j \neq k\) and \(A \in \mathcal{F}_k\), it follows that \(\pi_k^{-1}(A) \in \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j\). Therefore, \(\pi_k\) is measurable.



Lemma 30.2 Let \(\{(\Omega_j,\mathcal{F}_j)\}_{j=1}^d\) be a finite family of measurable spaces and, for \(k \in \{1, \dots, d\}\), let \(\pi_k: \prod_{j=1}^d \Omega_j \to \Omega_k\) be defined by \(\pi_k(\omega_1, \dots, \omega_d) = \omega_k\). Then \[
\begin{aligned}
\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j &= \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})\\
&=\sigma(\{\pi^{-1}_k(B_k) \mid 1 \le k \le d, B_k \in \mathcal{F}_k\}).
\end{aligned}
\]


Proof (Proof of Lemma 30.2). Let \(\mathcal{R} \triangleq \left\{ \prod_{j=1}^d B_j \;\middle|\; B_j \in \mathcal{F}_j \text{ for } 1 \le j \le d \right\}\) denote the collection of product rectangles on \(\Omega = \prod_{j=1}^d \Omega_j\). By Definition 30.1, the product \(\sigma\)-algebra is \(\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j = \sigma(\mathcal{R})\).
The second equality in the statement is Equation 30.4 applied to the family \(\{\pi_k\}_{k=1}^d\), i.e. it holds by definition of \(\sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})\); as recorded there, this is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) making every \(\pi_k\) measurable. It therefore remains to prove the first equality, which we do by mutual inclusion between \(\sigma(\mathcal{R})\) and \(\sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})\).

\((\subseteq)\) Inclusion: Let \(E \in \bigcup_{k=1}^d \pi_k^{-1}(\mathcal{F}_k)\). Then \(E = \pi_k^{-1}(B_k)\) for some \(k \in \{1, \dots, d\}\) and \(B_k \in \mathcal{F}_k\). We can express \(E\) as a product rectangle: \[
E = \pi_k^{-1}(B_k) = \Omega_1 \times \dots \times \Omega_{k-1} \times B_k \times \Omega_{k+1} \times \dots \times \Omega_d
\] Since \(\Omega_j \in \mathcal{F}_j\) for all \(j \neq k\) and \(B_k \in \mathcal{F}_k\), it follows that \(E \in \mathcal{R} \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{R})\). Thus, \(\bigcup_{k=1}^d \pi_k^{-1}(\mathcal{F}_k) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{R})\). Since \(\sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})\) is generated by this collection, we conclude: \[
\sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\}) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{R}) = \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j
\]
\((\supseteq)\) Inclusion: Let \(R = \prod_{j=1}^d B_j \in \mathcal{R}\) be an arbitrary product rectangle, where \(B_j \in \mathcal{F}_j\) for each \(j \in \{1, \dots, d\}\). Notice that \(R\) can be written as a finite intersection of preimages under projection maps: \[
R = \bigcap_{j=1}^d \pi_j^{-1}(B_j)
\] Indeed, for any \((\omega_1, \dots, \omega_d) \in \prod_{j=1}^d \Omega_j\): \[
\begin{aligned}
&(\omega_1, \dots, \omega_d) \in \bigcap_{j=1}^d \pi_j^{-1}(B_j) \\
&\iff \pi_j(\omega_1, \dots, \omega_d) = \omega_j \in B_j \text{ for all } j \\
&\iff (\omega_1, \dots, \omega_d) \in \prod_{j=1}^d B_j = R.
\end{aligned}
\] For each \(j\), \(B_j \in \mathcal{F}_j \implies \pi_j^{-1}(B_j) \in \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})\). Since a \(\sigma\)-algebra is closed under finite intersections, \(R \in \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})\). Thus, \(\mathcal{R} \subseteq \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})\), which implies: \[
\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j = \sigma(\mathcal{R}) \subseteq \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})
\]

Combining both inclusions yields \(\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j = \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})\), which together with the second equality noted above completes the proof.



Consequently, for finite \(J = \{1,\dots,d\}\) the rectangle definition Definition 30.1 and the cylinder definition Definition 30.3 agree, and the product \(\sigma\)-algebra is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\prod_{j=1}^d\Omega_j\) that makes all coordinate projections \(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_d\) measurable.
Borel \(\sigma\)-Algebra Identity: \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\).

Proof. \((\supseteq)\) Each projection \(\pi_j : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) is continuous, hence \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\)-measurable; so \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\) makes every \(\pi_j\) measurable and therefore contains \(\sigma(\{\pi_j \mid 1\le j\le d\}) = \bigotimes_{j=1}^d\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) by Lemma 30.2. \((\subseteq)\) Every open \(U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) is a countable union of open boxes \(\prod_{j=1}^d(a_j,b_j)\) with rational \(a_j < b_j\), and each such box is a measurable rectangle; hence \(U \in \bigotimes_{j=1}^d\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\). Since the open sets generate \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\), we get \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \subseteq \bigotimes_{j=1}^d\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\).
Caveat. The inclusion \((\subseteq)\) uses second countability of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) and does not hold for general topological spaces: if \(X\) is a discrete space of cardinality \(> \mathfrak{c}\), then \(\mathcal{B}(X) = 2^X\), \(X\times X\) is discrete so the diagonal \(\Delta\) is Borel in \(X \times X\), yet \(\Delta \notin \mathcal{B}(X) \otimes \mathcal{B}(X)\). In general one only has \(\mathcal{B}(X) \otimes \mathcal{B}(Y) \subseteq \mathcal{B}(X \times Y)\), with equality when \(X\) and \(Y\) are second countable.

title: 30  Lecture 14.2: Product Measure
text:
30.2 Product Measurability Lemma
The following lemma characterizes the measurability of functions into a product space in terms of the measurability of their component functions.

Lemma 30.3 Let \(\{(\Omega_j, \mathcal{F}_j)\}_{j \in J}\) and \((\Upsilon, \mathcal{B})\) be measurable spaces. A function \(f: \Upsilon \to \prod_{j \in J} \Omega_j\) is \(\mathcal{B} \,/\, \bigotimes_{j \in J} \mathcal{F}_j\)-measurable if and only if the component mapping \(\pi_k \circ f: \Upsilon \to \Omega_k\) is \(\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}_k\)-measurable for every \(k \in J\).


Proof (Proof of Lemma 30.3). Let \(\Omega \triangleq \prod_{j \in J} \Omega_j\) and let \(\mathcal{F} \triangleq \bigotimes_{j \in J} \mathcal{F}_j\) denote the product \(\sigma\)-algebra.
\((\Rightarrow)\) Forward Direction:
Assume \(f: \Upsilon \to \Omega\) is \(\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}\)-measurable.
Fix any \(k \in J\). By Lemma 30.1, the canonical projection map \(\pi_k: \Omega \to \Omega_k\) is \(\mathcal{F} \,/\, \mathcal{F}_k\)-measurable because \(\pi_k^{-1}(E_k) \in \mathcal{F}\) for all \(E_k \in \mathcal{F}_k\).
Since the composition of two measurable maps is measurable, the component map \(\pi_k \circ f: \Upsilon \to \Omega_k\) is \(\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}_k\)-measurable for every \(k \in J\).
\((\Leftarrow)\) Backward Direction:
Assume that \(\pi_k \circ f: \Upsilon \to \Omega_k\) is \(\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}_k\)-measurable for every \(k \in J\).
Define the generating collection of cylinder sets on \(\Omega\) by: \[
\mathcal{G} \triangleq \bigcup_{j \in J} \pi_j^{-1}(\mathcal{F}_j) = \left\{ \pi_j^{-1}(E_j) \;\middle|\; j \in J,\, E_j \in \mathcal{F}_j \right\}
\] By Definition 30.3, \(\mathcal{F} = \sigma(\mathcal{G})\). (For finite \(J\) this is consistent with Definition 30.1 by Lemma 30.2.)
To prove that \(f\) is \(\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}\)-measurable, we must show that \(f^{-1}(E) \in \mathcal{B}\) for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\). Consider the set of preimages under \(f\): \[
\mathcal{A} \triangleq \{ E \subseteq \Omega \mid f^{-1}(E) \in \mathcal{B} \}
\] Then \(\mathcal{A}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\), since preimages commute with complements and countable unions: \(f^{-1}(\Omega) = \Upsilon \in \mathcal{B}\), \(f^{-1}(E^c) = (f^{-1}(E))^c\), and \(f^{-1}(\bigcup_n E_n) = \bigcup_n f^{-1}(E_n)\).
Now, take any generating set \(A \in \mathcal{G}\). Then \(A = \pi_j^{-1}(E_j)\) for some \(j \in J\) and \(E_j \in \mathcal{F}_j\). Evaluating the preimage under \(f\) gives: \[
f^{-1}(A) = f^{-1}\left( \pi_j^{-1}(E_j) \right) = (\pi_j \circ f)^{-1}(E_j)
\] By hypothesis, \(\pi_j \circ f\) is \(\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}_j\)-measurable, so \((\pi_j \circ f)^{-1}(E_j) \in \mathcal{B}\). Thus, \(A \in \mathcal{A}\), which implies \(\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{A}\).
Since \(\mathcal{A}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra containing \(\mathcal{G}\), it contains the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by \(\mathcal{G}\): \[
\mathcal{F} = \sigma(\mathcal{G}) \subseteq \mathcal{A}
\] Hence, \(f^{-1}(E) \in \mathcal{B}\) for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\), proving that \(f\) is \(\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}\)-measurable.

Some Observations:

This lemma is often written more simply as: writing \(f_k \triangleq \pi_k \circ f : \Upsilon \to \Omega_k\) for the \(k\)-th component map of \(f\), the map \(f: \Upsilon \to \prod_{j \in J} \Omega_j\) is \(\mathcal{B} \,/\, \bigotimes_{j \in J} \mathcal{F}_j\)-measurable if and only if each component map \(f_k\) is \(\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}_k\)-measurable for all \(k \in J\).

title: 30  Lecture 14.2: Product Measure
text:
30.3 Tensor Product Functions
Given \(f_1: \Omega_1 \to \mathbb{R}\) and \(f_2: \Omega_2 \to \mathbb{R}\), their tensor product \(f_1 \otimes f_2: \Omega_1 \times \Omega_2 \to \mathbb{R}\) is defined by: \[
(f_1 \otimes f_2)(\omega_1, \omega_2) \triangleq f_1(\omega_1) \cdot f_2(\omega_2)
\tag{30.5}\]

Lemma 30.4 Let \(f_i : \Omega_i \to \mathbb{R}\) be \(\mathcal{F}_i\)-measurable for \(i = 1,2\). Then \(f_1 \otimes f_2\) is \((\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable.


Proof (Proof of Lemma 30.4). Note first that \(f_1 \otimes f_2 = (f_1 \circ \pi_1) \cdot (f_2 \circ \pi_2)\).

By Lemma 30.1 the coordinate projections \(\pi_i\) are \((\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2)/\mathcal{F}_i\)-measurable; since \(f_i\) is \(\mathcal{F}_i\)-measurable and compositions of measurable maps are measurable, \(f_1\circ\pi_1\) and \(f_2\circ\pi_2\) are \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable real-valued functions.
By Lemma 30.3, the pair map \[
\Phi \triangleq (f_1\circ\pi_1,\, f_2\circ\pi_2) : \Omega_1\times\Omega_2 \to \mathbb{R}^2
\] is \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2) \,/\, \big(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\otimes\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\big)\)-measurable, since both of its components are measurable. By the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra identity \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\otimes\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^2)\), \(\Phi\) is in fact \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^2)\)-measurable. (This step is exactly where second countability of \(\mathbb{R}\) is used.)
The multiplication map \(m:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\), \(m(x,y)=xy\), is continuous and hence \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^2)/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\)-measurable. Therefore \[
f_1\otimes f_2 = m\circ\Phi
\] is \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable.

title: 30  Lecture 14.2: Product Measure
text:
30.4 Iterated Integrals for Non-Negative Functions
The following theorem is the iterated-integral form of Tonelli’s theorem. It establishes the measurability of slice functions and the equality of iterated integrals for non-negative measurable functions on product spaces. It is logically prior to the product measure itself: it is what makes Corollary 30.1 possible. The form of Tonelli’s theorem that also identifies these iterated integrals with the integral against \(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2\) is Theorem 31.1 in Lecture 14.3.

Theorem 30.1 (Tonelli’s Theorem (Iterated-Integral Form)) Let \((\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1)\) and \((\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2)\) be measurable spaces and let \(f: \Omega_1 \times \Omega_2 \to [0, \infty]\) be a non-negative \((\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable function. Then:

Slice Measurability (no hypothesis on the measures is required):

For every fixed \(\omega_2 \in \Omega_2\), the slice function \(\omega_1 \mapsto f(\omega_1, \omega_2)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable.
For every fixed \(\omega_1 \in \Omega_1\), the slice function \(\omega_2 \mapsto f(\omega_1, \omega_2)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_2\)-measurable.


Assume in addition that \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) are measures on \((\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1)\) and \((\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2)\) that are \(\sigma\)-finite. Then:

Integrated Slice Measurability:

The function \(\omega_1 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable (as a map into \(([0,\infty],\mathcal{B}([0,\infty]))\)).
The function \(\omega_2 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_1} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_1(d\omega_1)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_2\)-measurable.

Equality of Iterated Integrals (both sides being elements of \([0,\infty]\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
&\int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2) \right) \mu_1(d\omega_1) \\
&= \int_{\Omega_2} \left( \int_{\Omega_1} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_1(d\omega_1) \right) \mu_2(d\omega_2)
\end{aligned}
\tag{30.6}\]



Remark 30.2 (\(\sigma\)-Finiteness Is Necessary in Parts 2 and 3). Let \(\Omega_1 = \Omega_2 = [0,1]\) with \(\mathcal{F}_1 = \mathcal{F}_2 = \mathcal{B}([0,1])\), let \(\mu_1 = \lambda\) be Lebesgue measure and let \(\mu_2\) be counting measure (which is not \(\sigma\)-finite on \([0,1]\)). The diagonal \[
D \triangleq \{(x,x) \mid x \in [0,1]\}
\] is closed in \([0,1]^2\), hence \(D \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^2) = \mathcal{B}([0,1])\otimes\mathcal{B}([0,1])\), so \(f = \mathbf{1}_D\) is product-measurable and non-negative: \[
f(x,y)=\mathbf{1}_D(x,y) =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } x=y,\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\Omega_1}\!\!\int_{\Omega_2} f \, d\mu_2\, d\mu_1 &= \int_{\Omega_1}\left(\int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_{\{x\}}(y)\mu_2(dy)\right) d\mu_1\\
&=\int_{\Omega_1}\mu_2(\{x\}) d\mu_1\\
&=\int_{[0,1]} 1 \, \lambda(dx) = 1,
\end{aligned}
\] \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\Omega_2}\!\!\int_{\Omega_1} f \, d\mu_1\, d\mu_2 &= \int_{\Omega_2}\left(\int_{\Omega_1} \mathbf{1}_{\{y\}}(x)\mu_1(dx) \right) \mu_2(dy)\\
&=\int_{[0,1]} 0 \, \mu_2(dy) = 0 .
\end{aligned}
\] Thus Equation 30.6 fails. Note that part 1 still holds here, as it must. The same example shows that uniqueness in Corollary 30.1 fails without \(\sigma\)-finiteness.


Proof (Proof of Theorem 30.1). Steps 1–3 prove all three assertions under the temporary hypothesis \[
\mu_1(\Omega_1) < \infty \quad\text{and}\quad \mu_2(\Omega_2) < \infty,
\] which is assumed throughout Steps 1–3. Step 4 removes it: it derives part 1 with no hypothesis on the measures at all, and parts 2–3 under \(\sigma\)-finiteness.

30.4.1 Step 1: Verification for Elementary Tensor Products
Let \(f = f_1 \otimes f_2\), where \(f_1 \in \mathbb{B}(\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1, \mathbb{R})\) and \(f_2 \in \mathbb{B}(\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2, \mathbb{R})\), i.e. \(f_i\) is bounded, real-valued and \(\mathcal{F}_i\)-measurable. By Lemma 30.4, \(f\) is \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable, and it is bounded, so \(f \in \mathbb{B}(\Omega_1\times\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2, \mathbb{R})\). Since \(\mu_1,\mu_2\) are finite and \(f_1,f_2\) are bounded, all integrals appearing below are finite real numbers, so no \(\infty - \infty\) or \(0\cdot\infty\) ambiguity can arise.

Slice Measurability: For fixed \(\omega_2 \in \Omega_2\), \(\omega_1 \mapsto (f_1 \otimes f_2)(\omega_1, \omega_2) = f_2(\omega_2) \cdot f_1(\omega_1)\) is a constant multiple of an \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable function, hence \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable. By symmetry, \(\omega_2 \mapsto f_1(\omega_1) f_2(\omega_2)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_2\)-measurable for fixed \(\omega_1\).
Integrated Slice Functions: Fix \(\omega_1 \in \Omega_1\). Since \(f_2\) is bounded and \(\mu_2(\Omega_2)<\infty\), \(f_2 \in L^1(\mu_2)\) and \(\int_{\Omega_2} f_2\,d\mu_2 \in \mathbb{R}\); since \(f_1(\omega_1) \in \mathbb{R}\) is a finite constant, it may be pulled out of the integral: \[
I_2(\omega_1) \triangleq \int_{\Omega_2} f_1(\omega_1) f_2(\omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2) = f_1(\omega_1) \int_{\Omega_2} f_2 \, d\mu_2
\] As \(\int_{\Omega_2} f_2 \, d\mu_2\) is a finite constant, \(I_2\) is a constant multiple of \(f_1\) and hence \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable (and bounded).
Equality of Iterated Integrals: \(I_2\) is bounded and \(\mu_1(\Omega_1)<\infty\), so \(I_2 \in L^1(\mu_1)\) and integrating over \(\Omega_1\) gives: \[
\int_{\Omega_1} I_2(\omega_1) \, \mu_1(d\omega_1) = \left( \int_{\Omega_1} f_1 \, d\mu_1 \right) \left( \int_{\Omega_2} f_2 \, d\mu_2 \right)
\] Reversing the roles of the two coordinates in items 2 and 3 yields the same product of finite numbers for the other iterated integral, establishing equality.




30.4.2 Step 2: Extension to Bounded Measurable Functions via Dynkin’s Theorem
Define the space of test functions \(\mathbb{M} \triangleq \{ f_1 \otimes f_2 \mid f_1 \in \mathbb{B}(\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1, \mathbb{R}),\, f_2 \in \mathbb{B}(\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2, \mathbb{R}) \}\).

\(\mathbb{M}\) is a Multiplicative System: For \(f_1 \otimes f_2, g_1 \otimes g_2 \in \mathbb{M}\), \((f_1 \otimes f_2) \cdot (g_1 \otimes g_2) = (f_1 g_1) \otimes (f_2 g_2) \in \mathbb{M}\) because products of bounded measurable functions remain bounded and measurable.
\(\mathbb{M}\) Generates \(\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2\): We check both inclusions.

\((\supseteq)\) For \(A_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1\) and \(A_2 \in \mathcal{F}_2\), \(\mathbf{1}_{A_1 \times A_2} = \mathbf{1}_{A_1} \otimes \mathbf{1}_{A_2} \in \mathbb{M}\), so \(A_1\times A_2 = (\mathbf{1}_{A_1}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{A_2})^{-1}(\{1\}) \in \sigma(\mathbb{M})\). Since \(\sigma(\mathbb{M})\) contains all measurable rectangles, \(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2 \subseteq \sigma(\mathbb{M})\).
\((\subseteq)\) By Lemma 30.4 every element of \(\mathbb{M}\) is \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable, so \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2\).

Hence \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) = \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2\).

Define \(\mathbb{H} \subseteq \mathbb{B}(\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2, \mathbb{R})\) as the collection of bounded measurable functions \(g\) satisfying:

For every fixed \(\omega_2 \in \Omega_2\) the map \(\omega_1 \mapsto g(\omega_1, \omega_2)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable, and for every fixed \(\omega_1 \in \Omega_1\) the map \(\omega_2 \mapsto g(\omega_1, \omega_2)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_2\)-measurable.
The map \(\omega_1 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_2} g(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable and the map \(\omega_2 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_1} g(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_1\) is \(\mathcal{F}_2\)-measurable. (These integrals are well defined by property (1), and are finite real numbers because \(g\) is bounded and \(\mu_1,\mu_2\) are finite.)
\(\int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} g(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 \right) d\mu_1 = \int_{\Omega_2} \left( \int_{\Omega_1} g(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_1 \right) d\mu_2\).

\(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}\): By Step 1, every \(f \in \mathbb{M}\) satisfies properties (1), (2), (3) above, so \(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}\).
We verify the remaining properties of \(\mathbb{H}\):

Vector Space containing \(1\): Let \(g, \tilde{g} \in \mathbb{H}\) and \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\). Property (1) for \(a g + b\tilde g\) is immediate. For (2) and (3), note that all four functions \(g(\cdot,\omega_2)\), \(g(\omega_1,\cdot)\), \(\tilde g(\cdot,\omega_2)\), \(\tilde g(\omega_1,\cdot)\) are bounded and \(\mu_1,\mu_2\) are finite, so every integral involved is a finite real number and linearity of the integral applies without any \(\infty-\infty\) ambiguity; consequently \[
\int_{\Omega_2}(a g + b\tilde g)(\omega_1,\cdot)\,d\mu_2 = a\!\int_{\Omega_2} g(\omega_1,\cdot)\,d\mu_2 + b\!\int_{\Omega_2} \tilde g(\omega_1,\cdot)\,d\mu_2,
\] which is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable, and the two iterated integrals of \(ag+b\tilde g\) agree because they do for \(g\) and for \(\tilde g\). Hence \(\mathbb{H}\) is a vector space. Since \(1 = 1 \otimes 1 \in \mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}\), the constant function \(1\) belongs to \(\mathbb{H}\).
Closed under Bounded Convergence: Let \(\{g_n\} \subset \mathbb{H}\) with \(|g_n(\omega_1, \omega_2)| \le M < \infty\) for all \(n\) and all \((\omega_1,\omega_2)\), and \(g_n \to g\) pointwise on \(\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\). Then \(g\) is \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable and \(|g|\le M\), so \(g \in \mathbb{B}(\Omega_1\times\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2,\mathbb{R})\).

Slice Limits: For fixed \(\omega_2\), \(g_n(\cdot,\omega_2) \to g(\cdot,\omega_2)\) pointwise, and each \(g_n(\cdot,\omega_2)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable by property (1) for \(g_n\); a pointwise limit of measurable functions is measurable, so \(g\) satisfies property (1) (and symmetrically in the other coordinate).
Slice Integrals: Define \(h_n(\omega_1) \triangleq \int_{\Omega_2} g_n(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2)\). Fix \(\omega_1\). Since \(|g_n(\omega_1,\cdot)| \le M\) and \(\mu_2(\Omega_2) < \infty\), the constant \(M\) is \(\mu_2\)-integrable and dominates the sequence. By the Dominated Convergence Theorem (DCT): \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} h_n(\omega_1) = \int_{\Omega_2} g(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2) \triangleq h(\omega_1)
\] Since each \(h_n\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable by property (2) for \(g_n\), their pointwise limit \(h\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable, verifying property (2) for \(g\) (and symmetrically in the other coordinate).
Iterated Integral Limit: Note that \(|h_n(\omega_1)| \le M \mu_2(\Omega_2) < \infty\) for all \(n\) and \(\omega_1\), and \(\mu_1(\Omega_1)<\infty\), so the constant \(M\mu_2(\Omega_2)\) is \(\mu_1\)-integrable and dominates \(\{h_n\}\). Applying DCT a second time with respect to \(\mu_1\): \[
\int_{\Omega_1} h(\omega_1) \, d\mu_1 = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_{\Omega_1} h_n(\omega_1) \, d\mu_1
\] By symmetry, the analogous limit holds for the reversed order of integration. Since the two iterated integrals agree for each \(g_n\) by property (3), and both sides converge, they agree for \(g\), verifying property (3).


All hypotheses of Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem (Theorem 29.1) are satisfied: \(\mathbb{M}\) is a multiplicative system, \(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}\), \(\mathbb{H}\) is a vector space of bounded functions containing \(1\) that is closed under bounded convergence, and \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) = \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2\). Therefore \[
\mathbb{H} \supseteq \mathbb{B}(\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2, \mathbb{R}),
\] i.e. every bounded \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable function satisfies (1), (2), (3).



30.4.3 Step 3: Extension to Non-Negative Functions
Let \(f: \Omega_1 \times \Omega_2 \to [0, \infty]\) be non-negative and \((\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable.

Truncation Sequence: Define \(f_n \triangleq \min\{f, n\}\). Since \(f\) is \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable as a map into \([0,\infty]\) and \(x \mapsto \min\{x,n\}\) is Borel, \(f_n\) is non-negative, bounded and \((\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable, hence real-valued and in \(\mathbb{B}(\Omega_1\times\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2,\mathbb{R})\). By the conclusion of Step 2, \(f_n \in \mathbb{H}\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), and \(f_n \uparrow f\) pointwise.
Slice Measurability: For fixed \(\omega_2\), \(f_n(\cdot, \omega_2) \uparrow f(\cdot, \omega_2)\) pointwise, and each \(f_n(\cdot,\omega_2)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable by property (1) of \(\mathbb{H}\). As a pointwise limit of measurable functions, \(\omega_1 \mapsto f(\omega_1, \omega_2)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable (as a map into \([0,\infty]\)). Symmetrically for the other coordinate.
Monotone Convergence Theorem: Fix \(\omega_1\). Since \(0 \le f_n(\omega_1,\cdot) \uparrow f(\omega_1,\cdot)\), MCT on \(\Omega_2\) gives: \[
I_{2, n}(\omega_1) \triangleq \int_{\Omega_2} f_n(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 \uparrow \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 \triangleq I_2(\omega_1)
\] Since each \(I_{2, n}\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable by property (2) of \(\mathbb{H}\), the pointwise limit \(I_2\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable (possibly \([0,\infty]\)-valued). Symmetrically for the other order.
Iterated Integrals: Since \(0 \le I_{2,n} \uparrow I_2\), applying MCT a second time on \(\Omega_1\): \[
\int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} f_n \, d\mu_2 \right) d\mu_1 \uparrow \int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} f \, d\mu_2 \right) d\mu_1
\] and symmetrically for the reversed order. Since the two iterated integrals agree for each \(f_n\) by property (3) of \(\mathbb{H}\), and both sides converge in \([0,\infty]\), taking \(n \to \infty\) establishes equality of the iterated integrals for \(f\).




30.4.4 Step 4: Extension to \(\sigma\)-finite Measures
The preceding three steps establish the theorem under \(\mu_1(\Omega_1) < \infty\) and \(\mu_2(\Omega_2) < \infty\). We now extend to the general \(\sigma\)-finite case.
Since \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) are \(\sigma\)-finite, choose increasing sequences \(A_k \nearrow \Omega_1\) in \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(B_k \nearrow \Omega_2\) in \(\mathcal{F}_2\) with \(\mu_1(A_k) < \infty\) and \(\mu_2(B_k) < \infty\) for all \(k \in \mathbb{N}\). (If \(\Omega_i = \bigcup_m C^{(i)}_m\) with \(\mu_i(C^{(i)}_m)<\infty\), replace \(C^{(i)}_m\) by \(\bigcup_{l \le m} C^{(i)}_l\), which is still of finite measure by finite subadditivity.)
Rather than passing to trace \(\sigma\)-algebras on \(A_k\) and \(B_k\), we truncate the measures on the original spaces. For \(k \in \mathbb{N}\) define \[
\mu_1^{(k)}(E) \triangleq \mu_1(E \cap A_k) \ \ (E \in \mathcal{F}_1), \qquad
\mu_2^{(k)}(F) \triangleq \mu_2(F \cap B_k) \ \ (F \in \mathcal{F}_2).
\] These are measures on \((\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1)\) and \((\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2)\) (countable additivity is inherited from \(\mu_i\)), and they are finite: \(\mu_1^{(k)}(\Omega_1) = \mu_1(A_k) < \infty\) and \(\mu_2^{(k)}(\Omega_2) = \mu_2(B_k) < \infty\). Moreover, for every non-negative \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable \(g_1\) and every non-negative \(\mathcal{F}_2\)-measurable \(g_2\), \[
\int_{\Omega_1} g_1 \, d\mu_1^{(k)} = \int_{\Omega_1} g_1 \, \mathbf{1}_{A_k} \, d\mu_1, \qquad \int_{\Omega_2} g_2 \, d\mu_2^{(k)} = \int_{\Omega_2} g_2 \, \mathbf{1}_{B_k} \, d\mu_2,
\tag{30.7}\] which holds for indicators by definition of \(\mu_i^{(k)}\), extends to non-negative simple functions by linearity, and to all non-negative measurable functions by MCT.

Part 1 needs no assumption on the measures. Apply Steps 1–3 with the (finite) zero measures \(\mu_1 \equiv 0\) and \(\mu_2 \equiv 0\) on \((\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1)\) and \((\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2)\): properties (2) and (3) in the definition of \(\mathbb{H}\) then hold trivially, while property (1) does not involve the measures at all. Steps 1–3 therefore yield that every non-negative \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable \(f\) has \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable and \(\mathcal{F}_2\)-measurable slices, for arbitrary measurable spaces \((\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1)\) and \((\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2)\). This proves part 1 of the theorem in full generality.
Finite-measure case applies to the truncated measures. Fix \(k\) and let \(f \ge 0\) be \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable. Applying Steps 1–3 to the finite measure spaces \((\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1,\mu_1^{(k)})\) and \((\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2,\mu_2^{(k)})\) and to \(f\) itself gives that \[
\omega_1 \longmapsto \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1,\omega_2)\, \mu_2^{(k)}(d\omega_2) = \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1,\omega_2)\,\mathbf{1}_{B_k}(\omega_2)\, \mu_2(d\omega_2)
\] (the equality being Equation 30.7) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable on all of \(\Omega_1\), and that \[
\int_{\Omega_1}\!\!\int_{\Omega_2} f \, d\mu_2^{(k)} \, d\mu_1^{(k)} = \int_{\Omega_2}\!\!\int_{\Omega_1} f \, d\mu_1^{(k)} \, d\mu_2^{(k)}.
\] Using Equation 30.7 twice on each side, and writing \(f_k \triangleq f \cdot \mathbf{1}_{A_k \times B_k}\) (so that \(f\,\mathbf{1}_{B_k}(\omega_2)\,\mathbf{1}_{A_k}(\omega_1) = f_k\)), this reads \[
\int_{\Omega_1} \int_{\Omega_2} f_k \, d\mu_2 \, d\mu_1 = \int_{\Omega_2} \int_{\Omega_1} f_k \, d\mu_1 \, d\mu_2,
\] and \(\omega_1 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_2} f_k(\omega_1,\omega_2)\,d\mu_2 = \mathbf{1}_{A_k}(\omega_1)\int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1,\omega_2)\mathbf{1}_{B_k}(\omega_2)\,d\mu_2\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable.
Monotone limit recovers \(f\): Because \(A_k\) and \(B_k\) are increasing, \(A_k \times B_k \nearrow \Omega_1\times\Omega_2\), so the single-indexed sequence \(f_k = f\cdot\mathbf{1}_{A_k\times B_k}\) satisfies \(0 \le f_k \uparrow f\) pointwise. By MCT applied to the inner integral, for every \(\omega_1\), \[
\int_{\Omega_2} f_k(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 \uparrow \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2.
\] Hence \(\omega_1 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable as the pointwise limit of the \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable functions from item 2, proving part 2 (symmetrically in the other coordinate).
Equality of iterated integrals: By item 3 the inner integrals increase, \(\int_{\Omega_2} f_k(\omega_1,\cdot)\,d\mu_2 \uparrow \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1,\cdot)\,d\mu_2\) for every \(\omega_1\), so MCT applied to the outer integral gives \[
\int_{\Omega_1} \int_{\Omega_2} f_{k} \, d\mu_2 \, d\mu_1 \uparrow \int_{\Omega_1} \int_{\Omega_2} f \, d\mu_2 \, d\mu_1,
\] and by symmetry the same limit holds for the reversed order. Since the two sides are equal at each stage \(k\) by item 2, and both converge in \([0,\infty]\), they are equal in the limit. This proves part 3 and completes the proof.

title: 30  Lecture 14.2: Product Measure
section: 30.5 Construction and Uniqueness of Product Measure
text:
30.5 Construction and Uniqueness of Product Measure

Corollary 30.1 (Existence and Uniqueness of the Product Measure) Let \((\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1, \mu_1)\) and \((\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2, \mu_2)\) be \(\sigma\)-finite measure spaces.

Existence and uniqueness. There exists exactly one measure \(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2\) on \(\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2\) satisfying \[
(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E_1 \times E_2) = \mu_1(E_1)\, \mu_2(E_2),
\tag{30.8}\] for all \(E_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1,\ E_2 \in \mathcal{F}_2\) with the convention \(0\cdot\infty = 0\). Moreover \(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2\) is \(\sigma\)-finite.
Representation by iterated integrals. For every \(E \in \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2\), \[
\begin{aligned}
(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E) &= \int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_E(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2) \right) \mu_1(d\omega_1) \\
&= \int_{\Omega_2} \left( \int_{\Omega_1} \mathbf{1}_E(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_1(d\omega_1) \right) \mu_2(d\omega_2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{30.9}\]



Proof (Proof of Corollary 30.1). For every \(E \in \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2\) the function \(\mathbf{1}_E\) is non-negative and \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable, so by Theorem 30.1 (parts 1 and 2) the inner integral \(\omega_1 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_E(\omega_1, \omega_2)\,d\mu_2\) is well defined for every \(\omega_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable. Hence the following definition is well-posed. Define: \[
(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E) \triangleq \int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_E(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 \right) d\mu_1.
\]

Non-negativity and empty set: Since \(\mathbf{1}_E \ge 0\), we have \((\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E) \ge 0\). Setting \(E = \emptyset\) gives \(\mathbf{1}_\emptyset = 0\), so \((\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(\emptyset) = 0\).
Countable Additivity: Let \(E = \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k\) with pairwise disjoint \(E_k \in \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2\). Disjointness gives \(\mathbf{1}_E = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{E_k}\) pointwise, and the partial sums \(S_N \triangleq \sum_{k \le N}\mathbf{1}_{E_k}\) satisfy \(0 \le S_N \uparrow \mathbf{1}_E\). Fix \(\omega_1\); by MCT on \(\Omega_2\) together with finite additivity of the integral, \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_E(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 &= \lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{N} \int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_{E_k}(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 \\
&= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_{E_k}(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 .
\end{aligned}
\] The partial sums of the right-hand side increase in \(N\), so applying MCT again on \(\Omega_1\) (and finite additivity there) gives \((\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty (\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E_k)\). Hence \(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2\) is a measure on \(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2\).
Rectangle Value: For \(E = E_1 \times E_2\) we have \(\mathbf{1}_{E_1\times E_2}(\omega_1,\omega_2) = \mathbf{1}_{E_1}(\omega_1)\mathbf{1}_{E_2}(\omega_2)\), so the inner integral evaluates as \(\int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_{E_1}(\omega_1)\mathbf{1}_{E_2}(\omega_2)\,d\mu_2 = \mathbf{1}_{E_1}(\omega_1)\,\mu_2(E_2)\) (with \(0\cdot\infty = 0\) when \(\omega_1 \notin E_1\) and \(\mu_2(E_2)=\infty\)). Integrating over \(\Omega_1\): \[
(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E_1 \times E_2) = \int_{\Omega_1} \mathbf{1}_{E_1}(\omega_1) \mu_2(E_2) \, d\mu_1 = \mu_1(E_1) \mu_2(E_2),
\] which is Equation 30.8. The equality of the two iterated integrals in Equation 30.9 is Theorem 30.1 part 3 applied to \(f = \mathbf{1}_E\), which is non-negative and \((\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)\)-measurable.
\(\sigma\)-finiteness of \(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2\) and uniqueness: The collection \[
\mathcal{P} \triangleq \{E_1 \times E_2 \mid E_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1,\, E_2 \in \mathcal{F}_2\}
\] is a \(\pi\)-system, since \((E_1 \times E_2) \cap (F_1 \times F_2) = (E_1 \cap F_1) \times (E_2 \cap F_2) \in \mathcal{P}\), and \(\sigma(\mathcal{P}) = \mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2\) by Definition 30.1.
By \(\sigma\)-finiteness we may choose increasing sequences \(A_m \nearrow \Omega_1\) and \(B_m \nearrow \Omega_2\) with \(\mu_1(A_m)<\infty\) and \(\mu_2(B_m)<\infty\) (replace a given countable cover by the unions of its initial segments). Put \[
S_m \triangleq A_m \times B_m \in \mathcal{P}.
\] Then \(S_m \nearrow \Omega_1\times\Omega_2\) and, by item 3, \((\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)(S_m) = \mu_1(A_m)\mu_2(B_m) < \infty\); in particular \(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2\) is \(\sigma\)-finite.
Now let \(\nu\) be any measure on \(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2\) satisfying Equation 30.8. Then \(\nu\) agrees with \(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2\) on \(\mathcal{P}\), and \(\nu(S_m) = \mu_1(A_m)\mu_2(B_m) < \infty\) with \(S_m \in \mathcal{P}\), \(S_m \nearrow \Omega_1\times\Omega_2\). By the uniqueness theorem for measures (Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem applied to \(\mathcal{L}_m \triangleq \{E \in \mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2 \mid \nu(E\cap S_m) = (\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)(E \cap S_m)\}\), which is a \(\lambda\)-system containing \(\mathcal{P}\), followed by continuity from below as \(m \to \infty\)), \(\nu = \mu_1\otimes\mu_2\) on \(\sigma(\mathcal{P}) = \mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2\). See also Lemma 32.1.

title: 31  Lecture 14.3: Tonelli and Fubini Theorems
text:
31.1 Tonelli’s Theorem for Non-Negative Functions
Let \((\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1, \mu_1)\) and \((\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2, \mu_2)\) be \(\sigma\)-finite measure spaces, and let \((\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2, \mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)\) be the product measure space.
crumbs: 31  Lecture 14.3: Tonelli and Fubini Theorems

title: 31  Lecture 14.3: Tonelli and Fubini Theorems
text:
Theorem 31.1 (Tonelli’s Theorem) Let \(f: \Omega_1 \times \Omega_2 \to [0, \infty]\) be a non-negative \((\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2) \,/\, \mathcal{B}([0, \infty])\)-measurable function. Then:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2} f \, d(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2) &= \int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2) \right) \mu_1(d\omega_1) \\
&= \int_{\Omega_2} \left( \int_{\Omega_1} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_1(d\omega_1) \right) \mu_2(d\omega_2)
\end{aligned}
\tag{31.1}\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 31.1). 

Indicator Functions: For \(f = \mathbf{1}_E\) with \(E \in \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2\), Equation 31.1 holds by definition of the product measure \(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2\).
Simple Functions: By linearity of integration, Equation 31.1 holds for non-negative simple functions \(f = \sum_{j=1}^k c_j \mathbf{1}_{E_j}\).
General Non-Negative Functions: For a general non-negative \(({\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2})\)-measurable \(f\), choose non-negative simple functions \(\varphi_n \uparrow f\) pointwise. By Step 2, Equation 31.1 holds for each \(\varphi_n\).

Inner MCT: For each fixed \(\omega_1 \in \Omega_1\), \(\varphi_n(\omega_1, \cdot) \uparrow f(\omega_1, \cdot)\) pointwise. By MCT on \((\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2, \mu_2)\): \[g_n(\omega_1) \triangleq \int_{\Omega_2} \varphi_n(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2) \uparrow \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2) \triangleq g(\omega_1).\] Since each \(g_n\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable (by Step 2), the pointwise limit \(g\) is \(\mathcal{F}_1\)-measurable.
Outer MCT: Since \(g_n \uparrow g\) pointwise, MCT on \((\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1, \mu_1)\) gives \(\int_{\Omega_1} g_n \, d\mu_1 \uparrow \int_{\Omega_1} g \, d\mu_1\).
Product MCT: Since \(\varphi_n \uparrow f\) on \(\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2\), MCT on the product space gives \(\int_{\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2} \varphi_n \, d(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2) \uparrow \int_{\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2} f \, d(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)\).

Since the three-way equality holds for each \(\varphi_n\), passing to the limit establishes Equation 31.1. The identity for the reversed integration order follows by symmetry.

title: 31  Lecture 14.3: Tonelli and Fubini Theorems
section: 31.2 Example: The Normalizing Constant for the Standard Normal Distribution
text:
31.2 Example: The Normalizing Constant for the Standard Normal Distribution
Consider \(f(x) = e^{-x^2/2} \ge 0\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Define \(I \triangleq \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-x^2/2} \, \lambda(dx)\). We evaluate \(I\) using Tonelli’s theorem on \(\mathbb{R}^2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
I^2 &= \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-x^2/2} \, \lambda(dx) \right) \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-y^2/2} \, \lambda(dy) \right) \\
&= \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x^2 + y^2)} \, d(\lambda \otimes \lambda)
\end{aligned}
\tag{31.2}\]

Exhaustion by Compact Disks: Define \[
\bar{D}_R \triangleq \{ (x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid x^2 + y^2 \le R^2 \}.
\] Note that as \(R \to \infty\), \(\mathbf{1}_{\bar{D}_R} \uparrow 1\) \(\lambda \otimes \lambda\)-a.s.
Monotone Convergence Theorem: \[
I^2 = \lim_{R \to \infty} \int_{\bar{D}_R} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x^2 + y^2)} \, dx dy
\tag{31.3}\]
Polar Coordinates Integration: \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\bar{D}_R} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x^2 + y^2)} \, dx dy &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} d\theta \int_{0}^{R} r e^{-r^2/2} \, dr\\
&= 2\pi \left[ -e^{-r^2/2} \right]_{0}^{R} \\
&= 2\pi \left( 1 - e^{-R^2/2} \right)
\end{aligned}
\tag{31.4}\]

Taking \(R \to \infty\) gives \(I^2 = 2\pi \implies I = \sqrt{2\pi}\).

title: 32  Lecture 15.1: Independence
text:
Definition 32.1 The conditional probability measure given \(B\), denoted \(P(\cdot \mid B): \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]\), is defined by: \[
P(A \mid B) \triangleq \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \quad \forall A \in \mathcal{F}
\tag{32.1}\]


Definition 32.2 Two events \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\) are independent if:
\[
P(A \cap B) = P(A) P(B)
\tag{32.2}\]
If \(P(B) > 0\), this is equivalent to \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\). If \(P(A) > 0\), it is equivalent to \(P(B \mid A) = P(B)\).


Closure under Complements: If \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, then so are \(\sigma(A)\) and \(\sigma(B)\) (i.e., \(A\) and \(B^c\), \(A^c\) and \(B\), \(A^c\) and \(B^c\) are independent).

Proof for \(A\) and \(B^c\): \[
\begin{aligned}
&A=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap B^c) \implies P(A) = P(A\cap B) + P(A\cap B^c) \\
&\implies P(A\cap B^c) = P(A) - P(A\cap B) = P(A) - P(A)P(B) \\
&\quad = P(A)(1 - P(B)) = P(A)P(B^c).
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 32  Lecture 15.1: Independence
text:
32.2 Independence of Collections of Events

Definition 32.3 (Independence of Collections of Events) Let \(\{ \mathcal{C}_i \}_{i \in I}\) be a family of collections of events, where \(\mathcal{C}_i \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) for each \(i \in I\).

Finite Family: Collections \(\mathcal{C}_1, \dots, \mathcal{C}_n\) are independent if for every non-empty subset \(J \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\) and every choice \(A_j \in \mathcal{C}_j\) (\(j \in J\)): \[
P\left( \bigcap_{j \in J} A_j \right) = \prod_{j \in J} P(A_j)
\tag{32.3}\]
Infinite Family: An arbitrary family \(\{ \mathcal{C}_i \}_{i \in I}\) is independent if every finite subfamily is independent.



Convenient Notation: If \(\Omega \in \mathcal{C}_i\) for all \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\), then condition Equation 32.3 reduces to verifying the single identity: \[
P\left( \bigcap_{i=1}^n A_i \right) = \prod_{i=1}^n P(A_i) \quad \forall A_i \in \mathcal{C}_i
\tag{32.4}\]
Pairwise vs. Mutual Independence: Pairwise independence (\(P(A_i \cap A_j) = P(A_i)P(A_j)\) for all \(i \neq j\)) does not imply mutual independence. For example, in two fair coin tosses with \(A = \{HH, HT\}\), \(B = \{HH, TH\}\), and \(C = \{HT, TH\}\), the events are pairwise independent with probabilities \(\frac{1}{2}\), but \(P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(\emptyset) = 0 \neq \frac{1}{8} = P(A)P(B)P(C)\).

title: 32  Lecture 15.1: Independence
text:
32.3 Uniqueness of Measures and \(\pi\)-Systems

Definition 32.4 A collection \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) is a \(\pi\)-system if it is closed under finite intersections: \[
A, B \in \mathcal{C} \implies A \cap B \in \mathcal{C}
\tag{32.5}\]


Lemma 32.1 (Uniqueness of Measures on \(\pi\)-Systems) Let \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a \(\pi\)-system. If \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are probability measures on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) such that \(\mu(A) = \nu(A)\) for all \(A \in \mathcal{C}\), then \(\mu = \nu\) on \(\sigma(\mathcal{C})\).


Proof. 

Define \(\mathbb{M} \triangleq \{ \mathbf{1}_B \mid B \in \mathcal{C} \}\). Since \(\mathcal{C}\) is a \(\pi\)-system, \(\mathbf{1}_A \cdot \mathbf{1}_B = \mathbf{1}_{A \cap B} \in \mathbb{M}\), so \(\mathbb{M}\) is a multiplicative system.
Let \(\mathbb{H} \triangleq \left\{ f \in B(\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \;\middle|\; \int_{\Omega} f \, d\mu = \int_{\Omega} f \, d\nu \right\}\). \(\mathbb{H}\) is a vector space containing \(1\) (since \(\mu(\Omega) = \nu(\Omega) = 1\)) and is closed under bounded convergence by the Dominated Convergence Theorem: if \(\{f_n\} \subset \mathbb{H}\) with \(|f_n| \le M\) and \(f_n \to f\) pointwise, then DCT with dominating function \(M\) (integrable since \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are probability measures) gives \(\int f_n \, d\mu \to \int f \, d\mu\) and \(\int f_n \, d\nu \to \int f \, d\nu\); since equality holds at each stage, it holds in the limit, so \(f \in \mathbb{H}\).
Since \(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}\), Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem implies \(B(\Omega, \sigma(\mathbb{M})) \subseteq \mathbb{H}\).
Because \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) = \sigma(\mathcal{C})\), taking \(f = \mathbf{1}_A\) for \(A \in \sigma(\mathcal{C})\) gives \(\mu(A) = \nu(A)\).



Remark 32.1 (Remark on Step 4). In Step 4, we claim that \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) = \sigma(\mathcal{C})\). This follows from the fact that \(\mathbb{M}\) consists of the indicator functions of the sets in \(\mathcal{C}\), and the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by these indicator functions is exactly the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by the original sets in \(\mathcal{C}\).

\(\sigma(\mathcal C)\subseteq\sigma(\mathbb M)\): Take any \(B\in\mathcal C\). Since \(B\in\mathcal C\), we have \(B\in\sigma(\mathcal C)\). Therefore its indicator function \(\mathbf1_B:\Omega\to\{0,1\}\) is \(\sigma(\mathcal C)\)-measurable. Indeed, \[
\{\omega:\mathbf1_B(\omega)=1\}=B\in\sigma(\mathcal C).
\] Thus every function in \(\mathbb M\) is \(\sigma(\mathcal C)\)-measurable. Hence the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by \(\mathbb M\) cannot be larger than \(\sigma(\mathcal C)\): \[
\sigma(\mathbb{M}) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{C}).
\]
\(\sigma(\mathcal C)\subseteq\sigma(\mathbb M)\): Now take any \(B\in\mathcal C\). By definition, \(\mathbf{1}_B\in\mathbb M\). Since \(\sigma(\mathbb M)\) makes every function in \(\mathbb M\) measurable, \(\mathbf{1}_B\) is \(\sigma(\mathbb M)\)-measurable. But then \[
B = \{\omega:\mathbf1_B(\omega)=1\} = \mathbf1_B^{-1}(\{1\}) \in\sigma(\mathbb M).
\] Therefore, \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \sigma(\mathbb{M})\). Hence, \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}) \subseteq \sigma(\mathbb{M})\).

title: 32  Lecture 15.1: Independence
text:
32.4 Extension of Independence to Generated \(\sigma\)-Algebras

Theorem 32.1 If \(\mathcal{C}_1, \dots, \mathcal{C}_n \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) are independent \(\pi\)-systems, then the generated \(\sigma\)-algebras \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}_1), \dots, \sigma(\mathcal{C}_n)\) are independent.


Proof. (Proof for \(n = 2\))
Fix \(B \in \mathcal{C}_2\).

Case 1 (\(P(B) = 0\)): For any \(A \in \mathcal{F}\), \(P(A \cap B) \le P(B) = 0 = P(A)P(B)\), so independence holds trivially.
Case 2 (\(P(B) > 0\)): Consider the conditional probability measure \(P(\cdot \mid B)\) on \(\mathcal{F}\). For all \(A \in \mathcal{C}_1\), independence of \(\mathcal{C}_1\) and \(\mathcal{C}_2\) implies \(P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = P(A)\).
Thus, the two probability measures \(P(\cdot \mid B)\) and \(P(\cdot)\) agree on the \(\pi\)-system \(\mathcal{C}_1\).
By Lemma 32.1, \(P(\cdot \mid B)\) and \(P(\cdot)\) agree on \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}_1)\). Hence, \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\) for all \(A \in \sigma(\mathcal{C}_1)\) and \(B \in \mathcal{C}_2\).

We have now established \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\) for all \(A \in \sigma(\mathcal{C}_1)\) and \(B \in \mathcal{C}_2\). To extend to \(B \in \sigma(\mathcal{C}_2)\), fix \(A \in \sigma(\mathcal{C}_1)\):

Case 1 (\(P(A) = 0\)): For any \(B \in \mathcal{F}\), \(P(A \cap B) \le P(A) = 0 = P(A)P(B)\), so independence holds trivially.
Case 2 (\(P(A) > 0\)): The two probability measures \(P(\cdot \mid A)\) and \(P(\cdot)\) agree on \(\mathcal{C}_2\): for all \(B \in \mathcal{C}_2\), \(P(B \mid A) = P(A \cap B)/P(A) = P(B)\). By Lemma 32.1 applied to the \(\pi\)-system \(\mathcal{C}_2\), \(P(\cdot \mid A)\) and \(P(\cdot)\) agree on \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}_2)\), giving \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\) for all \(B \in \sigma(\mathcal{C}_2)\).

Since \(A \in \sigma(\mathcal{C}_1)\) was arbitrary, \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}_1)\) and \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}_2)\) are independent. For \(n > 2\), the same two-step procedure is applied to each index in turn: at stage \(k\), fix an arbitrary choice of events from the already-extended \(\sigma\)-algebras and apply Lemma 32.1 to extend from \(\mathcal{C}_k\) to \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}_k)\).

title: 32  Lecture 15.1: Independence
text:
32.5 The Second Borel-Cantelli Lemma

Theorem 32.2 (Borel-Cantelli Lemma (II)) Let \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{F}\) be a sequence of independent events. If \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty P(A_n) = \infty\), then: \[
P(\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\}) = P\left( \limsup_{n \to \infty} A_n \right) = 1
\tag{32.6}\]


Proof. Recall that \(\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\} = \bigcap_{k=1}^\infty \bigcup_{n=k}^\infty A_n\). Taking complements gives \(\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\}^c = \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty \bigcap_{n=k}^\infty A_n^c\). The sets \(B_k \triangleq \bigcap_{n=k}^\infty A_n^c\) are increasing in \(k\) (larger \(k\) means fewer sets in the intersection), so by continuity of probability from below: \[
P(\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\}^c) = P\left( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty B_k \right) = \lim_{k \to \infty} P(B_k) = \lim_{k \to \infty} P\left( \bigcap_{n=k}^\infty A_n^c \right)
\]
For any fixed \(k \in \mathbb{N}\) and finite \(M \ge k\), by Theorem 32.1 each singleton \(\{A_n\}\) is a \(\pi\)-system, so the generated \(\sigma\)-algebras \(\sigma(A_n) = \{\emptyset, A_n, A_n^c, \Omega\}\) are mutually independent. Since \(A_n^c \in \sigma(A_n)\), the complements \(\{A_n^c\}\) are mutually independent: \[
P\left( \bigcap_{n=k}^M A_n^c \right) = \prod_{n=k}^M P(A_n^c) = \prod_{n=k}^M (1 - P(A_n))
\]
Using the elementary inequality \(1 - x \le e^{-x}\) (valid for all \(x \ge 0\)): \[
\prod_{n=k}^M (1 - P(A_n)) \le \prod_{n=k}^M e^{-P(A_n)} = \exp\left( -\sum_{n=k}^M P(A_n) \right)
\]
Taking \(M \to \infty\), since \(\sum_{n=k}^\infty P(A_n) = \infty\), we obtain: \[
\begin{aligned}
P\left( \bigcap_{n=k}^\infty A_n^c \right) &= \lim_{M \to \infty} P\left( \bigcap_{n=k}^M A_n^c \right) \\
&\le \lim_{M \to \infty} \exp\left( -\sum_{n=k}^M P(A_n) \right) = 0.
\end{aligned}
\] Thus \(P(\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\}^c) = \lim_{k \to \infty} 0 = 0 \implies P(\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\}) = 1\).

title: 32  Lecture 15.1: Independence
text:
32.6 Reconstruction and Interpretation Notes

Notational Standardizations:
