title: 34  Lecture 16.1: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (I)
text:
Definition 34.1 A sequence of random variables \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) taking values in a measurable space \((S, \mathcal{B}) = (\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) is independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) if all \(X_n\) are mutually independent and share a common probability law \(\mu_{X_n} = \mu\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).



Lemma 34.1 Let \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1), \dots, (S_N, \mathcal{B}_N)\) be measurable spaces and \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_N\) be probability measures on them. Define the product space: \[
\Omega \triangleq \prod_{n=1}^N S_n, \quad \mathcal{F} \triangleq \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n, \quad P \triangleq \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n
\tag{34.1}\]
Then the canonical projection maps \(X_n(\omega) \triangleq \pi_n(x_1, \dots, x_N) = x_n\) are independent random variables with marginal laws \(\mu_{X_n} = \mu_n\) for \(n = 1, \dots, N\).


Proof (Proof of Lemma 34.1). Measurability. Each projection \(X_n = \pi_n : \Omega \to S_n\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}_n)\)-measurable by Lemma 30.1 applied to the product \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F} = \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n\).
Joint distribution on rectangles. For any \(B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n\), the simultaneous event is the product rectangle: \[
\{X_1 \in B_1, \dots, X_N \in B_N\} = \bigcap_{n=1}^N \pi_n^{-1}(B_n) = B_1 \times \dots \times B_N.
\] Applying \(P = \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n\) and using the defining property of the product measure on rectangles: \[
\begin{aligned}
P(X_1 \in B_1, \dots, X_N \in B_N) &= \left(\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n\right)\!(B_1 \times \dots \times B_N) \\
&= \prod_{n=1}^N \mu_n(B_n).
\end{aligned}
\tag{34.2}\]
Marginal laws. Fix \(n \in \{1,\dots,N\}\) and \(B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n\). Setting \(B_j = S_j\) for all \(j \neq n\) in Equation 34.2, and using \(\mu_j(S_j) = 1\) (since each \(\mu_j\) is a probability measure): \[
P(X_n \in B_n) = \mu_n(B_n) \cdot \prod_{j \neq n} \mu_j(S_j) = \mu_n(B_n) \cdot \prod_{j \neq n} 1 = \mu_n(B_n).
\] Hence \(\mu_{X_n} = \mu_n\).
Independence. Substituting \(P(X_n \in B_n) = \mu_n(B_n)\) into Equation 34.2 gives: \[
P(X_1 \in B_1, \dots, X_N \in B_N) = \prod_{n=1}^N P(X_n \in B_n) \quad \forall\, B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n.
\] For any sub-family \(J \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) and \(B_j \in \mathcal{B}_j\) (\(j \in J\)), set \(B_j = S_j\) for \(j \notin J\); then \(\prod_{j \notin J} P(X_j \in S_j) = 1\), giving \(P\bigl(\bigcap_{j \in J}\{X_j \in B_j\}\bigr) = \prod_{j \in J} P(X_j \in B_j)\). Since this holds for all non-empty \(J\) and all \(B_j \in \mathcal{B}_j\), the random variables \(X_1, \dots, X_N\) are independent by Definition 33.1.

title: 34  Lecture 16.1: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (I)
section: 34.2 Example: Construction of Standard Normal Vectors
text:
34.2 Example: Construction of Standard Normal Vectors
To construct \(d\) i.i.d. \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) random variables on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(\gamma(x) = (2\pi)^{-1/2} e^{-x^2/2}\) be the standard Gaussian density with respect to Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\) on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\), and define \(d\mu = \gamma \, d\lambda\). The Gaussian integral \(\int_{\mathbb{R}} \gamma \, d\lambda = 1\) is what makes \(\mu\) a probability measure, which is required below.
Since \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) (the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra identity of Lecture 14.2), the space \((\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) carries the product measure \(P = \mu^{\otimes d}\) of Proposition 34.1. By Lemma 34.1 the coordinate projections \(X_n(x_1, \dots, x_d) = x_n\) are i.i.d. with common law \(\mu = \mathcal{N}(0,1)\); no computation of a joint density is needed for this conclusion.
The joint density is a consequence, not the reason. Define \[
\begin{aligned}
f(x_1, \dots, x_d) &\triangleq \prod_{j=1}^d \gamma(x_j) \\
&= (2\pi)^{-d/2} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2 \right) \\
&= (2\pi)^{-d/2} e^{-\frac{1}{2}\|x\|^2},
\end{aligned}
\tag{34.5}\] a non-negative Borel function on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
The two candidate reference measures agree. Let \(\lambda^{\otimes d}\) be the \(d\)-fold product of one-dimensional Lebesgue measure on \(\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\), which exists by Proposition 34.1 since \(\lambda\) is \(\sigma\)-finite, and let \(\lambda^d\) denote Lebesgue measure on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). The two \(\sigma\)-algebras coincide by the Borel identity. Let \[
\mathcal{R}_{\square} \triangleq \Bigl\{ \textstyle\prod_{j=1}^d (a_j, b_j] \;\Big|\; -\infty \le a_j \le b_j \le +\infty \Bigr\},
\] with the convention \((a, +\infty] \triangleq (a, +\infty)\), and where \(a_j = b_j\) is allowed so that \(\emptyset \in \mathcal{R}_{\square}\). Then \(\mathcal{R}_{\square}\) is a \(\pi\)-system, because \(\prod_j(a_j,b_j] \cap \prod_j(a_j',b_j'] = \prod_j (a_j \vee a_j', \, b_j \wedge b_j']\) (interpreting an interval with left endpoint \(\ge\) right endpoint as empty), and \(\sigma(\mathcal{R}_{\square}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Both \(\lambda^{\otimes d}\) and \(\lambda^d\) assign the value \(\prod_{j=1}^d (b_j - a_j)\) to such a box — for \(\lambda^{\otimes d}\) by Equation 34.2, for \(\lambda^d\) by its defining property. Since \(R_m \triangleq (-m, m]^d \in \mathcal{R}_{\square}\) increases to \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with \(\lambda^{\otimes d}(R_m) = (2m)^d < \infty\), the uniqueness argument of Corollary 30.1 (an increasing sequence of finite-measure sets inside the \(\pi\)-system) gives \[
\lambda^{\otimes d} = \lambda^d \quad\text{on } \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d).
\]
Computing the law. For any box \(R = \prod_{j=1}^d (a_j, b_j] \in \mathcal{R}_{\square}\) we have the tensor factorization \(f \cdot \mathbf{1}_R = \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \bigl( \gamma \cdot \mathbf{1}_{(a_j,b_j]} \bigr)\). Applying Theorem 31.1 to the two-factor splitting \(\lambda^{\otimes d} = \lambda^{\otimes (d-1)} \otimes \lambda\) supplied by Equation 34.1 — legitimate because \(f \mathbf{1}_R \ge 0\) is Borel and all factors are \(\sigma\)-finite — and iterating \(d - 1\) times, \[
\int_R f \, d\lambda^{\otimes d} = \prod_{j=1}^d \int_{(a_j, b_j]} \gamma \, d\lambda = \prod_{j=1}^d \mu\bigl((a_j, b_j]\bigr) = \mu^{\otimes d}(R),
\] the last step by Equation 34.2. Taking \(R = \mathbb{R}^d\) shows \(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \, d\lambda^{\otimes d} = 1\), so \(\nu(E) \triangleq \int_E f \, d\lambda^{\otimes d}\) defines a probability measure on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Since \(\nu\) and \(\mu^{\otimes d}\) are probability measures agreeing on the \(\pi\)-system \(\mathcal{R}_{\square}\) with \(\sigma(\mathcal{R}_{\square}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\), Lemma 32.1 yields \[
d\mu^{\otimes d} = f \, d\lambda^{\otimes d} = f \, d\lambda^d ,
\] i.e. the law of \((X_1, \dots, X_d)\) is the standard multivariate normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\).

title: 34  Lecture 16.1: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (I)
text:
34.2 Compact Infinite Product Spaces
To construct infinite sequences of random variables, we extend finite product measure spaces to infinite products. Let \(Q \triangleq [0, 1]^\mathbb{N} =\prod_{n=1}^\infty [0, 1] = \{ (x_n)_{n=1}^\infty \mid x_n \in [0, 1] \}\) and let \(p_n : Q \to [0,1]\), \(p_n(x) = x_n\), denote the coordinate maps. We equip \(Q\) with the product topology, i.e. the initial (coarsest) topology making every \(p_n\) continuous; a base is given by the finite cylinders \[
\bigcap_{i=1}^k p_{n_i}^{-1}(U_i), \qquad k \in \mathbb{N},\ n_1 < \dots < n_k,\ U_i \subseteq [0,1] \text{ open}.
\tag{34.6}\]
The product topology is not defined by a convergence criterion; the following lemma shows that on \(Q\) it is nevertheless metrizable, so that sequences do determine the topology. This is used twice below: to pass from sequential compactness to compactness in Theorem 34.1, and to identify \(\mathcal{B}(Q)\) in Lemma 34.3.

Lemma 34.2 (Metrizability of \(Q\)) The product topology on \(Q = [0,1]^\mathbb{N}\) is induced by the metric \[
\rho(x, y) \triangleq \sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n} |x_n - y_n| ,
\tag{34.7}\] and \(\rho\)-convergence is exactly coordinatewise (pointwise) convergence: \[
\begin{aligned}
&x^m = (x_n^m)_{n=1}^\infty \to x = (x_n)_{n=1}^\infty \text{ in } Q \\
&\iff x_n^m \to x_n \text{ in } [0, 1] \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{N}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{34.8}\] In particular \(Q\) is a separable metric space, and compactness, sequential compactness, closedness and sequential closedness in \(Q\) agree.


Proof (Proof of Lemma 34.2). The series in Equation 34.7 converges (terms bounded by \(2^{-n}\)), and \(\rho\) is clearly a metric: symmetry and the triangle inequality are inherited termwise, and \(\rho(x,y) = 0\) forces \(x_n = y_n\) for every \(n\).
\(\rho\)-convergence \(\Rightarrow\) coordinatewise. Fix \(n\); then \(|x_n^m - x_n| \le 2^n \rho(x^m, x)\).
Coordinatewise \(\Rightarrow\) \(\rho\)-convergence. Given \(\epsilon > 0\), pick \(N\) with \(\sum_{n > N} 2^{-n} < \epsilon/2\); the remaining finitely many terms satisfy \(\sum_{n \le N} 2^{-n}|x_n^m - x_n| < \epsilon/2\) for \(m\) large. (This is where \(\sum_n 2^{-n} < \infty\) is essential: the tail is uniformly small, which is why no analogue holds for uncountable products.)
\(\rho\) induces the product topology. Each \(p_n\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz up to the factor \(2^n\), hence \(\rho\)-continuous, so the product topology is coarser than the \(\rho\)-topology. Conversely, given \(x \in Q\) and \(\epsilon > 0\), choose \(N\) with \(\sum_{n > N} 2^{-n} < \epsilon/2\); the basic cylinder \(\bigcap_{n \le N} p_n^{-1}\bigl( (x_n - \epsilon/4, x_n + \epsilon/4) \cap [0,1] \bigr)\) is a product-open neighbourhood of \(x\) contained in the \(\rho\)-ball \(B_\rho(x, \epsilon)\). Hence the two topologies coincide.
The final assertions are the standard facts that in a metric space compactness and sequential compactness are equivalent, and that closed sets are exactly the sequentially closed sets. Separability follows since finitely supported rational sequences are \(\rho\)-dense.


Theorem 34.1 (Sequential Compactness of \([0, 1]^\mathbb{N}\)) Every sequence \(x^{(1)},x^{(2)},\ldots\in Q\) has a subsequence \(x^{(m_k)}\) and some \(x\in Q\) such that \(x^{(m_k)}\to x\) coordinatewise, i.e., \[
x_n^{(m_k)}\to x_n \qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb N.
\] That is, \(Q = [0,1]^\mathbb{N}\) is sequentially compact; by Lemma 34.2 it is therefore also compact.


Proof (Proof of Theorem 34.1). (Cantor’s Diagonal Argument)
Let \((x^{(m)})_{m \ge 1}\) be an arbitrary sequence in \(Q\).
Step 1: Construct nested convergent subsequences. Apply the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem (every bounded sequence in \(\mathbb{R}\) has a convergent subsequence) inductively:

Base case (\(j = 1\)): \((x_1^{(m)})_{m \ge 1} \subseteq [0,1]\) is bounded. By Bolzano-Weierstrass, extract a subsequence \(m^{(1)}(k)\) such that \(x_1^{(m^{(1)}(k))} \to x_1 \in [0,1]\) as \(k \to \infty\).
Inductive step (\(j \ge 2\)): Given the subsequence \(m^{(j-1)}\), apply Bolzano-Weierstrass to \((x_j^{(m^{(j-1)}(k))})_{k \ge 1} \subseteq [0,1]\) to extract a further subsequence \(m^{(j)}(k)\) of \(m^{(j-1)}(k)\) such that \(x_j^{(m^{(j)}(k))} \to x_j \in [0,1]\) as \(k \to \infty\).

The limits lie in \([0,1]\) because \([0,1]\) is closed. (This recursive extraction uses the axiom of dependent choice; we shall not comment on such uses again.)
This yields nested subsequences \(m^{(1)}, m^{(2)}, \ldots\) — each \(m^{(j)}\) a subsequence of \(m^{(j-1)}\) — satisfying: \[
x_j^{(m^{(j)}(k))} \to x_j \in [0,1] \quad \text{as } k \to \infty, \quad \forall j \ge 1.
\]
Step 2: Define the diagonal sequence. Set \(d_k \triangleq m^{(k)}(k)\) — the \(k\)-th element of the \(k\)-th subsequence. This is strictly increasing: since \(m^{(k+1)}\) is a subsequence of \(m^{(k)}\), write \(m^{(k+1)}(j) = m^{(k)}(\sigma_k(j))\) for a strictly increasing function \(\sigma_k\) satisfying \(\sigma_k(j) \ge j\). Then: \[
d_{k+1} = m^{(k+1)}(k+1) = m^{(k)}\!\left(\sigma_k(k+1)\right) \ge m^{(k)}(k+1) > m^{(k)}(k) = d_k.
\]
Step 3: Coordinatewise convergence. Fix any \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). For every \(k \ge n\), \(m^{(k)}\) is a subsequence of \(m^{(n)}\) (by transitivity of nesting: \(m^{(k)} \subset m^{(k-1)} \subset \cdots \subset m^{(n)}\)). Hence \(d_k = m^{(k)}(k) = m^{(n)}(l_k)\) for a unique index \(l_k\), since \(m^{(n)}\) is strictly increasing, hence injective. Moreover \(l_k\) is strictly increasing in \(k \ge n\): if \(l_{k+1} \le l_k\) then \(d_{k+1} = m^{(n)}(l_{k+1}) \le m^{(n)}(l_k) = d_k\), contradicting Step 2. Therefore \(l_k \to \infty\), and \((x_n^{(d_k)})_{k \ge n}\) is a subsequence of the convergent sequence \((x_n^{(m^{(n)}(l))})_{l \ge 1}\): \[
x_n^{(d_k)} = x_n^{(m^{(n)}(l_k))} \xrightarrow{\;k \to \infty\;} x_n.
\] The finitely many terms with \(k < n\) do not affect the limit. Since \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) was arbitrary, \(x^{(d_k)} \to x = (x_n)_{n \ge 1} \in Q\) coordinatewise.


Corollary 34.1 (Countable Finite Intersection Property) If \(\{K_m\}_{m=1}^\infty\) is a sequence of closed subsets of \(Q\) such that \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m K_i \neq \emptyset\) for all \(m \in \mathbb{N}\), then \(\bigcap_{i=1}^\infty K_i \neq \emptyset\).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 34.1). (Each \(K_m\) is automatically non-empty, by the hypothesis with \(m\) in place of the index.) For each \(m \in \mathbb{N}\), choose \(x^m \in \bigcap_{i=1}^m K_i\). By Theorem 34.1 there are indices \(m_1 < m_2 < \cdots\) and \(x \in Q\) with \(x^{m_l} \to x\) in \(Q\).
Fix \(i \in \mathbb{N}\). Since \(m_l \to \infty\), choose \(l_0\) with \(m_{l_0} \ge i\). For every \(l \ge l_0\) we have \(m_l \ge m_{l_0} \ge i\), hence \[
x^{m_l} \in \bigcap_{j=1}^{m_l} K_j \subseteq K_i .
\] Thus \(x\) is the limit of a sequence lying in \(K_i\), and \(K_i\) is closed, hence sequentially closed by Lemma 34.2; therefore \(x \in K_i\). As \(i \in \mathbb{N}\) was arbitrary, \(x \in \bigcap_{i=1}^\infty K_i\).

title: 34  Lecture 16.1: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (I)
text:
34.3 Kolmogorov Extension Theorem on \([0, 1]^\mathbb{N}\)
The Kolmogorov Extension Theorem provides a method to construct infinite sequences of random variables with prescribed finite-dimensional distributions.






NoteNotation from here on



From this point onward, and throughout Lecture 16.2, \(p_n : Q \to [0,1]\) denotes the \(n\)-th coordinate map, \(p_n(x) = x_n\), and \[
\pi_n : Q \to [0,1]^n, \qquad \pi_n(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_n),
\] denotes the projection onto the first \(n\) coordinates. This supersedes the earlier use of \(\pi_n\) in this lecture for the \(n\)-th coordinate projection of a finite product \(\prod_{k=1}^N S_k\).


Before stating the theorem we must know that the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of the topological space \(Q\) coincides with the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by the cylinder sets, on which the theorem prescribes \(P\). This is exactly what makes the uniqueness assertion meaningful; it uses that the product is countable and each factor is second countable, and it fails for uncountable products, where the cylinder \(\sigma\)-algebra is strictly smaller than the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra.

Lemma 34.3 (Borel Sets of \(Q\) are the Cylinder Sets) For every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(\mathcal{B}([0,1]^n) = \bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}([0,1])\); in particular \(B \times [0,1] \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^{n+1})\) whenever \(B \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)\). Moreover \[
\mathcal{B}(Q) = \sigma\bigl( p_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \bigr) = \sigma\Bigl( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \pi_n^{-1}\bigl( \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n) \bigr) \Bigr) ,
\tag{34.9}\] and the collection \(\mathcal{A} \triangleq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \pi_n^{-1}\bigl( \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n) \bigr)\) is an algebra, hence in particular a \(\pi\)-system, generating \(\mathcal{B}(Q)\).


Proof (Proof of Lemma 34.3). Finite-dimensional identity. Open boxes \(\prod_{k=1}^n I_k\) with \(I_k \subseteq [0,1]\) relatively open with rational endpoints form a countable base of the (second-countable, metric) space \([0,1]^n\). Every open \(G \subseteq [0,1]^n\) is therefore a countable union of such boxes, each of which lies in \(\bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}([0,1])\); hence \(\mathcal{B}([0,1]^n) \subseteq \bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}([0,1])\). Conversely each coordinate projection \(\operatorname{pr}_k : [0,1]^n \to [0,1]\) is continuous, hence Borel, so \(\operatorname{pr}_k^{-1}(\mathcal{B}([0,1])) \subseteq \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)\) for every \(k\); since \(\bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}([0,1]) = \sigma(\operatorname{pr}_1, \dots, \operatorname{pr}_n)\) by Lemma 30.2, the reverse inclusion follows. Combining this with the associativity identity Equation 34.1 gives \(\mathcal{B}([0,1]^{n+1}) = \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n) \otimes \mathcal{B}([0,1])\), so \(B \times [0,1] \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^{n+1})\) for \(B \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)\).
\(\supseteq\) in Equation 34.9. Each \(p_n\) is continuous for the product topology, hence Borel measurable, so \(\sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N}) \subseteq \mathcal{B}(Q)\). Furthermore \(\pi_n = (p_1, \dots, p_n)\) has all components \(\sigma(p_1, \dots, p_n)\)-measurable, so by Lemma 30.3 it is \(\sigma(p_1, \dots, p_n) \,/\, \bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}([0,1])\)-measurable; by the finite-dimensional identity this means \(\pi_n^{-1}(\mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)) \subseteq \sigma(p_1, \dots, p_n)\). Hence the second and third \(\sigma\)-algebras in Equation 34.9 coincide, and both are contained in \(\mathcal{B}(Q)\).
\(\subseteq\) in Equation 34.9. By Lemma 34.2 the metric \(\rho\) of Equation 34.7 induces the product topology. Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be the countable collection of finite cylinders \(\bigcap_{k \le N} p_k^{-1}(I_k)\) with \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) and each \(I_k \subseteq [0,1]\) relatively open with rational endpoints. The argument in the proof of Lemma 34.2 shows that for every \(x \in Q\) and \(\epsilon > 0\) there is a member of \(\mathcal{U}\) containing \(x\) and contained in \(B_\rho(x, \epsilon)\) (choose \(N\) with \(\sum_{n > N} 2^{-n} < \epsilon/2\) and rational-endpoint intervals of length \(< \epsilon/2\) around \(x_1, \dots, x_N\)). Hence \(\mathcal{U}\) is a countable base, so every open \(G \subseteq Q\) is a countable union of members of \(\mathcal{U}\), and each member of \(\mathcal{U}\) lies in \(\sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N})\). Therefore \(G \in \sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N})\) and \(\mathcal{B}(Q) \subseteq \sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N})\). (Countability of \(\mathcal{U}\) is exactly what fails for uncountable products.)
\(\mathcal{A}\) is an algebra. \(Q = \pi_1^{-1}([0,1]) \in \mathcal{A}\); complements are handled within a fixed level since \(Q \setminus \pi_n^{-1}(B) = \pi_n^{-1}([0,1]^n \setminus B)\); and two cylinders of orders \(m \le n\) can be brought to the common order \(n\) via \(\pi_m^{-1}(B) = \pi_n^{-1}(B \times [0,1]^{n-m})\), after which unions are taken inside \(\mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)\). Finally \(\sigma(\mathcal{A}) = \sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N}) = \mathcal{B}(Q)\).


Theorem 34.2 (Kolmogorov Extension Theorem (Compact Base Space)) For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), let \(\nu_n\) be a probability measure on \(([0, 1]^n, \mathcal{B}([0, 1]^n))\). Suppose the sequence \(\{\nu_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) satisfies the projective consistency condition: \[
\nu_{n+1}(B \times [0, 1]) = \nu_n(B) \quad \forall B \in \mathcal{B}([0, 1]^n), \, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
\tag{34.10}\] which is meaningful by Lemma 34.3. Then there exists a unique probability measure \(P\) on \((Q, \mathcal{B}(Q))\) such that \[
P\bigl( \pi_n^{-1}(B) \bigr) = \nu_n(B) \quad \forall B \in \mathcal{B}([0, 1]^n), \, \forall n \in \mathbb{N},
\tag{34.11}\] equivalently \(P \circ \pi_n^{-1} = \nu_n\) for every \(n\); that is, \(\{\nu_n\}\) is exactly the family of finite-dimensional distributions of \(P\).

Three comments on the statement.

Notation. In Equation 34.11 the cylinder \(\pi_n^{-1}(B)\) is often written \(B \times Q\), using the canonical homeomorphism \(Q \cong [0,1]^n \times [0,1]^{\{n+1, n+2, \dots\}}\). Strictly, \(B \times Q\) is not a subset of \(Q\), and we use \(\pi_n^{-1}(B)\) throughout.
Uniqueness. Uniqueness is immediate from Lemma 34.3 and Lemma 32.1: Equation 34.11 determines \(P\) on the \(\pi\)-system \(\mathcal{A}\), and \(\sigma(\mathcal{A}) = \mathcal{B}(Q)\). Existence is the substantive assertion.
Scope of the consistency condition. Equation 34.10 only requires consistency under deletion of the last coordinate. For a family indexed by the initial segments \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) this is enough: iterating it gives \(\nu_m\bigl( B \times [0,1]^{m-n} \bigr) = \nu_n(B)\) for all \(m > n\). For families indexed by arbitrary finite subsets \(F\) of a general index set \(T\), the condition must be strengthened to include permutation consistency, \(\nu_{\sigma F} = \nu_F \circ \sigma^{-1}\), in addition to marginal consistency.

Finally, the hypothesis that the base space is the compact interval \([0,1]\) is not a technical convenience: the theorem is false for general measurable state spaces. The proof converts finite additivity on the cylinder algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) into countable additivity by an inner-regularity argument, using Theorem 35.1 (in the form Corollary 35.1, which applies to the cubes \([0,1]^n\)) together with Corollary 34.1. The proof is given in Lecture 16.2; the case of \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\) is then obtained by transporting the problem to \((0,1)^\mathbb{N} \subseteq Q\) along a homeomorphism \(\mathbb{R} \cong (0,1)\).

Example 34.4 Let \(\lambda\) denote the uniform probability measure on \([0,1]\). For each \(n\), define \(\nu_n=\lambda^{\otimes n}\) the \(n\)-fold product measure on \(([0,1]^n,\mathcal B([0,1]^n))\). Thus, \(\nu_n\) is the joint distribution of \(n\) independent \(U[0,1]\) random variables. We want to check that \[
\nu_{n+1}(B\times[0,1])=\nu_n(B)
\] for every \(B\in\mathcal B([0,1]^n)\).
Suppose \(B=B_1\times\cdots\times B_n\), where each \(B_j\in\mathcal B([0,1])\). Then \[
B\times[0,1] = B_1\times\cdots\times B_n\times[0,1].
\] Because \(\nu_{n+1}=\lambda^{\otimes(n+1)}\), we have \[
\begin{aligned}
\nu_{n+1}(B\times[0,1]) &= \lambda(B_1)\cdots\lambda(B_n)\lambda([0,1])\\
&= \lambda(B_1)\cdots\lambda(B_n),
\end{aligned}
\] because \(\lambda([0,1])=1\). But \(\nu_n(B) = \lambda(B_1)\cdots\lambda(B_n)\). Therefore, \[
\nu_{n+1}(B\times[0,1]) = \nu_n(B).
\]
Suppose \(\nu_2=\lambda\otimes\lambda\) describes the joint distribution of \((X_1,X_2)\) and \(\nu_3=\lambda\otimes\lambda\otimes\lambda\) describes the joint distribution of \((X_1,X_2,X_3)\). Take, for example, \(B=[0,0.3]\times[0.5,0.8]\). Then \[
B\times[0,1] = [0,0.3]\times[0.5,0.8]\times[0,1].
\] The consistency condition says \[
\nu_3\left( [0,0.3]\times[0.5,0.8]\times[0,1] \right) = \nu_2\left( [0,0.3]\times[0.5,0.8] \right).
\] Indeed, \((0.3)(0.3)(1)=0.09\) while \((0.3)(0.3)=0.09\). The third coordinate contributes nothing because we allow it to take any value in \([0,1]\).
Thus the family \(\nu_1=\lambda\), \(\nu_2=\lambda^{\otimes2}\), \(\nu_3=\lambda^{\otimes3}\),\(\ldots\) is projectively consistent. Kolmogorov’s theorem then gives a unique probability measure \(P\) on \(Q=[0,1]^{\mathbb N}\) such that \[
P\circ\pi_n^{-1}=\lambda^{\otimes n} \qquad\forall n.
\] In other words, the theorem constructs the probability law of an infinite sequence \((X_1,X_2,X_3,\ldots)\) of independent \(U[0,1]\) random variables from its finite-dimensional distributions.
So the conceptual picture is: \[
\underbrace{\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3,\ldots}_{\text{finite-dimensional distributions}} \quad\xrightarrow{\text{Kolmogorov Extension}}\quad \underbrace{P}_{\text{law of the infinite sequence}}
\]

title: 34  Lecture 16.1: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (I)
text:
34.5 Reconstruction and Interpretation Notes

Notational Standardizations:

Formulated Cantor’s diagonal extraction \(m_j(k)\) explicitly to complete the sequential compactness proof of \(Q = [0, 1]^\mathbb{N}\).
Standardized product cylinder notation \(B \times Q \subseteq Q\) corresponding to finite dimensional marginal evaluation \(B \in \mathcal{B}([0, 1]^n)\).

title: 35  Lecture 16.2: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (II)
text:
Definition 35.1 A Borel measure \(\mu\) on \((X, \mathcal{B}(X))\) is called:

Outer-regular: \(\mu(B) = \inf \{ \mu(V) \mid B \subseteq V, \, V \text{ open} \}\) for all \(B \in \mathcal{B}(X)\).
Inner-regular: \(\mu(B) = \sup \{ \mu(K) \mid K \subseteq B, \, K \text{ compact} \}\) for all \(B \in \mathcal{B}(X)\).
Radon measure: \(\mu\) is finite on compact sets (\(\mu(K) < \infty\) for all compact \(K \subseteq X\); on a locally compact Hausdorff space this is equivalent to being locally finite) and both inner- and outer-regular.



Remark 35.1 (Two Conventions for “Radon”). Two cautionary remarks about the word Radon.

Relation to Definition 11.1. In Lecture 5.1 a Radon measure on \(\mathbb{R}\) was defined by the purely local condition \(\mu((a,b]) < \infty\) for all bounded intervals, with no regularity requirement. On \(\mathbb{R}^d\) the two notions in fact coincide, but we do not prove this in general: Theorem 35.1 below establishes it for finite Borel measures, which is the only case used in this lecture. Whenever regularity is invoked below, it is Theorem 35.1 (or its Corollary 35.1) that is being used, never Definition 11.1.
Strong versus weak inner regularity. Many texts require inner regularity only on open sets (together with outer regularity on all Borel sets). The definition above, demanding inner regularity on all Borel sets, is the stronger “tight” form. The two are not equivalent on a general locally compact Hausdorff space, but they agree for finite Borel measures on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) by Theorem 35.1, so no ambiguity arises here.



Theorem 35.1 Every finite Borel measure \(\mu\) on \((\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) (in particular, any probability measure) is a Radon measure.


Proof (Proof of Theorem 35.1). Finiteness on compact sets is immediate: \(\mu(K) \le \mu(\mathbb{R}^d) < \infty\) for every compact \(K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\). It remains to prove inner- and outer-regularity.
Write \(d(x,C) \triangleq \inf_{y \in C} |x - y|\) for the Euclidean distance from a point to a set (with \(d(x,\emptyset) \triangleq +\infty\)), and define the family of sets: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{F} \triangleq \bigl\{ B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \;\big|\;&
\forall \epsilon > 0,\ \exists\text{ open }V\text{ and closed }C\text{ such that}\\
& C \subseteq B \subseteq V
\text{ and }
\mu(V\setminus C)<\epsilon
\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Closed Sets are in \(\mathcal{F}\): Let \(C\) be closed. For \(k \in \mathbb{N}\), set \(V_k \triangleq \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^d \mid d(x, C) < 1/k \}\) (so \(V_k = \emptyset\) if \(C = \emptyset\)). Then each \(V_k\) is open, \(C \subseteq V_k\), the sequence \((V_k)\) is decreasing, and \(\bigcap_{k} V_k = \overline{C} = C\) because \(C\) is closed. Since \(\mu(V_1) \le \mu(\mathbb{R}^d) < \infty\), continuity from above gives \(\mu(V_k \setminus C) = \mu(V_k) - \mu(C) \to 0\). Given \(\epsilon > 0\), choose \(k\) with \(\mu(V_k \setminus C) < \epsilon\); the pair consisting of the closed set \(C\) itself and the open set \(V_k\) then witnesses \(C \in \mathcal{F}\).
Algebra Properties:

\(\emptyset \in \mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathbb{R}^d \in \mathcal{F}\), both being closed (item 1).
Let \(A \in \mathcal{F}\) and \(\epsilon > 0\). Choose \(C\) closed and \(V\) open with \(C \subseteq A \subseteq V\) and \(\mu(V \setminus C) < \epsilon\). Then \(V^c \subseteq A^c \subseteq C^c\) with \(V^c\) closed and \(C^c\) open. Since \(C^c \setminus V^c = C^c \cap V = V \setminus C\), we get \(\mu(C^c \setminus V^c) < \epsilon\). As \(\epsilon > 0\) was arbitrary, \(A^c \in \mathcal{F}\).
Let \(A_1, A_2 \in \mathcal{F}\) and \(\epsilon > 0\). Choose \(C_i \subseteq A_i \subseteq V_i\) with \(C_i\) closed, \(V_i\) open and \(\mu(V_i \setminus C_i) < \epsilon/2\). Then \(C_1 \cup C_2\) is closed, \(V_1 \cup V_2\) is open, \(C_1 \cup C_2 \subseteq A_1 \cup A_2 \subseteq V_1 \cup V_2\), and \((V_1 \cup V_2) \setminus (C_1 \cup C_2) \subseteq (V_1 \setminus C_1) \cup (V_2 \setminus C_2)\), so \(\mu((V_1 \cup V_2) \setminus (C_1 \cup C_2)) \le \mu(V_1 \setminus C_1) + \mu(V_2 \setminus C_2) < \epsilon\). As \(\epsilon > 0\) was arbitrary, \(A_1 \cup A_2 \in \mathcal{F}\).

Hence \(\mathcal{F}\) is an algebra (closure under finite intersections follows from complements and unions).
Closure under countable disjoint unions: Let \(A_n \in \mathcal{F}\) be pairwise disjoint and fix \(\epsilon > 0\). Choose \(C_n \subseteq A_n \subseteq V_n\) with \(\mu(V_n \setminus C_n) < \epsilon/2^{n+1}\). Set \(V = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty V_n\) (open) and \(D_N = \bigcup_{n=1}^N C_n\) (closed), so that \(D_N \subseteq A \triangleq \bigcup_n A_n \subseteq V\). Observe that: \[
V \setminus D_N \subseteq \bigcup_{n=1}^N (V_n \setminus C_n) \cup \bigcup_{n=N+1}^\infty V_n.
\] For \(n > N\), since \(C_n \subseteq A_n\) we have \(\mu(V_n) \le \mu(A_n) + \mu(V_n \setminus C_n)\). By subadditivity: \[
\mu(V \setminus D_N) \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(V_n \setminus C_n) + \sum_{n=N+1}^\infty \mu(A_n) < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \sum_{n=N+1}^\infty \mu(A_n).
\] Since \(\mu\) is finite and the \(A_n\) are disjoint, \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n) = \mu(A) \le \mu(\mathbb{R}^d) < \infty\), so \(\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty \mu(A_n) < \epsilon/2\) for \(N\) sufficiently large. Hence \(\mu(V \setminus D_N) < \epsilon\) for such \(N\), and since \(\epsilon > 0\) was arbitrary, \(A = \bigcup_n A_n \in \mathcal{F}\).
\(\mathcal{F}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra: Given any (not necessarily disjoint) \(A_n \in \mathcal{F}\), apply disjointification: set \(B_1 = A_1\) and \(B_n = A_n \setminus \bigcup_{k=1}^{n-1} A_k\) for \(n \ge 2\). Since \(\mathcal{F}\) is an algebra (Step 2), each \(B_n \in \mathcal{F}\). The \(B_n\) are pairwise disjoint and \(\bigcup_n A_n = \bigsqcup_n B_n\), so \(\bigcup_n A_n \in \mathcal{F}\) by the disjoint case above. Together with \(\mathbb{R}^d \in \mathcal{F}\) and closure under complements, \(\mathcal{F}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra.
Since \(\mathcal{F}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra containing all closed sets, \(\mathcal{F} \supseteq \sigma(\text{closed sets}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Combined with \(\mathcal{F} \subseteq \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\) by definition, \(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\).

For any \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \mathcal{F}\), the definition of \(\mathcal{F}\) provides, for each \(n\), a closed set \(C_n \subseteq B\) with \(\mu(B \setminus C_n) < 1/n\), establishing inner-regularity with closed sets. Setting \(K_n = C_n \cap \bar{B}^d(0, n)\) gives compact \(K_n \subseteq B\) with \[
\mu(B \setminus K_n) \le \mu(B \setminus C_n) + \mu(C_n \setminus \bar{B}^d(0,n)) < \frac{1}{n} + \mu(B \setminus \bar{B}^d(0,n)) \to 0
\] as \(n \to \infty\) (using \(B \setminus \bar{B}^d(0,n) \downarrow \emptyset\) and continuity from above for the finite measure \(\mu\)). Hence \(\mu(K_n) \to \mu(B)\), establishing full inner-regularity. For outer-regularity, given \(\epsilon > 0\) take \(C \subseteq B \subseteq V\) with \(\mu(V \setminus C) < \epsilon\) as in the definition of \(\mathcal{F}\); then \(V \setminus B \subseteq V \setminus C\), so \(\mu(V) = \mu(B) + \mu(V \setminus B) \le \mu(B) + \epsilon\), and since \(\epsilon > 0\) was arbitrary the infimum over open \(V \supseteq B\) equals \(\mu(B)\).
Note where the two hypotheses enter. Everything up to the previous paragraph uses only that \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is a metric space and that \(\mu\) is finite, and yields inner regularity by closed sets; this part is valid in any metric space. The upgrade from closed to compact sets uses the Heine–Borel theorem (a closed bounded subset of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is compact) together with \(\sigma\)-compactness of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and does fail in general metric spaces.



Corollary 35.1 (Regularity on Borel Subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\)) Let \(E \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\), give \(E\) the subspace topology, and let \(\mathcal{B}(E)\) be its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra. Let \(\nu\) be a finite Borel measure on \((E, \mathcal{B}(E))\). Then \(\nu\) is inner-regular by compact sets: \[
\nu(B) = \sup\{ \nu(K) \mid K \subseteq B, \ K \text{ compact} \} \qquad \forall B \in \mathcal{B}(E),
\] where “compact” may equivalently be read in \(E\) or in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), compactness being intrinsic to a subset. In particular every probability measure \(\nu_n\) on \(([0,1]^n, \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n))\) is inner-regular by compact sets.


Proof (Proof of Corollary 35.1). Step 0: identification of \(\mathcal{B}(E)\). The collection \(\mathcal{D} \triangleq \{ A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \mid A \cap E \in \mathcal{B}(E) \}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra (preimages under the inclusion \(E \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d\) commute with complements and countable unions) and contains every open \(A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\), since \(A \cap E\) is open in \(E\). Hence \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \subseteq \mathcal{D}\), i.e. \(\{A \cap E \mid A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\} \subseteq \mathcal{B}(E)\). Conversely \(\{A \cap E \mid A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(E\) containing all sets open in \(E\), so it contains \(\mathcal{B}(E)\). Therefore \[
\mathcal{B}(E) = \{ A \cap E \mid A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \},
\] and because \(E \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\) every such \(A \cap E\) is itself Borel in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), giving \[
\mathcal{B}(E) = \{ A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \mid A \subseteq E \} \subseteq \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d).
\]
Step 1: transfer. Define \(\hat{\nu}(A) \triangleq \nu(A \cap E)\) for \(A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\); this is well defined by Step 0, is countably additive because \(\nu\) is and \(A \mapsto A \cap E\) preserves disjointness and countable unions, and is finite with \(\hat\nu(\mathbb{R}^d) = \nu(E) < \infty\). Hence \(\hat\nu\) is Radon by Theorem 35.1. For \(B \in \mathcal{B}(E)\) we have \(B \subseteq E\), so \(\hat\nu(B) = \nu(B)\) and \[
\nu(B) = \hat{\nu}(B) = \sup\{ \hat{\nu}(K) \mid K \subseteq B, \ K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \text{ compact} \}.
\] Every such \(K\) satisfies \(K \subseteq B \subseteq E\), so \(K\) is compact in the subspace topology of \(E\) as well (compactness of a set depends only on its own subspace topology), and \(\hat{\nu}(K) = \nu(K)\). The final claim follows with \(E = [0,1]^n\), which is closed, hence Borel, in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

title: 35  Lecture 16.2: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (II)
section: 35.2 Proof of the Kolmogorov Extension Theorem
text:
35.2 Proof of the Kolmogorov Extension Theorem
Let \(Q = [0, 1]^\mathbb{N}\) equipped with the product topology and its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(Q)\). We prove Theorem 34.2, whose hypotheses (a projectively consistent family \(\{\nu_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) of probability measures on \(([0,1]^n, \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n))\)) and conclusion (existence and uniqueness of \(P\) on \((Q, \mathcal{B}(Q))\) with \(P \circ \pi_n^{-1} = \nu_n\)) are stated there.

Proof (Proof of Theorem 34.2). 

Cylinder Algebra: For \(j \in \mathbb{N}\), let \(p_j:Q\to[0,1]\) be the \(j\)-th coordinate projection, \(p_j((x_k)_{k=1}^\infty)=x_j\). Let \(\pi_n:Q\to[0,1]^n\) be the projection onto the first \(n\) coordinates: \[
\pi_n(x)=(p_1(x),\ldots,p_n(x))=(x_1,\ldots,x_n),
\] and write \(Q_{>n} \triangleq [0,1]^{\{n+1,n+2,\ldots\}}\) for the remaining coordinates. Under the canonical bijection \(Q \cong [0,1]^n \times Q_{>n}\) we have \(\pi_n^{-1}(B) = B \times Q_{>n}\); we use the unambiguous form \(\pi_n^{-1}(B)\) from now on. Define the \(\sigma\)-algebra of cylinder sets determined by the first \(n\) coordinates by \[
\mathcal{C}_n
\triangleq \{\pi_n^{-1}(B)\mid B\in\mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)\}
=\sigma(\pi_n)=\sigma(p_1,\ldots,p_n).
\tag{35.1}\] The inverse images of Borel sets form the \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\sigma(\pi_n)\). Moreover, each \(p_j\) with \(j\le n\) is \(\sigma(\pi_n)\)-measurable because \(p_j=\operatorname{pr}_j\circ\pi_n\) with \(\operatorname{pr}_j\) continuous, while \(\pi_n=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) is \(\sigma(p_1,\ldots,p_n)/\bigotimes_{k\le n}\mathcal{B}([0,1])\)-measurable by Lemma 30.3, and \(\bigotimes_{k \le n}\mathcal{B}([0,1]) = \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)\) by Lemma 34.3. These two inclusions prove \(\sigma(\pi_n)=\sigma(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\).
The collection \(\mathcal{A} \triangleq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \mathcal{C}_n\) is exactly the algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) of Lemma 34.3, and by that lemma \[
\sigma(\mathcal{A})=\sigma(p_j:j\in\mathbb{N})=\mathcal{B}(Q).
\] (This last identity is where countability of the index set and second countability of \([0,1]\) are used; for an uncountable product the inclusion \(\sigma(\mathcal{A}) \subseteq \mathcal{B}(Q)\) can be strict.) Note also that \(\mathcal{C}_m \subseteq \mathcal{C}_n\) for \(m \le n\), since \(\pi_m^{-1}(B) = \pi_n^{-1}(B \times [0,1]^{n-m})\) and \(B \times [0,1]^{n-m} \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)\) by Lemma 34.3; hence any finite collection of elements of \(\mathcal{A}\) lies in a common \(\mathcal{C}_n\), which is used repeatedly below.
Finitely Additive Set Function: Define \(P_0: \mathcal{A} \to [0, 1]\) by \(P_0(\pi_n^{-1}(B)) \triangleq \nu_n(B)\). This is well-defined: if \(\pi_m^{-1}(B) = \pi_n^{-1}(B')\) with \(m \le n\), then applying the surjection \(\pi_n\) gives \(B' = B \times [0,1]^{n-m}\), so iterating the consistency condition \(n-m\) times gives \(\nu_n(B') = \nu_m(B)\). Finite additivity holds because two disjoint elements of \(\mathcal{A}\) may be written at a common order \(n\) as \(\pi_n^{-1}(B_1)\), \(\pi_n^{-1}(B_2)\); disjointness and surjectivity of \(\pi_n\) force \(B_1 \cap B_2 = \emptyset\), whence \[
P_0\bigl(\pi_n^{-1}(B_1) \cup \pi_n^{-1}(B_2)\bigr) = \nu_n(B_1 \cup B_2) = \nu_n(B_1) + \nu_n(B_2).
\] In particular, \(P_0(Q) = \nu_1([0,1]) = 1\), so \(P_0\) is a finitely additive probability set function on the algebra \(\mathcal{A}\). Being non-negative and finitely additive on an algebra, \(P_0\) is also monotone and finitely subadditive there; both facts are used below.
Countable Additivity via Compactness: We show that \(P_0\) is a premeasure on \(\mathcal{A}\). Since \(P_0\) is finitely additive with \(P_0(Q) = 1 < \infty\), Proposition 11.1 (equivalence of items 1 and 4) reduces this to: \[
B_n \in \mathcal{A},\ B_n \downarrow \emptyset \ \Longrightarrow \ P_0(B_n) \to 0 .
\] Since \((B_n)\) is decreasing and \(P_0\) is monotone, \(P_0(B_n)\) is non-increasing and bounded, so the limit exists; suppose towards a contradiction that \[
\lim_{n\to\infty} P_0(B_n) = \inf_{n} P_0(B_n) = \epsilon > 0 .
\]

Cylinder representation. Write \(B_n = \pi_{m_n}^{-1}(C_n)\) with \(m_n \in \mathbb{N}\) and \(C_n \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^{m_n})\), so that \(P_0(B_n) = \nu_{m_n}(C_n)\) by Step 2. (No re-indexing to a common or monotone order is needed: the argument below applies Corollary 34.1 directly to closed sets, rather than building a point of \(\bigcap_n B_n\) coordinate by coordinate.)
Compact inner approximation. Each \(\nu_{m_n}\) is a probability measure on \([0,1]^{m_n}\), hence inner-regular by compact sets by Corollary 35.1. Since \(\nu_{m_n}(C_n) < \infty\), we may choose a compact \(K_n' \subseteq C_n\) with \[
\nu_{m_n}(C_n \setminus K_n') < \frac{\epsilon}{2^{n+1}} .
\]
Cylinders over the compacta. Put \(K_n \triangleq \pi_{m_n}^{-1}(K_n') \subseteq B_n\). Since \(\pi_{m_n} : Q \to [0,1]^{m_n}\) is continuous (its components \(p_1, \dots, p_{m_n}\) are) and \(K_n'\) is compact, hence closed in \([0,1]^{m_n}\), the set \(K_n\) is closed in \(Q\). Also \(K_n \in \mathcal{A}\), and \(B_n \setminus K_n = \pi_{m_n}^{-1}(C_n \setminus K_n')\), so \[
P_0(B_n \setminus K_n) = \nu_{m_n}(C_n \setminus K_n') < \frac{\epsilon}{2^{n+1}} .
\]
Set \(H_n \triangleq \bigcap_{i=1}^n K_i\). Then \(H_n \in \mathcal{A}\) (a finite intersection of cylinders), \(H_n\) is closed in \(Q\), and \(H_n \subseteq K_n \subseteq B_n\).
Estimate the difference. Since \(H_n \subseteq B_n\) we have \(B_n \setminus H_n = \bigcup_{i=1}^n (B_n \setminus K_i)\), and \(B_n \subseteq B_i\) for \(i \le n\) (because \((B_n)\) is decreasing), so \(B_n \setminus K_i \subseteq B_i \setminus K_i\). Using finite subadditivity and monotonicity of \(P_0\) from Step 2: \[
\begin{aligned}
P_0(B_n \setminus H_n) &= P_0\left( \bigcup_{i=1}^n (B_n \setminus K_i) \right) \\
&\le \sum_{i=1}^n P_0(B_n \setminus K_i) \\
&\le \sum_{i=1}^n P_0(B_i \setminus K_i) \\
&< \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\epsilon}{2^{i+1}} < \frac{\epsilon}{2}
\end{aligned}
\tag{35.2}\]
Since \(H_n \subseteq B_n\) and \(P_0\) is finitely additive, \(P_0(B_n) = P_0(H_n) + P_0(B_n \setminus H_n)\), whence, using \(P_0(B_n) \ge \epsilon\), \[
P_0(H_n) = P_0(B_n) - P_0(B_n \setminus H_n) > \epsilon - \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \frac{\epsilon}{2} > 0 .
\]
In particular \(H_n = \bigcap_{i=1}^n K_i \neq \emptyset\) for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). The sets \(K_i\) are closed in \(Q\) and all their initial finite intersections are non-empty, so Corollary 34.1 applies and gives, using \(H_n \subseteq B_n\), \[
\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty B_n \supseteq \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty H_n = \bigcap_{i=1}^\infty K_i \neq \emptyset
\tag{35.3}\]
This contradicts \(B_n \downarrow \emptyset\). Hence \(P_0(B_n) \to 0\) whenever \(B_n \downarrow \emptyset\), so \(P_0\) is a premeasure on the algebra \(\mathcal{A}\).

Extension and uniqueness. \((Q, \mathcal{A}, P_0)\) is a finite premeasure space, so by the measure extension theorem Theorem 9.2, \(P_0\) extends to a measure \(P\) on a \(\sigma\)-algebra containing \(\sigma(\mathcal{A}) = \mathcal{B}(Q)\); restricting to \(\mathcal{B}(Q)\) gives a measure with \(P(Q) = P_0(Q) = 1\) and \[
P(\pi_n^{-1}(B)) = P_0(\pi_n^{-1}(B)) = \nu_n(B) \qquad \forall n \in \mathbb{N},\ \forall B \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n),
\] which is Equation 34.11. Uniqueness holds because \(\mathcal{A}\) is an algebra, hence a \(\pi\)-system, generating \(\mathcal{B}(Q)\), and Equation 34.11 determines \(P\) on \(\mathcal{A}\); apply Lemma 32.1. (This is the same argument already recorded after the statement of Theorem 34.2 in Lecture 16.1.)

title: 35  Lecture 16.2: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (II)
section: 35.3 Extensions to \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\) and Infinite i.i.d. Sequences
text:
35.3 Extensions to \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\) and Infinite i.i.d. Sequences
Throughout this section \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\) carries the product topology, \(p_n : \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}\) is the \(n\)-th coordinate map and \(\pi_n : \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^n\), \(\pi_n(x) = (x_1,\dots,x_n)\), is the projection onto the first \(n\) coordinates. The product topology on \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\) is induced by the metric \[
\rho_\mathbb{R}(x,y) \triangleq \sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n}\bigl( |x_n - y_n| \wedge 1 \bigr),
\] by the same computation as in Lemma 34.2, and the countable family of finite cylinders \(\bigcap_{k \le N} p_k^{-1}(I_k)\) with \(I_k \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) an open interval with rational endpoints is a base. Repeating verbatim the argument of Lemma 34.3 — which used only countability of the index set and second countability of the factor — gives \[
\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}) = \sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N}) = \bigotimes_{n=1}^\infty \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) = \sigma\Bigl( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \pi_n^{-1}\bigl( \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \bigr) \Bigr),
\tag{35.4}\] the third equality being Definition 30.2 and the fourth using \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) = \bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\). Moreover \(\bigcup_{n} \pi_n^{-1}(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n))\) is an algebra, hence a \(\pi\)-system, generating \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N})\).

Corollary 35.2 (Kolmogorov Extension Theorem on \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\)) Let \(\nu_n\) be probability measures on \((\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n))\), \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), satisfying projective consistency \[
\nu_{n+1}(B \times \mathbb{R}) = \nu_n(B) \qquad \forall B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n),\ \forall n \in \mathbb{N} .
\tag{35.5}\] Then there exists a unique probability measure \(P\) on \((\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}))\) such that \[
P\bigl( \pi_n^{-1}(B) \bigr) = \nu_n(B) \qquad \forall B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n),\ \forall n \in \mathbb{N},
\tag{35.6}\] equivalently \(P \circ \pi_n^{-1} = \nu_n\) for every \(n\).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 35.2). Uniqueness. By Equation 35.4 the sets \(\pi_n^{-1}(B)\) form a \(\pi\)-system generating \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N})\) on which Equation 35.6 prescribes \(P\); since \(P\) is a probability measure, Lemma 32.1 gives uniqueness. It remains to prove existence.
Transport to the cube. Fix a homeomorphism \(\alpha: \mathbb{R} \to (0, 1)\) (e.g. \(\alpha(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x \frac{1}{\pi(1+t^2)} \, dt\), the Cauchy CDF), and let \(\beta \triangleq \alpha^{-1} : (0,1) \to \mathbb{R}\). Extend \(\beta\) to a Borel map \(\bar\beta : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}\) by setting \(\bar\beta(0) = \bar\beta(1) \triangleq 0\). Both \(\alpha\) and \(\bar\beta\) are Borel measurable, so the coordinatewise maps \[
\alpha^n : \mathbb{R}^n \to (0,1)^n, \qquad \bar\beta^{\,n} : [0,1]^n \to \mathbb{R}^n, \qquad \bar\beta^{\,\infty} : Q \to \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}
\] are Borel measurable — for \(\bar\beta^{\,\infty}\) this is Lemma 30.3 applied to the components \(\bar\beta \circ p_k\), together with Equation 35.4. Note \(\bar\beta^{\,n} \circ \alpha^n = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^n}\) and \(\alpha^n \circ \bar\beta^{\,n} = \mathrm{id}\) on \((0,1)^n\).
Define \(\tilde\nu_n\) on \(([0,1]^n, \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n))\) as the pushforward of \(\nu_n\) under \(\alpha^n\): \[
\tilde{\nu}_n(A) \triangleq \nu_n\bigl((\alpha^n)^{-1}(A \cap (0, 1)^n)\bigr), \qquad A \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n) .
\] Each \(\tilde\nu_n\) is a probability measure with \(\tilde\nu_n\bigl((0,1)^n\bigr) = \nu_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = 1\).
Consistency of \(\{\tilde{\nu}_n\}\). For \(A \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)\) we have \((A \times [0,1]) \cap (0,1)^{n+1} = (A \cap (0,1)^n) \times (0,1)\), and \(\alpha^{-1}((0,1)) = \mathbb{R}\), so \[
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{\nu}_{n+1}(A \times [0,1]) &= \nu_{n+1}\!\left((\alpha^n)^{-1}(A \cap (0,1)^n) \times \mathbb{R}\right) \\
&= \nu_n\!\left((\alpha^n)^{-1}(A \cap (0,1)^n)\right) = \tilde{\nu}_n(A),
\end{aligned}
\] the middle equality being Equation 35.5. Hence \(\{\tilde{\nu}_n\}\) is projectively consistent in the sense of Equation 34.10.
Existence. By Theorem 34.2 there is a probability measure \(\tilde{P}\) on \((Q, \mathcal{B}(Q))\) with \(\tilde{P} \circ \pi_n^{-1} = \tilde\nu_n\) for every \(n\). Define \[
P \triangleq \tilde{P} \circ \bigl( \bar\beta^{\,\infty} \bigr)^{-1},
\] a probability measure on \((\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}))\) since \(\bar\beta^{\,\infty}\) is measurable. (The values assigned to \(\bar\beta\) at the endpoints \(0,1\) are irrelevant: \((0,1)^\mathbb{N} = \bigcap_n \pi_n^{-1}\bigl((0,1)^n\bigr) \in \mathcal{B}(Q)\) and \(\tilde{P}\bigl(\pi_n^{-1}((0,1)^n)\bigr) = \tilde\nu_n((0,1)^n) = 1\) for every \(n\), so \(\tilde{P}\bigl((0,1)^\mathbb{N}\bigr) = 1\) and \(\bar\beta^{\,\infty}\) agrees \(\tilde P\)-a.s. with the inverse of the coordinatewise map induced by \(\alpha\).)
Verification of Equation 35.6. Fix \(n\) and \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)\). Since \(\pi_n \circ \bar\beta^{\,\infty} = \bar\beta^{\,n} \circ \pi_n\), \[
P\bigl(\pi_n^{-1}(B)\bigr) = \tilde{P}\Bigl( \bigl(\bar\beta^{\,\infty}\bigr)^{-1}\bigl(\pi_n^{-1}(B)\bigr) \Bigr) = \tilde{P}\Bigl( \pi_n^{-1}\bigl( (\bar\beta^{\,n})^{-1}(B) \bigr) \Bigr) = \tilde{\nu}_n\bigl( (\bar\beta^{\,n})^{-1}(B) \bigr).
\] Writing \(A \triangleq (\bar\beta^{\,n})^{-1}(B)\) we have \(A \cap (0,1)^n = \{ y \in (0,1)^n \mid \beta^n(y) \in B \} = \alpha^n(B)\), hence \((\alpha^n)^{-1}\bigl(A \cap (0,1)^n\bigr) = B\) and therefore \(\tilde\nu_n(A) = \nu_n(B)\). Thus \(P(\pi_n^{-1}(B)) = \nu_n(B)\).

title: 35  Lecture 16.2: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (II)
text:
35.4 Existence of Infinite i.i.d. Sequences

Theorem 35.2 Let \(\{\mu_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be an arbitrary sequence of Borel probability measures on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\). There exists a probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) and a sequence of independent random variables \(X_n: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P) \to (\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) such that \(\mu_{X_n} = \mu_n\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 35.2). Set \(\Omega \triangleq \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\) and \(\mathcal{F} \triangleq \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}) = \sigma(\{\pi_n \mid n \in \mathbb{N}\})\).

Define finite product measures \(\nu_n \triangleq \bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mu_k\) on \((\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n))\).
The sequence \(\{\nu_n\}\) satisfies projective consistency: \(\nu_{n+1}(B \times \mathbb{R}) = \nu_n(B) \cdot \mu_{n+1}(\mathbb{R}) = \nu_n(B)\).
By Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem on \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\), there exists a unique probability measure \(P\) on \((\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}))\) such that \(P(B \times \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}) = \nu_n(B)\) for all \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)\).
Set \(X_n \triangleq \pi_n\) (the \(n\)-th coordinate projection). For any \(B_1, \dots, B_n \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\): \[
\begin{aligned}
P(X_1 \in B_1, \dots, X_n \in B_n) &= P(B_1 \times \dots \times B_n \times \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}) \\
&= \nu_n(B_1 \times \dots \times B_n) \\
&= \prod_{k=1}^n \mu_k(B_k)
\end{aligned}
\tag{35.5}\] Hence \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are independent with marginal laws \(\mu_{X_n} = \mu_n\).

title: 35  Lecture 16.2: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (II)
text:
35.5 Reconstruction and Interpretation Notes

Notational Standardizations:

Expanded compactness contradiction step \(P_0(H_n) > \epsilon/2\) explicitly showing finite intersection preservation[cite: 11, 12].
Standardized product cylinder identification for single coordinate evaluation \(\pi_n: \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}\).

title: 36  Lecture 17.1: Kolmogorov’s 0-1 Law
text:
Definition 36.1 For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), define the sequence’s tail \(\sigma\)-algebras: \[
\mathcal{T}_n \triangleq \sigma(X_n, X_{n+1}, X_{n+2}, \dots) = \sigma(X_k \mid k \ge n)
\tag{36.1}\]
The tail \(\sigma\)-algebra (or tail field) \(\mathcal{T}\) of the sequence \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) is: \[
\mathcal{T} \triangleq \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty \mathcal{T}_n = \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty \sigma(X_k \mid k \ge n)
\tag{36.2}\]
Events \(E \in \mathcal{T}\) are called tail events. A random variable \(Y\) is tail-measurable if it is \(\mathcal{T}\)-measurable.

title: 36  Lecture 17.1: Kolmogorov’s 0-1 Law
section: 36.2 Examples and Counterexamples of Tail Events
text:
36.2 Examples and Counterexamples of Tail Events

Convergence Events: The events \(\{\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n\text{ exists}\}\) and, in the real-valued case, \(\{\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n>0\}\) are tail events. Indeed, for every \(N\), whether the sequence converges and the value of its limit are determined entirely by \((X_N,X_{N+1},\ldots)\); consequently these events belong to \(\sigma(X_k:k\ge N)\) for every \(N\), and hence to \(\mathcal T\).
Partial Sums \(S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n X_k\):

\(\{\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n\text{ exists}\}\in\mathcal T\). For every fixed \(N\) and \(n\ge N\), \[
S_n=S_{N-1}+\sum_{k=N}^nX_k.
\] Adding the fixed finite random vector \(S_{N-1}\) does not affect convergence as \(n\to\infty\). Thus convergence of \((S_n)\) is equivalent to convergence of the tail partial sums \((\sum_{k=N}^nX_k)_{n\ge N}\), an event in \(\sigma(X_k:k\ge N)\). Since this holds for every \(N\), the event is in \(\mathcal T\).
\(\{ \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{S_n}{b_n} > 0 \} \in \mathcal{T}\) for normalizing constants \(b_n \to \infty\), because for any fixed \(N\): \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{S_n}{b_n} &= \frac{S_{N-1}}{b_n} + \frac{\sum_{k=N}^n X_k}{b_n} \\
\frac{S_{N-1}}{b_n}&\longrightarrow 0,
\end{align*}
\tag{36.3}\] and therefore \[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_n}{b_n}
=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{k=N}^nX_k}{b_n}.
\] The right-hand side is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_k:k\ge N)\). Since \(N\) is arbitrary, the event belongs to \(\mathcal T\).

Non-Tail Event: \(\{ X_1 < 1 \} \notin \mathcal{T}\) in general, as \(X_1\) is not measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_2, X_3, \dots)\).
Identical RV Dependency: If \(X_1 = X_2 = X_3 = \dots\), then \(\sigma(X_n, X_{n+1}, \dots) = \sigma(X_1)\) for all \(n\), so \(\mathcal{T} = \sigma(X_1)\).

title: 36  Lecture 17.1: Kolmogorov’s 0-1 Law
text:
36.3 Kolmogorov’s 0-1 Law

Theorem 36.1 (Kolmogorov’s 0-1 Law) Let \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of independent random variables on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\). If \(E \in \mathcal{T}\) is any tail event, then: \[
P(E) = 0 \quad \text{or} \quad P(E) = 1
\tag{36.4}\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 36.1). Throughout, we use the following elementary fact twice, so we isolate it once:

Fact. If \((\mathcal H_m)_{m\ge1}\) is a non-decreasing sequence of \(\sigma\)-algebras (\(\mathcal H_m\subseteq\mathcal H_{m+1}\)), then \(\mathcal H\triangleq\bigcup_{m\ge1}\mathcal H_m\) is an algebra, hence in particular a \(\pi\)-system. Indeed, \(\Omega\in\mathcal H_1\subseteq\mathcal H\); if \(A\in\mathcal H\), then \(A\in\mathcal H_m\) for some \(m\), so \(A^c\in\mathcal H_m\subseteq\mathcal H\); and if \(A\in\mathcal H_m\), \(B\in\mathcal H_{m'}\), then both lie in \(\mathcal H_{\max(m,m')}\) by monotonicity, so \(A\cap B,\,A\cup B\in\mathcal H_{\max(m,m')}\subseteq\mathcal H\).


The past \(\mathcal B_n\) and the strict future \(\mathcal T_{n+1}\) are independent. For \(n\in\mathbb N\), define \[
  \mathcal{B}_n \triangleq \sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_n),
  \qquad
  \mathcal{T}_{n+1}\triangleq\sigma(X_{n+1},X_{n+2},\ldots).
  \] Fix \(n\). Since \(\{X_k\}_{k\ge1}\) are independent, Definition 33.1 gives that \(\sigma(X_1),\ldots,\sigma(X_m)\) are independent \(\sigma\)-algebras for every \(m\). For \(m>n\), applying Lemma 33.2 with the two blocks \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\{n+1,\ldots,m\}\) shows that the block-generated \(\sigma\)-algebras \[
  \begin{align*}
  &\mathcal B_n=\sigma\big(\sigma(X_1)\cup\cdots\cup\sigma(X_n)\big)
  \quad\text{and}\\
  &\sigma(X_{n+1},\ldots,X_m)=\sigma\big(\sigma(X_{n+1})\cup\cdots\cup\sigma(X_m)\big)
  \end{align*}
  \] are independent.

Applying the Fact above to the increasing sequence \(\mathcal H_k\triangleq\sigma(X_{n+1},\ldots,X_{n+k})\), \(k\ge1\), shows that \[
  \mathcal C_n\triangleq\bigcup_{m>n}\sigma(X_{n+1},\ldots,X_m)
  \] is a \(\pi\)-system. Since every \(X_{n+1},X_{n+2},\ldots\) appears as a coordinate of some \(\sigma(X_{n+1},\ldots,X_m)\subseteq\mathcal C_n\), we get \(\sigma(\mathcal C_n)=\sigma(X_{n+1},X_{n+2},\ldots)=\mathcal T_{n+1}\).
Every \(A\in\mathcal B_n\) and \(C\in\mathcal C_n\) lie, respectively, in \(\mathcal B_n\) and in \(\sigma(X_{n+1},\ldots,X_m)\) for some \(m>n\), so the independence established above gives \(P(A\cap C)=P(A)P(C)\). Thus \(\mathcal B_n\) and \(\mathcal C_n\) are independent \(\pi\)-systems, so Theorem 32.1 shows that the generated \(\sigma\)-algebras \(\sigma(\mathcal B_n)=\mathcal B_n\) and \(\sigma(\mathcal C_n)=\mathcal T_{n+1}\) are independent.
Finally, independence of \(\mathcal B_n\) and \(\mathcal T_{n+1}\) means \(P(A\cap C)=P(A)P(C)\) for all \(A\in\mathcal B_n\) and \(C\in\mathcal T_{n+1}\); since \(\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal T_{n+1}\), this identity holds in particular for all \(C\in\mathcal T\), so \(\mathcal B_n\) and \(\mathcal T\) are independent.

\(\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots)\) is generated by an algebra. The \(\sigma\)-algebras \(\mathcal B_n\) increase with \(n\), so applying the Fact above to \(\mathcal H_n\triangleq\mathcal B_n\) shows that \[
  \mathcal{A} \triangleq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \mathcal{B}_n
  \] is an algebra, hence a \(\pi\)-system, and (since \(\mathcal A\) is literally this union) \[
  \sigma(\mathcal A)=\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots).
  \]
Every tail event \(E\) is independent of all of \(\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots)\). Fix \(E\in\mathcal T\). For every \(A\in\mathcal A\), there is an \(n\) with \(A\in\mathcal B_n\), so Step 1 gives \(P(A\cap E)=P(A)P(E)\); that is, \[
  \mathcal D_E\triangleq\{A\in\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots):P(A\cap E)=P(A)P(E)\}
  \] satisfies \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal D_E\). We check \(\mathcal D_E\) is a \(\lambda\)-system:

\(\Omega\in\mathcal D_E\), since \(P(\Omega\cap E)=P(E)=P(\Omega)P(E)\).
Closed under complements: if \(A\in\mathcal D_E\), then \(E=(A\cap E)\sqcup(A^c\cap E)\) is a disjoint union, so \[
\begin{align*}
P(A^c\cap E)&=P(E)-P(A\cap E)=P(E)-P(A)P(E)\\
&=\big(1-P(A)\big)P(E)=P(A^c)P(E),
\end{align*}
\] i.e. \(A^c\in\mathcal D_E\).
Closed under countable disjoint unions: if \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\in\mathcal D_E\) are pairwise disjoint with union \(A\), then \(A\cap E=\bigsqcup_iA_i\cap E\) is also a disjoint union, so countable additivity gives \[
\begin{align*}
P(A\cap E)&=\sum_iP(A_i\cap E)=\sum_iP(A_i)P(E)\\
&=P(E)\sum_iP(A_i)=P(E)P(A),
\end{align*}
\] i.e. \(A\in\mathcal D_E\).


Thus \(\mathcal D_E\) is a \(\lambda\)-system containing the \(\pi\)-system \(\mathcal A\), so Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem gives \(\sigma(\mathcal A)\subseteq\mathcal D_E\). By Step 2, \(\sigma(\mathcal A)=\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots)\), so \(E\) is independent of every event in \(\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots)\).

Self-independence forces \(P(E)\in\{0,1\}\). Because \(\mathcal T_1\subseteq\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots)\) and \(\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal T_1\), the tail event \(E\) itself belongs to \(\sigma(X_1, X_2, \dots)\), so Step 3 applies with \(A=E\), giving \(E\) independent of itself: \[
\begin{align*}
&P(E) = P(E \cap E) = P(E) P(E) = P(E)^2\\
& \implies P(E) \in \{0, 1\}
\end{align*}
\tag{36.5}\]

title: 36  Lecture 17.1: Kolmogorov’s 0-1 Law
text:
36.4 Applications and Consequences

36.4.1 Borel-Cantelli Dichotomy
Let \((A_n)_{n\ge1}\) be independent events and define their tail \(\sigma\)-algebra by \[
\mathcal T_A\triangleq\bigcap_{N=1}^\infty\sigma(A_n:n\ge N),
\] where \(\sigma(A_n:n\ge N)\) means the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by the events \(A_N,A_{N+1},\ldots\). Equivalently, this is the tail \(\sigma\)-algebra of the independent indicator random variables \(\mathbf1_{A_n}\).
The event that infinitely many \(A_n\) occur is \[
\{A_n\text{ i.o.}\}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_n
=\bigcap_{m=1}^\infty\bigcup_{n=m}^\infty A_n.
\] It also has the following equivalent indicator-function representations: \[
\mathbf 1_{\{A_n\text{ i.o.}\}}
=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\mathbf 1_{A_n}
=\mathbf 1_{\left\{\sum_{n=1}^\infty\mathbf 1_{A_n}=\infty\right\}},
\] and hence \[
\{A_n\text{ i.o.}\}
=\left\{\limsup_{n\to\infty}\mathbf 1_{A_n}=1\right\}
=\left\{\sum_{n=1}^\infty\mathbf 1_{A_n}=\infty\right\}.
\] Indeed, for each \(\omega\in\Omega\), the sequence \(\mathbf 1_{A_n}(\omega)\) takes only the values \(0\) and \(1\). Its limsup equals \(1\), equivalently its series diverges to \(\infty\), exactly when \(\omega\) belongs to infinitely many of the events \(A_n\).
Fix \(N\in\mathbb N\). Removing the first \(N-1\) events cannot change whether infinitely many events occur, so \[
\{A_n\text{ i.o.}\}
=\bigcap_{m=N}^\infty\bigcup_{n=m}^\infty A_n.
\] Every event on the right belongs to \(\sigma(A_n:n\ge N)\); hence \(\{A_n\text{ i.o.}\}\in\sigma(A_n:n\ge N)\). Since this holds for every \(N\), \[
\{A_n\text{ i.o.}\}\in\mathcal T_A.
\] Kolmogorov’s 0-1 law therefore gives \(P(A_n\text{ i.o.})\in\{0,1\}\). The Borel-Cantelli lemmas identify which value occurs:

If \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty P(A_n)<\infty\), then Theorem 19.3 gives \(P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0\). Independence is not needed in this case.
If \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty P(A_n)=\infty\), then independence and Theorem 32.2 give \(P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1\).

Thus, for independent events, \[
P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=
\begin{cases}
0,&\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty P(A_n)<\infty,\\
1,&\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty P(A_n)=\infty.
\end{cases}
\]


36.4.2 Normalized Partial-Sum Limits
Let \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) be independent \(\mathbb R^d\)-valued random variables, let \[
S_n\triangleq\sum_{k=1}^nX_k,
\] and let \((b_n)\) be positive constants with \(b_n\to\infty\). Fix \(c\in\mathbb R^d\) and consider \[
E_c\triangleq\left\{\frac{S_n}{b_n}\to c\right\}.
\] For every fixed \(N\) and every \(n\ge N\), \[
\frac{S_n}{b_n}
=\frac{S_{N-1}}{b_n}+\frac{\sum_{k=N}^nX_k}{b_n}.
\] For each \(\omega\in\Omega\), the vector \(S_{N-1}(\omega)\) is fixed as \(n\to\infty\), and therefore \[
\frac{S_{N-1}(\omega)}{b_n}\longrightarrow0.
\] Consequently, \[
E_c
=\left\{\frac{\sum_{k=N}^nX_k}{b_n}\to c\right\}.
\] The event on the right depends only on \(X_N,X_{N+1},\ldots\) and is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_k:k\ge N)\). For example, writing \(\|\cdot\|\) for the Euclidean norm, it has the explicit measurable representation \[
\bigcap_{r=1}^\infty\bigcup_{M=N}^\infty\bigcap_{n=M}^\infty
\left\{\left\|\frac{\sum_{k=N}^nX_k}{b_n}-c\right\|<\frac1r\right\}.
\] Since \(N\) was arbitrary, \(E_c\in\mathcal T\). Kolmogorov’s 0-1 law now yields \[
P\left(\frac{S_n}{b_n}\to c\right)=P(E_c)\in\{0,1\}.
\] The 0-1 law determines only that the probability is extreme; additional information about the distributions of the \(X_n\) and the normalization \(b_n\) is needed to determine whether it is \(0\) or \(1\).

title: 36  Lecture 17.1: Kolmogorov’s 0-1 Law
section: 36.5 Tail-Measurable Functions and Constant A.S. Realizations
text:
36.5 Tail-Measurable Functions and Constant A.S. Realizations
The following result shows that if a random variable \(Y\) is determined by the entire infinite sequence \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\), then we can approximate \(Y\) arbitrarily well in \(L^1\) using a function of only finitely many \(X_i\)’s.

Proposition 36.1 Let \(Y\) be a bounded \(\sigma(X_1, X_2, \dots)\)-measurable random variable. For any \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) and a Borel function \(F:(\mathbb R^d)^N\cong\mathbb R^{dN}\to\mathbb R\) such that: \[
\mathbb{E}\left[ |Y - F(X_1, \dots, X_N)| \right] < \epsilon,
\tag{36.6}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 36.1). Throughout, write \[
\mathcal B_n\triangleq\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_n),\qquad
\mathcal A\triangleq\bigcup_{n\ge1}\mathcal B_n,\qquad
\mathcal G\triangleq\sigma(\mathcal A)=\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots),
\] and recall the elementary identity \[
\mathbb E\left|\mathbf1_A-\mathbf1_B\right|=P(A\triangle B),
\qquad A\triangle B\triangleq(A\setminus B)\cup(B\setminus A).
\tag{36.7}\]
Step 1: \(\mathcal A\) is an algebra. The \(\sigma\)-algebras \(\mathcal B_n\) increase in \(n\), since \(\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\subseteq\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_{n+1})\). Hence \(\Omega\in\mathcal B_1\subseteq\mathcal A\); if \(A\in\mathcal A\), then \(A\in\mathcal B_n\) for some \(n\) and \(A^c\in\mathcal B_n\subseteq\mathcal A\); and if \(A\in\mathcal B_m\), \(A'\in\mathcal B_n\), then both lie in \(\mathcal B_{\max(m,n)}\), so \(A\cup A'\in\mathcal B_{\max(m,n)}\subseteq\mathcal A\). Thus \(\mathcal A\) is an algebra (it is in general not a \(\sigma\)-algebra).
Step 2: every \(B\in\mathcal G\) is approximable in probability by sets of \(\mathcal A\). Since \(\mathcal A\) is an algebra (Step 1) generating \(\mathcal G=\sigma(\mathcal A)\) and \(P\) is a finite measure, Part 3 of Proposition 10.1 (with \(\mu=P\), which is trivially \(\sigma\)-finite since \(P(\Omega)=1<\infty\)) applies to every \(B\in\mathcal G\), as \(P(B)\le1<\infty\): for every \(\delta>0\) there exists \(A\in\mathcal A\) with \[
P(A\triangle B)<\delta .
\]
Step 3: approximate \(Y\) by a \(\mathcal G\)-measurable simple function. Let \(M<\infty\) be such that \(|Y|\le M\) everywhere, and put \(h\triangleq\epsilon/4\). Choose an integer \(r\) with \(rh>M\) and define, for \(j=-r,\ldots,r-1\), the disjoint half-open intervals \(I_j\triangleq[jh,(j+1)h)\), which cover \([-rh,rh)\supseteq[-M,M]\), together with \(B_j\triangleq Y^{-1}(I_j)\in\mathcal G\) and \(a_j\triangleq jh\). Then \[
s\triangleq\sum_{j=-r}^{r-1}a_j\mathbf1_{B_j}
\] is a \(\mathcal G\)-measurable simple function taking finitely many values, and by construction \(|Y(\omega)-s(\omega)|\le h\) for every \(\omega\) (since \(Y(\omega)\in I_j\Rightarrow Y(\omega)-a_j\in[0,h)\) on the unique \(j\) with \(\omega\in B_j\)), whence \[
\mathbb E|Y-s|\le h=\frac\epsilon4<\frac\epsilon2 .
\] The sum has \(r'\triangleq 2r\) terms, and \(K\triangleq\max_j|a_j|=rh<\infty\).
Step 4: replace the sets \(B_j\) by sets of \(\mathcal A\). By Step 2, for each \(j\) choose \(A_j\in\mathcal A\) with \[
P(A_j\triangle B_j)<\frac{\epsilon}{2r'(K+1)} .
\] Put \(\varphi\triangleq\sum_ja_j\mathbf1_{A_j}\). By the triangle inequality in \(L^1\) and Equation 36.7, \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb E\left|s-\varphi\right|
&\le\sum_j|a_j|\,\mathbb E\left|\mathbf1_{B_j}-\mathbf1_{A_j}\right|\\
&=\sum_j|a_j|\,P(A_j\triangle B_j)\\
&< r'\cdot K\cdot\frac{\epsilon}{2r'(K+1)}<\frac\epsilon2 .
\end{align*}
\]
Step 5: realize \(\varphi\) as a Borel function of finitely many \(X_i\). Each \(A_j\) lies in \(\mathcal A\), so there is \(n_j\) with \(A_j\in\mathcal B_{n_j}\). Set \(N\triangleq\max_jn_j\); by monotonicity of the \(\mathcal B_n\), every \(A_j\in\mathcal B_N\), so each \(\mathbf1_{A_j}\) — and hence the finite linear combination \(\varphi\) — is \(\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_N)\)-measurable. Regarding \((X_1,\ldots,X_N)\) as the vector of its \(dN\) real coordinates, Theorem 15.2 supplies a Borel function \(F:\mathbb R^{dN}\to\mathbb R\) with \[
\varphi=F(X_1,\ldots,X_N)\quad\text{everywhere on }\Omega .
\]
Step 6: conclusion. Combining Steps 3 and 4 with the triangle inequality, \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb E\left[\left|Y-F(X_1,\ldots,X_N)\right|\right]
&=\mathbb E|Y-\varphi|
\le\mathbb E|Y-s|+\mathbb E|s-\varphi|\\
&<\frac\epsilon2+\frac\epsilon2=\epsilon .
\end{align*}
\]


Example 36.1 (An infinite weighted sum) Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Define \(Y=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{-n}X_n\). Since \(0\leq X_n\leq1\), \[
0\leq Y \leq \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{-n} =1.
\] Thus \(Y\) is bounded. Moreover, \(Y = X_1/2+X_2/4+X_3/8+\cdots\) is clearly \(\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots)\)-measurable. For each \(N\), define \[
F_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N) = \sum_{n=1}^N2^{-n}x_n.
\]
This is a continuous, hence Borel function \(F_N​:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}\). The approximation error is exactly the tail: \[
Y-F_N(X_1,\ldots,X_N) = \sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}2^{-n}X_n.
\] Since \(0\leq X_n\leq1\), we have \[
Y-F_N(X_1,\ldots,X_N) \leq \sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}2^{-n}=2^{-N}
\] Therefore, \[
\mathbb E\left[ |Y-F_N(X_1,\ldots,X_N)| \right] \leq 2^{-N}.
\] Given any \(\epsilon>0\), choosing \(N\) such that \(2^{-N}\) yields the result.

The next result shows that if \(Y\) depends only on the infinitely remote future of an independent sequence, then there is actually no randomness left in \(Y\).

Proposition 36.2 Let \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be independent random variables. If \(Y\) is a real-valued tail-measurable random variable (\(\mathcal{T}\)-measurable), then \(Y\) is constant almost surely: \[
\exists c \in \mathbb{R} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad Y = c \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{36.8}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition 36.2). 

Consider the cumulative distribution function \(F_Y(t) \triangleq P(Y \le t)\) for \(t \in \mathbb{R}\).
Because \(Y\) is \(\mathcal{T}\)-measurable, the event \(\{Y \le t\} \in \mathcal{T}\) for every \(t \in \mathbb{R}\).
By Kolmogorov’s 0-1 Law, \(P(Y \le t) \in \{0, 1\}\) for all \(t \in \mathbb{R}\).
\(F_Y: \mathbb{R} \to \{0, 1\}\) is a non-decreasing, right-continuous function satisfying \(\lim_{t \to -\infty} F_Y(t) = 0\) and \(\lim_{t \to \infty} F_Y(t) = 1\).
Define \(S\triangleq\{t\in\mathbb R:F_Y(t)=1\}\) and \(c\triangleq\inf S\). The limits of the CDF at \(\pm\infty\) imply that \(S\) is non-empty and bounded below, so \(c\in\mathbb R\). If \(t<c\), then \(t\notin S\) and hence \(F_Y(t)=0\). If \(s>c\), the definition of the infimum gives some \(u\in S\) with \(u<s\); monotonicity then gives \(F_Y(s)\ge F_Y(u)=1\), so \(F_Y(s)=1\). Taking \(s\downarrow c\) and using right-continuity yields \(F_Y(c)=1\).
Finally, \[
P(Y<c)=P\left(\bigcup_{m=1}^\infty\{Y\le c-1/m\}\right)
=\lim_{m\to\infty}F_Y(c-1/m)=0,
\] by continuity from below. Therefore \(P(Y=c)=P(Y\le c)-P(Y<c)=1-0=1\), so \(Y=c\) almost surely.



Example 36.2 (The limsup of an independent Bernoulli sequence) Let \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be independent with \(X_n\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_n)\), i.e. \[
P(X_n=1)=p_n,\qquad P(X_n=0)=1-p_n,\qquad 0<p_n<1,
\] and set \[
Y\triangleq\limsup_{n\to\infty}X_n .
\] Each individual \(X_n\) is genuinely random (it is non-degenerate, since \(0<p_n<1\)), yet Proposition 36.2 forces \(Y\) to be deterministic. We verify this and identify the constant.
Step 1: \(Y\) is tail-measurable. Fix \(N\in\mathbb N\). Discarding the first \(N-1\) terms of a sequence does not change its limsup, so \[
Y=\limsup_{n\to\infty}X_n=\inf_{m\ge N}\ \sup_{n\ge m}X_n .
\] For each \(m\ge N\), the function \(\sup_{n\ge m}X_n\) is a countable supremum of \(\sigma(X_k:k\ge N)\)-measurable functions, hence \(\sigma(X_k:k\ge N)\)-measurable; the countable infimum over \(m\ge N\) is then also \(\sigma(X_k:k\ge N)\)-measurable. Thus \(Y\) is \(\mathcal T_N\)-measurable for every \(N\), so \[
Y\ \text{is}\ \mathcal T=\bigcap_{N\ge1}\mathcal T_N\ \text{-measurable}.
\] By Proposition 36.2 there exists \(c\in\mathbb R\) with \(Y=c\) a.s. Since \(X_n\in\{0,1\}\) we already know \(Y\in\{0,1\}\) pointwise, so necessarily \(c\in\{0,1\}\).
Step 2: identifying \(c\) via Borel-Cantelli. Put \(A_n\triangleq\{X_n=1\}\), so that \(P(A_n)=p_n\) and the events \(A_n\) are independent. Because \(X_n\) takes only the values \(0\) and \(1\), \[
\left\{\limsup_{n\to\infty}X_n=1\right\}=\{A_n\ \text{i.o.}\},
\qquad
\left\{\limsup_{n\to\infty}X_n=0\right\}=\{A_n\ \text{i.o.}\}^c .
\] Hence:

If \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty p_n=\infty\), then Theorem 32.2 (which uses independence) gives \(P(A_n\ \text{i.o.})=1\), so \[
Y=1\quad\text{a.s.},\qquad c=1 .
\]
If \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty p_n<\infty\), then Theorem 19.3 gives \(P(A_n\ \text{i.o.})=0\); almost every \(\omega\) therefore satisfies \(X_n(\omega)=0\) for all large \(n\), and \[
Y=0\quad\text{a.s.},\qquad c=0 .
\]

Step 3: two concrete instances.

\(p_n=\tfrac12\) for all \(n\) (fair coin tosses): \(\sum_n p_n=\infty\), so \(\limsup_n X_n=1\) almost surely. Every finite block \((X_1,\ldots,X_N)\) is completely undetermined, but “a head occurs infinitely often’’ is certain.
\(p_n=2^{-n}\): \(\sum_n p_n=1<\infty\), so \(\limsup_n X_n=0\) almost surely, i.e. only finitely many \(1\)’s ever appear.

Step 4: the CDF picture behind the proof. In the first instance the distribution function of \(Y\) is \[
F_Y(t)=P(Y\le t)=
\begin{cases}
0,&t<1,\\
1,&t\ge1,
\end{cases}
\] which indeed takes only the values \(0\) and \(1\), as Step 3 of the proof asserts, and \[
c=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:F_Y(t)=1\}=1
\] is exactly the constant produced in Step 5 of the proof. In the second instance \(F_Y\) is the same function shifted to \(0\), and \(c=0\).
Step 5: independence is essential. If we drop independence and take \(X_1=X_2=\cdots\) with \(X_1\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), then \(\mathcal T=\sigma(X_1)\) and \[
Y=\limsup_{n\to\infty}X_n=X_1 ,
\] which is \(\mathcal T\)-measurable but takes the values \(0\) and \(1\) each with probability \(1/2\). So \(Y\) is not a.s. constant: the conclusion of Proposition 36.2 genuinely requires the independence hypothesis.
Step 6: constancy does not reveal the value. The same argument applied to \(Y'\triangleq\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^nX_k\) (a tail-measurable random variable, by the invariance computation in Equation 36.3 with \(b_n=n\)) shows only that \(Y'\) is a.s. equal to some constant. For i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) variables that constant turns out to be \(p\), but identifying it requires a law of large numbers, not the 0-1 law.
