title: Appendix A — Limsups, Liminfs and Extended Limits
section: A.3 Liminfs, Limsups, and Supremum Conventions
text:
A.3 Liminfs, Limsups, and Supremum Conventions

Definition A.3 For any subset \(\Lambda \subset \overline{\mathbb{R}}\), \(\sup \Lambda\) denotes the least upper bound and \(\inf \Lambda\) denotes the greatest lower bound. We enforce the following extended conventions:

\(\sup \Lambda = +\infty\) if \(+\infty \in \Lambda\) or if \(\Lambda\) is not bounded above in \(\mathbb{R}\).
\(\inf \Lambda = -\infty\) if \(-\infty \in \Lambda\) or if \(\Lambda\) is not bounded below in \(\mathbb{R}\).
\(\sup \emptyset = -\infty\) and \(\inf \emptyset = +\infty\).



Definition A.4 (Limit Superior and Limit Inferior) For a sequence of real numbers \(\{x_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{R}\), we define: \[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} x_n := \lim_{n \to \infty} \left( \inf \{x_k : k \ge n\} \right) = \sup_{n \ge 1} \inf_{k \ge n} x_k,
\tag{A.3}\] \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} x_n := \lim_{n \to \infty} \left( \sup \{x_k : k \ge n\} \right) = \inf_{n \ge 1} \sup_{k \ge n} x_k.
\tag{A.4}\] We also write \(\varliminf_{n \to \infty} x_n\) for \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} x_n\), and \(\varlimsup_{n \to \infty} x_n\) for \(\limsup_{n \to \infty} x_n\).


Remark A.2. Let \(a_n := \inf \{x_k : k \ge n\}\) and \(b_n := \sup \{x_k : k \ge n\}\). Since the set \(\{x_k : k \ge n+1\} \subset \{x_k : k \ge n\}\), taking infima and suprema yields that \(\{a_n\}\) is non-decreasing (\(a_n \le a_{n+1}\)) and \(\{b_n\}\) is non-increasing (\(b_n \ge b_{n+1}\)). Monotone sequences in \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) always have well-defined limits in \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), which establishes why the limits in Equation A.3 and Equation A.4 always exist.


Proposition A.1 Let \(\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) and \(\{b_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be sequences in \(\mathbb{R}\).

\(\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n \le \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n\). Furthermore, \(\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = A \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}\) exists if and only if \[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n = \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n = A.
\]
There exists a subsequence \(\{a_{n_k}\}_{k=1}^\infty\) such that \(\lim_{k \to \infty} a_{n_k} = \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n\). Similarly, there exists a subsequence \(\{a_{m_k}\}_{k=1}^\infty\) such that \(\lim_{k \to \infty} a_{m_k} = \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n\).
The subadditivity of \(\limsup\) holds: \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} (a_n + b_n) \le \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n + \limsup_{n \to \infty} b_n,
\tag{A.5}\] provided the right-hand side is not of the indeterminate form \(\infty - \infty\).
If \(a_n \ge 0\) and \(b_n \ge 0\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), then \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} (a_n b_n) \le \left( \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n \right) \cdot \left( \limsup_{n \to \infty} b_n \right),
\tag{A.6}\] provided the right-hand side is not of the form \(0 \cdot \infty\) or \(\infty \cdot 0\).



Proof (Proof of Proposition A.1). Proof of Item 1: Since \(\inf\{a_k : k \ge n\} \le \sup\{a_k : k \ge n\}\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), taking \(n \to \infty\) shows \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n \le \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n\).
Now suppose \(\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = A \in \mathbb{R}\) exists. For every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists \(N(\epsilon) \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \(|A - a_n| \le \epsilon\) for all \(n \ge N(\epsilon)\), which implies \[
A - \epsilon \le a_k \le A + \epsilon \quad \text{for all } k \ge N(\epsilon).
\] Taking infimum and supremum over \(k \ge N(\epsilon)\) gives \[
A - \epsilon \le \inf_{k \ge N(\epsilon)} a_k \le \sup_{k \ge N(\epsilon)} a_k \le A + \epsilon.
\] Taking \(n \to \infty\), we obtain \[
A - \epsilon \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n \le \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n \le A + \epsilon.
\] Since \(\epsilon > 0\) is arbitrary, \(A = \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n = \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n\).
If \(A = +\infty\), then for any \(M > 0\), \(a_k \ge M\) for all \(k \ge N(M)\). Thus \(\inf_{k \ge N} a_k \ge M\), which implies \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n \ge M\). As \(M\) is arbitrary, \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n = \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n = +\infty\). The case \(A = -\infty\) is symmetric.
Conversely, if \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n = \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n = A \in \mathbb{R}\), then for any \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \(A - \epsilon \le \inf_{k \ge N} a_k \le \sup_{k \ge N} a_k \le A + \epsilon\). Consequently, \(A - \epsilon \le a_n \le A + \epsilon\) for all \(n \ge N\), proving that \(\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = A\).
Proof of Items 2–4: Left as an exercise.


Example A.1 To illustrate strict inequality in Equation A.5, set \(a_n = (-1)^n\) and \(b_n = (-1)^{n+1}\). Then \(a_n + b_n = 0\) for all \(n\), so \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} (a_n + b_n) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} (a_n + b_n) = \liminf_{n \to \infty} (a_n + b_n) = 0.
\] However, \(\limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n = 1\) and \(\limsup_{n \to \infty} b_n = 1\). Thus: \[
0 = \limsup_{n \to \infty} (a_n + b_n) < \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n + \limsup_{n \to \infty} b_n = 1 + 1 = 2.
\] Similarly, \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n = -1\) and \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} b_n = -1\), yielding: \[
0 = \liminf_{n \to \infty} (a_n + b_n) > \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n + \liminf_{n \to \infty} b_n = -2.
\]


Remark A.3. If \(a_n \le b_n\) for a.a. \(n\), then \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n \le \limsup_{n \to \infty} b_n \quad \text{and} \quad \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} b_n.
\] In particular, if \(a_n = b_n\) for a.a. \(n\), their limsups and liminfs are equal. Furthermore, for any constant \(b \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\limsup_{n \to \infty} (a_n + b) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n + b\) and \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} (a_n + b) = \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n + b\).


Lemma A.2 If \(\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{R}\) and \(\{b_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{R}\) such that \(b = \lim_{n \to \infty} b_n\) exists in \(\mathbb{R}\), then \[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} (a_n + b_n) = \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n + b.
\]


Proof (Proof of Lemma A.2). Given \(\epsilon > 0\), choose \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \(b - \epsilon \le b_n \le b + \epsilon\) for all \(n \ge N\). Then for all \(n \ge N\), \[
a_n + b - \epsilon \le a_n + b_n \le a_n + b + \epsilon.
\] Taking the \(\liminf\) across this inequality and using Remark A.3 yields \[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n + b - \epsilon \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} (a_n + b_n) \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n + b + \epsilon.
\] Since \(\epsilon > 0\) is arbitrary, taking \(\epsilon \downarrow 0\) yields \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} (a_n + b_n) = \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n + b\). \(\blacksquare\)

text: A.4 Infinite Sums and Classical Convergence Theorems
crumbs: A  Limsups, Liminfs and Extended Limits

title: Appendix A — Limsups, Liminfs and Extended Limits
text:
A.5 Non-negative Infinite Sums

Definition A.5 For any sequence \(a_n \in [0, \infty]\), we define the infinite sum as \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n := \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=1}^N a_n = \sup_{N \in \mathbb{N}} \sum_{n=1}^N a_n.
\tag{A.7}\]


Remark A.4. If \(a_n, b_n \in [0, \infty]\) and \(\lambda > 0\), then \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n + \lambda b_n) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n + \lambda \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n.
\] Indeed, finite sums are linear, and taking limits of non-decreasing sequences preserves linear combinations: \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n + \lambda b_n) &= \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=1}^N (a_n + \lambda b_n) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \left[ \sum_{n=1}^N a_n + \lambda \sum_{n=1}^N b_n \right] \\
&= \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=1}^N a_n + \lambda \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=1}^N b_n = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n + \lambda \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n.
\end{aligned}
\]


Proposition A.2 (Monotone Convergence Theorem (MCT) for Sums) Suppose that for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(\{f_n(i)\}_{i=1}^\infty\) is a sequence in \([0, \infty]\) such that \(f_n(i) \uparrow f(i)\) as \(n \to \infty\) for each \(i \in \mathbb{N}\) (i.e., \(f_n(i)\) is non-decreasing in \(n\) and \(\lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(i) = f(i)\)). Then \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i) = \sum_{i=1}^\infty \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(i) = \sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i).
\tag{A.8}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition A.2). Let \(M := \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i)\) (which exists in \([0, \infty]\) as the sequence of sums is non-decreasing).
Since \(f_n(i) \le f(i)\) for all \(n\) and \(i\), taking sums yields \(\sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i) \le \sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i)\) for all \(n\). Taking \(n \to \infty\) yields \[
M \le \sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i).
\] Conversely, for any fixed \(N \in \mathbb{N}\), using the linearity of finite limits gives \[
\sum_{i=1}^N f(i) = \sum_{i=1}^N \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(i) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^N f_n(i) \le \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i) = M.
\] Taking \(N \to \infty\) on the left side shows \(\sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i) \le M\). Combining both inequalities yields \(M = \sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i)\). \(\blacksquare\)


Proposition A.3 (Tonelli’s Theorem for Sums) If \(\{a_{k,n}\}_{k,n=1}^\infty \subset [0, \infty]\), then \[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,n}.
\tag{A.9}\]


Proof (Proof of Proposition A.3). Proof 1 (via MCT). For each \(k\), define \(S_N(k) := \sum_{n=1}^N a_{k,n}\). Notice that \(S_N(k) \ge 0\) and \(S_N(k) \uparrow \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n}\) as \(N \to \infty\). Applying the Monotone Convergence Theorem for sums (Proposition A.2) with \(f_N(k) = S_N(k)\) yields \[
\lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{k=1}^\infty S_N(k) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \lim_{N \to \infty} S_N(k) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n}.
\] On the other hand, interchanging finite sums gives \[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty S_N(k) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^N a_{k,n} = \sum_{n=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,n}.
\] Taking \(N \to \infty\) yields \(\lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{k=1}^\infty S_N(k) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,n}\), proving Equation A.9.
Proof 2 (via Supremum). Let \(M := \sup \left\{ \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{n=1}^N a_{k,n} : K, N \in \mathbb{N} \right\}\) and \(L := \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n}\).
For any fixed \(K, N \in \mathbb{N}\): \[
\sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{n=1}^N a_{k,n} \le \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n} \le \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n} = L.
\] Taking the supremum over \(K, N\) yields \(M \le L\).
Conversely, \(L = \lim_{K \to \infty} \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{n=1}^N a_{k,n}\). Since \(\sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{n=1}^N a_{k,n} \le M\) for all \(K, N\), taking limits yields \(L \le M\). Thus \(L = M\). By exact symmetry of indices in the definition of \(M\), \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,n} = M = L\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: Appendix A — Limsups, Liminfs and Extended Limits
text:
A.6 Summable Sequences and Linearity

Definition A.6 (Absolute Summability) A sequence \(\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{R}\) is said to be summable (or absolutely convergent) if \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n| < \infty\).
For a summable sequence \(\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\), we define its positive and negative parts by \(a_n^+ := \max(a_n, 0)\) and \(a_n^- := \max(-a_n, 0)\), so that \(a_n = a_n^+ - a_n^-\) and \(|a_n| = a_n^+ + a_n^-\). The sum is defined as: \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n := \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^+ - \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^-.
\tag{A.10}\]


Remark A.5. From Equation A.10, the triangle inequality for infinite series holds: \[
\begin{align*}
\left| \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \right| &= \left| \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^+ - \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^- \right| \\
&\le \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^+ + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^- \\
&= \sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n^+ + a_n^-) \\
&= \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|.
\end{align*}
\]


Proposition A.4 (Linearity of Infinite Sums) If \(\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) and \(\{b_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) are summable sequences in \(\mathbb{R}\) and \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\), then \(\{a_n + \lambda b_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) is summable, and \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n + \lambda b_n) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n + \lambda \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n.
\]


Proof. Proof. Let \(c_n := a_n + \lambda b_n\). By the triangle inequality, \(|c_n| \le |a_n| + |\lambda| |b_n|\). Thus: \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty |c_n| \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n| + |\lambda| \sum_{n=1}^\infty |b_n| < \infty,
\] proving \(\{c_n\}\) is summable.
First, assume \(\lambda \ge 0\). Since \(c_n = c_n^+ - c_n^- = a_n^+ - a_n^- + \lambda(b_n^+ - b_n^-)\), rearranging terms yields non-negative identities: \[
c_n^+ + a_n^- + \lambda b_n^- = c_n^- + a_n^+ + \lambda b_n^+.
\] Summing both sides over \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) and using Remark A.4 gives \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n^+ + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^- + \lambda \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n^- = \sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n^- + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^+ + \lambda \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n^+.
\] Rearranging finite real quantities gives \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n^+ - \sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n^- = \left( \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^+ - \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^- \right) + \lambda \left( \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n^+ - \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n^- \right),
\] which is \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n + \lambda \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n\).
Finally, for \(\lambda = -1\), observe that \((-a_n)^+ = a_n^-\) and \((-a_n)^- = a_n^+\). Thus, \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-a_n) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^- - \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^+ = -\left( \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^+ - \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^- \right) = -\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n.
\] Combining this with \(\lambda \ge 0\) completes the proof for all \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\).


Proposition A.5 (Fubini’s Theorem for Sums) Suppose \(\{a_{k,n}\}_{k,n=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{R}\) is double-indexed and satisfies \[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_{k,n}| < \infty.
\] Then: \[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,n}.
\tag{A.11}\]

title: Appendix A — Limsups, Liminfs and Extended Limits
section: A.7 Convergence Theorems: Fatou and DCT for Sums
text:
A.7 Convergence Theorems: Fatou and DCT for Sums

Proposition A.6 (Fatou’s Lemma for Sums) Suppose that for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(\{h_n(i)\}_{i=1}^\infty\) is a sequence in \([0, \infty]\). Then \[
\sum_{i=1}^\infty \liminf_{n \to \infty} h_n(i) \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty h_n(i).
\tag{A.12}\]


Proposition A.7 (Dominated Convergence Theorem (DCT) for Sums) Suppose that for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(\{f_n(i)\}_{i=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{R}\) and \(\{g_n(i)\}_{i=1}^\infty \subset [0, \infty)\) satisfy:

\(\sum_{i=1}^\infty g_n(i) < \infty\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).
Pointwise limits \(f(i) := \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(i)\) and \(g(i) := \lim_{n \to \infty} g_n(i)\) exist for every \(i \in \mathbb{N}\).
Domination condition: \(|f_n(i)| \le g_n(i)\) for all \(i, n \in \mathbb{N}\).
\(\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty g_n(i) = \sum_{i=1}^\infty g(i) < \infty\).

Then: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i) = \sum_{i=1}^\infty \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(i) = \sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i).
\tag{A.13}\]

title: Appendix A — Limsups, Liminfs and Extended Limits
text:
A.8 Examples and counterexamples

Example A.2 (Failure of Fubini / Interchanging Limits) Let \(\{S_{m,n}\}_{m,n=1}^\infty\) be a double sequence of real numbers such that \(\lim_{m \to \infty} S_{m,n} = 1\) for all \(n\) and \(\lim_{n \to \infty} S_{m,n} = 0\) for all \(m\). For instance, take \(S_{m,n} = \mathbf{1}_{\{m \ge n\}}\) or \(S_{m,n} = \frac{m}{m+n}\).
Define \(\{a_{i,j}\}_{i,j=1}^\infty\) via discrete mixed differences (with \(S_{m,0} = S_{0,n} = 0\)): \[
a_{m,n} := S_{m,n} - S_{m-1,n} - S_{m,n-1} + S_{m-1,n-1}.
\] This choice ensures that \(S_{m,n} = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}\). Consequently: \[
\begin{align*}
&\sum_{i=1}^\infty \sum_{j=1}^\infty a_{i,j} = \lim_{i \to \infty} \lim_{j \to \infty} S_{i,j} = 0\\
& \neq 1 = \lim_{j \to \infty} \lim_{i \to \infty} S_{i,j} = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \sum_{i=1}^\infty a_{i,j}.
\end{align*}
\tag{A.14}\]
Evaluating \(a_{m,n}\) explicitly for \(S_{m,n} = \mathbf{1}_{\{m \ge n\}}\) gives: \[
\begin{align*}
a_{m,n} &= \mathbf{1}_{\{m \ge n\}} - \mathbf{1}_{\{m-1 \ge n\}} - \mathbf{1}_{\{m \ge n-1\}} + \mathbf{1}_{\{m-1 \ge n-1\}} \\
&= \mathbf{1}_{\{m = n\}} - \mathbf{1}_{\{m = n-1\}}.
\end{align*}
\tag{A.15}\] Thus, \(a_{m,n} = 1\) if \(m = n\), \(a_{m,n} = -1\) if \(n = m+1\), and \(a_{m,n} = 0\) otherwise.
Fixing \(n\), the row sum yields \(\sum_{m=1}^\infty a_{m,n} = \mathbf{1}_{\{n = 1\}}\). Fixing \(m\), the column sum yields \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{m,n} = 0\). Thus: \[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{m=1}^\infty a_{m,n} = 1 \quad \neq \quad 0 = \sum_{m=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{m,n}.
\] Notice that \(\sum_{m=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_{m,n}| = \infty\), confirming why Fubini’s Theorem (Proposition A.5) does not apply.


Example A.3 (Continuous Counterexample on \(\mathbb{R}_+^2\)) A continuous analog of Example A.2 is constructed on \([0, \infty)^2\) via: \[
h(x,y) = \mathbf{1}_{\{x \le y \le x+1\}} - \mathbf{1}_{\{x+1 < y \le x+2\}}.
\tag{A.16}\]
Integrating with respect to \(y\) for a fixed \(x \ge 0\): \[
\int_0^\infty h(x,y) \, dy = \int_x^{x+1} 1 \, dy - \int_{x+1}^{x+2} 1 \, dy = 1 - 1 = 0.
\] Integrating with respect to \(x\) for a fixed \(y \ge 0\): \[
\int_0^\infty h(x,y) \, dx = y \mathbf{1}_{\{y \le 1\}} + (2-y) \mathbf{1}_{\{1 \le y \le 2\}}.
\] Taking iterated integrals yields: \[
\int_0^\infty \left( \int_0^\infty h(x,y) \, dy \right) dx = \int_0^\infty 0 \, dx = 0,
\] while \[
\int_0^\infty \left( \int_0^\infty h(x,y) \, dx \right) dy = \int_0^1 y \, dy + \int_1^2 (2-y) \, dy = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1.
\] Hence, \(\int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty h(x,y) \, dy \, dx = 0 \neq 1 = \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty h(x,y) \, dx \, dy\).

section: A.10 Exercise 1.1: Fubini’s Theorem for Sums
text:
A.10 Exercise 1.1: Fubini’s Theorem for Sums

Exercise A.1 Prove Proposition 1.15 (Proposition A.5).


Proof. Solution / Proof. Let \(a_{k,n}^+ := \max(a_{k,n}, 0)\) and \(a_{k,n}^- := \max(-a_{k,n}, 0)\). Then \(a_{k,n} = a_{k,n}^+ - a_{k,n}^-\) and \(|a_{k,n}| = a_{k,n}^+ + a_{k,n}^-\). Since \(a_{k,n}^+, a_{k,n}^- \le |a_{k,n}|\), Tonelli’s Theorem for non-negative double sums (Proposition A.3) implies: \[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^+ = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^+ \le \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_{k,n}| < \infty,
\] and \[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^- = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^- \le \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_{k,n}| < \infty.
\] For each \(k \in \mathbb{N}\), \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_{k,n}| < \infty\), so \(S_k := \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n}\) converges absolutely and equals \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^+ - \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^-\). By Proposition A.4, \(\{S_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\) is summable because \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty |S_k| \le \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_{k,n}| < \infty\).
Using the linearity of summable series: \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n} &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \left( \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^+ - \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^- \right) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^+ - \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^- \\
&= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^+ - \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^- = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left( \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^+ - \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,n}^- \right) \\
&= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,n}.
\end{aligned}
\] This completes the proof.

title: Appendix A — Limsups, Liminfs and Extended Limits
section: A.11 Exercise 1.2: Fatou’s Lemma for Sums
text:
A.11 Exercise 1.2: Fatou’s Lemma for Sums

Exercise A.2 Prove Proposition 1.17 (Proposition A.6).


Proof. Solution / Proof. For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) and \(i \in \mathbb{N}\), define \(f_n(i) := \inf_{m \ge n} h_m(i)\).
By construction:

\(f_n(i) \le h_n(i)\) for all \(n, i \in \mathbb{N}\).
\(f_n(i)\) is non-decreasing in \(n\) for each \(i \in \mathbb{N}\).
\(\lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(i) = \sup_{n \ge 1} \inf_{m \ge n} h_m(i) = \liminf_{n \to \infty} h_n(i)\).

Applying the Monotone Convergence Theorem for sums (Proposition A.2) to the non-decreasing sequence \(f_n(i)\) yields: \[
\sum_{i=1}^\infty \liminf_{n \to \infty} h_n(i) = \sum_{i=1}^\infty \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(i) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i) = \liminf_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i).
\] Since \(f_n(i) \le h_n(i)\) for all \(i\), monotonicity of sums implies \(\sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i) \le \sum_{i=1}^\infty h_n(i)\) for all \(n\). Taking the \(\liminf\) as \(n \to \infty\) gives: \[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i) \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty h_n(i).
\] Combining these two results proves Equation A.12.
crumbs: A  Limsups, Liminfs and Extended Limits

title: Appendix A — Limsups, Liminfs and Extended Limits
section: A.12 Exercise 1.3: Dominated Convergence Theorem for Sums
text:
A.12 Exercise 1.3: Dominated Convergence Theorem for Sums

Exercise A.3 Prove Proposition 1.18 (Proposition A.7).


Proof. Solution / Proof. Since \(|f_n(i)| \le g_n(i)\), we have \(g_n(i) + f_n(i) \ge 0\) and \(g_n(i) - f_n(i) \ge 0\) for all \(n, i \in \mathbb{N}\).
Step 1: Lower bound via \(g_n + f_n\). Define \(h_n(i) := g_n(i) + f_n(i) \ge 0\). Applying Fatou’s Lemma (Proposition A.6) to \(h_n\): \[
\sum_{i=1}^\infty \liminf_{n \to \infty} (g_n(i) + f_n(i)) \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty (g_n(i) + f_n(i)).
\] Since \(\lim_{n \to \infty} g_n(i) = g(i)\) exists, \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} (g_n(i) + f_n(i)) = g(i) + \liminf_{n \to \infty} f_n(i) = g(i) + f(i)\). Using Lemma A.2 with \(b_n = \sum_{i=1}^\infty g_n(i) \to \sum_{i=1}^\infty g(i) < \infty\): \[
\sum_{i=1}^\infty g(i) + \sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i) \le \sum_{i=1}^\infty g(i) + \liminf_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i).
\] Subtracting the finite quantity \(\sum_{i=1}^\infty g(i)\) from both sides yields: \[
\sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i) \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i).
\tag{A.17}\]
Step 2: Upper bound via \(g_n - f_n\). Define \(k_n(i) := g_n(i) - f_n(i) \ge 0\). Applying Fatou’s Lemma (Proposition A.6) to \(k_n\): \[
\sum_{i=1}^\infty \liminf_{n \to \infty} (g_n(i) - f_n(i)) \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty (g_n(i) - f_n(i)).
\] Using \(\liminf_{n \to \infty} (g_n(i) - f_n(i)) = g(i) - \limsup_{n \to \infty} f_n(i) = g(i) - f(i)\) and \(\liminf (-a_n) = -\limsup a_n\): \[
\sum_{i=1}^\infty g(i) - \sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i) \le \sum_{i=1}^\infty g(i) - \limsup_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i).
\] Subtracting \(\sum_{i=1}^\infty g(i)\) and multiplying by \(-1\) reverses the inequality: \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i) \le \sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i).
\tag{A.18}\]
Step 3: Conclusion. Combining Equation A.17 and Equation A.18 with Proposition A.1 (Item 1) gives: \[
\sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i) \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i) \le \limsup_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i) \le \sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i).
\] Thus \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^\infty f_n(i) = \sum_{i=1}^\infty f(i)\), completing the proof.

text:
A.13 Reconstruction and Gap Analysis

A.13.1 Transcriptions, Interpretations, and Corrections

Lemma 1.2 Notation & Wording: Fixed typographical errors in Item 1 (“\(for^1 a.a. n\)”) and clarified definition of almost all indices. Corrected typos in the limit law conditions (\(\infty - \infty\), \(\pm \infty \cdot 0\)).
Proof of Proposition 1.5, Item 1: Restructured the case-by-case epsilon and bounding argument for infinite limits where the handwritten note had incomplete fragment sentences.
Example 1.16 Equations: Reconstructed step-by-step algebra for \(a_{m,n} = S_{m,n} - S_{m-1,n} - S_{m,n-1} + S_{m-1,n-1}\). In particular, added explicit step-by-step evaluations for \(S_{m,n} = \mathbf{1}_{\{m \ge n\}}\) where the original notes skipped intermediate indicator function combinations.

title: Appendix B — Basic Metric and Topological Space Notions
text:
Definition B.1 (Pseudo-Metric and Metric Spaces) Let \(X\) be a non-empty set. A function \(d \colon X \times X \to [0, \infty)\) is called a pseudo-metric on \(X\) if \(d\) is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality:

Symmetry: \(d(x, y) = d(y, x)\) for all \(x, y \in X\).
Triangle Inequality: \(d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)\) for all \(x, y, z \in X\).

If we further assume that \(d\) is non-degenerate in the sense that \(d(x, y) = 0\) if and only if \(x = y\), then \(d\) is called a metric on \(X\). The pair \((X, d)\) is called a metric space.
Any subset \(Y \subseteq X\) of a (pseudo-)metric space \((X, d)\) is naturally a (pseudo-)metric space equipped with the restricted function \(\left.d\right|_{Y \times Y}\).


Example B.1 (Standard Metric Spaces)  

Let \(X = \mathbb{R}\). The standard metric is \(d(x, y) = |y - x|\). Another bounded metric on \(\mathbb{R}\) is given by \(d(x, y) = |\tan^{-1}(y) - \tan^{-1}(x)|\).
Let \(X = \mathbb{R}^d\). The standard Euclidean distance metric is given by \(d(x, y) = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{d}(y_j - x_j)^2}\). Subspaces such as the unit sphere \(S^{d-1} \subset \mathbb{R}^d\) inherit this metric.
Let \(X = C([0, 1], \mathbb{C})\) denote the space of continuous complex-valued functions on \([0, 1]\). Then \[d(f, g) := \max_{x \in [0, 1]} |f(x) - g(x)|\] is a metric on \(X\), whereas \[d_{1/2}(f, g) := \max_{x \in [0, 1/2]} |f(x) - g(x)|\] is a pseudo-metric on \(X\) (since non-zero functions vanishing on \([0, 1/2]\) satisfy \(d_{1/2}(f, 0) = 0\)).
Any normed vector space \((X, \|\cdot\|)\) is a metric space with induced metric \(d(x, y) := \|x - y\|\). In particular, \(L^p(\mu)\) spaces (for \(p \in [1, \infty]\)) are metric spaces.
Let \(X\) denote the space of \(C^1\)-periodic functions on \(\mathbb{R}\) with period \(1\). Then \[d(f, g) := \max_{x \in [0, 1]} |f'(x) - g'(x)|\] defines a pseudo-metric on \(X\).




Definition B.2 (Open and Closed Balls) Let \((X, d)\) be a metric space.

The open ball centered at \(x \in X\) with radius \(\delta > 0\) is defined by \[B(x, \delta) \equiv B_x(\delta) := \{y \in X \colon d(x, y) < \delta\}.\]
The closed ball centered at \(x \in X\) with radius \(\delta > 0\) is defined by \[C_x(\delta) := \{y \in X \colon d(x, y) \le \delta\}.\]



Definition B.3 (Sequence Convergence) A sequence \(\{x_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty} \subset X\) is said to converge to a point \(x \in X\) (denoted \(x_n \to x\) as \(n \to \infty\)) if \(\lim_{n \to \infty} d(x, x_n) = 0\).
If \(x_n \to x\) and \(x_n \to y\), then by the triangle inequality: \[d(x, y) \le d(x, x_n) + d(x_n, y) \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty,\] which implies \(d(x, y) = 0\). When \(d\) is non-degenerate (a metric), \(x = y\), ensuring unique limits. For general pseudo-metrics, limits are unique up to distance zero.


Definition B.4 (Bounded, Closed, and Open Sets)  

A set \(E \subset X\) is bounded if \(E \subset B(x, R)\) for some \(x \in X\) and \(R < \infty\).
A set \(F \subset X\) is closed if every convergent sequence \(\{x_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty} \subset F\) has its limit in \(F\). We denote this by \(F \sqsubset X\).
A set \(V \subset X\) is open if its complement \(V^c := X \setminus V\) is closed. We denote this by \(V \subset_o X\).
The collection of all open subsets of \(X\) relative to \(d\) is denoted by \(\tau_d\).



Exercise B.1 Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a collection of closed subsets of \(X\). Show that \(\bigcap \mathcal{F} := \bigcap_{F \in \mathcal{F}} F\) is closed. Furthermore, show that finite unions of closed sets are closed: if \(\{F_k\}_{k=1}^{K}\) are closed sets, then \(\bigcup_{k=1}^{K} F_k\) is closed. (By taking complements, this implies that \(\tau_d\) is closed under finite intersections and arbitrary unions.) Show by example that a countable union of closed sets need not be closed.


Proof. 

Arbitrary Intersections: Let \(\{x_n\} \subset \bigcap_{F \in \mathcal{F}} F\) with \(x_n \to x\). For each \(F \in \mathcal{F}\), \(\{x_n\} \subset F\). Since \(F\) is closed, \(x \in F\). Thus \(x \in \bigcap_{F \in \mathcal{F}} F\), proving the intersection is closed.
Finite Unions: Let \(\{x_n\} \subset \bigcup_{k=1}^{K} F_k\) with \(x_n \to x\). By the pigeonhole principle, there exists at least one \(k_0 \in \{1, \dots, K\}\) such that \(F_{k_0}\) contains an infinite subsequence \(\{x_{n_j}\}\). Since \(x_{n_j} \to x\) and \(F_{k_0}\) is closed, \(x \in F_{k_0} \subset \bigcup_{k=1}^{K} F_k\).
Counterexample: In \(\mathbb{R}\) with the standard metric, \(F_n = [1/n, 1 - 1/n]\) is closed for each \(n \ge 2\), but \(\bigcup_{n=2}^{\infty} F_n = (0, 1)\), which is open and not closed.



Exercise B.2 Show that \(V \subset X\) is open if and only if for every \(x \in V\) there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that \(B_x(\delta) \subset V\). In particular, show \(B_x(\delta)\) is open for all \(x \in X\) and \(\delta > 0\).


Proof. 

\((\Rightarrow)\) Suppose \(V\) is open, so \(V^c\) is closed. Assume for contradiction that there exists \(x \in V\) such that for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(B_x(1/n) \not\subset V\). Then choose \(x_n \in B_x(1/n) \cap V^c\). Then \(x_n \in V^c\) and \(d(x_n, x) < 1/n \to 0\), so \(x_n \to x\). Since \(V^c\) is closed, \(x \in V^c\), contradicting \(x \in V\).
\((\Leftarrow)\) Suppose for every \(x \in V\), there exists \(\delta_x > 0\) such that \(B_x(\delta_x) \subset V\). Let \(\{x_n\} \subset V^c\) be a sequence with \(x_n \to x\). If \(x \in V\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that \(B_x(\delta) \subset V\). But \(x_n \to x\) implies \(x_n \in B_x(\delta) \subset V\) for large \(n\), contradicting \(x_n \in V^c\). Thus \(x \in V^c\), so \(V^c\) is closed and \(V\) is open.
Open Ball Openness: Let \(y \in B_x(\delta)\) and set \(\epsilon = \delta - d(x, y) > 0\). If \(z \in B_y(\epsilon)\), then \(d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z) < d(x, y) + \epsilon = \delta\). Thus \(B_y(\epsilon) \subset B_x(\delta)\), proving \(B_x(\delta)\) is open.



Definition B.5 (Neighborhoods) A subset \(A \subset X\) is a neighborhood of \(x \in X\) if there exists an open set \(V \subset_o X\) such that \(x \in V \subset A\). \(A\) is an open neighborhood of \(x\) if \(A\) is open and \(x \in A\).


Lemma B.1 (Continuity of Distance to a Set) For any non-empty subset \(A \subset X\), define the distance function \(d_A \colon X \to [0, \infty)\) by \[d_A(x) := \inf \{d(x, a) \colon a \in A\}.\] Then \(d_A\) is 1-Lipschitz continuous: \[|d_A(x) - d_A(y)| \le d(x, y) \quad \forall x, y \in X. \tag{B.1}\]
In particular, if \(x_n \to x\) in \(X\), then \(d_A(x_n) \to d_A(x)\) as \(n \to \infty\). Moreover, for any \(\epsilon > 0\), the set \(F_\epsilon := \{x \in X \colon d_A(x) \ge \epsilon\}\) is closed in \(X\).


Proof. Let \(a \in A\) and \(x, y \in X\). By the triangle inequality: \[d_A(x) \le d(x, a) \le d(x, y) + d(y, a).\] Taking the infimum over \(a \in A\) yields \[d_A(x) \le d(x, y) + d_A(y) \implies d_A(x) - d_A(y) \le d(x, y).\] Swapping \(x\) and \(y\) gives \(d_A(y) - d_A(x) \le d(x, y)\), establishing Equation B.1.
If \(x_n \to x\), then \(|d_A(x) - d_A(x_n)| \le d(x, x_n) \to 0\), proving continuity.
Now let \(\{x_n\} \subset F_\epsilon\) with \(x_n \to x\). Since \(d_A(x_n) \ge \epsilon\) for all \(n\), continuity implies \[d_A(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} d_A(x_n) \ge \epsilon,\] so \(x \in F_\epsilon\), proving that \(F_\epsilon\) is closed.


Corollary B.1 (Joint Continuity of Metric) The metric function \(d \colon X \times X \to [0, \infty)\) satisfies \[|d(x, y) - d(x', y')| \le d(x, x') + d(y, y'). \tag{B.2}\]


Proof. Applying Lemma B.1 with singletons \(A = \{y\}\) and \(A = \{y'\}\) alongside the real triangle inequality: \[\begin{align*}
|d(x, y) - d(x', y')| &\le |d(x, y) - d(x, y')| + |d(x, y') - d(x', y')| \\
&\le d(y, y') + d(x, x'). \tag*{$\blacksquare$}
\end{align*}\]


Example B.2 For \(x \in X\) and \(\delta > 0\), \(C_x(\delta)\) and \(B_x(\delta)^c\) are closed. Indeed, if \(\{y_n\} \subset C_x(\delta)\) with \(y_n \to y\), then \(d(y_n, x) \le \delta\) for all \(n\). By Corollary B.1, \(d(y, x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} d(y_n, x) \le \delta\), so \(y \in C_x(\delta)\).


Lemma B.2 (Approximating Open Sets from Inside by Closed Sets) Let \(A \subset X\) be closed and let \(F_\epsilon := \{x \in X \colon d_A(x) \ge \epsilon\}\). Then \(F_\epsilon \uparrow A^c\) as \(\epsilon \downarrow 0\).


Proof. For any \(x \in A\), \(d_A(x) = 0\), so \(F_\epsilon \subset A^c\) for all \(\epsilon > 0\), implying \(\bigcup_{\epsilon > 0} F_\epsilon \subset A^c\). Conversely, let \(x \in A^c\). Since \(A^c\) is open, there exists \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \(B_x(\epsilon) \subset A^c\), which means \(d(x, y) \ge \epsilon\) for all \(y \in A\). Thus \(d_A(x) \ge \epsilon\), so \(x \in F_\epsilon\). Finally, \(F_\epsilon \subset F_{\epsilon'}\) whenever \(\epsilon' \le \epsilon\), completing the monotonic union \(F_\epsilon \uparrow A^c\).


Definition B.6 (Closure, Density, and Separability) Let \(A \subset X\).

The closure of \(A\), denoted \(\overline{A}\), is defined as \[\overline{A} := \{x \in X \colon \exists \{x_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty} \subset A \text{ with } x_n \to x\}.\]
\(A\) is dense in \(X\) if \(\overline{A} = X\).
A metric space \((X, d)\) is separable if it contains a countable dense subset \(D \subset X\).



Exercise B.3 Given \(A \subset X\), show that \(\overline{A}\) is closed and satisfies \[\overline{A} = \bigcap \{F \subset X \colon A \subset F \text{ and } F \text{ is closed}\}. \tag{B.3}\] That is, \(\overline{A}\) is the smallest closed set containing \(A\).


Proof. Let \(C = \bigcap \{F \subset X \colon A \subset F, F \text{ is closed}\}\).

\(\overline{A} \subset C\): Let \(x \in \overline{A}\), so \(x_n \to x\) for some \(\{x_n\} \subset A\). If \(F\) is any closed set containing \(A\), then \(\{x_n\} \subset F\), so its limit \(x \in F\). Thus \(x \in C\).
\(C \subset \overline{A}\): It suffices to show \(\overline{A}\) is closed (since \(A \subset \overline{A}\) trivially). Let \(\{y_k\} \subset \overline{A}\) with \(y_k \to y\). For each \(k\), choose \(x_k \in A\) with \(d(x_k, y_k) < 1/k\). Then \(d(x_k, y) \le d(x_k, y_k) + d(y_k, y) \to 0\), so \(x_k \to y \implies y \in \overline{A}\). Hence \(\overline{A}\) is closed, which implies \(C \subset \overline{A}\).



Exercise B.4 Let \(D \subset X\) be dense in \((X, d)\) and let \(E \subset X\) be such that for every \(x \in D\), there exists a sequence \(\{x_n\} \subset E\) converging to \(x\). Show that \(E\) is dense in \(X\).


Proof. Let \(x \in X\) and \(\epsilon > 0\). Since \(D\) is dense in \(X\), there exists \(y \in D\) with \(d(x, y) < \epsilon / 2\). Since \(E\) approximates \(D\), there exists \(z \in E\) with \(d(y, z) < \epsilon / 2\). By the triangle inequality, \(d(x, z) < \epsilon\). Thus \(x \in \overline{E}\), proving \(\overline{E} = X\).


Exercise B.5 Suppose \((X, d)\) contains an uncountable subset \(\Lambda \subset X\) such that there exists \(\epsilon > 0\) with \(d(a, b) \ge \epsilon\) for all \(a, b \in \Lambda\) with \(a \neq b\). Show that \((X, d)\) is not separable.


Proof. Suppose \(D \subset X\) is dense. For each \(a \in \Lambda\), the open ball \(B_a(\epsilon/2)\) must contain at least one point \(d_a \in D\). Since \(d(a, b) \ge \epsilon\) for distinct \(a, b \in \Lambda\), the balls \(\{B_a(\epsilon/2)\}_{a \in \Lambda}\) are pairwise disjoint. Thus the map \(a \mapsto d_a\) is an injection from the uncountable set \(\Lambda\) into \(D\), implying \(D\) must be uncountable. Hence no countable dense subset exists.

section: B.2 Metric Spaces as Topological Spaces
text:
B.2 Metric Spaces as Topological Spaces

Definition B.7 (Topological Space) Let \(X\) be a set. A topology on \(X\) is a collection \(\tau\) of subsets of \(X\) satisfying:

\(\emptyset \in \tau\) and \(X \in \tau\).
\(\tau\) is closed under arbitrary unions: if \(\{V_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A} \subset \tau\), then \(\bigcup_{\alpha \in A} V_\alpha \in \tau\).
\(\tau\) is closed under finite intersections: if \(V_1, \dots, V_n \in \tau\), then \(\bigcap_{i=1}^{n} V_i \in \tau\).

The pair \((X, \tau)\) is a topological space, and sets \(V \in \tau\) are called open. A set \(F \subset X\) is closed if \(F^c \in \tau\). Let \(\tau_x = \{V \in \tau \colon x \in V\}\) denote the open neighborhoods of \(x\). Every metric space \((X, d)\) naturally forms a topological space \((X, \tau_d)\).


Definition B.8 (Topological Operations) Let \((X, \tau)\) be a topological space and \(A \subset X\).

Closure: \(\overline{A} := \bigcap \{F \subset X \colon A \subset F, F^c \in \tau\}\).
Interior: \(A^\circ := \bigcup \{V \in \tau \colon V \subset A\}\).
Neighborhood: \(A\) is a neighborhood of \(x\) if \(x \in A^\circ\).
Accumulation Points: \(\mathrm{acc}(A) := \{x \in X \colon V \cap (A \setminus \{x\}) \neq \emptyset \text{ for all } V \in \tau_x\}\).
Boundary: \(\mathrm{bd}(A) := \overline{A} \setminus A^\circ\).



Remark B.1. The dual relations between interior and closure are given by: \[(A^\circ)^c = \overline{A^c} \quad \text{and} \quad (\overline{A})^c = (A^c)^\circ. \tag{B.4}\] Hence the boundary satisfies \(\mathrm{bd}(A) = \overline{A} \cap \overline{A^c}\).


B.2.1 Continuity

Definition B.9 (Pointwise Continuity (Metric)) Let \((X, \rho)\) and \((Y, d)\) be metric spaces. A function \(f \colon X \to Y\) is continuous at \(x \in X\) if for all \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that \[d(f(x), f(x')) < \epsilon \quad \text{whenever} \quad \rho(x, x') < \delta. \tag{B.5}\] \(f\) is continuous if it is continuous at every \(x \in X\).


Lemma B.3 (Local Continuity Characterizations) Let \((X, \rho)\) and \((Y, d)\) be metric spaces and \(f \colon X \to Y\). The following are equivalent for \(x \in X\):

\(f\) is continuous at \(x\).
For all neighborhoods \(A \subset Y\) of \(f(x)\), \(f^{-1}(A)\) is a neighborhood of \(x\).
For all sequences \(\{x_n\} \subset X\) with \(x_n \to x\), \(f(x_n) \to f(x)\) in \(Y\).



Proof. 

\((1 \Rightarrow 2)\): If \(A\) is a neighborhood of \(f(x)\), there exists \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \(B_{f(x)}(\epsilon) \subset A\). By continuity, pick \(\delta > 0\) satisfying Equation B.5. Then \(B_x(\delta) \subset f^{-1}(B_{f(x)}(\epsilon)) \subset f^{-1}(A)\), so \(f^{-1}(A)\) is a neighborhood of \(x\).
\((2 \Rightarrow 3)\): Suppose \(x_n \to x\). For any \(\epsilon > 0\), \(B_{f(x)}(\epsilon)\) is a neighborhood of \(f(x)\), so \(f^{-1}(B_{f(x)}(\epsilon))\) is a neighborhood of \(x\), containing \(B_x(\delta)\) for some \(\delta > 0\). Since \(x_n \to x\), \(x_n \in B_x(\delta)\) for almost all \(n\), so \(f(x_n) \in B_{f(x)}(\epsilon)\) for almost all \(n\). Thus \(f(x_n) \to f(x)\).
\((3 \Rightarrow 1)\): We prove \(\neg 1 \Rightarrow \neg 3\). If \(f\) is not continuous at \(x\), there exists \(\epsilon > 0\) such that for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), there is \(x_n \in X\) with \(\rho(x_n, x) < 1/n\) but \(d(f(x_n), f(x)) \ge \epsilon\). Then \(x_n \to x\) but \(f(x_n) \not\to f(x)\).



Lemma B.4 (Global Continuity Characterizations) Let \((X, \rho)\) and \((Y, d)\) be metric spaces and \(f \colon X \to Y\). The following are equivalent:

\(f\) is continuous on \(X\).
\(f^{-1}(V) \in \tau_\rho\) for all \(V \in \tau_d\) (preimages of open sets are open).
\(f^{-1}(C)\) is closed in \(X\) for all closed \(C \subset Y\).
For all convergent sequences \(x_n \to x\) in \(X\), \(f(x_n) \to f(x)\) in \(Y\).



Proof. Equivalence of (2) and (3) follows immediately from \(f^{-1}(C^c) = [f^{-1}(C)]^c\). Equivalence of (1), (2), and (4) follows from applying Lemma B.3 pointwise across \(X\).


Definition B.10 (Continuity in Topological Terms) Let \((X, \tau_X)\) and \((Y, \tau_Y)\) be topological spaces.

\(f \colon X \to Y\) is continuous at \(x \in X\) if for every open neighborhood \(V \in \tau_Y\) of \(f(x)\), there exists an open neighborhood \(U \in \tau_X\) of \(x\) such that \(U \subset f^{-1}(V)\).
\(f\) is globally continuous if \(f^{-1}(\tau_Y) \subset \tau_X\). The set of continuous functions is denoted \(C(X, Y)\).



Exercise B.6 Show \(f \colon X \to Y\) is continuous under Definition 2.19 if and only if \(f\) is continuous at all points \(x \in X\).


Proof. 

\((\Rightarrow)\) If \(f^{-1}(V) \in \tau_X\) for all \(V \in \tau_Y\), then given \(x \in X\) and \(V \in \tau_Y\) with \(f(x) \in V\), set \(U = f^{-1}(V) \in \tau_X\). Then \(x \in U\) and \(U \subset f^{-1}(V)\), so \(f\) is continuous at \(x\).
\((\Leftarrow)\) Let \(V \in \tau_Y\). For every \(x \in f^{-1}(V)\), continuity at \(x\) provides \(U_x \in \tau_X\) with \(x \in U_x \subset f^{-1}(V)\). Then \(f^{-1}(V) = \bigcup_{x \in f^{-1}(V)} U_x\), which is open as an arbitrary union of open sets.



Exercise B.7 Show \(f \colon X \to Y\) is continuous if and only if \(f^{-1}(C)\) is closed in \(X\) for all closed subsets \(C \subset Y\).


Proof. This follows directly from set operations: \(C \subset Y\) is closed \(\iff Y \setminus C\) is open. Since \(f^{-1}(Y \setminus C) = X \setminus f^{-1}(C)\), \(f^{-1}(Y \setminus C)\) is open \(\iff f^{-1}(C)\) is closed.


Definition B.11 (Homeomorphism) A map \(f \colon X \to Y\) between topological spaces is a homeomorphism if \(f\) is bijective, \(f\) is continuous, and its inverse \(f^{-1} \colon Y \to X\) is continuous.


Example B.3 By Lemma B.1, \(d_A \colon X \to [0, \infty)\) is continuous. Setting \(A = \{x\}\), the map \(y \mapsto d(y, x)\) is continuous for each fixed \(x \in X\).


Exercise B.8 (Joint Continuity Criterion) Let \(X, Y, Z\) be metric spaces and \(F \colon X \times Y \to Z\) be a function such that:

For each \(x \in X\), \(y \mapsto F(x, y)\) is continuous, and these maps are locally equi-continuous in \(x\): for all \((a, b) \in X \times Y\), \[\lim_{y \to b} \sup_{x \in B_X(a, r)} d(F(x, y), F(x, b)) = 0 \quad \text{for some } r > 0. \tag{B.6}\]
There exists a dense subset \(Y_0 \subset Y\) such that \(x \mapsto F(x, y)\) is continuous for fixed \(y \in Y_0\).

Show: 1. \(x \mapsto F(x, y)\) is continuous for all \(y \in Y\). 2. \(F \colon X \times Y \to Z\) is jointly continuous on \(X \times Y\).


Proof. 

Fix \(y \in Y\) and \(a \in X\). Let \(b = y\). By local equicontinuity, choose \(r > 0\) such that Equation B.6 holds. For \(\epsilon > 0\), choose \(y_0 \in Y_0 \cap B_Y(b, \delta)\) such that \(\sup_{x \in B_X(a, r)} d(F(x, y_0), F(x, y)) < \epsilon / 3\). Since \(x \mapsto F(x, y_0)\) is continuous, choose \(\delta_x > 0\) such that \(d(F(x, y_0), F(a, y_0)) < \epsilon / 3\) whenever \(d(x, a) < \delta_x\). By triangle inequality: \[d(F(x, y), F(a, y)) \le d(F(x, y), F(x, y_0)) + d(F(x, y_0), F(a, y_0)) + d(F(a, y_0), F(a, y)) < \epsilon.\]
To prove joint continuity at \((a, b)\), write: \[d(F(x, y), F(a, b)) \le d(F(x, y), F(x, b)) + d(F(x, b), F(a, b)).\] For \(\epsilon > 0\), local equicontinuity bounds the first term by \(\epsilon / 2\) for \(y\) near \(b\) uniformly in \(x \in B_X(a, r)\). Continuity of \(x \mapsto F(x, b)\) bounds the second term by \(\epsilon / 2\) for \(x\) near \(a\).



Lemma B.5 (Urysohn’s Lemma for Metric Spaces) Let \((X, d)\) be a metric space and let \(A, B \subset X\) be disjoint closed subsets. Then \[f(x) = \frac{d_B(x)}{d_A(x) + d_B(x)} \tag{B.7}\] defines a continuous function \(f \colon X \to [0, 1]\) such that \(\left.f\right|_A \equiv 1\) and \(\left.f\right|_B \equiv 0\).


Proof. By Lemma B.1, \(d_A\) and \(d_B\) are continuous. Since \(A\) and \(B\) are closed and disjoint, \(d_A(x) + d_B(x) > 0\) for all \(x \in X\). Thus \(f\) is continuous as the quotient of continuous functions with a non-zero denominator. If \(x \in A\), \(d_A(x) = 0 \implies f(x) = 1\). If \(x \in B\), \(d_B(x) = 0 \implies f(x) = 0\).


Corollary B.2 If \(A, B \subset X\) are disjoint closed sets, there exist disjoint open sets \(U, V \subset X\) such that \(A \subset U\) and \(B \subset V\).


Proof. Let \(f\) be the Urysohn function from Lemma B.5. Set \(U = \{f > 1/2\}\) and \(V = \{f < 1/2\}\).

B.3 Completeness in Metric Spaces

Definition B.12 (Cauchy Sequences and Completeness)  

A sequence \(\{x_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) in \((X, d)\) is Cauchy if \(\lim_{m, n \to \infty} d(x_n, x_m) = 0\).
A metric space \((X, d)\) is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges to a limit in \(X\).



Exercise B.9 Let \((X, d)\) be a pseudo-metric space.

Show every convergent sequence is Cauchy.
If \(x_n \to x\) and \(y_n \to y\), show \(d(x_n, y_n) \to d(x, y)\).
If \(\{x_n\}, \{y_n\}\) are Cauchy, show \(\lim_{n \to \infty} d(x_n, y_n)\) exists in \([0, \infty)\).



Proof. 

If \(x_n \to x\), then \(d(x_n, x_m) \le d(x_n, x) + d(x, x_m) \to 0\) as \(n, m \to \infty\).
By Corollary B.1, \(|d(x_n, y_n) - d(x, y)| \le d(x_n, x) + d(y_n, y) \to 0\).
By Corollary B.1, \(|d(x_n, y_n) - d(x_m, y_m)| \le d(x_n, x_m) + d(y_n, y_m) \to 0\), so \(\{d(x_n, y_n)\} \subset \mathbb{R}\) is Cauchy and hence converges.



Exercise B.10 Let \((X, d)\) be complete and \(A \subset X\). Show \((A, \left.d\right|_{A \times A})\) is complete if and only if \(A\) is closed in \(X\).


Proof. 

\((\Rightarrow)\) Let \(\{x_n\} \subset A\) with \(x_n \to x \in X\). Then \(\{x_n\}\) is Cauchy in \(A\), so completeness of \(A\) implies \(x_n \to a \in A\). Uniqueness of limits gives \(x = a \in A\), so \(A\) is closed.
\((\Leftarrow)\) Let \(\{x_n\} \subset A\) be Cauchy. Since \(X\) is complete, \(x_n \to x \in X\). Since \(A\) is closed, \(x \in A\).



Exercise B.11 (Completion of a Metric Space) Given a metric space \((X, d)\), construct its complete completion \((\overline{X}, \overline{d})\) with an isometry \(i \colon X \to \overline{X}\) having dense image \(i(X) \subset \overline{X}\).


Proof. 

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be the set of Cauchy sequences in \(X\). For \(a, b \in \mathcal{C}\), define \(d_{\mathcal{C}}(a, b) = \lim_{n \to \infty} d(a_n, b_n)\). \(d_{\mathcal{C}}\) satisfies symmetry and triangle inequality.
Define \(a \sim b \iff d_{\mathcal{C}}(a, b) = 0\). This is an equivalence relation. Let \(\overline{X} = \mathcal{C} / \sim\) and \(\overline{d}(\overline{a}, \overline{b}) = d_{\mathcal{C}}(a, b)\). \((\overline{X}, \overline{d})\) is a valid metric space.
Map \(i(x) = \overline{(x, x, x, \dots)}\). \(i\) is isometric and \(i(X)\) is dense in \(\overline{X}\).
Completeness of \(\overline{X}\): Let \(\{\overline{a}^{(m)}\}\) be Cauchy in \(\overline{X}\). For each \(m\), pick \(b_m \in X\) such that \(\overline{d}(i(b_m), \overline{a}^{(m)}) < 1/m\). Then \(b = \{b_m\} \in \mathcal{C}\) and \(\overline{a}^{(m)} \to \overline{b}\).



Definition B.13 (Lipschitz Functions) Let \((X, d)\) be a pseudo-metric space and \(U \subset X\). A function \(f \colon U \to \mathbb{C}\) is \(\mathrm{Lip}\)-\(K\) on \(U\) (for \(K > 0\)) if \[|f(y) - f(x)| \le K d(x, y) \quad \forall x, y \in U. \tag{B.8}\]


Lemma B.6 (Extension of Lipschitz Functions) Let \(f \colon U \to \mathbb{C}\) be \(\mathrm{Lip}\)-\(K\) on \(U \subset X\). Then \(f\) extends uniquely to a \(\mathrm{Lip}\)-\(K\) function \(\hat{f} \colon \overline{U} \to \mathbb{C}\).


Proof. For \(x \in \overline{U}\), pick \(\{x_n\} \subset U\) with \(x_n \to x\). Since \(|f(x_n) - f(x_m)| \le K d(x_n, x_m)\), \(\{f(x_n)\} \subset \mathbb{C}\) is Cauchy. Define \(\hat{f}(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} f(x_n)\). This is independent of the sequence choice and satisfies \(|\hat{f}(x) - \hat{f}(y)| \le K d(x, y)\) for all \(x, y \in \overline{U}\).

title: Appendix B — Basic Metric and Topological Space Notions
text:
B.4 Sequential Compactness

Definition B.14 (Sequential Compactness) A metric space \((Y, \rho)\) is sequentially compact if every sequence \(\{y_n\} \subset Y\) contains a convergent subsequence.



B.4.1 A “Little” Tychonoff Theorem
Let \(\Lambda\) be a countable index set and let \((Y_\lambda, \rho_\lambda)\) be compact metric spaces for each \(\lambda \in \Lambda\). Given sequences \(\{y_\lambda(n) \colon n \in \mathbb{N}\} \subset Y_\lambda\), there exists an increasing sequence of indices \(\{n_k\}_{k=1}^{\infty} \subset \mathbb{N}\) such that \(\lim_{k \to \infty} y_\lambda(n_k)\) exists in \(Y_\lambda\) for all \(\lambda \in \Lambda\).



Proof. Without loss of generality, let \(\Lambda = \mathbb{N}\). Since \(Y_1\) is compact, there exists an infinite sequence of indices \(\Gamma_1 \subset \mathbb{N}\) such that \(\{y_1(n)\}_{n \in \Gamma_1}\) converges. Inductively, for \(\lambda \ge 2\), choose an infinite subset \(\Gamma_\lambda \subset \Gamma_{\lambda-1}\) such that \(\{y_\lambda(n)\}_{n \in \Gamma_\lambda}\) converges.
Construct the diagonal sequence \(n_k\) by: \[n_1 = \min \Gamma_1, \quad n_2 = \min (\Gamma_2 \cap (n_1, \infty)), \quad \dots, \quad n_k = \min (\Gamma_k \cap (n_{k-1}, \infty)).\] By construction, \(n_k \in \Gamma_\lambda\) for all \(k \ge \lambda\). Thus \(\{y_\lambda(n_k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty}\) is a tail-subsequence of \(\{y_\lambda(n)\}_{n \in \Gamma_\lambda}\), so \(\lim_{k \to \infty} y_\lambda(n_k)\) exists for every \(\lambda \in \Lambda\).

text:
B.5 Supplementary Remarks

B.5.1 Boundary and Closed Ball Warnings

Lemma B.7 Let \((X, \|\cdot\|)\) be a normed vector space with metric \(d(x, y) = \|x - y\|\). Then \[\overline{B_x(\epsilon)} = C_x(\epsilon) \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{bd}(B_x(\epsilon)) = \{y \in X \colon d(x, y) = \epsilon\}. \tag{B.9}\]


Proof. We show \(C_x(\epsilon) \subset \overline{B_x(\epsilon)}\). Let \(y \in C_x(\epsilon)\) and \(v = y - x\), so \(\|v\| \le \epsilon\). Define \(\alpha_n = 1 - 1/n\) and \(y_n = x + \alpha_n v\). Then \(d(x, y_n) = \alpha_n \|v\| < \epsilon\), so \(y_n \in B_x(\epsilon)\). Moreover, \(d(y, y_n) = (1 - \alpha_n) \|v\| \to 0\), showing \(y_n \to y \implies y \in \overline{B_x(\epsilon)}\).

text:
B.6 Chapter Exercises

Exercise B.12 (Fast Cauchy Criterion) Let \(\{x_n\} \subset X\) and \(\epsilon_n = d(x_n, x_{n+1})\). Show that for \(m > n\), \[d(x_n, x_m) \le \sum_{k=n}^{m-1} \epsilon_k \le \sum_{k=n}^{\infty} \epsilon_k. \tag{B.10}\] Conclude that if \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d(x_n, x_{n+1}) < \infty\), then \(\{x_n\}\) is Cauchy. Furthermore, show \(d(x, x_n) \le \sum_{k=n}^{\infty} \epsilon_k\) when \(x_n \to x\).


Proof. Repeated triangle inequality gives \(d(x_n, x_m) \le \sum_{k=n}^{m-1} d(x_k, x_{k+1}) \le \sum_{k=n}^{\infty} \epsilon_k\). If \(\sum \epsilon_k < \infty\), the tail sum goes to \(0\) as \(n \to \infty\), making \(\{x_n\}\) Cauchy. Taking \(m \to \infty\) in \(d(x_n, x_m) \le \sum_{k=n}^{\infty} \epsilon_k\) yields \(d(x_n, x) \le \sum_{k=n}^{\infty} \epsilon_k\).


Exercise B.13 (Completeness via Absolutely Summable Series) Show that \((X, d)\) is complete if and only if every sequence \(\{x_n\} \subset X\) satisfying \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d(x_n, x_{n+1}) < \infty\) converges in \(X\).


Proof. 

\((\Rightarrow)\) Follows directly from Exercise B.12.
\((\Leftarrow)\) Let \(\{x_n\}\) be Cauchy. Choose a subsequence \(n_1 < n_2 < \dots\) such that \(d(x_n, x_m) < 2^{-j}\) for all \(n, m \ge n_j\). Set \(y_j = x_{n_j}\). Then \(d(y_j, y_{j+1}) < 2^{-j}\), so \(\sum d(y_j, y_{j+1}) < \infty\). By hypothesis, \(y_j \to x\). Since a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges to the same limit, \(x_n \to x\).



Exercise B.14 Suppose \(f \colon [0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)\) is a \(C^2\) function with \(f(0) = 0, f' > 0, f'' \le 0\). Show that \(d(x, y) = f(\rho(x, y))\) is a metric for any metric space \((X, \rho)\). In particular, \(d(x, y) = \frac{\rho(x, y)}{1 + \rho(x, y)}\) is a metric.


Proof. Concavity (\(f'' \le 0\)) and \(f(0) = 0\) imply subadditivity: \(f(a + b) \le f(a) + f(b)\) for \(a, b \ge 0\). Thus \(d(x, z) = f(\rho(x, z)) \le f(\rho(x, y) + \rho(y, z)) \le f(\rho(x, y)) + f(\rho(y, z)) = d(x, y) + d(y, z)\).


Exercise B.15 Let \(\{(X_n, d_n)\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be metric spaces and \(X = \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} X_n\). For \(x, y \in X\), define \[d(x, y) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2^{-n} \frac{d_n(x(n), y(n))}{1 + d_n(x(n), y(n))}. \tag{B.11}\] Show that: 1. \((X, d)\) is a metric space. 2. \(x_k \to x\) in \((X, d)\) iff \(x_k(n) \to x(n)\) in \(X_n\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). 3. \((X, d)\) is complete if \((X_n, d_n)\) is complete for all \(n\).


Proof. 

Metric properties follow from Exercise B.14 and dominated convergence of the sum.
\((\Rightarrow)\) \(2^{-n} \frac{d_n(x_k(n), x(n))}{1 + d_n(x_k(n), x(n))} \le d(x_k, x) \to 0 \implies x_k(n) \to x(n)\). \((\Leftarrow)\) DCT on counting measure.
Componentwise Cauchy sequences converge componentwise; their product converges in \((X, d)\).



Exercise B.16 Let \(A \subset X\) be dense.

If \(F, G \colon X \to Y\) are continuous and \(\left.F\right|_A = \left.G\right|_A\), then \(F = G\) on \(X\).
If \(Y\) is complete and \(f \colon A \to Y\) is uniformly continuous, \(f\) extends uniquely to a continuous \(F \colon X \to Y\).
Give an example of continuous \(f \colon \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}\) that does not extend continuously to \(\mathbb{R}\).



Proof. 

Set \(C = \{x \in X \colon F(x) = G(x)\}\). \(C\) is closed (as preimage of diagonal under continuous map \((F, G)\)) and contains dense \(A\), so \(C = X\).
For \(x \in X\), pick \(\{a_n\} \subset A\) with \(a_n \to x\). Uniform continuity implies \(\{f(a_n)\}\) is Cauchy in \(Y\). Define \(F(x) = \lim f(a_n)\).
Let \(f(q) = 1/(q - \sqrt{2})\) for \(q \in \mathbb{Q}\). \(f\) is continuous on \(\mathbb{Q}\) but unbounded near \(\sqrt{2}\), so no continuous extension to \(\mathbb{R}\) exists.

title: 11  Lecture 5.1. Radon Measure
text:
11.3 Proof of Theorem 11.1

Uniqueness: If \(G: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is another non-decreasing right-continuous function satisfying \(\mu((a, b]) = G(b) - G(a)\), then for all \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\): \[G(b) - G(a) = F(b) - F(a) \implies G(b) = F(b) + [G(0) - F(0)].\]
Setting \(C = G(0) - F(0)\), we have \(G(x) = F(x) + C\), establishing uniqueness up to a constant \(C \in \mathbb{R}\).
Existence: Define \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) centered at \(0\) by: \[
F(x) :=
\begin{cases}   
\mu((0, x]), & x \ge 0, \\    
-\mu((x, 0]), & x < 0.    
\end{cases}
\tag{11.3}\]

Interval Measure Identity: For any \(a < b\), set additive subtraction yields \(\mu((a, b]) = F(b) - F(a)\).
Monotonicity: For \(x \le y\), set inclusion \((0, x] \subseteq (0, y]\) (or \((y, 0] \subseteq (x, 0]\) for negative values) together with monotonicity of \(\mu\) implies \(F(x) \le F(y)\).
Right-Continuity: Fix \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) and let \(x_n \downarrow x\) with \(x_n > x\). Then \((x, x_1] \setminus (x_n, x_1] = (x, x_n] \downarrow \emptyset\). By continuity of measure from above for finite measure sets: \[
F(x_n) - F(x) = \mu((x, x_n]) \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0.
\]
Thus, \(F(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} F(x_n)\), proving right-continuity.


By the Measure Extension Theorem, \(\mu\) is the unique extension of \(\mu_F\) to \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\).

title: 11  Lecture 5.1. Radon Measure
text:
11.5 Proof of Proposition 11.1

(1) \(\Rightarrow\) (2): Let \(A_n \uparrow A \in \mathcal{A}\). Set \(B_1 = A_1\) and \(B_n = A_n \setminus A_{n-1} \in \mathcal{A}\) for \(n \ge 2\). The sequence \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) is pairwise disjoint with \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n = A\) and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^N B_n = A_N\). By countable additivity: \[
\mu(A) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=1}^N \mu(B_n) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \mu(A_N).
\]
(2) \(\Rightarrow\) (1): Let \(\{B_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathcal{A}\) be pairwise disjoint with \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n = B \in \mathcal{A}\). Define \(A_N := \bigcup_{n=1}^N B_n \in \mathcal{A}\). Then \(A_N \uparrow B\). Applying (2): \[
\mu(B) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \mu(A_N) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=1}^N \mu(B_n) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(B_n).
\]
Equivalence of (3)–(4) for Finite Measures: Follows directly by complementary set subtraction: \(\mu(B \setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\) whenever \(A \subseteq B\) and \(\mu(B) < \infty\).

title: 12  Lecture 5.2: Lebesgue Measure
text:
12.2 Translation Invariance
For any translation \(\tau \in \mathbb{R}\) and interval \(J = (a, b]\), we have \(J + \tau = (a + \tau, b + \tau]\), so: \[
\lambda(J + \tau) = (b + \tau) - (a + \tau) = b - a = \lambda(J).
\tag{12.2}\] By the extension and uniqueness theorems, this implies:

\(\lambda(A + \tau) = \lambda(A)\) for all \(A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\).
\(\lambda^*(E + \tau) = \lambda^*(E)\) for all arbitrary subsets \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}\).

title: 13  Lecture 6.1: Random Variables Motivation
text:
Example 13.1 Coin Tossing. Consider tossing a fair coin \(N\) times. The individual outcomes are sequences of heads (\(H\)) and tails (\(T\)), such as \(HTHH\). We might be interested in a summary numerical measurement, such as \(X = \text{\# heads}\). In this specific outcome, \(X = 3\). We can then consider events defined by conditions on \(X\), such as \(\{X \le 3\}\) or \(\{X \ge 2\}\).


Example 13.2 Dart Board. Consider throwing a dart at a circular dartboard of radius \(R\). The point where the dart lands can be represented in polar coordinates as \((r, \theta)\). A natural summary quantity is \(R\), the distance from the center. An outcome might be \((r, \theta) = \left(0.15, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) (or \((0.15, 0)\)), yielding \(R = 0.15\). We are then interested in events such as \(\{R \le 0.25\}\).






Outcomes are elements \(\omega \in \Omega\).
Events are measurable subsets of \(\Omega\), i.e., elements of \(\mathcal{F}\).



The state space \(S\) could be \(\mathbb{C}\).
\(S\) is usually \(\mathbb{R}\).
If \(S = \mathbb{R}^d\), we usually call \(X\) a random vector.


Remark 13.1 (Random Variable versus Random Function). The term “random variable” is a misnomer. A random variable is not a variable in the sense of algebra, but rather a function. It is a function that takes an outcome \(\omega \in \Omega\) and returns a real number \(X(\omega) \in \mathbb{R}\). The “random” part refers to the fact that the outcome \(\omega\) is random, and thus \(X(\omega)\) is also random. Historically, we should perhaps call them “random functions,” but the very old “variable” terminology has stuck since its usage by Laplace in the early 19th century.

title: 23  Lecture 11.1: Radon-Nikodym
text:
23.4 Takeaways

Absolute continuity is the right condition for densities. A measure \(
u\) admits a non-negative measurable density with respect to \(\mu\) if and only if \(
u \ll \mu\): every \(\mu\)-null set must also be \(
u\)-null. This is both necessary (integrating over a null set gives zero) and, given \(\sigma\)-finiteness, sufficient.
The Radon-Nikodym Theorem requires \(\sigma\)-finiteness. Without this hypothesis on both \(\mu\) and \(
u\), the density may fail to exist or fail to be unique \(\mu\)-a.e. The theorem guarantees both existence and \(\mu\)-a.e. uniqueness of \(ho = d
u/d\mu\) under \(\sigma\)-finiteness.
The chain rule holds for Radon-Nikodym derivatives. If \(
u \ll \mu \ll \lambda\) are \(\sigma\)-finite, then \(
u \ll \lambda\) and \( rac{d
u}{d\lambda} =  rac{d
u}{d\mu}\cdot rac{d\mu}{d\lambda}\) \(\lambda\)-a.e. This mirrors the classical chain rule for derivatives.
The Lebesgue Decomposition is unique and exhaustive. Every \(\sigma\)-finite \(
u\) splits uniquely as \(
u = 
u_a + 
u_s\) with \(
u_a \ll \mu\) and \(
u_s \perp \mu\). On \((\mathbb{R}^d, \lambda)\) the singular part refines further into a pure-point part \(
u_{pp}\) (countable weighted Diracs) and a singular-continuous part \(
u_{sc}\) (no atoms, yet supported on a Lebesgue-null set).
Singular-continuous measures are genuinely exotic. The Devil’s Staircase shows that a measure can be continuous (no atoms) while being entirely supported on a Lebesgue-null set (the Cantor set). Such measures arise naturally in fractal geometry and as limiting distributions in certain probabilistic constructions.
The ball-ratio formula is specific to \(\mu = \lambda\). The geometric interpretation \( rac{d
u}{d\lambda}(x) = \lim_{\epsilon\downarrow 0} rac{
u(B_\epsilon(x))}{\lambda(B_\epsilon(x))}\) is the Lebesgue Differentiation Theorem, valid \(\lambda\)-a.e. when \(
u\ll\lambda\). It does not extend to arbitrary reference measures without additional structure (e.g., doubling conditions).

title: 29  Lecture 14.1: Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem
section: 29.6 Step 1: \(\mathbb{H}\) Is an Algebra of Functions
text:
29.6 Step 1: \(\mathbb{H}\) Is an Algebra of Functions
\(\mathbb{H}\) is already a vector space containing \(1\); we must show it is closed under pointwise multiplication. For any \(f \in \mathbb{H}\), define: \[
\mathbb{H}^f \triangleq \{ g \in \mathbb{H} \mid f \cdot g \in \mathbb{H} \}
\tag{29.6}\]

\(\mathbb{H}^f \subseteq \mathbb{H}\) is a linear subspace.
\(\mathbb{H}^f\) is closed under bounded convergence: if \(g_n \in \mathbb{H}^f\) with \(|g_n| \le M\) and \(g_n \to g\), then \(f \cdot g_n \to f \cdot g\) boundedly, so \(f \cdot g \in \mathbb{H} \implies g \in \mathbb{H}^f\).
If \(f \in \mathbb{M}\), then \(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}^f\) (since \(\mathbb{M}\) is a multiplicative system). Thus \(\mathbb{H}(\mathbb{M}) \subseteq \mathbb{H}^f \subseteq \mathbb{H}\), which implies \(\mathbb{H}^f = \mathbb{H}\) for all \(f \in \mathbb{M}\).
Repeating the argument for an arbitrary \(f \in \mathbb{H}\), we conclude \(\mathbb{H}^f = \mathbb{H}\) for all \(f \in \mathbb{H}\). Hence \(\mathbb{H}\) is an algebra.

title: 38  Lecture 18.1: Strong Law of Large Numbers (I)
text:
38.5 Takeaways

Two roads beyond WLLN. The Chebyshev-based WLLN for uncorrelated \(L^2\) sequences only yields convergence in probability. Reaching the Strong Law requires either weakening the moment assumption to \(L^1\), strengthening the mode of convergence to almost sure, or both — this lecture lays the groundwork for the \(L^1\) i.i.d. case proved in full in 19-1-SLLN2.qmd.
Truncation needs independence. Truncating \(X\) at level \(M\) preserves integrability and boundedness for free, but destroys uncorrelatedness in general. This is why the SLLN program (unlike the \(L^2\)-WLLN) is built on full independence rather than mere uncorrelatedness.
Tail equivalence lets us swap sequences. Two sequences that agree eventually (in the summable-probability sense of Definition 38.1) have identical almost-sure limits of their scaled partial sums (Proposition 38.1), via Borel-Cantelli. This is the key device that lets us replace an arbitrary \(L^1\) sequence with a more tractable truncated one without changing the a.s. limit of \(S_n/n\).
The \(L^1\) tail bound is the engine. Lemma 38.1 converts a single moment bound \(E[|X|]<\infty\) into summability of tail probabilities, which is exactly the hypothesis Borel-Cantelli needs. Applied to an i.i.d. \(L^1\) sequence, it shows \(X_n\) is tail equivalent to its self-truncation \(X_n \mathbf{1}_{\{|X_n|\le n\}}\) (Corollary 38.1) — so proving the SLLN for the bounded-in-\(n\) truncated sequence suffices for the original one.
Infinite mean still has a strong law. When only \(E[X_n^-]<\infty\) but \(E[X_n]=+\infty\), truncating from above at a finite level \(M\) and letting \(M\to\infty\) via monotone convergence shows \(S_n/n \to +\infty\) a.s. (Corollary 38.2), extending the SLLN philosophy beyond the integrable case.
Net effect: these reduction tools (tail equivalence + truncation) turn the general \(L^1\) Strong Law into a problem about uniformly truncated, tail-equivalent sequences — precisely the setup exploited in the next lecture’s full proof of Kolmogorov’s SLLN.
crumbs: 38  Lecture 18.1: Strong Law of Large Numbers (I)

title: 39  Lecture 18.2: Kolmogorov Convergence Criterion
text:
39.4 Takeaways

Uncorrelated is enough for \(L^2\), but not for a.s. Proposition 39.1 shows that summable variances alone give \(L^2\) convergence of the centered series via completeness of \(L^2\) (Cauchy criterion). Getting almost sure convergence out of the same hypothesis requires the stronger structure of independence, packaged through Kolmogorov’s Maximal Inequality.
The Maximal Inequality controls the whole path, not just the endpoint. Unlike Chebyshev’s inequality, which bounds \(P(|S_n|\ge\epsilon)\), Theorem 39.1 bounds the probability that the running maximum \(S_n^* = \max_{j\le n}|S_j|\) ever exceeds \(\epsilon\), at the same variance cost \(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2}\sum \operatorname{Var}(Y_j)\). The stopping-time decomposition at \(\tau\) is what upgrades a single-time bound into a uniform, path-wise one.
Maximal inequality \(\Rightarrow\) Cauchy tails \(\Rightarrow\) a.s. convergence. Theorem 39.2 chains the maximal inequality over shrinking tails \((m,n]\to(m,\infty)\) to show the oscillation \(R_m = \sup_{j,k\ge m}|S_j - S_k|\) vanishes in probability, hence a.s.; this is exactly the Cauchy criterion for real sequences applied pathwise.
Centering can be added back for free. Since the mean series \(\sum \mathbb{E}[Y_n]\) is a deterministic (non-random) sequence, once it converges, adding it back to the a.s./\(L^2\)-convergent centered series preserves both modes of convergence — so the criterion applies equally to \(\sum Y_n\) itself whenever the means don’t obstruct convergence.
Random harmonic series is the paradigmatic example. \(\sum \frac{X_n}{n}\) for i.i.d. Rademacher \(X_n\) has \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_n) = 1/n^2\), summable, and zero mean, so the criterion immediately gives almost sure convergence — a result that fails for the ordinary (non-random sign) harmonic series, highlighting how independence and cancellation, not absolute summability, drive a.s. convergence here.
Looking ahead: this variance-summability criterion is one half of the machinery (together with truncation from 18-1-SLLN1.qmd) needed to prove the full Kolmogorov Strong Law of Large Numbers in 19-1-SLLN2.qmd.

title: 40  Lecture 19.1: Strong Law of Large Numbers (II)
text:
40.5 Takeaways

Kronecker’s Lemma is the analytic engine, not a probability result. It is a purely deterministic statement about real sequences: if a weighted series \(\sum x_k/b_k\) converges, the Cesàro-type average \(\frac{1}{b_n}\sum_{k=1}^n x_k\) vanishes. Its power in probability comes from applying it pathwise, i.e., separately to almost every \(\omega\) after a.s. convergence of a random series has been established some other way (typically via Kolmogorov’s Convergence Criterion).
The two-step recipe: variance-summability \(\to\) Kronecker. Every SLLN-type result in this lecture (thm-kolmogorov-slln-full, thm-l2-slln-general) follows the same pattern: (1) truncate/normalize so that \(\sum \operatorname{Var}(X_n/b_n) < \infty\), invoke Kolmogorov’s Convergence Criterion to get a.s. convergence of the centered weighted series, then (2) apply Kronecker’s Lemma to convert that series convergence into convergence of the Cesàro-type average \(S_n/b_n\).
Truncation tail bounds are delicate. Converting a second-moment tail sum like \(\sum_{n\ge x} n^{-2}\) into a bound linear in \(x\) requires care with the constants — a naive integral shift can produce a bound that fails on part of the range (as seen with the constant \(2\) vs. \(4\) in thm-kolmogorov-slln-full’s proof). Always verify such min-type bounds hold on the entire range, not just asymptotically.
Normalization rate trades off against moment assumptions. The comparison table makes explicit the tradeoff: the classical SLLN needs only \(L^1\) with \(b_n=n\); weaker moments (\(L^p\), \(p\in(1,2)\)) force a slower-growing normalization \(b_n = n^{1/p}\) (Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund); while retaining \(L^2\) but allowing heterogeneity lets \(b_n\) grow anywhere from just above \(\sqrt n\) (with a log-power correction) to \(n^{1/2+p}\), so long as \(\sum 1/b_n^2 < \infty\).
The Law of the Iterated Logarithm is the sharp boundary. Where the SLLN only tells us \(S_n/b_n \to 0\), the LIL identifies the exact almost-sure growth envelope \(b_n = \sqrt{2s^2 n \log\log n}\) at which \(\limsup (S_n-n\alpha)/b_n = 1\) — showing that no normalization growing strictly slower than \(\sqrt{n\log\log n}\) can force a.s. convergence to \(0\) for general finite-variance i.i.d. sequences.
Net effect: together with the truncation and tail-equivalence tools from 18-1-SLLN1.qmd and the Maximal Inequality from 18-2-Kolmogorov-Convergence-Criterion.qmd, this lecture completes the full proof of Kolmogorov’s Strong Law of Large Numbers and situates it within a broader family of normalization-rate results.

title: 41  Lecture 19.2: Renewal Theory
text:
41.5 Takeaways

SLLN is the frequentist interpretation’s mathematical backbone. Applying SLLN to indicator variables \(\mathbf{1}_A^{(n)}\) shows that the long-run relative frequency of an event converges almost surely to its probability — turning “probability as long-run frequency” from an informal heuristic into a theorem.
Renewal counts are the functional inverse of arrival times. \(N_t\) and \(S_n\) are related by the sandwich \(S_{N_t} \le t < S_{N_t+1}\), and this single inequality is the mechanical device that converts the SLLN statement about \(S_n/n\) (indexed by \(n\)) into a statement about \(N_t/t\) (indexed by \(t\)) — the Elementary Renewal Theorem is essentially SLLN viewed through the “inverse” of the arrival-time process.
Composition with a random time index is pathwise, not probabilistic. The recurring technique — “if \(a_n \to L\) a.s. and \(N_t \to \infty\) a.s., then \(a_{N_t} \to L\) a.s.” — is just ordinary real-sequence composition applied to almost every fixed \(\omega\) separately. It requires no independence between the index process \(N_t\) and the sequence \(a_n\), which is what lets it apply even when \(N_t\) is built from both \(\{X_n\}\) and \(\{Y_n\}\) in the alternating renewal setting.
Alternating renewal processes reduce to a ratio of means. The long-run operational fraction \(\mathbb{E}[X_1]/(\mathbb{E}[X_1]+\mathbb{E}[Y_1])\) falls out of two applications of the same machinery: the Elementary Renewal Theorem applied to the combined cycle length \(X_n+Y_n\) (for the rate \(N_t/t\)), and SLLN applied to \(\{X_n\}\) alone (for the average uptime per cycle) — the partial/incomplete final cycle contributes nothing in the limit, by Lemma 41.1.
The \(L^1\) tail lemma keeps reappearing. Lemma 41.1 is proved by the same tail-sum-plus-Borel-Cantelli pattern used throughout the SLLN lectures (18-1-SLLN1.qmd, 19-1-SLLN2.qmd): bound \(\sum_n P(|X_n|/n \ge \epsilon)\) using Lemma 38.1, then upgrade “eventually small” to “convergent to \(0\)” via a countable intersection over \(\epsilon_k = 1/k\).
Net effect: renewal theory is a direct application area for the Strong Law machinery built in Lectures 18–19, translating discrete-index a.s. convergence results into continuous-time (in \(t\)) a.s. convergence statements about counting and occupation-time processes.

title: 43  Lecture 20.2: Cramer’s LDP-Part II
section: 43.3 Existence and Uniqueness of the Maximizer \(t_\epsilon\)
text:
43.3 Existence and Uniqueness of the Maximizer \(t_\epsilon\)
The whole proof hinges on the existence of a point at which the supremum defining \(\Psi^*(\epsilon)\) is attained. This is not automatic — it is exactly where the hypothesis \(\epsilon < b\) enters — so we prove it.

Lemma 43.1 (Attainment of the Legendre Supremum) Assume \(\dot X_1\) is exponentially integrable, non-degenerate, and \(\mathbb{E}[\dot X_1] = 0\). For every \(\epsilon\) with \(0 < \epsilon < b = \operatorname*{ess\,sup}\dot X_1\) there exists a unique \(t_\epsilon \in \mathbb{R}\) with \[
\Psi'(t_\epsilon) = \epsilon ,
\] it satisfies \(t_\epsilon > 0\), and the supremum is attained there: \[
\Psi^*(\epsilon) = \sup_{t \ge 0}\{\epsilon t - \Psi(t)\} = \epsilon t_\epsilon - \Psi(t_\epsilon) < \infty .
\]


Proof. By Part I, \(\Psi\) is real-analytic on \(\mathbb{R}\) and, by non-degeneracy, strictly convex; hence \(\Psi'\) is continuous and strictly increasing. Moreover \(\Psi(0) = 0\) and \(\Psi'(0) = \mathbb{E}[\dot X_1] = 0\).
Claim: \(\Psi'(t) \uparrow b\) as \(t \to +\infty\).
Upper bound. If \(b < \infty\) then \(\dot X_1 \le b\) a.s., so \(\dot X_1 e^{t\dot X_1} \le b\,e^{t\dot X_1}\) pointwise a.s. and \[
\Psi'(t) = \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\dot X_1 e^{t\dot X_1}\right]}{M(t)} \le \frac{b\,M(t)}{M(t)} = b .
\] If \(b = \infty\) the bound is vacuous.
Lower bound. First, \(\frac{1}{t}\Psi(t) \to b\) as \(t \to +\infty\). Indeed, for any \(c < b\) we have \(p_c := \mathbb{P}(\dot X_1 > c) > 0\) by definition of the essential supremum, so \[
M(t) \ge \mathbb{E}\left[e^{t\dot X_1}\mathbb{I}_{\{\dot X_1 > c\}}\right] \ge e^{tc} p_c
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{\Psi(t)}{t} \ge c + \frac{\log p_c}{t} \xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{} c ,
\] and letting \(c \uparrow b\) gives \(\liminf_{t\to\infty}\Psi(t)/t \ge b\); conversely \(M(t) \le e^{tb}\) when \(b<\infty\), so \(\Psi(t)/t \le b\). Second, convexity of \(\Psi\) together with \(\Psi(0)=0\) gives the tangent-line inequality \(0 = \Psi(0) \ge \Psi(t) + \Psi'(t)(0-t)\), i.e. \[
\Psi'(t) \ge \frac{\Psi(t)}{t}\qquad (t > 0).
\] Combining, \(\liminf_{t\to\infty}\Psi'(t) \ge b\), which with the upper bound proves the claim.
Conclusion. \(\Psi'\) is a continuous, strictly increasing map with \(\Psi'(0) = 0\) and \(\sup_{t>0}\Psi'(t) = b\). Since \(0 < \epsilon < b\), the intermediate value theorem supplies a point \(t_\epsilon > 0\) with \(\Psi'(t_\epsilon) = \epsilon\), and strict monotonicity makes it unique. Finally, \(g(t) := \epsilon t - \Psi(t)\) is concave and differentiable with \(g'(t_\epsilon) = \epsilon - \Psi'(t_\epsilon) = 0\); a stationary point of a concave function is a global maximum, so \(\Psi^*(\epsilon) = g(t_\epsilon) = \epsilon t_\epsilon - \Psi(t_\epsilon)\), which is finite. \(\blacksquare\)

title: 45  Lecture 21.2: Law of Rare Events
text:
45.6 Takeaways

The Law of Rare Events is a non-asymptotic theorem, not a limit theorem.
Theorem 45.1 states that for any \(n\) and any \(p_1, \dots, p_n \in [0,1]\), the sum of independent Bernoulli variables satisfies \(d_{\text{TV}}(S_n, N) \le \sum_{j=1}^n p_j^2\) where \(N \sim \text{Poisson}(\sum_j p_j)\). There is no hypothesis that the \(p_j\) be small, equal, or that \(n \to \infty\): the bound is an explicit error estimate valid at every fixed \(n\), which is exactly what makes it usable in applications. The classical statement “Binomial \(\to\) Poisson” is the corollary Corollary 45.1 obtained by specializing to \(p_j = \lambda/n\), giving the quantitative rate \(\lambda^2/n\).
The bound is driven by the exact Bernoulli–Poisson distance \(p(1 - e^{-p})\).
Both proofs reduce to the single-coordinate computation \(d_{\text{TV}}(\text{Bernoulli}(p), \text{Poisson}(p)) = p(1 - e^{-p})\) from Lecture 21.1, followed by the elementary bound \(1 - e^{-p} \le p\). The quadratic term \(p_j^2\) is therefore a relaxation: the sharper conclusion \(d_{\text{TV}}(S_n, N) \le \sum_{j=1}^n p_j(1 - e^{-p_j})\) holds and is strictly better whenever the \(p_j\) are not negligible.
Two proof strategies, one estimate: convolution versus coupling.
The first proof is analytic: Lemma 45.1 says total variation is subadditive under convolution, so the error accumulates one coordinate at a time. The second is probabilistic: it builds all \(2n\) variables from \(n\) i.i.d. uniforms via inverse-CDF sampling and bounds the disagreement probability directly. Both routes produce the same sum \(\sum_j p_j(1 - e^{-p_j})\), since both localize the discrepancy to individual coordinates — the convolution bound is, in effect, the coupling argument done at the level of measures.
Coupling converts a distance between measures into a probability of disagreement.
Definition 45.1 fixes the marginals \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) while leaving the dependence structure free, and Lemma 45.2 gives \(d_{\text{TV}}(\mu, \nu) \le \mathbb{P}(X \ne Y)\) for every such choice. The strategy is therefore to design a coupling that makes \(X\) and \(Y\) agree as often as possible: any coupling yields a valid upper bound, and a clever one yields a sharp bound. Here the design step is to drive \(Z_j\) and \(M_j\) from the same uniform \(U_j\), which forces them to agree except on the two small intervals \((1 - p_j, e^{-p_j}]\) and \((\alpha_j(1), 1]\).
The union bound is what makes the error additive.
The passage from the single-coordinate estimate to the global one rests on \(\{T \ne M\} \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^n \{Z_j \ne M_j\}\): the two sums can only differ if some coordinate pair differs. This is why the total error is a sum of \(n\) per-coordinate errors, and why the bound degrades linearly in \(n\) while each term is quadratic in \(p_j\) — a trade-off that is favorable precisely in the “rare events” regime where \(\max_j p_j\) is small relative to \(1/\sqrt{n}\).
Total variation and Wasserstein measure different things.
\(d_{\text{TV}}\) asks whether \(X\) and \(Y\) differ; \(W_p\) of Definition 45.2 asks how far apart they are, and so is sensitive to the geometry of the state space. Neither topology dominates the other on \(\text{Prob}_p(\mathbb{R}^d)\): \(\delta_{1/n} \to \delta_0\) in \(W_p\) but not in \(d_{\text{TV}}\), while \((1 - \tfrac1n)\delta_0 + \tfrac1n \delta_{n^2} \to \delta_0\) in \(d_{\text{TV}}\) but not in \(W_p\). On uniformly bounded supports the comparison \(W_p \le D \cdot d_{\text{TV}}^{1/p}\) does hold. Total variation is the right tool here because Bernoulli and Poisson laws live on the common discrete space \(\mathbb{N}_0\), where “differ” is the natural unit of error.
