title: 34  Lecture 16.1: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (I)
text:
Definition 34.1 Let \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be a measurable space and let \(X_n : (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P) \to (S, \mathcal{B})\), \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), be measurable maps defined on a common probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), with laws (pushforward measures) \(\mu_{X_n} \triangleq P \circ X_n^{-1}\). The sequence \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) is independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) if:

Independence. \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) is independent in the sense of Definition 33.1; explicitly, for every finite subfamily \(X_{n_1}, \dots, X_{n_k}\) with \(n_1 < \dots < n_k\) and all \(B_1, \dots, B_k \in \mathcal{B}\), \[
P\Bigl( \bigcap_{i=1}^k \{ X_{n_i} \in B_i \} \Bigr) = \prod_{i=1}^k P(X_{n_i} \in B_i).
\]
Identical distribution. There is a single probability measure \(\mu\) on \((S, \mathcal{B})\) with \(\mu_{X_n} = \mu\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).

Independence of an infinite family is thus a condition on finite subfamilies only. Unless stated otherwise we take \((S, \mathcal{B}) = (\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\); nothing in the definition requires this choice.



Proposition 34.1 (Existence and Uniqueness of Finite Product Measures) Let \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1, \mu_1), \dots, (S_N, \mathcal{B}_N, \mu_N)\) be \(\sigma\)-finite measure spaces with \(N \ge 2\), and set \(S \triangleq \prod_{n=1}^N S_n\). Then, under the canonical bijection \(S \cong \bigl( \prod_{n=1}^{N-1} S_n \bigr) \times S_N\), \[
\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n = \Bigl( \bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mathcal{B}_n \Bigr) \otimes \mathcal{B}_N ,
\tag{34.1}\] and there exists a unique measure \(\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n\) on \(\bigl( S, \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n \bigr)\) satisfying \[
\Bigl( \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n \Bigr)(B_1 \times \dots \times B_N) = \prod_{n=1}^N \mu_n(B_n) \quad \forall\, B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n .
\tag{34.2}\] This measure is \(\sigma\)-finite, and it is a probability measure whenever every \(\mu_n\) is.


Proof (Proof of Proposition 34.1). Associativity of the product \(\sigma\)-algebra (Equation 34.1). Write \(\mathcal{C} \triangleq \bigl( \bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mathcal{B}_n \bigr) \otimes \mathcal{B}_N\).
(\(\subseteq\)) Every \(N\)-fold rectangle satisfies \(B_1 \times \dots \times B_N = (B_1 \times \dots \times B_{N-1}) \times B_N\), a two-factor rectangle whose first side lies in \(\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mathcal{B}_n\). Hence all \(N\)-fold rectangles lie in \(\mathcal{C}\), and since \(\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n\) is generated by these rectangles (Definition 30.1), \(\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n \subseteq \mathcal{C}\).
(\(\supseteq\)) By Lemma 30.1 each coordinate projection \(\pi_n : S \to S_n\) is \(\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n\)-measurable, so by Lemma 30.3 the map \(\pi_{1:N-1} \triangleq (\pi_1, \dots, \pi_{N-1}) : S \to \prod_{n=1}^{N-1} S_n\) is \(\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n \,/\, \bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mathcal{B}_n\)-measurable. Under the canonical bijection \(S \cong \bigl( \prod_{n=1}^{N-1} S_n \bigr) \times S_N\) the two coordinate projections of the two-factor product are exactly \(\pi_{1:N-1}\) and \(\pi_N\), so Lemma 30.2 applied with \(d = 2\) gives \[
\mathcal{C} = \sigma\bigl( \{ \pi_{1:N-1}^{-1}(A) \mid A \in \textstyle\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mathcal{B}_n \} \cup \{ \pi_N^{-1}(B_N) \mid B_N \in \mathcal{B}_N \} \bigr).
\] Each generator lies in \(\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n\): the sets \(\pi_{1:N-1}^{-1}(A)\) by the measurability of \(\pi_{1:N-1}\) just established, and the sets \(\pi_N^{-1}(B_N)\) by Lemma 30.1. Hence \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n\).
Existence. Induct on \(N\). For \(N = 2\) the assertion is Corollary 30.1, which also shows that the product of two \(\sigma\)-finite measures is \(\sigma\)-finite. For \(N > 2\), let \(\nu \triangleq \bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mu_n\) be the (\(\sigma\)-finite) measure supplied by the induction hypothesis and define \[
\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n \triangleq \nu \otimes \mu_N ,
\] which is a measure on \(\bigl( \bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mathcal{B}_n \bigr) \otimes \mathcal{B}_N = \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n\) by Equation 34.1, and is \(\sigma\)-finite by Corollary 30.1. On rectangles, \[
(\nu \otimes \mu_N)(B_1 \times \dots \times B_N) = \nu(B_1 \times \dots \times B_{N-1}) \, \mu_N(B_N) = \prod_{n=1}^N \mu_n(B_n),
\] using the induction hypothesis. If every \(\mu_n\) is a probability measure, then taking \(B_n = S_n\) gives \(\bigl( \bigotimes_n \mu_n \bigr)(S) = \prod_n \mu_n(S_n) = 1\).
Uniqueness. The collection \(\mathcal{R} \triangleq \bigl\{ \prod_{n=1}^N B_n \mid B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n \bigr\}\) is a \(\pi\)-system, since \(\prod_n B_n \cap \prod_n B_n' = \prod_n (B_n \cap B_n')\), and \(\sigma(\mathcal{R}) = \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n\) by Definition 30.1. By \(\sigma\)-finiteness choose, for each \(n\), an increasing sequence \(A^{(n)}_m \nearrow S_n\) with \(\mu_n(A^{(n)}_m) < \infty\) (replace a given countable cover by the unions of its initial segments, which still have finite measure by finite subadditivity). Put \[
R_m \triangleq \prod_{n=1}^N A^{(n)}_m \in \mathcal{R} .
\] Then \(R_m \nearrow S\) and any measure \(\kappa\) on \(\bigotimes_{n=1}^N\mathcal{B}_n\) satisfying Equation 34.2 has \(\kappa(R_m) = \prod_n \mu_n(A^{(n)}_m) < \infty\). Thus \(\mathcal{R}\) contains an increasing sequence of sets exhausting \(S\) that has finite measure under every such \(\kappa\). Consequently, if \(\kappa\) and \(\kappa'\) both satisfy Equation 34.2 then they agree on \(\mathcal{R}\) and, exactly as in the uniqueness step of Corollary 30.1 (Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem applied to the \(\lambda\)-system \(\{E \mid \kappa(E \cap R_m) = \kappa'(E \cap R_m)\}\) for each fixed \(m\), followed by continuity from below as \(m \to \infty\)), \(\kappa = \kappa'\) on \(\sigma(\mathcal{R}) = \bigotimes_{n=1}^N\mathcal{B}_n\). Taking \(\kappa = \bigotimes_n \mu_n\) also shows this measure is \(\sigma\)-finite. In the probability case, where \(S \in \mathcal{R}\) has measure \(1\), the conclusion is also immediate from Lemma 32.1.



\(X_n\) has a particular distribution \(\mu_n\), and
\(X_1,\ldots,X_N\) are independent.



Lemma 34.1 Let \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1), \dots, (S_N, \mathcal{B}_N)\) be measurable spaces and \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_N\) be probability measures on them. Define the product space: \[
\Omega \triangleq \prod_{n=1}^N S_n, \quad \mathcal{F} \triangleq \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n, \quad P \triangleq \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n
\tag{34.3}\] where \(P\) is the product measure of Proposition 34.1. Then \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) is a probability space, and the canonical projections \[
X_n(\omega) \triangleq \pi_n(\omega) = x_n, \qquad \omega = (x_1, \dots, x_N) \in \Omega,
\] are independent random variables with marginal laws \(\mu_{X_n} = \mu_n\) for \(n = 1, \dots, N\).


Proof (Proof of Lemma 34.1). Probability space. By Proposition 34.1 the product measure \(P\) exists, is unique, and satisfies \(P(\Omega) = \prod_{n=1}^N \mu_n(S_n) = 1\), so \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) is a probability space and the maps \(X_n\) below are genuine random variables.
Measurability. Each projection \(X_n = \pi_n : \Omega \to S_n\) is \((\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}_n)\)-measurable by Lemma 30.1 applied to the product \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F} = \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n\).
Joint distribution on rectangles. For any \(B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n\), the simultaneous event is the product rectangle: \[
\{X_1 \in B_1, \dots, X_N \in B_N\} = \bigcap_{n=1}^N \pi_n^{-1}(B_n) = B_1 \times \dots \times B_N.
\] Applying \(P = \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n\) and using the defining property Equation 34.2 of the product measure on rectangles: \[
\begin{aligned}
P(X_1 \in B_1, \dots, X_N \in B_N) &= \left(\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n\right)\!(B_1 \times \dots \times B_N) \\
&= \prod_{n=1}^N \mu_n(B_n).
\end{aligned}
\tag{34.4}\]
Marginal laws. Fix \(n \in \{1,\dots,N\}\) and \(B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n\). Setting \(B_j = S_j\) for all \(j \neq n\) in Equation 34.4, and using \(\mu_j(S_j) = 1\) (since each \(\mu_j\) is a probability measure): \[
P(X_n \in B_n) = \mu_n(B_n) \cdot \prod_{j \neq n} \mu_j(S_j) = \mu_n(B_n) \cdot \prod_{j \neq n} 1 = \mu_n(B_n).
\] Hence \(\mu_{X_n} = \mu_n\).
Independence. Substituting \(P(X_n \in B_n) = \mu_n(B_n)\) into Equation 34.4 gives: \[
P(X_1 \in B_1, \dots, X_N \in B_N) = \prod_{n=1}^N P(X_n \in B_n) \quad \forall\, B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n.
\] For any sub-family \(J \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) and \(B_j \in \mathcal{B}_j\) (\(j \in J\)), set \(B_j = S_j\) for \(j \notin J\); then \(\prod_{j \notin J} P(X_j \in S_j) = 1\), giving \(P\bigl(\bigcap_{j \in J}\{X_j \in B_j\}\bigr) = \prod_{j \in J} P(X_j \in B_j)\). This reduction is needed because Definition 33.1 demands the product rule for every finite subfamily, not merely for the full family. Since it holds for all non-empty \(J\) and all \(B_j \in \mathcal{B}_j\), the random variables \(X_1, \dots, X_N\) are independent by Definition 33.1.



Example 34.1 (Repeated coin tosses) Suppose we want to construct three independent coin tosses, where the probability of heads is \(p\). For each toss, let \[
S_n=\{H,T\}, \qquad \mathcal B_n=2^{S_n},
\] and define the probability measure \(\mu_n(\{H\})=p\) and \(\mu_n(\{T\})=1-p\). The lemma tells us to construct \[
\Omega = \{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}.
\] Thus, an outcome is something like \(\omega=(H,T,H)\). Define the coordinate random variables \[
X_1(\omega)=\omega_1,\qquad X_2(\omega)=\omega_2,\qquad X_3(\omega)=\omega_3.
\] So, for example, \(X_1(H,T,H)=H\), \(X_2(H,T,H)=T\), and \(X_3(H,T,H)=H\). The probability measure is \(P=\mu_1\otimes\mu_2\otimes\mu_3\). Now consider the outcome \(\{X_1=H,X_2=T,X_3=H\}\). This is exactly the singleton \(\{(H,T,H)\}\). Therefore, \[
P(X_1=H,X_2=T,X_3=H) = p(1-p)p.
\] In other words, \(P(H,T,H)=p^2(1-p)\). The product measure automatically gives us the multiplication rule for independent experiments.


Example 34.2 (Example with different distributions) Suppose we want three independent random variables: \(X_1\sim N(0,1)\), \(X_2\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\), and \(X_3\sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Take \[
S_1=\mathbb R,\qquad S_2=\{0,1\},\qquad S_3=[0,1],
\] and \[
\Omega=\mathbb R\times\{0,1\}\times[0,1].
\] Then define \(X_1(x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_1\), \(X_2(x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_2\), and \(X_3(x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_3\). The product measure \[
P = N(0,1) \otimes \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) \otimes \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)
\] guarantees that \(X_1\), \(X_2\), and \(X_3\) are independent and have exactly the desired marginal distributions. Thus, the lemma is not merely about coin tosses. It provides a general construction principle:
Choose the marginal distributions\(\implies\)take their product measure\(\implies\)the coordinate variables are independent.


Example 34.3 (Construction of Standard Normal Vectors) To construct \(d\) i.i.d. \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) random variables on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(\gamma(x) = (2\pi)^{-1/2} e^{-x^2/2}\) be the standard Gaussian density with respect to Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\) on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\), and define \(d\mu = \gamma \, d\lambda\). The Gaussian integral \(\int_{\mathbb{R}} \gamma \, d\lambda = 1\) is what makes \(\mu\) a probability measure, which is required below.
Since \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) (the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra identity of Lecture 14.2), the space \((\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) carries the product measure \(P = \mu^{\otimes d}\) of Proposition 34.1. By Lemma 34.1 the coordinate projections \(X_n(x_1, \dots, x_d) = x_n\) are i.i.d. with common law \(\mu = \mathcal{N}(0,1)\); no computation of a joint density is needed for this conclusion.
The joint density is a consequence, not the reason. Define \[
\begin{aligned}
f(x_1, \dots, x_d) &\triangleq \prod_{j=1}^d \gamma(x_j) \\
&= (2\pi)^{-d/2} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2 \right) \\
&= (2\pi)^{-d/2} e^{-\frac{1}{2}\|x\|^2},
\end{aligned}
\tag{34.5}\] a non-negative Borel function on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
The two candidate reference measures agree. Let \(\lambda^{\otimes d}\) be the \(d\)-fold product of one-dimensional Lebesgue measure on \(\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\), which exists by Proposition 34.1 since \(\lambda\) is \(\sigma\)-finite, and let \(\lambda^d\) denote Lebesgue measure on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). The two \(\sigma\)-algebras coincide by the Borel identity. Let \[
\mathcal{R}_{\square} \triangleq \Bigl\{ \textstyle\prod_{j=1}^d (a_j, b_j] \;\Big|\; -\infty \le a_j \le b_j \le +\infty \Bigr\},
\] with the convention \((a, +\infty] \triangleq (a, +\infty)\), and where \(a_j = b_j\) is allowed so that \(\emptyset \in \mathcal{R}_{\square}\). Then \(\mathcal{R}_{\square}\) is a \(\pi\)-system, because \(\prod_j(a_j,b_j] \cap \prod_j(a_j',b_j'] = \prod_j (a_j \vee a_j', \, b_j \wedge b_j']\) (interpreting an interval with left endpoint \(\ge\) right endpoint as empty), and \(\sigma(\mathcal{R}_{\square}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Both \(\lambda^{\otimes d}\) and \(\lambda^d\) assign the value \(\prod_{j=1}^d (b_j - a_j)\) to such a box — for \(\lambda^{\otimes d}\) by Equation 34.2, for \(\lambda^d\) by its defining property. Since \(R_m \triangleq (-m, m]^d \in \mathcal{R}_{\square}\) increases to \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with \(\lambda^{\otimes d}(R_m) = (2m)^d < \infty\), the uniqueness argument of Corollary 30.1 (an increasing sequence of finite-measure sets inside the \(\pi\)-system) gives \[
\lambda^{\otimes d} = \lambda^d \quad\text{on } \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d).
\]
Computing the law. For any box \(R = \prod_{j=1}^d (a_j, b_j] \in \mathcal{R}_{\square}\) we have the tensor factorization \(f \cdot \mathbf{1}_R = \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \bigl( \gamma \cdot \mathbf{1}_{(a_j,b_j]} \bigr)\). Applying Theorem 31.1 to the two-factor splitting \(\lambda^{\otimes d} = \lambda^{\otimes (d-1)} \otimes \lambda\) supplied by Equation 34.1 — legitimate because \(f \mathbf{1}_R \ge 0\) is Borel and all factors are \(\sigma\)-finite — and iterating \(d - 1\) times, \[
\int_R f \, d\lambda^{\otimes d} = \prod_{j=1}^d \int_{(a_j, b_j]} \gamma \, d\lambda = \prod_{j=1}^d \mu\bigl((a_j, b_j]\bigr) = \mu^{\otimes d}(R),
\] the last step by Equation 34.2. Taking \(R = \mathbb{R}^d\) shows \(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \, d\lambda^{\otimes d} = 1\), so \(\nu(E) \triangleq \int_E f \, d\lambda^{\otimes d}\) defines a probability measure on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Since \(\nu\) and \(\mu^{\otimes d}\) are probability measures agreeing on the \(\pi\)-system \(\mathcal{R}_{\square}\) with \(\sigma(\mathcal{R}_{\square}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\), Lemma 32.1 yields \[
d\mu^{\otimes d} = f \, d\lambda^{\otimes d} = f \, d\lambda^d ,
\] i.e. the law of \((X_1, \dots, X_d)\) is the standard multivariate normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\).

title: 35  Lecture 16.2: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (II)
text:
35.4 Existence of Infinite Independent Sequences

Theorem 35.2 (Existence of Infinite Independent Sequences) Let \(\{\mu_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be an arbitrary sequence of Borel probability measures on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\). There exists a probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) and a sequence of independent random variables \(X_n: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P) \to (\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) such that \(\mu_{X_n} = \mu_n\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). In particular, taking \(\mu_n = \mu\) for every \(n\) produces an i.i.d. sequence with common law \(\mu\), so i.i.d. sequences with an arbitrary prescribed marginal law exist.


Proof (Proof of Theorem 35.2). Set \(\Omega \triangleq \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\) and \(\mathcal{F} \triangleq \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}) = \sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N})\) by Equation 35.4. All the random variables constructed below are defined on this single space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), as Definition 33.1 requires.

Define the finite product measures \(\nu_n \triangleq \bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mu_k\) on \(\bigl(\mathbb{R}^n, \bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\bigr) = (\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n))\), the identification of the two \(\sigma\)-algebras being the Borel identity of Lecture 14.2; these exist and are unique probability measures by Proposition 34.1 (for \(n = 1\) read \(\nu_1 = \mu_1\)).
Projective consistency. The map \(B \mapsto \nu_{n+1}(B \times \mathbb{R})\) is the pushforward of \(\nu_{n+1}\) under the projection \(\operatorname{pr}_{1:n} : \mathbb{R}^{n+1} \to \mathbb{R}^n\) (measurable by Lemma 30.3), hence a probability measure on \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)\); so is \(B \mapsto \nu_n(B)\). On a rectangle \(B = B_1 \times \dots \times B_n\) they agree, since by Equation 34.2 \[
\begin{aligned}
\nu_{n+1}(B_1 \times \dots \times B_n \times \mathbb{R}) &= \Bigl( \prod_{k=1}^n \mu_k(B_k) \Bigr) \mu_{n+1}(\mathbb{R})\\
& = \prod_{k=1}^n \mu_k(B_k) = \nu_n(B).
\end{aligned}
\] Rectangles form a \(\pi\)-system generating \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)\) by Definition 30.1 together with \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) = \bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\), so Lemma 32.1 gives \(\nu_{n+1}(B \times \mathbb{R}) = \nu_n(B)\) for all \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)\), i.e. Equation 35.5 holds.
By Corollary 35.2 there is a unique probability measure \(P\) on \((\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}))\) with \(P(\pi_n^{-1}(B)) = \nu_n(B)\) for all \(n\) and all \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)\).
Set \(X_n \triangleq p_n\), the \(n\)-th coordinate map, which is \(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\)-measurable by Lemma 30.1. For any \(n\) and any \(B_1, \dots, B_n \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) we have \(\bigcap_{k=1}^n \{X_k \in B_k\} = \pi_n^{-1}(B_1 \times \dots \times B_n)\), so \[
\begin{aligned}
P(X_1 \in B_1, \dots, X_n \in B_n) &= P\bigl( \pi_n^{-1}(B_1 \times \dots \times B_n) \bigr) \\
&= \nu_n(B_1 \times \dots \times B_n) \\
&= \prod_{k=1}^n \mu_k(B_k) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{35.7}\]
Marginals. Fixing \(k \le n\) and setting \(B_j = \mathbb{R}\) for \(j \ne k\) in Equation 35.7 gives \(P(X_k \in B_k) = \mu_k(B_k)\), i.e. \(\mu_{X_k} = \mu_k\).
Independence. Let \(J \subseteq \mathbb{N}\) be finite and non-empty, \(n \triangleq \max J\), and \(B_j \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) for \(j \in J\). Setting \(B_j = \mathbb{R}\) for \(j \in \{1,\dots,n\} \setminus J\) in Equation 35.7 and using step 5, \[
P\Bigl( \bigcap_{j \in J} \{X_j \in B_j\} \Bigr) = \prod_{j \in J} \mu_j(B_j) = \prod_{j \in J} P(X_j \in B_j) .
\] Since this holds for every finite \(J\), the family \(\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) is independent in the sense of Definition 33.1.



Example 35.1 Suppose we want random variables \(X_1,X_2,X_3,\ldots\) such that \[
X_n=
\begin{cases} 1,&\text{with probability }p_n,\\
0,&\text{with probability }1-p_n,
\end{cases}
\] where the probabilities can be different for every \(n\). For example, let \(p_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\). Thus, \[
X_1\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}\left(\frac12\right), \, X_2\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}\left(\frac13\right), \, X_3\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}\left(\frac14\right), \,\ldots
\] and we want all these random variables to be independent. The theorem says that such an infinite sequence exists. Let’s construct it explicitly. For each \(n\), define \[
\mu_n = \frac{n}{n+1}\delta_0 + \frac{1}{n+1}\delta_1,
\] where \(\delta_x\) denotes the point mass at \(x\). So \(\mu_n(\{1\})=\frac{1}{n+1}\) and \(\mu_n(\{0\})=\frac{n}{n+1}\). Our goal is therefore to construct independent \(X_n\) satisfying \(X_n \sim \mu_n\) for \(n=1,2,3,\ldots\).
Let \(\Omega=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\). An element of \(\Omega\) is an entire infinite sequence: \[
\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\ldots), \, \omega_n\in\{0,1\}.
\] For example, \(\omega=(0,1,0,0,1,0,1,\ldots)\) is one possible outcome. Think of \(\omega\) as describing the outcomes of all infinitely many coin tosses. We equip \(\Omega\) with the product \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal F = \bigotimes_{n=1}^\infty 2^{\{0,1\}}\), where \(2^{\{0,1\}}\) is the power set of \(\{0,1\}\). For each coordinate, define the probability measure \[
\mu_n = \frac{n}{n+1}\delta_0+\frac{1}{n+1}\delta_1.
\] The infinite product probability measure is \[
P=\bigotimes_{n=1}^\infty\mu_n.
\] This is the probability measure that makes the coordinates behave according to their specified distributions and makes them independent. Schematically, \[
(\Omega,\mathcal F,P) = \left( \{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}, \bigotimes_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{\{0,1\}}, \bigotimes_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu_n \right).
\] Now define the \(n\)th coordinate map: \(X_n(\omega)=\omega_n\). For example, if \(\omega=(0,1,0,0,1,0,\ldots)\), then \[
X_1(\omega)=0,\, X_2(\omega)=1,\, X_3(\omega)=0,\, X_4(\omega)=0,\,\ldots.
\] So each \(X_n\) simply looks at the \(n\)th coordinate. The event \(\{X_n=1\}\) consists of all sequences whose \(n\)th coordinate equals \(1\): \(\{X_n=1\} = \{\omega\in\Omega:\omega_n=1\}\). Therefore, \(P(X_n=1) = \mu_n(\{1\}) = \frac{1}{n+1}\). Similarly, \(P(X_n=0) = \mu_n(\{0\}) = \frac{n}{n+1}\). Hence, \(X_n\) has the desired Bernoulli distribution: \(X_n \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}\left(\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\). Thus, \(\mu_{X_n} = \mu_n\).
The entire sample space can be visualized as
\[
\begin{array}{cccccc}
\omega &=& (\omega_1,&\omega_2,&\omega_3,&\omega_4,\ldots)\\
&&\downarrow&\downarrow&\downarrow&\downarrow\\
&&X_1(\omega)&X_2(\omega)&X_3(\omega)&X_4(\omega)
\end{array}
\] For example, \(\omega=(0,1,0,0,1,0,0,\ldots)\) produces \[
(X_1(\omega),X_2(\omega),X_3(\omega),X_4(\omega),X_5(\omega),\ldots) = (0,1,0,0,1,\ldots).
\] So an element \(\omega\) is itself an infinite realization, while \(X_n\) extracts its \(n\)th component. This is the central idea behind the product-space construction.


Example 35.2 (Infinitely many independent Uniform\((0,1)\) random variables) Suppose we want \(X_1,X_2,X_3,\ldots\) to satisfy \(X_n\sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) for every \(n\). The theorem tells us that such a sequence exists. Let’s construct it.
Let \(\lambda\) denote Lebesgue measure on \([0,1]\). The Uniform\((0,1)\) probability measure is \(\mu(A)=\lambda(A)\) for all \(A\in\mathcal B([0,1])\), because \(\lambda([0,1])=1\). Thus, \(([0,1],\mathcal B([0,1]),\lambda)\) is the desired probability space for a single Uniform\((0,1)\) random variable.
Take \(\Omega=[0,1]^{\mathbb N}\). An element of \(\Omega\) is an infinite sequence \[
\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\ldots), \qquad \omega_n\in[0,1].
\] For example, \(\omega=(0.374,0.821,0.156,\ldots)\) is one possible outcome. The sample space therefore contains every possible infinite sequence of numbers in \([0,1]\). Equip it with the product \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal F = \bigotimes_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathcal B([0,1])=\mathcal B([0,1])^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). For every coordinate, we want the Uniform\((0,1)\) distribution. Therefore define \(P=\bigotimes_{n=1}^{\infty}\lambda=\lambda^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). Thus, the probability space can be written as \[
(\Omega, \mathcal F, P)=([0,1]^{\mathbb N}, \bigotimes_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathcal B([0,1]), \bigotimes_{n=1}^{\infty}\lambda).
\]
Define the coordinate maps \[
X_n: \underbrace{([0,1]^{\mathbb N},\mathcal B([0,1])^{\otimes\mathbb N},\lambda^{\otimes\mathbb N})}_{\text{probability space}} \longrightarrow \underbrace{([0,1],\mathcal B([0,1]))}_{\text{measurable codomain space}},
\] with \(X_n(\omega)=\omega_n\). Why is \(X_n\) Uniform\((0,1)\)? Consider any Borel set \(A\subseteq[0,1]\). We have \[
\{X_n\in A\} = \{\omega:\omega_n\in A\}.
\] This is the cylinder set \[
[0,1]\times\cdots\times[0,1] \times A \times[0,1]\times\cdots,
\] where \(A\) occurs in the \(n\)th position. By the definition of the product measure, \[
\begin{aligned}
P(X_n\in A) &= P([0,1]\times\cdots\times A\times\cdots)\\
&= \prod_{j\neq n}\lambda([0,1])\cdot\lambda(A)\\
&=\lambda(A).
\end{aligned}
\] Since \(\lambda(A)\) is precisely the Uniform\((0,1)\) probability of \(A\), we conclude that \(X_n \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\).

title: 35  Lecture 16.2: Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem (II)
section: 35.3 Extensions to \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\) and Infinite Independent Sequences
text:
35.3 Extensions to \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\) and Infinite Independent Sequences
Throughout this section \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\) carries the product topology, \(p_n : \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}\) is the \(n\)-th coordinate map and \(\pi_n : \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^n\), \(\pi_n(x) = (x_1,\dots,x_n)\), is the projection onto the first \(n\) coordinates. The function \((a,b) \mapsto |a-b| \wedge 1\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}\) inducing its usual topology, so \[
\rho_\mathbb{R}(x,y) \triangleq \sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n}\bigl( |x_n - y_n| \wedge 1 \bigr)
\] is a well-defined metric on \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\) (the truncation \(\wedge\,1\) is what makes the series converge), and the argument of Lemma 34.2 shows verbatim that \(\rho_\mathbb{R}\) induces the product topology, that \(\rho_\mathbb{R}\)-convergence is coordinatewise convergence, and that the countable family of finite cylinders \(\bigcap_{k \le N} p_k^{-1}(I_k)\) with \(I_k \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) an open interval with rational endpoints is a base. In particular \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\) is a separable metrizable space; it is in fact Polish, since \(\rho_\mathbb{R}\) is complete. Repeating the argument of Lemma 34.3 mutatis mutandis — it used only countability of the index set and second countability of the factor, not compactness — gives \[
\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}) = \sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N}) = \bigotimes_{n=1}^\infty \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) = \sigma\Bigl( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \pi_n^{-1}\bigl( \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \bigr) \Bigr),
\tag{35.4}\] where the second equality is Definition 30.3 (the product \(\sigma\)-algebra is by definition generated by the coordinate maps) and the third uses the Borel identity \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) = \bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\) of Lecture 14.2. Moreover \(\bigcup_{n} \pi_n^{-1}(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n))\) is an algebra, hence a \(\pi\)-system, generating \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N})\).

Corollary 35.2 (Kolmogorov Extension Theorem on \(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\)) Let \(\nu_n\) be probability measures on \((\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n))\), \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), satisfying projective consistency \[
\nu_{n+1}(B \times \mathbb{R}) = \nu_n(B) \qquad \forall B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n),\ \forall n \in \mathbb{N} .
\tag{35.5}\] Then there exists a unique probability measure \(P\) on \((\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}))\) such that \[
P\bigl( \pi_n^{-1}(B) \bigr) = \nu_n(B) \qquad \forall B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n),\ \forall n \in \mathbb{N},
\tag{35.6}\] equivalently \(P \circ \pi_n^{-1} = \nu_n\) for every \(n\).


Proof (Proof of Corollary 35.2). Uniqueness. By Equation 35.4 the sets \(\pi_n^{-1}(B)\) form a \(\pi\)-system generating \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N})\) on which Equation 35.6 prescribes \(P\); since \(P\) is a probability measure, Lemma 32.1 gives uniqueness. It remains to prove existence.
Transport to the cube. Fix a homeomorphism \(\alpha: \mathbb{R} \to (0, 1)\) (e.g. \(\alpha(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x \frac{1}{\pi(1+t^2)} \, dt\), the Cauchy CDF), and let \(\beta \triangleq \alpha^{-1} : (0,1) \to \mathbb{R}\). Extend \(\beta\) to a Borel map \(\bar\beta : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}\) by setting \(\bar\beta(0) = \bar\beta(1) \triangleq 0\). Both \(\alpha\) and \(\bar\beta\) are Borel measurable, so the coordinatewise maps \[
\alpha^n : \mathbb{R}^n \to (0,1)^n, \qquad \bar\beta^{\,n} : [0,1]^n \to \mathbb{R}^n, \qquad \bar\beta^{\,\infty} : Q \to \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}
\] are Borel measurable — for \(\bar\beta^{\,\infty}\) this is Lemma 30.3 applied to the components \(\bar\beta \circ p_k\), together with Equation 35.4. Note \(\bar\beta^{\,n} \circ \alpha^n = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^n}\) and \(\alpha^n \circ \bar\beta^{\,n} = \mathrm{id}\) on \((0,1)^n\).
Define \(\tilde\nu_n\) on \(([0,1]^n, \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n))\) as the pushforward of \(\nu_n\) under \(\alpha^n\): \[
\tilde{\nu}_n(A) \triangleq \nu_n\bigl((\alpha^n)^{-1}(A \cap (0, 1)^n)\bigr), \qquad A \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n) .
\] Each \(\tilde\nu_n\) is a probability measure with \(\tilde\nu_n\bigl((0,1)^n\bigr) = \nu_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = 1\).
Consistency of \(\{\tilde{\nu}_n\}\). Let \(A \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)\) and abbreviate \(S \triangleq A \cap (0,1)^n\). Two set identities are used. First, \[
(A \times [0,1]) \cap (0,1)^{n+1} = S \times (0,1),
\] and second, since \(\alpha^{n+1}\) acts coordinatewise and \(\alpha^{-1}\bigl((0,1)\bigr) = \mathbb{R}\), \[
(\alpha^{n+1})^{-1}\bigl( S \times (0,1) \bigr) = (\alpha^{n})^{-1}(S) \times \alpha^{-1}\bigl((0,1)\bigr) = (\alpha^{n})^{-1}(S) \times \mathbb{R} .
\] Therefore \[
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{\nu}_{n+1}(A \times [0,1]) &= \nu_{n+1}\Bigl( (\alpha^{n+1})^{-1}\bigl( (A \times [0,1]) \cap (0,1)^{n+1} \bigr) \Bigr) \\
&= \nu_{n+1}\bigl( (\alpha^n)^{-1}(S) \times \mathbb{R} \bigr) \\
&= \nu_n\bigl( (\alpha^n)^{-1}(S) \bigr) = \tilde{\nu}_n(A),
\end{aligned}
\] the third equality being Equation 35.5. Hence \(\{\tilde{\nu}_n\}\) is projectively consistent in the sense of Equation 34.10.
Existence. By Theorem 34.2 there is a probability measure \(\tilde{P}\) on \((Q, \mathcal{B}(Q))\) with \(\tilde{P} \circ \pi_n^{-1} = \tilde\nu_n\) for every \(n\). Define \[
P \triangleq \tilde{P} \circ \bigl( \bar\beta^{\,\infty} \bigr)^{-1},
\] a probability measure on \((\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}))\) since \(\bar\beta^{\,\infty}\) is measurable. (The values assigned to \(\bar\beta\) at the endpoints \(0,1\) are irrelevant: \((0,1)^\mathbb{N} = \bigcap_n \pi_n^{-1}\bigl((0,1)^n\bigr) \in \mathcal{B}(Q)\) and \(\tilde{P}\bigl(\pi_n^{-1}((0,1)^n)\bigr) = \tilde\nu_n((0,1)^n) = 1\) for every \(n\), so \(\tilde{P}\bigl((0,1)^\mathbb{N}\bigr) = 1\) and \(\bar\beta^{\,\infty}\) agrees \(\tilde P\)-a.s. with the inverse of the coordinatewise map induced by \(\alpha\).)
Verification of Equation 35.6. Fix \(n\) and \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)\). Since \(\pi_n \circ \bar\beta^{\,\infty} = \bar\beta^{\,n} \circ \pi_n\), \[
P\bigl(\pi_n^{-1}(B)\bigr) = \tilde{P}\Bigl( \bigl(\bar\beta^{\,\infty}\bigr)^{-1}\bigl(\pi_n^{-1}(B)\bigr) \Bigr) = \tilde{P}\Bigl( \pi_n^{-1}\bigl( (\bar\beta^{\,n})^{-1}(B) \bigr) \Bigr) = \tilde{\nu}_n\bigl( (\bar\beta^{\,n})^{-1}(B) \bigr).
\] Writing \(A \triangleq (\bar\beta^{\,n})^{-1}(B)\) we have \(A \cap (0,1)^n = \{ y \in (0,1)^n \mid \beta^n(y) \in B \} = \alpha^n(B)\), hence \((\alpha^n)^{-1}\bigl(A \cap (0,1)^n\bigr) = B\) and therefore \(\tilde\nu_n(A) = \nu_n(B)\). Thus \(P(\pi_n^{-1}(B)) = \nu_n(B)\).


Remark 35.2 (What the Transport Argument Actually Uses). The specific choice of the Cauchy CDF is irrelevant. The only properties of \(\mathbb{R}\) used above are:

\(\mathbb{R}\) is homeomorphic to a Borel subset \((0,1)\) of the compact metrizable space \([0,1]\), so that the finite-dimensional laws transport to \([0,1]^n\) and the transported laws charge \((0,1)^n\) fully;
the inverse homeomorphism extends to a Borel map \([0,1] \to \mathbb{R}\) (any extension will do, since the added set is \(\tilde P\)-null).

By the Borel isomorphism theorem every uncountable Polish space is Borel isomorphic to \([0,1]\), so the same argument yields the Kolmogorov extension theorem with an arbitrary Polish state space in place of \(\mathbb{R}\). Some such hypothesis is genuinely needed: the theorem is false for arbitrary measurable state spaces.

title: 30  Lecture 14.2: Product Measure
text:
30.6 Takeaways

The product \(\sigma\)-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles in finite products and by finite-coordinate cylinder sets in arbitrary products. It is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra making all coordinate projections measurable.
In an uncountable product, product-measurable sets depend on at most countably many coordinates; unrestricted products need not be product measurable. This is why the definition uses cylinders.
A map into a product space is measurable exactly when each of its coordinate maps is measurable. In particular, tensor products of measurable functions are measurable on the product space.
For a product-measurable set or non-negative product-measurable function, its coordinate sections are measurable. Under \(\sigma\)-finite measures, integrating a non-negative function over either coordinate produces a measurable function, and the two iterated integrals agree.
The product measure \(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2\) is the unique \(\sigma\)-finite measure on \(\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2\) satisfying \[
(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E_1 \times E_2) = \mu_1(E_1)\mu_2(E_2).
\] It can equivalently be computed by integrating the indicator of a measurable set in either order.

title: 33  Lecture 15.2: Independent Random Variables
text:
33.8 Takeaways

Independence is independence of information. A family \(\{X_i\}_{i\in I}\) is independent precisely when the generated \(\sigma\)-algebras \(\{\sigma(X_i)\}_{i\in I}\) are independent. Equivalently, the probability factorization must hold for every finite collection of distinct indices and measurable sets in their respective state spaces.
It suffices to test generating classes. To prove independence, one may verify the factorization on a \(\pi\)-system generating each state-space \(\sigma\)-algebra, provided the test is made for every finite subfamily. For real-valued random variables, this yields the CDF criterion: independence is equivalent to factorization of the joint CDF into the marginal CDFs.
Independence is product factorization of the joint law. For a finite family, \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are independent if and only if \[
\mu_{(X_1,\ldots,X_n)}=\mu_{X_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\mu_{X_n}.
\] Consequently, independence is also equivalent to factorization of expectations of products of bounded measurable functions.
Products factor when integrability is available. If independent real-valued random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) belong to \(L^1\), then their product is in \(L^1\) and \[
\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i=1}^n X_i\right]=\prod_{i=1}^n\mathbb{E}[X_i].
\] In particular, independent \(L^2\) random variables are uncorrelated, but the converse fails.
Independence survives measurable transformations on disjoint blocks. Independent \(\sigma\)-algebras remain independent after grouping them into disjoint blocks. Therefore, measurable functions of disjoint blocks of independent random variables are themselves independent.
For bounded real-valued variables, all mixed moments characterize independence. If \(|X_i|\le M\) a.s. for a common finite \(M\), then independence is equivalent to factorization of every mixed moment. The converse uses polynomial approximation on \([-M,M]\), bounded convergence, and the bounded continuous-function criterion.

title: 37  Lecture 17.2: Convolution
text:
\(\lambda\) denotes Lebesgue measure on \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))\) (Definition 12.1), and \(d\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure is defined as the \(d\)-fold product \[
\lambda^d \triangleq \lambda^{\otimes d} \quad \text{on} \quad \textstyle\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d),
\tag{37.1}\] which exists, is unique, and is \(\sigma\)-finite by Corollary 30.1; the identification of the product \(\sigma\)-algebra with \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\) is the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra identity of Lecture 14.2. By associativity of the product construction, \(\lambda^{d} \otimes \lambda^{d} = \lambda^{2d}\) and \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \otimes \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{2d})\).
\(s: \mathbb{R}^{2d} \to \mathbb{R}^d\) denotes the addition map \(s(x, y) \triangleq x + y\). It is continuous, hence Borel measurable.
For \(B \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) and \(y \in \mathbb{R}^d\) we write \(B - y \triangleq \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d \mid x + y \in B\}\) for the translate of \(B\) by \(-y\). This is not a set difference. If \(B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\) then \(B - y = \tau_y^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)\), where \(\tau_y(x) \triangleq x + y\) is a homeomorphism.

title: 24  Lecture 11.2: Laws Revisited
text:
24.3 Application to Random Vectors
Let \((S, \mathcal{S}) = (\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))\) and let \(\mathbf{X}: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}) \to \mathbb{R}^d\) be a Borel-measurable random vector.

Law of \(\mathbf{X}\): The measure \(\mu_{\mathbf{X}} \triangleq \mathbf{X}_* \mathbb{P} = \mathbb{P} \circ \mathbf{X}^{-1}: \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \to [0, 1]\) defines the distribution (law) of \(\mathbf{X}\).
Expectation of \(g(\mathbf{X})\): By Equation 24.1, for any integrable or non-negative Borel-measurable \(g: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\): \[
\mathbb{E}[g(\mathbf{X})] = \int_{\Omega} (g \circ \mathbf{X}) \, d\mathbb{P} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} g \, d(\mathbf{X}_* \mathbb{P}) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} g \, d\mu_{\mathbf{X}}.
\tag{24.3}\] In particular, for a real-valued random variable \(X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\): \[
\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int_{\mathbb{R}} g \, d\mu_X.
\]

If \(F_X(t) \triangleq \mathbb{P}(X \le t)\) denotes the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of \(X\), then \(\mu_X\) is the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure \(\mu_{F_X}\) associated with \(F_X\). When \(g\) is Riemann-Stieltjes integrable (e.g., continuous), or when \(F_X\) is absolutely continuous with Radon-Nikodym derivative (density) \(f_X = F_X'\): \[
\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int_{\mathbb{R}} g(t) \, dF_X(t) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} g(t) f_X(t) \, dt.
\]
Upshot: Knowledge of the law \(\mu_X\) is sufficient to compute the expectation of any measurable function of \(X\).

Example 24.1 (Change of Variables via a Push-Forward Probability Measure) Consider the probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)=((0,1),\mathcal{B}((0,1)),\lambda)\), where \(\lambda\) is Lebesgue measure restricted to \((0,1)\). Define the random variable \(X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\) by \[
X(\omega)
=
\begin{cases}
0, & 0<\omega\leq \frac12,\\
1, & \frac12<\omega<1.
\end{cases}
\] Thus, \(X\) maps the entire interval \((0,\frac12]\) to \(0\) and the entire interval \((\frac12,1)\) to \(1\): \[
(0,1)
\quad\xrightarrow{\quad X\quad}\quad
\{0,1\}.
\]
The distribution of \(X\) is the push-forward probability measure \(P_X = X_* P\). For \(B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\), \[
P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B)).
\] In particular, \[
P_X(\{0\})=P(X^{-1}(\{0\}))=P\left(\left(0,\frac12\right]\right)=\frac12,
\] and \[
P_X(\{1\})=P(X^{-1}(\{1\}))=P\left(\left(\frac12,1\right)\right)=\frac12.
\] Thus, \(X\) has a Bernoulli\((1/2)\) distribution. Now let \(g(x)=3x+2\). The change-of-variables proposition gives \[
\int_{\mathbb{R}}g(x)\,dP_X(x)
=
\int_{\Omega}g(X(\omega))\,dP(\omega).
\] We can verify this directly. On the original probability space, \[
g(X(\omega))
=
\begin{cases}
2, & 0<\omega\leq \frac12,\\
5, & \frac12<\omega<1.
\end{cases}
\] Therefore, \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\Omega}g(X(\omega))\,dP(\omega)
&=
2P\left(\left(0,\frac12\right]\right)
+
5P\left(\left(\frac12,1\right)\right)\\
&=
2\left(\frac12\right)
+
5\left(\frac12\right)\\
&=
\frac72.
\end{aligned}
\] On the other hand, integrating directly with respect to the distribution of \(X\) gives \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}g(x)\,dP_X(x)
&=
g(0)P_X(\{0\})
+
g(1)P_X(\{1\})\\
&=
2\left(\frac12\right)
+
5\left(\frac12\right)\\
&=
\frac72.
\end{aligned}
\] Hence, \[
\int_{\Omega}g(X)\,dP
=
\int_{\mathbb{R}}g(x)\,dP_X(x)
=
\frac72.
\] The important point is that the original sample space \(\Omega=(0,1)\) is no longer needed once we know the distribution \(P_X\). The push-forward measure \(P_X\) summarizes how the probability measure \(P\) is transported through \(X\). In general, \[
\mathbb{E}[g(X)]
=
\int_{\Omega}g(X(\omega))\,dP(\omega)
=
\int_Sg(x)\,dP_X(x).
\] Thus, to integrate a function of a random variable, we can either integrate over the original sample space or integrate directly over the state space of the random variable using its distribution.

title: 24  Lecture 11.2: Laws Revisited
text:
24.4 Moments and Tail Behavior
For \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), the \(n\)-th moment of \(X\) is: \[
\mathbb{E}[X^n] = \int_{\mathbb{R}} t^n \, \mu_X(dt).
\]

Proposition 24.2 (Moment Hierarchy) Let \(X\) be a real-valued random variable and \(0 \le q < p\). If \(\mathbb{E}[|X|^p] < \infty\), then \(\mathbb{E}[|X|^q] < \infty\).


Proof (Proof of Proposition 24.2). Split the integral at \(|t| = 1\): \[
\mathbb{E}[|X|^q] = \int_{|t| < 1} |t|^q \, \mu_X(dt) + \int_{|t| \ge 1} |t|^q \, \mu_X(dt).
\]
For the first term, \(|t|^q \le 1\) on \(\{|t| < 1\}\), so: \[
\int_{|t| < 1} |t|^q \, \mu_X(dt) \le \mu_X(\mathbb{R}) = 1 < \infty.
\]
For the second term, \(|t|^q \le |t|^p\) on \(\{|t| \ge 1\}\) (since \(p > q\)), so: \[
\int_{|t| \ge 1} |t|^q \, \mu_X(dt) \le \int_{|t| \ge 1} |t|^p \, \mu_X(dt) \le \mathbb{E}[|X|^p] < \infty.
\]
Combining both terms gives \(\mathbb{E}[|X|^q] < \infty\).

Thus, if a random variable has a finite \(p\)-th absolute moment, then it has finite absolute moments of every order \(q\in[0,p)\).

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
section: 50.2 Skorohod Representation for Converging Normal Distributions
text:
50.2 Skorohod Representation for Converging Normal Distributions
Consider the sequence of probability measures \(\mu_n = N\left(\frac{1}{n},1\right)\) for \(n\geq 1\) and let \(\mu=N(0,1)\). We first observe that \(\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\). Indeed, the CDF of \(\mu_n\) is \(F_n(x)=\Phi\left(x-\frac{1}{n}\right)\), where \(\Phi\) is the CDF of the standard normal distribution. Since \(x-\frac{1}{n}\longrightarrow x\) and \(\Phi\) is continuous, \(F_n(x) = \Phi\left(x-\frac{1}{n}\right) \longrightarrow \Phi(x) = F(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). Hence \(\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\).
Skorohod’s Representation Theorem tells us that there exists a common probability space on which random variables with these distributions can be constructed so that they converge almost surely. We now construct such random variables explicitly.

50.2.0.1 Step 1: Start with a uniform random variable
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)=([0,1],\mathcal{B}([0,1]),\lambda)\), where \(\lambda\) denotes Lebesgue measure, and define \(U(\omega)=\omega\). Then \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\).


50.2.0.2 Step 2: Transform the uniform random variable
Define \(Y=\Phi^{-1}(U)\) and, for each \(n\geq1\), \(Y_n=\frac{1}{n}+\Phi^{-1}(U)\). The important feature of this construction is that the same random variable \(U\) is used for every \(Y_n\) and for \(Y\).


50.2.0.3 Step 3: Verify the distribution of \(Y\)
We first show that \(Y\sim N(0,1)\). For any \(y\in\mathbb{R}\), \[
\begin{aligned}
P(Y\leq y)
&=
P\left(\Phi^{-1}(U)\leq y\right)\\
&=
P\left(U\leq\Phi(y)\right).
\end{aligned}
\] The second equality follows because \(\Phi\) is strictly increasing. Since \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) and \(\Phi(y)\in(0,1)\), \(P\left(U\leq\Phi(y)\right)=\Phi(y)\). Therefore, \(P(Y\leq y)=\Phi(y)\). Thus the CDF of \(Y\) is \(\Phi\), so \(Y\sim N(0,1)=\mu\).


50.2.0.4 Step 4: Verify the distribution of \(Y_n\)
We now show that \(Y_n\sim N\left(\frac1n,1\right)=\mu_n\). For any \(y\in\mathbb{R}\), \[
\begin{aligned}
P(Y_n\leq y)
&=
P\left(\frac1n+\Phi^{-1}(U)\leq y\right)\\
&=
P\left(\Phi^{-1}(U)\leq y-\frac1n\right)\\
&=
P\left(U\leq
\Phi\left(y-\frac1n\right)\right)\\
&=
\Phi\left(y-\frac1n\right).
\end{aligned}
\] But \(F_n(y)=\Phi\left(y-\frac1n\right)\) is the CDF of \(N(1/n,1)\). Hence \(Y_n\sim N\left(\frac1n,1\right)=\mu_n\). Thus the construction preserves all the required marginal distributions: \[
P\circ Y_n^{-1}=\mu_n,
\qquad
P\circ Y^{-1}=\mu.
\]


50.2.0.5 Step 5: Verify almost-sure convergence
The construction makes the convergence particularly simple. We have \[
Y_n-Y
=\left(\frac1n+\Phi^{-1}(U)\right)-\Phi^{-1}(U)
=\frac1n.
\] Therefore, for every \(\omega\in\Omega\), \(|Y_n(\omega)-Y(\omega)|=\frac1n\longrightarrow0\). Hence \(Y_n\longrightarrow Y\) for every \(\omega\in\Omega\).

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
50.11 Mathematical Review and Required Corrections
This section records a mathematical audit of the chapter. It is deliberately separate from the lecture text so that the corrections are explicit rather than silently incorporated. No issue below is classified as CRITICAL. The four MAJOR issues are local and repairable, but they should be corrected before the chapter is used as a graduate-level text.

50.11.1 Critical and Major Issues
Location: Inverting the CDF & Generalized Inverses, opening ordinary-inverse argument
Severity: MAJOR
Problem: The assertion that a strictly increasing CDF is invertible as a map from \(\mathbb R\) onto \((0,1)\) is false. Strict increase does not rule out jump discontinuities, so the range of \(F\) can omit nonempty intervals.
Why it is a problem: For example, let \[
\mu=\frac12\delta_0+\frac12N(0,1).
\] Its CDF is strictly increasing because of the normal component, but it has a jump of size \(1/2\) at \(0\). Consequently, an ordinary inverse \(F^{-1}(u)\) is undefined for values \(u\) strictly between \(F(0-)\) and \(F(0)\). The displayed expression \(F^{-1}:(0,1)\to\mathbb R\) and the subsequent inverse-image calculation therefore do not follow from strict increase alone.
Correction: Replace the hypothesis by “\(F\) is continuous and strictly increasing.” Under that hypothesis, the CDF limits at \(\pm\infty\) imply that \(F\) maps \(\mathbb R\) bijectively onto \((0,1)\), and \[
\{u\in(0,1):F^{-1}(u)\le t\}=(0,F(t)].
\] Alternatively, omit the ordinary-inverse paragraph and introduce the generalized inverse immediately. This defect affects only the motivational argument, not the later generalized-inverse proof.
Location: Skorohod Representation for Converging Normal Distributions, Steps 1, 2, and 5
Severity: MAJOR
Problem: The construction uses \(\Omega=[0,1]\) and defines \(Y=\Phi^{-1}(U)\) as an \(\mathbb R\)-valued random variable. However, \(\Phi^{-1}(0)=-\infty\) and \(\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty\), so \(Y\) and \(Y_n\) are not \(\mathbb R\)-valued at the two endpoints. Moreover, \(Y_n-Y\) is undefined there, making the claim of convergence for every \(\omega\in\Omega\) false as written.
Why it is a problem: A random variable with codomain \(\mathbb R\) must take a finite real value at every point of its domain. Null sets may be ignored in an almost-sure assertion, but they cannot be ignored when the functions themselves are claimed to be everywhere \(\mathbb R\)-valued or when pointwise subtraction is performed there.
Correction: Use \[
(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)=((0,1),\mathcal B((0,1)),\lambda)
\] and \(U(\omega)=\omega\). Then \(Y_n-Y=1/n\) for every \(\omega\in(0,1)\). An alternative is to retain \([0,1]\), assign arbitrary finite values to all \(Y_n\) and \(Y\) at \(0\) and \(1\), and assert almost-sure convergence rather than convergence everywhere.
Location: Proof of Technical Properties of \(F^\leftarrow\) and \(F^\rightarrow\), Property 3
Severity: MAJOR
Problem: The proof section proves Properties 1 and 2 but does not prove Property 3. Property 3 is then used essentially in the quantile-transformation lemma and in Step 1 of the Skorohod proof.
Why it is a problem: The omitted result is not merely decorative: the implication \[
y<F^\leftarrow(u)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F(y)<u
\] is the step that permits weak convergence of the CDFs to control the lower limit of the quantiles. The property is true, but the chapter advertises a proof of all technical properties and leaves this one unproved.
Correction: First note that \(q:=F^\leftarrow(u)\) is finite. If \(y<q\), the definition of supremum gives some \(z\) with \(y<z\le q\) and \(F(z)<u\); monotonicity then yields \(F(y)\le F(z)<u\). If \(y>q\), then \(F(y)<u\) would put \(y\) in the set whose supremum is \(q\), a contradiction; hence \(F(y)\ge u\). Taking a sequence \(y_k\downarrow q\) and using right-continuity gives \[
F(q)=\lim_{k\to\infty}F(y_k)\ge u.
\] Finally, \(F(y)<u\) for every \(y<q\) implies \(F(q-)\le u\). Thus \[
F(q-)\le u\le F(q),
\] and both bullet-point implications in Property 3 follow.
Location: Continuous Mapping Theorem, proof of Part 2 (Step 6)
Severity: MAJOR
Problem: Step 6 reuses the set \(\Omega^*\) from Steps 1–2, but that set was constructed only to ensure continuity of \(g\circ f\) at \(Y(\omega)\). Continuity of \(g\circ f\) does not imply continuity of \(f\).
Why it is a problem: The inclusion \[
\operatorname{Disc}(g\circ f)\subseteq\operatorname{Disc}(f)
\] has the wrong direction for the inference made in Step 6. If \(g\) is constant, then \(g\circ f\) is continuous everywhere even when \(f\) is discontinuous. Thus the previously defined \(\Omega^*\) need not be a set on which \(f\) is continuous at \(Y(\omega)\).
Correction: For Part 2 define a new full-measure set \[
\Omega_f:=\Omega_1\cap\{\omega:Y(\omega)\notin\operatorname{Disc}(f)\}.
\] Because \(Y\) has law \(\mu_X\) and \(P(X\in\operatorname{Disc}(f))=0\), one has \(\lambda(\Omega_f)=1\). For \(\omega\in\Omega_f\), \(Y_n(\omega)\to Y(\omega)\) and \(f\) is continuous at \(Y(\omega)\), so \(f(Y_n(\omega))\to f(Y(\omega))\). The bound \(|f(Y_n)|\le M\) then permits DCT. The conclusion of Part 2 is correct; only its proof needs this repair.


50.11.2 Minor Issues
Location: Introduction & Motivation, first paragraph
Severity: MINOR
Problem: Saying that weak convergence is “strictly weaker than” convergence almost surely, in probability, and in \(L^p\) suppresses the fact that the latter modes compare random variables on a common probability space, whereas convergence in distribution depends only on their laws. The value or range of \(p\) is also unstated.
Why it is a problem: Without a common probability space, almost-sure, probability, and \(L^p\) convergence are not defined. For \(L^p\) convergence one also needs finite \(p\)th moments, normally with \(1\le p<\infty\) in these notes.
Correction: State: “For random variables defined on a common probability space, almost-sure convergence and convergence in probability imply convergence in distribution; for \(1\le p<\infty\), \(L^p\) convergence also implies convergence in probability. None of the converses holds in general.”
Location: Skorohod’s Representation Theorem and Note on the General Metric Space Proof
Severity: MINOR
Problem: The theorem is stated for separable metric spaces, while the note describes the general proof as being for Polish spaces and the chapter proves only the case \(S=\mathbb R\). The theorem is a legitimate standard result, but the exact scope of what is stated, cited, and proved should be distinguished.
Why it is a problem: The classical representation result is valid when the limiting law is concentrated on a separable subset; in particular, the stated separable-metric-space version is valid. Completeness is not needed for the stated conclusion. Nevertheless, the present chapter does not prove that general version.
Correction: Add “The general separable-metric-space theorem is quoted here as a standard result; this chapter proves only the case \(S=\mathbb R\).” If a proof is intended, provide a precise reference. Do not suggest that Polishness is required unless the theorem statement is correspondingly restricted.
Location: Note on the General Metric Space Proof and Takeaway 5
Severity: MINOR
Problem: The phrase “a well-chosen infinite product measure introducing precise correlations” is misleading. A product of the marginal laws gives independent coordinates and ordinarily does not produce the required coupling. The later assertion that the construction proceeds via kernels and the Kolmogorov extension theorem is only one possible proof architecture and is not established in this chapter.
Why it is a problem: What is needed is a suitable joint law on a product space, not generally the product of the prescribed marginal laws. Calling it a product measure obscures the essential dependence introduced by the coupling.
Correction: Replace the description by: “The general proof constructs a suitable joint coupling measure on an auxiliary probability space, for example through nested partitions or probability kernels. It is not generally the product of the marginal measures.”
Location: Generalized CDF Inverses, definition
Severity: MINOR
Problem: The definition treats the supremum and infimum as finite real numbers without stating why the defining sets are nonempty and bounded in the required directions.
Why it is a problem: Suprema and infima can otherwise take extended-real values. Their finiteness is needed for \(F^\leftarrow\) and \(F^\rightarrow\) to be maps from \((0,1)\) into \(\mathbb R\) and for all later evaluations at these points to be meaningful.
Correction: For \(u\in(0,1)\), use \[
\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0,
\qquad
\lim_{x\to+\infty}F(x)=1.
\] These limits show that \(\{x:F(x)<u\}\) and \(\{x:F(x)>u\}\) are nonempty. They also provide, respectively, a finite upper bound and a finite lower bound, so both generalized inverses are finite.
Location: Generalized CDF Inverses, discrete example
Severity: MINOR
Problem: The phrase “the last point at which the CDF is strictly below \(0.7\)” is inaccurate. The set \(\{y:F(y)<0.7\}=(-\infty,1)\) has no last point.
Why it is a problem: A supremum need not belong to the set whose supremum it is; this distinction is central to generalized inverses.
Correction: Say “the supremum, or right boundary, of the set on which the CDF is strictly below \(0.7\).”
Location: Technical Properties, Property 3
Severity: MINOR
Problem: The text attributes the entire display to right-continuity. Only the inequality \(u\le F(F^\leftarrow(u))\) uses right-continuity; the left-limit inequality and the two strict-side implications follow from the definition of the supremum and monotonicity.
Why it is a problem: The current wording conceals which hypotheses justify which conclusions.
Correction: Separate the supremum/monotonicity argument from the final use of right-continuity, as in the corrected proof under the corresponding MAJOR issue.
Location: Quantile Transformation, statement
Severity: MINOR
Problem: The notation \(Y^*\lambda\) is inconsistent with the earlier pushforward notation and conventionally suggests a pullback. The distribution is a pushforward measure.
Why it is a problem: Measures are pushed forward by measurable maps; using pullback notation can reverse the direction of the construction.
Correction: Write \[
Y_*\lambda=\lambda\circ Y^{-1}=\mu_Y=\mu
\] or use the equally standard notation \(Y_\#\lambda\).
Location: Proof of Skorokhod’s Theorem (\(S=\mathbb R\)), paragraph after the definition of \(Y_n,Y\)
Severity: MINOR
Problem: The expressions \(Y_n\overset d=\mu_n\) and \(Y\overset d=\mu\) compare random variables with measures and are therefore ill-typed.
Why it is a problem: Equality in distribution compares random variables or random elements; equality of a law with a measure is ordinary equality of measures.
Correction: Write \[
\mathcal L(Y_n)=\mu_n,
\qquad
\mathcal L(Y)=\mu,
\] or \(Y_n\sim\mu_n\) and \(Y\sim\mu\).
Location: Continuous Mapping Theorem, statement
Severity: MINOR
Problem: The underlying probability spaces of \(X_n\) and \(X\) are not stated. They need not be common for convergence in distribution, but \(P(X\in\operatorname{Disc}(f))\) uses the probability measure associated with \(X\).
Why it is a problem: Using a single unintroduced symbol \(P\) can incorrectly suggest that all variables must be defined on one space.
Correction: Say that \(X_n\) and \(X\) are real-valued random variables, possibly on different probability spaces, and write \[
\mu_X(\operatorname{Disc}(f))=0.
\] This condition is intrinsic to the law of \(X\).
Location: Continuous Mapping Theorem, Steps 1 and 4
Severity: MINOR
Problem: Expressions such as \(\lambda(Y\in A)\) are informal, and the same unindexed expectation notation is used for variables on the coupling space and variables on their original spaces.
Why it is a problem: Formally, \(\lambda\) measures subsets of \((0,1)\), not propositions in the state space; expectations on different probability spaces are distinct integrals.
Correction: Write \(\lambda(Y^{-1}(A))\) or \(\lambda\{\omega:Y(\omega)\in A\}\), use \(\mathbb E_\lambda\) for the coupled variables, and express transfer by laws as \[
\mathbb E_\lambda[h(Y_n)]
=\int h\,d\mu_n
=\mathbb E_{P_n}[h(X_n)].
\]
Location: Entire chapter
Severity: STYLE
Problem: The transliterations “Skorohod” and “Skorokhod” are both used.
Why it is a problem: Both forms occur in the literature, so this is not a mathematical error, but inconsistent spelling makes cross-references and indexing less reliable.
Correction: Choose one spelling and use it throughout. “Skorokhod” is common in current English-language probability texts.


50.11.3 Results Verified as Correct
The following arguments are mathematically correct once the local issues above are repaired or clarified:

The convergence of the normal CDFs \(\Phi(x-1/n)\to\Phi(x)\) proves \(N(1/n,1)\Rightarrow N(0,1)\) because the limiting CDF is continuous everywhere.
The normal quantile construction has the stated marginal laws away from the endpoint defect, and on \((0,1)\) it converges pointwise.
Both generalized-inverse formulas are standard and correct, and the values computed in the discrete example are correct.
The ordering \(F^\leftarrow(u)\le F^\rightarrow(u)\), the flat-spot equivalence, pairwise disjointness of the associated intervals, and countability of \(E\) are correct.
The quantile identity \[
\{u\in(0,1):F^\leftarrow(u)\le t\}=(0,1)\cap(0,F(t)]
\] is correct. Because these sublevel sets are Borel for every \(t\), it also establishes Borel measurability of \(F^\leftarrow\); taking Lebesgue measure establishes the pushforward law.
In the real-line Skorohod proof, weak convergence implies \(F_n(y)\to F(y)\) at every continuity point \(y\) of \(F\). The lower- and upper-bound arguments for the quantiles are correct. A CDF has at most countably many discontinuities, so its continuity points are dense; the limiting arguments \(y\uparrow Y(x)\) and \(y\downarrow Y(x)\) are therefore justified.
The set \(E\) is countable and hence Lebesgue-null, so convergence for every \(x\in(0,1)\setminus E\) gives almost-sure convergence.
In the continuous mapping proof, \(\operatorname{Disc}(g\circ f)\subseteq\operatorname{Disc}(f)\) for continuous \(g\), DCT applies because \(g\) is bounded on the probability space, and testing against every \(g\in C_b(\mathbb R)\) establishes weak convergence of the image laws.
Equality of laws permits transfer of expectations of bounded Borel functions. After the full-measure set in Step 6 is corrected, the bounded-expectation conclusion is valid.
The final warning is correct: the representation theorem constructs a new coupling and does not assert \(X_n\to X\) almost surely on the original probability space.



50.11.4 Recurring Patterns
The recurring issues are not failures of the central quantile idea. They are boundary and typing issues: endpoint values of inverse CDFs, finiteness of generalized inverses, confusion between a random variable and its law, and ambiguity about which probability measure governs an event or expectation. The chapter should also separate results quoted for general spaces from results actually proved for \(\mathbb R\).


50.11.5 Assumptions to Make Explicit
The following correct results would benefit from explicit hypotheses or justifications:

Modes stronger than convergence in distribution require random variables on a common probability space; \(L^p\) convergence requires the relevant finite moments.
The generalized inverses are finite because every probability CDF tends to \(0\) at \(-\infty\) and to \(1\) at \(+\infty\).
CDF convergence is used only at continuity points of the limiting CDF, exactly as required by the one-dimensional characterization of weak convergence.
A real CDF has at most countably many discontinuities, so its continuity set is dense.
The discontinuity set of a real-valued function is Borel; thus \(\mu_X(\operatorname{Disc}(f))\) is defined. The stated Borel measurability of \(f\) is additionally needed so that \(f(X_n)\), \(f(X)\), and their expectations are measurable.
DCT is applied on a probability space, so the constant dominating functions are integrable.
The general representation theorem is standard and valid as stated for separable metric \(S\), but only the \(S=\mathbb R\) case is proved in this chapter.



50.11.6 Overall Assessment
The chapter has the correct central strategy and its main real-line quantile-convergence argument is sound. There are no critical failures and no false final theorem or corollary. Nevertheless, the ordinary-inverse paragraph and the normal example are false as written at specific points, Property 3 has a genuine missing proof, and Part 2 of the continuous mapping proof uses an invalid inference about continuity. Accordingly, the chapter is not yet mathematically ready for use as a graduate-level text without correction. After the four major repairs and the listed notation and assumption clarifications, it would be suitable at that level.

title: 50  Lecture 23.3: Skorohod’s Theorem
text:
50.5 Proof of Skorohod’s Theorem (\(S = \mathbb{R}\))

Proof (Proof of Theorem 50.1 for \(S = \mathbb{R}\)). Let \(\mu_n, \mu \in \text{Prob}\left(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\right)\) with \(\mu_n \Rightarrow \mu\). Let \(F_n = F_{\mu_n}\) and \(F = F_\mu\) be their corresponding CDFs.
Define our probability space as \(\Omega = (0, 1)\), \(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{B}((0, 1))\), and \(P = \lambda\) (Lebesgue measure). Define the sequence of random variables: \[
Y_n(u) := F_n^\leftarrow(u), \quad Y(u) := F^\leftarrow(u), \quad \forall u \in (0, 1).
\] These are real-valued and Borel measurable by Lemma 50.1, which also gives \[
\mathcal{L}(Y_n) = \mu_n \quad \forall n \ge 1,
\qquad
\mathcal{L}(Y) = \mu,
\] establishing conclusions 1 and 2 of Theorem 50.1. To obtain conclusion 3, it suffices to show that \(Y_n(u) \to Y(u)\) for every \(u \in (0,1) \setminus E\), where \[
E = \{ t \in (0, 1) : F^\leftarrow(t) < F^\rightarrow(t) \}
\] is defined in terms of the limit CDF \(F\) only. By Property 2, \(E\) is at most countable, hence \(\lambda(E) = 0\), so this yields \(Y_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} Y\).
Throughout we use two standard facts. First, since \(\mu_n \Rightarrow \mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), we have \(F_n(y) \to F(y)\) at every \(y \in \text{Cont}(F)\). Second, \(\text{Cont}(F)\) is dense in \(\mathbb{R}\), because the monotone bounded function \(F\) has at most countably many discontinuities.
Step 1: Lower Bound, \(\liminf_{n\to\infty} Y_n(u) \ge Y(u)\).
Fix \(u \in (0,1)\) (this step does not require \(u \notin E\)). Choose \(y \in \text{Cont}(F)\) with \(y < Y(u) = F^\leftarrow(u)\); such \(y\) exist by density of \(\text{Cont}(F)\) and finiteness of \(Y(u)\). By the second implication in Property 3, since \(y < F^\leftarrow(u)\), we have \(F(y) < u\).
Since \(y\) is a continuity point of \(F\), we have \(F_n(y) \to F(y)\). Because \(F(y) < u\), for all sufficiently large \(n\) we have \(F_n(y) < u\). Therefore, by definition of \(Y_n(u) = F_n^\leftarrow(u)\), the point \(y\) lies in the set whose supremum defines \(Y_n(u)\): \[
Y_n(u) = \sup \{ y' : F_n(y') < u \} \ge y.
\] Taking the limit inferior as \(n \to \infty\) gives: \[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} Y_n(u) \ge y.
\] Since this holds for every \(y \in \text{Cont}(F)\) with \(y < Y(u)\), and such \(y\) can be taken with \(y \uparrow Y(u)\) by density, we obtain: \[
\liminf_{n \to \infty} Y_n(u) \ge Y(u).
\]
Step 2: Upper Bound, \(\limsup_{n\to\infty} Y_n(u) \le Y(u)\).
Now fix \(u \in (0,1) \setminus E\) and choose \(y \in \text{Cont}(F)\) with \(y > Y(u)\). Since \(u \notin E\), we have \(Y(u) = F^\leftarrow(u) = F^\rightarrow(u) = \inf \{ y' : F(y') > u \}\). This is the only place where \(u \notin E\) is used. Thus \(y > F^\rightarrow(u)\). Since the set \(\{y': F(y') > u\}\) is closed upward (non-decreasingness of \(F\): if \(F(z)>u\) and \(z'\ge z\) then \(F(z')\ge F(z)>u\)) and \(F^\rightarrow(u)\) is its infimum, any \(y > F^\rightarrow(u)\) belongs to the set, i.e.~\(F(y) > u\).
Since \(y \in \text{Cont}(F)\), \(F_n(y) \to F(y) > u\), so for all sufficiently large \(n\), \(F_n(y) > u\). Because \(F_n\) is non-decreasing, \(F_n(y) > u\) makes \(y\) an upper bound for \(\{z : F_n(z) < u\}\) (any \(z > y\) satisfies \(F_n(z) \ge F_n(y) > u\)), so \(Y_n(u) = \sup\{z : F_n(z) < u\} \le y\). Taking the limit superior as \(n \to \infty\) gives: \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} Y_n(u) \le y.
\] Taking \(y \downarrow Y(u)\) over continuity points \(y \in \text{Cont}(F)\) yields: \[
\limsup_{n \to \infty} Y_n(u) \le Y(u).
\]
Conclusion. Combining both steps: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} Y_n(u) = Y(u), \quad \forall u \in (0, 1) \setminus E.
\] Since \(\lambda(E) = 0\), we conclude \(Y_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} Y\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: 51  Lecture 24.1: Complex Integration and Dynkin’s Theorem
text:
53.1 Notation and Conventions
Throughout this section \(\Omega\) is a non-empty set. For a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{G}\) on \(\Omega\) and \(\mathbb{K} \in \{\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{C}\}\) we write \[
\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{K}}(\Omega, \mathcal{G}) \triangleq \{ f: \Omega \to \mathbb{K} \mid f \text{ is bounded and } \mathcal{G}/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{K})\text{-measurable} \}.
\] We set \(\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{K}}(\Omega) \triangleq \mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{K}}(\Omega, 2^\Omega)\) so that \(\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{K}}(\Omega)\) is the set of all bounded \(\mathbb{K}\)-valued functions on \(\Omega\). In this notation \(\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{R}}(\Omega, \mathcal{G})\) is the space written \(\mathbb{B}(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, \mathbb{R})\) in Theorem 29.1. The symbol \(\mathcal{B}(\cdot)\) is reserved for Borel \(\sigma\)-algebras.

Definition 53.1 (Bounded Convergence, Complex Case) A set \(\mathcal{H}\) of \(\mathbb{C}\)-valued functions on \(\Omega\) is closed under bounded convergence if for every sequence \(\{f_n\} \subseteq \mathcal{H}\) satisfying

\(\sup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \sup_{\omega \in \Omega} |f_n(\omega)| < \infty\), and
\(f_n(\omega) \to f(\omega) \in \mathbb{C}\) for every \(\omega \in \Omega\),

the limit \(f\) belongs to \(\mathcal{H}\). For \(\mathbb{R}\)-valued families this reduces to Definition 29.1.

For a family \(M\) of \(\mathbb{C}\)-valued functions on \(\Omega\), \(\sigma(M)\) denotes the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) making every \(f \in M\) measurable: \[
\sigma(M) \triangleq \sigma\big( f^{-1}(B) : f \in M, \, B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{C}) \big).
\] Since a \(\mathbb{C}\)-valued \(f\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable if and only if \(\operatorname{Re}(f)\) and \(\operatorname{Im}(f)\) are, we also have \(\sigma(M) = \sigma\big( \{ \operatorname{Re}(f), \operatorname{Im}(f) : f \in M \} \big)\).

Theorem 53.1 (Complex Dynkin’s Multiplicative Systems Theorem) Let \(\mathcal{H} \subseteq \mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}(\Omega)\) be a \(\mathbb{C}\)-vector subspace containing the constant function \(1\) and closed under bounded convergence in the sense of Definition 53.1. Let \(M \subseteq \mathcal{H}\) be a multiplicative system (i.e., \(f, g \in M \implies fg \in M\)) that is closed under complex conjugation (\(\bar{M} \subseteq M\)).
Then \(\mathcal{H}\) contains all bounded, \(\mathbb{C}\)-valued, \(\sigma(M)\)-measurable functions: \[\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}(\Omega, \sigma(M)) \subseteq \mathcal{H}\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 53.1). Step 1 (\(M_0\) is a conjugation-closed algebra). Let \(M_0 := \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{C}}(M \cup \{1\})\). Since \(\mathcal{H}\) is a \(\mathbb{C}\)-vector subspace containing \(M\) and \(1\), we have \(M_0 \subseteq \mathcal{H}\). It is an algebra: for \(f_i, g_j \in M \cup \{1\}\) and \(a_i, b_j \in \mathbb{C}\), \[
\Big( \sum_i a_i f_i \Big) \Big( \sum_j b_j g_j \Big) = \sum_{i, j} a_i b_j (f_i g_j) \in M_0,
\] because \(f_i g_j \in M \cup \{1\}\) (\(M\) is multiplicative and \(1\) is the multiplicative unit). It is closed under conjugation because \(\overline{\sum_i a_i f_i} = \sum_i \bar{a}_i \bar{f}_i\), with \(\bar{f}_i \in M \cup \{1\}\) by the hypothesis \(\bar{M} \subseteq M\).
Step 2 (real parts). Define the sets of real-valued elements \[\mathcal{H}^{\mathbb{R}} := \{ f \in \mathcal{H} : \operatorname{Im}(f) = 0 \}, \qquad M_0^{\mathbb{R}} := \{ f \in M_0 : \operatorname{Im}(f) = 0 \}.\]

\(1 \in \mathcal{H}^{\mathbb{R}}\), and \(\mathcal{H}^{\mathbb{R}}\) is an \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector subspace of \(\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{R}}(\Omega)\).
\(\mathcal{H}^{\mathbb{R}}\) is closed under bounded convergence in the sense of Definition 29.1: if \(f_n \in \mathcal{H}^{\mathbb{R}}\) are uniformly bounded and converge pointwise to \(f\), then \(f \in \mathcal{H}\) since \(\mathcal{H}\) is closed under bounded convergence, and \(f\) is real-valued as a pointwise limit of real-valued functions.
Since \(M_0\) is closed under conjugation (Step 1), every \(f \in M_0\) decomposes into elements of \(M_0^{\mathbb{R}}\): \[\operatorname{Re}(f) = \frac{f + \bar{f}}{2} \in M_0^{\mathbb{R}}, \qquad \operatorname{Im}(f) = \frac{f - \bar{f}}{2i} \in M_0^{\mathbb{R}}\]
\(M_0^{\mathbb{R}} \subseteq M_0 \cap \mathcal{H}^{\mathbb{R}}\), and \(M_0^{\mathbb{R}}\) is a real multiplicative system: if \(f, g \in M_0^{\mathbb{R}}\) then \(fg \in M_0\) because \(M_0\) is an algebra, and \(fg\) is real-valued, hence \(fg \in M_0^{\mathbb{R}}\).

Step 3 (\(\sigma(M) = \sigma(M_0) = \sigma(M_0^{\mathbb{R}})\)). This is the only place where the hypothesis \(\bar{M} \subseteq M\) is used.

(\(\sigma(M) \subseteq \sigma(M_0^{\mathbb{R}})\)) For \(f \in M\) we have \(\operatorname{Re}(f), \operatorname{Im}(f) \in M_0^{\mathbb{R}}\) by Step 2, so both are \(\sigma(M_0^{\mathbb{R}})\)-measurable, and therefore so is \(f = \operatorname{Re}(f) + i \operatorname{Im}(f)\).
(\(\sigma(M_0^{\mathbb{R}}) \subseteq \sigma(M_0) \subseteq \sigma(M)\)) Every element of \(M_0\) is a finite \(\mathbb{C}\)-linear combination of elements of \(M \cup \{1\}\), hence \(\sigma(M)\)-measurable.

Step 4 (conclusion). By Step 2 the pair \(M_0^{\mathbb{R}} \subseteq \mathcal{H}^{\mathbb{R}} \subseteq \mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{R}}(\Omega)\) satisfies all hypotheses of the real Dynkin Multiplicative Systems Theorem (Theorem 29.1), so \[\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{R}}(\Omega, \sigma(M_0^{\mathbb{R}})) \subseteq \mathcal{H}^{\mathbb{R}}\]
Now let \(g \in \mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}(\Omega, \sigma(M))\) and write \(g = u + iv\). Then \(u, v\) are \(\sigma(M)\)-measurable and \(|u|, |v| \le |g|\) are bounded, so by Step 3, \[u, v \in \mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{R}}(\Omega, \sigma(M_0^{\mathbb{R}})) \subseteq \mathcal{H}^{\mathbb{R}} \subseteq \mathcal{H}.\] Since \(\mathcal{H}\) is a \(\mathbb{C}\)-vector subspace, \(g = u + iv \in \mathcal{H}\). Thus, \(\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}(\Omega, \sigma(M)) \subseteq \mathcal{H}\).

title: 54  Lecture 25.2: Fourier Inversion
text:
54.11 Example: Laplace Distribution
Let \(X\) have characteristic function \(\phi_X(\xi)=\frac{1}{1+\xi^2}\). We have \[
\int_{\mathbb R}|\phi_X(\xi)|\,d\xi = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1+\xi^2}\,d\xi.
\] Since \(\frac{d}{d\xi}\arctan(\xi)=\frac{1}{1+\xi^2}\), we obtain \[
\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1+\xi^2}\,d\xi &= \lim_{a\to\infty} \int_{-a}^{a}\frac{1}{1+\xi^2}\,d\xi\\
&= \lim_{a\to\infty} \left[\arctan(\xi)\right]_{-a}^{a}\\
&= \lim_{a\to\infty} \left(\arctan(a)-\arctan(-a)\right)\\
&= \lim_{a\to\infty}2\arctan(a)\\
&=2\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=\pi.
\end{aligned}
\] Thus, the density inversion formula applies. Therefore \(X\) has a continuous density \[
f_X(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\mathbb R} \frac{e^{-i\xi x}}{1+\xi^2}\,d\xi.
\] We can evaluate this integral using the known Fourier transform pair \[
\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-i\xi x}}{1+\xi^2}\,d\xi = \pi e^{-|x|}.
\] Hence \(f_X(x)=\frac12e^{-|x|}\). Thus the inversion formula recovers the Laplace density directly from its characteristic function: \[
\boxed{ \phi_X(\xi)=\frac{1}{1+\xi^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f_X(x)=\frac12e^{-|x|}. }
\]

title: 55  Lecture 25.3: The Continuity Theorem
text:
55.6 Takeaways

On \(\mathbb{R}^d\), a characteristic function is a complete distributional fingerprint: if two probability measures have the same characteristic function, then they are equal.
Pointwise convergence of characteristic functions is not enough by itself; the crucial extra hypothesis is continuity at the origin. This ensures the limit function is a genuine characteristic function and prevents pathological non-tight behavior.
Lévy’s continuity theorem turns Fourier-space convergence into weak convergence of laws: if \(\hat{\mu}_n(\xi) \to \varphi(\xi)\) for all \(\xi\) and \(\varphi\) is continuous at \(0\), then there exists a probability measure \(\mu\) with \(\varphi = \hat{\mu}\) and \(\mu_n \implies \mu\).
The proof hinges on tightness and Prokhorov’s theorem: from pointwise convergence of characteristic functions, one obtains tightness, hence relative compactness of the sequence, and every subsequential limit must have the same Fourier transform.
In practice, the continuity theorem is the Fourier-analytic bridge between transform convergence and distributional convergence. It is the standard tool for proving CLTs and other weak-limit results by checking pointwise convergence of characteristic functions.

title: 59  Lecture 27.2: Lindberg-Feller CLT
text:
59.8 Two Examples

Example 59.1 (A triangular array of many small summands) Let \(X_{n,k}=\frac{Z_k}{\sqrt n}\) for \(k=1,\ldots,n\), where \(Z_1,Z_2,\ldots\) are i.i.d. with \(\mathbb E[Z_k]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[Z_k^2]=1\). Then \[
S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_{n,k} = \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k.
\] This is the familiar standardized sum from the classical CLT, but viewed as a triangular array. The variables in each row are independent and centered, and \(\operatorname{Var}(X_{n,k}) = \frac1n\). Therefore \(\sum_{k=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_{n,k}) = n\frac1n =1\). Moreover, \(\max_{1\le k\le n}\operatorname{Var}(X_{n,k}) = \frac1n\to0\). Therefore (DV) holds.
For any \(\varepsilon>0\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb E\left[ X_{n,k}^2 \mathbf 1\{|X_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\} \right] &= n\mathbb E\left[ \frac{Z_1^2}{n} \mathbf 1\left\{ \frac{|Z_1|}{\sqrt n}>\varepsilon \right\} \right]\\ &= \mathbb E\left[ Z_1^2 \mathbf 1\{|Z_1|>\varepsilon\sqrt n\} \right].
\end{aligned}
\] Since \(Z_1^2\mathbf 1\{|Z_1|>\varepsilon\sqrt n\} \longrightarrow0\) almost surely and \(0\le Z_1^2\mathbf 1\{|Z_1|>\varepsilon\sqrt n\} \le Z_1^2\) with \(\mathbb E[Z_1^2]<\infty\), the DCT gives \[
\mathbb E\left[ Z_1^2 \mathbf 1\{|Z_1|>\varepsilon\sqrt n\} \right]\to0.
\] Hence (Lind) holds. Therefore, by the sufficiency part, \[
S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n X_{n,k} = \frac{1}{\sqrt n} \sum_{k=1}^n Z_k \overset{w}{\longrightarrow} N(0,1).
\]


Example 59.2 (Why the Feller condition matters) Now consider a deliberately constructed array: \(X_{n,1}=Z\) and \(X_{n,k}=0\) for \(k=2,\ldots,n\), where \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\). Then \[
S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_{n,k}=Z
\] for every \(n\). Consequently, \(S_n\xrightarrow{w}\mathcal N(0,1)\). So we have convergence to the normal distribution. But
\[
\max_{1\le k\le n} \operatorname{Var}(X_{n,k}) = \operatorname{Var}(X_{n,1}) = \operatorname{Var}(Z) = 1,
\] So DV fails. And Lindeberg’s condition also fails. For, say, \(\varepsilon=1/2\), \[
\begin{aligned} \sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb E[ X_{n,k}^2 \mathbf 1\{|X_{n,k}|>\varepsilon\} ] &= \mathbb E[ Z^2\mathbf 1\{|Z|>1/2\} ]\\ &>0
\end{aligned}
\] for every \(n\). Thus, the classical CLT does not imply (Lind) without (DV). This is exactly why the Feller condition appears in the necessity theorem.

title: 60  Lecture 27.3: Random Permutations
text:
Theorem 60.1 (Lyapunov’s Condition) The standard triangular array \(\{X_{n,k}\}\) satisfies Lyapunov’s condition with exponent \(\delta = 2\): \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb{E}[X_{n,k}^4] = 0.
\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 60.1). Expanding the centered 4th moment for \(X_k \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/k)\): \[
\mathbb{E}\left[ \left( X_k - \frac{1}{k} \right)^4 \right] = \mathbb{E}\left[ X_k^4 - 4 X_k^3 \frac{1}{k} + 6 X_k^2 \frac{1}{k^2} - 4 X_k \frac{1}{k^3} + \frac{1}{k^4} \right].
\] Since \(X_k \in \{0, 1\}\), \(X_k^m = X_k\) for all \(m \ge 1\). Using \(\mathbb{E}[X_k] = \frac{1}{k}\): \[
\mathbb{E}\left[ \left( X_k - \frac{1}{k} \right)^4 \right] = \frac{1}{k} - \frac{4}{k^2} + \frac{6}{k^3} - \frac{4}{k^4} + \frac{1}{k^4} \le \frac{1}{k} + \frac{15}{k^2}.
\]
Summing over \(k=1, \dots, n\) and dividing by \(\sigma_n^4\): \[
\sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb{E}[X_{n,k}^4] = \frac{1}{\sigma_n^4} \sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb{E}\left[ \left( X_k - \frac{1}{k} \right)^4 \right] \le \frac{1}{\sigma_n^4} \left( \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{k} + 15 \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{k^2} \right).
\]
Since \(\sigma_n^2 \sim \log n\), for all sufficiently large \(n\), \[
\sigma_n^2 \ge \frac{1}{2}\log n.
\] Also, \(H_n \le \log n+1\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^n k^{-2}<2\). Hence, for all sufficiently large \(n\), \[
\sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb{E}[X_{n,k}^4]
\le \frac{4}{(\log n)^2}(\log n+31)
\longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]

title: 59  Lecture 27.2: Lindberg-Feller CLT
text:
59.8 Examples

Example 59.1 (A triangular array of many small summands) Let \(X_{n,k}=\frac{Z_k}{\sqrt n}\) for \(k=1,\ldots,n\), where \(Z_1,Z_2,\ldots\) are i.i.d. with \(\mathbb E[Z_k]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[Z_k^2]=1\). Then \[

\end{aligned}
\] Since \(Z_1^2\mathbf 1\{|Z_1|>\varepsilon\sqrt n\} \longrightarrow0\) almost surely and \(0\le Z_1^2\mathbf 1\{|Z_1|>\varepsilon\sqrt n\} \le Z_1^2\) with \(\mathbb E[Z_1^2]<\infty\), the DCT gives \[
