title: 66  Lecture 30.2: Conditional Expectation-Part I
text:
66.4 Conditioning on Discrete Random Variables
Let \(S\) be a countable set equipped with the discrete \(\sigma\)-algebra \(2^S\), and let \(Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,2^S)\) be measurable with \(\mathbb{P}(Y=s)>0\) for all \(s\in S\). The pre-images \(\{Y^{-1}(\{s\})\}_{s \in S}\) form a countable partition of \(\Omega\) generating \(\mathcal{G} = \sigma(Y)\).
For \(X \in L^1(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\), the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]\) is defined as:
\[
\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y](\omega) = \sum_{s \in S} \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = s] \mathbb{I}_{\{Y = s\}}(\omega) = \sum_{s \in S} \frac{\mathbb{E}[X \mathbb{I}_{\{Y = s\}}]}{\mathbb{P}(Y = s)} \mathbb{I}_{\{Y = s\}}(\omega).
\]
Define \(g:S\to\mathbb R\) by \(g(s)=\mathbb E[X\mid Y=s]\). Since \(S\) has the discrete \(\sigma\)-algebra, \(g\) is measurable, and:
\[
\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y](\omega) = g(Y(\omega)), \quad \text{where } g(s) = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = s] = \frac{\mathbb{E}[X \mathbb{I}_{\{Y = s\}}]}{\mathbb{P}(Y = s)}.
\]

title: 66  Lecture 30.2: Conditional Expectation-Part I
text:
66.5 Smoothing and Orthogonality Properties
The fundamental characterization of conditional expectation is given by its action under integration against \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable functions.

Theorem 66.1 (The Smoothing / Projection Property) Let \(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be a partition of \(\Omega\) with \(\mathbb{P}(A_n) > 0\), and let \(\mathcal{G} = \sigma(\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty)\). If \(X \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) and \(Y \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{G}, \mathbb{P})\), then:
\[
\mathbb{E}[X Y] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] Y].
\] Moreover, \(\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]\in L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,\mathbb P)\) and \[
\left\|\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]\right\|_2\le\|X\|_2.
\]


Proof (Proof of Theorem 66.1). 

Step 1 (Finitely supported atomwise \(Y\)): Consider \(Y = \sum_{k=1}^N \beta_k \mathbb{I}_{A_k}\) for some \(N < \infty\). Because the partition atoms are disjoint (\(\mathbb{I}_{A_n}\mathbb{I}_{A_k} = \delta_{nk}\mathbb{I}_{A_k}\)), the product reduces pointwise to a finite sum:
\[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \cdot Y
= \left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb{E}_{A_n}[X]\,\mathbb{I}_{A_n}\right)\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^N \beta_k\,\mathbb{I}_{A_k}\right)
= \sum_{k=1}^N \beta_k\,\mathbb{E}_{A_k}[X]\,\mathbb{I}_{A_k}.
\]
The infinite sum in \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) collapses to \(N\) surviving terms: for each fixed \(\omega \in A_j\), only the \(n = j\) term in \(\sum_n \mathbb{E}_{A_n}[X]\mathbb{I}_{A_n}\) is nonzero, and the factor \(\mathbb{I}_{A_j}(\omega)\) from \(Y\) is also 1 only if \(j \le N\). Taking expectations — now a finite sum so linearity needs no justification — and substituting \(\mathbb{E}_{A_k}[X]\,\mathbb{P}(A_k) = \mathbb{E}[X\mathbb{I}_{A_k}]\) (from Lemma 66.1) gives:
\[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\,Y]
&= \sum_{k=1}^N \beta_k\,\mathbb{E}_{A_k}[X]\,\mathbb{P}(A_k)\\
&= \sum_{k=1}^N \beta_k\,\mathbb{E}[X\mathbb{I}_{A_k}]\\
&= \mathbb{E}\!\left[X\sum_{k=1}^N \beta_k\,\mathbb{I}_{A_k}\right]\\
&= \mathbb{E}[XY].
\end{align*}
\]
Step 2 (General \(Y \in L^2(\mathcal{G})\)): Since \(Y\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, it takes a constant value \(\beta_k\) on each \(A_k\). Define the finite truncations \[Y_m = \sum_{k=1}^m \beta_k\,\mathbb{I}_{A_k}.\] Each \(Y_m\) is a finite simple \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable function, so Step 1 gives \(\mathbb{E}[XY_m] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\,Y_m]\). Since every \(\omega\) belongs to exactly one \(A_k\), we have \(Y_m(\omega) = Y(\omega)\) for all \(m \ge k\), hence \(Y_m \to Y\) pointwise and \(|Y_m| \le |Y|\). DCT applies to both limits:

For \(\lim_m \mathbb{E}[XY_m]\): the dominating function is \(|XY_m| \le |X||Y| \in L^1\), since \(\mathbb{E}[|X||Y|] \le \|X\|_2\|Y\|_2 < \infty\) by Cauchy–Schwarz.
For \(\lim_m \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\,Y_m]\): the dominating function is \(|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]||Y| \in L^1\). On each atom \(A_n\), \(|\mathbb{E}_{A_n}[X]| \le \mathbb{E}_{A_n}[|X|]\) by the triangle inequality \(|\mathbb{E}[Z]| \le \mathbb{E}[|Z|]\). Therefore, exchanging the countable sum and expectation via MCT on non-negative terms: \[\mathbb{E}[|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]||Y|] \le \sum_n \mathbb{E}_{A_n}[|X|]\,|\beta_n|\,\mathbb{P}(A_n) = \mathbb{E}[|X||Y|] \le \|X\|_2\|Y\|_2 < \infty.\]

Passing to the limit on both sides:
\[
\mathbb{E}[X Y] = \lim_{m \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[X Y_m] = \lim_{m \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] Y_m] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] Y].
\]

Finally, the measurability corollary gives \(\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]\in L^0(\mathcal G)\). On each \(A_n\), the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality under \(\mathbb P_{A_n}\) yields \[
\left|\mathbb E_{A_n}[X]\right|^2\le\mathbb E_{A_n}[X^2].
\] Therefore, using MCT for the non-negative series, \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\left[\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]^2\right]
&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left|\mathbb E_{A_n}[X]\right|^2\mathbb P(A_n) \\
&\le\sum_{n=1}^\infty\mathbb E_{A_n}[X^2]\mathbb P(A_n) \\
&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\mathbb E[X^2\mathbb I_{A_n}]
=\mathbb E[X^2].
\end{aligned}
\] Thus \(\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]\in L^2(\mathcal G)\) and \(\|\mathbb E_{\mathcal G}[X]\|_2\le\|X\|_2\).


Corollary 66.2 (Law of Total Expectation) Under the hypotheses of Theorem 66.1, taking \(Y = \mathbb{I}_\Omega = 1\) yields:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]] = \mathbb{E}[X].
\]

title: 68  Lecture 31.2: Conditional Expectation-Part II
section: 68.9 Remark on Averaging Property with Indicator Functions
text:
68.9 Remark on Averaging Property with Indicator Functions
The averaging property can be particularly useful when \(Y\) is taken as an indicator function of a \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable set \(A \in \mathcal{G}\): \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \mathbb{1}_A] = \mathbb{E}[X \mathbb{1}_A].
\] This shows that the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X]\) correctly averages \(X\) over the sets in \(\mathcal{G}\).
In terms of integral notation, the averaging property with indicator functions can be written as: \[
\int_A \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}[X] \, dP = \int_A X \, dP.
\] Thus, the conditional expectation preserves the integral of \(X\) over every event whose occurrence can be determined from \(\mathcal G\). That is why it is called the averaging property.
Finally, note that the indicator function characterization is equivalent to the averaging property for all bounded \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable functions, since any such function can be approximated by linear combinations of indicator functions.

title: 73  Lecture 33.2: Regular Conditional Distributions
text:
Theorem 73.1 (Conditional Expectation via Disintegration Kernel) Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) be a probability space, \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) and \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) be measurable spaces, and \(X: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) and \(Y: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) be random variables.
Let \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = (X, Y)^* \mathbb{P} \in \mathcal{P}(S_1 \times S_2, \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\) denote the joint pushforward distribution, and let \(\mu_X = X^* \mathbb{P} \in \mathcal{P}(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) denote the marginal distribution of \(X\).
If there exists a probability kernel \(Q\) from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) such that \[
\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes Q,
\tag{73.1}\] then for any \(f \in L^1(S_1 \times S_2, \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2, \mu_{(X,Y)})\) (or \(f \ge 0\)), we have \(\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X] = g(X)\) a.s., where \[
g(x) = \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy).
\tag{73.2}\] In short, \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X = x] = \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy).
\]


Remark 73.1 (Pushforward Distribution). Note that \(\mu_X = X^* \mathbb{P} \in \mathcal{P}(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) is the pushforward distribution of \(X\): \[
\mu_X(A) = \mathbb{P}(X \in A) = \mathbb{P}(X^{-1}(A)) \quad \text{for all }A \in \mathcal{B}_1.
\] Similarly, \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = (X,Y)^* \mathbb{P} \in \mathcal{P}(S_1 \times S_2, \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\) is the pushforward distribution of the pair \((X,Y)\): \[
\mu_{(X,Y)}(A \times B) = \mathbb{P}(X \in A, Y \in B) = \mathbb{P}((X,Y)^{-1}(A \times B)),
\] for all \(A \in \mathcal{B}_1, B \in \mathcal{B}_2\).


Proof (Proof of Theorem 73.1). By the characterization of conditional expectation, \(g(X) = \mathbb{E}[f(X,Y) \mid X]\) a.s. if and only if:

\(g(X)\) is \(\sigma(X)\)-measurable: this holds automatically because \(g\) is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable (by Lemma 72.1 applied to \(Q\)), and any measurable function of \(X\) is \(\sigma(X)\)-measurable.
For all bounded test functions \(h \in \mathcal{B}_b(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\): \[
\mathbb{E}\big[ f(X, Y) h(X) \big] = \mathbb{E}\big[ g(X) h(X) \big].
\]

It therefore suffices to verify condition (ii).
Case 1: Bounded Measurable Functions:
Assume \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S_1 \times S_2, \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\). By Change of Variables and the disintegration assumption \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes Q\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\big[ f(X, Y) h(X) \big] &= \int_{S_1 \times S_2} f(x, y) h(x) \, \mu_{(X,Y)}(dx \, dy) \\
&= \int_{S_1 \times S_2} f(x, y) h(x) \, (\mu_X \otimes Q)(dx \, dy) \\
&\stackrel{\text{Fubini}}{=} \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) h(x) \, \mu_X(dx) \\
&= \int_{S_1} g(x) h(x) \, \mu_X(dx) \\
&= \mathbb{E}\big[ g(X) h(X) \big].
\end{aligned}
\]
Case 2: Integrable Functions (\(f \in L^1\)):
If \(f \in L^1(\mu_{(X,Y)})\), define \(f_n = (f \wedge n) \vee (-n)\). Each \(f_n\) is bounded, so by Case 1, \(g_n(X) = \mathbb{E}[f_n(X,Y) \mid X]\) a.s., where \(g_n(x) = \int_{S_2} f_n(x, y) \, Q(x, dy)\).
As \(n \to \infty\), \(f_n \to f\) in \(L^1(\mathbb{P})\). By \(L^1\)-contractivity of conditional expectation, \(g_n(X) \to \mathbb{E}[f(X,Y) \mid X]\) in \(L^1(\mathbb{P})\). Concurrently: \[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{E}\left[ \left| g_n(X) - g(X) \right| \right] \\
&= \int_{S_1} \left| \int_{S_2} f_n(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) - \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right| \mu_X(dx) \\
&\le \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} |f_n(x, y) - f(x, y)| \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu_X(dx) \\
&= \int_{S_1 \times S_2} |f_n(x, y) - f(x, y)| \, (\mu_X \otimes Q)(dx \, dy) \\
&= \|f_n - f\|_{L^1(\mu_{(X,Y)})} \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\end{aligned}
\] Thus \(g(X) = \mathbb{E}[f(X,Y) \mid X]\) a.s.


Example 73.1 Suppose \(X\sim N(0,1)\) and, conditional on \(X=x\), \(Y\mid X=x\sim N(x,1)\). Thus, we can write \(Y=X+\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,1)\) is independent of \(X\). The conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=x\) is represented by the kernel \[
Q(x,dy)=\phi(y-x)\,dy,
\] where \(\phi\) is the standard normal density. Now consider the joint function \(f(x,y)=xy\). We want to calculate \(\mathbb E[XY\mid X]\). According to the theorem, \[
\mathbb E[XY\mid X=x] = \int_{\mathbb R}xy\,Q(x,dy).
\] Since \(x\) is fixed inside the conditional expectation, \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[XY\mid X=x] &=x\int_{\mathbb R}y\,Q(x,dy)\\ &=x\,\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].
\end{aligned}
\] But under the kernel \(Q(x,\cdot)\), \(Y\mid X=x\sim N(x,1)\), so \(\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]=x\). Therefore, \(\mathbb E[XY\mid X=x]=x^2\), and hence \(\mathbb E[XY\mid X]=X^2\).
The important point is that we do not need to work with the joint density of \((X,Y)\). We only need to know: \[
\boxed{Q(x,\cdot)=\text{the distribution of }Y\text{ when }X=x.}
\] Once we know this conditional distribution, the theorem tells us exactly how to calculate conditional expectations: \[
\boxed{ \mathbb E[f(X,Y)\mid X] = \int f(X,y)\,Q(X,dy). }
\] For example, with \(f(x,y)=y^2\), we immediately obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[Y^2\mid X=x] &=\int y^2 Q(x,dy)\\
&=x^2+1,
\end{aligned}
\] because \(Y\mid X=x\sim N(x,1)\). Hence \(\mathbb E[Y^2\mid X]=X^2+1\). So the kernel provides a recipe: fix the observed value of \(X\), use the corresponding distribution \(Q(x,\cdot)\) for \(Y\), and average the function \(f(x,Y)\) with respect to that distribution.

title: 73  Lecture 33.2: Regular Conditional Distributions
text:
73.2 Regular Conditional Distributions (RCD)
This raises a crucial question: Can we always find a probability kernel \(Q\) such that \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes Q\)? Note that if such a kernel exists and \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) is countably generated, it is unique \(\mu_X\)-almost surely. To that end, we define the regular conditional distribution (RCD) of \(Y\) given \(X\) as a probability kernel \(Q\) satisfying the conditional expectation property in Theorem 73.1.

Definition 73.1 (Regular Conditional Distribution) Let \(X: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) and \(Y: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) be random variables. A probability kernel \(Q\) from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) is called a regular conditional distribution (RCD) of \(Y\) given \(X\) if for every \(B \in \mathcal{B}_2\): \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_{\{Y\in B\}} \mid \sigma(X)] = \mathbb{P}(Y \in B \mid X) = Q(X, B) \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{73.3}\] Equivalently, for every bounded measurable function \(h \in \mathcal{B}_b(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\): \[
\mathbb{E}[h(Y) \mid X] = \int_{S_2} h(y) \, Q(X, dy) \quad \text{a.s.}
\tag{73.4}\]

The following result shows that \(Q\) is an RCD \(\implies\) \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes Q\). That is, an RCD is equivalent to a disintegration of the joint distribution.

Proposition 73.1 (Equivalence of RCD and Product Disintegration) If \(Q\) is a regular conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X\), then \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes Q\). Consequently, \(Q\) is unique \(\mu_X\)-almost surely if \(\mathcal{B}_2\) is countably generated.


Proof. To show \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes Q\), test on measurable rectangles \(A \times B \in \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{(X,Y)}(A \times B) &= \mathbb{P}(X \in A, Y \in B) \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{I}_A(X) \mathbb{I}_B(Y) \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{I}_A(X) \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_B(Y) \mid X] \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{I}_A(X) Q(X, B) \right] \quad \\
&= \int_A Q(x, B) \, \mu_X(dx) \\
&= (\mu_X \otimes Q)(A \times B).
\end{aligned}
\] where the third equality uses the averaging property of conditional expectation, the fourth equality uses the RCD definition in Equation 79.1, and the last equality uses the definition of the product measure in Definition 72.2. Since measures agreeing on generating rectangles agree on \(\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\), we have \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes Q\). Uniqueness \(\mu_X\)-a.s. follows directly from the kernel uniqueness theorem.


Remark 73.2 (Heuristic: The Product Rule “Jazzed Up”). To understand why an RCD extends from single-variable functions \(h(Y)\) to joint functions \(f(X,Y)\), consider \(f(x,y) = g(x) h(y)\): \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X] &= \mathbb{E}[g(X) h(Y) \mid X] \\
&= g(X) \mathbb{E}[h(Y) \mid X] \\
&= g(X) \int_{S_2} h(y) \, Q(X, dy) \\
&= \int_{S_2} f(X, y) \, Q(X, dy).
\end{align*}
\] The formal proposition establishes that this identity extends linearly and continuously to all joint integrable functions \(f(X, Y)\).

The reverse implication in Proposition 73.1 is also true: \(Q\) is an RCD of \(Y|X\) \(\iff\) \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes Q\).

title: 73  Lecture 33.2: Regular Conditional Distributions
text:
73.3 Existence of Regular Conditional Distributions
Does an RCD always exist for arbitrary measurable spaces? The answer is No! However, an RCD is guaranteed to exist whenever the target space \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) is “nice enough”—specifically, a Standard Borel Space (a space measure-isomorphic to a Borel subset of a Polish space). Below are two standard explicit constructions.

title: 73  Lecture 33.2: Regular Conditional Distributions
text:
73.6 Takeaways






TipKey Takeaways



1. RCDs Are the Rigorous Version of “Conditioning on \(X = x\).” A regular conditional distribution (RCD) of \(Y\) given \(X\) is a probability kernel \(Q: S_1 \times \mathcal{B}_2 \to [0,1]\) such that \(\mathbb{P}(Y \in B \mid X) = Q(X, B)\) a.s. for every \(B \in \mathcal{B}_2\). Unlike the naive conditional probability \(\mathbb{P}(Y \in B \mid X = x)\), which requires \(\mathbb{P}(X = x) > 0\), the kernel \(Q(x, \cdot)\) is defined simultaneously for all \(x\) with a single measurability condition, making it well-suited for continuous random variables.
2. RCD \(\Longleftrightarrow\) Disintegration of the Joint Distribution. A kernel \(Q\) is an RCD of \(Y\) given \(X\) if and only if \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes Q\) (the semi-direct product measure from Lecture 33.1). The forward direction follows by testing on rectangles using the tower property; the reverse follows from the generalized Fubini theorem. The two conditions are therefore interchangeable.
3. Computing Conditional Expectations from the RCD. When \(\mu_{(X,Y)} = \mu_X \otimes Q\), the conditional expectation of any jointly measurable \(f\) is given by \[
\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y) \mid X = x] = \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy),
\] for any \(f\) that is bounded or \(L^1(\mu_{(X,Y)})\). The proof verifies the two conditions for conditional expectation: (i) \(\sigma(X)\)-measurability (automatic since \(g(x) = \int f(x,y) Q(x,dy)\) is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable), and (ii) the integral characterization \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)h(X)] = \mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)h(X)]\) for all bounded \(h\), which follows from Fubini applied to \(\mu_X \otimes Q\). The \(L^1\) case is obtained by truncation and \(L^1\)-contractivity of conditional expectation.
4. Explicit Constructions of RCDs.

Density case: If \((X,Y)\) has joint density \(f_{X,Y}\) with respect to \(\nu_1 \otimes \nu_2\), set \(Q(x, B) = \int_B f_{Y|X}(y|x) \nu_2(dy)\). This is an RCD because \((\mu_X \otimes Q)(A \times B) = \int_A \int_B f_{X,Y}(x,y) \nu_2(dy) \nu_1(dx) = \mu_{(X,Y)}(A \times B)\) by Fubini, where the key cancellation is \(f_{Y|X}(y|x) \cdot f_X(x) = f_{X,Y}(x,y)\) on \(\{f_X > 0\}\).
Discrete case: If \(Y\) takes values in a countable set \(S_2\), set \(Q(x, \{y\}) = \mathbb{P}(Y = y \mid X = x)\) for \(\mathbb{P}(X = x) > 0\). Verification uses the countable additivity of conditional probability: \(Q(x, B) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(X = x, Y \in B)}{\mathbb{P}(X = x)} = \mathbb{P}(Y \in B \mid X = x)\).

5. Existence and Uniqueness. An RCD of \(Y\) given \(X\) need not exist for arbitrary measurable spaces, but is guaranteed to exist whenever \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) is a Standard Borel space (measure-isomorphic to a Borel subset of a Polish space). When it exists and \(\mathcal{B}_2\) is countably generated, the RCD is unique \(\mu_X\)-almost surely: if \(Q\) and \(\widetilde{Q}\) are both RCDs, then \(\mu_X \otimes Q = \mu_X \otimes \widetilde{Q}\), and the uniqueness theorem from Lecture 33.1 gives \(Q(x, \cdot) = \widetilde{Q}(x, \cdot)\) for \(\mu_X\)-a.e. \(x\).

title: 79  Lecture 36.2: Probability Kernels Revisited
text:
79.9 Takeaways

Notation. A probability kernel is denoted \(q\) (not \(Q\)); its associated Markov transition operator is denoted \(Q\) (not \(L\)), with \((Qf)(x) = \int_{S_2} f(y)\,q(x,\mathrm{d}y)\).
Kernels vs. operators. A probability kernel \(q\) and its transition operator \(Q\) carry the same information: \(q(x,B) = (Q\mathbb{I}_B)(x)\), and \(Q\) is recovered from \(q\) by integration (Equation 79.4). Theorem 79.1 shows \(Q\) is exactly a Markov transition operator iff it is linear, unit-preserving, positive, and continuous under bounded pointwise limits — the last property is what forces \(q(x,\cdot)\) to be countably additive, not merely finitely additive.
Regular conditional distributions are kernels. A regular conditional distribution \(q_{Y\vert X}\) is a probability kernel satisfying \(\mathbb{P}(Y \in B \mid X) = q_{Y\vert X}(X,B)\) a.s. (Definition 79.2). Existence is guaranteed whenever the space \(Y\) takes values in is standard Borel; no topological condition on the space of \(X\) is needed. Explicit constructions are available in the independent, density, and discrete cases, with the kernel extended arbitrarily off the (necessarily \(\mathbb{P}_X\)-null) degenerate set.
Uniqueness is subtle. Two kernels that induce the same action on a measure \(
u\) (i.e. \(
u q_1 = 
u q_2\)) need not agree \(
u\)-a.e. (Lemma 79.1). Genuine a.e.-uniqueness requires the stronger hypothesis that \(q_1(x,B) = q_2(x,B)\) for \(
u\)-a.e. \(x\), for every \(B\) — this is the condition that actually arises when comparing two regular conditional distributions of the same \(Y\) given \(X\).
Composition and disintegration. Kernels compose via the Chapman–Kolmogorov formula \((q_1q_2)(x,C) = \int_{S_2} q_2(y,C)\,q_1(x,\mathrm{d}y)\), dually to operator composition \(Q_1Q_2\). Iterating kernels \(q_1,\dots,q_n\) against an initial law \(
u\) builds a unique finite-dimensional product measure (Equation 79.7), which on product functions collapses to the nested operator expression \(\mathbb{E}_
u[f_1 Q_1(f_2 Q_2(\cdots Q_n(f_{n+1})\cdots))]\) (Proposition 79.2) — the finite-dimensional precursor to the Markov semigroup construction used in later lectures.

title: 80  Lecture 37.1: Markov Processes
text:
80.8 Takeaways

Markov property. An adapted process is Markov with respect to \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\) if conditioning on the whole past \(\mathcal{F}_s\) is the same as conditioning on the present \(X_s\), for every bounded measurable test function.
Transition kernels. On a standard Borel state space, \(\mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_s] = (Q_{s,t}f)(X_s)\) for a probability kernel \(q_{s,t}\) that is unique only \(\mu_{X_s}\)-almost everywhere.
Chapman–Kolmogorov. The Markov property implies \(Q_{r,t} = Q_{r,s}Q_{s,t}\) only almost everywhere with respect to \(\mu_{X_r}\), with exceptional sets depending on \((r,s,t)\). For this reason a Markov process is defined via a transition family satisfying Chapman–Kolmogorov at every point.
Both clauses are needed. A Chapman–Kolmogorov family satisfying Equation 80.9 does not make a process Markov; Example 80.1 (the pairwise independent triple \(X_2 = X_0 \oplus X_1\)) shows that the Markov property is a genuinely separate condition on the joint law.
Independent increments. An \(\mathbb{R}^d\)-valued process whose increments are independent of the past (including the initial value) is Markov with the translation kernel \(q_{s,t}(x,B) = \mathbb{P}(x + X_t - X_s \in B)\). Independence of the increments among themselves is not enough.
Discrete time. The one-step kernels determine everything via \(Q_{m,n} = Q_{m,m+1} \cdots Q_{n-1,n}\), and the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation becomes a sum over intermediate states (matrix multiplication for countable \(S\)).
Finite-dimensional distributions. The law of \((X_{t_0}, \dots, X_{t_n})\) is \(\nu_0(dx_0)\,q_{t_0,t_1}(x_0,dx_1)\cdots q_{t_{n-1},t_n}(x_{n-1},dx_n)\). Hence the initial law and the transition kernels determine the law of the process on the product \(\sigma\)-algebra.

title: 72  Lecture 33.1: Probability Kernels-Part 1
section: 72.2 Formal Definition of a Probability Kernel
text:
72.2 Formal Definition of a Probability Kernel
A probability kernel is a function in one variable and a probability measure in another variable. It is a generalization of the conditional distribution of one random variable given another.

Definition 72.1 (Probability Kernel) Let \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) and \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) be two measurable spaces. A function \(Q: S_1 \times \mathcal{B}_2 \to [0, 1]\) is called a probability kernel (or Markov kernel) from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) if it satisfies two conditions:

Measure Property: For every fixed \(x \in S_1\), the mapping \[
Q(x, \cdot): \mathcal{B}_2 \to [0, 1], \quad B \mapsto Q(x, B),
\] is a probability measure on \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\).
Measurability Property: For every fixed \(B \in \mathcal{B}_2\), the mapping \[
Q(\cdot, B): S_1 \to [0, 1], \quad x \mapsto Q(x, B),
\] is \(\mathcal{B}_1 / \mathcal{B}([0, 1])\)-measurable.


Some remarks on the definition:

Note that the domain of \(Q\) is \(S_1 \times \mathcal{B}_2\), where the first argument is a point in \(S_1\) and the second argument is a measurable set in \(\mathcal{B}_2\). The range of \(Q\) is the interval \([0, 1]\), representing probabilities.
If we think of \(Q\) as measure of \(y\) for a fixed \(x\), the notation we used when integrating with respect to \(Q\) is \[
\int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy),
\] where

\(x\) is fixed,
\(y\) is the variable of integration, and
\(Q(x, \cdot)\) is the probability measure on \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) for each fixed \(x \in S_1\).

This is consistent with the notation for integrating with respect to a measure \(\mu\) on \((S, \mathcal{B})\), where we write \(\int_S f(y) \, \mu(dy)\) rather than \(\int_S f(y) \, d\mu(y)\).
Since \(Q(x, \cdot): \mathcal{B}_2 \to [0, 1]\) is probability measure is on \((S_2,\mathcal B_2)\) for each fixed \(x \in S_1\), it satisfies the usual properties of a probability measure:

Non-negativity: \(Q(x, B) \ge 0\) for all \(B \in \mathcal{B}_2\).
Normalization: \(Q(x, S_2) = 1\).
Countable Additivity: For any countable collection \(\{B_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}\) of disjoint sets in \(\mathcal{B}_2\), \[
Q\Big(x, \bigcup_{i \in \mathbb{N}} B_i\Big) = \sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} Q(x, B_i).
\]

The mapping \(x \mapsto Q(x, B)\) is \(\mathcal{B}_1 / \mathcal{B}([0, 1])\)-measurable:
\[
\{x \in S_1 : Q(x, B) \in A\} \in \mathcal{B}_1,
\] for all \(A \in \mathcal{B}([0, 1])\).


Example 72.1 (Standard Examples of Probability Kernels)  

Constant / Product Measure Kernel: If \(\nu \in \mathcal{P}(S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) is a fixed probability measure, then \[
Q(x, B) := \nu(B) \quad \forall x \in S_1, \; B \in \mathcal{B}_2
\] is a probability kernel. This is called a constant kernel or product measure kernel. Note that this defines a probability kernel from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) for any measurable space \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\).
Conditional Density Kernel: If \((X, Y)\) has joint density \(f_{X,Y}(x, y)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^k\), then \[
\begin{align*}
Q(x, B) &:= \int_B f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) \, dy \\
&=
\begin{cases}
\frac{\int_B f_{X,Y}(x, y) \, dy}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^k} f_{X,Y}(x, y) \, dy} & \text{if } f_X(x) > 0, \\
\nu_0(B) & \text{if } f_X(x) = 0,
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
\] where \(\nu_0 \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^k, \mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}^k})\) is an arbitrary probability measure. This defines a probability kernel from \((\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}^d})\) to \((\mathbb{R}^k, \mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}^k})\).



Example 72.2 (A Bernoulli probability kernel) A very simple example is a kernel describing a Bernoulli random variable whose success probability depends on the value of \(x\). Let \(S_1=S_2=\mathbb R\), and \(\mathcal B_1=\mathcal B_2=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\). Define \[
Q(x,B) = (1-p(x))\mathbf 1_B(0)+p(x)\mathbf 1_B(1), \qquad B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R),
\] where, for example, \(p(x)=\frac{e^x}{1+e^x}\). Thus, for each \(x\), \(Q(x,\cdot)\) is the probability distribution of a Bernoulli random variable with success probability \(p(x)\): \[
Y\mid X=x \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}\left(\frac{e^x}{1+e^x}\right).
\]

Measure property: Fix \(x\in\mathbb R\). Then \[
Q(x,B) = (1-p(x))\mathbf 1_B(0)+p(x)\mathbf 1_B(1).
\] This is the probability measure that assigns \(Q(x,\{0\})=1-p(x)\) and \(Q(x,\{1\})=p(x)\). Since \(0\leq p(x)\leq1\), we have \(Q(x,\mathbb R)=1-p(x)+p(x)=1\). Moreover, because it is a weighted sum of the point-mass probability measures \(\delta_0\) and \(\delta_1\), it is a probability measure on \((\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))\).
Measurability property: Now fix \(B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\). We need to show that \(x\mapsto Q(x,B)\) is measurable. There are only four possibilities concerning whether \(0\) and \(1\) belong to \(B\). For example, if \(0\in B\) and \(1\notin B\), then \(Q(x,B)=1-p(x) =\frac{1}{1+e^x}\), which is a continuous, hence measurable, function of \(x\). If \(0\notin B\) and \(1\in B\), then \(Q(x,B)=p(x) =\frac{e^x}{1+e^x}\), which is also continuous. If both \(0,1\in B\), then \(Q(x,B)=1\), and if neither belongs to \(B\), then \(Q(x,B)=0\). Therefore \(x\mapsto Q(x,B)\) is measurable for every \(B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\).

The easiest way to visualize the kernel is \(x\longmapsto Q(x,\cdot)\). It takes an input \(x\) and returns a probability distribution. For example, \(x=0\Rightarrow p(0)=\frac12\), so \(Q(0,\cdot) = \frac12\delta_0+\frac12\delta_1\). At \(x=1\), \(p(1)=\frac{e}{1+e}\approx0.731\), so \(Q(1,\cdot) = 0.269\,\delta_0+0.731\,\delta_1\). At \(x=-1\), \(p(-1)=\frac{1}{1+e}\approx0.269\), so \(Q(-1,\cdot) = 0.731\,\delta_0+0.269\,\delta_1\). Thus the kernel is essentially a family of probability distributions indexed by \(x\).
Suppose \(X\) itself is a random variable. We can then use the kernel to define the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X\): \(\mathbb P(Y\in B\mid X) = Q(X,B)\). For example, \[
\mathbb P(Y=1\mid X) = Q(X,\{1\}) = \frac{e^X}{1+e^X}.
\] The measurability condition guarantees that this is a legitimate random variable: \(Q(X,B)\) is measurable whenever \(X\) is measurable.

title: 72  Lecture 33.1: Probability Kernels-Part 1
text:
72.3 Measurability and Integration Properties
The following lemma establishes the measurability of integral functions with respect to a probability kernel. It says that integrating a measurable function with respect to a probability kernel preserves measurability in the remaining variable.

Lemma 72.1 (Measurability of Integral Functions) Let \(Q\) be a probability kernel from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\). If \(f: S_1 \times S_2 \to \mathbb{R}\) is \((\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\)-measurable and is either bounded or non-negative, then the function \[
g(x) := \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy)
\tag{72.1}\] is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable.


Proof. We divide the proof into two main stages: bounded functions and non-negative functions (via Monotone Convergence).
Step 1: Bounded Measurable Functions Let \(\mathbb{H}\) be the vector space of bounded, \((\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\)-measurable functions \(f: S_1 \times S_2 \to \mathbb{R}\) for which \(x \mapsto \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy)\) is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable.
Let \(\mathbb{M} = \{ \mathbb{I}_{B_1 \times B_2} : B_1 \in \mathcal{B}_1, B_2 \in \mathcal{B}_2 \}\) be the collection of indicator functions of measurable rectangles. Note that \(\mathbb{M}\) is a multiplicative system — closed under pointwise products, since \(\mathbb{I}_{B_1 \times B_2} \cdot \mathbb{I}_{C_1 \times C_2} = \mathbb{I}_{(B_1 \cap C_1) \times (B_2 \cap C_2)} \in \mathbb{M}\) — and generates \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) = \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\). For any indicator function \(f = \mathbb{I}_{B_1 \times B_2}\) where \(B_1 \in \mathcal{B}_1\) and \(B_2 \in \mathcal{B}_2\): \[
\int_{S_2} \mathbb{I}_{B_1 \times B_2}(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) = \mathbb{I}_{B_1}(x) \int_{S_2} \mathbb{I}_{B_2}(y) \, Q(x, dy) = \mathbb{I}_{B_1}(x) Q(x, B_2).
\] Since \(\mathbb{I}_{B_1}(\cdot)\) is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable and \(Q(\cdot, B_2)\) is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable by definition of a probability kernel, their product is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable. Thus, \(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}\). \(\mathbb{H}\) also includes constant functions, so it contains the constant function \(1\).
Next, we will show that \(\mathbb{H}\) is closed under bounded monotone convergence. By linearity of integration, \(\mathbb{H}\) is a vector space. Furthermore, if \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathbb{H}\) is a sequence of bounded non-negative functions such that \(f_n \uparrow f\) with \(f\) bounded, then by the Dominated Convergence Theorem (or Monotone Convergence Theorem) applied to the probability measure \(Q(x, \cdot)\) for each \(x \in S_1\): \[
g_n(x) = \int_{S_2} f_n(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \longrightarrow \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) = g(x) \quad \forall x \in S_1.
\] As a pointwise limit of \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable functions \(g_n\), \(g\) is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable. By Dynkin’s Multiplicative System Theorem, \(\mathbb{H}\) contains all bounded \(\sigma(\mathbb{M})\)-measurable functions: \(\mathbb{B}(\sigma(\mathbb{M}))\subseteq \mathbb{H}\). But \(\sigma(\mathbb{M}) = \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\), so we conclude that \(x \mapsto \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy)\) is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable for all bounded \((\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\)-measurable functions \(f\).
Step 2: Non-Negative Measurable Functions If \(f \ge 0\) is \((\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\)-measurable, define the truncated sequence \(f_n(x, y) = f(x, y) \wedge n\). Each \(f_n\) is bounded and measurable, so \(x \mapsto \int_{S_2} f_n(x, y) \, Q(x, dy)\) is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable by Step 1. Since \(f_n \uparrow f\), the Monotone Convergence Theorem yields: \[
\int_{S_2} f_n(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \uparrow \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \quad \text{pointwise for all } x \in S_1.
\] Being the pointwise limit of a non-decreasing sequence of measurable functions, \(x \mapsto \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy)\) is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable.


Remark 72.1. The lemma is essentially a parameterized integration theorem. The ordinary result says that if \(f(x,y)\) is measurable, then integrating out \(y\) gives a measurable function of \(x\). Here the measure with respect to which we integrate also depends on \(x\): \[
g(x)=\int f(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)
\] The kernel’s measurability condition is exactly what makes this dependence on \(x\) well behaved.

title: 72  Lecture 33.1: Probability Kernels-Part 1
section: 72.4 Construction of the Semi-Direct Product Measure \(\mu \otimes Q\)
text:
72.4 Construction of the Semi-Direct Product Measure \(\mu \otimes Q\)
In the previous section, we defined a probability kernel \(Q\) from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\). We now show how to construct a probability measure \(\mu \otimes Q\) on the product space \((S_1 \times S_2, \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\) given a probability measure \(\mu\) on \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) and a probability kernel \(Q\).

Definition 72.2 (Product Measure \(\mu \otimes Q\)) Let \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) be a probability measure on \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\), and let \(Q\) be a probability kernel from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\). We define a set function \(\mu \otimes Q\) on measurable rectangles \(B_1 \times B_2 \in \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\) by: \[
\begin{align*}
(\mu \otimes Q)(B_1 \times B_2) &:= \int_{B_1} Q(x, B_2) \, \mu(dx)\\
&= \int_{S_1} \mathbb{I}_{B_1}(x) Q(x, B_2) \, \mu(dx).
\end{align*}
\] This extends uniquely to a probability measure on \((S_1 \times S_2, \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\), defined for any \(C \in \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\) by: \[
(\mu \otimes Q)(C) := \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} \mathbb{I}_C(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx).
\]

Some observations on the definition:

When \(Q\) is a constant kernel \(Q(x, \cdot) = \nu(\cdot)\) for all \(x \in S_1\), then \(\mu \otimes Q\) reduces to the standard product measure \(\mu \otimes \nu\) on \((S_1 \times S_2, \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\): \[
\begin{align*}
(\mu \otimes Q)(B_1 \times B_2) &= \int_{B_1} Q(x, B_2) \, \mu(dx) \\
&= \int_{B_1} \nu(B_2) \, \mu(dx) \\
&= \nu(B_2) \mu(B_1) \\
&= (\mu \otimes \nu)(B_1 \times B_2).
\end{align*}
\]
If we define \(C_x := \{ y \in S_2 : (x, y) \in C \}\), then we can write: \[
\begin{align*}
(\mu \otimes Q)(C) &= \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} \mathbb{I}_C(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx) \\
&= \int_{S_1} Q(x, C_x) \, \mu(dx).
\end{align*}
\] where \(Q(x, C_x)=\int_{S_2}\mathbb{I}_C(x,y)Q(x,dy)\) is the probability of the “slice” \(C_x\) under the measure \(Q(x, \cdot)\).


Remark 72.2 (Well-Definedness as a Probability Measure). To verify that \[
\mu\otimes Q\in\mathcal P(S_1\times S_2,\mathcal B_1\otimes\mathcal B_2),
\] we verify the defining properties of a probability measure.

Non-negativity: For every \(C\in\mathcal B_1\otimes\mathcal B_2\), \[
(\mu\otimes Q)(C)
=\int_{S_1}\int_{S_2}
\mathbb I_C(x,y)Q(x,dy)\mu(dx)
\ge 0,
\] since \(\mathbb I_C\ge0\) and both \(Q(x,\cdot)\) and \(\mu\) are non-negative measures.
Total Mass: \[
\begin{aligned}
(\mu\otimes Q)(S_1\times S_2)
&=
\int_{S_1}\left[\int_{S_2} \mathbb{I}_{S_1 \times S_2}(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right] \mu(dx) \\
&=
\int_{S_1}\left[\int_{S_2} 1 \cdot Q(x, dy) \right] \mu(dx)\\
&= \int_{S_1} Q(x, S_2) \, \mu(dx)\\
&= \int_{S_1} 1 \, \mu(dx)\\
&= \mu(S_1) = 1.
\end{aligned}
\] where the third equality follows because for each fixed \(x\), \(Q(x,⋅)\) is a probability measure on \(S_2\) and therefore \(Q(x,S_2)=1\).
Countable Additivity: Let \(\{C_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\subseteq\mathcal B_1\otimes\mathcal B_2\) be pairwise disjoint. Then, \(\mathbb I_{\cup_{k=1}^\infty C_k}(x,y)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\mathbb{I}_{C_k}(x,y)\). Since the partial sums on the right-hand side increase monotonically, the Monotone Convergence Theorem gives \[
\begin{aligned}
(\mu\otimes Q)\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty C_k\right)
&=
\int_{S_1}\int_{S_2}
\sum_{k=1}^\infty\mathbb I_{C_k}(x,y)Q(x,dy)\mu(dx)\\
&=
\sum_{k=1}^\infty
\int_{S_1}\int_{S_2}
\mathbb I_{C_k}(x,y)Q(x,dy)\mu(dx)\\
&=
\sum_{k=1}^\infty(\mu\otimes Q)(C_k).
\end{aligned}
\] Hence \(\mu\otimes Q\) is countably additive.



Example 72.3 The measure \(\mu\otimes Q\) describes a two-stage experiment:

Draw \(X\sim\mu\).
Given \(X=x\), draw \(Y\sim Q(x,\cdot)\).

Then \(\mu\otimes Q\) is the joint distribution of \((X,Y)\).
Suppose \(S_1=S_2=\mathbb R\), \(X\sim\mu\), and conditional on \(X=x\), \(Y\mid X=x\sim N(x,1)\). Then define \[
Q(x,B) = \int_B \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(y-x)^2/2}\,dy.
\] The joint distribution of \((X,Y)\) is \(\mu\otimes Q\). For example, \[
\begin{aligned}
P(X\in B_1,Y\in B_2) &= (\mu\otimes Q)(B_1\times B_2)\\
&= \int_{B_1} P(Y\in B_2\mid X=x)\,\mu(dx)\\
&= \int_{B_1} Q(x, B_2) \, \mu(dx)
\end{aligned}
\] This is precisely the familiar formula \[
P(X\in B_1,Y\in B_2) = \int_{B_1} P(Y\in B_2\mid X=x)\,P_X(dx).
\] So the abstract notation \(\mu\otimes Q\) is essentially a rigorous measure-theoretic formulation of “first draw \(X\), then draw \(Y\) according to a distribution that depends on \(X\).”

title: 72  Lecture 33.1: Probability Kernels-Part 1
section: 72.5 Generalized Fubini’s Theorem for Probability Kernels
text:
72.5 Generalized Fubini’s Theorem for Probability Kernels
The following result gives a generalized version of Fubini’s theorem for the semi-direct product measure \(\mu\otimes Q\). It expresses integration with respect to \(\mu\otimes Q\) as an iterated integral: first integrate with respect to the kernel \(Q(x,\cdot)\), and then integrate with respect to \(\mu\).

Lemma 72.2 (Integration with Respect to \(\mu \otimes Q\)) Let \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) and let \(Q\) be a probability kernel from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\). If \(f: S_1 \times S_2 \to \mathbb{R}\) is \((\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\)-measurable and is either bounded or non-negative (\(f \ge 0\)), then: \[
\begin{align*}
&\int_{S_1 \times S_2} f(x, y) \, d(\mu \otimes Q)\\
&=\int_{S_1 \times S_2} f(x, y) \, (\mu \otimes Q)(d(x,y)) \\
&= \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx).
\end{align*}
\tag{72.2}\]


Proof (Proof of Lemma 72.2). The proof proceeds by extending Equation 72.2 from the simplest functions to the full class via the standard monotone-class machinery.
Step 1: Indicator Functions:
For \(f = \mathbb{I}_C\) with \(C \in \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\), Equation 72.2 holds directly from the definition of \(\mu \otimes Q\) (Definition 72.2): \[
\begin{align*}
&\int_{S_1 \times S_2} \mathbb{I}_C(x, y) \, d(\mu \otimes Q) = (\mu \otimes Q)(C)\\
&= \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} \mathbb{I}_C(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx).
\end{align*}
\] In the special case \(C = B_1 \times B_2\), the inner integral simplifies as \(\int_{S_2} \mathbb{I}_{B_1 \times B_2}(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) = \mathbb{I}_{B_1}(x) Q(x, B_2)\), recovering \((\mu \otimes Q)(B_1 \times B_2) = \int_{B_1} Q(x, B_2) \, \mu(dx)\).
Step 2: Non-Negative Simple Functions:
Let \(f = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \, \mathbb{I}_{C_i}\) with \(c_i \ge 0\) and pairwise disjoint \(C_i \in \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\). By linearity of integration on both sides and Step 1 applied to each \(\mathbb{I}_{C_i}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
&\int_{S_1 \times S_2} f \, d(\mu \otimes Q)
= \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \, (\mu \otimes Q)(C_i) \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} \mathbb{I}_{C_i}(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx) \\
&= \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \, \mathbb{I}_{C_i}(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx) \\
&= \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx).
\end{aligned}
\] (The interchange of the finite sum with the integrals is justified by linearity.)
Step 3: Non-Negative Measurable Functions:
Let \(f \ge 0\) be \((\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\)-measurable. By the standard approximation theorem, there exist non-negative simple functions \(f_n \uparrow f\) pointwise. Step 2 gives Equation 72.2 for each \(f_n\): \[
\begin{align*}
\int_{S_1 \times S_2} f_n \, d(\mu \otimes Q) = \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} f_n(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx).
\end{align*}
\]

Left side: By the Monotone Convergence Theorem applied to \(\mu \otimes Q\), \[\int_{S_1 \times S_2} f_n \, d(\mu \otimes Q) \uparrow \int_{S_1 \times S_2} f \, d(\mu \otimes Q).\]
Right side: For each fixed \(x\), MCT applied to \(Q(x, \cdot)\) gives \(\int_{S_2} f_n(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \uparrow \int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy)\). The resulting pointwise non-decreasing sequence of \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable functions (measurable by Lemma 72.1) converges, and another application of MCT applied to \(\mu\) gives \[
\begin{align*}
&\int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} f_n(x,y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx) \\
&\uparrow \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} f(x,y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx).
\end{align*}
\]

Passing to the limit in the identity for \(f_n\) establishes Equation 72.2 for \(f\).
Step 4: Bounded Measurable Functions:
Let \(f\) be bounded and \((\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\)-measurable. Decompose \(f = f^+ - f^-\) where \(f^+ = \max(f, 0)\) and \(f^- = \max(-f, 0)\) are both bounded, non-negative, and jointly measurable. Applying Step 3 to each: \[
\begin{aligned}
&\int_{S_1 \times S_2} f \, d(\mu \otimes Q)
= \int_{S_1 \times S_2} f^+ \, d(\mu \otimes Q) - \int_{S_1 \times S_2} f^- \, d(\mu \otimes Q) \\
&= \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} f^+(x,y) \, Q(x,dy) \right) \mu(dx) - \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} f^-(x,y) \, Q(x,dy) \right) \mu(dx) \\
&= \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} \bigl[f^+(x,y) - f^-(x,y)\bigr] \, Q(x,dy) \right) \mu(dx) \\
&= \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} f(x,y) \, Q(x,dy) \right) \mu(dx).
\end{aligned}
\] (The subtraction is valid since both \(f^+\) and \(f^-\) are bounded, so both integrals are finite.)


Remark 72.3. The result in Lemma 72.2 has a very simple probabilistic interpretation. Suppose \(X\sim\mu\) and, conditional on \(X=x\), \(Y\mid X=x\sim Q(x,\cdot)\). Then \((X,Y)\sim\mu\otimes Q\). Consequently, \[
\mathbb E_{\mu\otimes Q}[f(X,Y)] = \mathbb E_\mu \left[ \mathbb E_{Q(X,\cdot)}[f(X,Y)] \right].
\] In other words, \[
\boxed{ \text{joint expectation} = \text{expectation of the conditional expectation}. } \] This is essentially the law of iterated expectations, expressed in measure-theoretic kernel notation. One particularly useful consequence is \[\int_{S_1\times S_2}f(x,y)\,(\mu\otimes Q)(d(x,y)) = \int_{S_1} \mathbb E_Q[f(x,Y)\mid X=x]\,\mu(dx),
\] which makes the connection with conditional distributions very transparent.


Example 72.4 Let \(S_1=S_2=\mathbb R\), \(\mathcal{B}_1=\mathcal{B}_2=\mathcal{B}(\mathbb R)\), and let \(\mu\) be the distribution of \(X\). Define the probability kernel \(Q(x,dy) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(y-x)^2/2}\,dy\). Thus, for each fixed \(x\), \(Y\mid X=x\sim N(x,1)\). The semi-direct product measure \(\mu\otimes Q\) is therefore the joint distribution of \((X,Y)\).
Take \(f(x,y)=y\). The kernel Fubini lemma says \[
\int_{\mathbb R^2}y\,(\mu\otimes Q)(d(x,y)) = \int_{\mathbb R} \left[ \int_{\mathbb R}y\,Q(x,dy) \right]\mu(dx).
\] Now consider the inner integral. Since \(Y\mid X=x\sim N(x,1)\), \(\int_{\mathbb R}y\,Q(x,dy) = \mathbb E[Y\mid X=x] = x\). Therefore, \(\int_{\mathbb R^2}y\,(\mu\otimes Q)(d(x,y)) = \mathbb E[X]\). Hence \(\mathbb E[Y]=\mathbb E[X]\). This is exactly what we would expect because \(\mathbb E[Y\mid X]=X\).
Take instead \(f(x,y)=xy\). Then the kernel Fubini formula gives \[
\int_{\mathbb R^2}xy\,(\mu\otimes Q)(d(x,y)) = \int_{\mathbb R} \left[ \int_{\mathbb R}xy\,Q(x,dy) \right]\mu(dx).
\] Since \(x\) is fixed in the inner integral, \[
\int_{\mathbb R}xy\,Q(x,dy) = x\int_{\mathbb R}y\,Q(x,dy) = x^2.
\] Consequently, \[
\int_{\mathbb R^2}xy\,(\mu\otimes Q)(d(x,y)) = \int_{\mathbb R}x^2\,\mu(dx)
\] or, in probabilistic notation, \(\mathbb E[XY]=\mathbb E[X^2]\). Again, this follows from \(\mathbb E[XY\mid X] = X\mathbb E[Y\mid X] = X^2\).

The following corollary gives the integrability criterion needed to extend the preceding kernel Fubini formula from bounded or non-negative functions to arbitrary integrable functions.

Corollary 72.1 (Integrability Criterion for \(\mu \otimes Q\)) Suppose \(f \in L^1(S_1 \times S_2, \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2, \mu \otimes Q)\). Then:

The integral \(\int_{S_2} |f(x, y)| \, Q(x, dy) < \infty\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x \in S_1\).
The partial integral mapping \[
g(x) =
\begin{cases}
\int_{S_2} f(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) & \text{if } \int_{S_2} |f(x, y)| \, Q(x, dy) < \infty,
\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\] is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable and belongs to \(L^1(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1, \mu)\).
The identity Equation 72.2 continues to hold.



Remark 72.4 (Conceptual Point). This corollary is the exact analogue of the standard Fubini theorem: \[
f\in L^1(\mu\otimes\nu) \quad\Longrightarrow
\begin{cases}
f(x,\cdot)\in L^1(\nu)\text{ for a.e. }x \\
x\mapsto\int f(x,y)\,\nu(dy)\in L^1(\mu).
\end{cases}
\] The only difference is that here the measure in the inner integral is allowed to depend on \(x\): \[
\nu(dy) \longrightarrow Q(x,dy).
\]


Proof (Proof of Corollary 72.1). Since \(f \in L^1(\mu \otimes Q)\), we have \(\|f\|_{L^1} = \int_{S_1 \times S_2} |f(x, y)| \, (\mu \otimes Q)(dx \, dy) < \infty\). By Lemma 72.2 applied to \(|f| \ge 0\): \[
\int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} |f(x, y)| \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx) = \|f\|_{L^1} < \infty.
\] Because the outer integral is finite, the non-negative integrand \(\int_{S_2} |f(x, y)| \, Q(x, dy)\) must be finite \(\mu\)-a.e. Thus \(\mu(\{ x \in S_1 : \int_{S_2} |f(x, y)| \, Q(x, dy) = \infty \}) = 0\).
Decomposing \(f = f^+ - f^-\), both \(f^+, f^- \in L^1(\mu \otimes Q)\). Applying linearity to the set where the integrals are finite gives: \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{S_1} g(x) \, \mu(dx) &= \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} f^+(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx) - \int_{S_1} \left( \int_{S_2} f^-(x, y) \, Q(x, dy) \right) \mu(dx) \\
&= \int_{S_1 \times S_2} f^+(x, y) \, (\mu \otimes Q)(dx \, dy) - \int_{S_1 \times S_2} f^-(x, y) \, (\mu \otimes Q)(dx \, dy) \\
&= \int_{S_1 \times S_2} f(x, y) \, (\mu \otimes Q)(dx \, dy).
\end{aligned}
\]
