section: 72.6 Uniqueness and Equivalence of Product Measures
text:
72.6 Uniqueness and Equivalence of Product Measures
The following result characterizes when two probability kernels induce the same semi-direct product measure. The forward implication always holds, while the reverse implication requires a countability condition on the target measurable space.

Lemma 72.3 (Almost-Sure Equality of Kernels and Product Measures) Let \(Q\) and \(\widetilde{Q}\) be probability kernels from \((S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\) to \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\), and let \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1)\).

Forward Implication: If \(Q(x, \cdot) = \widetilde{Q}(x, \cdot)\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x \in S_1\), then \(\mu \otimes Q = \mu \otimes \widetilde{Q}\) on \(\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\).
Reverse Implication: If \((S_2, \mathcal{B}_2)\) is countably generated (i.e., its \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}_2\) possesses a countable generator), then \(\mu \otimes Q = \mu \otimes \widetilde{Q}\) implies: \[
Q(x, \cdot) = \widetilde{Q}(x, \cdot) \quad \text{for } \mu\text{-almost every } x \in S_1.
\]



Proof (Proof of Lemma 72.3). Proof of Forward Implication (\(\Longrightarrow\)) Assume \(Q(x, \cdot) = \widetilde{Q}(x, \cdot)\) for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x \in S_1\). By Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) Theorem, it suffices to verify equality on measurable rectangles \(B_1 \times B_2 \in \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\): \[
\begin{align*}
(\mu \otimes Q)(B_1 \times B_2) &= \int_{B_1} Q(x, B_2) \, \mu(dx) \\
&= \int_{B_1} \widetilde{Q}(x, B_2) \, \mu(dx) \\
&= (\mu \otimes \widetilde{Q})(B_1 \times B_2).
\end{align*}
\] Hence \(\mu \otimes Q = \mu \otimes \widetilde{Q}\).
Proof of Reverse Implication (\(\Longleftarrow\)) Assume \(\mu \otimes Q = \mu \otimes \widetilde{Q}\). Testing on rectangles \(B_1 \times B_2 \in \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\): \[
\int_{B_1} Q(x, B_2) \, \mu(dx) = \int_{B_1} \widetilde{Q}(x, B_2) \, \mu(dx) \quad \forall B_1 \in \mathcal{B}_1, \, B_2 \in \mathcal{B}_2.
\] Rearranging terms: \[
\int_{B_1} \left( Q(x, B_2) - \widetilde{Q}(x, B_2) \right) \mu(dx) = 0 \quad \forall B_1 \in \mathcal{B}_1.
\] Setting \(B_1 = \{ x \in S_1 : Q(x, B_2) - \widetilde{Q}(x, B_2) > 0 \} \in \mathcal{B}_1\): the integrand is non-negative on \(B_1\) and the integral equals zero, so \(\mu\{Q(\cdot, B_2) > \widetilde{Q}(\cdot, B_2)\} = 0\). Setting \(B_1 = \{ x \in S_1 : Q(x, B_2) - \widetilde{Q}(x, B_2) < 0 \} \in \mathcal{B}_1\): the integrand is non-positive on \(B_1\) and the integral equals zero, so \(\mu\{Q(\cdot, B_2) < \widetilde{Q}(\cdot, B_2)\} = 0\). Together, \(Q(x, B_2) = \widetilde{Q}(x, B_2)\) for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x \in S_1\). Let \(N_{B_2} = \{ x \in S_1 : Q(x, B_2) \neq \widetilde{Q}(x, B_2) \}\), so \(\mu(N_{B_2}) = 0\).
Since \(\mathcal{B}_2\) is countably generated, there exists a countable algebra \(\mathcal{A}_2 \subseteq \mathcal{B}_2\) generating \(\mathcal{B}_2\). Define the exceptional set: \[
N := \bigcup_{B \in \mathcal{A}_2} N_B.
\] As a countable union of \(\mu\)-null sets, \(\mu(N) = 0\). For any fixed \(x \notin N\), \(Q(x, B) = \widetilde{Q}(x, B)\) for all \(B \in \mathcal{A}_2\). By the uniqueness of extension in Carathéodory’s / Dynkin’s Theorem, two probability measures agreeing on a generating algebra \(\mathcal{A}_2\) must coincide on all of \(\mathcal{B}_2\). Thus, \(Q(x, \cdot) = \widetilde{Q}(x, \cdot)\) for all \(x \notin N\).

title: 72  Lecture 33.1: Probability Kernels-Part 1
text:
72.7 Takeaways






TipKey Takeaways



1. Probability Kernels Generalize Conditional Distributions. A probability kernel \(Q: S_1 \times \mathcal{B}_2 \to [0,1]\) is simultaneously a probability measure in its second argument (for each fixed \(x\)) and a measurable function in its first argument (for each fixed \(B\)). This two-in-one structure is the rigorous formalization of a family of conditional distributions \(\{Q_x\}_{x \in S_1}\), as illustrated by \(Q_x(B) = \int_B f_{Y|X}(y|x)\,dy\) in the density setting. Any fixed probability measure \(\nu\) defines a constant (trivial) kernel \(Q(x,\cdot) = \nu\).
2. Integration Against a Kernel Preserves Measurability. For a jointly measurable \(f: S_1 \times S_2 \to \mathbb{R}\) that is bounded or non-negative, the partial integral \[x \mapsto \int_{S_2} f(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)\] is \(\mathcal{B}_1\)-measurable. The proof uses the Multiplicative System Theorem: indicator functions of measurable rectangles form a multiplicative system inside \(\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\), and the class \(\mathbb{H}\) of functions for which the conclusion holds is a vector space closed under bounded monotone limits. Since \(\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}\), the theorem forces all bounded jointly measurable functions into \(\mathbb{H}\); non-negative functions are then handled by truncation and MCT.
3. The Semi-Direct Product Measure \(\mu \otimes Q\). Given \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}(S_1)\) and a kernel \(Q\), the formula \[
(\mu \otimes Q)(C) = \int_{S_1} Q(x, C_x)\,\mu(dx), \qquad C_x := \{y \in S_2 : (x,y) \in C\},
\] defines a probability measure on \((S_1 \times S_2, \mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2)\), verified via non-negativity, total mass \(= 1\) (since \(Q(x, S_2) = 1\) for each \(x\)), and countable additivity (via MCT for the indicator sum). When \(Q(x,\cdot) = \nu\) (constant kernel), \(\mu \otimes Q\) reduces to the ordinary product measure \(\mu \otimes \nu\).
4. Generalized Fubini–Tonelli Theorem. For any \(f\) that is jointly measurable and bounded, non-negative, or \(L^1(\mu \otimes Q)\): \[
\int_{S_1 \times S_2} f(x,y)\,d(\mu \otimes Q) = \int_{S_1}\!\left(\int_{S_2} f(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)\right)\mu(dx).
\] This reduces to classical Fubini–Tonelli when \(Q\) is constant. For \(f \in L^1(\mu \otimes Q)\): applying this identity to \(|f|\) shows the inner integral is finite \(\mu\)-a.e., and the full identity then follows by splitting \(f = f^+ - f^-\).
5. Uniqueness: Kernels Are Determined \(\mu\)-Almost Everywhere. Two kernels \(Q\) and \(\widetilde{Q}\) satisfy \(\mu \otimes Q = \mu \otimes \widetilde{Q}\) if and only if \(Q(x,\cdot) = \widetilde{Q}(x,\cdot)\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\) (the reverse direction requires \(\mathcal{B}_2\) to be countably generated).

Forward: Agreement \(\mu\)-a.s. implies equal integrals over every \(B_1\) for every \(B_2\), so the two product measures agree on all rectangles, hence on all of \(\mathcal{B}_1 \otimes \mathcal{B}_2\) by Dynkin’s theorem.
Reverse: Testing against \(B_1 = \{Q(\cdot, B_2) > \widetilde{Q}(\cdot, B_2)\}\) and \(B_1 = \{Q(\cdot, B_2) < \widetilde{Q}(\cdot, B_2)\}\) separately gives \(\mu\)-a.s. equality for each fixed \(B_2\). Countable generation of \(\mathcal{B}_2\) yields a single \(\mu\)-null exceptional set \(N\) (a countable union of null sets) outside of which \(Q(x,\cdot) = \widetilde{Q}(x,\cdot)\) on a generating algebra, and hence on all of \(\mathcal{B}_2\) by Carathéodory’s uniqueness theorem.

title: 81  Lecture 37.2: Kolmogorov Extension Theorem
text:
81.6 Takeaways

The reverse problem. Given a consistent family of finite-dimensional distributions \(\{\mu_\Lambda\}_{\Lambda \subseteq T, \, |\Lambda| < \infty}\) (Definition 81.2), Kolmogorov’s Extension Theorem produces an actual process on the canonical product space \((S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\) realizing exactly those marginals, with no restriction on the cardinality of \(T\).
Standard Borel is the right hypothesis. The theorem genuinely needs \((S,\mathcal{B})\) to be standard Borel; this is what lets the classical, tightness-based countable-index theorem (Corollary 35.2, Lecture 16.2) be bootstrapped to an arbitrary index set \(T\) by reducing countable additivity on the cylinder algebra to countable additivity on the countable sub-product \(S^L\) determined by any given decreasing sequence of cylinder sets.
Cylinder sets behave like a generating algebra. Every measurability, well-definedness, and limit argument in the proof reduces to one fact: finite-dimensional projections \(\pi_\Lambda\) factor consistently (\(\pi_\Lambda = p_\Lambda^{\Lambda'}\circ\pi_{\Lambda'}\)) and are surjective, so set relations transfer freely between a cylinder set on \(S^T\) and any of its finite-dimensional representations.
Canonical construction of Markov processes. An initial law \(\nu\) together with a Chapman–Kolmogorov-consistent transition family \(\{Q_{s,t}\}_{s\le t}\) determines a unique probability measure \(\mathbb{P}^\nu\) on \((S^T,\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\) under which the coordinate process is Markov with exactly these ingredients — provided \(T\) has a least element \(0\), so that “initial law” is meaningful.
Mind the starting point. When assembling the finite-dimensional law \(\mu_\Lambda\) for \(\Lambda = \{t_0 < \dots < t_n\}\) not containing \(0\), the correct marginal at \(t_0\) is \(\nu Q_{0,t_0}\) — the law \(\nu\) pushed forward through the transition kernel from \(0\) to \(t_0\) — not \(\nu\) itself; using \(\nu\) directly would silently assume \(\nu\) is invariant under the transition semigroup.
Chapman–Kolmogorov consistency and the Markov property are separate. Verifying that \(\{\mu_\Lambda\}\) is projectively consistent only uses the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations; it says nothing yet about conditioning on the whole past. The Markov property itself is established separately, in Step 2, via a generating class of finite-dimensional cylinder functions and Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem.

title: 82  Lecture 38.1: Path Space
text:
82.7 Takeaways

Law of a process vs. the canonical coordinate process. Any stochastic process \(X\) on an arbitrary probability space has a well-defined law \(P_X \in \mathcal{P}(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\) (Definition 82.1), but \(X\) need not literally be the coordinate process constructed by the Kolmogorov Extension Theorem — the two share only their finite-dimensional distributions.
The product \(\sigma\)-algebra is too small for path properties. Every \(E \in \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\) depends on only countably many coordinates (Remark 82.1), so for \(T = [0,\infty)\), sets like \(C([0,\infty),\mathbb{R})\) that genuinely depend on uncountably many coordinates are not \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\)-measurable at all.
Brownian motion and the Poisson process as Markov processes built from the KET. Both are specified by an initial law together with a transition kernel (Gaussian, resp. Poisson), which is readily checked to satisfy Chapman–Kolmogorov; the Kolmogorov Extension Theorem then produces a process with the correct finite-dimensional distributions, including independent increments and (for a Markov process with a translation-invariant kernel) the correct marginal law of each increment. What the KET construction does not automatically provide is path regularity (continuity for BM, cadlag unit-jump paths for the Poisson process) — these are additional facts (Kolmogorov’s continuity theorem, explicit series or renewal constructions) that must be established separately, and that require \(N_0 = 0\) (resp. \(B_0 = 0\)) to even be meaningful.
The arrival-time characterization genuinely needs path regularity. Showing that the jump times of a Poisson process have i.i.d. \(\text{Exp}(\lambda)\) increments (Proposition 82.1) requires not just independent Poisson increments but also that \(N\) has non-decreasing, right-continuous, unit-jump paths starting at \(0\) — without this, the hitting times \(X_n = \inf\{t : N_t = n\}\) need not correspond to literal jump times of the path.
Moral: transition kernels do not determine sample path properties. Two processes with identical finite-dimensional distributions (e.g. \(N\) and its left-continuous modification \(M = N_{-}\)) can have incompatible path properties (right- vs. left-continuity); selecting a version with the “correct” regularity is a separate construction, not a consequence of the finite-dimensional distributions (Remark 82.2).

title: 83  Lecture 38.2: Time-Homogeneous Markov Processes
text:
83.6 Takeaways

Time homogeneity collapses \(\{Q_{s,t}\}\) to a semigroup. The reduction \(Q_{s,t} = Q_{0,t-s}\) (Definition 83.1), combined with the general Chapman-Kolmogorov equations Equation 83.1 that any transition family already satisfies, implies — rather than merely renames — the one-parameter semigroup law \(Q_sQ_t=Q_{s+t}\), \(Q_0=\mathrm{Id}\) (Definition 83.2). A time-homogeneous Markov process is exactly a Markov process whose transition operators reduce this way.
The canonical family \(\{\mathbb{P}^\nu\}_{\nu}\). Fixing the semigroup \((Q_t)_{t\ge0}\), all finite-dimensional distributions — and hence, via the Kolmogorov Extension Theorem, a canonical probability measure \(\mathbb{P}^\nu\) on path space — are determined by the initial law \(\nu\) alone; \(\mathbb{P}^x := \mathbb{P}^{\delta_x}\) is the Dirac/single-starting-point case.
The shift property (Theorem 83.1) is the rigorous form of “restarting the process at \(X_t\).” Statement 1 (measurability of \(x \mapsto \mathbb{E}^x[F(X_\cdot)]\)) holds for any measurable transition kernel family and does not use time homogeneity. Statement 2 — that conditioning the shifted path functional \(F(X_{t+\cdot})\) on the whole past \(\mathcal{F}_t\) is the same as conditioning on \(X_t\) alone, and equals \(\mathbb{E}^{X_t}[F(X_\cdot)]\) — genuinely uses time homogeneity (to identify the post-\(t\) kernels with the original ones) and is the basis for the strong Markov property developed in later lectures.
Proof technique: reduce to cylinder functions via the Multiplicative Systems Theorem. As in Theorem 78.1 (Lecture 36.1), the argument is carried out first for finite products \(f_0(w(t_0))\cdots f_n(w(t_n))\) of bounded measurable functions — a multiplicative system generating \(\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}\) — and then extended to all of \(\mathcal{B}_b(S^T,\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})\) by checking that the class of functionals satisfying statements 1–2 is a vector space, containing \(1\), closed under bounded convergence.

title: 84  Lecture 39.1: Markov Matrix
text:
84.5 Takeaways

Time-homogeneity collapses Chapman–Kolmogorov to iterating one operator. Because \(Q_{s,t}\) depends only on \(t-s\) (Lecture 38.2), the discrete-time family \((Q_n)_{n\ge0}\) satisfies \(Q_{n+m}=Q_nQ_m\) (Equation 84.1), and induction from \(Q_0=\mathrm{Id}\) gives \(Q_n=Q_1^n\) (Equation 84.2): the entire dynamics is encoded in the single 1-step operator \(Q_1\).
Translation-invariant walks give \(Q_1\) as convolution with the step law. For the random walk \(X_n=\sum_{k\le n}\xi_k\) (Example 84.1), \((Q_1f)(x)=\int f(x+y)\,\mu_{\xi_1}(\mathrm dy)\) because shifting the start to \(x\) only shifts the increment \(\xi_1\), not its law. The simple random walk on \(\mathbb Z\) (Equation 84.6) is the lattice special case \((Q_1f)(x)=pf(x+1)+(1-p)f(x-1)\), which is symmetric only when \(p=1/2\); otherwise the walk has nonzero drift \(2p-1\).
Not every chain is translation-invariant. The Ehrenfest urn (Example 84.2) shows a genuinely state-dependent kernel: the probability of moving left or right depends on the current occupancy \(i\), not just on a fixed increment law, yet it is still a time-homogeneous Markov chain.
On a countable state space, operators become matrices. With \(S\) countable, \(Q_1\) is represented by the stochastic matrix \(P=(P_{ij})\) (Definition 84.1, Equation 84.11), \(Q_n\) by \(P^n\) (Equation 84.12), and the evolution of the marginal law by row-vector times matrix, \(\boldsymbol\nu_n=\boldsymbol\nu_0P^n\) (Equation 84.13). Conversely, any stochastic matrix is the transition matrix of some chain, via the Kolmogorov extension theorem.
Marginals alone do not determine the chain. \(\boldsymbol\nu_n=\boldsymbol\nu_0P^n\) only tracks one-time distributions; joint (multi-time) distributions need the Markov property explicitly, e.g. \(\mathbb P(X_n=j,X_m=k)=[\boldsymbol\nu_0P^n]_j[P^{m-n}]_{jk}\) for \(n<m\) (Remark 84.2) — the full finite-dimensional distributions are recovered by chaining transition matrices across the gaps between observation times.
Finite chains have a natural graph picture. A stochastic matrix \(P\) on a finite \(S\) is equivalent to a weighted directed graph with edge weights \(P_{ij}\); time-homogeneity means these weights do not change with \(n\), setting up the graph-theoretic tools (communicating classes, periodicity, stationary distributions) developed in later lectures.

title: 85  Lecture 39.2: Markov Generator
text:
85.6 Takeaways

The generator turns the semigroup law into a differential equation. Since \((Q_t)_{t\ge0}\) satisfies \(Q_{t+s}=Q_tQ_s\), \(Q_0=\mathrm{Id}\) (Equation 85.1), if \(Q_t=e^{tA}\) for some operator \(A\), then \(A\) is recovered as the one-sided derivative \(A=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(Q_t-\mathrm{Id})/t\) (Equation 85.2), and conversely the whole semigroup is reconstructed from \(A\) by exponentiating. The generator is thus the “infinitesimal description” of a Markov process.
On a finite state space, generators are exactly the \(Q\)-matrices. Proposition 85.1 shows \(Q_t=e^{tA}\) defines a valid Markov semigroup iff \(A\) has non-negative off-diagonal entries and zero row sums — the classical intensity-matrix conditions. The (\(\Leftarrow\)) direction is proved via the shift trick \(A=B-cI\) with \(B\ge0\) entrywise, which simultaneously gives positivity of \(Q_t\) (via the non-negative series \(e^{tB}\)) and conservation of probability (via \(A\mathbf 1=0 \Rightarrow A^k\mathbf 1 = 0\) for \(k\ge1\)).
Not every Markov semigroup has a generator. Example 85.1 exhibits a perfectly valid semigroup (\(Q_t=P\) for all \(t>0\), \(Q_0=\mathrm{Id}\)) that is discontinuous at \(t=0\) whenever \(|S|\ge2\), so no bounded \(A\) with \(Q_t=e^{tA}\) can exist (such a family is automatically continuous at \(0\)). Existence of a generator is therefore a genuine extra hypothesis (continuity of \(t\mapsto Q_t\) at \(t=0\)), not automatic.
Bounded generators: the Poisson process. For the Poisson process, \(A=\lambda(T-\mathrm{Id})\) (forward-shift minus identity, scaled by the rate \(\lambda\)) is a bounded operator on \(\mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{N}_0)\) (Theorem 85.1), so \(Q_t=e^{tA}\) holds literally as a convergent operator-norm series — the discrete-state-space picture carries over verbatim to the countably infinite case because \(\|A\|\le2\lambda<\infty\).
Unbounded generators: Brownian motion. The generator of Brownian motion is \(Af=\tfrac12f''\) (Proposition 85.2), proved via a second-order Taylor expansion of \(f(x+B_t)\) combined with dominated convergence. Unlike the Poisson case, \(A\) cannot be bounded on all of \(\mathcal{B}_b(\mathbb{R})\): it is not even classically defined outside \(C_b^2(\mathbb{R})\), since indicator-type functions have no second derivative and their smooth approximations have second derivatives blowing up (Remark 85.3). This is the generic situation for diffusions, not a pathology specific to Brownian motion.
Domain restriction, not boundedness, is the right generalization. The Brownian/Poisson contrast shows that “bounded generator on \(\mathcal{B}_b\)” is too strong a requirement for continuous-state-space processes; the correct framework (Feller semigroups, restricting to \(C_0(\mathbb{R})\) with a dense domain \(\mathcal{D}(A)\)) is what must replace it, motivating the operator-theoretic machinery developed in Lecture 40.1.

title: Probability Theory
text:
Probability Theory I
The first part consists of 41 lectures on the fundamentals of probability theory. We begin with the Banach–Tarski paradox by showing that we cannot define a set function on all subsets of a unit circle in the complex plane that satisfies the usual properties of a measure. This motivates the need for a rigorous theory of measure, which forms the foundation of probability theory. We then introduce sigma-algebras, measures, and related concepts, and discuss the construction of measures from pre-measures defined on algebras, showing how these measures can be extended to complete measures on sigma-algebras, including the construction of Lebesgue and Radon measures. This part then continues with measurable functions (random variables) and their properties. We introduce integration theory for measurable functions, including the Lebesgue integral, and develop three important convergence theorems: the Monotone Convergence Theorem, Fatou’s Lemma, and the Dominated Convergence Theorem. We then cover product measures and Tonelli’s and Fubini’s theorems for iterated integration, followed by independence of events and random variables.
We then discuss Kolmogorov’s extension theorem for constructing stochastic processes with specified finite-dimensional distributions, Kolmogorov’s zero-one law governing the long-run behavior of independent sequences, and convolution as a tool for computing the distribution of a sum of independent random variables. We introduce Kolmogorov’s convergence criterion, which paves the way for the Strong Law of Large Numbers and the study of almost sure convergence of series of independent random variables. We finally close this part by applying the Strong Law of Large Numbers to basic concepts in renewal theory.






Figure 1: Probability Theory I

title: Probability Theory
text:
Probability Theory II
The second part consists of 44 lectures. We start with Cramér’s Large Deviations Principle, which provides a framework for understanding the probabilities of rare events in terms of the Legendre transform of the cumulant generating function. We then introduce total variation distance and Wasserstein distance for quantifying the difference between probability measures. We then move on to study weak and vague convergence of probability measures, and explore their implications for the convergence of random variables. We cover Prokhorov’s theorem and its applications to tightness and relative compactness of probability measures. The skorokhod representation theorem is also discussed, providing a powerful tool for constructing almost surely convergent sequences of random variables that mirror the weak convergence of their distributions.
We then discuss characteristic functions and their role in studying the distributions of random variables. Characteristic functions provide a powerful tool for analyzing convergence in distribution, as well as for deriving properties of sums of independent random variables. This set the stage for the central limit theorem and other limit theorems in probability theory.
The conditional probability and expectation are covered in detail, including their definitions and fundamental properties through seven lectures. We cover probability kernels and their role in defining conditional distributions and constructing new probability measures from existing ones through three lectures. This set the stage for rigorous treatment of Markov processes and their properties in the subsequent lectures.

title: 86  Lecture 40.1: Operator Norm Continuity
text:
86.8 Takeaways

The operator norm \(\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} = \sup_{\Vert{}f\Vert{}\le1}\Vert{}Af\Vert{}\) turns boundedness of a linear operator into a Lipschitz condition, and it is submultiplicative: \(\Vert{}AT\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} \le \Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}\Vert{}T\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}}\) (Lemma 86.1). This single inequality is the engine behind everything else in this lecture: it controls powers \(A^n\), the exponential series \(e^{tA}\), and products/limits of operators such as \(Q_t(Q_h - I)\).
On a Banach space \(B\), the space of bounded linear operators \((\mathcal{L}(B), \Vert{}\cdot\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}})\) is itself a Banach space (in fact a Banach algebra), so absolutely convergent operator series converge. This is what makes the operator exponential \(e^{tA} = \sum_{n\ge0} t^nA^n/n!\) well-defined and bounded whenever \(A\) is bounded (Corollary 86.1).
For a countable state space \(S\), bounded operators on \(\mathcal{B}(S)\) that arise from a matrix kernel \(q(i,j)\) are exactly characterized by \(\Vert{}A\Vert{}_{\mathrm{op}} = \Vert{}q\Vert{}_\infty\), the supremum of absolute row sums (Proposition 86.1)—but not every bounded operator on \(\mathcal{B}(S)\) arises this way, because \((\ell^\infty(S))^*\) is strictly larger than \(\ell^1(S)\).
The central result, Theorem 86.1, shows that operator norm continuity at a single time \(t=0\), together with the semigroup (Chapman–Kolmogorov) property \(Q_{s+t}=Q_sQ_t\), is already enough to force the entire semigroup to collapse to the simplest possible form: \(Q_t = e^{tA}\) for a bounded generator \(A\). This is special to the operator-norm topology—the semigroup property alone does not buy differentiability; continuity at one point is essential, and it must hold in operator norm, not merely strongly.
This is also a genuine limitation: most interesting continuous-time Markov chains and diffusions (e.g., Brownian motion, birth-death chains on infinite state spaces) have unbounded generators, so \(Q_t\) is only strongly (pointwise) continuous at \(t=0\), not operator norm continuous. The uniformly continuous case treated here is the technically simplest instance of the general Hille–Yosida theory of \(C_0\)-semigroups, in which the generator is replaced by a closed, densely defined operator \(A: \mathcal{D}(A) \subset B \to B\), and the exponential series is replaced by a more delicate construction (e.g., via the resolvent \((\lambda I - A)^{-1}\)).

title: 87  Lecture 40.2: Bounded Generators
text:
87.1 Introduction
In continuous-time Markov process theory, the transition operators \((Q_t)_{t \ge 0}\) form a semigroup of bounded linear operators on the space of bounded measurable functions. A central question in the analytical theory of Markov processes is the differentiability of the mapping \(t \mapsto Q_t\) with respect to the operator norm and the existence of a generator operator \(A\).
In these notes, we establish that under uniform operator-norm continuity at \(t = 0^+\), the semigroup \((Q_t)_{t \ge 0}\) is operator-norm differentiable for all \(t \in [0, \infty)\), the generator \(A\) is a bounded operator, and \(Q_t\) can be represented explicitly as an operator exponential \(Q_t = e^{tA}\).

title: 87  Lecture 40.2: Bounded Generators
text:
87.2 Main Theorem

Theorem 87.1 (Bounded Generator Theorem) Let \((S, \mathcal{B})\) be a measurable space, and let \((Q_t)_{t \ge 0}\) be a semigroup of Markov transition operators on \(\mathcal{B}_b(S)\), the Banach space of real-valued, bounded, \(\mathcal{B}\)-measurable functions endowed with the supremum norm \(\|f\|_\infty = \sup_{x \in S} |f(x)|\). That is, each \(Q_t\) is a linear, positivity-preserving operator with \(Q_t 1 = 1\), and the family satisfies the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations \[
Q_0 = I, \qquad Q_{s+t} = Q_s Q_t \quad \text{for all } s, t \ge 0.
\tag{87.1}\] Suppose further that \((Q_t)_{t \ge 0}\) is operator-norm continuous at \(t = 0^+\): \[
\lim_{t \downarrow 0} \|Q_t - I\|_{\text{op}} = 0,
\tag{87.2}\] where \(I\) denotes the identity operator on \(\mathcal{B}_b(S)\).
Then:

The mapping \(t \mapsto Q_t\) is operator-norm differentiable on \([0, \infty)\) (one-sided at \(t = 0\)).
The infinitesimal generator defined by
\[
A := \lim_{h \downarrow 0} \frac{Q_h - I}{h} = \left. \frac{d}{dt} Q_t \right|_{t=0^+}
\tag{87.3}\]
exists in the operator norm and satisfies \(\|A\|_{\text{op}} < \infty\).
For all \(t \ge 0\), the transition operator is given by the operator exponential
\[
Q_t = e^{tA} := \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n!} A^n,
\tag{87.4}\]
where the series converges uniformly in the operator norm on compact subintervals of \([0, \infty)\).
In particular, \((Q_t)_{t \ge 0}\) satisfies the Kolmogorov forward and backward differential equations:
\[
\frac{d}{dt} Q_t = Q_t A = A Q_t, \quad Q_0 = I.
\tag{87.5}\]

title: 87  Lecture 40.2: Bounded Generators
text:
87.3 Motivational Example: Poisson Process

Example 87.1 (Discrete State Space Poisson Process) Consider a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda > 0\) on the state space \(S = \mathbb{N}_0 = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\) equipped with the discrete \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}_0)\). The transition probabilities are given by: \[
q_t(i, j) = \mathbb{P}(X_t = j \mid X_0 = i) = e^{-\lambda t} \frac{(\lambda t)^{j-i}}{(j-i)!} \mathbb{I}_{\{j \ge i\}},
\tag{87.6}\] for \(i, j \in \mathbb{N}_0\). We verify condition (Equation 87.2) directly. Since \(\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}_0)\) is discrete, \(Q_t - I\) is represented by the matrix kernel \(q_t(i,j) - \delta_{ij}\), and by the row-sum operator-norm formula (Proposition 86.1, Lecture 40.1): \[
\begin{aligned}
\|Q_t - I\|_{\text{op}} &= \sup_{i \in \mathbb{N}_0} \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} |q_t(i, j) - \delta_{ij}| \\
&= \sup_{i \in \mathbb{N}_0} \left( |q_t(i, i) - 1| + \sum_{j > i} q_t(i, j) \right) \\
&= \sup_{i \in \mathbb{N}_0} \left( |e^{-\lambda t} - 1| + e^{-\lambda t} \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(\lambda t)^k}{k!} \right) \\
&= (1 - e^{-\lambda t}) + e^{-\lambda t} (e^{\lambda t} - 1) \\
&= 2(1 - e^{-\lambda t}).
\end{aligned}
\]
As \(t \downarrow 0\), we have:
\[
\lim_{t \downarrow 0} \|Q_t - I\|_{\text{op}} = \lim_{t \downarrow 0} 2(1 - e^{-\lambda t}) = 0.
\]
Thus, the Poisson process semigroup is uniformly operator-norm continuous at \(t = 0\). The infinitesimal generator \(A\) corresponds to the infinite matrix:
\[
A_{ij} = \left. \frac{d}{dt} q_t(i,j) \right|_{t=0^+} = \begin{cases} -\lambda & \text{if } j = i, \\ \lambda & \text{if } j = i+1, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
\]

title: 87  Lecture 40.2: Bounded Generators
text:
87.4 Proof of the Main Theorem
We break the proof into several logical steps.

87.4.1 Step 1: Norm Boundedness of \(Q_t\) and Continuity on \([0, \infty)\)
Since \((Q_t)_{t \ge 0}\) are Markov transition operators, they preserve positivity and satisfy \(Q_t 1 = 1\). Consequently, for any \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\), \[
\|Q_t f\|_\infty = \sup_{x \in S} |Q_t f(x)| \le \sup_{x \in S} Q_t |f|(x) \le \|f\|_\infty Q_t 1 = \|f\|_\infty.
\] Thus, \(\|Q_t\|_{\text{op}} \le 1\) for all \(t \ge 0\). Now, let \(t \ge 0\). For any \(h > 0\), using the Chapman–Kolmogorov identity \(Q_{t+h} = Q_h Q_t\) (Equation 87.1) and submultiplicativity of the operator norm (cf. Lemma 86.1, Lecture 40.1): \[
\begin{aligned}
\|Q_{t+h} - Q_t\|_{\text{op}} &= \|(Q_h - I) Q_t\|_{\text{op}} \\
&\le \|Q_h - I\|_{\text{op}} \|Q_t\|_{\text{op}} \\
&\le \|Q_h - I\|_{\text{op}} \xrightarrow[h \downarrow 0]{} 0.
\end{aligned}
\] Similarly, for \(t > h > 0\), using \(Q_t - Q_{t-h} = (Q_h - I) Q_{t-h}\) (again from Equation 87.1, since \(Q_t = Q_hQ_{t-h}\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
\|Q_t - Q_{t-h}\|_{\text{op}} &= \|(Q_h - I) Q_{t-h}\|_{\text{op}}\\
&\le \|Q_h - I\|_{\text{op}} \|Q_{t-h}\|_{\text{op}} \\
&\le \|Q_h - I\|_{\text{op}} \xrightarrow[h \downarrow 0]{} 0.
\end{aligned}
\] Hence, \(t \mapsto Q_t\) is operator-norm continuous on \([0, \infty)\). In particular, \(s \mapsto \|I - Q_s\|_{\text{op}}\) is continuous on \([0,\infty)\), and \(\|Q_s\|_{\text{op}} \le 1\) for every \(s \ge 0\); both facts will be used repeatedly below.



87.4.2 Step 2: Equivalence of Global Differentiability and Local Differentiability at \(t=0^+\)
Consider the right difference quotient for \(h > 0\):
\[
\frac{Q_{t+h} - Q_t}{h} = \frac{Q_h - I}{h} Q_t = Q_t \frac{Q_h - I}{h}.
\]
Suppose there exists a bounded linear operator \(B \in \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B}_b(S))\) such that \(\lim_{h \downarrow 0} \frac{Q_h - I}{h} = B\) in the operator norm. Then:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\| \frac{Q_{t+h} - Q_t}{h} - Q_t B \right\|_{\text{op}} &= \left\| Q_t \left( \frac{Q_h - I}{h} - B \right) \right\|_{\text{op}}\\
& \le \|Q_t\|_{\text{op}} \left\| \frac{Q_h - I}{h} - B \right\|_{\text{op}} \\
& \le \left\| \frac{Q_h - I}{h} - B \right\|_{\text{op}} \xrightarrow[h \downarrow 0]{} 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
so the right-derivative of \(t\mapsto Q_t\) exists at every \(t\ge0\) and equals \(Q_tB\).
For \(t > 0\) we must also check the left difference quotient, since differentiability at an interior point is a two-sided notion. For \(0 < h < t\), Step 1 gives \(Q_t - Q_{t-h} = (Q_h - I)Q_{t-h}\), so \[
\frac{Q_t - Q_{t-h}}{h} = \frac{Q_h - I}{h}\,Q_{t-h}.
\] Hence \[
\begin{aligned}
\left\| \frac{Q_t - Q_{t-h}}{h} - BQ_t \right\|_{\text{op}}
&= \left\| \left(\frac{Q_h - I}{h} - B\right) Q_{t-h} + B(Q_{t-h} - Q_t) \right\|_{\text{op}} \\
&\le \left\| \frac{Q_h - I}{h} - B \right\|_{\text{op}} \|Q_{t-h}\|_{\text{op}} + \|B\|_{\text{op}} \|Q_{t-h} - Q_t\|_{\text{op}} \\
&\le \left\| \frac{Q_h - I}{h} - B \right\|_{\text{op}} + \|B\|_{\text{op}} \|Q_{t-h} - Q_t\|_{\text{op}} \xrightarrow[h \downarrow 0]{} 0,
\end{aligned}
\] where the first term vanishes by hypothesis and the second vanishes because \(h \mapsto Q_{t-h}\) is operator-norm continuous at \(h=0\) (Step 1) and \(B\) is bounded. Thus the left-derivative at \(t\) also exists and equals \(BQ_t\). Moreover \(Q_tB=BQ_t\): this is immediate from the identity \(\frac{Q_h-I}{h}Q_t = Q_t\frac{Q_h-I}{h}\) established above, which holds for every \(h>0\) (not merely in the limit) and whose two sides converge, as \(h\downarrow0\), to \(BQ_t\) and \(Q_tB\) respectively. Hence the right- and left-derivatives at \(t\) coincide, and \(t\mapsto Q_t\) is (two-sided) differentiable at every \(t>0\).
This shows that \(\frac{d}{dt} Q_t\) exists (two-sided for \(t>0\), one-sided at \(t=0\)) at every point \(t \ge 0\) if and only if \(A = \lim_{h \downarrow 0} \frac{Q_h - I}{h}\) exists at \(t = 0^+\) as a bounded operator, in which case:
\[
\frac{d}{dt} Q_t = Q_t A = A Q_t.
\]



87.4.3 Step 3: Gårding’s Regularization Trick
To prove that \(A = \lim_{h \downarrow 0} \frac{Q_h - I}{h}\) exists, it suffices to show that \(t \mapsto Q_t\) is right-differentiable at some \(t \ge 0\). We employ a technique due to Lars Gårding.

Definition 87.1 (Gårding Averaging Operator) For any \(\varepsilon > 0\), define the linear operator \(B_\varepsilon\) on \(\mathcal{B}_b(S)\) by:
\[
B_\varepsilon = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \int_0^\varepsilon Q_s \, ds,
\tag{87.7}\]
meaning that for any \(f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\) and \(x \in S\):
\[
(B_\varepsilon f)(x) = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \int_0^\varepsilon (Q_s f)(x) \, ds.
\]
This is well defined: for fixed \(f\) and \(x\), the map \(s \mapsto (Q_sf)(x)\) is continuous and bounded by \(\|f\|_\infty\) (Step 1), so the Riemann integral exists and \(|(B_\varepsilon f)(x)| \le \|f\|_\infty\). Measurability of \(x \mapsto (B_\varepsilon f)(x)\) follows because it is the pointwise limit, as \(n \to \infty\), of the Riemann sums \(\frac{\varepsilon}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n (Q_{k\varepsilon/n}f)(x)\), each of which is a finite linear combination of the measurable functions \(Q_{k\varepsilon/n}f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\). Hence \(B_\varepsilon f \in \mathcal{B}_b(S)\) and \(B_\varepsilon \in \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B}_b(S))\) with \(\|B_\varepsilon\|_{\text{op}} \le 1\).

Applying \(B_\varepsilon\) to \(Q_t\), and using the Chapman–Kolmogorov identity \(Q_s Q_t = Q_{s+t}\) (Equation 87.1), we obtain:
\[
B_\varepsilon Q_t = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \int_0^\varepsilon Q_s Q_t \, ds = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \int_0^\varepsilon Q_{s+t} \, ds = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \int_t^{t+\varepsilon} Q_u \, du.
\tag{87.8}\]
By Step 1, \(u \mapsto Q_u\) is continuous in the operator norm on all of \([0,\infty)\), and \(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B}_b(S))\) is a Banach space (Corollary 86.1, Lecture 40.1); hence \(t \mapsto \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\int_t^{t+\varepsilon} Q_u\,du\) is the difference of two indefinite Riemann integrals of a continuous Banach-space-valued function and is therefore differentiable in both directions (two-sided for \(t>0\), one-sided at \(t=0\)) by the vector-valued Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, with derivative:
\[
\frac{d}{dt} \left( B_\varepsilon Q_t \right) = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} [Q_{t+\varepsilon} - Q_t].
\tag{87.9}\]



87.4.4 Step 4: Invertibility of \(B_\varepsilon\) for Small \(\varepsilon > 0\)
To recover the differentiability of \(Q_t\) from \(B_\varepsilon Q_t\), we show that \(B_\varepsilon\) is an invertible operator for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon > 0\).
Define \(T_\varepsilon := I - B_\varepsilon\). We attempt to construct the inverse \(C_\varepsilon := B_\varepsilon^{-1}\) using a Neumann geometric series:
\[
C_\varepsilon = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} T_\varepsilon^n = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (I - B_\varepsilon)^n.
\tag{87.10}\]
If the series converges in operator norm, we have:
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_\varepsilon B_\varepsilon &= \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=0}^N T_\varepsilon^n (I - T_\varepsilon) \\
&= \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=0}^N (T_\varepsilon^n - T_\varepsilon^{n+1}) \\
&= \lim_{N \to \infty} (I - T_\varepsilon^{N+1}) = I,
\end{aligned}
\]
and similarly \(B_\varepsilon C_\varepsilon = I\).
Since \(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B}_b(S))\) is a Banach space (Corollary 86.1, Lecture 40.1), the Neumann series converges in operator norm whenever \(\|T_\varepsilon\|_{\text{op}} < 1\): absolute convergence, \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty \|T_\varepsilon^n\|_{\text{op}} \le \sum_{n=0}^\infty \|T_\varepsilon\|_{\text{op}}^n < \infty\), implies convergence in a Banach space. We estimate \(\|T_\varepsilon\|_{\text{op}}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|I - B_\varepsilon\|_{\text{op}} &= \sup_{\|f\|_\infty = 1} \left\| f - \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \int_0^\varepsilon Q_s f \, ds \right\|_\infty \\
&= \sup_{\|f\|_\infty = 1} \left\| \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \int_0^\varepsilon (f - Q_s f) \, ds \right\|_\infty \\
&\le \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \int_0^\varepsilon \|I - Q_s\|_{\text{op}} \, ds.
\end{aligned}
\]
By the Mean Value Theorem for integrals, since \(s \mapsto \|I - Q_s\|_{\text{op}}\) is continuous on \([0,\varepsilon]\) (Step 1) and \(\|I - Q_0\|_{\text{op}} = 0\), there exists \(s^*=s^*(\varepsilon) \in [0, \varepsilon]\) such that:
\[
\frac{1}{\varepsilon} \int_0^\varepsilon \|I - Q_s\|_{\text{op}} \, ds = \|I - Q_{s^*(\varepsilon)}\|_{\text{op}}.
\]
Since \(0 \le s^*(\varepsilon) \le \varepsilon\), we have \(s^*(\varepsilon) \downarrow 0\) as \(\varepsilon \downarrow 0\); combined with condition (Equation 87.2), i.e. \(\lim_{s \downarrow 0}\|I-Q_s\|_{\text{op}}=0\), this gives \(\lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \|I - Q_{s^*(\varepsilon)}\|_{\text{op}} = 0\). Thus, for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon > 0\), we have:
\[
\|T_\varepsilon\|_{\text{op}} = \|I - B_\varepsilon\|_{\text{op}} < 1.
\]
Hence, \(B_\varepsilon\) is invertible on \(\mathcal{B}_b(S)\) with continuous inverse \(C_\varepsilon = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (I - B_\varepsilon)^n\).



87.4.5 Step 5: Existence of the Generator \(A\) and Solution of the ODE
Using the invertibility of \(B_\varepsilon\) from Step 4, we write \(Q_t = C_\varepsilon (B_\varepsilon Q_t)\) for every \(t \ge 0\). Setting \(t = 0\) (recall \(Q_0 = I\) by Equation 87.1) and using the fixed, bounded operator \(C_\varepsilon\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{h \downarrow 0} \frac{Q_h - I}{h} &= \lim_{h \downarrow 0} C_\varepsilon \left( \frac{B_\varepsilon Q_h - B_\varepsilon Q_0}{h} \right) \\
&= C_\varepsilon \left[ \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} (B_\varepsilon Q_t) \right] \\
&= C_\varepsilon \left( \frac{Q_{\varepsilon} - I}{\varepsilon} \right),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the second equality uses continuity of the bounded linear map \(X \mapsto C_\varepsilon X\) on \(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B}_b(S))\) (so the limit can be passed inside \(C_\varepsilon\)), and the third equality is (Equation 87.9) evaluated at \(t=0\). Hence the limit \[
A := \lim_{h \downarrow 0} \frac{Q_h - I}{h} = C_\varepsilon \left( \frac{Q_\varepsilon - I}{\varepsilon} \right)
\] exists in operator norm and is bounded, being a composition of the bounded operators \(C_\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon^{-1}(Q_\varepsilon - I)\): \[
\|A\|_{\text{op}} \le \|C_\varepsilon\|_{\text{op}} \cdot \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\|Q_\varepsilon - I\|_{\text{op}} < \infty.
\]
Since \(A\) now exists as a bounded linear operator, Step 2 applies and shows that \(t \mapsto Q_t\) is operator-norm differentiable at every \(t \ge 0\) (two-sided for \(t>0\), one-sided at \(t=0\)), with \[
\frac{d}{dt} Q_t = Q_t A = A Q_t, \qquad Q_0 = I,
\tag{87.11}\] proving parts 1, 2, and 4 of the theorem.
Finally, we show part 3, \(Q_t = e^{tA}\). Since \(A\) is bounded, Equation 87.4 defines \(e^{tA}\) as a bounded operator for every \(t\), with the series converging absolutely and uniformly on compact \(t\)-intervals (comparison with \(\sum_n |t|^n\|A\|_{\text{op}}^n/n!=e^{|t|\|A\|_{\text{op}}}\)); in particular \(e^{-tA}\) is well defined and commutes with \(A\) and with \(Q_t\) for every \(t\) (via Equation 87.11 and the fact that \(A\) commutes with every power of itself). Define \(F(t) := Q_t e^{-tA} \in \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B}_b(S))\). Term-by-term differentiation of the (uniformly convergent) power series for \(e^{-tA}\) gives \(\frac{d}{dt}e^{-tA} = -Ae^{-tA}\), so by the Leibniz (product) rule for operator-norm-differentiable \(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B}_b(S))\)-valued functions and Equation 87.11, \[
F'(t) = (Q_tA)e^{-tA} + Q_t(-Ae^{-tA}) = Q_tAe^{-tA} - Q_tAe^{-tA} = 0 \quad \text{for all } t \ge 0.
\] Since \(F\) is continuously differentiable with \(F'\equiv0\), the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for Banach-space-valued functions gives \(F(t) = F(0) = Q_0e^{0} = I\) for all \(t\ge0\), i.e. \(Q_t = e^{tA}\). This same computation shows that \(e^{tA}\) is the unique operator-norm-differentiable solution of the Cauchy problem \(\frac{d}{dt}X_t = AX_t\), \(X_0 = I\): applying it to any such solution \(X_t\) in place of \(Q_t\) gives \(X_te^{-tA}\equiv I\), hence \(X_t = e^{tA}\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: 87  Lecture 40.2: Bounded Generators
text:
87.5 Concluding Remarks

Scope of Uniform Continuity: The condition \(\lim_{t \downarrow 0} \|Q_t - I\|_{\text{op}} = 0\), together with the Chapman–Kolmogorov property (Equation 87.1), guarantees that the generator \(A\) is a bounded operator.
General Markov Chains vs. General State Spaces: For general continuous-state Markov processes (e.g., Brownian motion), uniform continuity in the operator norm is typically too restrictive, and \(A\) is generally an unbounded, densely defined operator under the weaker notion of strong continuity (\(L^p\) or \(C_0\)-semigroups). By contrast, for continuous-time Markov chains on discrete state spaces with bounded jump rates (i.e. \(\sup_i q_i < \infty\) for the Q-matrix), uniform operator-norm continuity does hold; this can be shown via uniformization (dominating the chain by a Poisson clock of rate \(\Lambda := \sup_i q_i\)), though we do not prove it here. The converse direction — passing from a bounded Q-matrix to operator-norm continuity — is thus the natural converse of Theorem 87.1, not a restatement of it.

title: 87  Lecture 40.2: Bounded Generators
text:
87.6 Takeaways

A semigroup of Markov transition operators \((Q_t)_{t\ge0}\) (linear, positivity-preserving, \(Q_t1=1\), satisfying \(Q_0=I\) and the Chapman–Kolmogorov law \(Q_{s+t}=Q_sQ_t\)) that is merely continuous at the single point \(t=0\) in the operator norm is automatically continuous and (one-sided/two-sided) differentiable on all of \([0,\infty)\), with a bounded generator \(A\). This is the content of Theorem 87.1, re-proved here by a method different from Lecture 40.1.
The key mechanism, due to Gårding, is to replace the semigroup by its short-time averages \(B_\varepsilon = \varepsilon^{-1}\int_0^\varepsilon Q_s\,ds\). Operator-norm continuity at \(t=0\) forces \(B_\varepsilon \to I\) in operator norm as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), so \(B_\varepsilon\) is invertible (via a Neumann series) for small \(\varepsilon\); the generator is then extracted algebraically as \(A = C_\varepsilon(Q_\varepsilon - I)/\varepsilon\), where \(C_\varepsilon = B_\varepsilon^{-1}\).
Differentiability at an interior point \(t>0\) is a two-sided condition: both the right-quotient \((Q_{t+h}-Q_t)/h\) and the left-quotient \((Q_t-Q_{t-h})/h\) must converge to the same limit as \(h\downarrow0\). Both are controlled by the Chapman–Kolmogorov identity together with the uniform bound \(\|Q_s\|_{\text{op}}\le1\) and the operator-norm continuity of \(s\mapsto Q_s\) established in Step 1.
Once \(A\) is known to be bounded, \(Q_t=e^{tA}=\sum_{n\ge0}t^nA^n/n!\) is the unique operator-norm-differentiable solution of \(\frac{d}{dt}X_t=AX_t=X_tA\), \(X_0=I\); uniqueness follows from differentiating \(F(t)=X_te^{-tA}\) and finding \(F'\equiv0\).
The discrete-state-space Poisson process illustrates the theorem concretely: the row-sum operator norm gives \(\|Q_t-I\|_{\text{op}}=2(1-e^{-\lambda t})\to0\), so the semigroup is uniformly operator-norm continuous and its generator is the familiar bounded birth generator \(A_{ii}=-\lambda\), \(A_{i,i+1}=\lambda\), \(A_{ij}=0\) otherwise.
This “bounded generator” regime is the technically simplest case of semigroup theory. It fails for most continuous-state-space Markov processes (e.g. diffusions), where the generator is only densely defined and unbounded, and one must instead invoke the Hille–Yosida theorem for strongly continuous (\(C_0\)) semigroups — the subject of the general theory this lecture pair (40.1–40.2) specializes.
